tool.heroSubtitle: Revelation never quotes the Old Testament outright, yet no New Testament book refers to it more. See both texts side by side, why they don't match, and what John does with them.

footer.text: The method. An echo is a place where the New Testament borrows Old Testament words or pictures without quoting them. Revelation has no formal quotations at all, so every entry here is an echo. Each one shows both texts, says what matches, why the wording differs, and what John does with it. Nothing goes in without a named source: a commentary, a study Bible or a lecture that points to the link. Possible echoes need two sources. The reasons a text does not match are eight: two texts woven together, following the Greek Old Testament, following the Hebrew, the same picture in new words, applied to someone new, turned upside down, following a whole scene, and read as coming true.

The grades follow G. K. Beale's commentary on Revelation. A clear echo uses nearly the same words, shares the core meaning, and could hardly come from anywhere else. A probable echo is less close in wording but carries an idea or a pattern that can be traced to that one passage. A possible echo is only generally like its source in words or ideas. Where Beale gives a grade, the entry says so. Where he does not, the grade is drawn here by his definitions, and the entry says that too.

entries.title: Revelation 1:1, what must soon take place
entries.summary: John opens his book with Daniel's words about what must take place, and changes Daniel's in the last days to soon.
entries.plain: **A coach who tells the team that the future starts tonight is borrowing a famous line and changing its clock.** John's first sentence borrows from Daniel 2, where God shows a king what must happen in the last days. John keeps the words about showing what must happen. Then he changes the time. Daniel looked far ahead. John says it will happen soon.
entries.same: Both texts say that God shows what must take place. The Greek phrase is the same in both books: ha dei genesthai, what must happen. Both speak of a hidden plan being revealed, and both pass it through a go-between. Beale counts the verb to reveal five times in Daniel 2.
entries.differs: Daniel says these things will happen in the last days. John says they will happen soon (en tachei). Beale calls the swap deliberate. He reads it as a word about time, not speed. What Daniel put far in the future, Beale says, John sees beginning in his own day. The setting changes too. Daniel explains a dream to a pagan king. John passes on a vision from God, through Jesus and an angel, to the churches.
entries.turn: John sets his whole book under Daniel 2. That dream ends with a stone that smashes the empires and grows into a kingdom that fills the earth. By opening with Daniel's words, John tells small churches under Rome that the kingdom of that dream is near. Beale finds the same Daniel phrase again at 1:19, 4:1 and 22:6, at the hinges of the book.
entries.not: **Not Daniel's time phrase.** John keeps Daniel's words about what must take place, but he drops in the last days and writes soon in their place. The echo is in the words about God's plan, not in the timing.
entries.deeper: Beale grades this a clear allusion. He notes that revelation, God showing, what must come to pass and making known occur together only in Daniel 2 and Revelation 1:1. The shared Greek is deixai (to show), ha dei genesthai (what must take place) and the verb semaino (to make known by signs), which the old Greek of Daniel 2 also uses. In Daniel 2:28 the Greek reads ep' eschaton ton hemeron, in the last days; John puts en tachei, quickly. Beale argues the substitution means the defeat of evil and the kingdom Daniel expected had begun with Christ's death and resurrection, while its completion is still to come. In his list of uses this is a possible indirect fulfillment: no formula such as it is written, yet an Old Testament prophecy is treated as coming true. He also reads the whole of chapter 1 as framed by Daniel 2, opening at 1:1 and closing at 1:19-20. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible notes that God had sent revelations through angels before, in Daniel 9 and Zechariah 1-6.
entries.dissent: The sources agree the wording comes from Daniel 2. They differ on soon. Beale holds that fulfillment has begun and will be completed at the end. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible reads near in 1:3 as a claim on the reader now. The CSB Study Bible reads soon as urgency rather than a timetable, and answers critics who say the prophecy failed. MacArthur reads soon as a stress on how near Christ's return is. At 1:3 he calls that return the next event in God's plan, though it may be put off so long that people doubt it will come. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible notes that many futurists read the book's events as still ahead and treat 1:19 as its outline.

aw.s: The book opens as a revelation God gave Jesus, sent by his angel to his servant John, with a blessing on the one who reads it aloud and on those who hear. It then greets seven churches in Asia like a letter, from the one who is, was and is to come, and from Jesus, ruler of the kings of the earth, who is coming with the clouds.

entries.title: Revelation 1:4, him who is and who was and who is to come
entries.summary: John's name for God takes the Greek form of the name given at the burning bush, the one who is, and adds who was and who is to come.
entries.plain: **A speaker who quotes a famous line in a second language can end up with words that sound new.** At the burning bush God gives his name as I AM. The old Greek translation turned that into the one who is. John uses that Greek form for God, then adds two more phrases: who was, and who is coming. He even breaks a rule of Greek grammar to keep the name as Exodus has it.
entries.same: The core words are the same in Greek: ho on, the one who is. That is how the Greek Old Testament puts God's name in Exodus 3:14. John uses the same two words for God in 1:4 and again in 1:8.
entries.differs: An English Bible reads I AM WHO I AM at the bush, because it follows the Hebrew. John follows the Greek translation, which says the one who is. He then adds two phrases Exodus does not have: who was, and who is coming. Beale traces that expansion to Isaiah's names for God as first and with the last, and to Jewish retellings of the name. John also keeps the name in the wrong case after the word from, so that it looks just as it does in Exodus.
entries.turn: John greets the churches from the God of the exodus, the one who rescued Israel from Pharaoh. The added words make him Lord of the past and of what is coming. To churches facing Rome, Beale says, the name promises that God rules history and will finish it. In 1:8 God speaks the same name himself, with the Almighty.
entries.not: **Not a slip in John's Greek.** Scribes later added God after the word from to fix the grammar. Beale and other commentators hold that John broke the rule on purpose, to point readers back to Exodus.
entries.deeper: The Hebrew of Exodus 3:14 is ehyeh asher ehyeh, I will be what I will be, or I am who I am. The Greek translation reads ego eimi ho on, I am the one who is, and then ho on has sent me. Revelation 1:4 reads apo ho on kai ho en kai ho erchomenos. After apo (from) Greek needs the genitive case, but John leaves ho on in the nominative, the form it has in Exodus. Beale calls the grammar intentional and says some manuscripts insert God after from to smooth it. He traces the three-part title to Exodus 3:14 together with Isaiah 41:4, 43:10, 44:6 and 48:12, and to later Jewish expansions: in the Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on Deuteronomy 32:39 God names himself in all three tenses: present, past and future. Those targums are later than John, as Beale's dates show. Keener adds that the title also resembles an occasional Greek title for an eternal deity. The grade is drawn here by Beale's definitions: ho on is identical and the solecism points to it. Beale's category is analogical use joined to stylistic use.
entries.heiser: Heiser follows Beale and says the broken grammar is deliberate: the name stays as Exodus 3:14 has it in Greek, like a red flag sending readers back to the bush. He adds a point from McDonough and Pausanias. Greek writers said of Zeus that he was, is and will be, and Zeus was hailed as the Most High. Heiser concludes that John's added words answer that claim: "it's very clear that John's taking a swipe at Zeus". He also notes, after Aune, that Philo used the same Greek name for God and was never called a blasphemer.
entries.dissent: Beale and Keener note Greek parallels: Pausanias records Zeus was, Zeus is, Zeus will be. Beale thinks the pagan formula may have prompted John to use the Jewish one as an answer to it. Keener says the title is related to the Greek formula but especially reflects Exodus. Heiser, after McDonough, goes further and calls the added words a deliberate answer to Zeus. Beale rejects the view that John borrowed only from Deuteronomy 32:39, since its first and last parts do not match his.

entries.title: Revelation 1:4, the seven spirits before the throne
entries.summary: The seven spirits before God's throne draw on Zechariah's lampstand, whose seven lamps are the eyes of the Lord and point to God's Spirit.
entries.plain: **A band can quote a famous riff in just three notes, and fans still hear the whole song.** John sends greetings from seven spirits before God's throne. Later he calls them seven lamps of fire and seven eyes sent through all the earth. Those pictures come from Zechariah 4, where seven lamps on a gold lampstand stand for God's Spirit and for his eyes.
entries.same: The number seven, the lamps, and the link to God's Spirit. In Zechariah a word about God's Spirit explains the seven lamps (4:6). Then they are called God's eyes, which look over the whole earth (4:10). Revelation 4:5 and 5:6 use the same lamps and eyes for the seven spirits.
entries.differs: Zechariah never says seven spirits. He sees seven lamps, and the angel speaks of God's one Spirit. John turns the seven lamps into a name, the seven spirits. In 1:4 he gives only that name. The lamps and the eyes come later, in 4:5 and 5:6. Beale calls 1:4 a paraphrase, and takes the meaning from those later verses.
entries.turn: In Zechariah the Spirit helps Israel finish the temple against all odds. John greets churches from the same Spirit. Beale reads it as the power that makes the church a burning lamp of witness. The place of the spirits, before the throne, shows them ready to carry out God's will.
entries.not: **Not a list of seven Holy Spirits.** Sources that read the phrase as the Spirit take seven as a number of fullness, and the ESV Study Bible says Revelation treats the Spirit as one person.
entries.deeper: Beale reads seven spirits as a figure for the Holy Spirit at work, since it stands in a greeting formula with God and Christ. He calls the wording part of a paraphrased allusion to Zechariah 4:2-7, as Revelation 4:5 and 5:6 show, where the seven spirits are also seven burning lamps and seven eyes sent out over the earth. In the Greek of Zechariah 4:2 the lampstand is all gold with seven lamps (hepta lychnoi) on it; 4:6 says not by power but by my Spirit; 4:10 calls the seven the eyes of the Lord looking on all the earth. Beale also thinks Isaiah 11:2 may stand behind the phrase, since the Greek of Isaiah 11:2 lists the Spirit's gifts and Revelation 5:5-6 joins the root of Jesse to the seven spirits. Walton notes that Zechariah's seven eyes are the lamps and may be the same seven eyes set on the stone in 3:9. The grade is drawn here: the wording is not close, but the pattern runs back to Zechariah 4.
entries.heiser: Heiser ties the seven spirits to the stars and angels of 1:16, 1:20 and 3:1, and the lamps to Zechariah 4:10, the eyes of the Lord that range over the whole earth. Following Oppenheim, he reads those eyes as God's heavenly agents, who watch and report, as in Zechariah 1 and 6 and Job 1. Since people cannot see the whole earth but spirits can, he says the picture has to apply to every church. He calls it divine council imagery. He also reads Beale's suggestion of Isaiah 11:2-3 behind the seven spirits.
entries.dissent: Not everyone reads the seven spirits as the Holy Spirit. Keener thinks the seven archangels of Jewish tradition more likely (compare 8:2), though he grants Isaiah 11:2 as possible. The CSB Study Bible leaves three options: the angels of the churches, other angels, or the fullness of the Spirit in Isaiah 11:2. Beale and the ESV Study Bible take it as the Spirit. Fekkes, as Beale reports, doubts the Isaiah link.

entries.title: Revelation 1:5, the faithful witness, the firstborn, the ruler of kings
entries.summary: The three titles John gives Jesus all come from Psalm 89, a psalm about God's promise to David's line.
entries.plain: **When a new leader is introduced with three phrases from an old oath of office, people know which office is meant.** John gives Jesus three titles: faithful witness, firstborn from the dead, and ruler over earth's kings. All three come from Psalm 89. That psalm is about God's oath to King David: his line will last forever, and his heir will be the highest of the kings.
entries.same: Three phrases. Psalm 89:27 makes David's heir the firstborn and highest of the kings of the earth. Psalm 89:37 speaks of a faithful witness in the sky. In the Greek the words match closely: ho martys ... pistos (faithful witness), prototokos (firstborn), and the kings of the earth.
entries.differs: In the psalm the faithful witness is the moon, a sign in the sky that David's throne will last. John makes the witness Jesus himself. The firstborn in the psalm is a royal heir. John adds from the dead, so the first rank comes through resurrection. The psalm says highest of the kings; John says ruler of the kings. He also gathers phrases from two verses into one line.
entries.turn: John reads Jesus as the heir the psalm was waiting for. His death and rising made him king for good, over the very rulers who threatened the churches. Beale notes that the kings of the earth are usually God's enemies in Revelation. The titles also hold out a model: the faithful witness who died and rose is the pattern for believers under pressure.
entries.not: **Not a claim that Jesus was the first being created.** Beale reads firstborn as rank, the heir's place, gained by rising from the dead, as Colossians 1:18 also has it.
entries.deeper: Beale says commentators are surely right to see Psalm 88(89):27, 37 here, since all three phrases occur there. The Greek of Psalm 89:27 (88:28 in the Greek numbering) has prototokon ... hypselon para tois basileusi tes ges; 89:37 (88:38) has ho martys en ourano pistos. John's ho martys ho pistos, ho prototokos stands in the nominative after apo, where Greek grammar wants the genitive. Beale reads this as the same kind of flag as in 1:4: the phrase keeps the case it had in the psalm. Jewish writings read Psalm 89:27 of the Messiah (Midrash Rabbah on Exodus 19:7). Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible also point to Psalm 89:27, and the study Bible sets it against the Roman emperor's claim to rule subject kings. The grade is drawn here: three phrases from one psalm, close in wording. Beale's category is analogical use, raised to a higher level.
entries.dissent: Some see other sources for faithful witness. Fiorenza, as Beale reports, adds Isaiah 55:4, where David is made a witness to the peoples, and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible also cites Isaiah 55:4. Beale adds Isaiah 43:10-13, where Israel is God's witness. These are offered beside Psalm 89, not in place of it.

entries.title: Revelation 1:6, a kingdom and priests
entries.summary: What God promised Israel at Mount Sinai, to be a kingdom of priests, John says Jesus has made of his people.
entries.plain: **A school can hand a famous founder's motto to a new class, and the motto now names them.** At Mount Sinai God told Israel that they would be a kingdom of priests. John says Jesus has already made his people a kingdom and priests. John applies Israel's title to everyone Jesus has freed, from every nation.
entries.same: Both join two ideas, a kingdom and priests, to name God's people. Both follow a rescue: Israel's from Egypt, and the church's by Jesus' blood. In Exodus the people are God's own treasure (19:5). John begins with the one who loves us.
entries.differs: Three things change. The Hebrew says a kingdom of priests, and the Greek translation says a royal priesthood. John writes two nouns, a kingdom, priests, as the Targum, an Aramaic paraphrase, also does (Keener). Exodus speaks of the future, you shall be. John speaks of a fact, he has made us. And the people named are not one nation but all who are freed from their sins.
entries.turn: John hands Israel's vocation to the church. Priests stand between God and people and bring God's presence near. Beale reads the verse as a present office: believers already serve as kings and priests, by bearing faithful witness as Jesus did. Revelation 5:10 and 20:6 return to the same line.
entries.not: **Not a claim that Israel is erased.** John widens Israel's calling to people from every nation (5:9-10). The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible speaks of believers grafted into Israel's heritage, not of a swap.
entries.deeper: Beale calls this a clear allusion to Exodus 19:6. The Hebrew is mamleket kohanim, a kingdom of priests; the Greek translation reads basileion hierateuma, a royal priesthood; Revelation has basileian, hiereis, kingdom, priests. Keener notes that the Targum of the verse also reads a kingdom and priests. Beale lists Jewish readings that make two offices of it: Targum Neofiti has kings and priests, and Jubilees 16:18 and Philo have kingdom and priesthood. He argues the believers' reign has begun now, citing the aorist he made, the parallel in 5:10, and 1:9, where John shares the kingdom. In Beale's terms this is universalization: a title given to Israel is applied to a people from every tribe and nation. 1 Peter 2:9 uses the same verse for the church. Walton's commentary is not cited here; the Jewish Study Bible notes that later Jewish tradition read the verse as a duty for the whole people to live by a code of holiness.
entries.heiser: Heiser calls verses 5 and 6 proof of his reading of the chapter: Israel's calling to be priests who bring God's presence to the nations is now the church's. He reads Tabb's note on the Hebrew and Greek of Exodus 19:6 and the treasured possession of 19:4-5. He adds a caution: "the church is a new Israel it's not the new Israel". John, he says, treats the church as the rightful outcome of Israel, not a replacement.
entries.dissent: Commentators split on when believers reign. Beale argues they reign now, in a hidden way, through faithful endurance. Others he names, such as Fiorenza and Beckwith, hold that the reign is only future (20:6; 22:5) and that believers are now priests and citizens of the kingdom. MacArthur reads the kingdom as God's rule, entered now by faith, with believers as priests who may come before God. At 1:9 he names their eager hope of Christ's thousand-year reign on earth. The CSB Study Bible says the wording may mean believers are already a kingdom and priests. Manuscripts differ too: some read for us instead of us, and some kings and priests.

entries.title: Revelation 1:7, coming with the clouds
entries.summary: John weaves Daniel's son of man coming with the clouds into Zechariah's mourning for the one who was pierced, and widens the mourners from Israel's tribes to all the earth's.
entries.plain: **A song can join two famous tunes so smoothly that the crowd hears one melody.** John does that here. He takes the one who comes with the clouds from Daniel 7. He joins it to Zechariah 12, where people look on the one they pierced and mourn. Then he widens the mourners. In Zechariah they are Israel's tribes. In John they are all the tribes of the earth.
entries.same: From Daniel 7:13, coming with the clouds, word for word in the Greek (meta ton nephelon). From Zechariah 12:10, those who pierced him, and they will mourn over him (kopsontai ep' auton). From Zechariah 12:12, the tribes who mourn.
entries.differs: John weaves two prophets into one line. He adds every eye and of the earth, so the mourning is no longer Israel's alone. For pierced, John agrees with the Hebrew of Zechariah; the Greek translation has a different word there, treated with scorn. In Zechariah God says they will look on me. John has see him, and the one pierced is Jesus.
entries.turn: Two prophecies meet in one man. Daniel's figure is given rule over every nation. Zechariah's pierced one is mourned at last. John says both are Jesus, the one the world rejected. Beale reads the mourning as repentance spreading to the nations, and the coming as a process through history that ends in a final coming.
entries.not: **Not two quotations side by side.** John never names either prophet. He blends their words into his own sentence, as Matthew 24:30 also does.
entries.deeper: Beale calls the verse two Old Testament citations. Daniel 7:13 supplies coming with the clouds; the Aramaic has im ananei shemaya, with the clouds, and the Greek of Daniel in the vault's interlinear (the version called Theodotion) has meta ton nephelon, as John does. Zechariah 12:10 supplies the pierced one and the mourning; the Hebrew is asher daqaru, whom they pierced, while the Greek translation reads katorchesanto, they treated despitefully. John's exekentesan follows the Hebrew sense, as John 19:37 does. Beale shows two additions that widen the text: every eye, and of the earth after all the tribes, which he traces to Zechariah 14:17 and the peoples and tribes of Daniel 7:14. He calls it universalization, the same move as Exodus 19:6 in 1:6. Matthew 24:30 already joins Daniel 7 and Zechariah 12, and Beale thinks it may have shaped John. Unseen Realm adds that coming on the clouds was a title of the god Baal, and that the Old Testament gives it to Yahweh. The grade is drawn here; Beale calls the verse citations.
entries.heiser: Heiser's lecture reads 1:7 for its first line. Coming with the clouds, he says, was a stock title of Baal, the rider of the clouds. The Hebrew Bible uses the picture five times: four of Yahweh (Deuteronomy 33:26; Psalm 68:33; Psalm 104:3; Isaiah 19:1) and the fifth of the son of man in Daniel 7:13. So Daniel shows two divine figures, which he links to the early Jewish idea of two powers in heaven. He does not discuss Zechariah 12:10 in this lecture.
entries.dissent: Is the mourning repentance or terror? Beale and the CSB Study Bible read it as saving repentance, since the mourners grieve over him, not over themselves. The ESV Study Bible says most scholars read it as a reaction to judgment, and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible leaves both open. MacArthur reads the coming as Christ's return with God's glory cloud fully seen, and splits the mourners. Those who pierced him are the Jews who bore the blame for his death, named in Zechariah 12:10 as David's house and Jerusalem's people, and they will one day repent in truth. The mourning of the earth's other peoples he reads as guilt and fear of punishment. On Zechariah itself, the Jewish Study Bible notes the Hebrew is unclear about who is pierced and reads it as someone from the nations; the Talmud applies it to a messiah from the house of Joseph.

aw.n: Revelation 1:1-8, a revelation sent as a letter
aw.s: The book opens as a revelation God gave Jesus, sent by his angel to his servant John, with a blessing on the one who reads it aloud and on those who hear. It then greets seven churches in Asia like a letter, from the one who is, was and is to come, and from Jesus, ruler of the kings of the earth, who is coming with the clouds.

entries.title: Revelation 1:8, the Alpha and the Omega
entries.summary: God names himself with the opening and closing letters of the Greek alphabet, a fresh way to say what Isaiah says: God is first and last.
entries.plain: **Saying from A to Z says the same thing as from start to finish, with different words.** In Isaiah God calls himself first and last. In Revelation 1:8 he says it with letters: Alpha and Omega, the opening and closing letters of the Greek alphabet. The picture is Isaiah's. The words are new.
entries.same: The idea: God stands at the beginning and the end. Isaiah says it in words, first and last. Revelation says it with the two ends of the alphabet. Later in the book John joins the two forms (22:13).
entries.differs: Isaiah never uses the alphabet. Alpha and Omega is John's own phrase. Beale calls it a merism: two far ends that stand for everything between. Keener notes that some Jewish teachers later did the same with the Hebrew alphabet, aleph to tav. In 1:8 the title sits beside the name from 1:4 and the Almighty, a common Greek word for the Lord of hosts.
entries.turn: John has God speak in his own voice, once at the start of the book and once near the end (21:6). The God who began history will finish it. In Isaiah that claim mocks the idols, which cannot say what will happen. Here it backs every promise the book will make.
entries.not: **Not a quote from Isaiah.** The Alpha and Omega words are not in Isaiah. Beale says the title could well have been shaped by reflection on Isaiah 41-48; it is a new phrase for an old claim.
entries.deeper: Beale thinks the Alpha and Omega pair likely grew out of thinking on Isaiah 41-48, because first and last in 1:17 is based on Isaiah 41:4, 44:6 and 48:12, and the threefold name in 1:8 also links to Isaiah. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible says the title evokes Isaiah's first and last; the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible also cites Isaiah 44:6. Keener notes that Greco-Roman writers called the supreme god the first, but that Isaiah 41:4, Josephus and Philo had already called Israel's God first and last. Beale adds Aune's note that the letters AO stood for a divine name in the magical papyri, perhaps as a polemic. The Almighty (pantokrator) is the usual Greek rendering of the Lord of hosts in the Septuagint, and appears often in Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi. The grade is drawn here: the idea is traceable to Isaiah, the wording is not.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Isaiah 41:4, 43:10, 44:6 and 48:12 alongside the threefold name, and notes that Revelation later explains Alpha and Omega as the first and the last (21:6; 22:13). He says John mixes the wording so that it fits the Father and the Son alike. He calls Isaiah 43:10 the big one: before God no god was formed, and none after.

entries.title: Revelation 1:10, in the Spirit, a voice like a trumpet
entries.summary: John's call borrows Ezekiel's words for being taken up by the Spirit and hearing a voice behind him, and the trumpet voice of Mount Sinai.
entries.plain: **A new judge who takes the oath with the old wording is saying the office has not changed.** John describes his call in the words of earlier prophets. Like Ezekiel, he is in the Spirit and hears a loud voice behind him. The voice sounds like a trumpet, as on the day God came down on Sinai to speak with Moses. John is claiming the place of a prophet like them.
entries.same: From Ezekiel 3:12, the Spirit takes the prophet, and he hears behind him a great sound. The Greek is close: ekousa opiso mou phonen (John) and ekousa katopisthen mou phonen (Ezekiel). From Exodus 19:16, a trumpet that sounds very loud as God comes down on the mountain.
entries.differs: Two scenes are joined in one sentence. In Ezekiel the sound behind him is a great rumbling; in Exodus the loud thing is a trumpet. John hears one loud voice like a trumpet. Beale notes that John's grammar bends here too: the word saying agrees with trumpet instead of voice, which may stress the Sinai trumpet. The setting is new as well: John is on Patmos on the Lord's day.
entries.turn: John says his book comes the way the prophets' books came. The Spirit seizes him as it seized Ezekiel. The voice he hears is like the voice at Sinai, where God gave his word through Moses. Beale adds that commands to write in the prophets often carried judgment, a hint of what is coming.
entries.not: **Not a claim that John is Moses or Ezekiel.** The echo puts John in their line as a messenger, with the same authority.
entries.deeper: Beale says John's commission uses the language of Ezekiel's repeated rapture in the Spirit (Ezekiel 2:2; 3:12, 14, 24; 11:1; 43:5), giving him prophetic authority like that of the Old Testament prophets. The great voice as a trumpet evokes the voice Moses heard at Sinai (Exodus 19:16, 19-20). In Greek, the participle legouses (saying) should agree with the voice but is genitive, agreeing with the trumpet; Beale suggests the bend underlines the Exodus 19 background, and finds the same bend in 4:1. Keener says the trumpet sound may allude to Exodus 19:16, and notes Ezekiel's visionary state; the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible and the ESV Study Bible cite Ezekiel 3:12 for in the Spirit. The CSB Study Bible's cross-references list both. The grade is drawn here by Beale's definitions: the phrasing is traceable to these scenes, but no single text supplies all of it.
entries.dissent: Jeske, as Beale reports, sees Micah 3:8 as the only background for in the Spirit; Beale thinks Ezekiel at least as likely. Keener allows that in the Spirit may mean charismatic worship rather than a vision.

aw.s: On the island of Patmos, in the Spirit on the Lord's day, John hears a voice like a trumpet telling him to write to seven churches. He turns and sees one like a son of man among seven golden lampstands, holding seven stars, who holds the keys of death and Hades and explains what the stars and lampstands mean.

entries.title: Revelation 1:11, write what you see in a book
entries.summary: The command to write the vision in a book repeats a charge God gave Moses and the prophets.
entries.plain: **A reporter told to get it in writing knows the story will be read and checked later.** God told Moses to write his words in a book. He told Isaiah and Habakkuk to write their visions down too. John receives the same order. His vision is to be written and sent to the seven churches.
entries.same: The order to write. In the Greek of Exodus 17:14 and Isaiah 30:8, the order is to write in a book. John has the same phrase (grapson eis biblion).
entries.differs: The prophets wrote for Israel, often as a record against the people. John writes to seven named churches in Asia, and the book is to be sent like a letter. The wording is common in the Old Testament, so no one passage stands behind it.
entries.turn: The order puts John's book among the written words of God's messengers. Beale adds that such commands in the prophets often came with judgment, and Revelation's letters to the churches carry both warning and comfort.
entries.not: **Not a single source text.** The command is spread across the Old Testament, which is why this is only a possible echo.
entries.deeper: Beale hears in the order to write in a book the same charge God gave his prophets, citing the Greek of Exodus 17:14, Isaiah 30:8, Jeremiah 37:2 and 39:44 in Greek numbering, and Tobit 12:20. He adds that readers steeped in the Old Testament might notice that these commissions were often commands to record a witness against Israel. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible notes the parallel with Isaiah 30:8, Jeremiah 36:2 and Habakkuk 2:2, and the CSB Study Bible's cross-references list the same kind of texts. The grade is possible because the language is only generally similar to many texts.

entries.title: Revelation 1:12, turned to see the voice
entries.summary: John turns to see a voice, an odd phrase that may carry on the Sinai echo, where the people saw the voice.
entries.plain: **When a writer uses an odd turn of phrase, readers who know the old book catch where it came from.** John says he turned to see the voice. You cannot see a voice. But at Mount Sinai, in the Greek Old Testament, the people saw the voice and the trumpet's sound. John may be keeping up the Sinai picture from verse 10.
entries.same: The verb see with the noun voice. John has blepein ten phonen; the Greek of Exodus 20:18 has heora ten phonen, the people perceived the voice.
entries.differs: At Sinai the whole people see the voice and are afraid. John alone turns to see it. English Bibles of Exodus 20:18 read thunderings, since the Hebrew word can mean sounds or voices. The Greek translation chose voice, and John's phrase matches the Greek.
entries.turn: If the echo is meant, John's vision opens like Sinai, the place where God spoke his word to his people. Beale reads it as part of John's claim to speak with a prophet's authority.
entries.not: **Not a certain link.** It may simply be a way of saying John turned toward the speaker. Beale himself calls that reading possible.
entries.deeper: Beale offers two readings. The phrase may be a metonymy, the voice for the speaker. He also notes the Greek of Daniel 7:11 has the prophet attending to a voice, though there it is the boasting of God's enemy. He finds Exodus 20:18 more relevant: in the Greek, the people at Sinai see the voice and the trumpet's sound; after the allusion to Exodus 19 in 1:10, he reads the seeing of a voice as a continuation of it. Philo, Decalogue 46-47, stresses that the voice at Sinai was visible. Ezekiel 3:12-13 in Greek also has the prophet behold the voice of the creatures' wings. The CSB Study Bible's cross-reference at 1:12 points to Exodus 20:18. The grade is possible: the wording is close, but the phrase is short and could arise on its own.
entries.dissent: Beale lists Daniel 7:11 in Greek as a possible unconscious borrowing, and Exodus 20:18 as the more relevant source. Thomas, as Beale reports, takes it as a simple figure of speech for the speaker.

entries.title: Revelation 1:12, seven golden lampstands
entries.summary: Zechariah saw one gold lampstand with seven lamps; John sees seven gold lampstands, and is told they are the churches.
entries.plain: **A city can copy a famous fountain and build seven of them, one in each district.** Zechariah saw one gold lampstand with seven lamps on it. It stood for God's people, lit by his Spirit. John sees seven gold lampstands, and in verse 20 he is told they are the seven churches. Where Zechariah saw one lampstand, John sees seven.
entries.same: Gold lampstand, the number seven, and a vision that is then explained. In both books someone asks or tells what the lights mean (Zechariah 4:4-10; Revelation 1:20).
entries.differs: Zechariah has one lampstand with seven lamps. John has seven lampstands. Beale says the change from one to seven shows that the church is no longer one nation but people of every place. Zechariah's lamps are God's eyes. John's lampstands are churches, and the stars beside them are angels.
entries.turn: The lampstand stood in the tabernacle and the temple, near God's presence. Calling the churches lampstands says they are now where God's light shines in the world. Keener adds that the menorah was the best-known symbol of Judaism, so John claims the Jesus movement is part of Israel's story. Christ walks among them, tending them like a priest trims lamps.
entries.not: **Not seven separate religions.** The seven churches stand for the whole church, Beale says, since each letter ends with a word to all the churches.
entries.deeper: Beale grants a broad background in the tabernacle lampstand (Exodus 25 and 37; Numbers 8), but traces the image more narrowly to Zechariah 4:2, 10. His three reasons: the seven spirits of 1:4 (compare Zechariah 4:6); the vision and its explanation in 1:20 follow Zechariah's pattern; and Zechariah 4 is clearly used in Revelation 4:5 and 5:6 beside allusions to Daniel. In the Greek of Zechariah 4:2 the lampstand (lychnia) is all gold; John has hepta lychnias chrysas. Jewish writings read Zechariah's lampstand as Israel and identified it with the righteous of every age (Midrash Rabbah on Leviticus 30.2, Sifre Deuteronomy 10). Revelation 11:4 uses lampstands again for the witnessing church. Walton notes that Zechariah's lamp was a bowl lamp with forty-nine lights, unlike any excavated piece. The grade is drawn here: the pattern is traceable to Zechariah, the count is changed.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads the lampstands as branches of a menorah and traces them to Zechariah 4:1-2. With the Meyers' commentary he links the lamps, the eyes of 4:10 and the stone with seven eyes in Zechariah 3:9, which they read as temple building. He concludes that John is calling the church God's temple, where God's presence and his heavenly host now dwell, a line that runs to John 2 and Revelation 21:22. He calls believers the reconstituted divine council, already but not yet.
entries.dissent: Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible stress the menorah as the common symbol of Judaism in the cities of Asia, rather than Zechariah's vision in particular. Beale holds that Zechariah 4 is the specific source. They agree on what the lampstands mean, since 1:20 says it.

entries.title: Revelation 1:13, one like a son of man, robed and girded with gold
entries.summary: The figure among the lampstands is Daniel's one like a son of man, dressed like the shining man of Daniel 10 and the scribe in linen of Ezekiel 9.
entries.plain: **A painter can put a king's crown, a judge's robe and a priest's sash on one sitter.** John sees a figure like a son of man, the one who comes before God's throne in Daniel 7. He wears a long robe and a gold sash, like the shining man by the river in Daniel 10 and the man in linen in Ezekiel 9. John builds one figure out of several.
entries.same: One like a son of man (homoion huion anthropou) from Daniel 7:13. A man clothed and girded with gold from Daniel 10:5. A robe reaching to the feet (podere) and a belt from the Greek of Ezekiel 9:2.
entries.differs: Daniel 10 has the gold around the waist; John puts the gold sash across the chest. John's word for the robe, podere, is not in Daniel 10. It is in the Greek of Ezekiel 9:2 and in the Greek of Exodus for the high priest's robe. John also breaks a grammar rule again: like a son of man has the wrong case, as in 14:14, which Beale reads as pointing back to Daniel.
entries.turn: The son of man in Daniel receives an everlasting kingdom. The robe and sash were priestly clothing. Beale and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible read Jesus here as both king and priest, standing among the churches and tending them like lamps. He is also the one who came on the clouds in 1:7, now present with his people.
entries.not: **Not a lesser angel.** Borrowing an angel's features does not make Jesus an angel, the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible says; John gathers the grandest pictures he has.
entries.deeper: Beale finds most features of the figure in verses 13-15 in Daniel 7 and, above all, Daniel 10, with other texts adding detail. Son of man is from Daniel 7:13 (in Greek hos huios anthropou). The robe and gold come from Daniel 10:5, which the vault's Greek Daniel renders clothed in baddin, linen, and girded with gold of Uphaz. The word podere comes from the Greek of Ezekiel 9:2, 11, the man in a foot-length robe among the six destroyers, and from Exodus 28:4 and 29:5 for the high priest. Beale also notes that podere never describes a king's clothing in the Septuagint. The accusative huion after homoion is a solecism; scribes changed it to the dative. Keener reads the robe and girdle as a likely allusion to the high priest. Beale counts this cluster among his combined allusions and his literary prototypes: Revelation 1 follows the shape of Daniel 7. The grade is drawn here: son of man is Daniel's phrase word for word.
entries.heiser: Heiser traces the robe and gold sash to Daniel 10:5, paired with 10:16. He argues the man in linen there is neither Gabriel, who takes orders from him, nor Michael, who helps him and has equals. Linking the prince of the host in Daniel 8:11 with the commander of Yahweh's army in Joshua 5:14, he concludes, in his words I would argue, that the man is the angel of the Lord, God appearing as a man. So John is not comparing Jesus to a lesser angel. He piles up Daniel 7, Daniel 10 and Zechariah 1 and 4 to make the same point four times.
entries.dissent: Who is the man in Daniel 10? Walton notes he is usually identified as Gabriel, and Keener calls him the mighty angel. Others read him as more than an angel. The sources also weigh priest against king: Beale and Keener lean priestly, the ESV Study Bible gives both, and some commentators Beale names deny any priestly sense.

entries.title: Revelation 1:14, hair white like wool, white as snow
entries.summary: The white hair belongs in Daniel 7 to the Ancient of Days, God on his throne; John gives it to Jesus, the son of man.
entries.plain: **If an actor playing the prince walks on wearing the king's crown, the audience notices.** In Daniel 7 two figures stand apart. The Ancient of Days, God on the throne, has hair like pure wool and clothing white as snow. The son of man comes to him. John's son of man has the hair of the Ancient of Days. He gives God's look to Jesus.
entries.same: Hair white like wool, and the whiteness of snow. In the Greek, wool (erion) and snow (chion) appear in both verses.
entries.differs: In Daniel the snow describes the clothing and the wool describes the hair. John puts both on the head and the hair. And the person changes. In Daniel these features belong to the Ancient of Days, not to the son of man who comes before him. John blends the two figures.
entries.turn: This is the boldest move in the vision. John gives Jesus a feature that Daniel reserved for God. Beale reads it as showing Jesus' divine right to judge and his eternal life. Wright puts it simply: looking at Jesus, you see the Father.
entries.not: **Not a sign of old age.** White hair in Daniel marks the dignity and wisdom of the eternal judge (Keener, the ESV Study Bible), not frailty.
entries.deeper: Beale says the head and hair are taken from the Ancient of Days in Daniel 7:9, and that the transfer of the judge's attributes to Christ shows his role as the end-time divine judge and his eternal life. In the vault's Greek Daniel, 7:9 reads to endyma autou hosei chion leukon, his garment as white snow, and he thrix ... hosei erion katharon, the hair as pure wool. Beale notes a variant in the old Greek of Daniel 7:13 in which the son of man comes as the Ancient of Days, and suggests it may reflect a tradition that helped John. Keener, the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the ESV Study Bible, the CSB Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible all trace the hair to Daniel 7:9. The grade is drawn here: the words are nearly the same and the source is one passage.
entries.heiser: Heiser stresses that in Daniel 7 the white hair belongs to the Ancient of Days, not to the son of man. John gives it to Jesus anyway: "he blurs the distinction between them". Heiser reads this as John's view of Jesus as Yahweh in the flesh, written by the end of the first century at the latest. He ties the Ancient of Days' fiery wheeled throne to Ezekiel 1.
entries.dissent: The study Bibles differ on what white hair means: wisdom (ESV Study Bible, NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible), dignity of age (Keener), or wisdom and purity, joined with the transfiguration (CSB Study Bible). Beale stresses judgment and eternal life. None doubts the source.

entries.title: Revelation 1:14, eyes like a flame of fire
entries.summary: The fiery eyes come from the shining man in Daniel 10, whose eyes were like torches of fire.
entries.plain: **A cover version can keep a song's tune and change one word in the chorus.** In Daniel 10 a shining man appears to Daniel by a river. His eyes are like torches of fire. John's figure has eyes like a flame of fire. The picture is Daniel's; the word is a little different.
entries.same: Eyes and fire, in the same kind of portrait: a glorious man seen in a vision. In Greek both say his eyes were as something of fire (pyros).
entries.differs: Daniel's man has eyes like torches or lamps (lampades). John says flame (phlox). The word flame of fire appears in Daniel 7:9 too, for God's throne. John may have joined the two. He keeps the order of Daniel 10 through the next verses: eyes, then feet, then voice.
entries.turn: Fire that sees through everything is a picture of judgment. Beale notes that in 2:18-23 the one with eyes like fire searches hearts and gives each church what its deeds deserve. The ESV Study Bible says these eyes see through any front a church puts up.
entries.not: **Not a picture of anger alone.** The fire also stands for full knowledge, which can bring blessing as well as judgment (Beale).
entries.deeper: Beale says the description of the eyes and feet follows Daniel 10:6 in Greek. The vault's Greek Daniel reads hoi ophthalmoi autou hosei lampades pyros; John has hoi ophthalmoi autou hos phlox pyros. The words phlox pyros occur in Daniel 7:9 of the Ancient of Days' throne, a link noted here and not by the sources. Beale reads the eyes as judicial and ties them to 2:18, 23 and 19:12. Keener lists the features of the mighty angel of Daniel 10:5-6 among the sources of verses 13-15; the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the ESV Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible all cite Daniel 10:6. Walton notes that Daniel's five features (body, face, eyes, limbs, voice) also describe the throne-bearers of Ezekiel 1. The grade is drawn here: the picture is uniquely Daniel's, the wording is not identical.
entries.heiser: Heiser calls the fiery eyes a bit of an outlier: the picture is not entirely from Ezekiel 1, but such descriptions are used of God elsewhere. He reads the whole portrait as John fusing descriptions of Yahweh from different places into one picture of Jesus.

entries.title: Revelation 1:15, feet like bronze refined in a furnace
entries.summary: The bronze feet come from Daniel 10 and Ezekiel 1; the furnace may recall the fiery furnace of Daniel 3.
entries.plain: **A builder who reuses beams from three old barns can still make one sound frame.** The feet like gleaming bronze come from the shining man of Daniel 10. Ezekiel's living creatures, who carry God's throne, also have feet that sparkle like bronze. And the furnace may call to mind Daniel 3, where a fourth figure walked in the fire.
entries.same: Bronze. Daniel 10:6 has arms and legs like the sight of gleaming bronze; Ezekiel 1:7 has feet that sparkle like bronze. Revelation has feet like fine bronze. Daniel 3 and Revelation both have a furnace of fire.
entries.differs: Daniel 10 speaks of arms and legs, not feet. John's word for bronze, chalkolibanon, is rare, and appears in neither Daniel nor Ezekiel. The furnace is John's addition; Beale thinks it echoes the furnace of Daniel 3, and wonders whether the odd grammar of John's furnace phrase is meant to point there.
entries.turn: Bronze tested in fire stands for strength and purity. Beale reads it as moral purity that Christ will ask of the churches he walks among (compare 3:18). The ESV Study Bible says such feet will crush every opponent. The CSB Study Bible contrasts them with the statue's crumbling feet in Daniel 2.
entries.not: **Not an exact source text.** The phrase draws on several pictures at once, so no one verse matches it.
entries.deeper: Beale says the feet follow Daniel 10:6 in Greek, and the furnace again echoes Daniel 3:25 (verse 92 in the Greek numbering of Theodotion), with Ezekiel 1:27 perhaps near. He notes the genitive pepyromenes after the dative kamino, an irregular construction, and asks whether it imitates the genitive phrase for the burning furnace in the Greek of Daniel 3. Keener links the bronze feet both to the creatures under God's throne in Ezekiel 1:7 and to the angel of Daniel 10:6. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible connects the feet to Daniel 10:6 and Ezekiel 1:7, and the glowing metal to God's own glory in Ezekiel 1:27. The grade is drawn here: probable for the bronze, possible for the furnace.
entries.dissent: Beale offers the furnace of Daniel 3 as a likely echo. The study Bibles do not mention it. Beale himself asks the grammar question without settling it.

entries.title: Revelation 1:15, a voice like many waters
entries.summary: The voice like the roar of many waters is God's voice in Ezekiel 43:2 and Ezekiel 1:24, and John follows the Hebrew wording.
entries.plain: **A tribute band that plays a song from the original record, not a later cover, shows which version it knows.** Daniel's shining man had a voice like a crowd. John's figure has a voice like many waters. Those words come from Ezekiel, where God's glory returns to the temple with a sound like many waters. John's wording matches the Hebrew of Ezekiel, not the Greek translation.
entries.same: A voice like the sound of many waters. In Hebrew Ezekiel 43:2 reads kol mayim rabbim; John has phone hydaton pollon. Ezekiel 1:24 uses the same picture for the sound of the creatures' wings near God's throne.
entries.differs: The Greek translation of Ezekiel 43:2 does not say many waters; it compares the voice to an army camp. So John is closer to the Hebrew here. He also moves the voice from God to Jesus. And he skips the end of Daniel 10:6, where the man's voice is like a crowd, for Ezekiel's stronger image.
entries.turn: In Ezekiel the voice belongs to God himself, as his glory returns to the temple. John gives that voice to Jesus, standing among the lampstands. Beale reads it as another sign of Christ's divine nature, set, like Ezekiel's, in a temple scene.
entries.not: **Not a voice like Daniel's angel.** Daniel 10:6 has a crowd. John chose God's voice from Ezekiel instead, Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible both note.
entries.deeper: Beale says that just as Daniel 10:6 ends with the man's voice, so does John's portrait, but the language is taken from the Hebrew of Ezekiel 1:24 and 43:2, where God's voice is like the roar of many waters. In the vault's Septuagint, Ezekiel 43:2 reads phone tes paremboles hos phone diplasiazonton pollon, a sound of a camp like the voice of many; Ezekiel 1:24 has hos phonen hydatos pollou, like the sound of much water. The Hebrew of 43:2 is vekolo kekol mayim rabbim. Jewish writings placed Ezekiel's voice in the temple (Midrash Rabbah on Genesis 3.4). Vos, as Beale's introduction reports, counted the shift from Yahweh to the son of man as disregard for context; Beale answers that it is a change of application, since the son of man is plainly divine in Revelation 1. The grade is drawn here by Beale's definitions: the wording is nearly identical to the Hebrew and the setting is God's glory.
entries.heiser: Reading verse 15, Heiser says the bronze feet and the roar of many waters sound like Ezekiel 1 and 43, and that John is throwing it all in the blender.
entries.dissent: Vos takes the transfer of God's voice to the son of man as ignoring Ezekiel's context; Beale calls it a change of application. Keener adds that later Jewish traditions spoke of waters in the heavens.

entries.title: Revelation 1:16, a sharp two-edged sword from his mouth
entries.summary: The sword coming from his mouth joins Isaiah's servant, whose mouth God made a sharp sword, and Isaiah's king, who strikes the earth with his mouth.
entries.plain: **A speech can be said to cut deep; John paints the words as a blade.** In Isaiah 49 the servant says God turned his mouth into a sharp blade. In Isaiah 11 the coming king strikes the earth with what comes from his mouth. John joins the two. The sword from Jesus' mouth is his word, and it judges.
entries.same: A mouth, a sharp sword, and a word that strikes. The Greek of Isaiah 49:2 has a mouth as a sharp sword (machairan oxeian); John has a sharp two-edged sword (rhomphaia distomos oxeia).
entries.differs: In Isaiah 49 the mouth is like a sword; in John a sword comes out of the mouth. Isaiah 11:4 in Hebrew has the rod of his mouth, but the Greek translation has the word of his mouth. A sword fits that Greek reading better than a rod. John also uses a different Greek word for sword, the long blade (rhomphaia).
entries.turn: The king in Isaiah 11 judges the earth with his mouth. Jesus does the same. Beale shows that 19:15 adds Isaiah's words about striking the nations, so Isaiah 11 is uppermost. In 2:16 the same sword is turned on compromisers inside the church.
entries.not: **Not a call for Christians to fight.** The sword is in his mouth, not in a hand. It stands for his word of judgment, as the ESV Study Bible and the CSB Study Bible note.
entries.deeper: Beale says the sword is based on the prophecies of Isaiah 11:4 and 49:2, and that 19:15 shows Isaiah 11:4 is uppermost, since there the words to strike the nations follow. In the vault's Septuagint, Isaiah 49:2 reads ethēke to stoma mou hos machairan oxeian, and Isaiah 11:4 reads pataxei gen to logo tou stomatos autou, he will strike the earth with the word of his mouth; the Hebrew has beshevet piv, with the rod of his mouth. Beale cites 4 Ezra 13:10, where the son of man destroys the enemy with fire from his mouth, and the Wisdom of Solomon 18:15, where God's word is a warrior with a sharp sword. Keener reads Isaiah 49:2 of God's spokesperson and Isaiah 11:4 of the Messiah's decrees. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible cites Isaiah 11:4; the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible both. The grade is drawn here: the picture is traceable to Isaiah, the wording is close but not identical.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Beale and Moyise on Isaiah 11:4 and 49:2. Moyise notes that the Greek of Isaiah 11:4 has the word of his mouth where the Hebrew has the rod. Heiser draws the step himself: since John has a sword and not a rod, John is following the Greek here. He reads the image as conquest and judgment, and perhaps also as speaking the truth, and notes its return in 2:16 and 19:15.
entries.dissent: The sources weigh the two Isaiah texts differently. Beale puts Isaiah 11:4 first. Keener and Wright give both. The CSB Study Bible points to Hebrews 4:12 and the word of God. Beale adds that most see the Roman soldier's battle sword behind the word rhomphaia.

entries.title: Revelation 1:16, his face like the sun shining in its strength
entries.summary: The shining face uses the closing words of Deborah's song in Judges 5, where those who love God are like the sun rising in its strength.
entries.plain: **A victory speech that ends with a line from an old battle song links the two wins.** Deborah's song in Judges 5 ends with a wish: may those who love the Lord shine like the rising sun at full strength. John's figure has a face like the sun shining in its strength. Beale thinks John took the words from that song of victory.
entries.same: The sun, and its strength. In the Greek both end with en te dynamei autou or en dynamei autou, in his power.
entries.differs: In Judges the words are a wish for God's friends, the faithful people. John uses them of Jesus' own face. The Greek of Judges speaks of the sun rising; John says shining. The other features of the portrait follow Daniel 10, whose man had a face like lightning, but the wording here is Judges.
entries.turn: Judges 5 is a song of victory after a battle in which even the stars fought from heaven. Beale reads John's line as a picture of Christ as the victorious warrior, linked with the stars in his hand. The face that shines is the face of the winner.
entries.not: **Not proof that John had Judges open.** Beale grounds the link in wording. The study Bibles point instead to the transfiguration, where Jesus' face shone like the sun.
entries.deeper: Beale says the description still follows the outline of Daniel 10, but the actual wording is derived from Judges 5:31 in the Greek of Codex Vaticanus (B). The vault's Greek Judges reads hos he anatole tou heliou en dynamei autou, as the rising of the sun in its power; John has hos ho helios phainei en te dynamei autou. Beale links the warrior of Judges 5:31 with the stars that fought from heaven in 5:20, and notes Jewish writings that join Judges 5:31 with Daniel 12:3 (Sifre Deuteronomy 10 and 47). He suggests Judges 5:31 was seen as a type of the messianic warrior. The grade is drawn here: Beale treats the wording as derived, but no other source in the vault names Judges.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Beale on Judges 5:31 and the stars that fought from heaven in 5:20, which make Christ the divine warrior. He says the connections might be a little loose but are worth considering. He takes Beale's point that the image is warfare: Christ returns to judge those who oppose him, starting with compromise inside the churches.
entries.dissent: The CSB Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible read the shining face against Matthew 17:2, the transfiguration, and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible adds Psalm 84:11 and Isaiah 60:19. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible points to Greek and Jewish descriptions of shining beings. Beale mentions the transfiguration too, as anticipating Christ's reign.

entries.title: Revelation 1:16, seven stars in his right hand
entries.summary: The seven stars, explained in 1:20 as the angels of the churches, may draw on Daniel 12:3, where the wise shine like the stars.
entries.plain: **A logo can borrow a single star from an old flag and still carry its meaning.** John's figure holds seven stars, and 1:20 says they are the angels of the churches. Beale thinks the stars come from Daniel 12, where the wise among God's people will shine like the stars forever. In Daniel stars can also stand for angels.
entries.same: Stars, near the same heavenly man. In Daniel 12 the man in linen stands above the river (12:6-7), right after the stars of 12:3. In John he holds the stars in his hand.
entries.differs: Daniel 12:3 has the wise shining like stars, with no number. John has seven stars, a count that may come from Zechariah's seven lamps. Daniel's stars are people raised to glory. John's stars are angels of churches.
entries.turn: The hand means rule. Christ holds the churches' heavenly side as well as their earthly side, the lampstands. Beale reads the stars as the churches' place in heaven, and the angels as their heavenly representatives.
entries.not: **Not astrology.** The sources reject a star-fate reading. Keener notes that Jews often took the stars to be angels under God, and here the stars are in Jesus' hand.
entries.deeper: Beale says there is reason to view the stars as coming from Daniel, given the influence of Daniel 10 in the portrait: the man above the river in Daniel 12:6-7 is the one from Daniel 10, and the stars of 12:3 are the wise raised to glory. He suggests the seven may come from Zechariah 4's seven lamps, since Jewish writings equated Zechariah's lampstand with the stars of Daniel 12:3. 1 Enoch 90:20-25 has seven white ones and seventy stars, both angels, built on Daniel; 1 Enoch 21:3 has seven stars as seven angels; 1 Enoch 86:1-3 and 88:1 use stars for angels. He also mentions a possible polemic against imperial myths of a dead emperor's son ruling the stars. The grade is possible: the link is to pictures more than words.
entries.heiser: Heiser follows Beale: John draws the link between stars and angels from Daniel and from 1 Enoch, where seven white ones and seventy stars are angels (90:20-25) and seven stars are seven angels (21:3). He reads the stars, the angels and the seven spirits of 1:4 and 3:1 as one group.
entries.dissent: Readers differ on the angels of 1:20: heavenly angels (Beale, who argues they represent the churches), human messengers or leaders, or personifications of each church (the ESV Study Bible). Keener lists four views. On the stars' source, Keener points to Jewish usage of stars for angels without naming Daniel.

entries.title: Revelation 1:17, falling as though dead, and do not fear
entries.summary: John's response follows Daniel 10 step by step: the vision, the prophet falling face down, a touch that lifts him, and the words do not fear.
entries.plain: **A scene in a new film can follow an old classic beat for beat, and fans notice.** In Daniel 10 Daniel sees the shining man, falls face down, is touched by a hand, and hears do not fear. Then he receives a message. John's scene runs the same way. He falls at the figure's feet as though dead, is touched by his right hand, hears do not fear, and is given the message.
entries.same: The order of events, and the words do not fear (me phobou), which both texts have.
entries.differs: The match is in the sequence more than the wording. Daniel is set on his hands and knees by a hand; John is touched by the right hand of the one he sees. Daniel lies face down in a deep sleep; John falls like a dead man. And the one who lifts John is the one he saw, not a messenger sent by him.
entries.turn: The scene marks John as a prophet in Daniel's line. The comfort is the point. Beale reads do not fear as the main word of verses 12-18, addressed to churches afraid of suffering and death.
entries.not: **Not a fainting spell.** Falling down before God's glory is the usual response of prophets in Scripture (Ezekiel 1:28; Daniel 8:17), as the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible and Keener both note.
entries.deeper: Beale finds a four-step pattern from Daniel 8 and 10 in John's response: a vision, a fall in fear, strength from a heavenly being, and more revelation after it. He finds the word order and ideas closest to Daniel 10:8-20, which is the basis of the scene, with Ezekiel 1-3 nearby in vaguer form. Do not fear occurs twice in Daniel 10 (verses 12 and 19) but not in Daniel 8 or Ezekiel. The vault's Greek Daniel reads me phobou, Daniel in 10:12. Keener notes that revealers often touched and strengthened those who fell (Daniel 8:18; 10:10) and that God often told his servants not to be afraid. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible and the CSB Study Bible add Ezekiel 1:28 and Daniel 8:17. In Beale's terms this is a literary prototype: a scene shaped on an Old Testament sequence. The grade is drawn here: the sequence, not the wording, points to Daniel 10.

entries.title: Revelation 1:17, the first and the last
entries.summary: Jesus calls himself the first and the last, the title God uses for himself in Isaiah when he mocks the idols, and John's wording follows the Hebrew.
entries.plain: **A title can be so tied to one person that using it says who you are.** In Isaiah God calls himself first and last, and says no other god exists. In Revelation 1:17 Jesus claims the same title for himself. He takes God's own name from Isaiah. John's words also match the Hebrew of Isaiah, since the Greek translation never says last.
entries.same: The words first and last (protos and eschatos). The Hebrew of Isaiah 44:6 and 48:12 reads rishon and acharon, first and last.
entries.differs: The Greek translation of Isaiah does not use last. It says first and after these things (44:6), first and forever (48:12), first and into what is coming (41:4). John's eschatos fits the Hebrew, a link noted here from the texts, not from the sources. The larger change is the speaker: in Isaiah it is God; here it is the risen Jesus.
entries.turn: What Isaiah says of God alone, Jesus says of himself. Beale calls it a clear reference that shows Christ as a divine figure, sovereign over history. In Isaiah the title comforts Israel in exile, and the same chapters say do not fear. John's readers hear it as a reason not to fear death.
entries.not: **Not a lesser title.** In Isaiah the phrase is followed by there is no God but me. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible says it is precisely the title that marks out deity.
entries.deeper: Beale calls this a clear reference to Yahweh's self-predications in Isaiah 41:4, 44:6 and 48:12, with the same meaning as the formulas of 1:8: God's rule over history from start to end. He shows how the Isaiah texts were linked to Daniel 10 by shared phrases: do not fear in Isaiah 41:10 and 44:2, and God's right hand in 48:13. In the vault's Septuagint, Isaiah 44:6 reads ego protos kai ego meta tauta, 48:12 ego eimi protos kai ego eimi eis ton aiona, and 41:4 protos kai eis ta eperchomena. The Hebrew of 44:6 is ani rishon va'ani acharon, and of 48:12 ani rishon af ani acharon. John's ego eimi ho protos kai ho eschatos agrees with the Hebrew; Beale does not discuss the point, so the textual link is drawn here. Fekkes, cited by Beale, treats these titles at length. The ESV Study Bible says Jesus echoes the Lord's boast over the idols.
entries.heiser: Heiser notes that the first and the last, used of God in Isaiah 41:4, 44:6 and 48:12 and in Revelation 1:8, is said by Jesus in 1:17, who adds I died, and look, I am alive. He reads this as John applying God's language to Jesus within the opening chapter, long before the creeds.

entries.title: Revelation 1:18, the living one, alive forever
entries.summary: Living forever and ever was a way the Old Testament spoke of God; the risen Jesus says it of himself.
entries.plain: **Some phrases are kept for one person, like a family motto.** In Daniel, God is the one who lives forever. Moses' song has God swear as one who lives forever. Jesus says he is the living one, dead once and now alive forever and ever. He takes a phrase kept for God, and adds that he died.
entries.same: Living forever, said of the one who speaks. In Daniel 12:7 the man in linen swears by him who lives forever.
entries.differs: In the Old Testament the phrase belongs to God, who never dies. Jesus says I died, and look, I am alive. The forever life comes after a death, which no Old Testament text says of God.
entries.turn: Beale reads the phrase as another claim to deity, joined to the resurrection. The ever-living one died to free his people. Churches facing death are told that the one who holds their lives has been through death and come out.
entries.not: **Not a single quoted verse.** The phrase recurs in several places, so the echo is possible, not clear.
entries.deeper: Beale counts this as one more claim to deity, because living forever is a phrase the Old Testament keeps using of God: Deuteronomy 32:40, Daniel 4:34 in Theodotion, Daniel 12:7, and Sirach 18:1. He reads the threefold living, dead, living of 1:18 as modeled on the threefold name of 1:4 and 1:8. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible notes that the risen Christ lives forever like God, citing Daniel 4:34. The grade is possible: the phrase is general, and two sources name it.

entries.title: Revelation 1:18, the keys of death and Hades
entries.summary: The keys may recall Isaiah 22:22, where the steward of David's house is given the key that opens and shuts.
entries.plain: **Whoever holds the keys of a building runs it.** In Isaiah 22 a new steward is put over King David's house and given its key. What he opens no one shuts. Jesus says he holds the keys to death and to Hades, the place of the dead. Beale and others hear Isaiah 22 here, a link Revelation makes plainer in 3:7.
entries.same: A key that gives authority over a house or realm. Isaiah 22:21-22 also gives the steward a robe and sash, like the figure in 1:13.
entries.differs: Isaiah's steward holds the key of David's house. Jesus holds the keys to death and the grave. Isaiah 22 says nothing about death or Hades. The clear use of Isaiah 22:22 comes later, in 3:7, with the key of David.
entries.turn: The risen Jesus controls who is kept in death and who is released. Beale reads it as the result of the resurrection: the one once held by death now rules it. For churches facing martyrdom, Wright says, this is the news that he has the keys.
entries.not: **Not keys borrowed from the pagan gods.** Sources note Hekate and Anubis held keys to the underworld; Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible say Jewish texts gave those keys to God alone.
entries.deeper: Beale says the image could come from keys in the Targums or rabbinic writings, but Isaiah 22:22 is the more probable background, as 3:7 makes plain. He suggests Eliakim was read as a pattern for a royal and priestly servant to come, which would fit the priest-king picture of 1:13. Keener notes that whoever held the keys in a royal house had great authority, citing Isaiah 22:21-22, and that the Wisdom of Solomon 16:13 gives God authority over death and the gates of Hades. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cites Isaiah 22:22 with Matthew 16:19. Targum on Deuteronomy 28:12, as Beale reports, says God alone holds the key of the tombs. The grade is possible: the echo rests on the picture, and the clear use waits for 3:7.
entries.heiser: Heiser holds the keys over in the Revelation 1 lecture and takes them up with Revelation 3:7. There, reading Beale and Carson and Justin Bass, he says the key of David amplifies the keys of death and Hades: Jesus is Lord over life and death.
entries.dissent: Aune, as Beale reports, reads the keys as a polemic against the goddess Hekate, said to hold the keys of the world; Beale widens it to all the gods of the underworld. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible names Anubis and Hades. The CSB Study Bible links the keys to Matthew 16:18 rather than Isaiah.

entries.title: Revelation 1:19-20, what will take place after this, and the mystery
entries.summary: Chapter 1 ends as it began, with Daniel 2: what must take place after this, and a mystery revealed.
entries.plain: **A song that ends on the line it opened with tells you the whole thing hangs together.** Daniel 2 says God reveals mysteries and shows the king what will happen after this. John's first chapter closes on the same words. He is to write what will take place after this, and he is told the mystery of the stars and lampstands. Chapter 1 begins and ends with Daniel 2.
entries.same: The words after these things (meta tauta), what will happen, and mystery (mysterion). In Daniel 2:29 and 2:45 the Greek has ha dei genesthai meta tauta, and mysteries are revealed in 2:28-29.
entries.differs: John says ha mellei ginesthai, what is going to happen, where Daniel says what must happen. Beale treats it as a paraphrase, as Josephus also paraphrases Daniel. Daniel's mystery is the meaning of a king's dream. John's mystery is the meaning of the stars and lampstands: the churches on earth and their angels in heaven.
entries.turn: The mystery in Daniel was God's coming kingdom, shown to a king in a dream. John uses the same word for the stars and lampstands, and the meaning follows at once, as in Daniel. Beale reads mystery as fulfillment in an unexpected form: the kingdom present in weak, suffering churches with Christ among them.
entries.not: **Not a new source.** The words about what will take place after this come again from Daniel 2, already heard in 1:1, and mystery comes from the same chapter. Whether the verse also outlines the book is a separate question.
entries.deeper: Beale calls 1:19 the most important of a series of verses that allude to Daniel 2:28-29, 45 (with 1:1, 4:1 and 22:6). He reads meta tauta as carrying an end-time sense, since Daniel 2 uses it beside the latter days. Mysterion occurs in the Greek of the Hebrew Bible only in Daniel; mysteria precedes ha dei genesthai in Daniel 2:28-29, which, for Beale, confirms the link. He notes that the awkward start of 1:20, the mystery, without a connecting word, may tie it to the Daniel allusion. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible says 1:19 recalls Daniel 2:28-29, 45; the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible ties mystery in 1:20 to Daniel 2:27-30, 47. The grade is drawn here: Beale argues it at length but the wording is a paraphrase.
entries.dissent: Beale lists six readings of 1:19. He calls a strictly time-ordered outline the least plausible and prefers three that mix present and end time. Futurists, as the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible notes, read it as the book's outline, and the CSB Study Bible and the ESV Study Bible both map it onto chapters 1, 2-3 and 4-22. MacArthur reads it the same way: chapter 1 is the vision John has just seen, chapters 2-3 are the letters to the churches, and chapters 4-22 are the history still to come. On the source, Brown and Swete, as Beale reports, connect mystery to Daniel 2 but not 1:19.

entries.title: Revelation 2:1, these are the words of
entries.summary: Each of the seven letters opens with the stock line the prophets used before a word from the Lord, now spoken by Jesus.
entries.plain: **A press release that opens with the old royal formula tells you who is speaking before you read a word.** Each letter in Revelation 2 and 3 opens with one stock line. The Greek is tade legei, the line Amos, Zechariah and Ezekiel used to say the Lord was speaking. John puts Jesus in that place. The letters are prophecy, and the speaker takes the Lord's own part.
entries.same: The opening words, tade legei, these things says. The Greek of Amos 1:6 and Zechariah 1:3 opens a word from God the same way. In the prophets the Lord is the speaker; in Revelation the speaker is the risen Jesus.
entries.differs: In the prophets the formula is followed by the Lord, or the Lord of hosts. In the letters it is followed by a picture of Jesus taken from chapter 1. No single verse stands behind it, since the line opens dozens of oracles. The ESV Study Bible adds that kings used the same line for their decrees.
entries.turn: John sets Jesus in the seat of the God who spoke through the prophets. Beale draws two points. Christ takes up the role of the Lord. And the seven letters are prophetic messages, not ordinary mail.
entries.not: **Not a quotation of one prophet.** The line was a common way to open an oracle, so the echo is to a habit of speech.
entries.deeper: Beale counts the formula tade legei kyrios pantokrator, these things says the Lord Almighty, 21 times in the Minor Prophets, about 12 of them in Zechariah, where it opens a new unit as here. The shorter tade legei kyrios opens sayings at least 65 times in Ezekiel, about 30 in Jeremiah and 8 in Amos. The vault's Septuagint confirms the wording in Amos 1:6 and Zechariah 1:3, which are cited here as two examples; the choice of those two verses is drawn here. Keener notes that prophets borrowed the formula from royal edicts and messenger speech, and the ESV Study Bible gives 2 Chronicles 36:23 for the royal use. The grade is possible because the language is only generally like many texts.

aw.n: Revelation 2:1-7, Ephesus and the Nicolaitans
aw.s: To Ephesus the one who holds the seven stars praises a church that tested false apostles and hates the works of the Nicolaitans, but warns that it has abandoned its first love and may lose its lampstand. The one who conquers will eat from the tree of life in God's paradise.

entries.title: Revelation 2:4, the love you had at first
entries.summary: The first love Ephesus has left may recall Jeremiah 2:2, where God remembers Israel's love as a young bride in the wilderness.
entries.plain: **A couple who look at their wedding photos remember what they used to do for each other.** Jesus tells the church in Ephesus that it has left the love it had at first. Some sources hear Jeremiah 2, where God remembers how young Israel loved him like a bride and followed him through the desert. Ezekiel 16 tells the same story of a covenant like a marriage.
entries.same: The idea of an early love for God that has since cooled. Jeremiah 2:2 speaks of the love of Israel's youth. Ezekiel 16:8 tells of God entering a covenant with Israel when she was old enough for love.
entries.differs: John does not borrow the bride picture or any shared phrase. His word is agape, love, with first. The Greek of Jeremiah 2:2 also has agape, but for love at Israel's consecration; the Greek of Ezekiel 16:8 has no word for love at all. So the link is in the idea, not the wording.
entries.turn: Ephesus kept its doctrine clean and endured hard times. What it lost, Beale argues, was its outward love, the witness it once gave to its city. Heiser follows him. The remedy fits that reading: do the works you did at first.
entries.not: **Not a quotation of Jeremiah.** Jeremiah remembers Israel's love as a young bride in the desert. John uses the picture of a first love left behind, but not Jeremiah's words.
entries.deeper: The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible and Keener both say Jeremiah 2:2 fits if the love is for God, and a fellow-believer reading fits the hate of verse 6. The CSB Study Bible's cross-reference at 2:4 is Jeremiah 2:2. Beale names Jeremiah 2:2 and Ezekiel 16:8 for the view that the church lost its love for Christ, which he thinks is too narrow. He ties the lost love instead to Matthew 24:12-14, where the love of many grows cold just before the call to preach to every nation. In the vault's Septuagint, Jeremiah 2:2 reads agapes teleioseos sou, the love of your consecration, and Ezekiel 16:8 speaks of a time of resting and an oath of covenant. The grade is possible: the sources propose the link, and the wording is only generally similar.
entries.heiser: Heiser says the first love language seems to come from passages like Jeremiah 2:2 and Ezekiel 16:8, where Israel is God's bride. He then follows Beale. The church had not gone after other gods or false teachers; it had let its mission slide. He calls it a lapse in the covenant task, not in belief, and links it to Judges 2, where the angel of the Lord withdraws from Israel.
entries.dissent: The sources split on what love is meant. Beale and Heiser read it as love shown in witness to outsiders. Wright reads it as practical care for others, especially fellow Christians. The CSB Study Bible reads it as love for God. MacArthur reads it as love for Christ that had cooled into a cold, mechanical orthodoxy, which their sound doctrine and service could not replace. The ESV Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible say both love for Christ and love for one another may be in view.
