entries.title: Revelation 2:7, the tree of life in the paradise of God
entries.summary: The reward for the one who conquers is the tree of life from Genesis 2 and 3, now open again, set in Ezekiel's paradise of God.
entries.plain: **A family that wins back the old farm can sit under the tree their great-grandparents planted.** In Genesis God sets the tree of life in the garden, then bars the way to it after Adam and Eve sin. Jesus promises the one who conquers a right to eat from it. John places the tree in the paradise of God, a phrase from Ezekiel. Eden is open again.
entries.same: The tree of life (to xylon tes zoes), in the same Greek words as Genesis 2:9 and 3:22. Paradise (paradeisos), the Greek translation's word for the garden. Ezekiel 31:8 in Greek has the very phrase in the paradise of God.
entries.differs: Genesis speaks of the garden in Eden, not the paradise of God; John takes that phrase from Ezekiel 28:13 and 31:8. In Genesis 3 the tree is guarded so that no one may eat. John reverses the ban: now the winner is invited to eat. Genesis has no condition of conquering; John adds it.
entries.turn: The tree stands for God's life-giving presence, Beale says, lost when Adam and Eve were sent out. Christ promises it back. The same tree returns in 22:2 by the river of the new Jerusalem. Wright and the ESV Study Bible add a local edge: a sacred tree stood in the precinct of Artemis at Ephesus.
entries.not: **Not a picture of the cross as the tree.** Beale reads the tree as the effect of the cross, the restored presence of God, not the cross itself.
entries.deeper: In the vault's Septuagint, Genesis 2:9 has to xylon tes zoes en meso tou paradeisou and 3:22 warns lest he take from the tree of life and eat. Ezekiel 28:13 reads en te tryphe tou paradeisou tou theou, and Ezekiel 31:8 twice has en to paradeiso tou theou. John's phrase en to paradeiso tou theou is Ezekiel's word for word, joined to Genesis' tree. Beale lists early Jewish texts with the same hope: Testament of Levi 18:10-11, Psalms of Solomon 14:2-3 and 4 Ezra 8:52. He notes that the tabernacle lampstand was shaped like a tree, which ties the lampstand of 2:5 to the tree of 2:7. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible notes that many Jewish sources made Eden the destiny of the righteous. The grade is drawn here: the wording is the same and the scene is Eden's.
entries.heiser: Heiser calls the Old Testament roots of this verse very transparent. The believer's future on the new earth is modeled on Eden before the fall. He ties it to the mission: the gospel goes to the nations, the Lord returns, the nations are healed and Eden is renewed. A church that drops its witness delays that future.
entries.dissent: The sources agree on Genesis. They differ on the local color. Beale suggests a tree linked with Artemis or with Ephesus. Wright describes a tree in the Artemis precinct used for asylum. The ESV Study Bible names the date palm on the city's coins. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible mentions tree shrines in the temple estates.

aw.n: Revelation 2:1-7, Ephesus and the Nicolaitans
aw.s: To Ephesus the one who holds the seven stars praises a church that tested false apostles and hates the works of the Nicolaitans, but warns that it has abandoned its first love and may lose its lampstand. The one who conquers will eat from the tree of life in God's paradise.

entries.title: Revelation 2:7, whoever has ears, let them hear
entries.summary: The call to hear that closes every letter goes back through Jesus' parables to Isaiah 6 and Ezekiel 3, where some hear and some refuse.
entries.plain: **A teacher who says this part will be on the test knows only some students will take the hint.** Every letter ends with the same call to anyone with ears to listen. Jesus used it after his parables. Behind it stand Isaiah 6, where the people hear and do not understand, and Ezekiel 3, where the prophet is told to say let the hearer hear.
entries.same: Ears, and an order to hear. The Greek of Ezekiel 3:27 has ho akouon akoueto, the one who hears, let him hear. John has ho echon ous akousato, the one who has an ear, let him hear. Isaiah 6:9-10 speaks of ears that hear without understanding.
entries.differs: John's line is closest to the gospels, where Jesus ends his parables this way. Isaiah 6 is a word of judgment on a dull people; John aims the call at the churches. Ezekiel's wording is the nearest Old Testament match in the Greek. John adds a new close: listen to the Spirit's message for the churches.
entries.turn: Beale reads the line as it works in Isaiah and in Jesus' parables. The same message opens some eyes and closes others. Here it calls the church to listen. Like Israel, some churches are drifting toward idols. They must hear and turn back before the visions to come.
entries.not: **Not a polite sign-off.** In Isaiah and the gospels the call marks a message that divides its hearers.
entries.deeper: Beale traces the formula to the Synoptic saying, which itself alludes to Isaiah 6:9-10, with Ezekiel 3:27 and 12:2 and Jeremiah 5:21 nearby. In the vault's Septuagint, Isaiah 6:9 reads akoe akousete kai ou me synete, hearing you will hear and not understand, and Ezekiel 3:27 reads ho akouon akoueto kai ho apeithon apeitheito, let the hearer hear and the refuser refuse. Beale adds that idols have ears and do not hear (Psalm 115:4-8), so a church flirting with idols risks becoming as deaf as they are. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible names Isaiah 6:9-10 and Ezekiel 3:27 beside Matthew 11:15 and Mark 4:9. Keener compares the prophets' call to hear the word of the Lord. The grade is possible: the call comes through the gospels, and its Old Testament roots are general.
entries.dissent: Beale holds that John uses the saying with its Synoptic and Isaiah setting in mind. He reports others who think the formula had become a stock phrase and lost that setting. Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible note the gospel form without naming Isaiah.

entries.title: Revelation 2:10, tested for ten days
entries.summary: The ten days of testing at Smyrna recall Daniel and his friends, tested ten days for refusing the king's food.
entries.plain: **A coach who says the next ten days will show who you are is borrowing from a story every player knows.** Daniel and his three friends would not eat the Babylonian king's food. They asked to be tested for ten days. Jesus tells the believers in Smyrna they will be tested and have ten days of trouble. Their test, like Daniel's, is about loyalty under pressure from a pagan power.
entries.same: A test and ten days. The Greek of Daniel 1:12 reads peirason ... hemeras deka, test us ten days; 1:14 repeats it. John has peirasthete and hemeron deka, be tested and ten days.
entries.differs: Daniel's test was a diet, and the outcome was good health. Smyrna's test is prison and perhaps death. Daniel asks for the test; at Smyrna the devil brings it. John keeps the number and the testing and drops the food. The sources agree the time is short. Beale grants it could be ten literal days.
entries.turn: Beale reads the echo closely. Daniel's friends refused food dedicated to idols at the king's table, and that table meant loyalty to a king who thought himself divine. Smyrna's Christians faced the same kind of demand from the cult of the emperor. The short test before Daniel's greater trials also hints that worse may follow.
entries.not: **Not Daniel's test.** Daniel asked for ten days on vegetables and water. At Smyrna the ten days are prison and trouble from the devil. John borrows the number and the idea of a test, not the story.
entries.deeper: Beale calls the ten days an allusion to Daniel 1:12-15, where the testing for ten days is mentioned twice, and reads the number as figurative for a short but severe trial. He notes that Judaism and the early church held up Daniel and his friends as models for those who would rather suffer than worship idols, and that Polycarp, later bishop of Smyrna, died for refusing to call Caesar Lord. Keener reads the ten days as a symbol drawn from Daniel's small test in 1:12, the first of greater trials. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the ESV Study Bible, the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible and the CSB Study Bible's cross-references all name Daniel 1:12-14. The grade is drawn here: testing and ten days together point to that one chapter.
entries.dissent: The sources agree on Daniel 1. They differ on the number. Beale grants it could be literal but reads it, with Wright and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible, as a brief, bounded time of trial. Wright notes that a day can stand for a longer period in writing like John's. MacArthur says the jailing will be short. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible reads it as a sign of a swift execution to come.

aw.n: Revelation 2:8-11, Smyrna, poor and slandered
aw.s: To Smyrna the risen Jesus says he sees their hardship and poverty and the abuse they suffer from local opponents claiming to be the true Jews, whom he condemns in harsh terms. Some will be jailed for a short time; if they stay loyal even to death he will reward them with life.

entries.title: Revelation 2:13, Antipas, my faithful witness
entries.summary: Jesus gives the martyr Antipas his own title from Psalm 89, faithful witness, and keeps the psalm's grammar to show it.
entries.plain: **A captain who hands his own armband to a fallen teammate is saying they played the same game.** In 1:5 Jesus is the faithful witness, a title from Psalm 89. Now he gives the same title to Antipas, a believer killed at Pergamum. John even keeps the odd grammar he used in 1:5, so readers hear the same psalm again.
entries.same: Two words, witness and faithful (ho martys ... ho pistos). The Greek of Psalm 89:37 has ho martys en ourano pistos, the faithful witness in the sky. Isaiah 43:10 calls Israel God's witnesses.
entries.differs: In the psalm the witness is the moon. In 1:5 it is Jesus. Here it is a man who died for his faith. John adds my twice: my witness, my faithful one. The grammar is odd again: after in the days of, the name and title should change form, but John leaves them as the psalm has them.
entries.turn: Antipas shares his Lord's title because he shared his Lord's path, faithful to death. Beale reads the grammar as a pointer: the reader is sent back to 1:5 and the psalm, so that the martyr's witness is joined to Jesus' own. The ESV Study Bible says Jesus shares his title with Antipas.
entries.not: **Not a slip by a weak writer.** Beale argues the grammar is deliberate, as in 1:4 and 1:5, and rejects calling it a careless error.
entries.deeper: Beale notes that the phrase Antipas ho martys mou ho pistos mou follows in the days of, where Greek grammar wants the genitive. He rejects the view that this is a careless Semitism or uneducated style. Like the solecisms of 1:4 and 1:5, the nominative is kept because it belongs to the same Old Testament allusion as 1:5, the nominative ho martys ... pistos of Psalm 88(89):38(37) in Greek numbering. He adds Isaiah 43:10-12, where Israel is told twice you are my witnesses, also nominative, beside God and his servant. In the vault's Septuagint, Isaiah 43:10 reads ginesthe moi martyres kai ego martys, be my witnesses, and I am a witness. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible links Antipas to Jesus as faithful witness in 1:5 and 3:14. The grade is drawn here: the title is the psalm's, and Beale's case rests on the grammar.
entries.dissent: Beale reports scholars who explain the nominative as an undeclined Semitic name, or as a slip after the name. He answers that no undeclined form of Antipas has been found and that the same clause in 1:5 shows the pattern.

aw.n: Revelation 2:12-17, Pergamum, where Satan's throne is
aw.s: To Pergamum Jesus, who wields the sword of judgment, says they have stayed loyal in a city he calls Satan's seat, even after the martyrdom of Antipas. But some follow teaching like Balaam's that leads to idol meals and immorality. The faithful are promised hidden heavenly food and a white stone carrying a new name.

entries.title: Revelation 2:14-16, the teaching of Balaam
entries.summary: The false teachers at Pergamum are named after Balaam, who taught Moab how to lead Israel into idol feasts and immorality, and the Nicolaitans may be his namesakes in Greek.
entries.plain: **Calling a schemer a Judas tells everyone what kind of betrayal you mean.** Balaam was hired to curse Israel and could only bless. Then he showed Moab another way: lure Israel to idol feasts and sexual sin. Jesus says some at Pergamum hold the teaching of Balaam. The Nicolaitans, Beale and Heiser argue, carry Balaam's name in Greek form.
entries.same: Balaam and Balak by name, Israel's sons, eating idol sacrifices and sexual sin. The Greek of Numbers 25:1-2 has ekporneusai, to fornicate, and ephagen ... ton thysion ton eidolon, they ate the sacrifices of the idols. Numbers 31:16 blames Balaam's advice. Numbers 31:8 says he was killed by the sword.
entries.differs: Numbers never quotes Balaam's plan; it reports the result and later blames his counsel. John adds that Balaam taught Balak to set a stumbling block. He uses the word eidolothyta, food offered to idols, where Numbers has the sacrifices of their idols. The setting moves from Moab's camp to a Christian church.
entries.turn: Beale sees a principle carried across: then and now, the danger was closeness to pagan worship dressed as wisdom. The sword in 2:16 fits the story, since Balaam was threatened by the angel's sword and died by the sword. Heiser adds that Nicolaitan means one who conquers the people. Rabbis read Balaam's name the same way.
entries.not: **Not a ban on all meat from the market.** Beale and Heiser, following Witherington, read the idol food as meals eaten at pagan worship, the case Paul also forbids in 1 Corinthians 10.
entries.deeper: Beale traces the episode through Numbers 22:5 to 25:3 and 31:8, 16: Balaam could not curse Israel, so he advised Moab's women to draw Israel's men into feasts for their gods. Balaam became proverbial for the false teacher who works for gain (Deuteronomy 23:4; Nehemiah 13:2; 2 Peter 2:14-16; Jude 11). He notes that Balaam faced the drawn sword of the angel (Numbers 22:23, 31) and was killed by the sword (31:8; Joshua 13:22), the fate threatened in 2:16. In the vault's Septuagint, Numbers 31:8 reads apekteinan en rhomphaia, they killed with the sword, the same word as Revelation's rhomphaia. On the Nicolaitans, Beale notes that nika laon means he overcomes the people, and that rabbinic writings read Balaam's name as he consumes the people or lord over the people (Babylonian Talmud Sanhedrin 105a). Keener, the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the ESV Study Bible, the CSB Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible all name Numbers 25 and 31:16. The grade is drawn here: the names make the source certain.
entries.heiser: Heiser follows Aune and Beale. Nicolaitan was not a real sect but a label built from the name: nika laon, he conquers the people, matches a rabbinic reading of Balaam. The church fathers who traced it to Nicolas in Acts 6:5 had no basis, he says. Is this really repurposing the Old Testament? A little, he answers: John wants readers to feel that Pergamum is reliving the disaster of Balaam.
entries.dissent: The sources differ on the Nicolaitans. Beale and Heiser read the name as a play on Balaam, and Wright mentions the idea. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible says we can only guess, noting both the later link to Nicolas and the link to Balaam. The ESV Study Bible calls them a sect not identifiable with certainty. Keener notes that church fathers later called them a Gnostic sect.

entries.title: Revelation 2:17, the hidden manna
entries.summary: The hidden manna recalls the bread from heaven God gave Israel in the wilderness and the jar of it kept before the Lord.
entries.plain: **A grandmother who keeps one loaf from the wedding feast is saving a taste of the day for later.** In the wilderness God fed Israel with manna, bread from heaven. Moses had a jar of it set aside before the Lord for future generations. Jesus promises the one who conquers some of the hidden manna. Those who refuse the idol feasts of Pergamum will eat at God's own table.
entries.same: The word manna (manna). Exodus 16:32-34 has the jar of manna laid up before God for later generations. Psalm 78:24-25 calls it the bread of heaven and, in Greek, the bread of angels.
entries.differs: Exodus speaks of manna kept, not hidden; the hiddenness comes from Jewish tradition. 2 Maccabees 2:4-7 says Jeremiah hid the ark, and later writings expected the manna to return. The wilderness food was daily bread; John's manna is a reward for the one who conquers. And it is set against the idol meat of 2:14.
entries.turn: Beale reads the hidden manna as end-time fellowship with Christ, sealed at the marriage supper of the Lamb. Those who will not eat at pagan feasts are promised a better meal. Israel should have trusted God's bread in the desert instead of Moab's sacrifices. The same choice faces Pergamum.
entries.not: **Not a hunt for a lost jar.** The legends about the ark are background color. Beale and Keener read the manna as a picture of fellowship with Christ, not a relic to be found.
entries.deeper: Beale calls the manna a metaphor for end-time fellowship with Christ, citing John 6:31-35, and lists Jewish texts where manna marks the end-time hope: 2 Baruch 29:8, Sibylline Oracles 7.149 and the Babylonian Talmud Hagigah 12b. He ties the hiddenness to the tradition that Jeremiah hid the ark (Exodus 16:32 with 2 Maccabees 2:4-7), and to Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on Exodus 16:4, 15, where the manna lies hidden in the high heavens. In the vault's Septuagint, Exodus 16:33 has the manna put aside enantion tou theou eis diaterasin, before God for keeping, and Psalm 78:25 reads arton angelon, bread of angels. The CSB Study Bible notes that Israel ate idol food at Peor while God was still sending manna. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible and the CSB Study Bible's cross-references name Exodus 16:32-34. The grade is drawn here: manna can come from nowhere but the wilderness story.
entries.heiser: Heiser calls manna the food of angels, from Psalm 78:25, since it fell from heaven where angels live. He links it to the meals with God in Genesis 18 and Exodus 24 and to the marriage supper of the Lamb, and reads Beale's line that those who refuse pagan feasts get a seat at the table. He mentions the Targum traditions of hidden manna but stresses they are much later than John.
entries.dissent: The sources agree on Exodus 16. They differ on hidden. Beale reads it as revealed only at the end. Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible point to the hidden ark tradition. The ESV Study Bible reads the manna as God feeding his people now, as he fed Israel in the wilderness.

entries.title: Revelation 2:17, a white stone
entries.summary: The white stone may recall the manna, which Exodus calls white and Numbers likens to a gem, though the sources also point to stones used for votes and tickets.
entries.plain: **A pebble picked up at a wedding can be a keepsake and a ticket at once.** Jesus promises a white stone along with the hidden manna. Beale notes that the Old Testament describes manna as white, and as looking like a precious stone. A white stone also meant a vote to acquit and a pass to a feast. John may want all of these to ring at once.
entries.same: Whiteness and a stone joined to the manna. Exodus 16:31 says the manna was white (leukon). Numbers 11:7 compares its look to bdellium, and the Greek translation to crystal (krystallou). John's word is psephos leuke, a white pebble.
entries.differs: Neither Exodus nor Numbers calls the manna a stone. The link runs through comparison: white, and like a gem. John's word psephos was the pebble used for voting, which the Old Testament passages do not use. So the stone draws on Greek custom as much as on the manna story.
entries.turn: Beale reads the stone with the manna: it confirms the heavenly feast. White marks the purity of those who did not soil themselves at idol meals, and it marks their acquittal. The world's courts condemned them; Christ reverses the verdict and gives them a ticket to his supper.
entries.not: **Not a known object with one meaning.** Beale says there may be no single background, and the study Bibles list several customs.
entries.deeper: Beale says the white stone may be intentionally allusive, suggesting several compatible backgrounds. It was used as a vote to acquit (4 Maccabees 15:26; Acts 26:10) and sometimes as a pass to special occasions. It also strengthens the manna as a heavenly reward, since the Old Testament likens manna to white bdellium (Exodus 16:31; Numbers 11:7), and the Greek of Numbers 11:7 to the appearance of rock crystal. The vault's Septuagint confirms krystallou in Numbers 11:7 and leukon in Exodus 16:31. Beale adds a Jewish tradition that precious stones fell with the manna (Midrash on Psalm 78.4). The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible also says the stone recalls Exodus 16:31. The grade is possible: the sources propose it among several backgrounds.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Aune and Beale. Aune explains psephos as pebble, gem and vote, with white for acquittal. Heiser stresses Beale's further point that Exodus 16:31 and Numbers 11:7 liken manna to white bdellium or rock crystal, which he finds really interesting. His summary: the stone is a vote of approval, you belong here.
entries.dissent: Some see a priestly background: the two stones on the high priest's ephod bearing the tribes' names (Exodus 28:9-12). Beale reports it and finds it possible, and Wright mentions the names on the high priest's clothing. Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible stress Greek customs: jurors' white stones, admission tokens, and the black stone of Cybele.

aw.n: Revelation 2:12-17, Pergamum, where Satan's throne is
aw.s: To Pergamum Jesus, who wields the sword of judgment, says they have stayed loyal in a city he calls Satan's seat, even after the martyrdom of Antipas. But some follow teaching like Balaam's that leads to idol meals and immorality. The faithful are promised hidden heavenly food and a white stone carrying a new name.

entries.title: Revelation 2:17, a new name
entries.summary: The new name on the stone echoes Isaiah's promise that God will call his restored people by a new name.
entries.plain: **When a town wins its charter and takes a new name, the new name tells you its status has changed.** Isaiah 62 says God will call Zion by a new name, and Isaiah 65 says his servants will be called by another name. Jesus promises the one who conquers a new name written on the stone. Beale and Heiser read it, after 3:12, as God's and Christ's own name.
entries.same: A new name (onoma kainon). The Greek of Isaiah 62:2 has kalesei se to onoma sou to kainon, he will call you by your new name. Isaiah 65:15 has klethesetai onoma kainon, they will be called by a new name.
entries.differs: In Isaiah the name is spoken by the Lord over Jerusalem and God's servants. John has a name written on a stone that only the receiver knows. Isaiah's promise was to Israel restored; John gives it to whoever conquers at Pergamum. He also adds the secrecy, which is not in Isaiah.
entries.turn: Beale reads the new name as Israel's promised new standing, now given to the church as the people of the last days. The name marks belonging and God's presence, as 3:12 and 22:4 spell out. Isaiah 65 sets faithful servants against Israelites who ate at idol feasts, which suits Pergamum.
entries.not: **Not Isaiah's name for Zion.** In Isaiah 62 God gives Zion a new name before the nations. John turns the promise into a name given to the one who conquers.
entries.deeper: Beale calls the new name an allusion to Isaiah 62:2 and 65:15, noting the shared kaleo with onoma kainon, and perhaps Isaiah 56:5. In Isaiah 62 the new name signals Israel's royal status (62:3), God's restored presence (62:4) and a marriage with the Lord. Isaiah 65:15 contrasts God's servants with those who dedicate meals to idols (65:3-4, 11), and the Targum of Isaiah 65:6, 15 links the sword and the second death, both of which close the letter. The vault's Septuagint confirms both phrases. Beale reads 3:12 as the key: the name is God's name, the name of the new Jerusalem, and Christ's new name, all one. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible names Isaiah 62:2 and 65:15; the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible names Isaiah 56:5 and 62:2; the CSB Study Bible's cross-references give Isaiah 56:5 and 62:2. The grade is drawn here: the phrase new name with the verb to call points to these chapters.
entries.heiser: Heiser asks whether the name is God's or the believer's. Isaiah 62:2 and 65:15 do not settle it alone. Aune lands on God's or Jesus' name, and Heiser prefers Beale's simpler path: 3:12 answers 2:17. He calls it name theology, a mark of ownership, and reads the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:27, where God's name is put on Israel. The mark of the beast in chapter 13 is its dark mirror.
entries.dissent: Beckwith, as Beale reports, holds that the name belongs to the believer alone and draws on secret names used in magic. Beale answers that all overcomers receive the same name. MacArthur also reads the name as personal: a word from Christ to each one he loves, which no one but its holder knows, and which admits its holder to glory. The ESV Study Bible relates the new name to the Spirit making believers holy. Keener notes that a change of name in the Old Testament came with a promise (Genesis 17:5, 15).
sources: G. K. Beale, The Book of Revelation (New International Greek Testament Commentary), comment on 2:17c, and The New Name

entries.title: Revelation 2:18, the Son of God
entries.summary: The only use of Son of God in Revelation looks ahead to Psalm 2, quoted at the end of the letter, and may recall the son of God in Daniel's furnace.
entries.plain: **A letter signed with the heir's title warns the reader that the heir's rights come with it.** This letter opens with Jesus as the Son of God, the only time Revelation uses the title. It ends by quoting Psalm 2, where God tells his king, you are my Son. Beale also hears Daniel 3, where a figure like a son of God walks in the fire with Daniel's friends.
entries.same: The title son of God. The Greek of Psalm 2:7 reads huios mou ei sy, you are my son. Daniel 3:25 in the vault's Greek has the fourth figure homoia huio theou, like a son of God. Fire is in both Daniel 3 and Revelation 2:18.
entries.differs: Psalm 2 never says Son of God; God says my son. Daniel 3 has like a son of God, a heavenly helper. John uses a fixed title. The fiery eyes and bronze feet come from chapter 1 and Daniel 10, not from Psalm 2. So the title gathers two passages without quoting either.
entries.turn: The title prepares for the promise of Psalm 2 in verses 26-27. The Son who rules the nations will share his rule. Beale adds that it answers local claims, since Apollo, patron of Thyatira's guilds, and the emperor were both called sons of Zeus. As in Daniel 3, the Son protects the faithful in the fire.
entries.not: **Not a new picture of Jesus.** The eyes and feet repeat chapter 1. Only the title is new here.
entries.deeper: Beale reads Son of God as John's way of putting son of man from 1:13, since the eyes and feet come from 1:14-15. He hears Daniel 3:25 (and 3:92 in the Greek with its additions), where the friends are saved by one like a son of God, and a Jewish and Christian tradition that took Daniel 7's son of man and Daniel 3's son of God as one figure. The title also anticipates Psalm 2, cited at the end of the letter. Hemer, as Beale reports, ties the bronze to a Thyatiran trade and the title to Apollo Tyrimnaeus and the emperor. The ESV Study Bible connects the Son of God of verse 18 with Psalm 2:7-9, and the CSB Study Bible's cross-references give Psalm 2:7-9 at this verse. The grade is possible: the title is general and the link to Psalm 2 is through the letter's end.
entries.dissent: Hemer, as Beale reports, reads the title chiefly against Apollo and the emperor and plays down Daniel; Beale holds that both backgrounds count. Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible stress the local cult of Apollo and the emperor as son of a god without naming Daniel 3. The ESV Study Bible adds Ezekiel 1:27 behind the fiery description.

entries.title: Revelation 2:20-23, that woman Jezebel
entries.summary: The false prophetess at Thyatira is called Jezebel, after Ahab's queen who drew Israel into Baal worship and whose children came to ruin.
entries.plain: **Everyone knows what is meant when a politician is called a Benedict Arnold.** Jezebel was Ahab's queen. She brought Baal worship into Israel and led the king astray. At Thyatira a woman who calls herself a prophet teaches God's servants to join idol feasts and immorality. Jesus gives her Jezebel's name, and warns that her children will share Jezebel's end.
entries.same: The name Jezebel and the charge of fornication. The Greek of 2 Kings 9:22 speaks of the porneiai Iezabel, the harlotries of Jezebel; John uses porneusai and porneia. 1 Kings 21:25 says Jezebel his wife urged Ahab on. The death of her children echoes the fall of her house.
entries.differs: The Old Testament Jezebel was a queen, not a prophetess, though she kept hundreds of prophets of Baal. John adds the claim to prophesy and the teaching. Her harlotry in Kings is spiritual, worship of Baal. John also adds idol food. The setting moves from a palace to a church meeting.
entries.turn: Beale reads Jezebel as a label for a teacher or group that said Christians could join the trade guilds' idol meals and stay safe. Her sentence draws on Jezebel's fate: Ahab's house was struck down. Jezebel also looks ahead to the harlot Babylon of chapters 17 and 18, as Keener and the CSB Study Bible note.
entries.not: **Not proof that the woman's name was Jezebel.** The sources read the name as a nickname that brands her teaching.
entries.deeper: Beale traces Jezebel's influence through 1 Kings 16:31 and 21:25 and the Greek of 4 Kingdoms (2 Kings) 9:22, where porneia means spiritual adultery. He hears in your wife (a variant reading at 2:20) an echo of Iezabel he gyne autou, Jezebel his wife, which he cites from 3 Kingdoms 20:25 in Greek numbering; the vault's interlinear prints it at 1 Kings 21:25. The nominative he legousa after an accusative is, he argues, another deliberate solecism pointing to that phrase. The punishment recalls 1 Kings 21:17-29, 2 Kings 9:30-37 and 10:1-11. The vault's Septuagint confirms 1 Kings 16:31, where Ahab took Jezebel and served Baal. Keener notes she sponsored hundreds of prophets (1 Kings 18:19) and was accused of witchcraft (2 Kings 9:22). The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the ESV Study Bible, the CSB Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible all name 1 Kings 16 and 21. The grade is drawn here: the name settles it.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Jezebel as a symbol of pagan religion with sexual immorality and idol food, the same problem as Balaam's, now tolerated. To eat at those meals, after Paul in 1 Corinthians 10, is to sit at the table of demons. He notes John chose two famous villains, Balaam and Jezebel, to brand the teaching.
entries.dissent: The sources differ on who she was. The ESV Study Bible says many scholars think she was a real woman prophet. Beale prefers a group within the church, read through 2 John 1, while granting she may be one person. Some identify her with a local Sibyl, which Beale finds unlikely and Keener weighs. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible debates whether her sexual sin is literal.

entries.title: Revelation 2:23, he who searches minds and hearts
entries.summary: Jesus takes the Lord's words from Jeremiah 17:10, the one who searches the heart and repays by deeds, as his own.
entries.plain: **An auditor who says I see the books, not the brochure, is claiming to know what is really there.** In Jeremiah 17 the Lord says he searches the heart and tests the inner self, and repays each person by their ways. Jesus says the same of himself to Thyatira. The two claims stand together only in Jeremiah, Beale notes. Now they belong to Jesus.
entries.same: Hearts and kidneys, an old way to name the inner self. And a payment to each one by what they have done. The Greek of Jeremiah 17:10 has kardias and nephrous with dounai hekasto kata, to give to each according to.
entries.differs: Jeremiah's Greek uses etazon and dokimazon, examining and testing; John has eraunon, searching. Jeremiah repays by ways and the fruit of deeds; John by works. The order of heart and kidneys is reversed. And the speaker is now Jesus, not the Lord of Israel.
entries.turn: What God claimed in Jeremiah, Jesus claims at Thyatira: he sees motives no one else can. Beale notes that Jeremiah's setting is idolatry for gain inside Israel, which fits a church tempted by guild feasts. The fiery eyes of 2:18 are explained here.
entries.not: **Not an empty threat.** In Jeremiah and here the point is judgment that fits the truth about each person.
entries.deeper: Beale calls knowledge of kidneys and hearts a stock biblical idea for God's just judgment, and the formula I will give to each according to works a stock phrase too, but says Jeremiah 17:10 is uppermost because both expressions occur together only there. He notes that Jeremiah addresses Israelites who practice idolatry for economic gain (Jeremiah 17:3, 11; 11:10-17, 20). The vault's Septuagint confirms the wording. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible says the phrase recalls the Lord's self-description in Jeremiah 17:10. The CSB Study Bible's cross-references list Psalm 7:9, Jeremiah 11:20 and 17:10. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible names 1 Chronicles 28:9 and Psalm 7:9. The grade is drawn here: the pairing is unique to Jeremiah.
entries.dissent: The sources differ only on which verse is primary. Beale and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible point to Jeremiah 17:10. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible cites 1 Chronicles 28:9 and Psalm 7:9, and Keener speaks of Jewish names for God as the searcher of hearts.

entries.title: Revelation 2:26-27, authority over the nations, a rod of iron
entries.summary: Jesus quotes Psalm 2:8-9, the promise of the nations and the iron rod, in its Greek form, and shares it with the one who conquers.
entries.plain: **A founder who signs the company over to the whole team is sharing what was his alone.** In Psalm 2 God promises his king the nations and a rod of iron to break them like clay jars. Jesus received that rule from his Father. Now he promises it to the believer at Thyatira who holds on to the end. John follows the Greek translation, where the king shepherds with the rod.
entries.same: Nations, an iron rod and clay pots smashed. The Greek of Psalm 2:9 reads poimaneis autous en rhabdo sidera hos skeue kerameos syntripseis; John has poimanei autous en rhabdo sidera hos ta skeue ta keramika syntribetai.
entries.differs: The Hebrew of Psalm 2:9 has tero'em, you will break them. The Greek translation has poimaneis, you will shepherd. John follows the Greek. He changes you to he, so the promise passes to the believer. He turns the second verb into the pots are broken. And he adds as I received from my Father.
entries.turn: Psalm 2 was a royal psalm for David's heir. Jesus has received its authority, and he shares it with those who conquer. Beale reads the rule as beginning now, through faithful witness, and completed at the end. Keener notes a reader who did not know the Bible would have thought of the emperor.
entries.not: **Not a call to take power by force.** The authority is Christ's, received from his Father, and he shares it with those who conquer. The rod of Psalm 2 belongs to a shepherd as well as a king.
entries.deeper: Beale calls this a quotation of Psalm 2:8-9. He discusses the shepherd problem: the Masoretic vowels give a verb meaning to break, but the bare consonants could be read as a verb meaning to shepherd, which the Greek, Syriac and Vulgate followed. He suggests John or the translator saw a double sense: the rod destroys the rebels and guards God's people, as poimaino means destroy in some Greek texts (Micah 5:6; Jeremiah 6:3). Revelation itself uses poimaino for judgment in 19:15 and for shepherding in 7:17. Sefaria's Hebrew has tero'em beshevet barzel. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible says the verse closely follows the common Greek version and that rule could be translated shepherd. Midrash on Psalm 2 applied the psalm to both Messiah and Israel. The grade is drawn here: the wording is the Greek psalm almost word for word.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads verse 26 as a messianic psalm aimed at Jesus, now spoken of believers. Who rules the nations now? In the Deuteronomy 32 worldview, fallen gods do, whom Paul calls demons. At the end they are judged and displaced, and human believers inherit the nations, he says: "it's going to be you not them". He adds 1 Corinthians 6:3 and Psalm 82.
entries.dissent: The sources differ on timing. Beale reads the rule as begun now and completed at the end, with the rod as both protection and judgment, exercised through suffering witness. The CSB Study Bible places it after the second coming (20:4, 6), and the ESV Study Bible notes that premillennial readers see the millennium here. MacArthur places it in the thousand-year kingdom, when Christ will shepherd with an iron scepter, enforcing his will and guarding his flock, and believers will reign with him. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible adds Daniel 7:14, 22 behind the shared rule.

entries.title: Revelation 2:28, the morning star
entries.summary: The morning star promised to the one who conquers draws on Balaam's oracle of a star rising from Jacob, read as a sign of the Messiah's rule.
entries.plain: **A medal shaped like the king's own emblem says the wearer shares in his rule.** Balaam, of all people, foretold a star coming out of Jacob and a scepter rising from Israel. Jewish readers took that star as the Messiah. Jesus promises the one who conquers the morning star. In 22:16 he calls himself the morning star. So he shares his own royal sign.
entries.same: A star as a sign of the coming ruler. The Greek of Numbers 24:17 reads anatelei astron ex Iakob, a star will rise from Jacob. John has ton astera ton proinon, the morning star.
entries.differs: Numbers says a star will rise; John says the morning star. Beale suggests the verb to rise, anatello, which is also used of dawn, led to morning. Numbers speaks of a star and a scepter that crush Moab. John gives the star as a gift. The words are different; the picture is the same.
entries.turn: Psalm 2 and Numbers 24 sit side by side here, Beale notes. Both have a scepter and rule over nations. The Numbers prophecy came from Balaam, the villain of 2:14, which makes the pairing pointed. Romans used the morning star, Venus, as a sign of sovereignty, so Christ claims the title for his people.
entries.not: **Not Lucifer.** Isaiah 14:12 gives a star title to Babylon's king. The sources here read the star as Christ's royal sign, not the fallen one's.
entries.deeper: Beale says the star is most likely a symbol of messianic rule, as 22:16 shows, and that Numbers 24:14-20 confirms it: the future ruler is a rising star and scepter who crushes the princes of the nations. The Targums read the star as a king. He notes the same pairing of Psalm 2 and Numbers 24 in 2 Peter 1:17-19, and Jewish messianic readings of Numbers 24:17 in Testament of Levi 18:3, the Damascus Document 7.18-21 and 4QTestimonia 9-13. The vault's Septuagint confirms anatelei astron. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible calls the star undoubtedly that of Numbers 24:17 and notes that Psalm 2:9 and Numbers 24:17 share the word scepter. The ESV Study Bible, the CSB Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible all name Numbers 24:17. The grade is drawn here: the idea is traceable to that one oracle, the wording is not.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads the morning star as a symbol of messianic rule that Jesus shares with those who overcome, alongside authority over the nations. He says he has treated both at length in Unseen Realm and does not repeat it in the lecture.
entries.dissent: Some read the star as the promise that the righteous will shine like stars when raised, which Beale grants is possible but less likely. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible notes the image was applied to rulers in Isaiah 14:12, and the CSB Study Bible's cross-references give Isaiah 14:12. Keener stresses the Roman and astral background: authority over a powerful star.

aw.n: Revelation 2:18-29, Thyatira, the guilds and Jezebel
aw.s: To Thyatira the Son of God, with eyes like fire and feet like bronze, praises a growing church but rebukes it for tolerating Jezebel, a self-styled prophetess who leads his servants into immorality and idol food. Those who hold fast are promised authority over the nations and the morning star.

entries.title: Revelation 3:4-5, walking with me in white
entries.summary: The white garments promised at Sardis recall Daniel 11 and 12, where the faithful are made white through the time of trouble at the end.
entries.plain: **A uniform washed clean after a muddy match shows who stayed in the game.** A few at Sardis have not soiled their clothes. Jesus says they will walk with him in white. Daniel 11 and 12 promise that the wise will be refined and made white in the time of trouble at the end. Beale reads that promise as already coming true for those who stay faithful at Sardis.
entries.same: White as the mark of the faithful at the end. The Hebrew of Daniel 11:35 has lelaben, to make white; the Greek of Daniel 12:10 has ekleukanthosi, they will be made white. John has en leukois and himatiois leukois, in white garments.
entries.differs: Daniel speaks of people being made white, refined in trial. John speaks of white clothes, and of walking with Jesus. Daniel has no clothing at all. John adds the contrast with soiled garments, which Beale reads as stains from idol worship. The vault's Greek of Daniel 11:35 lacks the word white; only the Hebrew has it.
entries.turn: Beale reads the white robes as purity proved in the fire of persecution, the end-time trial Daniel foresaw, already begun. The book of life in the next clause also comes from Daniel 12:1. The same white robes return in 4:4, 6:11 and 7:14 for those who came through trial.
entries.not: **Not a prize for a moral performance.** Beale and Heiser read white as faithful loyalty under pressure and as belonging to God's people, not as a reward for being better.
entries.deeper: Beale calls the purification a fulfillment of Daniel 11-12, where the saints are made white through persecution, citing the Hebrew laben in Daniel 11:35 and 12:10 and ekleukaino in 12:10 in Theodotion's Greek. Sefaria's Hebrew of Daniel 11:35 has ulelaben; the vault's Greek Daniel, Theodotion's, has ekleukanthosi in 12:10 but not in 11:35. Beale ties 3:4-5 to 7:9, 13-14, where robes are washed white in the Lamb's blood, and notes that the Mishnah (Middoth 5.4) clothed unblemished priests in white. Keener notes temples in Asia Minor barred worshipers with soiled clothes. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible adds Isaiah 61:10. The grade is drawn here: the idea of being made white at the end is traceable to Daniel.
entries.heiser: Heiser notes that of 26 New Testament uses of leukos, white, 16 are in Revelation. Most scholars, he says, point to Daniel 11:35 and 12:1, 10, where the faithful are made white in the time of trouble and found written in the book. He follows Beale in gathering the promises (white robes, crowns, thrones, rule over nations) and reads them as believers joining God's ruling council.
entries.dissent: The sources weigh the backgrounds differently. Beale puts Daniel first and mentions festive, Roman and baptismal senses. Wright points to white robes worn in triumphs and by the newly baptized. Charles, as Beale reports, reads the clothing as resurrection bodies, which Beale doubts. Aune, as Heiser reports, hears Genesis 5:22 and 6:9 in walking with God.

aw.n: Revelation 3:1-6, Sardis, alive in name only
aw.s: To Sardis the one who holds the seven spirits and seven stars says the church has a reputation for being alive but is dead, and warns that he will come like a thief if it does not wake up. A few have not soiled their clothes; the one who conquers will walk with him in white and will not be blotted out of the book of life.

entries.title: Revelation 3:4-5, soiled clothes and white garments
entries.summary: Soiled clothes traded for white may also recall Zechariah 3, where the high priest's filthy garments are removed and he is clothed anew.
entries.plain: **A patient who leaves the hospital in fresh clothes has left more than the old gown behind.** In Zechariah 3 the high priest Joshua stands before the angel in filthy clothes. The angel has them taken off, says his guilt is gone, and has him dressed in clean robes. At Sardis some have soiled their clothes and some have not. The faithful will be dressed in white.
entries.same: Dirty garments set against new ones, and a person clothed by heaven. The Greek of Zechariah 3:4 removes ta himatia ta rypara, the filthy garments, and 3:5 has periebalon auton himatia, they put garments on him. John has himatia and periballo too.
entries.differs: Zechariah's clothes are dirty from guilt, and God removes it. At Sardis the faithful kept their own clothes clean, and the reward comes after. Zechariah never says white. John's word for soiled, emolynan, is not Zechariah's rypara. So the match is in the picture, not the words.
entries.turn: If the echo is in mind, white garments carry a note of being made right with God. The robes washed in 7:14 point the same way. Beale reports this reading and gives it a place. Still, he puts the weight on faithful witness under trial.
entries.not: **Not a firm source.** Beale mentions Zechariah only as a reading some hold, and the CSB Study Bible gives it as a cross-reference.
entries.deeper: Beale notes that some see a sense of justification behind the white garments, from a baptismal background, and cites the exchange of filthy garments for a clean robe in Zechariah 3, which stands for the taking away of iniquity. He adds that the robes made clean by the Lamb's blood in 7:14 may suggest the same, and that even the bride's linen in 19:8 carries a note of vindication. The CSB Study Bible's cross-references at 3:4 list Zechariah 3:3-4 with 2 Corinthians 7:1 and Revelation 14:4. In the vault's Septuagint, Zechariah 3:4 also dresses Joshua in a poderes, the foot-length robe of Revelation 1:13. That last link is drawn here. The grade is possible: two sources point to it, and the wording is only generally similar.
entries.dissent: Beale says the white garments mainly mark faithful witness that has stayed free of idolatry. He reports the justification reading, which draws on Zechariah 3, as a further note. Keener stresses temple customs: soiled clothes barred worshipers in Asia Minor. Neither Keener nor the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible names Zechariah.

entries.title: Revelation 3:5, never blotted out of the book of life
entries.summary: The promise not to blot a name from the book of life joins Moses' plea in Exodus 32 and Psalm 69 to the book of the saved in Daniel 12.
entries.plain: **A club that promises your name will never come off the honor roll is answering the fear that it might.** Moses asked God to strike his own name from God's book if Israel could not be forgiven. Psalm 69 asks that enemies be struck from the list of the living. Daniel 12 says all whose names are written there will be saved. Jesus promises the one who conquers at Sardis that his name stays.
entries.same: The verb to blot out and a book of names. The Greek of Exodus 32:33 reads exaleipso autous ek tes biblou mou, I will blot them out of my book. Psalm 69:28 has exaleiphthetosan ek biblou zonton, let them be blotted from the book of the living. John has ou me exaleipso to onoma autou ek tes biblou tes zoes.
entries.differs: Exodus and the psalm threaten blotting out; John turns it into a promise that it will not happen. He calls it the book of life, close to the psalm's book of the living. Daniel 12:1 gives the book of those delivered but not the verb. John weaves the three into one line.
entries.turn: Beale reads the line within Daniel's scheme of two kinds of books: a book of life for the faithful and books of deeds for judgment (Daniel 7:10; 12:1-2). The promise assures the faithful few at Sardis. Beale also hears a warning to the many with a name for being alive.
entries.not: **Not a settled answer on losing salvation.** The sources disagree on what blotting out implies. Beale reads it as a guarantee; Heiser, after Aune, as proof that faithfulness matters.
entries.deeper: Beale calls the phrase an allusion to Daniel 12:1-2 and to Exodus 32:32-33 and Psalm 69(68):28, where names written in God's book are blotted out. He notes that those two texts have one book, while Revelation, like Daniel, has more than one, so the Exodus and psalm wording is read through Daniel. Isaiah 4:3, the remnant in Jerusalem written for life, may also stand behind 3:5 and 21:27. The vault's Septuagint confirms exaleipho in Exodus 32:32-33 and Psalm 69:28, and has en te biblo in Daniel 12:1. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible says the image most directly stems from Exodus 32:32-33, later applied to a heavenly book (Psalm 69:28; Daniel 12:1). Keener notes that Greek and Roman cities struck expelled citizens from their rolls. The grade is drawn here: verb and book match Exodus and the psalm closely.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Aune: a name can be erased, so fidelity to God, not any predestinarian system, is why a name is written. Originally to be blotted out meant to die (Exodus 32:32-33; Psalm 69:27-28; Isaiah 4:3). He ties the book to the judgment scenes of Daniel 7:9-10 and 1 Enoch, and further back to the Mesopotamian tablets of destiny. He calls election access to the truth, not a guarantee.
entries.dissent: The sources disagree on the meaning. Beale holds that true believers' names were written before history and cannot be erased; the line assures and warns. Aune, as Heiser reports, and Heiser read the possibility of erasure as showing that ongoing loyalty is required. The CSB Study Bible reads the book as the names of the eternally elect.

entries.title: Revelation 3:7, the key of David
entries.summary: Jesus applies to himself Isaiah 22:22, where God gives the steward Eliakim the key of David's house to open and shut.
entries.plain: **The person handed the master key decides which doors open.** In Isaiah 22 God removes a proud steward and puts Eliakim in charge of King David's palace. He lays the key of David's house on his shoulder: what he opens no one shuts. Jesus says he holds the key of David now. At Philadelphia, shut out of the synagogue, he opens the door.
entries.same: The key of David and the paired clauses about opening and shutting. The vault's Greek of Isaiah 22:22 has ten kleida oikou Dauid, the key of David's house. Then come the open and shut clauses. John has ho echon ten klein Dauid, ho anoigon kai oudeis kleisei.
entries.differs: Isaiah has the key of David's house laid on the steward's shoulder. John shortens it to the key of David and drops the shoulder. Isaiah's man is a servant over the palace; John's is the king himself. The open and shut wording is close, though John puts it in his own grammar.
entries.turn: In 1:18 Jesus held the keys to death and the grave. Here, Beale says, the key of David is set in their place to stress the same rule: Jesus decides who enters the kingdom. To a church pushed out of the synagogue, Keener notes, the true ruler of David's house welcomes them.
entries.not: **Not a passing comparison.** Beale reads Eliakim as a pattern pointing to Christ, the prime minister of a small kingdom foreshadowing the king of a greater one.
entries.deeper: Beale calls the line a quotation of Isaiah 22:22 and reads it as an indirect typological prophecy, not a mere analogy. He gives five reasons. David's name in the New Testament carries messianic overtones. Eliakim is called my servant (22:20), a phrase used thirteen times in Isaiah 40-53. The key on his shoulder, his role as father and his throne of glory echo Isaiah 9:6-7. Revelation 3:9 alludes to servant passages. And the Targum of Isaiah 22:22 gives Eliakim the key of the sanctuary. Walton notes Eliakim's seal impressions and the large keys of the period. Sefaria's Hebrew has maftach beit David al shikhmo. The vault's Greek also has a second clause, I will give him the glory of David. The grade follows Beale's word quotation.
entries.heiser: Heiser, reading Beale and Carson, says the key of David is put in place of the keys of death and Hades to amplify the same claim. He reads Eliakim's name as God will raise up, striking for a risen Jesus. Since the kingdom is the new Eden without death, he says, both keys mean one thing: Jesus is Lord of everlasting life and death.
entries.dissent: The sources differ on the name and the point. Heiser reads Eliakim as God will raise up; Walton reads it as may El establish. Beale stresses rule over who enters the kingdom; the ESV Study Bible joins Isaiah 22:22 to Matthew 16:19; the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible stresses the steward's control of entry to the palace and also cites Isaiah 45:1-2.

aw.n: Revelation 3:7-13, Philadelphia and the key of David
aw.s: To Philadelphia the one who holds the key of David sets before a weak but faithful church an open door no one can shut. Those of the synagogue of Satan will bow at their feet, and the one who conquers will be a pillar in God's temple, bearing the name of the new Jerusalem.

entries.title: Revelation 3:8, an open door no one can shut
entries.summary: The open door set before Philadelphia may echo Isaiah 45:1, where God opens doors before Cyrus that will not be shut.
entries.plain: **A small shop that finds the city gates opened for it can trade far beyond its size.** In Isaiah 45 God promises to open doors before King Cyrus, gates that will not be shut. Philadelphia has little power. Jesus tells it he has opened a door for it, and no one will close it. Beale thinks Isaiah's promise to the weak lies behind it.
entries.same: Doors opened by God that will not be shut. The Greek of Isaiah 45:1 reads anoixo emprosthen autou thyras ... ou synkleisthesontai, I will open doors before him and they will not be shut. John has thyran eneogmenen, hen oudeis dynatai kleisai, an open door no one can shut.
entries.differs: Isaiah's doors are city gates opened before a conqueror. John's single door is set before a weak church. Isaiah's word for shut is synkleio; John uses kleio, as in 3:7. The Isaiah link rests on the picture and a few shared words.
entries.turn: Beale reads it as a promise to a weak people. Israel was small before its foes but would be made strong through God's work with Cyrus; Philadelphia's small witness will be made effective among its opponents. Perhaps, he says, the key of 3:7 led John's thought from Isaiah 22 to Isaiah 45.
entries.not: **Not a sure source.** Beale proposes it and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible cites it in passing; other sources read the door through Paul's open doors for mission.
entries.deeper: Beale argues that the heavy use of Isaiah 40-60 in 3:7-9 makes an allusion to Isaiah 45:1 likely in 3:8, setting the two Greek texts side by side. He suggests the language of Isaiah 45:1 has merged with Isaiah 22:22. The vault's Septuagint confirms the wording. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, commenting on 3:7, cites Isaiah 45:1-2 and Ezekiel 44:2 beside Isaiah 22. Beale also reads the open door as entry to the kingdom and, with Acts 14:27 and 1 Corinthians 16:9, as opportunity for witness. The grade is possible: two sources propose it, and the wording is only partly shared.
entries.dissent: The sources read the door differently. The ESV Study Bible weighs Paul's open doors for ministry and prefers the door into God's sanctuary (4:1). The CSB Study Bible reads a door to heaven and the kingdom. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible leans to access to the kingdom.

entries.title: Revelation 3:9, bowing down at your feet
entries.summary: Isaiah's picture of nations bowing at Israel's feet is turned around: opponents who call themselves Jews will bow before the church at Philadelphia.
entries.plain: **When the old school bully ends up asking the new kid for help, the story has turned around.** Isaiah promised that nations who oppressed Israel would one day come and bow at Israel's feet. Jesus tells the church at Philadelphia that its Jewish opponents will come and bow before its feet. Beale reads it as the prophecy coming true with the roles reversed. He calls this his clearest example of an echo turned upside down.
entries.same: Coming and bowing at the feet. The Greek of Isaiah 60:14 has poreusontai pros se ... kai proskynesousin epi ta ichne ton podon sou, they will come to you and bow at the soles of your feet. John has hexousin kai proskynesousin enopion ton podon sou. Isaiah 49:23 and 45:14 repeat the bowing.
entries.differs: In Isaiah the Gentile nations bow to Israel. In John the ones who bow claim to be Jews, and the church is the one bowed to. Isaiah speaks of soles of feet or licking dust; John says before your feet. John drops the gifts and chains of Isaiah 45 and 60.
entries.turn: Beale reads an ironic fulfillment. In Isaiah the nations bow before Israel. In his reading the Gentile church has become true Israel by faith, and the synagogue that rejects Jesus plays the part of the nations. Beale argues the bowing is not grudging; it leads to their own rescue, as Isaiah's nations were saved. Heiser and Beale both compare Romans 11.
entries.not: **Not a charter for hatred of Jews.** John is a Jew rebuking one local group that handed believers over, Heiser says. Isaiah's picture of foes bowing is turned on that group.
entries.deeper: Beale calls the clause a collective allusion to Isaiah 45:14, 49:23 and 60:14, and Psalm 86:9, all predicting that Gentiles will bow before Israel and Israel's God. This is what Beale's introduction calls an inverted use: the prophecy is fulfilled in reverse, with Christ in the role of Yahweh. He supports the reading of salvation from the open door of 3:8, from Isaiah 60:11 in Revelation 21:25-26, and from 1 Corinthians 14:25. In the vault's Septuagint, Isaiah 60:14 has proskynousin and the feet, 49:23 has proskynesousi soi and the dust of your feet, and 45:14 has proskynesousi soi. Keener, the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the ESV Study Bible, the CSB Study Bible's cross-references and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible all name these chapters of Isaiah. Beale's introduction gives this verse as an example of inverted use. The grade is drawn here: the coming and bowing at the feet are Isaiah's.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Beale and Carson: Isaiah 45:14, 49:23 and 60:14 promise Gentiles bowing to Israel, and here the prophecy is fulfilled in an ironic inversion, with ethnic Israelites in the role of the Gentiles. He calls the anti-Semitic reading incoherent: the writer is a Jew, the target is a persecuting subset, and in Romans 11 the opposition becomes a step toward Israel's salvation.
entries.dissent: The sources differ on what the bowing means. Beale reads conversion. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible speaks of vindication of believers before their persecutors. Wright compares Joseph's brothers bowing in Genesis 42. Fekkes, as Beale reports, sees no thought of conversion here. MacArthur, pointing back to his note on 2:9, reads the opponents as Jews by birth who were not true Jews in Paul's sense (Romans 2:28) and who joined pagans against the church. Keener notes Jewish hopes that kings would bow to Israel at the end.

entries.title: Revelation 3:9, they will learn that I have loved you
entries.summary: God's word to Israel in Isaiah 43:4, I have loved you, is spoken to the church before its opponents, in the same three Greek words.
entries.plain: **A parent who says in front of the whole class that's my kid makes the point public.** In Isaiah 43 God tells Israel that it is precious to him and that he loves it. Jesus tells the church at Philadelphia that its opponents will learn that he has loved it. John applies to a church words God first spoke to Israel.
entries.same: The words I have loved you. The Greek of Isaiah 43:4 reads kai ego egapesa se; John has ego egapesa se, the same three words.
entries.differs: In Isaiah God speaks to Israel, his chosen, in exile. In John the hearers are a church, and the ones who will learn of God's love are Jewish opponents. Isaiah ties the love to ransoming Israel with other nations; John ties it to the church's endurance. Keener adds Malachi 1:2, where God says I have loved you to Israel.
entries.turn: Beale reads a second reversal beside the bowing: God shows his love for persecuted Israel before the nations, and now he shows it for the church before the synagogue. The roles turn, but the promise stands. Heiser reads it as Gentiles brought into God's family.
entries.not: **Not a quotation of Isaiah 43:4.** John takes God's word of love for Israel before the nations and sets it in a new scene: a church before its local opponents.
entries.deeper: Beale says the prophecy that God would show his love for persecuted Israel before the nations is fulfilled in reverse here, as apparently in Isaiah 43:4, and in the Greek of Isaiah 41:8, 44:2, 60:10 and 63:9. The vault's Septuagint confirms ego egapesa se in Isaiah 43:4, matching John's wording exactly; that match is drawn here from the comparison. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible names Isaiah 43:4 and especially Malachi 1:2, and adds Isaiah 49:7, where kings see that God has chosen his servant. The CSB Study Bible's cross-references at 3:9 give Isaiah 43:4. Keener suggests Malachi 1:2. The grade is drawn here: the words are identical, though the phrase is common.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Beale and Carson on Isaiah 43:4: they will know that I have loved you is an Old Testament promise to persecuted Israel, now applied to the Gentile church. He reads the chapter: God disinherits the nations, Israel is his own family, and he will gather its children from every direction. Now the family includes Gentiles who believe.
entries.dissent: The sources name different verses. Beale and the CSB Study Bible point to Isaiah 43:4. Keener suggests Malachi 1:2, where God loves Jacob and hates Esau. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible lists both and adds Isaiah 49:7.

entries.title: Revelation 3:10, the hour of trial
entries.summary: The hour of trial coming on the whole world may echo Daniel 12, the time of trouble at the end when God's people are delivered.
entries.plain: **A storm warning that names the hour tells people to get ready, not to panic.** Daniel 12 speaks of a time of trouble like no other, when God's people whose names are written are rescued. Jesus promises Philadelphia that he will keep it from the hour of trial coming on the whole world. Beale, Heiser and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible hear Daniel here.
entries.same: A coming time of trouble for the whole world, testing, and a promise to God's people. Daniel 12:10 speaks of many tested and purified. John has he hora tou peirasmou, the hour of testing, and peirasai, to test.
entries.differs: The Greek of Daniel in the vault says kairos thlipseos, a time of trouble, not an hour. Beale cites the older Greek translation, which has that hour. Daniel speaks of a nation's distress; John of the whole inhabited world. John adds that the trial falls on those who dwell on the earth.
entries.turn: Daniel 12 speaks of a time of trouble that refines the wise and exposes the wicked. John promises a faithful church that Christ will keep it from a coming hour of trial. That hour will fall on the whole world. Beale reads Daniel's double effect here. He ties the line to 7:14, where saints come out of the great trouble.
entries.not: **Not a quotation of Daniel 12.** Daniel speaks of a time of distress unlike any before. John's words for the hour of trial are his own, with Daniel's picture behind them.
entries.deeper: Beale says 3:10 may well allude to Daniel 12:1, 10 in the older Greek, where that hour is described as the day of tribulation and many are tested and sanctified. He cites Gundry on John 17:15, the only other New Testament use of keep from, where Jesus asks that his followers be kept from the evil one, not taken out of the world. The vault's Greek of Daniel is Theodotion's and reads kairos thlipseos in 12:1, so the hour wording cannot be checked here; that limit is noted here. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible ties the hour of trial to Daniel 12:1-2. Keener notes that Allen Kerkeslager reads the hour as the day of judgment. The grade is possible: the idea is shared, and the key word cannot be confirmed in the vault's Greek.
entries.heiser: Heiser says the verse is not a promise that keeping faith spares you from every hardship. It refers to the ultimate day of the Lord, the final judgment, which God's family will not suffer. He calls it probably an allusion to Daniel 12:1, the time of trouble when those written in the book are delivered.
entries.dissent: The sources disagree on keep from. Beale and the ESV Study Bible read protection through the trial, and Heiser reads protection from the final judgment. The CSB Study Bible thinks removal before the trial more likely and names the pretribulation view. MacArthur reads the hour as the seven years of tribulation still to come, set out in chapters 6-19, the same as Daniel's seventieth week (Daniel 9:24-27) and Jacob's time of distress (Jeremiah 30:7). He takes keep from, whose preposition means out of, as support for the church being taken up before it, the pretribulation rapture. Kerkeslager, as Beale and Keener report, reads the hour as Christ's final coming in judgment.

entries.title: Revelation 3:12, a pillar in the temple of my God
entries.summary: The promise of a lasting place and a name in God's temple recalls Isaiah 56:5, where outsiders receive a place in God's house and a name that will not be cut off.
entries.plain: **A plaque with your name on the wall of the house means you belong there for good.** Isaiah 56 speaks to foreigners and eunuchs who were kept out. God promises them a place in his house. He promises a name that lasts longer than children. Believers at Philadelphia were pushed out of the synagogue. Jesus says they will be pillars in God's temple and never leave.
entries.same: A place in God's house and a lasting name. The Greek of Isaiah 56:5 promises en to oiko mou ... topon onomaston, in my house a named place, and onoma aionion, an everlasting name. John has a pillar in the temple, a name written on it, and a promise never to go out.
entries.differs: Isaiah speaks of a place and a name within God's walls. John makes the person a pillar and writes God's name on it. Isaiah's name is better than sons and daughters; John's names are God's, the city's and Christ's. Beale adds Isaiah 22:23, where Eliakim is fixed like a peg, which some Greek witnesses render as a pillar.
entries.turn: Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible read the promise against exclusion. Those the synagogue shut out have a lasting place in God's temple. Beale stresses lasting presence. The new Jerusalem has no temple building, since God himself fills it (21:22). Unlike Eliakim's family, Christ's people will never be removed.
entries.not: **Not a promise about stone columns.** The pillar stands for a permanent place among God's people, as Wright and Beale note.
entries.deeper: Beale says Isaiah 56:5 is probably evoked together with Isaiah 62:2 and 65:15, given the Jewish attitude to Gentile Christians in Philadelphia. The Greek's named place suits the threefold writing of a name. He also hears Isaiah 22:23: Eliakim's relatives hang on him like a peg, and some Greek witnesses, Vaticanus among them, read I will set up as a pillar. The vault's interlinear has stēso auton archonta, I will establish him as ruler, so that reading cannot be checked here. Keener calls Isaiah 56:5 the primary allusion. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible says the verse recalls Isaiah 56:5 and Deuteronomy 23:1. Beale notes Philadelphia suffered earthquakes more than any of the other cities. The grade is drawn here: a place and a name in God's house point to Isaiah 56.
entries.dissent: The sources differ on the background of the pillar. Beale weighs Isaiah 22:23. Keener notes pillars bore dedication inscriptions and could stand for God's people (Exodus 24:4). MacArthur reads the pillar as a secure, lasting place in God's presence. By his note at 7:15 the temple is God's heavenly throne; he also expects a temple on earth in the thousand years (Ezekiel 40-48), and none in the eternal state, where God himself is the temple. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible contrasts temples felled by the earthquake and perhaps the Jerusalem temple destroyed in 70.

entries.title: Revelation 3:12, the name of the city of my God
entries.summary: Writing the name of God's city on the faithful may recall the last verse of Ezekiel, where the new city's name is The Lord Is There.
entries.plain: **A city that names itself after its founder tells you who it belongs to.** Ezekiel's book ends with a city whose name will be The Lord Is There. Jesus promises to write God's name on the faithful. He will also write the name of God's city, the new Jerusalem. Beale hears Ezekiel: the city's name speaks of God living among his people.
entries.same: The name of the city of the last days, tied to God's presence. The Greek of Ezekiel 48:35 has to onoma tes poleos, the name of the city. John has to onoma tes poleos tou theou mou, adding of my God.
entries.differs: Ezekiel gives the city's name, The Lord Is There. John never states the name; he writes it on people. Ezekiel's city stands around the new temple; John's comes down from heaven. In the vault's Greek, Ezekiel 48:35 even loses the name: it reads the name of the city shall be its name.
entries.turn: The name of the city goes with God's name and Christ's new name, and Beale reads all three as one thing: God's presence with his people. Revelation 21 describes the city in words drawn from Ezekiel's temple vision. Philadelphia had taken a new name from Caesar after an earthquake; the faithful will carry God's.
entries.not: **Not the name Jerusalem written on a forehead.** The sources read the names as marks of belonging and presence.
entries.deeper: Beale says the promise recalls Ezekiel 48:35, where the name of the new Jerusalem is The Lord Is There because his temple and glory dwell in it. He cites the Babylonian Talmud Baba Bathra 75b, which repoints the Hebrew to read the Lord is its name, and notes that Midrash on Psalm 21.2 and Pesikta de Rab Kahana 22.5a give the Messiah and the city God's name. Sefaria's Hebrew reads veshem ha'ir miyom YHWH shammah. The vault's Greek reads the same consonants as its name, not there. That reading of the Greek is drawn here. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible names Jeremiah 33:16 and Ezekiel 48:35, and the CSB Study Bible's cross-references give Ezekiel 48:35. The grade is possible: three sources point to it, and the wording is only the name of the city.
entries.dissent: The sources stress different things. Beale reads the names as God's presence and draws in Ezekiel's temple. The ESV Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible note Philadelphia's earlier renaming for Caesar. MacArthur reads the new Jerusalem as the capital city of heaven, where those who conquer hold citizenship forever, and God's name on them as his character stamped on those who belong to him. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible adds Jeremiah 33:16, where Jerusalem is called The Lord Our Righteousness.

entries.title: Revelation 3:14, the Amen, the faithful and true witness
entries.summary: Jesus' titles to Laodicea draw on Isaiah 65:16, the God of Amen, and Isaiah 43:10, God's witnesses, both tied to the new creation.
entries.plain: **A signature at the bottom of a contract says this is binding.** In Isaiah 65 God is named the God of Amen, the God whose word holds. Right after, he promises a new heaven and earth. Isaiah 43 calls God and his servant witnesses. Jesus takes the name Amen for himself and calls himself a witness who is faithful and true. Beale reads beginning of God's creation as the new creation his rising began.
entries.same: Amen as a name, and the ideas faithful and true. The Hebrew of Isaiah 65:16 has Elohei amen twice, the God of Amen. The Greek translation renders it ton theon ton alethinon, the true God. John has ho Amen, ho martys ho pistos kai alethinos.
entries.differs: The Greek translation turns Isaiah's Amen into true. John keeps the Hebrew word as a name, then adds faithful and true, as if translating it twice. Isaiah speaks of God; John of Jesus. Witness comes from Isaiah 43:10 and Psalm 89, not from Isaiah 65. And Beale ties beginning of creation to Isaiah 65:17, the new heavens and earth.
entries.turn: Beale reads the titles as one claim: Jesus is the faithful witness, and his resurrection is the start of God's new creation. To a lukewarm church whose witness has gone quiet, he presents himself as the witness to follow. He also comes as the true judge who will spit out the unfaithful.
entries.not: **Not a claim that Jesus was the first thing God made.** Beale and the ESV Study Bible read beginning as the start and ruler of creation, not its first product.
entries.deeper: Beale argues that Isaiah 65:15-16 primarily stands behind the Amen title. In the Bible only Isaiah 65:16 and Revelation 3:14 use Amen as a name. The Greek versions of Isaiah 65:16 differ: the Septuagint has the true God, Aquila and Jerome have faithfully, and Symmachus keeps amen. Together, Beale notes, they give almost the same amplified reading as Revelation 3:14. Isaiah 43:10-12 adds witness: Israel, God and his servant are witnesses to a new act of creation, from the beginning. The vault's Septuagint confirms ton alethinon in 65:16; Sefaria's Hebrew has beElohei amen. Beale reads the beginning as the new creation launched by the resurrection, building on firstborn of the dead in 1:5. The grade is drawn here: Amen as a name occurs only in Isaiah 65:16.
entries.dissent: Silberman and Montgomery, as Beale reports, read Amen as a misreading of amon, master workman, in Proverbs 8:30, with beginning from Proverbs 8:22. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible links beginning to the divine titles first and last in Isaiah 41:4, 44:6 and 48:12. MacArthur reads beginning as originator of creation, against a claim, which he thinks was alive at Laodicea, that Christ was created. The CSB Study Bible reads originator of creation, Christ as agent of creation. Keener points to 2 Corinthians 1:20.

aw.n: Revelation 3:14-22, Laodicea, lukewarm and rich
aw.s: To Laodicea the faithful and true witness says the church is neither cold nor hot but lukewarm, and he will spit it out. It thinks itself rich but is poor, blind and naked; he counsels it to buy gold, white clothes and eye salve, and stands at the door and knocks.

entries.title: Revelation 3:17, I am rich
entries.summary: The Laodicean boast of riches echoes Ephraim's boast in Hosea 12:8, a wealthy people blind to its sin.
entries.plain: **A man who brags about his bank balance at his own bankruptcy hearing has missed the point.** In Hosea 12 Ephraim says: I have become rich, I have found wealth, and no one will find sin in all my work. The church at Laodicea says the same kind of thing. Jesus answers that it is poor, blind and naked.
entries.same: The boast of having become rich. The Greek of Hosea 12:8 reads peploutēka, I have become rich; John has plousios eimi kai peploutēka, I am rich and have become rich, the same verb form.
entries.differs: Hosea's Ephraim adds that no sin will be found in him; Laodicea says it needs nothing. John adds a list of what the church really is: poor, blind, naked and more. Hosea speaks of a nation; John of a church. Hosea 12:8 in English is 12:9 in the Hebrew Bible.
entries.turn: Beale reads the echo with its context: Hosea's Israel was a merchant growing rich by fraud and credited its wealth to its idols. Laodicea, he suggests, prospered by going along with the trade guilds and their gods. The boast was a sign of compromise, not of blessing.
entries.not: **Not a rule that wealth is sin.** The sources read the charge as self-sufficiency and compromise that made the church blind to its need.
entries.deeper: Beale says the unique wording and thought shared by Hosea 12:8 and Revelation 3:17 suggest an intentional allusion, not a coincidence, as many think. He points to Hosea 12:7, where Israel is a merchant with false scales, and to Hosea 2:5, 8, where Israel credits its idols for its wealth. He sets Laodicea against Smyrna: poor but rich there, rich but poor here. The vault's Septuagint confirms peploutēka; Sefaria's Hebrew of Hosea 12:9 has asharti, I have become rich. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible cites Hosea 12:8 for the church's pride, the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible says the boast recalls it, and the CSB Study Bible's cross-references give Hosea 12:8 and Zechariah 11:5. The grade is drawn here: the boast and the verb match Hosea.
entries.dissent: The sources weigh Hosea against local history. Beale argues for a deliberate allusion. The ESV Study Bible, Keener and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible stress that Laodicea refused imperial aid after the earthquake of 60 and rebuilt from its own wealth. The CSB Study Bible's cross-references add Zechariah 11:5.
