entries.title: Revelation 3:18, buy from me
entries.summary: Jesus' advice to buy gold, clothes and salve from him may echo Isaiah 55:1, where God invites the penniless to come and buy without money.
entries.plain: **A host who says you can't pay here, just come in, turns a shop into a feast.** In Isaiah 55 God calls the thirsty and the penniless to come and buy food and drink, though they have no cash. Jesus tells the rich church at Laodicea to buy from him gold refined in fire, white clothes and salve for its eyes. What they need, they can get only from him.
entries.same: The call to buy from God what money cannot buy. The Greek of Isaiah 55:1 repeats agorasate, buy. John has agorasai par' emou, to buy from me.
entries.differs: Isaiah calls the poor to buy without money; John tells a church that thinks it is rich to buy. Isaiah offers water, wine and milk. John offers gold, white garments and eye salve, things Laodicea's banks, wool trade and medical school were known for. Isaiah never mentions any of them.
entries.turn: The ESV Study Bible reads it as grace. The Laodiceans had nothing to pay with, so they could only receive, like the poor in Isaiah. Beale reads it as a call to renew their bond with Christ. He alone holds the true riches, clothing and sight.
entries.not: **Not a hint that grace has a price.** The sources read the buying as receiving what Christ freely gives.
entries.deeper: Beale says the church's malaise cannot be cured by the resources of idolatrous society or its own, only by buying true spiritual resources from Christ, with a cross-reference to Isaiah 55:1-3. He reads refined gold as a biblical idiom for a life purified of sin (Job 23:10; Malachi 3:2-3) and the shame of nakedness as the prophets' language for idolatry (Ezekiel 16:36; 23:29). The ESV Study Bible says they could purchase only by grace, as the Lord once invited spiritual paupers to buy without money (Isaiah 55:1-4). The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible also cites Isaiah 55:1-3. The vault's Septuagint confirms agorasate and aneu argyriou, without money. The grade is possible: three sources point to it, and the wording shares only the verb to buy.
entries.dissent: The sources stress the local background in different ways. Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible tie the three items to Laodicea's banking, black wool and Phrygian eye salve. Beale accepts the background but warns against giving each item its own allegory. The CSB Study Bible's cross-references give Zechariah 13:9 for refined gold and Isaiah 20:4 and Ezekiel 23:29 for nakedness.

entries.title: Revelation 3:19, those I love I rebuke and discipline
entries.summary: Jesus' word that he rebukes and disciplines those he loves takes up Proverbs 3:11-12, the father's discipline of the son he loves.
entries.plain: **A coach who stays after practice to correct you is showing he still believes in you.** Proverbs 3 tells a son not to resent the Lord's correction. A father corrects the son he cares for, and so does God. Jesus tells the lukewarm church that his sharp words are of the same kind. He rebukes and disciplines those he loves. So they should be zealous and repent.
entries.same: Love that shows itself in correction. The Greek of Proverbs 3:11 has elenchomenos, being rebuked, and 3:12 has paideuei, he disciplines. John has elencho kai paideuo, I rebuke and discipline, with those I love.
entries.differs: Proverbs speaks of the Lord and a son; John's speaker is Jesus. Proverbs uses agapa for love; John uses philo. John pulls rebuke from 3:11 and discipline from 3:12 into one line. And he adds the command: be zealous and repent.
entries.turn: Beale reads the line as a sign that the harsh words of verses 15-18 are not yet rejection but a father's correction. The church still has time. Yet the threat of 3:16 stands if they will not repent. Hebrews 12:5-6 quotes the same proverb for a suffering church.
entries.not: **Not a claim that every hardship is punishment.** The proverb, and this letter, speak of correction meant to bring repentance.
entries.deeper: Beale reads the reproof as a mark of love for children, not judicial wrath, citing Proverbs 3:12 and Psalms of Solomon 10:1-3 and 14:1. In the vault's Septuagint, Proverbs 3:11 reads mede eklyou hyp' autou elenchomenos and 3:12 hon gar agapa kyrios paideuei. That John's two verbs come from the two lines of the proverb is drawn here from the comparison. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the ESV Study Bible, the CSB Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible all name Proverbs 3:11-12 or 3:12, the last two adding Hebrews 12. Keener compares the many prophetic rebukes of Israel. The grade is drawn here: the pairing of love and discipline is the proverb's.
entries.dissent: The sources agree on Proverbs 3. Keener points instead to the general pattern of prophetic rebukes of Israel. The ESV Study Bible pictures a loving father; Beale, a husband renewing a bond, which he develops in verse 20.

entries.title: Revelation 3:20, I stand at the door and knock
entries.summary: Jesus knocking at the door echoes the Song of Songs, where the beloved knocks and asks to be let in.
entries.plain: **A husband knocking softly on the bedroom door after a quarrel is asking to be let back in.** In the Song of Songs the beloved knocks at night and calls: open to me. Jesus tells the church at Laodicea that he stands at the door and knocks. Whoever hears and opens will have him as a guest at their table. Beale reads it as a lover asking for the bond to be renewed.
entries.same: A voice, a knock at the door and a call to open. The Greek of the Song 5:2 reads phone adelphidou mou krouei epi ten thyran; anoixon moi, the voice of my beloved knocks on the door, open to me. John has krouo, epi ten thyran, phones mou and anoixe.
entries.differs: In the Song the woman hears and hesitates. In John the one knocking speaks, and the response is left open: if anyone hears. The Song ends with longing; John promises a meal together. The beloved becomes Jesus, and the woman becomes the church.
entries.turn: Beale reads it as an invitation to renew a relationship already begun, not a first call to faith. Jewish teachers read open to me in the Song as God's call to Israel to repent. The meal may look toward the Lord's Supper and the messianic banquet.
entries.not: **Not a quotation of the Song.** The Song's lover knocks and asks to be let in. John gives the knock to Christ at the door of a church, in his own words.
entries.deeper: Beale says the invitation is probably dependent on Song of Songs 5:2, setting the two Greek texts side by side. He notes that Jewish commentators read open to me in the Song as a call for Israel's repentance within a covenant (Midrash Rabbah on Exodus 33.3 and on the Song 5.2). He also allows a model in Luke 12:36-37, where servants open to the returning master who then serves them. The vault's Septuagint confirms the wording. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible hears either a lover coming back (Song 5:2) or a master (Luke 12:36). The grade is drawn here: knock, door, voice and open together point to the Song.
entries.dissent: The sources weigh the Song against the gospels. Beale and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible give the Song first and Luke second. The ESV Study Bible reads the master of the house returning (Luke 12:35-36; James 5:9) and does not name the Song. Beale and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible read the call as addressed to the complacent church. MacArthur sets aside the common reading of Christ knocking at a person's heart. He reads a church that carried Christ's name with no true believer in it: the letter is the knock, and Christ would come in if one member turned to him in saving faith. Keener compares John 10:1-4 and Matthew 24:33.

entries.title: Revelation 4:1, an open door, a trumpet voice, come up here
entries.summary: John's call into heaven borrows the opened heavens of Ezekiel 1 and the scene at Sinai, where a trumpet sounded and Moses was called up the mountain.
entries.plain: **A new player who is waved into the coaches' room knows the door opened for a reason.** John sees an open door in heaven. The voice he heard in chapter 1, loud as a trumpet, tells him to come up. Ezekiel saw the heavens opened before he saw God's throne. At Sinai a trumpet blast came before God spoke, and God called Moses up the mountain. John is called up in the same way.
entries.same: Three things line up. Heaven opens before a vision, as in Ezekiel 1:1, where the Greek says the heavens were opened. A voice sounds like a trumpet, as the trumpet rang out at Sinai (Exodus 19:16). And there is a call to go up: God summoned Moses to the peak, and he climbed (anebe). John hears anaba hode, come up here.
entries.differs: Ezekiel saw the whole sky opened; John sees one door. At Sinai a real trumpet sounded. Here it is a voice that sounds like one, the voice of 1:10. Moses climbed a mountain; John is taken up in the Spirit. Beale adds that one Greek word is in the wrong case after voice, as in 1:10, and he reads the slip as a pointer back to Exodus 19.
entries.turn: John is cast as a prophet called into God's council, like Moses at Sinai and Ezekiel by the river. What he sees there carries God's authority, and he must report it to the churches. Beale and Wright both say the call is for John alone, to let him see the plan behind events.
entries.not: **Not a trumpet blast for the rapture.** The verse speaks of a voice like a trumpet. Heiser, Beale and Wright reject reading the church's removal from the earth into the call to come up, and so does MacArthur, who reads chapters 4 to 22 as events still to come.
entries.deeper: Beale hears echoes of Ezekiel's visions and of Exodus 19 in the second half of 4:1. The participle lalouses (speaking) is genitive where grammar wants the accusative, and he calls the irregularity an intended pointer to Exodus 19:16-19, as at 1:10; later scribes corrected it. Legon, masculine where a feminine is expected, he takes as a deliberate echo of the Greek Old Testament's idiom. Keener says come up here may allude to God calling Moses up the mountain (Exodus 19:24; 24:12; 34:2) and that the opened heavens follow the pattern of Ezekiel 1:1; the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible makes both links and adds Exodus 24:9-12, the first throne vision in Scripture. In the vault's Septuagint, Ezekiel 1:1 has the heavens opened (enoichthesan); Revelation has a door opened (thyra eneogmene). The CSB Study Bible's cross-references at 4:1 list Exodus 19:19 and 20:18. The grade is drawn here by Beale's definitions: each piece traces to a scene, but no single text gives them all.
entries.heiser: Heiser says plainly that the verse does not say a trumpet sounded. It is a voice as loud as a trumpet, so it has no link to rapture passages. Reading Aune, he ties the trumpet to the Sinai theophany in Exodus 19:16 and 20:18, and adds Aune's note that Greek texts compared Athena's voice to a trumpet and called thunder the trumpet of Zeus. His point is that God is speaking: the risen Christ speaks with God's authority, as God spoke to Moses after the trumpet from the cloud.
entries.dissent: Many futurist readers, Beale reports, take come up here and the phrase after this as a sign that the church leaves the earth before the judgments. Beale, Wright and Heiser reject that reading. MacArthur, a futurist, rejects it too: the command is for John alone, taken up to heaven for a time in the Spirit. He finds the church's place in heaven elsewhere. He reads the elders of 4:4 as the church, already crowned before the judgments start, and he takes 3:10 as support for the church being taken out before the seven-year tribulation. The CSB Study Bible leaves open whether John was taken up into heaven or stayed in the Spirit on Patmos.

entries.title: Revelation 4:1, what must take place after this
entries.summary: The voice promises to show John what must take place after this, the Daniel 2 phrase that already framed the book at 1:1 and 1:19.
entries.plain: **A tour guide who repeats the same line at every new stop is telling you the tour follows one plan.** The voice says it will show John what must happen after this. The words come from Daniel 2, where God shows a king the empires to come and the kingdom that will replace them. John used the same words in 1:1 and 1:19. Now they open the long middle of the book.
entries.same: The Greek matches Daniel 2:29 and 2:45 closely: ha dei genesthai meta tauta, what must happen after these things. In both, God shows (deixo) what he has decided will happen.
entries.differs: In Daniel the phrase sits inside a dream about kingdoms. John uses it as a heading for all the visions that follow. Beale takes after this as Daniel's last days in other words, so the visions cover the whole end time, begun but not yet finished. He finds the wording closest to the Greek of Daniel 2:29 and 2:45, perhaps blended with the other Daniel 2 phrases.
entries.turn: John tells suffering churches that what follows is God's decree, not chance. Beale says the allusion means God knows events, has decided them and guides them. The phrase also marks the hinges of the book: 1:1, 1:19, 4:1 and 22:6.
entries.not: **Not Daniel's dream carried over whole.** John takes Daniel's words for what must happen after this, but not the statue or its kingdoms. In his hands the phrase becomes a heading over the visions that follow.
entries.deeper: Beale calls this a clear reference to Daniel 2:28-29, used as in 1:1 and 1:19: deixo soi ha dei genesthai meta tauta. In the vault's Greek of Daniel (the version called Theodotion), 2:29 and 2:45 read ha dei genesthai meta tauta. Dei (must) expresses divine determination. Beale argues that meta tauta is close in sense to Daniel's ep' eschaton ton hemeron (in the last days) and to the New Testament's phrases for the last days already begun, so the visions of 4:2-22:5 are eschatological in scope, realized and unrealized. He rejects the view that meta tauta opens verse 2, given the parallels at 1:10 and 22:6. The CSB Study Bible also ties the phrase to 1:19 and to the body of the book. The grade is Beale's.
entries.dissent: Most futurist commentators, Beale reports, read 4:1 as the start of events still future. Johnson, following Keil on Daniel, argues the visions concern a period after the churches of the letters. MacArthur reads 1:19 as the outline of the whole book, so 4:1 opens its third part: chapters 4 to 22 tell of events that follow the church age. Beale holds that after this only marks the next vision, and that the visions mix past, present and future. He answers that Daniel's own last days included Nebuchadnezzar's present reign, and that the visions cover the last days already begun. The ESV Study Bible describes chapters 4 and 5 as events that come after the struggles of the first-century churches.

entries.title: Revelation 4:2-11, the whole scene modeled on Daniel 7
entries.summary: Beale finds fourteen features of Daniel 7's heavenly court in Revelation 4 and 5, in nearly the same order, with Ezekiel 1 and Isaiah 6 woven in.
entries.plain: **A film can follow an old classic scene by scene while changing every costume.** Beale lines up chapters 4 and 5 with Daniel 7. Both have thrones set in heaven, God seated, fire, crowds of servants, books opened, a figure who comes to receive a kingdom, and saints who reign. The order is nearly the same. Ezekiel 1 and Isaiah 6 supply many of the details along the way.
entries.same: A sequence. Thrones are set in heaven, God sits, his look is described, and fire comes before him. Servants stand around him, books are opened, and a figure comes near to receive power over all peoples. The seer is troubled, an attendant explains, the saints receive the kingdom, and God's endless rule is praised. Both visions also have a sea.
entries.differs: The order shifts in places. In Daniel the books open before the son of man arrives; in Revelation the Lamb comes first. John's servants around the throne are far more detailed than Daniel's. Many details come from other scenes: the creatures and the jewels from Ezekiel 1, the six wings and the song from Isaiah 6. Beale says these were drawn in because they are so like Daniel 7.
entries.turn: Daniel 7 is a court. It judges the beasts and gives the kingdom to the son of man and to the saints. By building on it, John shows the churches this court in session. Beale reads chapters 4 and 5 as the start of that fulfillment: the kingdom handed over through the Lamb's death and rising.
entries.not: **Not a claim that every line comes from Daniel.** Beale himself says that in 4:1 to 5:1 Ezekiel 1 and 2 supply more allusions than Daniel does. His case rests on the order of the whole scene, read as one vision.
entries.deeper: Beale argues that chapters 4 and 5 form one structure, closer to Daniel 7:9ff. than to any other Old Testament vision. His fourteen elements run from the opening vision wording (Daniel 7:9, with 7:2, 6-7; Revelation 4:1), thrones set (7:9a; 4:2a, 4a), God's appearance (7:9c; 4:3) and fire (7:9d-10a; 4:5), through books opened (7:10; 5:2-5, 9), the figure who approaches for authority (7:13-14; 5:5-7) and all peoples, nations and tongues (7:14; 5:9), to the seer's distress and counsel (7:15-16; 5:4-5), the saints' reign (7:18, 22, 27; 5:10) and God's eternal reign (7:27; 5:13-14). He counts about 23 allusions to Daniel in the two chapters, half from Daniel 7. Ezekiel 1-2 lacks five of the elements and its outline fades after 5:1, so Beale calls Daniel 7 the magnet that drew in Ezekiel 1, Isaiah 6 and Exodus 19. In his list of uses this is a literary prototype. The grade is his: the Daniel framework is probable. Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible stress Isaiah 6 and Ezekiel 1; Wright adds Micaiah's council in 1 Kings 22.
entries.heiser: Heiser calls Revelation 4 and 5 a divine council scene that uses the Old Testament covenant lawsuit form, and says scholars largely agree. He reads Beale's fourteen parallels from Beale and Carson's commentary. He says they make it plain that Daniel 7 is a council courtroom and that John is building on it. John then fills the throne room with pieces of Ezekiel 1 and Isaiah 6. All three are council scenes, and each stresses God's rule as judge.
entries.dissent: Not everyone accepts Daniel 7 as the model. Ruiz, Beale reports in his introduction, is unconvinced, above all by the claim that Daniel 7, not Ezekiel, is the pattern for chapters 4 and 5; Beale replies that Ruiz does not weigh the verbal allusions to Daniel or the outlines of Daniel 7, Ezekiel 1 and Isaiah 6 closely enough. Goulder finds broad portions of Ezekiel, in Ezekiel's order, behind Revelation 4, 5 and later sections. Moyise concludes that Ezekiel provides more of the model than Daniel. Many commentators, Beale notes, take Ezekiel as the pattern for chapter 4 or for 4:1-5:1, among them Caird and Sweet. Prigent hears the synagogue morning liturgy; Aune, the ceremony of the Roman imperial court. MacArthur reads chapters 4 and 5 as worship in heaven before the judgments that follow the church age.

entries.title: Revelation 4:2, a throne in heaven with one seated on it
entries.summary: John sees God enthroned in heaven, the scene the prophets saw before him in Ezekiel 1, Isaiah 6 and Daniel 7.
entries.plain: **When someone describes a palace hall, people who have been there fill in the rest.** Caught up in the Spirit, John sees a throne set in heaven and someone sitting on it. The prophets had seen this before. Isaiah saw the Lord seated high in the temple. Ezekiel saw a throne above the creatures with a figure like a man on it. Daniel saw thrones set out and an ancient figure take his place.
entries.same: A throne in heaven and God seated on it. Isaiah 6:1 in Greek has the Lord sitting (kathemenon) on a throne (thronou). Ezekiel 1:26 has the likeness of a throne with a figure above it. Daniel 7:9 has thrones set (etethesan) and the Ancient of Days seated. John has a throne set (ekeito) and one seated (kathemenos).
entries.differs: John names no one. He says only that someone sat on the throne, and he describes him by light and stone, not by shape. Ezekiel saw the form of a man; Daniel saw white clothing and white hair. Beale suggests that John's verb, was set, may echo Daniel's thrones being set in place.
entries.turn: The throne is the center of the vision: Beale counts it seventeen times in chapters 4 and 5. Everything in heaven is placed around it, and the judgments that follow come from it. For churches under pressure, the first sight in heaven is that God still rules.
entries.not: **Not a new picture of heaven.** The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible notes that God is enthroned in the earlier visions, and that John, like Ezekiel, gets there by the Spirit, not by a dangerous climb.
entries.deeper: Beale says the Old Testament theophanies form the background, with Ezekiel 1 uppermost, since the phrases that follow refer to it clearly. Because Daniel 7 and Ezekiel 1 share the same order, the seated figure could echo either, but the plural thrones of 4:4 and the Danielic frame favor linking ekeito with Daniel 7:9a. He also hears Isaiah 6:1 and 1 Kings 22:19 in 4:2b, 8 and 9: like those prophets, John is summoned into the Lord's council. Keener lists Isaiah 6, Ezekiel 1, Exodus 24:9-11, 1 Kings 22:19 and Daniel 7:9-10 as the models for Jewish throne visions and contrasts John's restraint with later elaborations. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible's cross-references give the same set. In the Spirit recalls Ezekiel being lifted by the Spirit (Keener cites Ezekiel 11:1, 24; the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, Ezekiel 2:2 and 3:12). The grade is drawn here: the scene is unmistakable, but no single text supplies the wording.
entries.heiser: Heiser says the throne and the one seated on it plainly match Daniel 7, Isaiah 6, Ezekiel 1 and 1 Kings 22. Reading Davis, he notes that all the major council scenes seat the head of the council on a throne, sometimes with members seated too, as Daniel 7's plural thrones show. Isaiah and Ezekiel set the throne inside the temple, he adds, because the temple is where God lives and rules.
entries.dissent: Aune, as Beale reports, sees a parody of Roman imperial court ceremony in the scene, and Keener also allows a contrast with the imperial court. Beale grants some force to that background but ranks it well behind the Old Testament and Jewish sources.

entries.title: Revelation 4:3, jasper and carnelian
entries.summary: John describes the one on the throne only by the gleam of jasper and carnelian, stones that the Greek of Ezekiel 28 and Exodus 28 lists together with emerald.
entries.plain: **A friend who can only say a sunset looked like fire and gold is telling you words ran out.** John does not describe God's face or form. He says the one on the throne looked like jasper and carnelian, two precious stones. Ezekiel's throne gleamed like a precious stone too. Lists with the same stones appear in Ezekiel 28 and in the high priest's breastplate in Exodus 28.
entries.same: Precious stones that carry God's glory. In the Greek, Ezekiel 28:13 names sardion (carnelian), smaragdos (emerald) and iaspis (jasper) in one list, the three stones of 4:3. In the Greek of Exodus 28:17-18 the same three stand in the first two rows of the breastplate.
entries.differs: Ezekiel's throne looked like sapphire, and the figure on it like a man. John swaps in jasper and carnelian and gives no human shape. He leaves the sapphire out here and saves it for the city wall in 21:19. English Bibles often name these stones differently, since the old names are hard to match with modern gems.
entries.turn: The stones do not stand for separate things, Beale and the ESV Study Bible agree. Together they show the glory around God. They also point ahead: jasper heads the stones of the new city in chapter 21, where God's glory fills everything. The throne room already shines with what the new creation will be.
entries.not: **Not a code in which each stone means something.** Beale and the ESV Study Bible both say the stones work together to show God's splendor, not one meaning apiece.
entries.deeper: Beale says references from Ezekiel 1:26, 28, from the Greek of Ezekiel 9:2 and 10:1, and from Ezekiel 28:13 have been combined, with reflections of Exodus 24:10 and especially Exodus 28:17-20. All are theophany or glory texts that mention a sapphire, and Ezekiel 28 and Exodus 28 stand out because all three of John's stones occur in them. The vault's Septuagint bears this out: Ezekiel 28:13 has sardion, smaragdon and iaspin; Exodus 28:17-18 has sardion, smaragdos and iaspis. Jasper ties 4:3 to 21:11, where the city has God's glory, shining like jasper. Walton notes that Ezekiel's sapphire is better taken as lapis lazuli, and that Mesopotamian texts paved the levels of heaven with stones, the lower heaven with jasper. Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible contrast John's restraint with the lavish thrones of other apocalypses. The grade is drawn here: the stones trace to these lists, but the wording is brief.
entries.heiser: Reading Aune, Heiser notes that Jewish throne scenes seldom use precious stones but Ezekiel 1 does, and that jasper, carnelian and crystal return in the new Jerusalem. He reads the stones as language for the place where God lives, and links jasper to Eden's geography in Genesis 2:12. He adds his own point from The Unseen Realm: the stones of Ezekiel 28 are not the high priest's breastplate, because the list does not match it; they describe God's dwelling, Eden, the garden mountain of God.
entries.dissent: Beale counts Exodus 28, the high priest's breastplate, among the strongest influences, with Ezekiel 28, since both lists hold all three stones. Heiser denies that Ezekiel 28's stones come from the breastplate and reads them, and John's, as the furnishings of God's home. Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible read the plain description mainly as a contrast with the emperor's pomp.

entries.title: Revelation 4:3, a rainbow around the throne
entries.summary: The rainbow around the throne comes from Ezekiel's vision of God's glory and recalls the bow God set in the clouds after the flood.
entries.plain: **A peace sign painted on a courthouse wall would tell everyone that mercy is part of the verdict.** Around God's throne John sees a rainbow that glows like an emerald. Ezekiel saw the brightness around God's throne shine like a rainbow after rain. After the flood God set his bow in the clouds as a promise never to destroy the earth with water again. Both pictures stand behind John's.
entries.same: A bow of light around the enthroned God. Ezekiel 1:28 compares the brightness around God to the bow seen in a cloud, and calls the sight the likeness of the Lord's glory. Genesis 9:13 has God's bow in the cloud as the sign of his covenant with the earth.
entries.differs: The Greek of Ezekiel 1:28 and Genesis 9:13 calls the bow toxon, the word for an archer's bow. John uses iris, a different word for a rainbow. Ezekiel's bow is a comparison for brightness; John sees an actual rainbow ringing the throne. And he adds a color: it looks like emerald.
entries.turn: Beale reads the rainbow as a sign that the coming judgments will be tempered with mercy, as the covenant with Noah promised. God stays merciful to his own people even while he judges. Wright calls it a mix of mercy, awe and beauty. Before any seal is broken, the throne already carries a promise.
entries.not: **Not proof that the flood story is the only source.** Most sources start from Ezekiel 1:28. The Genesis covenant is the added note that Beale, Wright, the CSB Study Bible and Heiser hear in it.
entries.deeper: Beale says the rainbow, as probably in Ezekiel 1:28, implies judgment tempered by mercy in view of the Noahic covenant; above all it evokes God's glory, since Ezekiel equates it with the appearance of the glory of the Lord, and Jewish writings cite Ezekiel 1:28 for it (Midrash on Psalms 89.18; Numbers Rabbah 14.3; Hagigah 16a). He also reads it as the first sign of new creation after the flood. In the vault's Septuagint, Ezekiel 1:28 has toxou and Genesis 9:13 to toxon; Revelation 4:3 has iris. Some manuscripts read hiereis (priests) for iris, an error of hearing. Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible cite Ezekiel 1:26, 28; the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible and the CSB Study Bible add Genesis 9. The grade is drawn here: the setting is plainly Ezekiel's, but the word differs.
entries.heiser: Heiser, after Aune, says the rainbow alludes to the brightness around the throne in Ezekiel 1:27-28, and notes that the Greek word for the bow there, toxon, is not John's word. He adds that readers will also think of the bow after the flood in Genesis 9:13. With Beale and Bauckham he reads it as a covenant sign: in a court that decides the fate of empires, it promises that God will not destroy all flesh and that a remnant will survive.
entries.dissent: The sources weigh the two backgrounds differently. Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible cite only Ezekiel. The CSB Study Bible reads the rainbow chiefly as the flood covenant, with judgment now coming by other means. Beale holds both, with glory first and mercy second.

entries.title: Revelation 4:4, twenty-four elders on thrones
entries.summary: The elders around the throne draw on Isaiah 24:23, where God reigns in glory before his elders, on the elders who saw God at Sinai, and on the twenty-four priestly orders of 1 Chronicles 24.
entries.plain: **A seating chart at a royal banquet tells the guests who sits nearest the king.** Around God's throne John sees twenty-four elders on thrones, dressed in white with gold crowns. Isaiah foresaw the Lord reigning on Zion with his glory shown before his elders. At Sinai, Israel's elders went up and saw God. King David divided the priests into twenty-four orders. The sources hear all three.
entries.same: Elders in God's presence who see his glory. Isaiah 24:23 in Greek has the Lord glorified before the elders (presbyteron), John's word (presbyterous). In Exodus 24:9-10 seventy elders of Israel saw God and the pavement under his feet. In 1 Chronicles 24 the priests serve in twenty-four divisions.
entries.differs: Isaiah and Exodus do not number the elders twenty-four, and they give them no thrones, white robes or crowns. The number comes from elsewhere: Keener says almost certainly from the priests' orders, Beale says perhaps. John adds thrones, which Daniel 7:9 also places around God. No source finds a single text that gives all of it.
entries.turn: Beale reads the elders as heavenly figures who stand for all God's people, Israel and the church, twelve and twelve. The churches that endure were promised white robes and crowns (2:10; 3:4-5, 21). Here those gifts are already given in heaven. Readers learn that their reward is real and that God's people already share his rule.
entries.not: **Not a settled identification.** The sources do not agree whether the elders are angels, glorified believers, or angels who stand for believers. Each reading has texts in its favor.
entries.deeper: Beale lists six identifications: stars, angels, Old Testament saints, angels representing all saints, patriarchs and apostles, and the twenty-four books of the Old Testament. He concludes they are probably angels identified with the twelve tribes and twelve apostles. He finds it likely that Isaiah 24:23 and Exodus 24:9-10 partly stand behind 4:4: in both, elders witness God's glory, and Jewish tradition read Isaiah's elders as Israel's (Targum of Isaiah 24:23). He calls the link to Exodus 24 obvious, since those elders saw God above a sapphire pavement. The number may follow David's twenty-four priestly orders, gatekeepers and singers (1 Chronicles 24:3-19; 25:6-31), which would explain the harps and incense of 5:8. Keener says the number almost certainly alludes to the priestly orders; the NIV Cultural Backgrounds, NIV Biblical Theology and ESV Study Bibles mention them beside the tribes and apostles. The Greek of Isaiah 24:23 has presbyteron. The grade is drawn here: several texts are named, none decisive.
entries.heiser: Reading Aune, Heiser says two Old Testament passages put a group of elders before Yahweh: Isaiah 24:23 and Exodus 24:9-10. He takes Isaiah's elders as members of the heavenly council, following Timothy Willis, and those of Exodus as humans. He notes that council members sit on thrones in Daniel 7:9, and mentions the suggestion that the number comes from the priestly courses of 1 Chronicles 23-24. His answer is that council members, glorified believers and star imagery are all in play at once.
entries.dissent: Beale holds that in Revelation only saints wear crowns and white robes or sit on thrones, and reads the elders as angels who represent the saints. Heiser counters that Daniel 7's council members sit on thrones and that the martyrs of 6:9-11 are distinct from the elders. He reads Isaiah 24:23 of heavenly elders, while Fekkes, as Beale reports, argues against that reading. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible leans to an angelic order, the CSB Study Bible to twelve tribes and twelve apostles, and Keener to the priestly orders. MacArthur reads the elders as the church, already crowned and glorified in heaven; Israel and those saved during the tribulation, he holds, are not yet raised at this point in the story.

entries.title: Revelation 4:5, lightning, rumbling and thunder
entries.summary: The storm that pours from the throne repeats the lightning and thunder of Sinai and the lightning that flashed from the fire among Ezekiel's creatures.
entries.plain: **A thunderclap in a film can tell you the hero has arrived before you see him.** Lightning, rumbling and thunder burst out of the throne. At Sinai the same storm broke over the mountain when God came down to give the law. In Ezekiel's vision lightning flashed out of the fire among the living creatures. John uses the storm to say that the God of Sinai is here.
entries.same: The storm signs of God's presence. Exodus 19:16 in Greek has voices (phonai) and lightnings (astrapai) on Sinai. Ezekiel 1:13 has lamps of fire, with lightning going out (exeporeueto) from the fire. Revelation 4:5 has lightnings, voices and thunders going out (ekporeuontai) from the throne.
entries.differs: At Sinai the storm covers a mountain; here it comes from the throne itself. Beale says the wording leans on the Greek of Ezekiel 1:13, with Sinai in second place, while most study Bibles name Sinai first. John also gives the list a future. It returns at 8:5, 11:19 and 16:18, growing each time, at the close of each series of judgments.
entries.turn: Since the same storm closes each round of judgments, Beale says 4:5 names God as their source. The churches learn that the coming troubles are not chaos. They come from the throne they have just seen, and God has not forgotten those who persecute them.
entries.not: **Not a weather report from heaven.** In Revelation the storm marks God's presence and his coming judgment, as the CSB Study Bible notes, not the climate of heaven.
entries.deeper: Beale says the order of Daniel 7:9 and Ezekiel 1:26ff. lies behind 4:5, since both put fire after the throne, and that the wording of 4:5a is shaped by the fiery theophany of Ezekiel 1:13 in Greek, with Exodus 19:16 in second place. In the vault's Septuagint, Ezekiel 1:13 reads ek tou pyros exeporeueto hos astrape, lightning going out from the fire, and Exodus 19:16 has phonai kai astrapai. The phrase recurs almost word for word at 8:5, 11:19 and 16:18, at the end of each series of seven, with additions; Beale credits the observation to Bauckham. Keener says the effects rehearse Sinai (Exodus 19:16; compare Ezekiel 1:4, 13). The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the ESV Study Bible, the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible and the CSB Study Bible cite Exodus 19:16 or 20:18. The grade is drawn here: the scene is plain, but the wording is shared by several texts.
entries.heiser: Heiser says the lightning and thunder take readers back to the Sinai theophany, as the trumpet did. Reading Aune, he notes that storm lists occur four times in Revelation (4:5; 8:5; 11:19; 16:18-21) and that they grew out of Exodus 19:16-18, which names thunder, lightning, a thick cloud, a trumpet and an earthquake. Fire, he adds, is a stock sign of God's presence.
entries.dissent: Beale gives the wording to Ezekiel 1:13 and gives Sinai a secondary place. Keener, the study Bibles and Heiser put Sinai first. Both scenes have lightning; the sources differ on which John had uppermost.

entries.title: Revelation 4:5, seven torches of fire, the seven spirits
entries.summary: The seven torches burning before the throne are Zechariah's seven lamps, which the prophet ties to God's Spirit, merged with the torches among Ezekiel's creatures.
entries.plain: **A logo printed on every page of a report soon tells readers whose report it is.** In front of the throne John sees seven torches of fire, and he calls them God's seven spirits. Zechariah saw a gold lampstand with seven lamps, and the angel explained them with a word about God's Spirit. Ezekiel saw something like torches moving among the creatures. John joins the two pictures.
entries.same: Seven lights and God's Spirit. Zechariah 4:2 has seven lamps (hepta lychnoi) on the lampstand, and 4:6 explains them by a word about God's Spirit. Ezekiel 1:13 in Greek has torches (lampadon) of fire among the creatures; John has seven torches (lampades) of fire.
entries.differs: Zechariah's word for lamp is lychnos; John uses lampas, a torch, the word of Ezekiel 1:13. Zechariah has one lampstand; here there is none, only seven torches burning before the throne. Zechariah's angel speaks of the Spirit; John names the torches the seven spirits outright, as in 1:4.
entries.turn: The torches before the throne show God's Spirit ready to act. In 5:6 the same seven spirits become the Lamb's eyes, sent out across the whole world. Beale reads the picture through Zechariah: the Spirit by whom God's work gets done against every obstacle.
entries.not: **Not a lampstand standing for a church.** In 1:20 the lampstands are the churches. Here there are torches, not lampstands, and John names them the spirits of God.
entries.deeper: Beale says the second half of 4:5 is clearly patterned after Zechariah 4:2-3, 10, where seven lamps are seen and then explained, which ties the lamps to the Spirit of Yahweh (4:6). Part of the wording of Ezekiel 1:13 has merged with it: the reference to Ezekiel's lamps drew in Zechariah's. The meaning is developed in 5:6. He also sees the lamps of the temple lampstand, part of the temple setting of the two chapters. The vault's Septuagint has lychnoi in Zechariah 4:2 and lampadon in Ezekiel 1:13; Revelation 4:5 has lampades pyros kaiomenai, and the verb kaio (burn) also describes Ezekiel's burning coals. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible calls the lamps an allusion to Zechariah 4:2; the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible says they allude to Ezekiel 1:13. The grade is drawn here from Beale's clearly patterned.
entries.heiser: Reading Aune, Heiser notes that early Judaism often held angels to be made of fire, so the seven torches may be seven angelic beings. Some read them as the temple lampstand, he says, but that leads back to Zechariah 4 anyway, where the Lord's seven eyes prove to be heavenly beings.
entries.dissent: The study Bibles differ on the source. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible names Zechariah 4:2 and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible names Ezekiel 1:13; Beale holds that both are merged. On the meaning, Beale reads the seven spirits as the Holy Spirit, while Aune, as Heiser reads him, allows seven angels.

entries.title: Revelation 4:6, a sea of glass like crystal
entries.summary: The glassy sea before the throne takes the crystal expanse of Ezekiel 1:22 and may recall the great bronze sea of Solomon's temple.
entries.plain: **A polished marble floor can make a hall look as if it stands on still water.** Before the throne John sees a glassy sea, as clear as crystal. Ezekiel saw an expanse above the creatures that gleamed like ice. Solomon's temple had a huge bronze basin called the sea. At Sinai the elders saw something like clear blue stone under God's feet. The sources hear one or more of these.
entries.same: Crystal under or before the throne. In the Greek of Ezekiel 1:22 the expanse over the creatures is like crystal (krystallou); John's sea is like crystal (krystallo). The Hebrew calls it a raqia, a firmament, gleaming like ice (qerach).
entries.differs: Ezekiel saw a firmament, not a sea. John turns the crystal floor into a sea of glass and places it before the throne. Solomon's sea was bronze, and the pavement at Sinai was sapphire. So no one text gives John's picture. He joins a crystal floor to the word sea.
entries.turn: The sea before the throne is calm. Beale suggests John hints that the sea, often a picture of chaos and the place the beasts rise from in Daniel 7, has been stilled by God's rule. At 15:2 the victors stand beside the same sea, and in 21:1 the sea is gone.
entries.not: **Not a sea taken from Ezekiel.** Ezekiel saw a crystal expanse, not water. No source reads John's sea as an ocean. MacArthur, like Beale and Keener, ties it to Ezekiel's crystal, and he takes it as the pavement before the throne.
entries.deeper: Beale weighs three backgrounds he finds compatible: the laver of Solomon's temple, God's holy separateness, and the heavenly counterpart of the Red Sea, supported by 15:2-4 and by the Mekilta on Exodus 14:16, where the sea became like glass. But he calls Ezekiel 1:22 the most prominent, confirmed by the wording and the Ezekiel allusions around it. He adds Caird's view that the sea carries a nuance of cosmic evil, which the Daniel 7 frame supports. Keener says the sea alludes to Solomon's sea (1 Kings 7:23; 2 Chronicles 4:2, 6) and the crystal firmament to Ezekiel 1:22; the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible names the bronze sea as the most direct source. The ESV Study Bible cites Exodus 24:10 and Ezekiel 1:22; the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible adds the waters divided in Genesis 1:7. Walton reads Ezekiel's expanse against Mesopotamian pictures of stone platforms in the heavens. The grade is drawn here: the crystal is Ezekiel's, the sea is not.
entries.heiser: Heiser reports Bruce Malina's reading without fully adopting it: God's throne sits above the firmament, the solid dome of Genesis 1:6, Job 37:18 and Psalm 29:10, and storms come from the throne, so the sea of glass before and under the throne is best taken as the firmament. Heiser says Malina never ties his astral reading to the Old Testament, a real weakness, but he treats the data as worth weighing.
entries.dissent: The sources pick different primary backgrounds. Beale and Keener give the crystal to Ezekiel 1:22; Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible give the sea to Solomon's bronze basin; the ESV Study Bible points to the sapphire pavement of Exodus 24:10; Malina, as Heiser reports, reads it as the firmament. Beale alone presses the Red Sea and the sea as a symbol of evil. MacArthur reads a crystal pavement, the floor of God's throne, after Exodus 24:10 and Ezekiel 1:22; he says heaven has no sea.

entries.title: Revelation 4:6-8, four living creatures full of eyes
entries.summary: The four creatures take the faces and eyes of Ezekiel's cherubim and the six wings of Isaiah's seraphim, blended into one new picture.
entries.plain: **A portrait painter can give one face the eyes of one parent and the smile of the other.** Around the throne John sees four living creatures, like a lion, an ox, a man and an eagle, covered with eyes and each with six wings. Ezekiel saw four creatures with those four faces and wheels covered with eyes. Isaiah saw beings with six wings above the Lord's throne. John blends the two.
entries.same: The name and the faces come from Ezekiel. Ezekiel 1:5 has four living creatures (zoa, the word John uses), and 1:10 gives them the faces of a man, a lion, an ox and an eagle. In the Greek, Ezekiel 1:18 and 10:12 have things full of eyes all around (kyklothen); John's creatures are full of eyes all around. The six wings (pteryges hex) are Isaiah 6:2's.
entries.differs: In Ezekiel each creature has four faces; in Revelation each has one. Ezekiel's creatures have four wings, Isaiah's seraphim six. In Ezekiel 1 it is the wheels, not the creatures, that are covered with eyes. John drops the wheels and gives the eyes to the creatures. And like Isaiah's seraphim, his creatures sing God's praise, which Ezekiel's never do.
entries.turn: The creatures stand for all of animate creation, many sources say, and they do what creation was made for: they praise God without rest. Their many eyes show that nothing escapes God's notice. In chapter 6 they will call out the riders, so the judgments start from the throne.
entries.not: **Not a list of the four Gospel writers.** Some early Christian writers read them that way, as Wright and Beale note, but Beale says the reading has no support in the text.
entries.deeper: Beale says John draws from Ezekiel 1:5-21, merged with the living creatures of Ezekiel 10:12-15, 20-22, and supplements the picture with the six wings of Isaiah 6. The living beings stand in the midst of and around the throne (kyklo), as the seraphim in the Greek of Isaiah 6:2 stood around (kyklo) the Lord. He reads the beings as symbolic, since they differ from both models: wings, position, faces and voice all vary. The eyes allude directly to Ezekiel 1:18 and 10:12, and perhaps to the Targum on Ezekiel 1:14, where the creatures are sent to do their Master's will. Keener says Ezekiel 10:12 covers the cherubim with eyes and that each of Ezekiel's creatures had all four faces. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the ESV Study Bible, the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible and the CSB Study Bible all name Ezekiel 1 and Isaiah 6. Walton notes Near Eastern winged guardians with lion, bull and eagle features. The grade is drawn here: the faces, eyes and wings could hardly come from anywhere else.
entries.heiser: Heiser says the creatures are on the surface Ezekiel's cherubim, but the six wings come from Isaiah's seraphim, so John blends his sources. He calls the eyes a deliberate change. In Ezekiel 1 and 10 the wheels are full of eyes, not the cherubim; John moves the eyes onto the creatures. After Daniel Block he notes that the Hebrew word for eye in Ezekiel 1:18 also means sparkle earlier in the chapter. He reads the wheels as star imagery: the God who rules the cycles of time is Israel's God, not Marduk.
entries.dissent: Keener and Beale read Ezekiel 10:12 as covering the cherubim themselves with eyes. Heiser says only the wheels are full of eyes and that 10:12 depends on how it is translated. Beale doubts the zodiac reading of the four faces, since an eagle is never part of the zodiac scheme; Heiser, after Block, ties the faces to the four cardinal points of the Babylonian zodiac.

entries.title: Revelation 4:8, holy, holy, holy
entries.summary: The creatures sing the threefold holy of Isaiah 6:3, but John changes Isaiah's title for God and replaces the earth full of his glory with the one who was, is and is coming.
entries.plain: **A choir can sing a famous anthem and change the last line so that it fits the day.** The creatures never stop calling God holy three times. That song comes from Isaiah 6, where the seraphim cry it to one another in the temple. John keeps the triple holy. He names God the Lord God Almighty, and in place of Isaiah's whole earth full of his glory he praises the one who was, is and is to come.
entries.same: The triple holy. Isaiah 6:3 in Greek has hagios, hagios, hagios kyrios, holy, holy, holy Lord, and Revelation 4:8 has the same four words. In both, heavenly beings next to the throne sing it without ceasing. The six wings in the same verse also come from Isaiah 6:2.
entries.differs: The Hebrew says YHWH tsevaot, Lord of hosts. The Greek of Isaiah keeps the Hebrew word as sabaoth. John writes ho theos ho pantokrator, God the Almighty. That is the form the Greek of Amos and other prophets uses for Lord of hosts. He drops Isaiah's line about the earth full of God's glory. He adds the three-part name from 1:4.
entries.turn: Isaiah's vision leads to judgment on a people who will not hear. Beale notes that Revelation later borrows the next verse, the temple filling with smoke, when God's anger is poured out in 15:8. So the song of holiness in 4:8 prepares for the judgments to come. They come from the God who rules all of time.
entries.not: **Not a new hymn made up for the church.** The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible notes that the song was already part of Jewish prayer. Beale says John takes it from Isaiah or from a tradition built on it.
entries.deeper: Beale says the influence of Isaiah 6 continues in 4:8b: the trisagion finds its background in Isaiah 6:3, perhaps directly, perhaps through a tradition based on it, and probably both. Isaiah 6 is drawn in because its theophany is so like Daniel 7 and Ezekiel 1. He traces the Lord God Almighty to its recurrent use in the Greek prophets (Amos 3:13; 4:13; Hosea 12:5; Nahum 3:5; Zechariah 10:3). In the vault's Septuagint, Amos 3:13 reads kyrios ho theos ho pantokrator, word for word Revelation's title, where the Hebrew has Yahweh, God of hosts. The second name, the one who was, is and is coming, comes from Exodus 3:14 and Jewish tradition (see 1:4). Jewish writings had the cherubim praise God without sleep (1 Enoch 39:11-14; 61:12; 2 Enoch 21:1). Keener and the NIV Biblical Theology and CSB Study Bibles all cite Isaiah 6:3. The grade is drawn here: the triple holy can hardly come from anywhere else.
entries.heiser: Heiser says the triple holy comes right out of Isaiah 6. That is one of three council scenes, with Daniel 7 and Ezekiel 1, that John blends to build the throne room. As in The Unseen Realm, he adds that Isaiah's seraphim may look like serpents as well as fire. They guard the throne. But he says the fire imagery does not depend on Isaiah 6 alone.
entries.dissent: Prigent and others, Beale reports, take the triple holy and the new song from the liturgy of the synagogue or early church. Beale answers that they are just as likely taken from the Old Testament. Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible note that the song had entered synagogue prayer, which allows both.

entries.title: Revelation 4:9, the one who lives forever and ever
entries.summary: God is praised twice as the one who lives forever and ever, a title Beale traces to Daniel 4:34 and 12:7, where God's endless life outlasts proud kings.
entries.plain: **A plaque that says founded long before you and still here after you puts every visitor in their place.** The creatures and elders praise the one who lives forever and ever. Daniel uses the same title twice. A humbled King Nebuchadnezzar praises the one who lives forever, and an angel swears by him. Beale hears both behind John's words.
entries.same: A title for God built on two words, live and forever. The Greek of Daniel 4:34 has to zonti eis tous aionas, to the one who lives forever. Daniel 12:7 has en to zonti eis ton aiona. Revelation 4:9 and 4:10 have to zonti eis tous aionas ton aionon, to the one who lives forever and ever.
entries.differs: John doubles the forever into forever and ever, as Revelation does throughout. In Daniel 4 a pagan king says it after God humbles him; in Daniel 12 an angel swears by it. In Revelation the heavenly court sings it in worship. The phrase also occurs elsewhere in the Old Testament, Beale grants, but the closest wording is Daniel's.
entries.turn: In Daniel the eternal God outlasts kings who made themselves gods and persecuted his people. Beale reads the same contrast here: God's endless reign outlasts the emperor's. It warns readers not to give divine honor to rulers, and it assures them that they will be vindicated.
entries.not: **Not a stock phrase with no source.** Beale grants that the phrase is found about five times outside Daniel. But he finds the two Daniel verses the closest, and the best fit for a scene built on Daniel 7.
entries.deeper: Beale says that forms of the phrase occur about five times in the Old Testament outside Daniel, but that the closest verbal parallels are Daniel 4:34 (Theodotion) and 12:7, each with a dative participle of zao (live) followed by a temporal aion phrase. These two form the most probable collective influence on 4:9b, and a phrase from Daniel suits a vision patterned on Daniel 7. In both Daniel texts God's eternity contrasts with the passing reigns of evil kings who claimed deity and persecuted God's people (Daniel 4:30-33; 11:36-37; 12:7). The threefold verbal introduction of 4:9-10 also matches Daniel 4:34, where Nebuchadnezzar blessed, praised and glorified the one who lives forever. The ESV Study Bible links the title to the creatures' praise of God's eternal life. The grade is Beale's: he calls the Daniel texts the most probable influence.
entries.dissent: Beale reads the title as a pointed contrast with rulers who claimed divine titles. The ESV Study Bible reads the same words as praise for God's eternal life, without the Daniel contrast. No source denies the Daniel link.

entries.title: Revelation 4:11, you created all things and by your will they exist
entries.summary: The elders' hymn to God as Creator, who made all things by his will, echoes Nebuchadnezzar's praise in Daniel 4, where God does as he wills in heaven and on earth.
entries.plain: **A worker who praises the boss for building the company is also saying the boss decides what happens next.** The elders throw down their crowns and praise God as worthy of glory, honor and power, because he made everything and everything exists by his will. Beale hears Daniel 4 behind it. There a humbled king praises the God who does as he wills in heaven and on earth.
entries.same: Praise of God's will over all things. The Greek of Daniel 4:35 has kata to thelema autou poiei, he acts according to his will, in heaven and on earth. Revelation 4:11 has dia to thelema sou, because of your will. Beale adds that the old Greek of Daniel calls God the one who created all things, as John does, and that glory, honor and power also gather in Daniel 4.
entries.differs: Daniel praises God's power in history: he does what he wills among heaven's armies and earth's people. John makes it creation: God created all things, and by his will they were and were created. Beale says the old Greek translation of Daniel had already read the verse in terms of creation. The speaker changes too, from a humbled king to the elders.
entries.turn: Beale says the hymn stresses that all things exist to serve God's purposes and that he carries out his will through all of history without being stopped. For persecuted Christians that means even their suffering sits inside his plan. Chapter 5 then shows how he carries the plan out: through the Lamb.
entries.not: **Not a hymn about the past alone.** Beale reads they were, then were created, as God keeping all things going and also starting them. So the praise looks at the present as well as the first creation.
entries.deeper: Beale finds the closest parallel to 4:11b in Nebuchadnezzar's closing hymn in Daniel 4: the old Greek of 4:37 calls God to ktisanti ta panta (the one who created all things) and gives his will, while Theodotion's 4:35 has God acting kata to thelema autou in heaven and on earth. He argues that the old Greek reads the Aramaic as creative rather than historical sovereignty. Both have aorist verbs of making followed by all things and a will construction. He adds dynamis and time in Daniel 4:34, 36 and doxa in 4:35-36 (old Greek), matching glory, honor and power, and finds a hint of a liturgy shaped by the Greek additions to Daniel 3. The vault's Septuagint gives Theodotion only, so the old Greek wording here rests on Beale. Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible note that Domitian liked to be called our Lord and God. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible lists Daniel 4:37 among heaped-up praises. The grade is drawn here: Beale finds no closer combination of wording, theme and setting.
entries.dissent: Two scholars Beale names, Jörns and Deichgräber, argue for a general Old Testament and Jewish background to the hymn, not Daniel 4. Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible read the title our Lord and God against the claims of the emperor Domitian. The study Bible adds that the Greek Old Testament already used the title for God (Psalm 99:8; 106:47).

entries.title: Revelation 5:1, a scroll written inside and on the back
entries.summary: The scroll in God's right hand, written on both sides, is Ezekiel's scroll of laments and woes, now given a reach that covers the whole world.
entries.plain: **A letter so full that the writer has run onto the back of the page tells you there is a lot of news.** In God's right hand John sees a scroll with writing on the inside and on the back. Ezekiel was shown the same kind of scroll, written front and back, full of laments, mourning and woe. John borrows Ezekiel's scroll, and with it a hint of what is inside: judgment.
entries.same: A scroll written on both sides. Ezekiel 2:10 in Greek has writing on the front and the back (ta emprosthen kai ta opisthen); Revelation has written inside and on the back (esothen kai opisthen). The Hebrew has panim ve'achor, front and back. Both scrolls are held out from heaven to a prophet.
entries.differs: Ezekiel's scroll is unrolled before him and he reads its woes; John's is sealed and no one can open it. Ezekiel's scroll was for Israel; John's covers the whole world. Beale says the change comes from joining Ezekiel's scroll with the books of Daniel 7 and 12, which have cosmic reach. John never says what the scroll holds.
entries.turn: Beale reads the scroll as God's plan of judgment and redemption, set in motion by Christ's death and resurrection and still to be completed. Heiser stresses that Ezekiel's book judges both Judah and the nations. The scroll is for the whole earth, and only the Lamb can put it into effect.
entries.not: **Not a scroll read out, as Ezekiel's was.** Ezekiel's scroll is spread open before him; John's stays sealed until the Lamb takes it. The sources differ on whether chapters 6 to 8 show what it holds.
entries.deeper: Beale says most have rightly heard Ezekiel 2:9b-10 in 5:1 and later speaks of the clear allusion to Ezekiel 2:10. The writing on the back connotes comprehensive contents, as in Ezekiel 2:10 and Zechariah 5:1-3. In his introduction he gives it as an example of universalization: the book of judgment aimed at Israel in Ezekiel 2:9 gains cosmic reach in 5:1 by being joined to the books of Daniel 7:10 and 12:4, 9. The Targum on Ezekiel 2:10 says the scroll held what had been from the beginning and what will be at the end. Beale weighs Roman wills sealed with seven seals and doubly written contracts, and thinks John may have combined them with Ezekiel. Keener, the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the ESV Study Bible and the CSB Study Bible all cite Ezekiel 2:9-10. The grade is Beale's.
entries.heiser: Following Aune, Heiser says the sealed scroll comes from Ezekiel 2:9-10 as a sign that the Lamb is being installed in office. The Ezekiel link, he says, settles it as a rolled scroll rather than a book with pages. The best clue to the contents is Ezekiel's: laments, mourning and woe, that is, judgment. Ezekiel judges Judah (chapters 4-24) and then the nations (25-32). So, he argues, the scroll targets the wicked among both, and Revelation is not about Jerusalem's fall alone.
entries.dissent: The sources split on how the contents come out. The CSB Study Bible and Heiser say nothing can be read until all seven seals are off, so chapter 6 shows what comes before the opening. Beale holds that each broken seal reveals and carries out part of the contents. On the form, Beale weighs a codex and a double legal deed; Keener reads a sealed legal document; Heiser and most commentators read a scroll. MacArthur reads the scroll as a deed, the title deed to the earth, as in Jeremiah 32, and each broken seal as a judgment of the coming tribulation.

entries.title: Revelation 5:1, sealed with seven seals
entries.summary: The seven seals merge Daniel's order to keep the book sealed until the end with Isaiah's sealed book that no one can read.
entries.plain: **An envelope marked do not open until a certain date tells you the news inside is waiting for its moment.** The scroll is sealed with seven seals. Daniel was told to seal up the book until the end, and was told again that the words stay sealed until then. Isaiah spoke of a sealed book that even a reader cannot read. John joins the two, and now the question is who can break the seals.
entries.same: A sealed book that hides God's plan. The Greek of Daniel 12:4 has sphragison to biblion, seal the book, and 12:9 has the words sealed (esphragismenoi). Isaiah 29:11 has the words of this sealed book (esphragismenou). Revelation 5:1 has a book (biblion) sealed (katesphragismenon) with seven seals.
entries.differs: Daniel's book stays closed until the end. In Revelation the time to open it has come, and the question is who can do it. John adds the number seven, the number of fullness in his book. Isaiah's sealed book stands for a people who cannot understand. Beale says John brings the texts together for their nearly identical wording and their shared idea of hidden judgment.
entries.turn: Daniel was told to close the book until the end. The Lamb now opens it. Beale reads this as a sign that Christ's death and resurrection have begun to fulfill Daniel, so the end time is underway. Heiser adds that the sealing may mean the wicked are blind to what is coming, while the righteous are told.
entries.not: **Not a quotation of Daniel or Isaiah.** John borrows the sealed book and joins the two texts for their wording. He adds the number seven, and he makes the opening of the book the Lamb's task alone.
entries.deeper: Beale says the phrase sealed with seven seals appears to merge Daniel 12 and Isaiah 29:11. He compares Daniel 12:4 (Theodotion) sphragison to biblion, Daniel 12:9 esphragismenoi hoi logoi, and Isaiah 29:11 hoi logoi tou bibliou tou esphragismenou toutou, which the vault's Septuagint confirms. The texts are joined for their almost identical wording and their common idea of a sealed book that hides revelation and is tied to judgment. Sealing and opening books in connection with end-time events, he says, occurs in the Old Testament only in Daniel 12 and 7. Isaiah 29:9-12 develops Isaiah 6:9-10, and in Isaiah 29:11-12 and Revelation 5:3-4 no one can read the sealed book. Comparing Daniel 12:4 with Revelation 5:9b, he argues that Christ's death has begun to fulfill Daniel, so the seals are now removed. Walton notes that official scrolls were rolled and sealed with string and a clay or wax seal. The CSB Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cross-reference Isaiah 29:11 and Daniel 12:4. The grade is drawn here: Daniel's sealing is close in wording, Isaiah's less so.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Beale's point that sealing and opening books tied to the end time is unique to Daniel 12. He weighs two forces: Isaiah 29:11, where the sealed book pictures blindness, as in the Isaiah 6 council scene, so the wicked are blindsided by judgment; and Daniel 12:4, 9, a book sealed so its contents stay hidden until God reveals them to the righteous. He suggests it may be both. He adds Aune's parallel in 1 Enoch 89:71-77, a sealed book of deeds opened for punishment.
entries.dissent: Fekkes, as Beale reports, rejects an allusion to Isaiah 29 here. Schlatter and Sweet hear Ezekiel 2 and Daniel 12 working together. Beale keeps Isaiah 29 for its almost identical wording. Heiser leaves open whether the sealing means blindness or concealment. Beale reads the opening of the seals as Daniel's end time begun through the Lamb's death. MacArthur reads it as the start of judgments still to come: each seal lets loose a judgment of the future tribulation.

entries.title: Revelation 5:2, who is worthy to open the book
entries.summary: The angel's question about opening the book recalls the court of Daniel 7, where the judgment sat and the books were opened.
entries.plain: **When a judge says the court will open the file, everyone knows the hearing has begun.** A mighty angel asks who has the right to open the book and break its seals. In Daniel's vision of God's court, the judges sat down and the books were opened. John's question takes that moment and asks who has the right to do the opening.
entries.same: The opening of books in God's court. The Greek of Daniel 7:10 has bibloi eneochthesan, books were opened. Revelation 5:2 has anoixai to biblion, to open the book, the same verb with a single book.
entries.differs: In Daniel the books are simply opened, and no one asks who may do it. John turns the moment into a question and a crisis: no one anywhere, above, on or below the earth, is able. Daniel has many books; John has one. And John's book is sealed, which Daniel 7 does not say.
entries.turn: The question shows that no created being has the right to carry out God's plan of judgment and redemption. That makes the answer in 5:5 and 5:9 stand out: the slain Lamb is worthy. The court of Daniel 7 is in session, and Christ alone may open its book.
entries.not: **Not proof that the books of Daniel 7 and the scroll are the same.** Daniel's books record deeds for judgment; Beale reads John's scroll as God's plan. The link is the court scene and the act of opening.
entries.deeper: Beale says the image of opened books from Daniel 7:10 comes into focus in 5:2b, comparing anoixai to biblion with Theodotion's bibloi eneochthesan; Revelation 20:12 uses the same Daniel text clearly. The verb lysai (to loose) the seals draws more from Daniel 12, where the textual tradition links lysis (unloosing) and sealing. The open book of Daniel 7 continues to hover in 5:3, with Isaiah 29:11-12. In his outline, books opened is element eight of the fourteen shared with Daniel 7. Walton notes that royal courts kept records of deeds, which in Daniel 7:10 are brought out as evidence against the beast. The grade is drawn here: the verb and the court setting match, within the Daniel 7 frame.
entries.heiser: Heiser lists the court that sat and the books that were opened among the signs that Daniel 7 is a courtroom scene behind Revelation 4 and 5. Reading Aune, he notes that Daniel 7 has only books being opened; the sealed scroll is brought in from Ezekiel 2.
entries.dissent: Beale makes Daniel 7:10 the leading influence on the book because it has cosmic reach. Aune, as Heiser reads him, says the sealed scroll does not come from Daniel 7 but from Ezekiel 2, with Daniel supplying only the opened books.

entries.title: Revelation 5:5, the Lion of the tribe of Judah
entries.summary: The elder names Jesus the Lion of the tribe of Judah, Jacob's blessing on Judah in Genesis 49, which Jewish tradition read of the Messiah.
entries.plain: **A team that keeps a lion as its badge is telling you how it plans to win.** One of the elders tells John to stop weeping, because Judah's Lion has won. On his deathbed Jacob called his son Judah a lion's cub and said the ruler's staff would not leave Judah. Jewish readers took that as a promise of the Messiah. John names Jesus as that Lion, the one who has won.
entries.same: Judah and a lion. The Hebrew of Genesis 49:9 calls Judah gur aryeh, a lion's cub; the Greek has skymnos leontos Iouda, a lion's cub, Judah. Revelation 5:5 has ho leon ho ek tes phyles Iouda, the lion from the tribe of Judah. Genesis 49:10 adds the ruler's staff that stays with Judah.
entries.differs: Genesis speaks of a tribe, Judah the lion's cub; John speaks of one person from that tribe. Jacob's lion crouches over its prey; John's lion has conquered, a word he adds. And John does not let the lion stand alone: when John turns to look, he sees a slain Lamb.
entries.turn: The Lion is the Messiah from Judah who rules the nations. Beale says the conquering word brings out the victory in the title, and Jesus fulfills it. Then John turns the image over: the lion wins by being the slain Lamb. Wright warns against both readings that keep only the lion and readings that keep only the lamb.
entries.not: **Not Jacob's lion unchanged.** Genesis 49 pictures a lion's cub crouching over its prey. John gives the title to one man and sets it beside a slain Lamb. Wright, Beale and the ESV Study Bible stress that the Lion conquers through the Lamb's death.
entries.deeper: Beale says the two titles of 5:5 come from Genesis 49:9 and Isaiah 11:1, 10, and that both concern a messianic figure who overcomes his enemy through judgment. A messianic reading of Genesis 49:9 occurs in the Targums Neofiti and Pseudo-Jonathan of Genesis 49:9-12, in later Jewish writings and in 4 Ezra 11:37 and 12:31-32, where a lion stands for the Messiah of David's seed; Qumran's 1QSb 5.21-29 joins Genesis 49:10 with the same hope. Beale thinks this tradition may have prompted John to combine the two texts. In his introduction he lists the lion from Judah among his analogical uses, a judging figure. Keener, the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the ESV Study Bible, the CSB Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible all cite Genesis 49:9-10, and Wright mentions the lion of 2 Esdras 11-12. Walton notes that a hand on the enemy's neck in 49:8 signals Judah's power. The grade is drawn here: the title can only come from Genesis 49.
entries.dissent: The sources agree on Genesis 49. They read the hard word Shiloh in 49:10 differently: Walton takes it as tribute brought to Judah, while the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible reads the verse of a ruler from Judah who will rule the nations. Keener notes that lions also adorned Torah shrines in Jewish art, but says the direct background is Genesis 49. Wright, Beale and the ESV Study Bible define the Lion's victory by the cross. MacArthur holds that the Lion's fierce strength, only glimpsed at the first coming, is shown in full at the moment this scene looks toward, while the Lamb's death is what makes him worthy to take the scroll.

entries.title: Revelation 5:5, the Root of David
entries.summary: The Root of David takes Isaiah's root of Jesse, the shoot from David's line who rules the nations, and puts David's name in place of his father's.
entries.plain: **Calling someone the founder of a family business, when he is also its newest heir, says more than either title alone.** The elder also calls Jesus the Root of David. Isaiah promised a shoot from the stump of Jesse, David's father, and called him the root of Jesse, a banner the nations will seek. John uses Isaiah's title and puts David in Jesse's place.
entries.same: The root. The Hebrew of Isaiah 11:10 has shoresh yishai, the root of Jesse, and the Greek he rhiza tou Iessai. Revelation 5:5 has he rhiza Dauid, the root of David. In Isaiah 11:10 the root rises to rule the nations; in Revelation he is able to open the scroll for the whole world.
entries.differs: Isaiah names Jesse, David's father; John names David. In Isaiah the shoot grows from the root, and the root then stands for the coming king. John takes the title straight to Jesus. The ESV Study Bible draws out the effect: Jesus is David's heir, and also the source of David's rule.
entries.turn: John joins a title of royal descent to the Lion from Judah. Both promise a ruler from David's line. He judges the wicked and brings the nations under God. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible notes that Isaiah's king slays the wicked. In Revelation he wins by his own death.
entries.not: **Not a new title made up by John.** It reworks Isaiah's root of Jesse. Paul uses the same verse of Jesus in Romans 15:12, as the ESV Study Bible and the CSB Study Bible note.
entries.deeper: Beale traces the root of David to Isaiah 11:1, 10 (compare Jeremiah 23:5; 33:15; Zechariah 3:8), and says the title shares the conquering sense brought out by overcome. He notes that the Greek of Isaiah 53:2 also uses root (rhiza) of the servant, which may have drawn the slain lamb of 5:6 into the scene, and that the seven gifts of the Spirit in the Greek of Isaiah 11:2 may have drawn in the seven eyes of Zechariah. In the vault's Septuagint, Isaiah 11:1 has ek tes rhizes Iessai and 11:10 he rhiza tou Iessai, ho anistamenos archein ethnon, the one rising to rule nations. Keener says the image is used of the Messiah in later texts and that the Dead Sea Scrolls combine the lion and the root. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the ESV Study Bible, the CSB Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cite Isaiah 11:1, 10, and Wright calls it Isaiah's great messianic prophecy. The grade is drawn here: the title can only come from Isaiah 11.
entries.dissent: The ESV Study Bible reads root as the source of David's line, so that Jesus stands before David as well as after him. Keener reads it as the shoot from the cut-off line of David, the heir who comes after the line seemed ended. Beale treats it as a messianic title of conquest without settling the sense of root.

entries.title: Revelation 5:6, a Lamb standing as if slain
entries.summary: The slain Lamb joins the Passover lamb that saved Israel to the servant of Isaiah 53, led like a sheep to the slaughter.
entries.plain: **A medal for bravery given to someone who was badly wounded tells the story of how the battle was won.** John turns to see the Lion and sees a Lamb, standing, yet bearing the marks of slaughter. The sources hear two lambs behind it. The Passover lamb's blood saved Israel in Egypt. And Isaiah's servant went like a sheep to be killed and carried the sins of others.
entries.same: A lamb that is slaughtered for others. Isaiah 53:7 in Greek has a sheep led to slaughter (sphagen) and a lamb (amnos) silent before its shearer; Revelation has a lamb as slain (esphagmenon), from the same root. Exodus 12:6 has the Passover lamb killed at evening, and its blood marks the houses that are spared.
entries.differs: John's word for lamb is arnion, not amnos, the word in the Greek of Isaiah 53:7 and in John 1:29. Neither Isaiah's sheep nor the Passover lamb stands up again; John's Lamb stands, alive, still marked by slaughter. And it has seven horns and seven eyes, nothing like an ordinary lamb. John names neither Passover nor Isaiah outright.
entries.turn: The Lion has won by being slain. Beale reads the death itself as the victory: by it the Lamb redeemed a people and made them a kingdom. The church's way of overcoming follows the same pattern of faithful suffering. Heiser warns against reading only weakness: the Lamb is also the warrior whose wrath the world fears.
entries.not: **Not a lamb that only looks dead.** Beale says the translation as though slain misleads; the Greek perfect means slain and still bearing it. The Lamb truly died and truly stands.
entries.deeper: Beale names two proposals, the Passover lamb and Isaiah 53:7, and says neither should be excluded, since both center on a sacrificed lamb that brings redemption and victory. Isaiah 53 brings the atoning sense, and its root (rhiza, 53:2) and lamb (amnos) may have joined it to Isaiah 11. Behind arnion may lie the Aramaic talya, meaning lamb, servant or boy, which would combine Passover and servant. The sinlessness of Isaiah 53:9 partly underlies the worthiness of 5:9. The perfect esphagmenon expresses an abiding state. Fekkes, as Beale reports, sees a mainly paschal background. Keener says the figure especially represents the Passover lamb; the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible combines Passover (Exodus 12:3-6), Isaiah 53:7 and Jeremiah 11:19; the ESV Study Bible and the CSB Study Bible cite Isaiah 53:7. The grade is drawn here: the sacrificed lamb traces to these texts, but John's wording is his own.
entries.heiser: Heiser, reading Aune, notes that arnion occurs 29 times in Revelation, all of Jesus except the beast of 13:11, while the Lamb of God in John 1:29 is a different word, amnos. He calls the picture multivalent: a sacrificed victim and also a conquering ruler, as 6:16 and 17:14 show. He adds that Passover was about rescue from the destroyer rather than forgiveness of sin, and that the Aramaic talya, lamb or servant, opens a link to Isaiah 53:7. He insists that the slain Lamb rules out dropping substitution from the atonement.
entries.dissent: The sources weigh Passover and Isaiah 53 differently. Keener and Fekkes favor Passover; the ESV Study Bible and the CSB Study Bible cite Isaiah 53; Beale and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible hold both, the study Bible adding Jeremiah 11:19. Heiser cautions that Passover was not a sin offering, and that without a specific reference by John the options stay open.
