entries.title: Revelation 5:6, seven horns
entries.summary: The Lamb's seven horns turn the horns of Daniel's beasts against them: the symbol of the enemy's power now marks the Messiah's.
entries.plain: **When a winning team wears the badge of the side it beat, the insult is part of the victory.** The Lamb has seven horns. In Daniel horns stand for kings and power, and they grow on the terrible fourth beast and on the ram. Beale says John borrows the beast's horns for the Lamb on purpose. The one who seemed defeated now carries the full power the enemy only pretended to have.
entries.same: Horns that stand for power and kingship. Daniel 7:7 in Greek gives the fourth beast ten horns (kerata), and 7:24 says the horns are kings. Daniel 8:3 has a ram with horns, standing. Revelation 5:6 has the Lamb standing with seven horns (kerata hepta).
entries.differs: In Daniel the horns belong to the beasts that persecute God's people. John puts them on the Lamb. Daniel's beast has ten horns, then three are uprooted; John's Lamb has seven, the number of fullness. Beale notes the grammar too: the word having is masculine, though lamb is neuter, which may point back to the beast that had ten horns.
entries.turn: Beale calls it ironic parody. The Lamb defeats the enemy with the enemy's own imagery, so the punishment fits the crime. The beast of chapter 13 will later mimic the Lamb, with a wound healed and horns like a lamb. Revelation's war is between the true power and its imitation.
entries.not: **Not a picture of a real animal.** Male lambs have two horns, the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible notes, not seven. The horns are a sign of complete power, not a description.
entries.deeper: Beale says the seven horns are probably linked to the beast's horns of Daniel 7. The Lamb replaces the son of man of Daniel 7:13, and one could even count seven horns left on the beast after three were uprooted (7:8). The same mimicry appears in 1 Enoch 90:9-13, 16, the Testament of Joseph 19:6-8 and Genesis Rabbah 99.2. He lists Daniel 7:7ff. in Revelation 5:6-7 among the ironic, retributive inversions of his introduction. Horns stand for power (Deuteronomy 33:17; 1 Kings 22:11; Psalm 89:17). The masculine echon may draw attention to eiche in the Greek of Daniel 7:7, the beast that had ten horns. Keener says horns as symbols of authority are rooted in Daniel 8; the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible cites Daniel 7:7-24 and 8:3-22, the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible Daniel 7:24 and 8:21-22, the CSB Study Bible Daniel 7:8, 20, 24, and the ESV Study Bible Psalm 18:2, Daniel 7:24 and Zechariah 1:18-21. The grade is Beale's probably.
entries.dissent: Beale reads the horns as a deliberate parody of Daniel 7's beast. Keener roots them in Daniel 8, and the study Bibles read them simply as a sign of royal power, with no turn against the beast. The ESV Study Bible adds Psalm 18:2 and Zechariah 1:18-21.

aw.n: Revelation 5:1-14, the sealed scroll and the Lamb
aw.s: In God's right hand is a scroll written on both sides and sealed with seven seals, and no one is worthy to open it until the Lion of Judah, the Root of David, appears as a Lamb that looks slain. The living creatures, the elders, countless angels and all creation worship him.

entries.title: Revelation 5:6, seven eyes sent into all the earth
entries.summary: The Lamb's seven eyes are the seven eyes of the Lord in Zechariah 3 and 4, which range over all the earth, now belonging to the Lamb.
entries.plain: **When the owner hands a new manager the master keys, everyone knows who runs the building now.** The Lamb has seven eyes, which John calls God's seven spirits, sent out across the world. In Zechariah seven eyes sit on a stone, and seven eyes belong to the Lord and roam the whole earth. In Zechariah they are God's eyes. Here they belong to the Lamb.
entries.same: Seven eyes over all the earth. Zechariah 4:10 in Greek has hepta ophthalmoi kyriou, seven eyes of the Lord, looking on all the earth (pasan ten gen). Zechariah 3:9 has seven eyes on one stone. Revelation 5:6 has seven eyes (ophthalmous hepta) sent into all the earth (pasan ten gen).
entries.differs: In Zechariah the eyes are the Lord's, watching the earth. John gives them to the Lamb and names them the seven spirits, sent out on mission. Zechariah's eyes look; John's are sent. And Zechariah's seven eyes on the stone are tied to removing the land's sin in one day, which John's slain Lamb has done.
entries.turn: Before, the seven spirits stayed before the throne (1:4; 3:1; 4:5). Beale says that the Lamb's death and resurrection make them his agents in all the world. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible draws the point out. Eyes that were God's now belong to Jesus, who appears as divine.
entries.not: **Not seven spirits with seven jobs.** Beale reads the seven spirits as a picture of the Holy Spirit in full. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible reads them as the fullness of God's Spirit.
entries.deeper: Beale says the consensus is that the phrase depends on Zechariah 3 and 4. In Zechariah 3:9 the seven eyes are tied to an inscription about removing the land's iniquity in one day; in Zechariah 4 the seven lamps (4:2) and seven eyes (4:10) are linked to Yahweh's Spirit. 2 Chronicles 16:9 adds that the Lord's eyes range through the earth to support his own. John has read Zechariah's eyes as Yahweh's Spirit and made both eyes and spirits the Lamb's. Isaiah 11, alluded to in 5:5, may have drawn Zechariah in, through the sevenfold Spirit of the Greek of Isaiah 11:2 and the shared images of root and branch. In the vault's Septuagint, Zechariah 4:10 has hepta houtoi ophthalmoi kyriou eisin hoi epiblepontes epi pasan ten gen. Keener, the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the ESV Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cite Zechariah 4:10. The grade is drawn here: close wording and the consensus Beale reports.
entries.dissent: Keener notes that Zechariah's eyes may be angels, modeled on the Persian king's messengers. So Revelation may mean the seven archangels of Jewish tradition, under Christ, rather than the Spirit. Beale and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible read the Holy Spirit. The ESV Study Bible reads the Lamb's full knowledge.

aw.n: Revelation 5:1-14, the sealed scroll and the Lamb
aw.s: In God's right hand is a scroll written on both sides and sealed with seven seals, and no one is worthy to open it until the Lion of Judah, the Root of David, appears as a Lamb that looks slain. The living creatures, the elders, countless angels and all creation worship him.

entries.title: Revelation 5:7, the Lamb comes and takes the scroll
entries.summary: The Lamb comes to the throne and takes the scroll, as one like a son of man comes before the Ancient of Days in Daniel 7:13-14 to receive a kingdom.
entries.plain: **A new chief executive who walks up and takes the keys from the founder's hand has just been given the company.** The Lamb comes and takes the scroll from the one seated on the throne. Daniel saw a figure like a human being come before the Ancient of Days and receive authority, glory and an everlasting kingdom. Beale says Daniel's scene stands behind John's.
entries.same: A figure who comes before God's throne to receive authority. Daniel 7:13 has one like a son of man coming (erchomenos) to the Ancient of Days; John's Lamb came (elthen) and took. Daniel 7:14 has authority, honor (time) and a kingdom given; in Revelation 5:12-13 the Lamb receives power, honor (time) and glory.
entries.differs: Daniel's figure is like a son of man and comes with the clouds. John's is a slain Lamb. Daniel says authority was given; John says the Lamb took the scroll. In Daniel the books open before the figure comes; in Revelation he comes in order to open the book. Heiser and Aune note that in neither text does the figure sit down on the throne.
entries.turn: Beale reads 5:7 as Christ taking up the reign of Daniel 7. He says it began with the death and rising. The power Daniel saw promised is handed over. Heiser and Aune call it an investiture. It shows in public the rule he has held since he rose. The full kingdom is still to come.
entries.not: **Not Daniel's scene repeated exactly.** Daniel's figure is like a son of man and comes with the clouds; John's is a slain Lamb who takes a scroll. When the handing over takes place is a separate question.
entries.deeper: Beale says Daniel 7:13 is the only Old Testament text where a divine, messianic figure approaches God's heavenly throne to receive authority, and that it should be seen behind 5:7. Both texts show one who comes (erchomai) before the throne to receive authority to reign after books have been opened. He adds the giving (didomi) of Daniel 7:14 and the receiving (paralambano) of 7:18 beside the taking (lambano) of 5:7, and, after Comblin, honor (Theodotion 7:14) and glory (the old Greek of 7:14) in 5:12-13, followed by universal acclaim. The reference results mainly from John's adherence to the pattern of Daniel 7:9ff. The perfect eilephen functions as an aorist. The CSB Study Bible calls Daniel 7:13-14 a parallel account and reads the taking as a transfer of authority. The vault's Greek of Daniel 7:14 has time and basileia. The grade is drawn here from Beale's reasoning.
entries.heiser: Heiser, with Aune, reads Revelation 5 as an investiture rather than an enthronement or a commissioning. Investiture establishes someone in an office already held informally. The Lamb never sits on the throne until the shared throne of God and the Lamb in 22:1. Aune notes, and Heiser stresses, that Daniel 7's son of man is given everlasting kingship but never sits down. Heiser places the grant of authority at the resurrection and ascension, an already but not yet.
entries.dissent: Beale and most commentators, he reports, read Revelation 5 as an enthronement, already begun, and Beale rejects van Unnik's argument against it. Aune and Heiser read an investiture, since the Lamb is not enthroned until 22:1. Lang and others, Beale notes, see chapter 5 as a second, future enthronement. Beale and Heiser place the handing over at Christ's resurrection and ascension. MacArthur sets chapters 4 and 5 after the church age, and he reads the scene as looking ahead: the new song anticipates the final redemption God is about to begin.

entries.title: Revelation 5:8, bowls of incense, the prayers of the saints
entries.summary: The elders' bowls of incense, which are the prayers of the saints, take up Psalm 141:2, where the psalmist asks that his prayer rise like incense.
entries.plain: **A thank-you card that smells of the giver's perfume makes the message feel present in the room.** The elders hold harps and gold bowls full of incense, and John says the incense is the prayers of God's people. In Psalm 141 David asks God to accept his prayer like incense before him. John makes the picture real in the heavenly temple: the prayers rise before the throne.
entries.same: Prayer as incense. Psalm 141:2 in Greek has he proseuche mou hos thymiama, my prayer as incense, before God. Revelation 5:8 has bowls full of incense (thymiamaton), which are the prayers (proseuchai) of the saints. The two key nouns are the same.
entries.differs: The psalm compares one man's prayer to incense; John says the incense is the prayers of all the saints. The psalmist offers it himself; in Revelation the elders bring it, in gold bowls, to the Lamb. Beale reads the psalm as a plea for God to vindicate the righteous, and finds that plea in the saints' prayers too.
entries.turn: The prayers are more than praise. Beale ties them to the cry of the martyrs in 6:9-11 and the incense of 8:3-5, which come before judgment falls on the earth. The ESV Study Bible draws the same line: the saints' pleas are heard and answered in God's judgments.
entries.not: **Not a picture of saints praying to the elders.** The elders carry the prayers to the throne. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible compares the Jewish tradition of a chief angel presenting God's people's prayers.
entries.deeper: Beale says Psalm 141:2 stands behind the picture of prayers as incense, a plea for God to defend the righteous by judging those who persecute them (compare Luke 1:9-10). The prayers are those of 6:9-11 and 8:3-4, requests that God defend his justice. The relative hai refers to the incense, not the harps. The harps fit the elders as the twenty-four orders of Levites who prophesied with lyres and harps (1 Chronicles 25:6-31). In the vault's Septuagint, Psalm 141:2 has proseuche and thymiama. Keener calls prayers as incense not uncommon (Psalm 141:2) and ties it to the heavenly altar of incense (8:3); the NIV Cultural Backgrounds and NIV Biblical Theology Study Bibles also cite Psalm 141:2. The grade is drawn here: both key words match, but the image was not rare.
entries.dissent: Beale reads the prayers mainly as pleas for vindication against persecutors. Keener reads the scene as worship in the heavenly temple, with the harps of the Levitical choir. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible holds both: the prayers are answered in the judgments of 6:9-11, 8:3-5 and 15:7-8.

entries.title: Revelation 5:9, a new song
entries.summary: The elders sing a new song, the Psalms' and Isaiah's call to praise God for a fresh victory, now sung to the Lamb.
entries.plain: **A crowd that makes up a new chant after a big win is saying no old song is big enough.** The creatures and elders sing a new song to the Lamb. The Psalms and Isaiah often call God's people to sing a new song when he wins a victory or does a new saving act. John's heaven sings one now, for the Lamb.
entries.same: The phrase new song. Psalm 144:9 in Greek has oden kainen, a new song, sung with a harp; Revelation 5:9 has oden kainen sung by elders who hold harps (5:8). Psalm 98:1 and Isaiah 42:10 call for a new song to the Lord.
entries.differs: In the Old Testament a new song is offered to God alone, the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible notes. John's new song is sung to the Lamb. The Psalms praise a victory over Israel's enemies; this song praises a death that redeemed people from every nation. The phrase occurs in many places, so no single psalm is its source.
entries.turn: Beale says a new song in the Old Testament always praises God's victory over the enemy, sometimes with thanks for creation. Here it praises the defeat of evil and sin through the Lamb. Beale also hears in the word new the new creation, begun, he says, by the Lamb's death. Chapter 21 calls it a new heaven and earth.
entries.not: **Not a quotation of one psalm.** The phrase appears in at least six psalms and in Isaiah. The grade is possible because the wording is general, even though the phrase itself matches exactly.
entries.deeper: Beale lists the new song texts (Psalms 33:3; 40:3; 96:1; 98:1; 144:9; 149:1; Isaiah 42:10) and says the song in the Old Testament is always praise for God's victory over the enemy. Kainos ties Christ's work to new creation: the vision flows from creation in 4:11, the hymns of 5:12-13 parallel 4:11, kainos marks the new creation in 21:1-5, and Jewish writings link the new song to the messianic age (Numbers Rabbah 15.11; Exodus Rabbah 23.11 on Psalm 98:1). Of the seven Old Testament uses, four are tied to God's act of creation. Keener says the temple's inspired psalms were called new songs and cites the same psalms; the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the CSB Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cite them too. Psalm 144:9 in Greek joins the new song and the harp, as 5:8-9 does, a link Beale points out. The grade is drawn here: the phrase is common to many texts.
entries.dissent: Prigent, as Beale reports, takes the new song directly from the paschal liturgy of John's church; Beale says it is just as likely taken from the Old Testament. Keener reads it as freshly inspired worship, like the temple singers' new songs. Beale hears the new creation already begun in the song. MacArthur reads it as looking ahead to the final redemption God is about to begin.

entries.title: Revelation 5:9, every tribe and language and people and nation
entries.summary: The list of every tribe, language, people and nation comes from Daniel, where the nations serve Israel's king or bow to Nebuchadnezzar's statue; John turns it into the people the Lamb has bought.
entries.plain: **A roll call once used to summon a conquered empire, read out now as the names of the guests at a feast, has changed its meaning completely.** The Lamb bought people for God out of every tribe, language, people and nation. Daniel repeats a list like this. It summons all nations to bow to Nebuchadnezzar's statue. In Daniel 7 all peoples, nations and languages serve the son of man. John turns those nations into the Lamb's own people.
entries.same: A list of peoples that covers the whole earth. The Greek of Daniel 7:14 has laoi, phylai, glossai, peoples, tribes, languages. The Greek of Daniel 3:4 has four: ethne, laoi, phylai, glossai. Revelation 5:9 has phyles, glosses, laou, ethnous, tribe, language, people, nation. The Aramaic of Daniel 7:14 has ammaya, ummaya velishanaya.
entries.differs: Daniel's lists are threefold in the Aramaic; John's has four nouns, like the Greek of Daniel 3:4. In Daniel 3 the nations are ordered to bow to a statue. In Daniel 7 they serve the son of man as subjects. John's nations are neither: they are bought by the Lamb's blood and made to rule with him. Beale calls this an intended inversion.
entries.turn: In Daniel the phrase named the nations under Israel's rule. Now, Beale says, those very nations reign with the Messiah. Heiser draws the same line: John takes Daniel 7's kingdom for all peoples and makes it the redeemed from every nation. The people of God is one people, drawn from all of them.
entries.not: **Not a promise that every person is saved.** Beale reads it as people from all races without distinction, not all people without exception, as 14:3-4 makes clear.
entries.deeper: Beale says the general consensus traces the phrase to Daniel, though it is not an exact copy. Theodotion's Daniel has phylai, glossai and laoi together in 3:4, 7; 4:1; 5:19; 6:26; 7:14, and the old Greek adds ethne in 3:2, 7. Since the Daniel 7:9ff. frame has the threefold phrase in 7:14, he thinks that verse sparked John's formula, which recurs in 7:9; 10:11; 11:9; 13:7; 14:6; 17:15, usually beside other Daniel allusions. In his introduction he lists it twice: under universalization, since Exodus 19:6's title now applies to a people from every nation, and under inverted uses, since in Daniel the phrase names nations made subject to Israel, and now those nations rule with the Messiah. The vault's Septuagint confirms the lists in Daniel 3:4 and 7:14. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible counts six such lists in Daniel and seven in Revelation; the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible contrasts the nations' false worship in Daniel 3:4-5. The grade is drawn here: close, though not exact, wording that only Daniel supplies.
entries.heiser: Heiser says the unity of the redeemed from every tribe, language, people and nation is by design. He reads Daniel 7:14, where all peoples, nations and languages serve the son of man, and 7:27, where the kingdoms under heaven go to the people of the holy ones, and says John equates that language with the redeemed. The kingdom is bigger than Israel, he adds, because Eden had no Jew and Gentile divide.
entries.dissent: Beale reads an inversion: Daniel's subject nations become rulers. The CSB Study Bible links the list instead to the Great Commission's all nations, and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible to the false worship of Daniel 3. Morris, Beale notes, doubts the Daniel link. Manuscripts differ on whether the Lamb bought us or bought people, and Beale leaves both readings open.

entries.title: Revelation 5:10, a kingdom and priests, reigning on the earth
entries.summary: The Lamb makes his people a kingdom and priests, Israel's calling from Exodus 19:6, woven with Daniel 7's promise that the saints will receive the kingdom.
entries.plain: **A charter first written for one town, now signed for a whole country, keeps its words and widens its reach.** The song says the Lamb made his people a kingdom and priests to God, and that they will rule on the earth. At Sinai God called Israel a kingdom of priests. In Daniel 7 the saints receive the kingdom. John weaves both into one line about the Lamb's people.
entries.same: Kingdom and priests, as in 1:6: Revelation has basileian kai hiereis, kingdom and priests, from Exodus 19:6. Daniel 7:22 has the holy ones take the kingdom (basileian), and 7:27 gives the kingdom under all heaven to the Most High's holy people. Revelation adds that they reign, or will reign, on the earth: manuscripts have basileuousin or basileusousin.
entries.differs: Exodus speaks to one nation chosen from all nations; John speaks of people from every nation. Daniel gives the kingdom to the saints of Israel; John gives it to the Lamb's redeemed. Exodus does not mention reigning, and Daniel does not mention priests; John joins the two. Manuscripts also differ between they reign and they will reign.
entries.turn: Beale reads 5:10 as the inaugurated fulfillment of Daniel 7: the saints already reign, because the Lamb's death made them a kingdom. Their reign looks ahead to the new earth too. Heiser stresses that the rule is on earth, the new Eden, and that the Lamb shares the authority he receives.
entries.not: **Not a reign only in heaven.** The song says on the earth. Beale, Heiser, MacArthur and the ESV Study Bible all read the rule as earthly. They differ on when it begins.
entries.deeper: Beale says Danielic influence on the peoples of 5:9 is clearer because, as in Daniel 7:14, the formula is followed by Christ giving the saints a kingdom and their reign (Daniel 7:18, 22b, 27a). The old Greek of 7:27 uses the infinitive basileusai (to reign), and both contexts share four elements. Exodus 19:6 is also present in kingdom and priests: Israel was chosen from all the nations (Exodus 19:5), and in 5:9 that election is widened through Daniel's formula to every tribe and nation. Exodus 19 is drawn in for its link to Passover and to Daniel's kingdom. On the text, the standard printed Greek editions prefer they will reign; Beale prefers the present they reign as the harder reading. The vault's Greek of Daniel 7:22 has ten basileian kateschon hoi hagioi. The ESV Study Bible and the CSB Study Bible cite Exodus 19:6 and 1:6. The grade is drawn here: the Exodus wording is as clear as in 1:6.
entries.heiser: Reading Aune, Heiser says John overlays the kingship language of Daniel 7:14-18 with the kingdom and priests of Exodus 19:6, grounding the investiture in Christ's sacrifice. He then breaks with most commentators: Daniel 7's holy ones and the people of those holy ones are two groups, the loyal heavenly council and human believers, given the same authority. Believers, he says, become the reconstituted council, ruling on the earth in a new Eden.
entries.dissent: Beale holds that the saints reign now, in an inaugurated kingdom. Commentators who prefer the future, he notes, place the reign in 20:4-6 or on the new earth; the CSB Study Bible says the promise is fulfilled in 20:6. Heiser reads Daniel's holy ones as heavenly beings joined by believers, against most commentators, who take both phrases as God's people. MacArthur points to his note on 20:2: the reign on the earth is Christ's rule for a literal thousand years after his return, with the saints reigning beside him.

entries.title: Revelation 5:11, myriads of myriads and thousands of thousands
entries.summary: The countless angels around the throne are counted in the numbers of Daniel 7:10, where thousands serve God and myriads stand before him.
entries.plain: **A stadium crowd too big to count is still described by borrowing the words of the last great crowd.** John hears the voices of countless angels around the throne, ten thousands of ten thousands and thousands of thousands. In Daniel's vision of God's court, thousands upon thousands served him and myriads upon myriads stood there. John uses the same numbers and turns their order around.
entries.same: Two huge numbers doubled. The Greek of Daniel 7:10 has chiliai chiliades and myriai myriades, thousands of thousands and myriads of myriads. Revelation 5:11 has myriades myriadon kai chiliades chiliadon. The Aramaic has elef alfin and ribbo ribvan. In both, the crowd surrounds God's throne.
entries.differs: Daniel names the thousands first, then the myriads; John reverses the order and starts with the larger number. Daniel's crowd serves and stands; John's sings. And in Daniel the next verse turns to the beast's boasting voice; John's angels speak with a great voice in praise.
entries.turn: The scene grows from the inner circle to the angels to all creation. Beale suggests that the angels' loud praise in 5:12 may answer the boastful voice of Daniel's beast in Daniel 7:11. Here, it is the slain Lamb who receives the acclaim.
entries.not: **Not a count of exactly how many angels there are.** Keener notes that ten thousand was the largest single number in Greek, so the doubled myriads simply mean beyond counting.
entries.deeper: Beale says it is generally recognized that the description is taken from Daniel 7:10 (compare 1 Enoch 40:1; 60:1; 71:8, which also allude to it). Such a clear picture from Daniel 7:10 is no surprise after the Daniel 7 influence in 5:2-10. The masculine legontes (saying) where a feminine is expected may be an attention-getting device pointing to Daniel 7:10. He wonders whether the host speaking with a great voice is a polemical counterpart to the beast's voice of great words in Daniel 7:11. In the vault's Greek of Daniel (Theodotion), 7:10 has chiliai chiliades and myriai myriades; the Hebrew text of the Aramaic has thousand thousands first, then ten thousand ten thousands. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds and NIV Biblical Theology Study Bibles and the CSB Study Bible's cross-references cite Daniel 7:10. The reversal of order is drawn here from the texts. The grade is drawn here: nearly identical wording, a setting that could hardly come from elsewhere.
entries.dissent: Beale traces the numbers straight to Daniel 7:10. Keener explains them from Greek counting and from Jewish texts that gave huge numbers of angels, without naming Daniel. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible adds Hebrews 12:22 and Jude 14.

entries.title: Revelation 5:12, power and wealth and wisdom
entries.summary: The angels' sevenfold praise of the Lamb may echo David's prayer in 1 Chronicles 29 and the gifts Daniel says God gave to kings.
entries.plain: **A toast that strings together every good word you can think of borrows from every toast you have ever heard.** The angels say the slain Lamb is worthy to receive power, wealth, wisdom, strength, honor, glory and praise. David's prayer in 1 Chronicles 29 heaps up power, glory and riches for God. Daniel praises God for wisdom and power, and says God gave a king power, strength and glory. John's list may draw on both.
entries.same: A string of royal honors. 1 Chronicles 29:11-12 joins greatness, power, glory and riches as God's. Daniel 2:20 gives God wisdom and might, and Daniel 2:37 says God gave the king kingdom, power, strength and glory. Revelation's list has power, wealth, wisdom, strength, honor, glory and blessing.
entries.differs: David gives the honors to God; Daniel 2:37 says God gave them to a pagan king. John gives them to the slain Lamb. His list has seven items, which neither source has. And the order is his own. Beale says the link to Daniel is probably indirect, through worship language that drew on it.
entries.turn: Beale says John uses the words Daniel used for kingship that God gives to another. Here they name the world rule given to the Lamb. The Lamb receives what Scripture gives to God alone, and the praise of 5:13 joins him with the one on the throne. Wright reads this as John's way of showing that the Lamb shares the creator's worship.
entries.not: **Not a quotation of a known hymn.** Beale and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible say only that such lists heap up praise and may echo these texts. The link is a matter of shared words, not a copied verse.
entries.deeper: Beale reports a study by Milling of the New Testament's closing words of praise. It finds 1 Chronicles 29:11-12 behind the set of dynamis (power), ploutos (wealth), ischys (might) and doxa (glory), and Daniel 2:20 behind sophia (wisdom), which is paired with power in Theodotion's 2:23. He adds that ischys, doxa and time occur together in the old Greek of Daniel 2:37 and 4:30, a combination found only twice more in the Greek Old Testament, and that in Daniel and Revelation the words come in the same order and describe kingship given by God to another. He thinks the influence is indirect, through a liturgy or John's long acquaintance with Daniel, combined with 1 Chronicles. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible cites 1 Chronicles 29:11-12 and Daniel 2:37 for heaped-up praise, and notes lists of seven in the Dead Sea Scrolls and the Mishnah. The grade is possible: the words are generally similar and spread over several texts.
entries.dissent: Delling, as Beale reports, sees a general Old Testament background rather than specific texts. Keener notes that the Passover service later listed seven praises, but thinks John's love of sevens makes the parallel likely coincidental.

entries.title: Revelation 5:13, every creature in heaven, on earth and in the sea
entries.summary: All creation praises God and the Lamb in the words that the Law and the Psalms use for God as maker of heaven, earth, sea and all that is in them.
entries.plain: **When every section of the orchestra plays the last chord together, the whole hall knows the piece is done.** John hears every creature in every part of the world praise God and the Lamb. They are above, on and below the earth, and in the sea. The Ten Commandments and Psalm 146 praise God for making sky, land, sea and all that fills them. John's chorus is that creation answering back.
entries.same: The parts of creation and all that fills them. The Greek of Exodus 20:11 and Psalm 146:6 lists heaven, earth and sea, then kai panta ta en autois, and all things in them. Revelation 5:13 lists heaven, earth, under the earth and sea. Then it has kai ta en autois panta, the same phrase in a new order.
entries.differs: Exodus and the psalm speak of God making all things. John has all things praising. He adds a fourth realm, under the earth, which the Old Testament texts do not list here. And the praise goes to two: the one on the throne and the Lamb. The ESV Study Bible and Beale point back to the creation hymn of 4:11.
entries.turn: Beale says the scene looks ahead to the end, when all creation will acclaim God and the Lamb, willingly or by force. Chapter 4 praised God as Creator; now creation itself praises its Creator and its Redeemer together. The ESV Study Bible compares the day when every knee bows (Philippians 2:10-11).
entries.not: **Not a claim that every creature is saved.** Beale reads the praise as including God's enemies, forced into submission, and notes that the evil are judged for refusing it in their lifetime.
entries.deeper: Beale says the fivefold praise of 5:13a may be a collective reflection of Exodus 20:11, Psalm 146:6 and Nehemiah 9:6, which praise God as maker of all his varied works and as the king who freed his people from slavery, which fits the kingdom and Passover themes. Daniel 2:38 and 4:37 in the old Greek may be part of the influence. The closing praise (blessing, honor, glory, dominion) traces to the old Greek of Daniel 4:30-31, he says, a combination found nowhere else in the Greek Old Testament. In the vault's Septuagint, Exodus 20:11 and Psalm 146:6 both have kai panta ta en autois. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible cites Exodus 20:11 and Psalm 146:6, with Psalm 96:11, Amos 9:6 and Haggai 2:6; the ESV Study Bible cites Psalm 146:6. The grade is possible: the wording is a common Old Testament phrase.
entries.dissent: Beale reads the praise as universal in the fullest sense, including forced submission. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible reads the fourfold division against Greek ideas of the gods ruling heaven, earth, sea and the underworld. Keener notes that Judaism expected the whole world to submit to God at the end but held it answered to him already.

entries.title: Revelation 6:2-8, four horses of four colors
entries.summary: The four horsemen are built on Zechariah's horses and chariots, sent out from God's presence to range over the earth, now sent to judge it.
entries.plain: **A director can reshoot an old classic with the same cast of characters and a darker ending.** Zechariah saw horses of different colors that God sent out to patrol the earth. Later he saw four chariots pulled by red, black, white and dappled horses. John sees four horses, white, red, black and pale, each called out as the Lamb breaks a seal. The colors and the sending come from Zechariah. The riders now bring war, hunger and death.
entries.same: Four horses marked by color, sent out from God's presence to cover the whole earth. Three colors match in Greek: white (leukos), red (pyrros) and black (melas). In Zechariah 6:5 the teams are the four winds of heaven that go out after standing before the Lord.
entries.differs: Zechariah sees groups of horses in chapter 1 and four chariot teams in chapter 6. John sees four single horses with riders. His fourth color is pale green (chloros), where Zechariah has dappled or spotted. In Zechariah the horses patrol and report. In John each rider carries out a judgment. Beale says the change from teams to riders matters little, since John could infer riders in the chariots.
entries.turn: In Zechariah the patrol finds the nations at ease while Jerusalem suffers, and God promises to act against them. John turns the patrol into the action. The Lamb opens each seal, a living creature calls, and a rider goes out. Beale reads it as Christ ruling over the disasters of history, using them to test his people and to judge their persecutors.
entries.not: **Not a code in which each color names a nation or a year.** Beale reads the colors as pictures of the plague each rider brings, and Heiser declines to spend time matching every color to Zechariah's.
entries.deeper: Beale calls Zechariah 6:1-8, with 1:8-15, the most obvious background, and says the colors in both books are almost identical. In the Greek of Zechariah 6:2-3 the teams are pyrroi, melanes, leukoi and poikiloi psaroi; 1:8 has pyrroi, psaroi, poikiloi and leukoi. Revelation has leukos, pyrros, melas and chloros. Zechariah 6:5 calls the teams the four winds of heaven, which Beale takes as one reason John has four. He reads the colors as metaphors: white for conquest, red for bloodshed, black for famine, pale green for death. Targum Zechariah 6 made the horsemen the evil angels of Daniel's four kingdoms, which Beale uses to argue that all four riders are evil powers under Christ's control. Keener, the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the ESV Study Bible, the CSB Study Bible, the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible and Wright all point to Zechariah 1 and 6. Walton notes that Zechariah 6 calls the teams spirits, the same word as winds. The grade is drawn here: a scene of colored horses sent out over the earth can hardly come from anywhere else.
entries.heiser: Heiser calls Zechariah 6:1-8, looped back to Zechariah 1, the most obvious source, and refuses to spend an episode reconciling each color. He draws four points. The figure among the myrtles may be the angel of Yahweh. The horsemen go out from God's throne in the council scene of chapters 4-5. The four horses cover the four corners of the earth. And chariots were weapons of war, so judgment is already present in Zechariah, where the teams go out against nations oppressing God's people. He links this to the angel of Yahweh as destroyer at Passover and concludes that here the Lamb is the destroying judge.
entries.dissent: Commentators differ on the first rider. Beale lists those who see Christ or the gospel (Psalm 45 and Revelation 19:11) and those who see a satanic imitator, and sides with the second. Keener, the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible and the ESV Study Bible point to the Parthian archers. Wright takes him as the conquering kings of the earth. MacArthur reads the riders as forces, not persons: the first brings a false and short peace, led by false messiahs and ending in the Antichrist, won by agreement and not by war. On the sequence, Beale argues the four plagues run at the same time, not one after another; the CSB Study Bible notes the parallel with the Olivet Discourse and places the seals before the tribulation. MacArthur places every seal inside a tribulation still to come, starting with the first.

aw.n: Revelation 6:1-8, four horsemen
aw.s: As the Lamb opens the first four seals, four riders go out: a crowned archer on a white horse bent on conquest, a rider on a red horse who takes peace from the earth, a rider with scales on a black horse while wheat sells at famine prices, and Death on a pale horse with Hades following.

entries.title: Revelation 6:5-6, scales and rationed grain
entries.summary: The rider with scales and the price of grain recall the curses and sieges in which bread was handed out by weight.
entries.plain: **When shops start weighing bread by the gram, everyone knows times are hard.** The third rider holds a pair of scales, and a voice names grain prices about a day's pay for a day's food. In the covenant curses of Leviticus 26, and in Ezekiel's siege of Jerusalem, God warns that bread will be eaten by weight. Elisha's prophecy in 2 Kings 7 also prices grain by the measure. John draws on that picture of hunger.
entries.same: Food measured out in hard times. In the Greek of Leviticus 26:26 and Ezekiel 4:16 bread is eaten by weight (en stathmo). 2 Kings 7:1 names a price for a measure of fine flour and of barley, as John's voice names prices for wheat and barley.
entries.differs: No single verse supplies John's wording. The scales are John's own picture, and his prices are in Roman money, a denarius. Leviticus and Ezekiel threaten Israel; John's famine strikes a wider world. And John adds a limit the older texts do not have: the oil and the wine are spared.
entries.turn: Beale reads the famine as a trial that hits believers hardest, since they could be shut out of trade for refusing the patron gods of the guilds. The same hunger falls on the unbelieving world as judgment. The limit on oil and wine shows the famine is real but held in check.
entries.not: **Not a price list taken from the Old Testament.** No older text gives John's prices or his denarius. What he shares with Leviticus, Ezekiel and 2 Kings is the picture of bread measured out in hunger.
entries.deeper: Beale notes the metaphorical use of scales for famine in Leviticus 26:26, 2 Kings 7:1 and Ezekiel 4:10, 16, and later says Leviticus 26:26, where the Greek speaks of affliction (thlipsis) and loaves given by weight, stands partly behind 6:5-6. Leviticus 26 is one of the covenant curse chapters he sees behind the whole of 6:1-8. The ESV Study Bible cites Deuteronomy 28:49-57 and 2 Kings 6:24-25 and 7:1-2 on siege prices, and the CSB Study Bible's cross-references list 2 Kings 6:25 and 7:1. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible and Keener explain the prices: a quart of wheat fed one worker for a day, and the prices ran far above normal. Beale adds that a lack of wheat, barley, oil and wine marks severe famine in Joel 1:10-11. The grade is possible: the picture is shared with several texts, and no one wording points to one source.
entries.dissent: The sources read the spared oil and wine differently. Beale sees basic foods that the poor still cannot afford, and rejects a sacramental reading. Keener and Wright see items of lesser need, or of the rich, left untouched while staples soar. MacArthur sees basic goods turned into luxuries that must be guarded. The ESV Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible mention Domitian's edict of AD 92 on the vineyards. On the famine itself, Beale finds no one event behind the verse. MacArthur reads a worldwide famine still to come, caused by the war of the second seal, with food rationed and a day's pay buying one person's food for a day.

aw.s: As the Lamb opens the first four seals, four riders go out: a crowned archer on a white horse bent on conquest, a rider on a red horse who takes peace from the earth, a rider with scales on a black horse while wheat sells at famine prices, and Death on a pale horse with Hades following.

entries.title: Revelation 6:8, Death and Hades
entries.summary: Death riding with Hades behind may echo Hosea 13:14, where God names death and Hades together as powers he will master.
entries.plain: **Naming two bullies together tells everyone they work as a pair.** The fourth rider is named Death, and Hades, the realm of the dead, follows him. In Hosea 13 God speaks to death and to Hades side by side, and asks where their sting has gone. Beale thinks John may be echoing that pairing. Here the pair are let loose, but their reach stops at a quarter of the world.
entries.same: Death and Hades named together as personal powers. The Greek of Hosea 13:14 has hades and thanatos in the same verse, and John has ho thanatos kai ho hades.
entries.differs: In Hosea God promises to rescue his people from Hades and death, and taunts both. In John they ride out to kill. Hosea 13:8 also has beasts of the field, which Beale links to the beasts in 6:8, but John's other wording comes from Ezekiel 14.
entries.turn: Beale reads Death and Hades as evil powers that act only because they are given authority. Christ already holds their keys (1:18), so even their work serves his purposes. The Hosea background, if it is meant, carries a promise: the powers that strike will one day be undone.
entries.not: **Not two separate monsters with their own kingdom.** The Greek Old Testament often uses death and Hades almost as one phrase for the grave, as Beale notes.
entries.deeper: Beale says the pair possibly echoes Hosea 13:8, 14, where Hades and death and the beasts of the field are judgments on Israel from which God will later redeem it; he also cites Isaiah 28:15. In the vault's Septuagint, Hosea 13:14 reads ek cheiros hadou ... ek thanatou, and then pou he dike sou, thanate ... pou to kentron sou, hade. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible lists Hosea 13:14 among biblical poems that personify Death and Hades, with Psalm 49:14, Psalm 116:3, Isaiah 28:15 and Habakkuk 2:5. The CSB Study Bible's cross-references at 6:8 give Hosea 13:14, and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cites it as well. Beale notes that in the Septuagint thanatos often stands for the Hebrew word for plague, so death here can mean pestilence. The grade is possible: the pairing is common, and only Beale argues for Hosea in particular.

aw.n: Revelation 6:1-8, four horsemen
aw.s: As the Lamb opens the first four seals, four riders go out: a crowned archer on a white horse bent on conquest, a rider on a red horse who takes peace from the earth, a rider with scales on a black horse while wheat sells at famine prices, and Death on a pale horse with Hades following.

entries.title: Revelation 6:8, sword, famine, plague and wild beasts
entries.summary: The four ways the riders kill are Ezekiel's four dreadful judgments on Jerusalem, now let loose over a fourth of the earth.
entries.plain: **A judge who reads out the old sentence word for word wants everyone to know which law applies.** Ezekiel 14 lists four judgments God sends on an unfaithful city: sword, famine, wild beasts and plague. John ends the four horsemen with the same four. The list was a covenant warning, the kind of sentence God named for idolatry. John applies it to a fourth of the whole earth.
entries.same: The same four judgments. The Greek of Ezekiel 14:21 has rhomphaia (sword), limos (famine), theria (beasts) and thanatos (death, meaning plague), and John uses the same four words. Both lists sum up the trials that come before them.
entries.differs: John changes the order, putting death third and beasts last. Ezekiel's evil beasts become beasts of the earth, a phrase Beale finds in Psalm 79:2. Ezekiel aims at Jerusalem. John aims at a fourth of the earth; Beale reads the part as standing for the whole world. Ezekiel 5:12 in the Greek also speaks of a fourth part.
entries.turn: Beale reads 6:8 as the summary of all four riders. In Ezekiel the judgments punish the idolatrous majority and test the faithful few. John keeps both purposes. The same trials purify Christians and punish those who persecute them or give in to idols.
entries.not: **Not a list made up for the occasion.** The four come from a fixed set of covenant curses that the prophets repeat, as Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible show.
entries.deeper: Beale says Ezekiel 14:21 is explicitly quoted in 6:8b as a summary of the trials before it, and that Ezekiel 14:12-23 is formative for the section. Ezekiel 14:21 itself sums up four judgments listed in 14:13-19 and develops the curses of Leviticus 26:18-28 and Deuteronomy 32:23-25. In the vault's Septuagint, 14:21 reads rhomphaian kai limon kai theria ponera kai thanaton; John has en rhomphaia kai en limo kai en thanato kai hypo ton therion tes ges. Beale notes that thanatos renders the Hebrew deber, plague, more than thirty times, twice in Ezekiel 14. He finds the phrase beasts of the earth in the Greek of Psalm 79:2, a psalm John uses again in 6:10. Keener calls the list closest to Ezekiel 14:21; the ESV Study Bible ties it to the curses on Jerusalem in Ezekiel 14:12-21; the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cites Ezekiel 14:21 with Deuteronomy 32:24-26; the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible adds Ezekiel 5:17. Beale also wonders whether the four sevenfold curses of Leviticus 26 shaped the four series of seven in the book. The grade is drawn here from Beale's word quoted.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Beale's comment on 6:8 aloud: Ezekiel 14:21 is quoted there as a summary of the trials before it, adding beasts. He stresses Beale's point that the four plagues need not come one after another. A scroll sealed seven times cannot be read until every seal is broken, the fourth rider sums up the first three, and the Gospel parallels list the trials in different orders. So the judgments may run at once, which he notes cuts against end-time systems that depend on a strict sequence.
entries.dissent: Beale argues the beasts may stand for the evil powers later called the beast, since every other use of the word in Revelation refers to them. Most study Bibles read the list as ordinary disasters of war: violence, hunger and disease. Beale himself grants that the four judgments may also follow one another logically, as war leads to famine and death. MacArthur reads the riders as forces that come in turn in a tribulation still to come: worldwide war, then famine from the ruined food supply, then death for a quarter of the world's people.

aw.s: As the Lamb opens the first four seals, four riders go out: a crowned archer on a white horse bent on conquest, a rider on a red horse who takes peace from the earth, a rider with scales on a black horse while wheat sells at famine prices, and Death on a pale horse with Hades following.

entries.title: Revelation 6:9, souls under the altar
entries.summary: The slain saints lie under the altar where the blood of sacrifices was poured out, so their deaths are pictured as offerings.
entries.plain: **A memorial set beside a chapel's altar says these lives were given up, and not wasted.** Under the law of Moses, the priest poured the rest of a sacrifice's blood out where the altar met the ground. John sees the souls of those killed for their witness under the altar in heaven. The picture turns their deaths into gifts laid before God. Beale adds that being so near God's throne also means they are kept safe.
entries.same: An altar, blood that has been shed, and the place at its base. In the Greek of Leviticus 4:7 the blood is poured out by the altar's foot (basis); John sees the slain under it (hypokato tou thysiasteriou).
entries.differs: Leviticus speaks of animal blood at the earthly altar. John speaks of souls of people, at a heavenly altar. The sources disagree on which altar is meant. Leviticus 4 names both: the incense altar gets blood on its horns, and the rest is poured out at the foot of the bronze altar for burnt offerings.
entries.turn: The slain saints share the pattern of the slain Lamb of chapter 5. Their deaths, offered in faithfulness, are not wasted. Beale reads the scene as comfort: they are close to God's throne, protected even though they lost their lives.
entries.not: **Not the rite of Leviticus moved to heaven.** Leviticus pours out the blood of animals at an earthly altar. No Old Testament text places the souls of the dead under an altar; that part of the picture is John's.
entries.deeper: Beale says the altar evokes the sacrificial nature of the saints' suffering, and that blood was poured at the base of the bronze altar (Leviticus 4:18, 30, 34), but he identifies the heavenly altar with the golden altar of incense near the holy of holies (Exodus 30:1-10; Leviticus 4:7), which is clearly meant in 8:3-5 and 9:13. He reads under the altar as near God's throne, a link Jewish writings also made. Keener lists Leviticus 4:7, 18, 25, 34 and others for blood at the base of the altar and calls the martyrs sacrifices. The ESV Study Bible and the CSB Study Bible cite Exodus 29:12; the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cites Leviticus 4:7 and leaves both altars open. In the Greek, Leviticus 4:7 has the blood poured para ten basin tou thysiasteriou, by the base of the altar. The grade is possible: the image is clear, but no source points to one verse, and the sources disagree on the altar.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Aune, who notes the two altars but does not choose, and Beale, who argues for the altar of incense. He is persuaded by Beale because later altars in the book are clearly the incense altar, next to the throne behind the veil. He reads the picture as protection: judgment goes out from the throne, while the souls of the faithful stay in God's presence. He also reports an astral reading, a constellation called the Altar above the Milky Way, which Aune rejects; Heiser says it at least belongs on the table.
entries.dissent: The sources differ over the altar. Beale argues for the incense altar, and MacArthur also takes it as probably the incense altar. The ESV Study Bible says the heavenly altar fills both roles, and Beale says the same of 8:3. Keener, the ESV Study Bible and the CSB Study Bible stress blood poured out at the foot of the bronze altar. They also differ on who the slain are. Beale takes them as a picture of all believers who suffer for their witness, comparing 20:4. MacArthur reads Christians martyred during a seven-year tribulation still to come.

aw.n: Revelation 6:9-17, souls under the altar and the great day of wrath
aw.s: At the fifth seal the souls of those killed for God's word cry out from under the altar, how long, and are given white robes and told to wait. At the sixth a great earthquake shakes the world, the sky rolls up like a scroll, and kings and slaves alike hide in the caves from the wrath of the Lamb.

entries.title: Revelation 6:10, how long until you avenge our blood
entries.summary: The martyrs' cry borrows Psalm 79, which asks how long God will wait and prays for vengeance for the blood of his servants.
entries.plain: **When people at a vigil sing an old protest song, they are joining a long line of protesters.** Psalm 79 grieves over Jerusalem's dead. It asks God how long he will be angry, and prays that the nations will see him avenge his servants' blood. The martyrs under the altar pray the same prayer. They ask how long, and they ask God to avenge their blood on the earth's people.
entries.same: The question how long (heos pote), and vengeance for the blood of God's servants. The Greek of Psalm 79:10 has he ekdikesis tou haimatos ton doulon sou; John has ekdikeis to haima hemon.
entries.differs: In the psalm the people speak for the dead. In John the dead speak for themselves. The psalm prays for the servants' blood; the martyrs say our blood. John adds a name for God, holy and true, and names the guilty: those who dwell on the earth, his usual term for unbelievers.
entries.turn: Beale reads the prayer as a plea for God's justice and good name, not personal revenge. He sees the answer come in stages. The saints must wait (6:11), the sixth seal shows the final judgment, and later the bowls and 19:2 say God has avenged their blood.
entries.not: **Not a call for Christians to take revenge.** The saints hand the matter to God, and Beale contrasts their prayer with personal vengeance.
entries.deeper: Beale says how long is the Greek Old Testament's usual question about when God will punish persecutors (Psalms 6:3; 13:1; 74:10; 79:5 and others; Daniel 8:13 and 12:6), and that will you not avenge our blood alludes to Psalm 79:10 in the Greek. In that psalm how long comes first (v. 5) and the bodies of the saints are given to the beasts of the earth (v. 2), the phrase used in 6:8. He thinks Deuteronomy 32 stands behind the psalm too. Keener cites Psalm 79:5, 10 among prayers for vindication; the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible lists Psalm 79:5; the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cites Psalm 79:4-6, 10; the CSB Study Bible's cross-references give Psalm 79:10. Walton notes how long occurs about twenty times in the Psalms, usually in laments. The grade is drawn here: the wording is close and the context matches.
entries.dissent: Beale and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible point to Psalm 79. The ESV Study Bible names Psalms 13:1 and 89:46 instead, and Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible add Genesis 4:10, where Abel's blood cries out. Beale reads the prayer as about God's justice; the CSB Study Bible stresses the Lord's vengeance that begins with the bowls. MacArthur sets the cry in the fifth seal of a tribulation still to come. God answers in his own time, once the number of martyrs he has set is complete, and the sixth seal begins the day of the Lord.

entries.title: Revelation 6:10, how long after the horsemen ride
entries.summary: In Zechariah the angel of the Lord asks how long, right after the horses report; John puts the same question right after his four horsemen.
entries.plain: **A sequel that repeats a famous line at the same point in the story wants you to remember the first film.** In Zechariah 1 the horsemen report that the nations are at rest. Then God's angel asks how long mercy will be held back from Jerusalem. God answers that he will act. In Revelation the question comes at the same place, after the four horsemen, from the slain saints.
entries.same: The question how long, asked right after a vision of horses sent over the earth. In both books the question is about God acting against nations that oppress his people.
entries.differs: In Zechariah the angel of the Lord asks on behalf of Jerusalem. In John the saints ask for themselves. The Greek wording differs: Zechariah 1:12 has heos tinos, John heos pote. And Zechariah's horses report that all is quiet, while John's horsemen are already the start of judgment.
entries.turn: In Zechariah God answers by promising to judge the nations at ease, and the horses of chapter 6 carry it out. Beale reads John the same way. The horsemen are already a partial answer. The sixth seal is the full one.
entries.not: **Not a word-for-word quotation.** The match is in the order of events and the question, not the Greek words.
entries.deeper: Beale says Zechariah 1:12 also inspired the saints' cry. There the question comes once the horses have toured the earth and found the oppressor nations at peace. God then promises to remove that peace (Zechariah 1:13-16), and the horses become the agents of judgment in Zechariah 6:1-8. In Revelation, he says, the horsemen of 6:2-8 are an implied partial answer, and 6:12-17 the full answer. In the vault's Septuagint Zechariah 1:12 reads heos tinos ou me eleeses ten Ierousalem, until when will you not show mercy to Jerusalem. Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible both list Zechariah 1:12 among the how long prayers. The link of the sequence is Beale's. The grade is drawn here: the question is common, but its place after a horse vision points to Zechariah.

entries.title: Revelation 6:10, holy and true, who avenges the blood of his sons
entries.summary: The Song of Moses calls God true and holy and promises he will avenge the blood of his sons; the martyrs appeal to that God.
entries.plain: **Quoting a promise back to the person who made it is a way of asking them to keep it.** The Song of Moses in Deuteronomy 32 praises God as true and just and holy. Its last verse promises that God will take vengeance for his children's blood. The martyrs call God holy and true and ask him to avenge their blood. Beale thinks they may be holding God to that song.
entries.same: God described as true, and God avenging the blood of his people. In the Greek, Deuteronomy 32:43 has to haima ton hyion autou ekdikeitai, he avenges the blood of his sons; John has ekdikeis to haima hemon.
entries.differs: The Song promises; the martyrs ask how long. The Song speaks of sons, the martyrs of our blood. For holy, the Greek of Deuteronomy 32:4 has hosios, while John here has hagios, a different word (a point drawn here).
entries.turn: The Song of Moses moves from judging Israel to judging the nations that oppress it. The martyrs appeal to the same pattern. Their persecutors will be judged, as the Song promised.
entries.not: **Not a direct quotation.** Beale offers the Song only as a possible reflection behind the cry, alongside Psalm 79.
entries.deeper: Beale says the attributes true and holy are applied to God together in the Old Testament only in Deuteronomy 32:4, where God judges Israel with the same judgments as Ezekiel 14:21 (Deuteronomy 32:24-25) and then punishes the persecutors of his people (32:43). He suggests there may be a reflection of Deuteronomy 32 in 6:10b, since Psalm 79 probably alludes to it. The CSB Study Bible's cross-references at 6:10 list Deuteronomy 32:43 first. In the vault's Septuagint, 32:4 has alethina ta erga autou ... dikaios kai hosios ho kyrios, and 32:43 has to haima ton hyion autou ekdikeitai kai ekdikesei. The grade is possible: two sources name the text, and the shared words are few.

entries.title: Revelation 6:12, sun black as sackcloth, moon like blood
entries.summary: The sixth seal darkens the sun and turns the moon to blood in Joel's words for the day of the Lord, with Isaiah's sackcloth sky.
entries.plain: **Some phrases mean the end of the world in any language, like the lights going out.** Joel said the sun would go dark and the moon turn to blood when the day of the Lord drew near. Isaiah pictured God clothing the sky in black like sackcloth. John puts the two together. When the sixth seal opens, the sun turns black like sackcloth and the whole moon becomes like blood.
entries.same: The sun darkened and the moon turned to blood, both from Joel 2:31 (helios, selene, haima). The sackcloth (sakkos) is from Isaiah 50:3. Isaiah 13:10 also darkens the sun and the moon at the day of the Lord.
entries.differs: Joel says the sun will turn to darkness. John says it becomes black as sackcloth, an image from Isaiah 50:3. John adds the whole moon, and a great earthquake first. Joel set the signs before the day; John sets them at the opening of the day itself.
entries.turn: Joel and Isaiah used these signs to announce the Lord's day of judgment on the nations. John sets them at the sixth seal, as God begins to answer the martyrs' prayer. Beale reads the seal as the start of the final judgment of the whole unbelieving world.
entries.not: **Not a quotation of Joel.** John keeps Joel's darkened sun and moon of blood. He changes the darkness to black sackcloth from Isaiah 50:3, adds the whole moon, and puts an earthquake first.
entries.deeper: Beale says the scene is drawn from a quarry of Old Testament texts for the dissolution of the cosmos: Isaiah 13:10-13, 24:1-6, 19-23, 34:4; Ezekiel 32:6-8; Joel 2:10, 30-31, 3:15-16; Habakkuk 3:6-11. He says Joel 2:31 stands behind the darkened sun and bloody moon, and that the sackcloth was suggested by Isaiah 50:3. In the vault's Septuagint, Joel 2:31 reads ho helios metastraphesetai eis skotos kai he selene eis haima; John has ho helios egeneto melas hos sakkos ... he selene hole egeneto hos haima. Isaiah 50:3 has hos sakkon. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible cites Isaiah 13:9-11, 24:21-23 and Joel 2:31; the CSB Study Bible links Joel 2:28-31; the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cites Isaiah 13:9-13 and Joel 2:10, 31; the CSB Study Bible's cross-references list Isaiah 13:10, 50:3 and Joel 2:10, 31. Walton reads Joel's signs as eclipses, feared as omens. The grade is drawn here.
entries.dissent: Beale and Wright read the signs as figurative, since the source texts describe the fall of Babylon, Edom, Egypt and Israel's enemies. Keener reads the passage as the end of the age. The ESV Study Bible notes that some take 6:13 as a meteor shower. MacArthur reads physical events still to come: a worldwide earthquake as all the earth's faults give way together, with volcanoes whose ash blackens the sun and turns the moon red. For him the sixth seal begins the day of the Lord, which runs on through the trumpets and the bowls.

entries.title: Revelation 6:13-14, stars falling like figs, the sky rolled up like a scroll
entries.summary: The falling stars and the sky rolled up like a scroll come from Isaiah 34:4, where the host of heaven is judged with the nations.
entries.plain: **A painter can borrow one striking image from an old master and everyone knows the source.** Isaiah 34 pictures God's anger at the nations and their host. The sky rolls up like a scroll, and the stars drop like leaves from a vine or fruit from a fig tree. John uses the same pictures. Stars fall like figs shaken by a strong wind, and the sky splits away, rolling up like a scroll.
entries.same: Stars falling, a fig tree, and the sky rolled like a scroll. The Greek is close: biblion (scroll) and the verb roll (helisso) in both, and the stars fall (pipto) in both.
entries.differs: Isaiah has leaves falling from the fig tree in the Greek, and withered fruit in the Hebrew. John has unripe figs shaken by a great wind, which fits the Hebrew fruit better than the Greek leaves (a point drawn here). Isaiah says the sky is rolled up; John says it is split off as a scroll is rolled.
entries.turn: In Isaiah the judgment falls on the nations and on the host of heaven at once. John moves the picture to the sixth seal, a judgment on the whole world. Beale reads the stars as heavenly powers behind the nations, judged together with the earthly ones.
entries.not: **Not a quotation of Isaiah 34:4.** John keeps the falling stars, the fig tree and the scroll. He changes Isaiah's falling leaves to unripe figs shaken by a gale, and has the sky split away.
entries.deeper: Beale calls Isaiah 34:4 the most formative of the texts behind 6:12-14, the one after which 6:13-14a is most closely patterned. In the vault's Septuagint, 34:4 reads takesontai pasai hai dynameis ton ouranon, kai heligesetai ho ouranos hos biblion, kai panta ta astra peseitai hos phylla ex ampelou kai hos piptei phylla apo sykes. Revelation has hoi asteres ... epesan ... hos syke ballei tous olynthous autes ... kai ho ouranos apechoristhe hos biblion helissomenon. The Hebrew of 34:4 has tseva hashamayim, the host of heaven, and ukhnovelet mitte'enah, like withered fruit from a fig. Beale notes that the Greek renders the host of heaven as the powers of the heavens and identifies them as stars. Keener, the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the ESV Study Bible, the CSB Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible all cite Isaiah 34:4. Walton says the image of the sky rolled like a scroll is unique in the Hebrew Bible, and that dimming stars meant defeated star gods. The grade is drawn here.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Beale's list of texts and then stresses Isaiah 34:4, where God is angry at the nations and at their host. He says that this word form, their host, always means things in the sky in the Hebrew Bible, never earthly armies, and that the Greek renders it with dunamis, a word for supernatural powers. So the falling stars mean the judgment of the powers of darkness along with earthly powers: "we're not talking about something NASA can defeat". He adds 1 Enoch's falling stars as rebel Watchers and calls this the worldview of Deuteronomy 32 and Daniel 10.
entries.dissent: Keener thinks the stars may symbolize angelic hosts but probably just show the cosmic scope of judgment. Beale and Heiser read them as powers. The ESV Study Bible reports a literal reading as a meteor shower, and Beale grants that a few of the source texts may be literal. MacArthur reads a massive asteroid or meteor shower, since the word star can name any body in the sky. He takes the vanished sky as a real change to the earth's atmosphere.

entries.title: Revelation 6:15, the kings of the earth and the great ones
entries.summary: The ranks of the powerful who hide begin with the same three groups Isaiah 34 dooms: kings, great ones and rulers.
entries.plain: **A roll call that starts with the same three names as an older list sends readers back to it.** In Isaiah 34, the chapter of the rolled-up sky, Edom's kings, rulers and great men come to nothing. John's list of those who hide from God starts with kings, great ones and commanders. It then widens to the rich, the strong, and everyone, slave or free.
entries.same: Kings and great ones under judgment. The Greek of Isaiah 34:12 has hoi basileis and hoi megistanes, the same two words John uses, with rulers (archontes) as the third.
entries.differs: Isaiah names Edom's leaders; John names the kings of the earth. John's third group are commanders of a thousand (chiliarchoi), not rulers. And John adds three more groups, ending with slave and free.
entries.turn: Beale says the same groups appear in 19:18-19 as allies of the beast. The list shows that God judges all alike, whatever their rank. The people who ran the world, and those who served them, stand together before the throne.
entries.not: **Not a judgment on the rich alone.** The list runs from kings to slaves, and Beale reads it as everyone who has made the earth an idol.
entries.deeper: Beale says the Septuagint has the kings, the rulers and the great ones only in Isaiah 34:12, and calls this nearly identical to the first three groups of 6:15 (he compares Psalm 2:2 as well). He notes it fits the use of Isaiah 34:4 just before, and that in both texts the groups are judged for oppressing God's people. In the vault's Septuagint, 34:12 reads hoi archontes autes ... hoi gar basileis autes kai hoi megistanes autes; John has hoi basileis tes ges kai hoi megistanes kai hoi chiliarchoi. Beale also finds six groups of people here matching six parts of the cosmos in 6:12-14. The grade is drawn here by Beale's definitions: the three nouns together are found in one Greek verse, right beside the verse John has just used. Only Beale names this link.

entries.title: Revelation 6:15-16, hiding in the caves and rocks
entries.summary: People hide in caves and among the rocks from the face of God, as Isaiah 2 pictured idolaters hiding from the terror of the Lord.
entries.plain: **Hiding under the covers does not stop the storm.** Isaiah 2 pictures idolaters running into caves and the cracks of the rocks to hide from the terror of the Lord. They throw away their idols as they go. John sees the whole world do the same. Kings and slaves hide in caves and rocks, from the face of God on the throne and the anger of the Lamb.
entries.same: Caves (spelaia) and rocks (petrai). Hiding from the face (apo prosopou) of the Lord. All three are in the Greek of Isaiah 2:10, 19 and 21.
entries.differs: In Isaiah people hide from the Lord's terror and his glory. In John they hide from God on his throne, and from the Lamb. Beale says the Lamb stands where Isaiah had the glory of God's majesty. In Isaiah the scene judges Israel's idolaters; in John it is the whole world.
entries.turn: Beale reads the borrowing as a sign that these people are idolaters. It also puts the Lamb in the place of God's own glory, so the Lamb judges as God does.
entries.not: **Not the same scene as Isaiah 2.** Isaiah's idolaters hide from the Lord's terror and throw away their idols. John's hide from God seated on his throne, and from the Lamb, and no idols are named.
entries.deeper: Beale says the hiding is based on a typological reading of God's judgment of Israel's idolaters in Isaiah 2:10, 18-21, with Jeremiah 4:29 possibly included. In the vault's Septuagint, Isaiah 2:19 reads eis ta spelaia kai eis tas schismas ton petron ... apo prosopou tou phobou kyriou kai apo tes doxes tes ischyos autou; John has eis ta spelaia kai eis tas petras ton oreon and apo prosopou tou kathemenou epi tou thronou kai apo tes orges tou arniou. Beale adds a typological allusion to Genesis 3:8, where Adam and Eve hide from the presence of God. Keener cites Isaiah 2:10 and 19-20; the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible cites Isaiah 2:19; the ESV Study Bible cites Isaiah 2:20-21; the CSB Study Bible's cross-references list Isaiah 2:10, 19, 21; the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cites Isaiah 2:19-21. Walton notes the bright aura of a god in Isaiah 2:10. The grade is drawn here.
entries.dissent: The sources weigh Isaiah 2 against Hosea 10:8. Keener says the scene reflects Hosea 10:8 and compares Isaiah 2. Beale treats Isaiah 2 as the basis of the hiding and Hosea 10 as the basis of the cry. Beale also hears Genesis 3:8, which no other source here mentions. On why they hide, Beale argues they seek to die away from God's presence, not to survive.

entries.title: Revelation 6:16, fall on us
entries.summary: The cry to the mountains and rocks to fall on them and hide them is Hosea's picture of idolaters facing judgment.
entries.plain: **Some lines are so tied to one scene that you can quote them without naming the play.** Hosea warned that the people of Samaria, ruined for their idols, would beg the mountains to cover them and the hills to fall on them. Jesus used the same words on the way to the cross. In Revelation people everywhere call on the mountains and rocks. They beg them to fall and hide them.
entries.same: A cry to the mountains to fall on us. The Greek is close: Hosea 10:8 has erousi tois oresi ... pesate eph' hemas; John has legousin tois oresin ... pesete eph' hemas.
entries.differs: Hosea pairs mountains and hills; John has mountains and rocks. Hosea asks first to be covered, then to be fallen on; John reverses the order and says hide us. And John adds what they hide from: the face of God and the anger of the Lamb.
entries.turn: In Hosea the cry follows the fall of Israel's altars. Beale says John uses it for the final judgment of idolaters everywhere. They would rather die under the rocks than face God and the Lamb.
entries.not: **Not a prayer for mercy.** The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible notes that they call on the mountains, not on God.
entries.deeper: Beale says the cry alludes to Hosea 10:8. Like Isaiah 2, Hosea pictures idolaters looking for shelter from God's anger among the hills and rocks; Jeremiah 4:29 is included as well. In the vault's Septuagint, Hosea 10:8 reads kai erousi tois oresi, kalypsate hemas, kai tois bounois, pesate eph' hemas; John has kai legousin tois oresin kai tais petrais, pesete eph' hemas kai krypsate hemas. Keener says the hiding and crying reflect Hosea 10:8; the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible quotes Hosea and notes its use in Luke 23:30; the ESV Study Bible, the CSB Study Bible's cross-references and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible all cite Hosea 10:8, and Wright names it as a scene the prophets described. The grade is drawn here: the wording is nearly identical.
entries.dissent: Wright reads the scene as huge political turmoil within history, asking why people would hide in caves if the universe were really ending. Beale reads it as the final judgment. Keener also sees the end of the age. MacArthur sets the scene in a tribulation still to come, when the world's people see for the first time where all their trouble comes from, after living as usual until then.

entries.title: Revelation 6:17, the great day, and who can stand
entries.summary: The closing cry joins Joel's great day of the Lord to the prophets' question of who can stand before God's anger.
entries.plain: **A speaker who ends with a famous question leaves the crowd to answer it.** Joel calls the day of the Lord great and asks who can endure it. Nahum asks who can stand before God's anger. Malachi asks who will stand at his coming. John ends the sixth seal with the same question. The great day of their anger has come, and who is able to stand?
entries.same: The great day (he hemera he megale) and a question about who can stand. Joel 2:11 in Greek calls the day great (megale) and asks who will be able to bear it. Nahum 1:6 and Malachi 3:2 both ask who will stand (hypostesetai).
entries.differs: The prophets speak of the day of the Lord. John speaks of the great day of their anger, God's and the Lamb's together. John's verb for stand is different (stathenai). He joins phrases from several prophets into one line.
entries.turn: Beale reads the change to Joel as one more sign that the Lamb is divine. The day of the Lord becomes the day of God and the Lamb. The question also sets up chapter 7. There John sees people who do stand before the throne.
entries.not: **Not a question with no answer.** The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible both note that 7:9 shows a crowd standing before the throne.
entries.deeper: Beale says that since Joel 2:10, 31 is partly behind 6:12, the section fittingly ends with what ends Joel 2:10-11, the great day of the Lord and who will be able to resist it, supplemented by Nahum 1:5-6 on Nineveh. He lists Isaiah 13:9, Zephaniah 1:14, 18 and Malachi 4:5 as possible further background. In the vault's Septuagint, Joel 2:11 has megale he hemera kyriou ... kai tis estai hikanos aute; Nahum 1:6 has apo prosopou orges autou tis hypostesetai; Malachi 3:2 has tis hypostesetai. Keener says the verse reflects especially Joel 2:11 and compares Malachi 3:2; the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible says the question adapts Joel 2:11 and cites Malachi 3:2; the ESV Study Bible cites Nahum 1:5-6 and Malachi 3:2; the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cites Joel 2:11 and Isaiah 13:9. The grade is drawn here: the phrases are traceable but spread over several texts.

entries.title: Revelation 7:1, four angels holding back the four winds
entries.summary: The four winds held back at the corners of the earth recall the four winds of heaven in Zechariah 6, the horse teams John has just used, and other prophets' winds of judgment.
entries.plain: **A dam holds back a flood only until the gates are opened.** In Zechariah 6 the four chariot teams are called the four winds of heaven, sent out over the earth. Jeremiah and Daniel also speak of four winds that bring judgment or turmoil. John sees four angels standing at the world's four corners. They hold the four winds in check. Nothing may harm land, sea or trees until God's servants are marked.
entries.same: Four winds (tessares anemoi) that sweep over the earth. Zechariah 6:5, Jeremiah 49:36 and Daniel 7:2 all use the phrase in Greek. In Zechariah and Jeremiah God sends the winds.
entries.differs: Zechariah's winds belong to heaven. John's winds belong to the earth. In Zechariah the winds go out at once; in John angels hold them back for a time. Jeremiah's winds scatter one nation, Elam. John's would harm the whole earth, sea and trees.
entries.turn: Beale reads the winds as the four horsemen of chapter 6 seen another way. The pause shows that God's people are marked before the woes begin. The same powers that harm the world cannot touch what God has sealed for himself.
entries.not: **Not Zechariah's chariots.** John keeps the four winds and drops the horses. In Zechariah the winds go out over the earth; here angels hold them back until God's servants are sealed.
entries.deeper: Beale identifies the four winds with the four horsemen of 6:1-8, because Zechariah 6:5 calls the horse teams the four winds of heaven, and John has just drawn on that chapter. He defends this reading of Zechariah 6:5 against translations that make the horses go toward the winds. He adds that Jeremiah 49:36, where four winds are God's agents against Elam, stands in the same tradition and may also be behind 7:2-3. In the vault's Septuagint, Zechariah 6:5 reads hoi tessares anemoi tou ouranou, Jeremiah 49:36 tessaras anemous, and Daniel 7:2 hoi tessares anemoi tou ouranou. The four corners of the earth recall Isaiah 11:12 and Ezekiel 7:2. Keener notes the winds were probably seen as angels even in Zechariah 6:5. The CSB Study Bible's cross-references list Isaiah 11:12, Jeremiah 49:36, Ezekiel 7:2, Daniel 7:2 and Zechariah 6:5. Walton notes that Zechariah's teams are called spirits, the same word as winds. The grade is drawn here: the phrase is shared, and the link to Zechariah rests on the context John has just used.
entries.dissent: Beale ties the winds to the horsemen of chapter 6. Mounce and Thomas, as Beale reports, deny the link, reading Zechariah 6:5 as horses going out toward the four winds. Keener reads the winds more generally as forces of nature under angels' care. Beale and Keener read the four corners and four winds as ordinary speech for the whole world. MacArthur reads the winds as all the earth's winds from every side, and the corners as the points of the compass; the angels stop the world's winds for a short pause.
