aw.n: Revelation 7:1-17, the sealing of the 144,000 and the crowd in white
aw.s: Four angels hold back the winds until God's servants are sealed on their foreheads, 144,000 from the tribes of Israel. Then John sees a crowd no one can count, from every nation, in white robes with palm branches, who have come out of the great tribulation and whom the Lamb will shepherd.

entries.title: Revelation 7:3, a seal on the foreheads of God's servants
entries.summary: Judgment waits until God's servants are sealed on their foreheads, as in Ezekiel 9 the faithful are marked before the slaughter in Jerusalem.
entries.plain: **Before a storm, a family paints a sign on the door so rescuers know who is inside.** In Ezekiel 9 a man in linen marks the brow of each person who mourns the city's sins. Only then may the executioners begin, and they must not touch anyone with the mark. In Revelation an angel tells the four angels to do no harm until God's servants are sealed on their foreheads.
entries.same: A mark on the foreheads (epi ta metopa in Ezekiel, epi ton metopon in John) of God's faithful, placed before judgment falls. In both, the harm must wait until the marking is done.
entries.differs: Ezekiel's mark is a letter, the Hebrew tav; the Greek translation calls it a sign (semeion). John calls it a seal (sphragis), the stamp of an owner. Ezekiel marks a few in one city. John seals the servants of God before harm comes on the whole earth.
entries.turn: In Ezekiel the mark spares the faithful when Jerusalem falls. Beale says John's seal protects faith more than bodies, since believers still suffer. Later the seal turns out to be the name of God and the Lamb (14:1; 22:4), set against the mark of the beast.
entries.not: **Not a visible tattoo.** Keener notes that Ezekiel's mark was not one people could see, and that Revelation presumably means it the same way.
entries.deeper: Beale calls Ezekiel 9 the best background for the sealing: God has an angel mark the true believers and has other angels kill the unfaithful. In the Hebrew of Ezekiel 9:4 the mark is tav, the last letter of the alphabet; Walton says in the old script it was an X or a + shape, and the Jewish Study Bible agrees. Beale doubts John knew the old letter shape. In the vault's Septuagint, 9:4 reads dos to semeion epi ta metopa ton andron, and 9:6 says do not approach anyone on whom is the sign. John has sphragisomen tous doulous tou theou hemon epi ton metopon auton. Beale cites Psalms of Solomon 15:6, 9, where God's mark is on the righteous and a mark of destruction on sinners. Keener says the sealing is taken directly from Ezekiel 9:4-6; the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible calls Ezekiel 9:4 the most important background; the ESV Study Bible, the CSB Study Bible's cross-references, the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible and Wright all cite Ezekiel 9. The grade is drawn here: the scene and its order could hardly come from anywhere else.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Moyise, who says the sealing is almost certainly modeled on Ezekiel 9:4-6, and he calls Ezekiel 9 surely John's source. He reads the whole chapter: the six executioners, the man in linen, the mark on those who groan over the abominations. With Moyise he notes that John stays close to Ezekiel, a mark that protects from slaughter, rather than Paul's language of sealing. Moyise also notes that in both books the sealing is followed by fire thrown from the altar (Ezekiel 10:2; Revelation 8:5).
entries.dissent: The sources differ on what the seal protects. Beale argues it guards faith and salvation, not bodies. Moyise, as Heiser reads him, rules out physical protection. Aune, also read by Heiser, says it protects from God's wrath, and Charles from demonic attack. Heiser himself keeps a physical element open, since the trumpets copy the plagues of Egypt. MacArthur reads the seal as God's name (14:1), a mark of ownership that protects the sealed while they carry out their mission.

entries.title: Revelation 7:3, the sign that turns the destroyer away
entries.summary: Behind the seal stands the Passover blood on the doors of Israel's houses, a sign that kept the destroyer out while Egypt was struck.
entries.plain: **A pass at the gate lets you through while others are stopped.** On the night of the last plague, blood on the doorposts marked Israel's houses. When God saw it, he passed over, and the destroyer did not enter. John's servants of God are sealed before the plagues of the trumpets begin. Beale thinks the Passover sign may stand behind both Ezekiel's mark and John's seal.
entries.same: A sign that marks God's own before a judgment, so that the harm passes them by. In the Greek of Exodus 12:13 the blood is a sign (semeion). The Greek of Ezekiel 9 uses that word for the mark.
entries.differs: In Exodus the sign is blood on a door. In John it is a seal on the forehead. Exodus protects the firstborn on one night; John's seal comes before a whole series of plagues. Exodus names no seal, and the link runs through the pattern, not shared words.
entries.turn: Beale notes that the trumpets and bowls that follow are modeled on the plagues of Egypt, and the sealed are protected from them. So the scene repeats the order of the exodus: God's people are marked, and then the blows fall on their oppressors.
entries.not: **Not a promise that believers never suffer.** Beale stresses that the sealed still pass through trials, and Heiser notes that the Israelites were not spared every plague either.
entries.deeper: Beale says the blood on the Hebrews' doors at Passover (Exodus 12:7, 13, 22-28) did the same work as Ezekiel's mark. In his view the Passover may lie behind both Ezekiel 9 and Revelation 7:2-3, since the seal protects believers from the trumpet and bowl plagues modeled on the exodus. Walton notes that marking those who will survive God's wrath is comparable to the blood on the doorposts, and that the two marks were linked early. Wright compares the sealing to the Passover blood that spared Israel from the angel of death. Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible note that God protected his people in Goshen during the plagues. In the vault's Septuagint, Exodus 12:13 reads estai to haima hymin en semeio, and 12:23 says the Lord will not let the destroyer (ton olothreuonta) enter. The grade is possible: the pattern is shared, the wording is not.
entries.heiser: Heiser calls Beale's link to Passover decisive, with one qualification. The trumpets and bowls copy the plagues, and the 144,000 are protected from them as Israel was at Passover. He is frustrated that Beale then turns the protection into a purely spiritual one. For Heiser the Old Testament data keeps a physical element on the table: in Egypt some plagues spared Israel, though the last one spared only houses marked with blood.
entries.dissent: Beale ends by saying John's seal protects faith, not bodies. Heiser thinks the same Passover evidence points to some physical protection as well. Wright says those sealed may still pass through great suffering. MacArthur reads the seal as God's protection of the 144,000 while they carry out their mission.

entries.title: Revelation 7:4, sealed from every tribe of Israel
entries.summary: Twelve thousand from each of twelve tribes draws on the prophets' hope that all the tribes of Israel would be gathered again.
entries.plain: **A family reunion that lists every branch of the family tree says no one has been forgotten.** The prophets hoped that God would gather Israel's scattered tribes and make them one again. Ezekiel 37 pictures Joseph's stick and Judah's stick joined in one hand. John hears the number of the sealed: twelve thousand from each of twelve tribes. The hope of a restored Israel stands behind the list.
entries.same: All twelve tribes of Israel, gathered and counted. In the Greek of Ezekiel 37:19 God takes the tribe (phyle) of Joseph and joins the tribes of Israel to the tribe of Judah. John lists tribe by tribe (ek phyles).
entries.differs: No prophet lists the tribes as John does. Ezekiel 48 includes Dan, first of all; John leaves Dan out. John lists Joseph and Manasseh but not Ephraim, and he counts Levi. Judah comes first. Bauckham, as Heiser reports, says this order matches no other list.
entries.turn: The sources differ on what John does with the hope. Heiser reads Jews who follow the Lamb, seen apart from the great crowd from every nation. Beale reads the twelve tribes as a picture of the whole church as the true Israel. MacArthur reads Jewish believers sealed in a tribulation still to come. All three tie the list to the promised gathering of the tribes.
entries.not: **Not a list copied from the prophets.** No Old Testament text names the tribes in John's order, leaves out Dan, or gives each tribe the same number.
entries.deeper: Keener says that whether the number is figurative or literal, the allusion is clearly to the Old Testament and Jewish hope for the restoration of the twelve tribes, and that the normal Jewish understanding was that the tribes would inherit the land together (Ezekiel 48). Beale lists the tradition of the restoration of all the tribes (Isaiah 11:10-13; 27:12-13; Jeremiah 31:7-9; Ezekiel 37:15-23) and argues John applies it to the church. Aune, as Heiser reads him, takes the equal number per tribe as a sign of interest in Israel's end-time restoration and cites Ezekiel 37:15-23. Bauckham, also read by Heiser, suggests the use of Joseph for Ephraim may come from Ezekiel 37:16, 19, where Joseph is linked to Ephraim. In the vault's Septuagint, Ezekiel 37:19 reads ten phylen Ioseph ten dia cheiros Ephraim. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible notes Dan was first in Ezekiel 48:1. The grade is possible: the hope is a theme, and no single verse supplies John's list.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads the 144,000 as ethnic Jews who are also followers of the Lamb: "they're Jews who follow the lamb". He agrees with Aune that the great crowd of 7:9 is a different group, since it cannot be counted, comes from every nation, stands in heaven, and has already come through the tribulation. Everything in 7:1-8 is Jewish and Old Testament in its sources. He warns end-time systems on both sides not to use this text to keep Jewish and Gentile believers apart, or to deny the difference.
entries.dissent: The sources split on who the 144,000 are. Heiser, with Aune, reads Jewish followers of Jesus, distinct from the crowd of 7:9. Beale, the ESV Study Bible and Wright read one group, the whole church, heard as a number and then seen as a crowd. The CSB Study Bible calls a literal Israel after a future conversion highly plausible. MacArthur reads a band of Jewish believers, 12,000 chosen from each tribe and sealed for protection, who bring many Jews and Gentiles to faith in a tribulation still to come, the firstfruits of a redeemed Israel. Keener leaves it open. On Dan's absence, Beale and the CSB Study Bible suggest idolatry; Bauckham calls it arbitrary; Heiser says the Dan tradition should not be dismissed but may be unanswerable.

entries.title: Revelation 7:4-8, counted tribe by tribe like an army
entries.summary: The tribe-by-tribe count has the form of the census in Numbers 1, where Moses counted Israel's fighting men by their tribes.
entries.plain: **A roll call by regiment tells you the people being counted are soldiers.** In Numbers 1 Moses counts the men able to go to war, tribe by tribe, with a number for each tribe. John hears a count of the same kind: twelve thousand from each tribe. Some read the 144,000 as God's army, mustered for a battle they will win by staying faithful.
entries.same: A list of Israel's tribes with a number for each one. The Greek of Numbers 1:21 counts from the tribe (ek tes phyles) of Reuben; John repeats from the tribe (ek phyles) twelve times.
entries.differs: In Numbers each tribe has a different total, and Levi is left out of the count for war. John gives every tribe the same number and includes Levi. He drops Dan. And no weapons appear; the count is of those sealed.
entries.turn: Beale, after Bauckham, reads the 144,000 as an army for a holy war fought the Lamb's way, by faithful suffering. In 7:14 they wash their robes, as soldiers washed after battle. In that reading the census form makes the sealed a people ready for conflict, though not with swords.
entries.not: **Not a call to arms.** Every source that sees an army here says the battle is fought by faith and witness, not by force.
entries.deeper: Beale, following Bauckham, notes that a census in the Old Testament was for military strength (Numbers 1:3, 18, 20; 26:2; 2 Samuel 24:1-9), that from the tribe of may echo Numbers 1:21 in Greek, and that the odd nominative sealed at the start and end of the list may echo the numbering formulas of Numbers 1:19 and 1:44. He adds that the War Scroll from Qumran used the census of Numbers 1 to organize its end-time army by twelve tribes. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible compares the form to a military census (Numbers 1:3, 18, 20; 26:2); the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible says the list may echo the census in Numbers 1-2; the CSB Study Bible compares Israel's camp in Numbers 2. In the vault's Septuagint, Numbers 1:21 reads he episkepsis auton ek tes phyles Rhouben. The grade is possible: the form fits, and the sources hedge.
entries.heiser: Heiser says the counting reminds anyone of the census lists in Numbers. He reads Aune: a census was usually for military strength (Numbers 1), which Revelation 14:4 seems to confirm, though Aune then pulls back because 7:4-8 has no war imagery and prefers restoration. Bauckham, Heiser notes, sees Judah first only in the military camp order of Numbers 2 and finds the military link weak. Heiser keeps it: he thinks the sprinkling of military language fits spiritual warfare.
entries.dissent: Bauckham's book, as Beale reports, argues strongly for an army. Aune, and Bauckham's War Scroll article, as Heiser reads them, find the military element faint. Heiser and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible keep the army reading as spiritual warfare. MacArthur reads the 144,000 as Jewish evangelists sent on a mission, not as an army.

entries.title: Revelation 7:5, Judah first
entries.summary: Judah heads the list, not Reuben the firstborn, because Jacob's blessing promised that the ruler would come from Judah.
entries.plain: **When a team lists its captain before the oldest player, the order makes a point.** Reuben was Jacob's firstborn, and most lists of the tribes begin with him. Jacob's blessing in Genesis 49 gives Judah the scepter and says his brothers will bow to him. John's list of the sealed begins with Judah. The tribe of the king now leads the tribes.
entries.same: Judah placed ahead of his brothers. In Genesis 49:8 the sons of Judah's father bow down to him, and 49:10 says a ruler will not leave Judah. In John, Judah stands first of the twelve.
entries.differs: Genesis gives no list at all; the echo lies in the order, not in shared words. Genesis says the brothers bow to Judah. John simply places Judah first and gives every tribe the same twelve thousand.
entries.turn: Revelation 5:5 has already called Jesus Judah's lion. Beale reads Judah's first place as the promised king taking his place at the head of the tribes. Through him, the Greek of Genesis 49:10 says, comes the hope of the nations.
entries.not: **Not a ranking of which tribe is better.** The equal numbers show every tribe sealed in full, with Judah first because of its king.
entries.deeper: Beale notes that Judah is rarely first in the Old Testament lists (Numbers 2:3; 34:19; Joshua 21:4; 1 Chronicles 12:23-37) and says the priority of Judah fulfills Genesis 49:8, that the other tribes will bow down to Judah. He adds that Ezekiel 37:15-19 develops Genesis 49:8 by placing all the tribes under Judah, and that the Greek of Genesis 49:10 makes the ruler the expectation of nations. In the vault's Septuagint, Genesis 49:10 reads ouk ekleipsei archon ex Iouda ... kai autos prosdokia ethnon. The CSB Study Bible says Judah comes first as the royal tribe (Genesis 49:9-10) into which Jesus was born. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible lists Judah first as the tribe of Israel's king (5:5; Genesis 49:8-10). The ESV Study Bible and Wright give the same reason without citing Genesis. The grade is possible: the echo rests on the order of a list, not on wording.

entries.title: Revelation 7:9, a crowd no one could count
entries.summary: The great multitude that no one could number recalls God's promise to Abraham and Jacob of descendants too many to count.
entries.plain: **A promise kept on a bigger scale than anyone expected is still the same promise.** God told Abraham to count the stars if he could, and told Jacob his offspring would be like sand too many to number. John now sees a crowd so large no one could count it. It is drawn from every nation and tribe, every people and tongue. Beale hears in it the promise of a countless family coming true.
entries.same: A multitude too large to number. The Greek of Genesis 32:12 and 16:10 has a seed that will not be counted (ouk arithmethesetai) for its multitude; John has a crowd which no one could count (arithmesai).
entries.differs: The promise in Genesis is to Abraham's offspring, Israel. John's crowd comes from every nation. Genesis looks ahead; John sees the crowd already standing before the throne in white robes.
entries.turn: Beale reads the crowd as the final fulfillment of the promise to Abraham. The descendants he was promised turn out to include people from every nation who belong to the Lamb. For Beale that makes the crowd one more way John calls the church God's Israel.
entries.not: **Not a denial that the crowd is huge but real.** Keener notes that innumerable meant too many to count, not infinite.
entries.deeper: Beale hears in the uncountable crowd the promise made to Abraham and to Jacob, citing above all the Greek of Genesis 32:13 (32:12 in English) and 16:10, with 13:16, 15:5, 22:17, 26:4 and Hosea 1:10. In the vault's Septuagint, Genesis 32:12 and 16:10 both have ouk arithmethesetai apo tou plethous. He reports Bauckham's view that 7:9 alludes to the promise of a multitude of nations (Genesis 17:4), signposted by putting nation first in the list, and qualifies it. He notes Jewish writings that saw the census of Numbers as a fulfillment of the same promise, which links the counted tribes to the uncountable crowd. The CSB Study Bible's cross-references at 7:9 list Genesis 15:5 and 32:12. The phrase every nation, tribe, people and language comes from Daniel, as at 5:9. The grade is drawn here: the idea is traceable to the patriarchal promise.
entries.dissent: Beale, the ESV Study Bible and Wright read the crowd as the same people as the 144,000, heard and then seen. Heiser, with Aune, reads them as Gentiles alongside the Jewish 144,000. Keener notes both readings. MacArthur reads two groups: the Jewish 144,000 on earth and, here, their converts from every people, saved in a tribulation still to come and now in heaven.

entries.title: Revelation 7:9, palm branches in their hands
entries.summary: The palm branches recall the Feast of Tabernacles, which Zechariah said the nations would one day keep.
entries.plain: **A crowd waving the flags of an old festival is joining its story.** At the Feast of Tabernacles Israel took palm branches and rejoiced before God. The feast remembered God's care in the wilderness after Egypt. Zechariah saw the nations coming up each year to keep it. John's crowd from every nation holds palm branches as they stand before the throne.
entries.same: Palm branches held in worship before God. The Greek of Leviticus 23:40 names branches of palm trees (phoinikon); John's crowd holds palms (phoinikes). Zechariah 14:16 has the nations keeping the feast (skenopegia).
entries.differs: Leviticus gives the feast to Israel. John's palm bearers come from every nation, as Zechariah foresaw. The feast is kept not in Jerusalem but before God's throne. John never names the feast.
entries.turn: Beale reads the scene as a heavenly Feast of Tabernacles. People from all nations celebrate their own exodus, God's protection through their wilderness, and their victory. The theme returns in 7:15, where God spreads his tent over them.
entries.not: **Not a victory sign and nothing more.** Palms did mark victory, but Beale and Keener tie them here to the feast of God's care in the wilderness.
entries.deeper: Beale calls palm branches an allusion to the Feast of Tabernacles (Leviticus 23:40, 43; Nehemiah 8:15; 2 Maccabees 10:7), a feast of thanks for harvest and a memory of Israel living in tents under God's protection. He notes palms also marked victory in 1 Maccabees 13:51. He suggests 7:9-17 may reflect Jewish readings of Zechariah 14, where Gentiles keep the feast. Keener says palm branches were especially used at Tabernacles and that the remnant of all nations would go up to keep it (Zechariah 14:16). The CSB Study Bible's cross-references give Leviticus 23:40 and John 12:13. In the vault's Septuagint, Leviticus 23:40 has kallynthra phoinikon, and Zechariah 14:16 tou heortazein ten heorten tes skenopegias. The grade is drawn here: Beale names an allusion, and the feast is the main use of palms in the law.
entries.dissent: Beale, backing Bauckham's army reading, notes that white robes and palms also marked military victory. Keener stresses the Feast of Tabernacles alone. Beale holds both together.

entries.title: Revelation 7:10, salvation belongs to our God
entries.summary: The crowd's shout that salvation belongs to God echoes the closing line of Psalm 3, a prayer for rescue from enemies.
entries.plain: **A team that chants a line from an old anthem is claiming its story.** Psalm 3 is David's prayer while enemies surround him. It ends by saying that salvation belongs to the Lord. The crowd before the throne shouts almost the same words. They credit their rescue to God, seated on his throne, and to the Lamb.
entries.same: Salvation said to belong to God. The Greek of Psalm 3:8 (3:9 in Greek numbering) reads tou kyriou he soteria; John has he soteria to theo hemon.
entries.differs: The psalm credits the Lord alone. John's crowd credits God on the throne and the Lamb together. The psalm is one man's prayer under attack; John's is a shout of a crowd that has come through.
entries.turn: Beale reads salvation here as rescue and victory over the powers that tried to break their faith. The victory belongs to God, not to them, and John gives the Lamb the same share as God.
entries.not: **Not a direct quotation.** The sources offer the psalm only as a comparison, and the words are common in worship.
entries.deeper: The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible compares Psalm 3:8 and 62:11, and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible compares Psalm 3:8 with Exodus 15:2. The CSB Study Bible's cross-references at 7:10 list Psalm 3:8 among many texts. Beale reads soteria here in its sense of deliverance and victory, citing Psalm 3 and its context of rescue from enemies, and Jonah 2:9. In the vault's Septuagint, the psalm verse reads tou kyriou he soteria. The grade is possible: the wording is close, but the phrase is short and common, and the sources only compare it.

aw.s: Four angels hold back the winds until God's servants are sealed on their foreheads, 144,000 from the tribes of Israel. Then John sees a crowd no one can count, from every nation, in white robes with palm branches, who have come out of the great tribulation and whom the Lamb will shepherd.

entries.title: Revelation 7:14, the great tribulation
entries.summary: The crowd comes out of the great tribulation, the time of distress Daniel 12:1 foretold, when God's people would be rescued.
entries.plain: **Calling a storm the big one tells everyone which storm you mean.** Daniel 12 speaks of a time of distress like none before it, when Michael stands up and God's people are rescued. Jesus called it great tribulation. An elder tells John who the crowd in white are. They have come through Daniel's time of trouble, the great tribulation.
entries.same: A time of great distress for God's people, from which they are brought through. Daniel 12:1 in Greek has thlipsis; John has he thlipsis he megale, the great tribulation.
entries.differs: Daniel describes distress like none before it. John names it the great tribulation, the phrase Jesus used in Matthew 24:21. Daniel's rescued people are those written in the book; John's crowd have washed their robes in the Lamb's blood. Neither text gives the time a length.
entries.turn: The crowd has come out of the distress, having passed through it. John ties Daniel's time of trouble to the Lamb's people, cleansed by his blood. Beale says the tribulation began with Jesus' sufferings and runs through the church age, rising at the end.
entries.not: **Not a phrase from Daniel.** Daniel speaks of a time of distress like none before it. The name great tribulation comes from Jesus in Matthew 24:21, which points back to Daniel.
entries.deeper: Beale calls Daniel 12:1 the likely origin of the great tribulation, since outside Revelation the phrase occurs in the New Testament only in Matthew 24:21, a fuller reference to Daniel 12:1. He notes the War Scroll expected God to protect the saints through Daniel's time of distress, and that 1 Maccabees 9:27 already saw a great tribulation in the second century BC. In the vault's Septuagint, Daniel 12:1 reads kairos thlipseos hoia ou gegonen. Keener says the phrase refers to Daniel 12:1; the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible says it probably evokes Daniel 12:1 with Matthew 24:21; the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible says it alludes to Daniel 12:1; the CSB Study Bible cross-references Daniel 12:1 and Mark 13:19. Heiser adds Jeremiah 30:7, the time of Jacob's distress, which scholars link to Daniel 12:1. The grade is drawn here: the phrase and the idea point to Daniel.
entries.heiser: Heiser rejects equating the great tribulation with the seventieth week of Daniel, since no verse ties tribulation to a week or seven years. Its Old Testament context, he says, is Daniel 12:1, with Jeremiah 30:7, the time of Jacob's trouble, and Matthew 24:21. Four things can be said for sure: it is tied to Daniel 12:1 and Jeremiah 30:7, linked to Matthew 24:21, comes before the final judgment, and involves persecution of believers. He reports Beale's view that it is already but not yet.
entries.dissent: The sources differ on when the tribulation happens. Beale says it began with Christ and runs through the church age. Heiser and Beale note that no text ties Daniel 12:1 to a seven-year span. MacArthur reads the great tribulation as the later half of a seven-year period still to come, Daniel's seventieth week. The crowd, in his reading, are people saved and killed in those years, who were not yet believers when the church was raptured before it. Charles and the futurists Beale names place it at the very end. The CSB Study Bible links it to the hour of testing in 3:10 and a possible rapture before it. The ESV Study Bible gives both views.

entries.title: Revelation 7:14, robes washed and made white
entries.summary: Being made white through trial comes from Daniel's last chapters, and the washing recalls the prophets' promise that sin would be made white as snow.
entries.plain: **Gold is not ruined by the furnace; it comes out purer.** Daniel 11 and 12 say that the wise will be tested and made white through the trials of the end. Isaiah and the psalms speak of sins washed and made white as snow. John's crowd has washed its robes, whitening them in the Lamb's blood. They were purified through the trial, by the Lamb's death.
entries.same: Being made white. Daniel 12:10 in Greek has many will be whitened (ekleukanthosi); John has they made them white (eleukanan). Isaiah 1:18 and Psalm 51:7 in Greek use the same verb for sins made white.
entries.differs: Daniel says the faithful are made white by testing. Isaiah says God will make scarlet sins white. John joins the two and adds what no Old Testament text could: the robes are made white in blood, the Lamb's. The paradox of whitening in blood is John's own.
entries.turn: Beale reads the robes as purity shown by faith that held on through trials. The faith is in the Lamb's death for them. For Beale the crowd fulfills Daniel's hope for faithful Israel, and the cleansing comes from the cross.
entries.not: **Not a picture Daniel paints.** Daniel's wise are made white by testing, and Isaiah's sins are made white as snow. No Old Testament text makes robes white in blood.
entries.deeper: Beale says the idea of being made white by persevering through tribulation is found in the Old Testament only in Daniel 11-12: Daniel 11:35 speaks of refining and making white until the end, and 12:10 has many purified and made white. He reports Bauckham's support for the Daniel background, and calls it the most plausible. In the vault's Theodotion Daniel, 12:10 reads eklegosi kai ekleukanthosi kai pyrothosi kai hagiasthosi polloi. Beale also hears Genesis 49:11, where Judah's ruler washes his robe in the blood of grapes, and Exodus 19:10, 14, where Israel washes garments before meeting God. He says the image generally reflects Isaiah 1:18, 64:6 and Zechariah 3:3-5. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible says washed white recalls the promises of Psalm 51:7 and Isaiah 1:18; the CSB Study Bible's cross-references list the same; the ESV Study Bible compares Psalm 51:7. The grade is drawn here: Beale names Daniel as the plausible background, but no single text supplies the whole picture.
entries.dissent: Beale reads the blood as Christ's atoning death, and MacArthur reads it the same way. Bauckham, as Beale reports, reads it mainly as the saints' own suffering, like soldiers washing after battle. Keener calls the image ritual: sacrificial blood purified things for worship. On who washed their robes, Beale argues for all the redeemed, since 22:14 uses the picture of everyone who enters the city. MacArthur reads people saved in a tribulation still to come and killed for their faith.

entries.title: Revelation 7:15, God will spread his tent over them
entries.summary: God sheltering his people with his tent joins Ezekiel's promise of God's dwelling with restored Israel and Isaiah's canopy over Zion.
entries.plain: **A host who pitches a tent over the guests is promising shade and safety.** Ezekiel 37 promises that God's dwelling will be with his restored people forever. Isaiah 4 pictures a cloud by day and fire by night, a canopy and shelter over Zion. John says the one on the throne will spread his tent over the crowd. Day and night they worship and serve in his temple.
entries.same: God dwelling over his people as in a tent. Ezekiel 37:27 in Greek promises God's dwelling (kataskenosis) among them; John has he will tent over them (skenosei). Isaiah 4:6 adds shelter from the heat (kaumatos), which John picks up in 7:16.
entries.differs: Ezekiel's promise is for Israel brought home and made one. John applies it to a crowd from every nation. Ezekiel and Isaiah speak of the land and Zion; John speaks of God's presence in heaven, before the throne.
entries.turn: Beale notes that Ezekiel said the nations would know God sanctifies Israel when his sanctuary is among them. John sees the nations themselves inside. The tent also carries on the Feast of Tabernacles from 7:9.
entries.not: **Not Ezekiel's temple plan.** John borrows Ezekiel's promise that God will dwell with his people, from 37:27. He does not draw on the temple described in Ezekiel 40-48.
entries.deeper: Beale calls being in his temple, with God tenting over them, a clear echo of Ezekiel 37:26-28, confirmed by 21:3, which quotes Ezekiel 37:27 more fully and is followed by the same allusions as 7:16-17. In the vault's Septuagint, Ezekiel 37:27 reads estai he kataskenosis mou en autois. He says Isaiah 4:4-6 may also be echoed. Keener says God's tabernacle as a refuge directly echoes Isaiah 4:5-6, a new exodus text; the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible says the shelter alludes to Isaiah 4:5-6; the ESV Study Bible compares Ezekiel 37:27. Isaiah 4:6 in Greek reads eis skian apo kaumatos kai en skepe. Beale suggests the verb skenoo may play on the Hebrew shekinah. The grade is Beale's own word for the Ezekiel link: a clear echo.
entries.dissent: Beale puts Ezekiel 37:27 first and Isaiah 4 second. Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible name Isaiah 4:5-6 and not Ezekiel. They agree the picture is God's shelter for his people. On the temple, Beale reads it here as the presence of God and the Lamb, as in 21:22. MacArthur reads it as God's throne in heaven. He expects a temple on earth during the thousand years (Ezekiel 40-48), and none in the eternal state, where God himself is the temple.

entries.title: Revelation 7:16-17, no more hunger or thirst, led to springs of water
entries.summary: The promise of no hunger, no thirst, no scorching sun, and a guide to springs of water is Isaiah 49:10, given now to the Lamb's people.
entries.plain: **A host who repeats the menu of an old feast promises the same meal.** In Isaiah 49 God promises exiles coming home that they will not hunger or thirst. Neither heat nor sun will strike them, and he will guide them to water. John says the same of the crowd before the throne. But now it is the Lamb who leads them, to springs of the water of life.
entries.same: The Greek runs almost word for word. Both have ou peinasousin oude dipsesousin, they will not hunger nor thirst. Both have the sun (helios) and the heat. Both lead them to springs of waters (pegon hydaton).
entries.differs: John adds anymore (eti) twice, since the crowd has known hunger. Isaiah's springs of water become springs of the water of life. In Isaiah the one who has mercy, God, leads them. In John the Lamb leads them, and he is also their shepherd.
entries.turn: Isaiah's promise was for Israel's return from exile. John sees it kept for a crowd from every nation, after their tribulation. Beale says Jewish readers applied the verse to the return of the ten tribes, and that John applies it to the church. The comfort also answers the famine of 6:5-6.
entries.not: **Not John's own promise.** The words are Isaiah's, spoken to exiles coming home. John adds the word anymore, the water of life, and the Lamb as the one who leads.
entries.deeper: Beale says John appeals to Isaiah 49:10, a result of Israel's restoration into God's presence. In the vault's Septuagint, Isaiah 49:10 reads ou peinasousin oude dipsesousin, oude pataxei autous kauson oude helios ... kai dia pegon hydaton axei autous; John has ou peinasousin eti oude dipsesousin eti oude me pese ep' autous ho helios oude pan kauma ... kai hodegesei autous epi zoes pegas hydaton. He adds that the shepherding comes from Isaiah 49:9, where they will be pastured. Keener says Revelation borrows the language of Isaiah 49:10; the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible sets the two side by side; the ESV Study Bible, the CSB Study Bible's cross-references and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible all cite Isaiah 49:10. Walton notes that Assyrian texts describe a just king's reign with food and drink for the needy, and that Isaiah's promises join the messianic profile. The grade is drawn here: the wording is nearly the same.
entries.dissent: The sources differ on when the promise is kept. Beale reads it as kept for the church, and notes that 22:17 already invites the thirsty to take the water of life now. MacArthur reads the crowd as believers saved and killed in a tribulation still to come, now sheltered in God's presence in heaven from all they suffered on earth.

entries.title: Revelation 7:17, the Lamb will be their shepherd
entries.summary: The Lamb shepherding his people takes the shepherd role God holds in Psalm 23 and promises to David's heir in Ezekiel 34.
entries.plain: **A story where the smallest lamb leads the flock turns the usual roles upside down.** In Psalm 23 the Lord is the shepherd who leads his sheep beside quiet waters. In Ezekiel 34 God promises one shepherd, his servant David, to tend his people. John says the Lamb, at the very heart of the throne, will shepherd them and lead them to water. The one who was slain now leads the flock.
entries.same: A shepherd who tends his people and leads them to water. The Greek of Ezekiel 34:23 has poimanei autous, he will shepherd them, exactly John's words. Psalm 23:1 has the Lord shepherds me (poimainei).
entries.differs: In the psalm the Lord is the shepherd; in Ezekiel it is David's heir. John gives the role to a Lamb, an animal of the flock. Beale says shepherd may stand in for Isaiah's word pastured, borrowed from Ezekiel.
entries.turn: Beale and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible read the Lamb as the divine shepherd. He stands where God stands in Psalm 23. Wright calls it a role reversal: the lamb becomes the shepherd, taking both the royal role and the divine one.
entries.not: **Not a weak leader.** Keener notes lambs were the weakest in the flock, yet this Lamb stands in the middle of the throne.
entries.deeper: Beale says the image of the Lamb shepherding comes from Isaiah 49:9-10, and that Psalm 23:1-2 may also be echoed, since there God shepherds his people and leads them to water. He suggests shepherd them (poimanei autous) replaces Isaiah's pastured because of Ezekiel 37:24 and 34:23, where David will be one shepherd over all Israel. In the vault's Septuagint, Ezekiel 34:23 reads kai poimanei autous ... kai estai auton poimen, and Psalm 23:1 kyrios poimainei me. The ESV Study Bible and the CSB Study Bible's cross-references cite Psalm 23:1-2, with Ezekiel 34:23 in the cross-references; the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cites Psalm 23:1-2 and Ezekiel 34:11-16; Wright names Psalm 23. The grade is possible: Beale says may be echoed, though Ezekiel's two words match John exactly.

entries.title: Revelation 7:17, God will wipe away every tear
entries.summary: The promise that God will wipe every tear comes from Isaiah 25:8, and John's verb is closer to the Hebrew than to the Greek translation.
entries.plain: **A parent drying a child's face after a bad dream is a picture everyone understands.** Isaiah 25 describes a feast for all peoples on God's mountain. God swallows up death and wipes the tears from every face. John ends the vision of the crowd with the same promise. God himself will dry every tear they cry.
entries.same: God removing every tear (pan dakryon). Both texts make God the one who does it and both say every tear.
entries.differs: The Greek translation of Isaiah 25:8 says the Lord took away (aphelen) every tear. The Hebrew says he will wipe (machah). John has will wipe away (exaleipsei), which matches the Hebrew sense, a point drawn here. Isaiah says from every face; John says from their eyes. John leaves out the reason Isaiah gives, death swallowed up, until 21:4.
entries.turn: In Isaiah the end of tears comes at the feast where death is defeated. Beale says John assumes that reason here and states it in 21:4. Those who suffered through the tribulation are comforted by God's own hand.
entries.not: **Not a promise for this life only.** Beale and the ESV Study Bible tie the promise to the new Jerusalem of 21:4.
entries.deeper: Beale calls this an allusion to the restoration promise of Isaiah 25:8, appended to the Isaiah 49:10 wording. In Isaiah the end of mourning comes because God will swallow up death, which John states in 21:4. In the vault's Septuagint, Isaiah 25:8 reads kai palin aphelen kyrios ho theos pan dakryon apo pantos prosopou. The Hebrew reads umachah adonai YHWH dim'ah me'al kol panim, and the Lord God will wipe tears from all faces. Revelation 7:17 has exaleipsei ho theos pan dakryon ek ton ophthalmon auton. The match of wipe to the Hebrew is drawn here; the sources do not discuss it. Keener says the verse alludes to Isaiah 25:8; the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the ESV Study Bible, the CSB Study Bible's cross-references and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible all cite it, and Wright links it to 21:4. The grade is drawn here: the words and the giver are the same.

entries.title: Revelation 8:1, silence in heaven
entries.summary: The silence when the seventh seal opens draws on the prophets' call for all the earth to be silent before the Lord as he rises to judge.
entries.plain: **A courtroom goes quiet just before the verdict is read.** Habakkuk tells the whole earth to hush, because God sits in his holy house. Zephaniah and Zechariah give the same order: God's day is close, and he has risen from his dwelling. When the Lamb opens the seventh seal, heaven falls silent for about half an hour. Beale reads the hush as the silence before judgment.
entries.same: Silence before God at the moment of judgment, tied to his holy temple. In all three prophets the Lord is in his holy dwelling or comes from it. The earth, or all flesh, is told to be silent.
entries.differs: The prophets command silence; John reports it. In the prophets the earth falls silent; in John it is heaven, where the praise of chapters 4-7 stops. The Greek translation of the three prophets says be in awe or take care (eulabeisthe), not be silent; John's word is sige, silence, closer to the Hebrew has (a point drawn here).
entries.turn: The prophets' hush before God the judge becomes a hush in heaven before judgment falls. Beale reads the seventh seal as the final judgment itself, not an empty pause. The prayers in 8:3-5 then rise in that quiet.
entries.not: **Not a quotation.** The prophets order the earth to hush before God. John reports a silence in heaven instead, and no prophet gives it a length of half an hour.
entries.deeper: Beale says the Old Testament links silence with judgment (Psalm 31:17; 115:17; Isaiah 47:5; Lamentations 2:10) and that Habakkuk 2:20 and Zechariah 2:13 matter most. In both the Lord judges from his holy temple in heaven, and the whole earth and every person must fall silent in awe. Zephaniah 1:7 adds temple imagery, with God about to slay like a sacrifice. He concludes the silence of 8:1 is probably drawn from this background. He adds Jewish ideas of a primeval silence before the new creation (4 Ezra 7:30) and of angels falling silent so prayers can be heard. In the vault's Septuagint the three verses read eulabeistho or eulabeisthe apo prosopou; the Hebrew of Habakkuk 2:20 and Zephaniah 1:7 has has, hush. Keener cites Habakkuk 2:20, Zephaniah 1:7 and Zechariah 2:13; the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible cites Zephaniah 1:7 and Zechariah 2:13; the ESV Study Bible cites Zephaniah 1:7-10 and Zechariah 2:13; the CSB Study Bible says the half hour echoes Zephaniah 1:7. The grade is drawn here: the idea is traceable, though three texts share it.
entries.heiser: Heiser walks through five readings. Charles's silence so the saints' prayers can be heard he finds less persuasive. Tonstad ties the silence to Isaiah 52:15, kings shutting their mouths at the servant. Aune weighs a return to primeval silence and lands on silence during the incense offering in the temple. Heiser prefers Beale: an appalled silence at the final judgment, drawn from Habakkuk 2:20, Zephaniah 1:7 and Zechariah 2:13, where Babylon is judged from the heavenly temple. He likes Beale's primeval silence too, since judgment undoes creation before God makes it new.
entries.dissent: The sources weigh the readings differently. Beale and Heiser favor silence before judgment. Wright, Keener and Beale also allow the Jewish idea that heaven's praise pauses so prayers can be heard. Aune, as Heiser reports, prefers temple silence during the incense rite. The CSB Study Bible calls it a literary break before the trumpets. On what the seal holds, Beale argues against an empty seal whose contents are the trumpets. MacArthur reads a silence of awe before the judgments to come, and takes the seventh seal to hold the seven trumpets and the seven bowls, which come quickly just before Christ returns.

entries.title: Revelation 8:2, seven trumpets
entries.summary: Seven trumpets in the hands of seven angels recall the seven priests with seven trumpets who went before the ark around Jericho.
entries.plain: **Seven horn blasts before a wall falls is a story children know.** At Jericho seven priests carried seven trumpets before the ark and blew them as Israel circled the city. On the seventh day the walls fell. John sees the seven angels who stand in God's presence receive seven trumpets. Each blast brings a judgment, and the seventh brings the end.
entries.same: Seven trumpets (hepta salpinges) blown by seven figures who serve before God. The Greek of Joshua 6:13 has seven priests carrying seven trumpets (tas hepta salpingas) before the ark.
entries.differs: At Jericho priests blow the trumpets on earth. In John angels hold them in heaven. Jericho's trumpets sound over seven days for one city. John's announce judgments on a third of land, sea and sky, and the seventh brings the kingdom of God (11:15).
entries.turn: Beale reads the trumpets as holy war. The saints do not fight; they wait for God to fight from heaven, as at Jericho. The first six blasts lead up to the last one. In the same way, six days of marching led to the fall of the walls.
entries.not: **Not a retelling of Jericho.** John borrows the seven trumpets and their priestly setting. There is no city to circle and no wall that falls.
entries.deeper: Beale says that in the Old Testament trumpets warned, judged, signaled victory, enthroned a king, and gathered God's people, and that the primary background here is the fall of Jericho, where trumpets announced victory in a holy war. He notes three matches. Seven priests blow seven trumpets at Jericho, and John's seven angels are priestly figures (15:5-6). The ark is present in both. And silence comes before the trumpets in both. Keener notes series of seven trumpeters in Joshua 6:6, 13 and in the temple (1 Chronicles 15:24; Nehemiah 12:41); Wright names Jericho as the most famous trumpet story. The CSB Study Bible's cross-references at 8:2 list Joshua 6:6. In the vault's Septuagint, Joshua 6:13 reads hoi hepta hiereis hoi pherontes tas hepta salpingas. Beale also hears the trumpet of Sinai (Exodus 19:16) and the War Scroll's trumpets. The grade is drawn here: the count and the setting point to Jericho.
entries.dissent: Beale and Wright point to Jericho. Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible also point to the temple's trumpets. On their purpose, Beale argues that, as at Jericho, the trumpets mark judgment already decided; the ESV Study Bible stresses warning. MacArthur says the trumpets mainly announce judgment about to fall, harsher than the seals and lighter than the bowls, during the last three and a half years. On the seven angels, Keener, Beale and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible name the seven archangels of Jewish tradition; Heiser prefers a company of destroying angels like Psalm 78:49.

entries.title: Revelation 8:3-4, incense with the prayers of the saints
entries.summary: Incense rising with the saints' prayers recalls the psalmist's plea that his prayer be set before God like incense.
entries.plain: **The smell of a kitchen tells the family dinner is on the way.** In Psalm 141 David asks that his prayer rise before God like incense, and that his lifted hands count as an evening offering. John sees an angel at the golden altar offer much incense with the prayers of all the saints. The smoke goes up before God. The prayers are heard.
entries.same: Prayer joined to incense (thymiama) rising before God. The Greek of Psalm 141:2 has my prayer (proseuche) as incense before you; John has incense with the prayers (proseuchais) going up before God.
entries.differs: In the psalm one man prays, and his prayer is likened to incense. In John an angel adds incense to the prayers of all the saints and brings them before the throne. The psalm is a simile; John shows the scene acted out in heaven.
entries.turn: The prayers here are, above all, the martyrs' cry from 6:10. Beale reads the rising smoke as a sign the prayers are accepted. The next verse shows the answer: fire thrown down to the earth.
entries.not: **Not prayers to the angel.** Beale notes the saints pray to God directly in 6:10; the angel only presents what God has already received.
entries.deeper: Beale says prayer as incense in the Old Testament connotes prayer accepted by God, citing Psalm 141:1-2, and that the fragrant smoke of incense in the temple signaled acceptance (Leviticus 16:12-13). He notes Psalm 141:2 sets prayer as incense beside the lifting of hands as the evening offering. In the vault's Septuagint, Psalm 141:2 reads kateuthyntheto he proseuche mou hos thymiama enopion sou. Revelation 8:4 has kai anebe ho kapnos ton thymiamaton tais proseuchais ton hagion. Keener says prayers are presented as incense, as in Psalm 141:2; the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible and the ESV Study Bible cite Psalm 141:2; the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible refers back to 5:8. Walton describes the incense altar before the veil and its daily incense. The grade is drawn here: the pairing of prayer and incense is traceable to the psalm, though the scene is new.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Beale and McDonough: prayer as incense in the Old Testament means prayer accepted by God (Psalm 141:2; Numbers 16:46), and fragrant smoke showed acceptance in the temple (Leviticus 16:12-13). The point, he says, is that God listens when his people pray as priests. Those people are the suffering believers of the book, and God answers with judgment. He ties the prayers to the martyrs' plea and sees them as the trigger for what follows.

entries.title: Revelation 8:3-5, a censer of fire from the altar
entries.summary: The angel with the golden censer acts like the high priest on the Day of Atonement, who took coals from the altar and laid incense on the fire before the Lord.
entries.plain: **A ritual that only one person may perform tells you what kind of day it is.** On the Day of Atonement the high priest took a censer full of live coals from the altar. He carried incense into the inner room and laid it on the coals in God's presence. John's angel stands at the altar with a golden censer, receives much incense, and later fills the censer with fire from the altar. Beale hears the Day of Atonement here.
entries.same: A censer, fire taken from the altar, and incense offered before God. The Greek of Leviticus 16:12 has fire from the altar (apo tou thysiasteriou); John has fire of the altar (ek tou pyros tou thysiasteriou).
entries.differs: Leviticus has the high priest; John has an angel. The priest's smoke covers the mercy seat so he will not die. John's smoke carries the prayers of the saints. And John's angel then throws the fire to the earth, which no priest did.
entries.turn: Beale reads the scene as God accepting the prayers of the saints and answering with judgment. Heiser reads the Day of Atonement as a reset, cleansing what was defiled. The judgments that follow undo a corrupt world before God makes it new.
entries.not: **Not a cleansing rite for the world's sin.** The fire goes out as judgment; the sources read the atonement link as background to accepted prayer, not as a new sacrifice.
entries.deeper: Beale says Revelation 8:3-5 echoes Leviticus 16:12-13. There the priest takes a censer of live coals from the altar, lays incense on the coals in God's presence, and its smoke covers the mercy seat. He adds that Exodus 30:8-10 links incense to the Day of Atonement, and that in Wisdom 18:21 Moses' prayer is likened to an atoning offering of incense. In the vault's Septuagint, Leviticus 16:12 reads lepsetai to pyreion pleres anthrakon pyros apo tou thysiasteriou, and 16:13 has epithesei to thymiama epi to pyr enanti kyriou. Revelation uses a different word for the censer (libanotos). The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible explains the golden censer from Leviticus 16:12; the ESV Study Bible notes the incense altar beside the veil (Exodus 30:1-10). The grade is drawn here: Beale names an echo, and the sequence of censer, coals and incense matches.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Beale and McDonough that 8:3-5 echoes Leviticus 16:12-13, the Day of Atonement. He builds on it: that day was a reset button, purging the sanctuary and restoring it as it was at the start. So the judgments after 8:2 undo a corrupt world, and the book ends in a new Eden, as if there had been no fall. The Lord hears his suffering priestly people and answers with devastating judgment, Heiser says, following them.
entries.dissent: Beale and Heiser hear the Day of Atonement. The ESV Study Bible and Keener read the scene through the temple's regular incense service. Beale notes the heavenly altar combines the incense altar and the altar of burnt offering, so the setting is mixed.

entries.title: Revelation 8:5, fire from the altar thrown on the earth
entries.summary: The angel fills the censer with fire and throws it to the earth, as the man in linen in Ezekiel 10 scatters coals from among the cherubim over Jerusalem, right after the faithful are marked.
entries.plain: **A story that runs in the same order as an older one invites you to read them side by side.** In Ezekiel 9 the faithful in Jerusalem are marked on their foreheads. In Ezekiel 10 the man in linen takes handfuls of glowing coals from between the cherubim. He scatters them over the city. John follows the same order. God's servants are sealed in chapter 7. Then an angel loads a censer with the altar's fire and hurls it down to the earth.
entries.same: A heavenly figure takes fire from God's presence and casts it on the place to be judged. The Greek of Ezekiel 10:2 has fill your hands with coals of fire (anthrakon pyros); John has the angel fill (egemisen) the censer from the fire.
entries.differs: Ezekiel's coals come from among the cherubim and the wheels; John's fire comes from the altar. Ezekiel scatters them on Jerusalem; John throws the fire on the earth. Ezekiel's man is the one who marked the faithful; John's angel is not said to be the sealing angel.
entries.turn: Beale says the pattern is deliberate. As the coals fell on Jerusalem after the faithful were marked, so judgment falls after God's servants are sealed. Those without the seal face what comes from the altar.
entries.not: **Not random fire.** It comes from the altar where the saints' prayers rose, so the sources read it as God's answer to 6:10.
entries.deeper: Beale says 8:3-5 is modeled to a great extent on Ezekiel 10:1-7, where a figure in the heavenly temple takes coals from among the cherubim and scatters them over Jerusalem. This comes right after Ezekiel 9, where those without the protective mark are slain. Since 7:3 is based on Ezekiel 9:4-6 and 8:3-5 on Ezekiel 10, he says, the pattern is intentional, combined with the memory of the Passover mark. In the vault's Septuagint, Ezekiel 10:2 reads pleson tas drakas sou anthrakon pyros ek mesou ton cheroubin kai diaskorpison epi ten polin. Beale notes that the Targum of Ezekiel 1:8 adds cherubim taking coals to sprinkle on the wicked. Moyise, as Heiser reads him, makes the same link. The CSB Study Bible's cross-references point instead to Leviticus 6:12-13 and Numbers 16:46. The grade is drawn here: the order of events matches.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Moyise in the Revelation 7 episode: the sealing in Ezekiel 9 is followed in 10:2 by the man in linen filling his hands with coals and scattering them, and John's sealing is followed by the censer of fire in 8:5. In the Revelation 8 episode he reads Beale and McDonough that 8:3-5 is modeled on Ezekiel 10:1-7. He reads the scene as day of the Lord imagery married to Sinai: God remembers his covenant, hears his people, and judges the agents of chaos.

entries.title: Revelation 8:5, thunder, voices, lightning and earthquake
entries.summary: The thunder, sounds, lightning and earthquake are the signs of God's coming at Sinai, repeated to close each series of judgments.
entries.plain: **A band that ends every set with the same chord tells you each set is over.** When God came down on Mount Sinai there were thunders, lightning, a loud trumpet, and the whole mountain shook. John uses those signs to close the seals here. He uses them again at the end of the trumpets (11:19) and the bowls (16:18). Each time the list grows, as the judgments come closer to the end.
entries.same: Sounds or voices (phonai), lightnings (astrapai), and thunder, with the shaking of a quake. The Greek of Exodus 19:16 has phonai kai astrapai; John has brontai kai phonai kai astrapai kai seismos.
entries.differs: Sinai adds a thick cloud, smoke and a trumpet. John keeps four items and adds an earthquake, where Exodus has the mountain shaking. At Sinai God came down to meet his people. Here the signs mark judgment falling on the earth.
entries.turn: Beale and Bauckham see the list grow through the book. It has three items at 4:5, four at 8:5, five at 11:19, and more at 16:18-21. Each marks the end of a series as the last judgment draws near. Heiser adds that Sinai was also where God made his covenant, so the signs carry promise for his people.
entries.not: **Not a weather report.** The sources read the signs as God's presence in judgment, borrowed from Sinai, not as a storm.
entries.deeper: Beale says this fourfold chain of cosmic disturbance has precedent in Exodus 19:16, 18, Psalm 77:18-19 and Isaiah 29:6, and that the Sinai theophany is partly in mind in 8:5, as it was in 4:5. He follows Bauckham in seeing a progressive sequence: lightnings, sounds and thunders in 4:5; thunders, sounds, lightnings and quaking in 8:5; adding great hail in 11:19 and 16:18-21. Since the formula ends the trumpets and bowls with the last judgment, he argues, it ends the seals the same way. In the vault's Septuagint, Exodus 19:16 reads egenonto phonai kai astrapai kai nephelai gnophodeis, and 19:18 has the mountain smoking. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible says 8:5 alludes to the Sinai theophany (Exodus 19:16-20); the CSB Study Bible's cross-references point back to 4:5. Beale adds that the trumpets that follow partly echo the Sinai trumpet. The grade is drawn here: the cluster is traceable to Sinai.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Beale and McDonough: the thunder, rumblings, lightning and earthquake have Old Testament precedent in Exodus 19:16, 18, Psalm 77:17-18 and Isaiah 29:6, and Sinai is partly in mind, as in 4:5. The same formula closes the trumpets and the bowls. He stresses Sinai's other side: there God, though frightening, made a covenant with a people he loved. By looping it in, John shows God remembering his covenant even as he judges.
entries.dissent: The sources differ on where the series stands in time. Beale, after Bauckham, reads the formula as closing each series with the last judgment, so the seals reach the end, as the trumpets and the bowls do. MacArthur reads one sequence: the seventh seal holds the trumpets, the thunder and lightning are God's fury and not a storm, and the earthquake is a real one, at least as strong as that of the sixth seal.

entries.title: Revelation 8:7, hail and fire mixed with blood
entries.summary: The first trumpet repeats the seventh plague on Egypt, hail with fire, adds blood, and spreads it from Egypt to the earth.
entries.plain: **A remake of a famous disaster film keeps the storm but moves it to a bigger city.** In the seventh plague God sent hail and fire on Egypt. It struck the land, the plants of the field and the trees. At the first trumpet, hail and fire are hurled down, blended with blood. Fire burns a third of the land and its trees, and all the green grass. Egypt's plague now falls on the world.
entries.same: Hail (chalaza) and fire (pyr) sent down together, striking the land, the plants and the trees. Exodus 9:23-25 in Greek has hail and fire on the earth and the trees of the field broken. Ezekiel 38:22 joins hail, fire and blood.
entries.differs: Exodus says hail did the most harm; John says fire burned things up. John adds blood, which Beale traces to the first plague or to Ezekiel 38:22. Exodus struck all Egypt; John limits the damage to a third, yet spreads it over the whole earth.
entries.turn: Beale reads the trumpets as the plagues of Egypt aimed at a world that persecutes God's people and serves idols. In his reading the same blows that broke Pharaoh now fall on a new Egypt. The sealed of chapter 7 are kept, as Israel was.
entries.not: **Not a copy of the seventh plague.** John keeps Egypt's hail and fire, adds blood, limits the harm to a third, and spreads it over the whole earth.
entries.deeper: Beale says the first five trumpets are patterned after five plagues of Egypt, and that 8:7 follows Exodus 9:22-25: in both, hail and fire from heaven strike three parts of creation, the land, the trees and the grass. One Greek manuscript of Exodus 9:23 even adds trumpets. In the vault's Septuagint, Exodus 9:23-24 has chalazan ... kai dietreche to pyr epi tes ges, and 9:25 says the hail broke all the trees of the field. Revelation has chalaza kai pyr memigmena en haimati. Beale adds that 8:7 also echoes Ezekiel 38:22, where God judges Gog with plague, blood, hail and fire; Jewish writers joined that verse to the hail plague. Keener, the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the ESV Study Bible, the CSB Study Bible, the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible and Wright all cite the seventh plague; the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible and the CSB Study Bible's cross-references add Ezekiel 38:22. Walton notes hail destroyed crops in late winter. The grade is drawn here.
entries.heiser: Heiser says anyone can see the overlap with the plagues of Egypt. He reads Beale and McDonough: the verse follows the hail and fire of Exodus 9:23-25. The Greek of Exodus lists the same three things, land, plants and trees. With them he notes the plague is cut to a third but spread from Egypt to the whole earth. He adds Beale's note that Ezekiel 38:22, the defeat of Gog, is also echoed, and that this repeated language matters for reading Revelation as cycles rather than a timeline.
entries.dissent: The sources differ on how to read the plague. Beale says the visions draw on Old Testament models full of figures of speech, so the burden of proof lies on a literal reading. Heiser, after Beale, reads the trumpets as cycles that retell the judgments, not a timeline. MacArthur reads a physical event still to come, in the last three and a half years: volcanoes set off by the earthquake of 8:5 throw down hail with burning lava, dust may turn the water red, and fire burns a third of the world's forests.

entries.title: Revelation 8:7, a third burned up
entries.summary: Judgment by thirds may come from Ezekiel 5, where Jerusalem is divided into thirds for fire, sword and scattering, and from Zechariah 13, where a third is brought through fire.
entries.plain: **Splitting something into thirds can make a point no pie chart needs to spell out.** Ezekiel shaves his hair and divides it into three parts: one burned, one cut with a sword, one scattered to the wind. Each third stands for a part of Jerusalem's people. Zechariah says two thirds will perish and a third will be refined in fire. John's trumpets strike one third of land, of trees and of sea.
entries.same: Judgment measured out in thirds, with fire as one of the means. Ezekiel 5:2 burns a third in the fire; Zechariah 13:8-9 brings a third through fire. John burns a third of the earth.
entries.differs: Ezekiel's thirds are thirds of a city's people, each with a different fate. John's are thirds of the earth, the trees, the sea and the sky. The Greek translation of Ezekiel 5 divides the people into fourths, not thirds. The Hebrew has thirds, so John's third matches the Hebrew of Ezekiel, a point drawn here.
entries.turn: Beale says Ezekiel's thirds sit inside a larger warning of famine, and the first trumpet also means famine. Zechariah adds that the same fire refines the faithful and destroys the rest. The limit to a third keeps these judgments partial, short of the end.
entries.not: **Not a copy of Ezekiel's thirds.** Ezekiel divides a city's people into three parts with three fates. John strikes a third of the land, the trees, the sea and the sky.
entries.deeper: Beale says the limit to a third is due above all to Ezekiel 5:2, 12, where Israel is divided into thirds and judged by fire, sword and scattering, inside a frame of famine (Ezekiel 4:9-17; 5:16-17). He adds that 8:7 might also evoke Zechariah 13:8-9, where the third that is left is brought through the fire and refined. In the vault's Septuagint, Ezekiel 5:2 and 5:12 speak of to tetarton, a fourth part, four times; the Hebrew of 5:12 has shelishit, a third, as the Hebrew of 5:2 also does. So John's thirds follow the Hebrew of Ezekiel, while the fourth of 6:8 matches the Greek. That textual point is drawn here. Zechariah 13:8 in Greek has to triton, the third. Aune, as Heiser reports, ties the thirds loosely to Ezekiel 5:2. The CSB Study Bible's cross-references at 8:7 list Ezekiel 5:12 and Zechariah 13:8-9. The grade is possible: Beale is confident, but the number is common and the other sources only list texts.
entries.heiser: Heiser says the source of the third is not clear. He reports Tonstad, who reads every third through the third of the stars in 12:4, which Heiser finds arbitrary. Aune ties the thirds loosely to Ezekiel 5:2, which Heiser thinks makes more sense but not much. He prefers Beale's other option, Zechariah 13:8-9, where the same fire refines the righteous and punishes the ungodly. He adds Moyise's observation that the trumpets follow the order of Joel 2-3 and Amos 1-3.
entries.dissent: The sources weigh the possible models differently. Beale puts Ezekiel 5 first and Zechariah 13 second. Heiser prefers Zechariah 13. Tonstad, as Heiser reports, reads the thirds from 12:4. Keener and the study Bibles note the escalation from a fourth (6:8) to a third to the whole (the bowls) without naming a source. On what the third means, Beale reads it as a sign that these woes are partial, short of the final judgment. MacArthur reads the fractions as real shares: a third of the earth's forests here, and a quarter of the world's people at 6:8.

entries.title: Revelation 8:8-9, a third of the sea became blood
entries.summary: The second trumpet turns a third of the sea to blood and kills its creatures, as the first plague turned the Nile to blood and killed its fish.
entries.plain: **A river turning red is a picture no one forgets.** In the first plague Moses struck the Nile, its water turned to blood, the fish died and no one could drink. At the second trumpet a burning mountain falls into the sea. One third of the sea turns to blood. One third of its creatures die, and one third of the ships are wrecked. The plague on Egypt's river now strikes the world's seas.
entries.same: Water turned to blood (haima) and the creatures in it dying. The Greek of Exodus 7:20-21 says the river turned to blood and the fish died. John has one third of the sea turned to blood and one third of its creatures dead.
entries.differs: Exodus strikes a river; John strikes the sea. Exodus kills all the fish; John kills a third of the creatures. John adds the burning mountain as the cause, and the loss of ships, which Exodus does not have. Beale traces the mountain to Jeremiah 51.
entries.turn: Beale reads the trumpet as judgment on the world's trade and food, a famine at sea. The ships point ahead to chapter 18, where sailors mourn Babylon. For Beale, Egypt's plague becomes a blow against the whole world system that oppresses God's people.
entries.not: **Not the Nile plague repeated.** Exodus strikes a river and kills all its fish. John strikes a third of the sea, adds a burning mountain, and wrecks ships.
entries.deeper: Beale calls a third of the sea became blood a direct allusion to Exodus 7:20, where Moses turns the Nile to blood, and notes that as the fish died there, a third of the sea creatures die here. In the vault's Septuagint, Exodus 7:20 reads metebale pan to hydor to en to potamo eis haima, and 7:21 says the fish died. Revelation has egeneto to triton tes thalasses haima. Beale suggests a shortage of water may be implied, since that was a major effect of the Nile plague, made explicit in the third trumpet. He notes Ezekiel 29:3-5, where Egypt's people are the fish of the Nile, and suggests the sea creatures may stand for people. Keener, the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the ESV Study Bible, the CSB Study Bible, the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible and Wright all cite the first plague. The grade is drawn here: Beale's direct allusion meets the clear grade.
entries.heiser: Heiser says the sea turning to blood is the plague reference that draws attention right back to Exodus, and calls it obvious. He reads the second and third trumpets together, since their language repeats. For the burning mountain and the ships he reads Beale's link to Babylon (see the next entry).
entries.dissent: The sources differ on how to read the scene. Beale reads it through its Old Testament models: the fire may picture severe famine, the lost ships a blow to sea trade, and the sea creatures may stand for people. The ESV Study Bible names Vesuvius as one example of a burning mountain. MacArthur reads a physical event still to come: a huge meteor or asteroid strikes the sea and its wave wrecks a third of the ships; the blood may be a red tide of dead micro-organisms, or real blood.

entries.title: Revelation 8:8, a great mountain burning with fire
entries.summary: The burning mountain thrown into the sea may come from Jeremiah 51, where God calls Babylon a destroying mountain he will make a burnt-out one.
entries.plain: **Calling a city a mountain tells you how big and proud it is.** In Jeremiah 51 God speaks against Babylon, the destroying mountain, and promises to roll it down and make it a burned-out mountain. Later the sea covers Babylon. At the second trumpet something like a great burning mountain is thrown into the sea. Beale reads it as the judgment of an evil kingdom like Babylon.
entries.same: A mountain that is set on fire under God's judgment. The Greek of Jeremiah 51:25 calls Babylon a mountain (oros) and promises to make it a mountain set on fire; John has a great mountain burning with fire (oros mega pyri kaiomenon).
entries.differs: Jeremiah names Babylon outright. John says only something like a mountain, and leaves it unnamed. In Jeremiah the mountain is burned where it stands; in John it is thrown into the sea. Jeremiah 51:42 does have the sea rising over Babylon.
entries.turn: Beale reads the mountain as an evil kingdom judged. He ties it to 18:21. There an angel throws a millstone into the sea and says Babylon will fall like it. For Beale the trumpet is an early blow against the world system that later bears Babylon's name.
entries.not: **Not a quotation of Jeremiah.** Jeremiah calls Babylon a destroying mountain to be burned where it stands. John says only something like a great burning mountain, and has it thrown into the sea.
entries.deeper: Beale says mountains can stand for kingdoms, and fire for judgment, so the burning mountain is an evil kingdom judged. He calls Jeremiah 51:25 an allusion here: I am against you, destroying mountain, and I will make you a burnt mountain. He supports it from the repeated allusion in 11:18, from the trumpet among the nations in Jeremiah 51:27, and from the stone thrown into the river in 51:63-64, the basis of 18:21. He adds that the Greek of Jeremiah 51:42 has the sea come up over Babylon. In the vault's Septuagint, 51:25 reads to oros to diephtharmenon ... kai doso se hos oros empepyrismenon. He also cites 1 Enoch 18:13 and 21:3, stars like great burning mountains. The ESV Study Bible says the imagery echoes Jeremiah 51:25, 42; the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible says it may recall Jeremiah 51:25; the CSB Study Bible's cross-references list it. The grade is drawn here: the wording is close and Beale gives several supports.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Beale at length: mountains can mean kingdoms, Jeremiah 51:25 calls Babylon a destroying mountain to be burned out, and 1 Enoch 18:13 and 21:3 use burning mountains for judged fallen angels. Following Beale, he says the language of chapter 8 repeats in chapter 18 and leads back to Babylon, the world system hostile to God, so the trumpets are judgments on those persecuting God's people. Babylon, he adds, is the Old Testament's poster child for anti-Eden.
entries.dissent: Keener says the parallel to Jeremiah 51:25, 42 is not as obvious, and points to a burning star thrown into the sea in the Sibylline Oracles; the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible suggests both may depend on Jeremiah. The ESV Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible mention volcanoes such as Vesuvius. Wright notes Jesus' saying about a mountain thrown into the sea (Mark 11:23). Beale reads the mountain as the object of judgment, not its tool, since mountains standing for nations are always judged in the Old Testament. MacArthur reads a huge meteor or asteroid wrapped in burning gases, whose impact raises a great wave.

entries.title: Revelation 8:10, a great star fell from heaven
entries.summary: The great burning star that falls from heaven may recall Isaiah 14:12, the fallen morning star used of the king of Babylon.
entries.plain: **A falling star in an old poem can stand for a fallen ruler.** Isaiah 14 mocks the king of Babylon. It cries out at how the morning star has fallen from heaven and been cut down to the ground. At the third trumpet a great star, burning like a torch, falls from heaven on the rivers and springs. Beale and others hear Isaiah's fallen star here.
entries.same: A heavenly light that falls from heaven (ek tou ouranou). The Greek of Isaiah 14:12 has the morning star (heosphoros) fallen out of heaven; John has a great star (aster megas) falling from heaven.
entries.differs: Isaiah's fall is a taunt over a proud king brought down to the pit. John's star burns like a torch and falls on the waters, poisoning them. Isaiah uses the name morning star; John names his star Wormwood. John does not say who or what the star is.
entries.turn: Beale reads the star as the angel that stands for a sinful nation, judged with it. If Isaiah 14 is in view, the judgment of Babylon's guardian falls along with Babylon. In that reading the trumpet links the fall of heavenly powers to the fall of earthly ones.
entries.not: **Not the star of 9:1.** That star is given a key to the abyss; the sources treat the two separately, though Beale reads both through the same wording.
entries.deeper: Beale says stars represent angels in Revelation, the Old Testament and later Judaism, and that these angels often stand for peoples and kingdoms. He reads the star as the angel of an evil kingdom undergoing judgment, here Babylon's, since 8:8 concerns Babylon. He says this becomes more convincing if 8:10 alludes to Isaiah 14:12-15, where the judgment of Babylon's king comes because its guardian, the star of the morning, has fallen from heaven. He cites a Jewish midrash reading the Nile plague as judgment on heavenly beings, with Isaiah 24:21. In the vault's Septuagint, Isaiah 14:12 reads pos exepesen ek tou ouranou ho heosphoros. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cites Isaiah 14:12 for falling stars; the CSB Study Bible's cross-references list it; Wright says the falling star echoes Isaiah 14:12, applied there to Babylon's king. The grade is possible: the sources hedge, and falling stars are common in apocalyptic writing.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Beale here as speaking the language of the Deuteronomy 32 worldview: a fallen star is an angelic power that stands for a sinful people, judged together with them. He notes Beale's rabbinic support, a midrash that reads the Nile plague as judgment on the Nile's god, citing Isaiah 24:21, where God punishes the host of heaven and the kings of the earth. He takes it as proof that the rabbis kept the theology of nations under heavenly rulers. He does not cite Isaiah 14 here.
entries.dissent: Beale reads the star as an angel judged along with its nation. He grants it could simply be an agent of judgment. The ESV Study Bible allows a meteorite if read literally, and the CSB Study Bible compares a meteorite hitting the earth. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible suggests readers in Asia may have thought of Artemis's image that fell from heaven. MacArthur reads another body from the sky, perhaps a comet because of its burning trail, that breaks up as it nears the earth and scatters over it.
