entries.title: Revelation 8:11, Wormwood
entries.summary: The star named Wormwood turns the waters bitter, the judgment Jeremiah announced on idolaters, and John's word follows the Hebrew, not the Greek translation.
entries.plain: **A bitter taste that matches a bitter wrong makes a fitting punishment.** In Jeremiah God says he will feed his people wormwood and give them poisoned water to drink, because they followed idols and false prophets. At the third trumpet the falling star is named Wormwood. One third of the waters turn bitter, and many die from drinking them.
entries.same: Wormwood and water that kills, given as judgment. The Hebrew of Jeremiah 9:15 (9:14 in Hebrew) and 23:15 has la'anah, wormwood, and poisoned water (mei rosh). John names the star Wormwood (Apsinthos) and makes the waters bitter.
entries.differs: The Greek translation of both verses has no wormwood. It says God will feed them distress or grief and give them bitter water or water of gall. John's Wormwood matches the Hebrew word, as Silva notes the Greek never uses it. Jeremiah aims at Israel and its prophets; John strikes a third of the world's waters.
entries.turn: Beale says the punishment fits the crime: as idolaters polluted the people, God pollutes their water. In his reading Babylon, the world system, has drawn earth-dwellers and some in the church into idolatry. The result is bitter suffering for both.
entries.not: **Not a word from the Greek Old Testament.** The Greek translation of Jeremiah never names wormwood. John's name for the star matches the Hebrew word la'anah.
entries.deeper: Beale says the scene is based on Jeremiah 9:15 and 23:15, where God feeds Israel wormwood and poisoned water because its leaders led it into Baal worship. He notes that everywhere else in the Old Testament wormwood is a metaphor for affliction from God's wrath (Deuteronomy 29:18; Proverbs 5:4; Lamentations 3:15, 19; Amos 5:7; 6:12), often tied to idolatry. In the vault's Septuagint, Jeremiah 9:15 reads psomizo autous anankas kai potio autous hydor choles, and 23:15 odynen ... hydor pikron; neither uses apsinthos. The Hebrew of both has la'anah and mei rosh. Silva, as Heiser reads him, says apsinthos is not found before the New Testament, that the Septuagint never uses it, but that Aquila used it for la'anah in Proverbs 5:4. So John's name agrees with the Hebrew word, a link drawn here from those facts. Keener, the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the ESV Study Bible, the CSB Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible all cite Jeremiah 9:15 or 23:15. Walton describes the plant. The grade is drawn here.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads the ESV Study Bible on the plant and then Silva's word study: the Greek word is not attested before the New Testament, the Septuagint does not use it, but Aquila renders la'anah in Proverbs 5:4 with it. He reads Jeremiah 9:15, where God feeds his people bitter food and bad water. Then he reads Beale. The punishment fits the crime of idolatry. Babylon, the world system, brings bitter judgment on the earth-dwellers and on the unfaithful in the church. He dismisses asteroid and volcano readings.
entries.dissent: The sources agree on Jeremiah. They differ on the star and on what the name points to. Beale reads the star as Babylon's angel, and he and Heiser read Wormwood through its Old Testament use for bitter judgment. The CSB Study Bible reads a meteorite causing pollution. MacArthur reads an event still to come, perhaps a comet, and takes wormwood as a bitter poison from a root that brings drunkenness and then death. The CSB Study Bible notes wormwood is bitter but not poisonous, and Silva, via Heiser, suggests bitterness and poison were linked in ancient speech.

entries.title: Revelation 8:11, the waters made bitter
entries.summary: Waters made bitter recall Marah, where Israel could not drink the bitter water until God made it sweet; here God makes sweet water bitter.
entries.plain: **A story can repeat an old scene in reverse to show the tables have turned.** Just after crossing the Red Sea, Israel came to Marah. The water there was too bitter to drink, until God showed Moses a piece of wood that made it sweet. At the third trumpet the waters turn bitter and people die from them. The miracle that saved Israel now runs the other way.
entries.same: Water too bitter to drink. The Greek of Exodus 15:23 says the water at Marah was bitter (pikron); John says the waters were made bitter (epikranthesan).
entries.differs: At Marah the water was already bitter and God made it sweet. In John good water is made bitter, and many die. Marah is a single spring in the desert; John strikes one third of all rivers and springs. The reversal is drawn here from the two texts; the sources only note the recall.
entries.turn: Marah came right after the exodus, a sign that God would heal his people. John turns the sign around for those who oppose God. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible sets these deadly waters against the springs of living water in 7:17.
entries.not: **Not one of the ten plagues.** Marah comes after the plagues, once Israel had crossed the sea. John blends it with the Nile plague in one trumpet.
entries.deeper: The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible says the bitter waters recall the first plague (Exodus 7:20-21) and the bitter water at Marah (Exodus 15:23), and contrast with the springs of living water of 7:17. Heiser says the water becoming bitter harks back to Marah, after the Red Sea crossing. In the vault's Septuagint, Exodus 15:23 reads ouk edynanto piein hydor ek Merras, pikron gar en; Revelation 8:11 has epikranthesan, they were made bitter. Beale draws a related contrast: the springs of water in 8:10 are linked to death, while the springs of 7:17 and 21:6 are linked to life. The grade is possible: two sources name Marah, and the shared word is short.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads the second and third trumpets together. The sea turning to blood points back to the first plague; the water becoming bitter, he says, harks back to the incident at Marah in Exodus 15, after the Red Sea crossing. He notes there is little difference between the two trumpets.

entries.title: Revelation 8:12, a third of the sun, moon and stars darkened
entries.summary: The fourth trumpet darkens a third of the lights in the sky, echoing the ninth plague, three days of darkness over Egypt.
entries.plain: **Turning the lights down on a stage tells the audience the scene has changed.** In the ninth plague Moses stretched out his hand and thick darkness covered Egypt for three days. Yet the Israelites had light where they lived. At the fourth trumpet, sun, moon and stars each lose a third of their light. A third of the day and a third of the night lose their light.
entries.same: Darkness sent as judgment from heaven on the oppressor. Exodus 10:22 in Greek has darkness (skotos) over the land; John has the lights struck so that a third of them is darkened (skotisthe).
entries.differs: Exodus has total darkness for three days over Egypt. John has partial darkness, a third of the day and night, over the world. Exodus does not name the sun, moon and stars; John strikes all three. Beale suggests the three days and Israel's light may lie behind the limit to a third.
entries.turn: Beale says the plague of darkness was aimed at Egypt's sun god. John's darkness falls on idolaters and on the world they trust instead of God. Jewish writers already read the plague as a picture of exile from God, and Beale reads the fourth trumpet the same way.
entries.not: **Not the sixth seal again.** There the whole sun, moon and stars are struck; here only a third, so Beale and the ESV Study Bible see a partial trial before the end.
entries.deeper: Beale says the woe is partly based on Exodus 10:21, three days of darkness over Egypt. That plague was in part an attack on Ra, Egypt's sun god. The limit to a third may come from the three days and from Israel's having light in their homes (Exodus 10:23). He notes Wisdom 17 read the plague as symbolic: the Egyptians became prisoners of darkness, cut off from providence. He also cites Ezekiel 32:7-8, Joel 2:10 and 3:15 and Amos 8:9. In the vault's Septuagint, Exodus 10:22 reads egeneto skotos gnophos thyella epi pasan gen Aigyptou treis hemeras. Keener, the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the ESV Study Bible, the CSB Study Bible, the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible and Wright all cite the ninth plague. Walton reads the darkness as a strike at Amon-Re. The grade is drawn here: the plague is the clear model, though the wording differs.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Aune. The fourth trumpet partly recalls the darkness of Exodus 10:21-22, a blow at Egypt's sun gods. The Wisdom of Solomon read that plague as exile from the true God. Amos 8:9 is likely in view too. Aune also wonders about the fourth day of creation, when sun, moon and stars were made. Then the trumpet would undo day four and return to chaos.
entries.dissent: Beale and Aune, as Heiser reports, both see Exodus 10. Aune also hears Genesis 1:14-19; the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible notes darkness as a symbol of the primordial world (Genesis 1:2). The CSB Study Bible weighs whether the lights shine for less time or less brightly. Beale reads the darkness as probably not literal, a picture of the idolaters' separation from God. MacArthur reads God really dimming the sun, moon and stars by a third for a time, so that the cold upsets weather, plants and living things.

entries.title: Revelation 8:12, the sun going down at noon
entries.summary: Amos 8:9, where God makes the sun set at noon in a judgment on Israel shaped by the plague on Egypt, may also stand behind the fourth trumpet.
entries.plain: **A writer can borrow a disaster from history and aim it at a new target.** Amos took the darkness of the Egyptian plague and turned it on Israel. He warned that God would make the sun set at midday and bring darkness in broad daylight. A famine of hearing God's word would follow. John's fourth trumpet darkens part of the day as well. Beale and others think Amos may be in the background.
entries.same: Daylight darkened as a judgment. The Greek of Amos 8:9 has the sun going down at midday and the light darkened (syskotasei) on the earth; John has a third of the day not shining.
entries.differs: Amos speaks of the sun alone, darkened at noon. John strikes sun, moon and stars, and only by a third. Amos aims at Israel's sins. John's trumpet strikes the world.
entries.turn: Beale says Amos modeled this warning on the plague of darkness. A famine of God's word was to follow. If John has Amos in mind, the darkness means God pulling away from those who reject him.
entries.not: **Not a firm link.** Beale says Amos possibly stands in the background; it adds to Exodus, it does not replace it.
entries.deeper: Beale says Amos 8:9 possibly stands in the background of 8:12. Amos shaped his warning to Israel on the Egyptian darkness, as the double mention of the Nile in 8:8 and the mourning for an only son in 8:10 show. It comes with a famine of hearing God's word (8:11-12), which Beale reads as God withdrawing his presence. In the vault's Septuagint, Amos 8:9 reads dysetai ho helios mesembrias, kai syskotasei epi tes ges en hemera to phos. Aune, as Heiser reads him, thinks John likely had Amos 8:9 in view as well, a judgment on Israel modeled on Egypt's plague. The CSB Study Bible's cross-references at 8:12 list Amos 8:9. The grade is possible: the sources hedge, and the wording is only partly shared.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Aune here: besides the plague of darkness, Amos 8:9 is likely part of John's reference, a judgment on apostate Israel modeled on what God did to Egypt. Heiser adds that the persecutor changes, from Egypt to Babylon, but the theme repeats.

entries.title: Revelation 8:13, an eagle crying woe
entries.summary: An eagle flying overhead and crying woe draws on the prophets' eagle of judgment, set beside a trumpet in Hosea 8:1 and beside woe in Jeremiah 4:13.
entries.plain: **A bird circling overhead can be a warning everyone below understands.** Hosea tells Israel to put the trumpet to its lips, because an enemy comes like an eagle over the Lord's house. Jeremiah sees an invader with horses swifter than eagles, and the people cry woe. John looks and hears an eagle flying in mid-heaven. It cries woe three times over the last three trumpets.
entries.same: An eagle (aetos) tied to judgment, a trumpet, and woe. Hosea 8:1 pairs the trumpet with an eagle over God's house; Jeremiah 4:13 has eagles and then woe to us (ouai hemin). John has the eagle, the trumpets and ouai three times.
entries.differs: In Hosea and Jeremiah the eagle is the enemy army itself. In John the eagle is a messenger that announces the woes; it does not attack. Jeremiah's people cry woe on themselves; John's eagle cries woe on those who dwell on the earth.
entries.turn: Beale reads the eagle as a bird hovering over prey, the unbelieving earth-dwellers. Its high place lets it warn the whole world. The worst three trumpets are still to come.
entries.not: **Not Rome's eagle.** Keener thinks the eagles on Roman army flags do not matter here. One study Bible says this eagle warns of a force fiercer than Rome.
entries.deeper: Beale says Old Testament announcements of judgment use the eagle as a metaphor for destruction (Deuteronomy 28:49; Jeremiah 4:13; 48:40; 49:22; Lamentations 4:19; Ezekiel 17:3; Hosea 8:1; Habakkuk 1:8), and that Hosea 8:1 and Jeremiah 4:13 are particularly relevant: the first sets a trumpet with an eagle against the Lord's house, the second has eagles, woe to us, and a trumpet sounded three times. In the vault's Septuagint, Hosea 8:1 has hos aetos epi oikon kyriou; Jeremiah 4:13 has kouphoteroi aeton hoi hippoi autou. ouai hemin; Deuteronomy 28:49 hosei hormema aetou. He adds that the eagle may be the eaglelike living creature of 4:7, and that Exodus 19:4 has God carry Israel on eagles' wings. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible lists Deuteronomy 28:49, Jeremiah 48:40, Hosea 8:1 and Habakkuk 1:8. The grade is possible: the image is widespread, and no text supplies John's scene.
entries.heiser: Heiser does not discuss Hosea or Jeremiah. He reads Aune and then Pilch and Malina on the eagle in mid-heaven: mid-heaven was a term for the ruling center of the sky, and the eagle was Zeus's messenger, or in astral lore the constellation Pegasus. For Heiser the point is that the God of Israel sends this eagle, another swipe at Zeus's claim to be most high, like 1:4.
entries.dissent: Beale and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible read the eagle through the prophets' bird of judgment, and Keener as a vulture over the dead. Aune, Pilch and Malina, as Heiser reports, read it against Zeus and astral lore. Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible also note the eagle as a symbol of God's protection (Exodus 19:4).

entries.title: Revelation 9:1, a star fallen from heaven
entries.summary: The star that has fallen from heaven and is handed the key to the Abyss may recall the fallen morning star of Isaiah 14:12, though the sources split on whether this star is good or evil.
entries.plain: **A night watchman with a ring of keys may be the guard or the burglar, and the story turns on which.** John sees a star that has already fallen to earth. It is a person, since it is handed the key to the Abyss, the deep prison of rebel spirits. Some sources hear Isaiah 14, where the bright morning star falls from heaven. Others read John's star as a loyal angel sent down with God's key.
entries.same: A star and a fall from heaven to earth. Isaiah 14:12 in Greek has the morning star falling out of heaven (exepesen ek tou ouranou). John has a star from heaven, fallen to the earth (ek tou ouranou peptokota eis ten gen).
entries.differs: Isaiah mocks a proud king of Babylon under the picture of a fallen star. John's star is handed a key and opens a pit. Isaiah says nothing of a key or of the Abyss. John never says he saw the star fall, only that it had fallen. Beale reads this star like the one in 8:10, which he ties to Isaiah 14. The CSB Study Bible lists Isaiah 14:12 in its margin.
entries.turn: The key is the point. Whoever opens the Abyss does it only because a key is given. Beale stresses that Christ, who holds the keys to death and Hades in 1:18, stays in control. Heiser draws the same lesson the other way round: Christ would not hand his key to a rebel.
entries.not: **Not a meteor.** The star is given a key and opens a shaft, so it is a being. Heiser says nobody argues that point, and Keener notes that many Jews took stars as angels.
entries.deeper: John uses the perfect participle peptokota, has fallen, and Beale reads it to mean John saw the star after its fall. Isaiah 14:12 in the Septuagint reads exepesen ek tou ouranou ho heosphoros, the morning star fell out of heaven. Beale reads 9:1 like the star of 8:10, which he links to Isaiah 14:12-15, where the star is Babylon's guardian thrust down to the pit. He adds that 1 Enoch 88:1-3 calls an evil angel a star fallen from heaven into an abyss, and that Jesus saw Satan fall like lightning in Luke 10:18. Beale also cites Isaiah 24:21-22, where God shuts the rebel host of heaven in a pit. In 1 Enoch 10 and 21 the Abyss is the prison of the angels who sinned before the flood, and Heiser's Reversing Hermon reads 9:1-10 as their release before final judgment. The CSB Study Bible lists Isaiah 14:12 among its cross-references for 9:1. The grade is drawn here: the falling star is shared, but only Beale argues for Isaiah, and only through 8:10.
entries.heiser: Heiser rejects Beale's evil star. He follows Aune: the star is an angel like the one in 20:1 who holds the same key, and not the Abaddon of 9:11. His candidate is the archangel whom 1 Enoch sets over Tartarus, the prison of the Watchers (1 Enoch 19:1; 20:1); 1 Enoch 20 gives that archangel's name as Uriel. Two angels with two keys make no sense, he argues, and Christ, who took the keys in 1:18, would not hand one to a rebel. So he is "skeptical of his skepticism", meaning Beale's. The released spirits go out to their own doom.
entries.dissent: Is the star good or evil? Beale says evil: 1 Enoch keeps falling-star language for fallen angels, and the star is probably the king of the Abyss in 9:11. The ESV Study Bible names it Satan, while noting that many scholars see a good angel. Heiser, after Aune, reads a good angel, the same one who holds the key in 20:1, and the CSB Study Bible calls that the most likely option. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible leaves both open. MacArthur reads an angelic being, probably Satan himself, unlike the stars that fall in 6:13 and 8:8.

aw.n: Revelation 9:1-21, the Abyss opened and the armies from the Euphrates
aw.s: At the fifth trumpet a fallen star is given the key to the Abyss, and from its smoke come locusts like horses with human faces, women's hair and scorpions' stings, under a king called Abaddon and Apollyon. At the sixth, four angels bound at the Euphrates are released with a cavalry of two hundred million that kills a third of humanity, yet the survivors do not repent.

entries.title: Revelation 9:2, smoke from the shaft darkens the sun
entries.summary: The smoke that pours from the Abyss and darkens the sun joins Joel's darkened sun to the land darkened by the locusts of Exodus and the furnace smoke over Sodom.
entries.plain: **Wildfire smoke can turn noon to dusk, and older people in town remember the last time.** When the shaft opens, smoke pours out like smoke from a huge kiln. The sun and the air go dark. Joel says the sun grows dark when the locust army comes. In Exodus the locusts covered Egypt until the land went black. Sodom's ruin rose like kiln smoke too.
entries.same: The sun goes dark. Joel 2:10 in Greek uses a related verb for sun and moon (syskotazo); John has eskotothe ho helios. The smoke of a furnace (kaminos) rises over Sodom in Genesis 19:28 and over Sinai in Exodus 19:18. In Exodus 10:15 the locusts darken the land.
entries.differs: John's darkness comes from smoke, not from locusts or from God's coming as in Joel. One verb covers the sun and the air. The darkened land of Exodus 10:15 is in the Hebrew; the Greek translation says instead that the land was ruined, a point drawn here. Genesis 19:28 has a furnace's vapor, while Exodus 19:18 has a furnace's smoke, as John does.
entries.turn: Darkness was a sign of judgment in Egypt and in Joel's day of the Lord. Beale reads the smoke as judgment spreading from the demonic world to people on earth. He adds that the darkness stands for the blindness that comes with it. Out of this smoke come the locusts of the next verse.
entries.not: **Not an eclipse or a volcano.** The smoke rises from the Abyss, which MacArthur calls the prison of demons, and Beale reads the darkening as a sign of judgment, as in Joel and Exodus.
entries.deeper: Beale calls the darkened sun an allusion to the repeated line in Joel 2:10, 31 and 3:15, with Exodus 10:15 partly included, where the locusts darkened the land; the Palestinian Targum on Exodus 10, he notes, says the sun went dark too. Joel's locusts are themselves modeled on Exodus 10, so the two fit. For the smoke he notes that smoke of a furnace is tied to judgment in the Septuagint, at Sodom in Genesis 19:28 and perhaps at Sinai in Exodus 19:18. In the vault's Septuagint, Genesis 19:28 reads atmis kaminou, vapor of a furnace, and Exodus 19:18 kapnos kaminou, smoke of a furnace, John's own words. The Hebrew of Exodus 10:15 says vatechshach haarets, the land grew dark, but the Septuagint has ephthare, the land was ruined; that difference is drawn here. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible notes that locusts could cloud the sky (Joel 2:2, 10). The ESV Study Bible hears the eighth plague and Joel. The CSB Study Bible lists Genesis 19:28, Exodus 19:18 and Joel 2:2, 10. The grade is drawn here: the sun and the smoke each have a clear source, but no single text holds both.

entries.title: Revelation 9:3, locusts came out onto the earth
entries.summary: Locusts coming out onto the earth repeat the eighth plague of Exodus 10, the next step in the plague pattern the trumpets follow.
entries.plain: **A remake can keep the plot of the old film and swap in a scarier monster.** The fifth trumpet follows the plagues on Egypt, as the earlier trumpets did. In Exodus 10 Moses stretches out his hand, and locusts come up over the land. Here locusts come out of the smoke onto the earth. But these locusts are given the power of scorpions. They are no ordinary insects.
entries.same: Locusts (akrides) coming onto the land or earth: epi ten gen in Exodus 10:12, eis ten gen in John. In both books the locusts come as God's judgment on people who will not turn.
entries.differs: In Exodus, Moses stretches his hand and the wind brings the locusts. In John they rise from the smoke of the Abyss. John adds the power of scorpions, which Exodus lacks. The verb shifts too: Exodus says let them come up, John says they came out. Beale and Keener say John has turned insects into something far worse, demonic powers.
entries.turn: The trumpets copy the order of the Exodus plagues: hail and fire, water to blood, darkness, now locusts. Beale says the pattern shows that God holds the reins of every plague. But this plague strikes people, not crops, and its agents come from the pit.
entries.not: **Not a swarm of ordinary locusts.** The insects come from the Abyss and sting like scorpions. Every source here, MacArthur included, reads them as more than locusts.
entries.deeper: Beale says the wording, locusts going out into the earth, rests on Exodus 10:12, which opens the locust plague, so the fifth trumpet is partly modeled on the plagues in form and theme. In the Septuagint Exodus 10:12 reads anabeto akris epi ten gen, let the locust come up on the land; John has exelthon akrides eis ten gen. Exodus 10:14 adds that there had never been such a swarm. Beale notes Wisdom of Solomon 16:9, where the Egyptians die from locust bites, and that the frogs of another plague become demonic spirits in Revelation 16:13. Keener says the plague recalls the eighth plague, transmuted into something far more terrifying with Joel's help. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the ESV Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible each name Exodus 10, and the CSB Study Bible lists Exodus 10:1-20. Heiser reads Beale's note on Exodus 10:12 in his lecture. The grade is drawn here: the locust plague is uniquely traceable to Exodus, but the wording is not close enough to call it clear.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads 9:3-10 as the release of the Watchers held in the Abyss. He begins by ruling out tanks and missiles, since these creatures may torment but not kill. Then he reads Beale at length on Exodus 10 and Joel to show how much of the scene comes from the Old Testament. To read it as black helicopters, he says, is to throw out the Old Testament John is using.
entries.dissent: What are the locusts? Beale, Heiser and the ESV Study Bible read demonic spirits. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible and Keener allow that a human army, perhaps Rome's Parthian enemies, colors the picture. The ESV Study Bible also mentions readers who see real locusts described in symbols. MacArthur reads demons that take the outward form of locusts, whose sting may bring spiritual as well as bodily pain.

entries.title: Revelation 9:4, not to harm the grass or any green thing
entries.summary: Locusts that may not touch grass, plants or trees turn the locusts of Exodus upside down, since those ate every green thing in Egypt.
entries.plain: **A guard dog trained to ignore the steak and go for the burglar has been taught against its nature.** Locusts eat green things. In Exodus 10 they ate every plant and left nothing green in Egypt. John's locusts are ordered to spare the grass, plants and trees. They may hurt only people who lack God's seal on their foreheads. The plague has switched targets.
entries.same: The green things (chloron) and trees of Exodus 10:15, where nothing green was left on the trees or in the fields. John names the grass, every green thing and every tree.
entries.differs: Exodus says the locusts ate it all. John says they must not touch it. The harm moves from crops to people, and only to those without God's seal. In Exodus the plagues also passed over Israel; in John the sealed of 7:3 are spared. The sources say the change shows these are not real locusts and that the judgment falls on rebels, not on nature.
entries.turn: The judgment is aimed. Beale says it strikes rebellious people, not the earth, and the sealed are kept from its harm as Israel was kept from the plagues. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible draws the same contrast with Exodus.
entries.not: **Not a contradiction of 8:7, where the grass burned.** Beale reads the order as a point about the target, people not nature, and the trumpets as overlapping in time.
entries.deeper: In the Septuagint Exodus 10:15 ends that no green thing (chloron ouden) was left on the trees or in the plants of the field. John writes that the locusts must not harm ton chorton tes ges oude pan chloron oude pan dendron, the grass of the earth, any green thing or any tree. Beale sets the two side by side: the Exodus locusts devoured everything, but John's are told to spare it and harm only unbelievers. He links the exception to the seal of 7:2-3 and to the plagues that did not touch Israel (Exodus 8:22-24; 9:4-7, 26; 10:21-23). The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible says locusts always devour plants (Exodus 10:15; Joel 1:4), but these are told not to. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible and the CSB Study Bible draw the conclusion that these are no normal locusts. Heiser reads Beale's comparison in the lecture. Beale's word here is a contrast, not his label for an inverted use, so the label and the grade are drawn here: the reversal of Exodus 10:15 is plain and uniquely traceable.
entries.dissent: Who are the sealed? Beale reads all true believers, whom God's seal keeps from the locusts' spiritual harm, as the plagues passed over Israel. MacArthur reads the two groups of chapter 7: the 144,000 Jewish evangelists and the people they bring to faith. The CSB Study Bible reads the 144,000 of Israel, perhaps with their converts.

entries.title: Revelation 9:6, people will seek death and not find it
entries.summary: People longing to die but unable to may recall Job's cry for a death that does not come and Jeremiah's people who would choose death over life.
entries.plain: **When a patient says the pain makes him want to die, the doctor hears how bad it is.** John says the sting will be so bad that people look for death and cannot reach it. Job spoke of the bitter who long for death and do not get it. Jeremiah said a guilty people would choose death over life. John's sufferers want the same, and death runs from them.
entries.same: A longing for death in the middle of suffering. Job 3:21 speaks of those who wait for death and it does not come. Jeremiah 8:3 has a people who will choose death over life. John has people who want death and do not get it.
entries.differs: No phrase is shared. John's two lines, seek and not find, desire and death flees, are his own. Job is one man's grief; Jeremiah is a judgment on idolaters. John's sufferers are under a plague. Beale lists these texts among many where pain makes death look better than life, without calling any one of them John's source.
entries.turn: John explains his own vision here: the torment is real, but it is limited. Beale reads it as inner anguish that drives people to despair while they still refuse to repent. Even death, the last way out, is denied them for the time God has set.
entries.not: **Not a quotation of Job.** John uses no words from either book, and the sources offer them only as parallels.
entries.deeper: Keener says only the worst suffering made people prefer death to life, citing Jeremiah 8:3. The CSB Study Bible lists Job 3:20-22 for this verse. Beale gives a wider list of the same idea: 1 Kings 19:1-4, Job 3, 6:8-9 and 7:15-16, Jeremiah 8:3 and 20:14-18, and Jonah 4:3, 8. In the vault's Septuagint, Job 3:21 speaks of those who long (himeirontai) for death and do not attain it, and Jeremiah 8:3 says they chose (heilonto) death rather than life. John's verbs are zeteo, seek, and epithymeo, desire, with the present pheugei, flees, which Beale calls a vivid prophetic present. He also points to Deuteronomy 28, where the plagues of Egypt fall on an idolatrous Israel with madness and dread of heart, as a frame for the torment. The grade is drawn here: two sources propose texts, but the likeness is in the idea only.

entries.title: Revelation 9:7, like horses ready for battle
entries.summary: The locusts that look like war horses and sound like chariots come from Joel 2, where a locust swarm is pictured as an army charging into battle.
entries.plain: **A sports writer who calls a fast team a cavalry charge is borrowing an old war picture.** Joel 2 describes a locust swarm as an army. They look like horses and run like cavalry. They sound like chariots rattling over the hills. John takes that picture whole. His locusts look like horses ready for war, and their wings roar like many chariots in a charge.
entries.same: Horses (hippoi) and battle. Joel 2:4 says the swarm looks like horses, and 2:5 that it is drawn up for battle (eis polemon); John's locusts are like horses made ready for battle (eis polemon). The sound of chariots (phone harmaton) is the same in Joel 2:5 and Revelation 9:9.
entries.differs: Joel's locusts are real insects pictured as an army. John's are demonic beings pictured as locusts, so the picture now runs both ways. He adds what Joel lacks: gold crowns, human faces, women's hair and iron breastplates. Joel's chariots leap on the mountain tops; John's chariot noise is the sound of wings. Joel's swarm eats Israel's land; John's harms only the unsealed.
entries.turn: Joel's locusts announced the day of the Lord, and a trumpet sounded at their coming (Joel 2:1, 15). Beale points out that a trumpet brings John's locusts too. So the fifth trumpet carries that day's dread to the whole world. Heiser presses the point: every detail is from the Old Testament, so none of it is a coded weapon.
entries.not: **Not attack helicopters.** Beale calls the hunt for modern war machines here misguided, and Heiser, Wright and the ESV Study Bible agree.
entries.deeper: Beale says the portrayal in 9:7-9 is based on Joel 1-2, and that Joel's locusts are themselves modeled on Exodus 10. In the Septuagint Joel 2:4 reads hos horasis hippon he opsis auton, their look is as the sight of horses, and 2:5 hos phone harmaton, as a sound of chariots, then a people drawn up eis polemon. John has homoia hippois hetoimasmenois eis polemon and hos phone harmaton hippon pollon trechonton eis polemon. Beale adds that the iron breastplates may partly recall the war horse of Job 39:19-25, which charges at the trumpet and leaps like a locust. Walton notes that ancient Near Eastern texts often pictured armies as locusts, and that Joel turns it round. Keener, the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible and the CSB Study Bible all point to Joel 2:4-5. The grade is drawn here by Beale's definitions: horses for battle and the sound of chariots are nearly word for word from Joel, and the locust setting points nowhere else.
entries.heiser: In the lecture Heiser reads Beale and McDonough: 9:7-9 is based on Joel 1-2, framed by the trumpet of Joel 2:1 and 2:15, and Joel is modeled on Exodus 10. He then reads Beale's longer list, with Job 39's war horse. His purpose, he says, is to show that all of it comes from the Old Testament, so the locusts are not helicopters or missiles. He calls the creatures the released Watchers, described in animal terms as ancient writers described demons.
entries.dissent: The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible and Keener think long hair and fierce horses also called to mind the Parthians, Rome's feared horsemen, though the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible adds that Parthian links in these verses are few. Beale and Heiser keep to the Old Testament and the demonic. MacArthur reads demonic creatures, the human faces marking them as beings who can reason.

entries.title: Revelation 9:7, horses like a swarm of locusts
entries.summary: Jeremiah 51 calls for horses like a multitude of locusts against Babylon at the sound of a trumpet, and John's horse-like locusts echo that call in its Greek form.
entries.plain: **A crowd can chant the rival team's own song back at them.** In Jeremiah 51 God calls the nations to war on Babylon. A trumpet sounds, and horses come up like a swarm of locusts. John's trumpet brings locusts like horses. The Greek translation of Jeremiah is closer to John than the Hebrew is, Beale says. The judgment once aimed at Babylon now falls on a world that acts like it.
entries.same: Horses and locusts in one picture, at a trumpet blast. The Greek of Jeremiah 51:27 says bring up horses against her like a multitude of locusts (hippon hos akridon plethos), after the call to blow the trumpet among the nations (salpisate). Jeremiah 51:14 promises to fill Babylon with men as with locusts.
entries.differs: Jeremiah likens horses to locusts; John likens locusts to horses. The Hebrew of 51:27 has bristly locusts, in Beale's rendering, while the Greek has a multitude of locusts, which Beale calls closer to Revelation. In Jeremiah the army attacks Babylon for Israel's sake. In John the targets are the earth-dwellers, who worship idols. This trumpet is also the fifth of seven.
entries.turn: Beale reads the echo as a sign of whom the woes strike. Jeremiah's horses struck Babylon, which served idols and harmed Israel and its temple. The woes strike idol-serving persecutors in the same way. The second trumpet already drew on the burning mountain of Jeremiah 51, so John is still in that chapter. Babylon will soon name the whole hostile world.
entries.not: **Not a separate army from Joel's.** John blends Joel and Jeremiah into one swarm.
entries.deeper: Beale counts echoes of Jeremiah 51:14, 27 here and gives three reasons. Jeremiah 51:27 opens with a call to sound the trumpet among the nations, as a trumpet brings these locusts. The second trumpet in 8:8-9 already drew on the burned mountain of Jeremiah 51:25, 63-64. And the Septuagint of 51:27 (28:27 in its order) is closer to Revelation than the Hebrew is. The vault's Septuagint reads anabibasate ep auten hippon hos akridon plethos, bring up horses against her like a multitude of locusts, and Jeremiah 51:14 has hos akridon, as locusts. John's Greek is homoia hippois. Beale adds the Targum on Jeremiah 51:26-27, where horses come speeding like a locust, and Isaiah 33:1-4. Keener says horses could be called as many as locusts (Jeremiah 51:27; 51:14), and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible cites Jeremiah 51:27 beside Joel 2:4. The grade is drawn here: three sources name the text and Beale gives a motive, but the wording is not identical.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Beale's case aloud and breaks in to underline it: the earlier trumpets used Jeremiah 51 and so does this one, and the Greek is closer than the Hebrew. Near the end of the lecture he names Joel 1-2 and Jeremiah 51 as the main passages John draws on here, part of a small set of texts John keeps returning to.

entries.title: Revelation 9:8, teeth like lions' teeth
entries.summary: The locusts' lion teeth come straight from Joel 1:6, where the locust nation has the teeth of a lion.
entries.plain: **A cartoonist who draws a shark's grin on a tax bill is borrowing a picture everyone knows.** Joel 1 describes a locust nation that strips the land bare. Its teeth are a lion's teeth. John gives his locusts the same lion teeth. With crowns, human faces and long hair, the picture is meant to frighten. These creatures tear.
entries.same: Teeth like a lion's. Joel 1:6 in Greek reads hoi odontes autou odontes leontos, its teeth are a lion's teeth. John has hoi odontes auton hos leonton, their teeth were like lions'.
entries.differs: Joel says the teeth are a lion's teeth; John says they were like lions'. Joel's lion teeth chew Israel's crops. John's locusts have been forbidden to touch crops, so their teeth point to harm done to people. John also adds women's hair, which nothing in Joel explains, Beale says.
entries.turn: Joel used the lion to show how much a swarm destroys. John uses it to show how savage the demonic swarm is. Keener notes that in Joel the picture would scare farmers, while in Revelation it calls up the lion's famous ferocity.
entries.not: **Not a description of a real insect.** The lion teeth are borrowed from Joel to show fury, not anatomy.
entries.deeper: Beale says the lion teeth are based on Joel 1:6, where the locusts are like a nation whose teeth are a lion's, and notes later Jewish writings that gave the Egyptian locusts lion teeth too, which would make the link between Exodus and Joel a natural one. Walton explains that comparing locusts to a lion was common in the ancient Near East because of the insect's coloring and the shape of its face and mouth, and that Joel pictures the swarm as an invading army. Keener, the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible and the CSB Study Bible all name Joel 1:6. For the hair, Beale finds no convincing parallel, though some think of locust antennae, and Keener thinks of long-haired Parthians. The vault's Septuagint confirms odontes leontos in Joel 1:6. The grade is drawn here: the phrase is almost identical to Joel 1:6, and lion-toothed locusts point to no other text.

entries.title: Revelation 9:11, Abaddon and Apollyon
entries.summary: The king of the locusts bears the Hebrew name Abaddon, the place of destruction that the Old Testament sets beside the grave, and a Greek name, Apollyon, the Destroyer.
entries.plain: **A gang that names its boss after the morgue is telling you what it does.** The locusts have a king. He is the angel of the Abyss, and his Hebrew name is Abaddon, a word Job, the Psalms and Proverbs use for the place of the dead beside Sheol. In Greek he is Apollyon, the Destroyer. John turns a place of ruin into a person who rules over ruin.
entries.same: The word itself. Abaddon is the Hebrew for destruction, the realm of the dead set beside Sheol in Job 26:6 and Proverbs 15:11 and beside the grave in Psalm 88:11. John spells it in Greek letters, Abaddon, and says the name is Hebrew.
entries.differs: In the Old Testament Abaddon is a place. John makes it a person, an angel and a king. He then gives a Greek name of his own, Apollyon, the Destroyer, which the Greek translation never uses. Where the Hebrew has Abaddon, the Greek translation of these verses has apoleia, destruction, from the same verb as Apollyon, a link drawn here.
entries.turn: Real locusts have no king, as Proverbs 30:27 says and Beale notes. These do, and their king is the angel of the pit of ruin. Beale reads him as Satan or one of his servants, working to bring people to death and ruin. Even this king rules only by God's leave.
entries.not: **Not a sure jab at Apollo.** Some hear the god Apollo in the name. Keener says the link is not clear. Beale and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible give it as a maybe.
entries.deeper: Beale says Abaddon transliterates the Hebrew for destruction, which the Old Testament sometimes equates with Sheol or death (Job 26:6; 28:22; Psalm 88:11; Proverbs 15:11; 27:20), and Apollyon is Greek for destroyer. The Hebrew of Psalm 88:12 (88:11 in English) reads baavaddon, in Abaddon, beside the grave; the vault's Septuagint of Psalm 88:11 has en te apoleia, and Proverbs 15:11 hades kai apoleia. John's Apollyon is the present participle of apollymi, the verb behind apoleia. Beale adds that at Qumran Abaddon is the home of Belial, that Exodus 12:23 calls the angel of the firstborn plague the destroyer, and that Amos 7:1 in Greek has a locust army led by king Gog. Both names stand in the nominative, he notes, as titles. Keener and the CSB Study Bible add Job 31:12 and Proverbs 27:20, and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible links the word with death and the realm of the dead. The grade is drawn here: the name is the Hebrew word itself and could come from nowhere else.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Aune: the angel named Abaddon or Apollyon in 9:11 is a different figure from the star of 9:1. The name occurs only here in the Bible and in a Dead Sea Scroll, 4Q280, where it is another way to name Belial. Abaddon, Aune says, is a Hebrew term for the realm of the dead, a poetic parallel to Sheol. Heiser leaves open whether this king is Satan. The Apollo pun the study guide credits to him is not in the lecture.
entries.dissent: Who is the king? Beale and the ESV Study Bible say Satan, or Satan's agent, and Beale takes him to be the star of 9:1 as well. Aune, as Heiser reports, keeps him distinct from that star and doubts he is Satan, since John names Satan elsewhere with other titles. On Apollyon, Beale, Keener and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible report a possible jab at Apollo, whom emperors such as Domitian claimed to embody; Keener says the allusion is not clear. MacArthur reads a high leader among Satan's forces, perhaps Satan himself, since demons have ranks as holy angels do.

entries.title: Revelation 9:14, the four angels bound at the great river Euphrates
entries.summary: Angels set loose at the Euphrates call up the prophets' armies from beyond that river, above all Jeremiah 46, where horsemen gather by the Euphrates on the day of the Lord's vengeance.
entries.plain: **For a town on a border, the bridge to the other side means danger.** For Israel the Euphrates was that border. Beyond it lay Assyria and Babylon, the armies God sent to judge his people. Jeremiah 46 pictures horsemen in armor massed by the Euphrates on the Lord's day of vengeance. John hears four angels set loose at the same river, with a huge cavalry behind them.
entries.same: The great river Euphrates. The Greek of Jeremiah 46:2 has the army at the river Euphrates (epi to potamo Euphrate), and John has those bound epi to potamo to megalo Euphrate. Both scenes have horsemen in armor, countless as locusts (Jeremiah 46:4, 23), and a day set by God (46:10).
entries.differs: Jeremiah's army is Babylon's against Egypt; Isaiah's is Assyria's against Judah. John's invaders are four angels and a cavalry beyond number, and they strike a third of humanity, not one kingdom. John also says the angels were bound, which no prophet says, and that God fixed the hour, day, month and year.
entries.turn: Beale says the river sums up where the last assault on the world was expected to come from. In John's day Rome feared the Parthians beyond it, as Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible note. John takes that fear and the prophets' armies and shows God unleashing both as judgment. The river returns at the sixth bowl in 16:12.
entries.not: **Not a modern army crossing the river.** MacArthur and Beale both read the four angels and their riders as demonic forces. The ESV Study Bible reads a picture of war's carnage.
entries.deeper: Beale says the river evokes the prophets' armies from beyond the Euphrates in the north, sent to judge Israel (Isaiah 5:26-29; 7:20; 8:7-8; Jeremiah 1:14-15; 6:1, 22; Ezekiel 38:6, 15; Joel 2:1-11) and the nations around it. The strongest echo, he says, is Jeremiah 46: horsemen like serpents and countless locusts, wearing breastplates, by the Euphrates (Septuagint 26:2; also 46:6, 10). The vault's Septuagint of 46:10 calls that day a day of vengeance in a land of the north at the river Euphrates, and 46:23 says the army outnumbers the locust. Beale also notes 1 Enoch 56:5-8, where angels stir up kings from the east, and that John's irregular participle in 9:14 may flag the allusion. The ESV Study Bible says Israel's captors Assyria and Babylon came from the Euphrates, and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cites Isaiah 8:7-8 and Jeremiah 1:14-15. The grade is drawn here: Beale gives the Jeremiah link with a motive, and river, horsemen and locusts together point to that chapter.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Beale and McDonough on the river: the four presumably wicked angels held at the Euphrates evoke the foe from the north whom God brings to judge Israel, and the echoes of Jeremiah 46 are especially strong. He adds his own point from The Unseen Realm. The north is also the cosmic north, Zaphon, Baal's mountain, so the threat is both human armies and supernatural evil.
entries.dissent: Are the four angels evil? Beale, the CSB Study Bible and Heiser, after Beale and McDonough, say yes. Beale also wonders whether they are the four winds held back in 7:1, and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible thinks they are those winds now let loose. The ESV Study Bible reads the scene as human warfare, while Beale and the CSB Study Bible read a demonic host, perhaps with human armies in it too. MacArthur says holy angels are never said to be bound, so these are fallen angels, held and then freed at God's command.

entries.title: Revelation 9:16, a double myriad of myriads
entries.summary: The cavalry's number doubles the myriads of myriads who stand before God in Daniel 7:10.
entries.plain: **A crowd can take an old cheer and shout it twice as loud.** John hears the size of the horse army: double myriads of myriads. A myriad is ten thousand. Daniel 7 used myriads of myriads for the angels before God's throne. John doubles the figure for a host of horsemen. Beale reads a host no one could count; the CSB Study Bible takes the sum as a real army.
entries.same: Myriads of myriads. Daniel 7:10 in Greek has myriai myriades, ten thousand myriads, standing before God. John has dismyriades myriadon, twice myriads of myriads, close to his own myriades myriadon in 5:11.
entries.differs: Daniel's myriads serve God at his throne. John's ride out to kill a third of humanity. John adds the prefix dis, twice, which no Old Testament verse has. He says he heard the number, as if to stress it, yet Beale says the plural form makes an exact sum impossible.
entries.turn: Beale reads the number as an uncountable host of demonic forces, and the doubling as a way to heighten it. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible notes that even this evil army carries out God's purpose. It outnumbers every army John's readers knew.
entries.not: **Not Daniel's heavenly host.** Daniel's myriads stand before God's throne. John's ride out to kill. The link is the number formula, not the scene.
entries.deeper: Beale argues that myrias without a numeral always means an immense, uncountable host, especially in the plural (Genesis 24:60; Deuteronomy 33:2; Daniel 7:10), and that 1 Enoch 40:1 already reads Daniel 7:10 that way. Revelation 5:11 alludes to Daniel 7:10 with myriades myriadon, and 9:16 adds dis-, twice, to intensify it. He also ties the countless horsemen to Jeremiah 46:23 and to armies as many as locusts in Judges 6:5 and 7:12. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible says some commentators compare the figure with God's hosts in Psalm 68:17 and Daniel 7:10. The vault's Greek Daniel 7:10 reads myriai myriades pareisteikeisan, ten thousand myriads stood by. The grade is drawn here: two sources propose Daniel 7:10, and the likeness is the number formula only.
entries.dissent: Is the number a count, and who are the riders? Beale reads an uncountable host, since the plural myriads never name an exact sum. The CSB Study Bible takes two hundred million as an army large enough to kill a third of humanity, and leans to a demonic army while allowing both. MacArthur reads a demon force, not a human army from Asia, since the kings from the east come with the seventh trumpet, not the sixth. Beale, the ESV Study Bible and Aune, as Heiser reports, read demons. Heiser argues the host must also include human armies, since in 20:7-10 the nations are deceived into marching on Jerusalem, and demons need no deceiving.

entries.title: Revelation 9:17-18, fire, smoke and sulfur from their mouths
entries.summary: Fire, smoke and sulfur pouring from the horses' mouths call up the fall of Sodom and Gomorrah, the one Old Testament scene with all three.
entries.plain: **Say fire and brimstone and most people think of one old story.** Sodom and Gomorrah fell under sulfur and fire from heaven, and smoke rose from the land like a kiln. John's horses breathe out the same three things, and a third of humanity dies. The judgment that once fell on two cities now rides out against the world.
entries.same: Fire (pyr), smoke and sulfur (theion). Genesis 19:24 has sulfur and fire rained on Sodom, and 19:28 the smoke going up like a furnace. Beale notes that the three occur together only in that story.
entries.differs: In Genesis the fire and sulfur fall from heaven. In John they come out of the horses' mouths. Genesis has no horses, lions or riders. John also calls the three plagues, the word for the plagues on Egypt. In the Greek of Genesis 19:28 the rising cloud is a vapor (atmis); John has kapnos, the smoke of 9:2.
entries.turn: Sodom became the Bible's picture of total judgment. Beale says the echo shows how deadly this trumpet is, a first act of the final judgment, which Revelation later describes with the same fire and sulfur (14:10; 19:20; 20:10; 21:8). The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible draws the same line forward.
entries.not: **Not dragons or flamethrowers to be named.** Beale reads the mouths as a figure for deadly lies. Keener sets the picture beside the fire-breathing beasts in the Wisdom of Solomon.
entries.deeper: Beale says the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19:24, 28) is uppermost in mind, since the exact combination of pyr, kapnos and theion occurs only there, and 9:2 already alluded to the same text; Deuteronomy 29:22-23 calls Sodom's ruin a plague. He adds that fire and smoke from the mouth picture God's judgment in 2 Samuel 22:9 (Psalm 18:8), and that the sea dragon of Job 41 breathes fire and smoke. In the vault's Septuagint, Genesis 19:24 has theion kai pyr and 19:28 atmis kaminou. Revelation 9:17 reads ek ton stomaton auton ekporeuetai pyr kai kapnos kai theion. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cites Genesis 19:24, 28 with Deuteronomy 29:22-23 and Luke 17:29. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible links the sulfur with Sodom (Genesis 19:24), and the CSB Study Bible lists Genesis 19:24 among many texts. Keener notes Wisdom of Solomon 11:17-20, where God could have sent new fire-breathing beasts. The grade is drawn here: the triad is unique to the Sodom story, but John moves it into a new picture.

entries.title: Revelation 9:19, tails like snakes
entries.summary: Horses whose tails are like snakes that bite may recall the snakes that struck Israel in the wilderness in Numbers 21.
entries.plain: **A warning sign with a coiled snake needs no words.** In Numbers 21 God sent snakes among Israel in the wilderness, and their bites killed many. John's horses have tails like snakes, with heads that wound. Two sources hear the wilderness snakes here. In Revelation the serpent also points to Satan, the ancient serpent of 12:9.
entries.same: Snakes (opheis) that harm people as a judgment. Numbers 21:6 in Greek has the deadly serpents that bit the people so that many died. John's horses have tails like serpents that wound with their heads.
entries.differs: Numbers has real snakes sent on Israel for its grumbling. John's snakes are tails on monstrous horses, sent on the unsealed. Numbers has no horses. The link is a shared picture, with no shared wording beyond the word for snakes.
entries.turn: Beale says the snake image ties these horses to Satan. In 12:9 and 20:2 Satan is the serpent, and he works by deceit. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible links the tails to Numbers 21 and to that ancient serpent.
entries.not: **Not Parthian archers alone.** Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible note the Parthian trick of shooting backward from horseback, but they offer it as one layer of the picture.
entries.deeper: Beale compares the horses to serpents that harm with poison, citing Numbers 21:6, where serpents punished sinful Israel with death in the wilderness, with Deuteronomy 32:24 and Jeremiah 8:17. He notes that Numbers 21:6 and Deuteronomy 8:15 speak of fiery serpents, which fits the threefold fire of 9:17-19, and that ophis in Revelation always names Satan. He also hears Job's sea dragon (Job 40-41) in the description, a reading Heiser repeats from Beale and McDonough. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible names Numbers 21:6-7 and 1 Corinthians 10:9. The vault's Septuagint of Numbers 21:6 reads tous opheis tous thanatountas, the deadly serpents. The grade is drawn here: two sources name the text, and the likeness is the picture of judging snakes.

entries.title: Revelation 9:20, idols that cannot see, hear or walk
entries.summary: The gold, silver, bronze, stone and wooden idols join Daniel's list of the gods Belshazzar praised to the Psalms' mockery of idols with feet that do not walk.
entries.plain: **A new song can list the things in a house the way an old hymn does, and listeners hear the hymn.** Daniel scolded Belshazzar for praising gods of metal, wood and stone, gods that do not see or hear. Psalm 115 mocks idols that have feet but do not walk. John joins the two. The survivors cling to idols that see nothing, hear nothing and go nowhere.
entries.same: The materials: gold, silver, bronze, stone and wood, the list of Daniel 5:4 and 5:23. The senses idols lack: in Daniel's Greek they do not see (blepousi) or hear (akouousi), and in Psalm 115:7 their feet do not walk (peripatesousin). John has blepein, akouein and peripatein.
entries.differs: John drops iron from Daniel's list and puts stone before wood. In place of Daniel's do not know, he takes walk from Psalm 115. Daniel speaks to one king; John speaks of all the survivors. And John puts demons first, a step Deuteronomy 32:17 takes and Daniel does not.
entries.turn: Belshazzar ignored the warning of his father's fall and went on praising idols, and that night he died. Beale sees the same refusal here. The plagues were warnings, and the survivors still cling to what cannot help them. The Psalms add a sting: those who make idols become like them, blind and deaf.
entries.not: **Not a list of materials for its own sake.** Beale reads it as the usual biblical mockery of idols, whose makers grow as senseless as the idols.
entries.deeper: Beale says the list of idols by material is closest to Daniel 5:4 and 5:23, with Psalms 115:4-7 and 135:15-17 and Deuteronomy 4:28; his note adds that Daniel 5:23 in Theodotion has all the metals and wood, while the Psalms and Deuteronomy have only two of the six. The vault's Greek Daniel 5:23 lists gold, silver, brass, iron, wood and stone and calls them gods that do not see, hear or know; Psalm 115:7 adds feet that do not walk (ou peripatesousin). Revelation 9:20 reads ta chrysa kai ta argyra kai ta chalka kai ta lithina kai ta xylina, ha oute blepein dynantai oute akouein oute peripatein. The ESV Study Bible names Daniel 5:23 with Psalms 115:4-8 and 135:15-18, and the CSB Study Bible lists Deuteronomy 4:28, Psalms 115:4-7 and 135:15-17 and Daniel 5:23. Keener and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cite the Psalms. The grade is drawn here by Beale's definitions: the list and the senses are nearly word for word from Daniel 5:23 and Psalm 115, and Beale gives the motive.

entries.title: Revelation 9:20, worshiping demons
entries.summary: Calling the worship of idols the worship of demons follows Deuteronomy 32:17 and Psalm 106:37, where Israel sacrificed to demons.
entries.plain: **A puppet show looks harmless until you see who works the strings.** Moses' song in Deuteronomy 32 says Israel sacrificed to demons, not to God. Psalm 106 says they gave their own children to demons. John says the same of those who survive the plagues. Their idols are only the front. Behind them stand demons, and that is who gets the worship.
entries.same: Demons (daimonia) as the real object of idol worship. The Greek of Deuteronomy 32:17 says they sacrificed to demons (daimoniois) and not to God, and Psalm 106:37 has sons and daughters given to demons.
entries.differs: Moses and the psalmist speak of Israel; John speaks of the rest of humanity. Their verb is sacrificed; John's is worship (proskyneo). John puts demons and idols side by side, joining what Deuteronomy says about demons to Daniel's list of idols. Paul makes the same move in 1 Corinthians 10:20.
entries.turn: The two halves belong together: demons behind, idols in front. Beale says idols are the tools demons use to keep people in the dark. That is why the demonic plagues do not lead to repentance: the demons would lose their hold.
entries.not: **Not a claim that idols have power of their own.** The idol is nothing; the demon behind it is the danger, as Paul says in 1 Corinthians 10:19-20.
entries.deeper: Beale prefaces the idol list with the idols' spiritual essence: demonic forces stand behind them, as in Deuteronomy 32:17 in the Septuagint, Psalm 96:5 (95:5 in Greek), Psalm 106:36-37, Jubilees 11:4, 1 Enoch 19:1 and 99:6-7, and 1 Corinthians 10:20. The vault's Septuagint of Deuteronomy 32:17 reads ethysan daimoniois kai ou theo, they sacrificed to demons and not to God; Psalm 106:37 has tois daimoniois. Revelation 9:20 has hina me proskynesousin ta daimonia, with the future after hina, a usage Beale discusses at 9:4. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cites Deuteronomy 32:16-17 for the spiritual essence of idols. Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible note that Jews widely held the gods of the nations to be demons. The grade is drawn here: the idea is uniquely traceable to these texts, though the verb differs.

aw.n: Revelation 9:1-21, the Abyss opened and the armies from the Euphrates
aw.s: At the fifth trumpet a fallen star is given the key to the Abyss, and from its smoke come locusts like horses with human faces, women's hair and scorpions' stings, under a king called Abaddon and Apollyon. At the sixth, four angels bound at the Euphrates are released with a cavalry of two hundred million that kills a third of humanity, yet the survivors do not repent.

entries.title: Revelation 9:21, murders, sorceries, sexual sin and thefts
entries.summary: The sins the survivors will not leave may follow the Ten Commandments and Jeremiah's temple sermon, where murder, adultery and theft go hand in hand with serving other gods.
entries.plain: **A rap sheet often reads like a list someone wrote long before.** In Jeremiah 7 the prophet stands at the temple gate. He names the crowd's sins: theft, murder, adultery, false oaths, incense to Baal, other gods. John's list after the idols is close: murders, sorceries, sexual sin, thefts. In both, false worship and wrongs against neighbors come together.
entries.same: Murder, sexual sin and theft listed beside the worship of other gods. Jeremiah 7:9 in Greek has phoneuete, you murder, and kleptete, you steal; John has phonon, murders, and klemmaton, thefts. The Ten Commandments ban murder, adultery and theft after banning other gods.
entries.differs: John adds sorceries (pharmaka), which neither Jeremiah 7:9 nor the commandments name. He has sexual immorality in general where they have adultery. Jeremiah speaks to Judah at the temple; John speaks of the whole unrepentant world.
entries.turn: Beale says the vices cannot be separated from idolatry: idolatry is the root and these grow from it. Wright puts it simply: people become like what they worship. So the refusal to turn from idols brings the refusal to turn from the rest.
entries.not: **Not a full list of sins.** John picks four that, the sources say, travel with idol worship in the Bible.
entries.deeper: Beale says the Ten Commandments may have inspired the list, since idolatry comes first there and three of the four sins follow, and he gives Jeremiah 7:5-11 first among texts that tie these vices to idolatry, with Hosea 3:1-4:2, Wisdom of Solomon 12:3-6 and 14:22-29, and Romans 1. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible links the evil deeds to idolatry by citing Jeremiah 7:5-11. The vault's Septuagint of Jeremiah 7:9 lists murder, adultery, theft, false oaths, incense to Baal and other gods. Wright writes that murder, magic, fornication and theft are forms of the blindness and deadness idols produce. The grade is drawn here: two sources propose Jeremiah 7, and the likeness is a list of vices tied to idolatry.

entries.title: Revelation 10:1, wrapped in a cloud, with legs like pillars of fire
entries.summary: The mighty angel comes robed in the marks of God's own presence: the cloud, the rainbow of Ezekiel 1, and legs like the pillar of fire that led Israel through the wilderness.
entries.plain: **A messenger who arrives in the king's robe and crown makes you wonder who he really is.** John sees a mighty angel come down. He is wrapped in a cloud, the way God came to Israel. A rainbow is over his head, like the bow around God's glory in Ezekiel 1. His legs are like pillars of fire, like the pillar that led Israel by night.
entries.same: The pillar of fire: Exodus 13:21 in Greek has stylo pyros, and John has styloi pyros. The bow in the cloud around God's glory in Ezekiel 1:28. A face like the sun and legs of fire recall the man of Daniel 10:6 and Christ in Revelation 1:15-16.
entries.differs: Exodus has one pillar leading a people; John has two fiery legs on one figure. Ezekiel's bow surrounds God's glory; John's rainbow sits on the angel's head, and his word iris is not Ezekiel's word for bow. Daniel's man has legs like polished bronze; John trades bronze for fire. The cloud is worn as clothing, which no single text says.
entries.turn: Each feature belongs elsewhere to God or to Christ. The cloud and the rainbow of 4:3 are God's. The shining face of 1:16 and the fiery feet of 1:15 are Christ's. Beale concludes that the angel is the divine angel of the Lord, Christ himself. The wilderness pillar, he says, promises God's guiding presence to his people in the wilderness of the world.
entries.not: **Not a mere giant.** Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible stress the angel's vast size, but the features John chose are the marks of God's presence.
entries.deeper: Beale says only God comes in a cloud in the Old Testament, with the possible exception of the son of man in Daniel 7:13. The rainbow is near Ezekiel 1:26-28, and the article carries over the rainbow of 4:3. The face like the sun repeats 1:16 and Matthew 17:2. The heavenly man of Daniel 10-12 is the model, he says, and the change from bronze feet (1:15; Daniel 10:6) to pillars of fire evokes God's presence in the wilderness (Exodus 13:20-22; 14:24). He also hears Exodus 19:9-19, where God descends in cloud and fire with thunder and a trumpet, echoed in 10:3-4, 7. In the vault's Septuagint, Exodus 13:21 has en stylo pyros and Ezekiel 1:28 hos horasis toxou, like the sight of a bow, in the cloud. Revelation 10:1 has he iris and hoi podes autou hos styloi pyros. The ESV Study Bible gives the same cluster: rainbow (4:3), cloud and face (1:7, 16), pillars (Exodus 13:21-22; 14:24). Beasley-Murray, Beale reports, thinks the pillar wording is coincidence. The grade is drawn here: each feature traces to a theophany, but the mix is John's.
entries.heiser: Heiser argues the mighty angel is Christ, in his words "the second person of the Trinity appearing as a man". He calls this angelomorphic christology: John borrows features used of God, of the angel of Yahweh, and of the man above Gabriel and Michael in Daniel. The cloud recalls Daniel 7, the rainbow Ezekiel 1:28 through 4:3, the face Revelation 1:16. Angel does not mean created, he says; the angel of the Lord is Yahweh himself, the one who bears God's name (Exodus 23:20-21). He disagrees with Bauckham, who keeps Christ and the revealing angel apart.
entries.dissent: Is the angel Christ? Beale and Heiser say yes, the divine angel of the Lord, and Beale adds the lion of 5:5 beside the roar of 10:3. The CSB Study Bible calls it unlikely, since Christ is never called an angel elsewhere in the New Testament. The ESV Study Bible gives both views, noting that many see simply another great angel. Charles proposed Gabriel, whose name sounds like mighty one; Aune, as Heiser reports, and Beale see no reason to name him. Keener treats him as a mighty angel over creation. MacArthur reads a created angel of the highest rank, since the word for another means one of the same kind.

aw.n: Revelation 10:1-11, the mighty angel and the little scroll
aw.s: A mighty angel robed in a cloud, with a rainbow over his head, plants one foot on the sea and one on the land, swears by the one who lives for ever that there will be no more delay, and gives John a little scroll to eat, sweet in his mouth and bitter in his stomach.

entries.title: Revelation 10:3, a loud cry like a lion roaring
entries.summary: The angel's lion-like cry echoes Amos 3:8, where the Lord has roared and the prophet must prophesy, the same chapter John draws on in 10:7.
entries.plain: **When the coach shouts from the sideline, the team knows the next play is coming.** Amos asks who will not fear when a lion roars, and who will not prophesy when the Lord speaks. John's angel cries out like a roaring lion, and thunders answer him. A few verses later John is told to prophesy again. The roar is the call that sets the prophet to work.
entries.same: A lion's roar as the voice from heaven. Amos 3:8 sets the lion's roar beside the Lord who speaks, and Hosea 11:10 has the Lord roar like a lion. John's angel cries out like a lion.
entries.differs: John's verb for the roar, mykatai, is not the Greek verb of Amos 3:8 or Hosea 11:10, ereuxetai, a difference drawn here. In Amos the lion pictures God; in John the roar comes from the angel. John ties the roar to seven thunders, which Amos does not have. Beale's reason for the link is three verses on: 10:7 clearly uses Amos 3:7.
entries.turn: In Amos the roar means God has spoken and the prophet cannot keep silent. John's roar opens his own new commission to prophesy (10:11). Beale reads the lion as another sign that the speaker is divine, like the Lion of Judah in 5:5. The ESV Study Bible says the roar could belong to that Lion.
entries.not: **Not the devil's roar.** The CSB Study Bible notes 1 Peter 5:8, where the devil prowls like a roaring lion, but reads this roar as speaking for the Lion of Judah.
entries.deeper: Beale calls it probable that the roar alludes to Amos 3:8, since 10:7 clearly alludes to Amos 3:7, and Amos 3:4-8 joins a lion's roar, a trumpet and the prophets as Revelation 10 does; he credits Bauckham. God's voice is likened to a lion's also in Isaiah 31:4 and Hosea 11:10, and 4 Ezra 11:37 and 12:31 picture the Messiah's judgment as a roaring lion. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cites Hosea 11:10, Amos 1:2 and 3:8. The ESV Study Bible pairs Amos 3:7-8 with the Lion of 5:5. The vault's Septuagint of Amos 3:8 reads leon ereuxetai, a lion will roar, while John writes hosper leon mykatai. Walton notes that a lion roars to freeze its prey as it rushes. The grade is Beale's own word: probable.

entries.title: Revelation 10:3-4, the seven thunders spoke
entries.summary: The seven thunders may recall Psalm 29, where the voice of the Lord thunders seven times, and Sinai, where God's voice came with thunder.
entries.plain: **A choir that sings one line seven times leaves no doubt whose song it is.** Psalm 29 says the voice of the Lord seven times, and it thunders over the waters. At Sinai God spoke amid thunder. When the angel cries out, seven thunders speak. John was about to write it down, but he is told to seal it. Two sources hear Psalm 29 in the seven.
entries.same: Thunder as God's voice (phone). Psalm 29:3 has the voice of the Lord over the waters while the God of glory thunders, and the phrase voice of the Lord runs seven times through the psalm. Exodus 19:16 has voices and lightning at Sinai.
entries.differs: Psalm 29 never says seven thunders; the seven is a count of its refrain. John's thunders speak words he could have written down. The psalm's thunder praises God's power, while John's message is held back. Both sources hedge: may be based on, says Beale, and may be an allusion, says the CSB Study Bible.
entries.turn: If the psalm stands behind them, the seven thunders are God's own voice of judgment. Their silence is God's choice. Beale reads them as one more set of seven judgments, like the seals, trumpets and bowls. This set John is not to reveal.
entries.not: **Not a hidden message to be decoded.** John was told to seal it and not write it. The CSB Study Bible cites Deuteronomy 29:29: hidden things belong to God.
entries.deeper: Beale says the thunders may rest on Psalm 29, whose punishing thunders are named the voice of the Lord seven times, and the psalm shows God sitting as king forever. The article, the seven thunders, may itself introduce the allusion. Jewish tradition called God's thunder at Sinai seven voices (Midrash Rabbah on Exodus 15.28) and used Psalm 29 to explain Exodus 19:16-19. The CSB Study Bible says the thunders may be an allusion to Psalm 29 and cites Deuteronomy 29:29 for the sealing. The vault's Septuagint of Psalm 29:3 (28:3 in its order) reads phone kyriou epi ton hydaton, ho theos tes doxes ebrontese. Revelation 10:3 reads elalesan hai hepta brontai tas heauton phonas. The grade is possible: both sources hedge, and the shared idea is thunder as God's voice.
entries.dissent: What were the thunders? Beale lists views: judgments God chose to cancel (Caird), plagues never released (Mounce), or a sevenfold series kept hidden, which he prefers. Keener connects them to the contents of the scroll. The ESV Study Bible says reporting them would only have delayed the end. MacArthur reads thunder in Revelation as the storm of God's fury about to fall on a sinful world, and the seal as keeping the message hidden until God's time.

aw.s: A mighty angel robed in a cloud, with a rainbow over his head, plants one foot on the sea and one on the land, swears by the one who lives for ever that there will be no more delay, and gives John a little scroll to eat, sweet in his mouth and bitter in his stomach.

entries.title: Revelation 10:4, seal up what the seven thunders said
entries.summary: The order to seal the thunders' words repeats the order given to Daniel to seal his vision, though elsewhere Revelation is told not to seal its words.
entries.plain: **A judge can order part of a file kept secret while the rest goes public.** Daniel was told to seal up his words until the end. John's book is the opposite: at its close he is told not to seal it, since the end is close. But here, once, he gets Daniel's order. The thunders' words stay sealed. John alone hears what his readers never will.
entries.same: The verb seal (sphragizo) for keeping a revelation hidden. Daniel 12:4 in Greek tells Daniel to seal the book (sphragison) until the time of the end, and 12:9 says the words are sealed. John hears sphragison, seal up.
entries.differs: Daniel seals a written book; John is told not to write at all. Daniel's seal holds until the end; John's thunders are sealed at its brink. In 22:10 the angel reverses Daniel for the rest of Revelation: do not seal. So 10:4 is the one place John is treated like Daniel.
entries.turn: Beale says sealing in Daniel never meant cancelling, only hiding how events will come true. John, unlike Daniel, understood what he heard but was not to tell it. The church lives with some of God's plans still hidden, as the ESV Study Bible says.
entries.not: **Not a lost chapter to be recovered.** Nothing was written down, so nothing was lost.
entries.deeper: Beale says the command reflects the command to Daniel from the angel who is the model for John's angel (Daniel 12:4, 7, 9 in Theodotion; also 8:26), with the shared verb sphragizo. In Daniel 12 the way the prophecy would be fulfilled was sealed, not revealed. He argues that sealing in apocalyptic writing never means cancelling, against Caird. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cites Daniel 8:26 and 12:4, 9 and contrasts 22:10, and the CSB Study Bible lists the same verses. Walton reads sealing in Daniel as authentication: the vision is confirmed when the set time passes. The vault's Greek Daniel 12:4 reads sphragison to biblion heos kairou synteleias, seal the book until the time of the end. The grade is drawn here: the shared verb and the Daniel 12 setting of 10:5-7 make the link uniquely traceable, though the wording is short.

aw.n: Revelation 10:1-11, the mighty angel and the little scroll
aw.s: A mighty angel robed in a cloud, with a rainbow over his head, plants one foot on the sea and one on the land, swears by the one who lives for ever that there will be no more delay, and gives John a little scroll to eat, sweet in his mouth and bitter in his stomach.

entries.title: Revelation 10:5-6, he raised his right hand and swore
entries.summary: The angel over sea and land who lifts his hand and swears by the one who lives forever replays Daniel 12:7, but where Daniel's oath set a time of waiting, John's says the delay is over.
entries.plain: **A judge who once said wait for the verdict now bangs the gavel.** In Daniel 12 a man in linen stands above the river. He lifts both hands to heaven and swears by the one who lives forever. His answer to the question how long is a long wait. John's angel stands on sea and land, lifts his hand, swears the same kind of oath, and says the waiting is over.
entries.same: A hand raised to heaven and an oath by the one who lives forever. The Greek of Daniel 12:7 has the man lift his right hand to heaven and swear by the one living forever (omosen en to zonti eis ton aiona); John has omosen to zonti eis tous aionas ton aionon. Both stand over waters: Daniel's man above the river, John's angel on the sea.
entries.differs: Daniel's man lifts both hands; John's angel lifts the right hand only. Daniel's oath sets a time of waiting; John's says the delay is over (chronos ouketi estai). John adds the Creator of heaven, earth and sea, and the mystery to be finished at the seventh trumpet. Beale says the idea of the oath has been changed: the end Daniel had to wait for is now at hand.
entries.turn: Daniel asked how long and was told to wait. The martyrs of 6:10 ask how long and are told to rest a little longer. Now the angel swears the delay is over. Keener says the point is that the time before the end has run out. John treats Daniel's oath as coming true.
entries.not: **Not a claim that time itself will stop.** Beale, Keener and Wright read chronos here as delay, not as the end of time.
entries.deeper: Beale calls the description a direct allusion to Daniel 12:7. An oath with en is unusual in Greek, he says, and conforms to Daniel; the SBL text prints the verse without en. Daniel 12:7 itself develops Deuteronomy 32:40, where God lifts his hand and swears to judge his enemies, and Beale thinks that text is also in mind; God swears oaths elsewhere too, so an oath does not rule out a divine speaker. The verb etelesthe in 10:7 again betrays Daniel 12:7 (syntelesthesetai in the Septuagint). For the sense of delay he and Keener point to Habakkuk 2:3, where the vision will not delay. Keener says John alludes to Daniel 12:7, where an angel swore there would be three and a half more years. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the ESV Study Bible (with Genesis 14:22 and Deuteronomy 32:40) and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cite Daniel 12:7, and the CSB Study Bible lists it. The creator phrase echoes Exodus 20:11, Nehemiah 9:6 and Psalm 146:6, Beale notes. The grade is drawn here by Beale's definitions: the oath words are nearly identical and the setting is unique.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Daniel 12:6-7, the man in linen above the waters, while identifying that man: he is neither Gabriel nor Michael but the prince of the host, the angel of the Lord, and Revelation 10 borrows his features. On the oath he answers an objection: if the angel is Christ, why swear by God? The Son swearing by the Father is no contradiction, he says, since the angel of the Lord serves God the Father. He does not draw out the no-more-delay parallel; that link comes from Beale and Keener.
entries.dissent: Does an oath show the angel is a creature? Beckwith and others, as Beale reports, say God or Christ would not swear. Beale answers that God swears in Deuteronomy 32 and elsewhere, and Heiser makes the same point. On timing, Charles and Ladd read the days of the seventh trumpet as a short final tribulation; Beale reads them as the end of history itself. MacArthur reads the end of delay as the opening of the day of the Lord's final plagues, the time the disciples asked about (Acts 1:6).
