entries.title: Revelation 10:7, the mystery of God, announced to his servants the prophets
entries.summary: The mystery God announced to his servants the prophets joins Amos 3:7, where God reveals his secret to his servants the prophets, to Daniel's word for a mystery God reveals.
entries.plain: **A company that promised a launch years ago can finally say, we told you this was coming.** Amos says the Lord does nothing without first showing his secret to his servants the prophets. Daniel calls God's plan a mystery that God reveals. John joins them. At the seventh trumpet God's mystery will be finished, just as he told his servants the prophets long ago.
entries.same: His servants the prophets: Amos 3:7 in Greek has tous doulous autou tous prophetas, and John has tous heautou doulous tous prophetas. And mystery (mysterion), the word Daniel 2:28 uses for what the God in heaven reveals.
entries.differs: Amos says God reveals his secret before he acts; John says the mystery will be finished. John's verb is euangelizo, announced as good news, which Amos lacks. Amos's Hebrew word is sod, secret counsel, which the Greek translation turned into paideia, instruction. John's mystery is closer to the Hebrew sense, a point drawn here. The word mystery itself is Daniel's.
entries.turn: Beale reads the mystery as God's plan in Daniel, now opening because Christ has begun the last days. Part of the secret, he says, is how it comes true: God wins through his people's apparent defeat, as Christ did. The CSB Study Bible says the prophets here are probably both Old and New Testament ones.
entries.not: **Not an esoteric secret for insiders.** In Daniel and in Paul a mystery is God's plan made known, as Beale and the ESV Study Bible stress.
entries.deeper: Beale calls 10:7 a clear allusion to Amos 3:7, combined with the mystery idea from Daniel, and notes the same Daniel and Amos pairing at Qumran (1QpHab 7.4-5). Amos 3:4-8 also has the lion's roar and the trumpet of Revelation 10. Mysterion has a latter-day sense in the Greek Old Testament only in Daniel (2:19, 27-30, 47), and the phrase his servants the prophets introduces Daniel 9 twice. The Hebrew of Amos 3:7 reads ki im gala sodo el avadav hanneviim, unless he reveals his secret to his servants the prophets; the vault's Septuagint has apokalypse paideian, reveals instruction. The CSB Study Bible says the phrase echoes the same wording in Amos 3:7, and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible and the ESV Study Bible cite Amos 3:7. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible counts the formula nearly twenty times in the Old Testament (on 11:18). The grade is Beale's: a clear allusion.
entries.dissent: What is the mystery? Beale says God's plan from Christ's exaltation to the end, carried out through the saints' suffering. The ESV Study Bible says God's plan to unite all things under Christ, including the wrath of the bowls. Kraft, as Beale reports, limits it to the resurrection of the dead, which Beale counts as only part of it. MacArthur reads the close of all things, when God judges sinners and sets up his just kingdom on the earth.

aw.n: Revelation 10:1-11, the mighty angel and the little scroll
aw.s: A mighty angel robed in a cloud, with a rainbow over his head, plants one foot on the sea and one on the land, swears by the one who lives for ever that there will be no more delay, and gives John a little scroll to eat, sweet in his mouth and bitter in his stomach.

entries.title: Revelation 10:8-10, take it and eat it
entries.summary: John's eating of the little scroll replays Ezekiel's call, where the prophet eats a scroll sweet as honey, and adds a bitter stomach that Ezekiel and Jeremiah also knew.
entries.plain: **A new reporter learns the job by reading the whole file before writing a word.** Ezekiel saw a hand holding a scroll. God told him to eat it, and in his mouth it was sweet as honey. Then he went out to speak hard words. John takes the little scroll the angel holds and eats it. It tastes sweet, then turns bitter inside him.
entries.same: Eating a scroll from a heavenly hand. Ezekiel 3:3 in Greek has it in my mouth as honey, sweet (hos meli glykazon); John has sweet as honey (glyky hos meli). Ezekiel 3:1 has eat (kataphage), the command John hears. Ezekiel's belly (koilia) is filled; John's belly turns bitter.
entries.differs: Ezekiel's scroll was written with lament and woe, yet tasted sweet. John adds bitterness in the stomach. Beale says it is not new: Ezekiel went away bitter (Ezekiel 3:14), and in Jeremiah 15:16-17 God's eaten words gave joy and then filled him with bitterness in the Greek. Ezekiel is sent to Israel; John to many peoples and kings. John's scroll is a little one.
entries.turn: Eating the scroll means taking God's message in whole before speaking it. The sweetness is God's good word; the bitterness is the judgment it holds and the grief of watching people refuse it. Beale says John, like Ezekiel, is being commissioned again as a prophet. Wright: the prophet can speak God's word only when it has become part of his own life.
entries.not: **Not a sign that John fell ill.** The bitterness, Beale says, is John's anguish at the judgment he must announce.
entries.deeper: Beale says the precise reference is clearly to Ezekiel 2:8-3:3: both prophets are told to take and eat a scroll, and for both it is sweet as honey in the mouth. Ezekiel's scroll held lament, mourning and woe (2:10), and he went away bitter (3:14). In Jeremiah 15:16-17 the prophet eats God's words, finds joy, and is filled with anger, which the Septuagint renders pikria, bitterness, the noun of John's verb pikraino. The vault's Septuagint confirms pikrias eneplesthen in Jeremiah 15:17, where the Hebrew has zaam, indignation. The Hebrew of Ezekiel 3:14 has mar, bitter, but the vault's Septuagint of 3:14 lacks it; so John's bitterness agrees with the Hebrew of Ezekiel and the Greek of Jeremiah, a point drawn here. Keener says the account is based on Ezekiel 2:8-3:3, and the ESV Study Bible, the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible and the CSB Study Bible agree. Walton says the eaten scroll belongs to Ezekiel's call: the words must be internalized. The grade is drawn here by Beale's definitions: the act and the honey are nearly identical and could come from nowhere else.
entries.heiser: Heiser says the eating of the scroll and the honey are right out of Ezekiel. He reads Beale and McDonough on Ezekiel 2:8-3:3, on Ezekiel's bitter response in 3:14, and on Jeremiah 15:16-17, where the Greek has bitterness for anger. His own point: God gave Ezekiel the scroll and God gave Jeremiah the words, and here the mighty angel gives the scroll to John. That, he says, is one more sign that the angel is divine.
entries.dissent: Is the little scroll the scroll of chapter 5? Bauckham argues they are the same book, as Beale reports. Beale grants a close link but holds that the diminutive biblaridion marks a smaller scroll for the church's task. In the Revelation 5 lecture Heiser reads a commentator who thinks the two are unlikely to be the same. Wright thinks they are one reality, and the CSB Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible leave both options open. MacArthur takes the little scroll to be the seven-sealed scroll of chapter 5, the title deed to the earth, now opened in full.

aw.s: A mighty angel robed in a cloud, with a rainbow over his head, plants one foot on the sea and one on the land, swears by the one who lives for ever that there will be no more delay, and gives John a little scroll to eat, sweet in his mouth and bitter in his stomach.

entries.title: Revelation 10:11, peoples, nations, languages and kings
entries.summary: John's commission to prophesy about peoples, nations, languages and many kings takes Daniel's formula for the whole world and adds kings.
entries.plain: **A roll call that starts with the usual names and then adds the bosses tells you who is in trouble.** Daniel uses a stock list for the whole world: peoples, nations and languages. In Daniel 7 all of them serve the son of man. John is told to prophesy again about peoples, nations, languages and many kings. Daniel's list now carries a warning for rulers.
entries.same: The world named by its peoples (laoi), nations (ethne) and languages (glossai). The Greek of Daniel 3:4 calls on nations, peoples, tribes and languages, and Daniel 7:14 has all peoples, tribes and languages serve the son of man. John has laois kai ethnesin kai glossais.
entries.differs: John drops Daniel's tribes here and adds many kings. In 5:9 and 7:9 the same formula names the redeemed; here it names those John must prophesy about, or against. Beale says kings is added because kings are judged in the later visions (16:12-14; chapters 17-19).
entries.turn: John's new message is for the whole world. It is the world Daniel saw ruled by beasts and then handed to the son of man. Beale reads the preposition epi as against: the stress is on judgment. The ESV Study Bible says that from here on the formula marks peoples who resist Christ, and kings who side with evil.
entries.not: **Not a list that changes meaning by accident.** The same formula praises the redeemed in 5:9; Beale says John turns it toward judgment on purpose from 10:11 on.
entries.deeper: Beale says the fourfold formula throughout Revelation is coined on the phrase repeated in Daniel, where it is universal (see his note on 5:9). In Daniel 3:4, 7 in Greek the formula comes just before and after the sound of a trumpet, and here it follows the seventh angel's trumpet of 10:7. Prophesy epi in the Septuagint usually means against, mostly in Ezekiel, so Beale prefers prophesy against. The CSB Study Bible lists Daniel 3:4, 7; 4:1; 5:19 and 7:14. The vault's Greek Daniel 3:4 reads ethne, laoi, phylai, glossai, and Daniel 7:14 hoi laoi, phylai kai glossai. Revelation 10:11 reads epi laois kai ethnesin kai glossais kai basileusin pollois. The grade is drawn here: the formula is uniquely Daniel's, but John varies it each time.
entries.dissent: About or against? Most translations say about, Beale notes; he argues for against, and the CSB Study Bible gives against in its margin. Feuillet, as Beale reports, sees a new mission to the nations replacing one to Israel; Beale disagrees. MacArthur reads a call to warn the world of the judgments still to come at the seventh trumpet and in the bowls.

entries.title: Revelation 10:11, prophesy again about many nations and kings
entries.summary: Two study Bibles hear in John's renewed commission Jeremiah's call as a prophet set over nations and kingdoms.
entries.plain: **A new manager may be handed the same job title as a famous predecessor.** At his call Jeremiah was told that God had set him over nations and kingdoms. Ezekiel was sent only to Israel. John is sent, like Jeremiah, to many peoples and kings. Two study Bibles hear Jeremiah's call in John's new commission.
entries.same: A prophet whose word reaches nations (ethne) and rulers. Jeremiah 1:10 in Greek sets the prophet over nations and kingdoms (basileias); John prophesies about nations and kings (basileusin).
entries.differs: Jeremiah has kingdoms; John has kings. Jeremiah's word roots up and plants; John's is mostly judgment, Beale says. Jeremiah is appointed once; John is told to prophesy again. The likeness is in scope, not in wording.
entries.turn: The point is reach. Ezekiel's scroll was for Israel, but John's word goes out like Jeremiah's, to the nations. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible adds that the nations must worship God and the Lamb, and those who side with Babylon face wrath.
entries.not: **Not a replacement for the Ezekiel echo.** The scroll of 10:8-10 is Ezekiel's; Jeremiah adds only the scope of the call.
entries.deeper: The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible notes that Ezekiel was to speak only to Israel (Ezekiel 3:1), but John, like Jeremiah (1:10), would prophesy to many peoples. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible ties the universal scope to Jeremiah's call as a prophet to the nations with authority over nations and kingdoms (Jeremiah 1:5, 10). Keener compares the oracles against the nations in Isaiah 13-23, Jeremiah 46-51, Ezekiel 25-32 and Amos 1-2. The vault's Septuagint of Jeremiah 1:10 reads kathestaka se semeron epi ethne kai epi basileias. Beale does not cite Jeremiah 1:10 here. The grade is possible: two study Bibles propose it, and the likeness is the range of the commission.

entries.title: Revelation 11:1, a measuring reed to measure the temple of God
entries.summary: John's measuring reed comes from Ezekiel 40, where a man with a measuring reed marks out the temple to come, and from Zechariah 2, where a man goes out to measure Jerusalem.
entries.plain: **A surveyor who stakes out a plot is claiming it for someone.** In Ezekiel 40 a man of bronze carries a measuring reed and maps a new temple. In Zechariah 2 a man sets out to measure Jerusalem, and God promises to be its wall of fire. John is handed a reed and told to measure God's temple, the altar and the worshipers. In Zechariah measuring marks what God claims and guards.
entries.same: A measuring reed (kalamos) for measuring God's temple. Ezekiel 40:3 in Greek has a man with a builder's line and a measuring reed (kalamos metrou); John is given a kalamos like a rod and told to measure (metreson). Zechariah 2:1-2 has a man with a measuring line going to measure Jerusalem.
entries.differs: In Ezekiel a heavenly man measures; here John is told to measure. Ezekiel measures buildings; John must also measure the people worshiping, which cannot literally be done. The measuring is ordered but never carried out, as Aune notes in Heiser's reading. John leaves the outer court unmeasured, which Ezekiel does not.
entries.turn: John hands the prophet the reed carried by Ezekiel's heavenly man and Zechariah's surveyor. In Zechariah measuring marks what God claims and will guard. Beale reads the measured temple as God's people, kept in faith while their bodies suffer, like the sealing of 7:3. MacArthur reads God's ownership of a temple rebuilt for the tribulation. Wright hears God's intent to dwell with his people, and Heiser and Aune read measuring as preservation.
entries.not: **Not Ezekiel's vision retold.** Ezekiel watches a heavenly man measure a whole temple complex. John is told to measure the temple, the altar and the worshipers, and to leave the outer court out.
entries.deeper: Beale says the measuring is best understood against Ezekiel 40-48, where an angel's measuring secures the end-time temple (the measuring words occur about thirty times each in that section's Septuagint), as Revelation 21:15-17 also draws on it. Measuring can mean protection (2 Samuel 8:2; Isaiah 28:16-17; Jeremiah 31:38-40; Zechariah 1:16) or judgment (2 Kings 21:13; Lamentations 2:8; Amos 7:7-9), and 1 Enoch 61:1-5 measures the righteous to preserve them. Keener cites Ezekiel 40:3-42:20 and Zechariah 2:1-5, where measuring praises God's house. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the ESV Study Bible and the CSB Study Bible cite Ezekiel 40:3, and Wright names Ezekiel 40 and Zechariah 2. Walton says Ezekiel's linen cord was for long distances and the reed for short ones. The vault's Septuagint of Ezekiel 40:3 has kalamos metrou in the man's hand. The grade is drawn here: the reed and the temple point to Ezekiel 40, while Zechariah 2 shares the act.
entries.heiser: Heiser says the image is drawn from Ezekiel 40:3. He follows Aune: measuring can mean planned destruction or protection, and here it means protection, since Zechariah 2:1-5 is even closer and 1 Enoch 61 measures the righteous to keep them. He notes the speaker is never named and the measuring never done. On whether this is the earthly temple, he sets out both cases and points to an irony: each system turns literal or symbolic here as its date for the book requires.
entries.dissent: Which temple? Aune, with most scholars as Heiser reports, takes the earthly temple of John's day, which implies a date before AD 70; others read the temple in heaven of 11:19 as defining 11:1. Beale reads Ezekiel's temple fulfilled in the church. Many dispensationalists, the ESV Study Bible reports, expect a rebuilt temple. Strand, as Beale reports, doubts the Ezekiel source at all. MacArthur reads the holy place of a temple rebuilt for the tribulation (Daniel 9:27; Matthew 24:15; 2 Thessalonians 2:4), with the bronze altar in its court.

aw.n: Revelation 11:1-14, the measured temple and the two witnesses
aw.s: John is told to measure God's temple and its worshipers but to leave out the outer court, given to the nations to trample for forty-two months. Two witnesses in sackcloth prophesy with the powers of Elijah and Moses, are killed by the beast from the Abyss and left unburied in the great city, then raised and taken up to heaven.

entries.title: Revelation 11:2, the nations will trample the holy city
entries.summary: Nations trampling the holy city draws on Daniel 8:13, where the holy place and the host are trampled, and on Isaiah 63:18, where enemies tread down God's sanctuary.
entries.plain: **A trampled garden is the image of a place left unguarded.** Daniel 8 asks how long the holy place will be trampled. Isaiah 63 laments that enemies have trodden down God's sanctuary. John hears that the outer court is left out of the measuring and handed to the nations. They will trample the holy city, though the inner shrine is kept.
entries.same: Enemies trampling God's holy place. Daniel 8:13 in Greek asks how long the holy place and the host will be trampled (sympatethesetai); Isaiah 63:18 says adversaries trampled (katepatesan) the sanctuary; John has patesousin, they will trample. Zechariah 12:3 in Greek makes Jerusalem a stone trampled by all the nations.
entries.differs: Daniel and Isaiah mourn the real sanctuary under foreign feet. John splits the court, which is handed over, from the temple, which is measured and kept. He names the holy city and the nations (ethne), as Luke 21:24 does, and adds a time, forty-two months.
entries.turn: Beale reads the trampled court and city as God's true people in their earthly exposure: they suffer, but their worship is kept safe. The ESV Study Bible gives the other view, that literal Jerusalem is meant. Either way the picture comes from Daniel's crisis under Antiochus, read forward.
entries.not: **Not a quotation of Daniel or Isaiah.** John takes the trampling from both but names the holy city and the nations in his own words, as Luke 21:24 also does.
entries.deeper: Beale says the persecution fulfils Daniel's word that the sanctuary and the host would be trodden down (Daniel 8:13 in Theodotion; also 1 Maccabees 3:45, 51; 4:60), and Isaiah 63:18 uses similar words. Zechariah 12:3 in the Septuagint may also be partly in mind, he says, citing Bauckham. Bauckham reads Daniel 8:11, the place of his sanctuary was cast down or cast out, behind John's order to cast out the outer court. Keener cites Isaiah 63:18 and 1 Maccabees. The ESV Study Bible cites Daniel 8:13 with Luke 21:24, and the CSB Study Bible lists Luke 21:24. The vault's Septuagint has Daniel 8:13 to hagion kai he dynamis sympatethesetai and Isaiah 63:18 katepatesan to hagiasma sou. The grade is drawn here: the trampled sanctuary is traceable to Daniel 8 and Isaiah 63, though the verb varies.
entries.dissent: Is the court the church, apostates, or Israel? Beale lists five views and holds that court and city stand for the true people exposed to harm. Charles and others, Beale reports, see the apostate church; dispensational readers see a future Jerusalem; preterists see the city of AD 70. Keener allows a spiritual temple, as at Qumran. MacArthur reads Jerusalem trampled in the future by the Antichrist's forces, the unmeasured court standing for the unbelieving nations God rejects.

entries.title: Revelation 11:2-3, forty-two months and 1,260 days
entries.summary: Forty-two months and 1,260 days are three and a half years, Daniel's span for the season when God's people are under attack.
entries.plain: **Half a week on a work schedule means the job is cut short, not finished.** Daniel speaks of three and a half times, three and a half years, when God's holy ones are handed over. John uses that span three ways. The city is trampled for forty-two months. The witnesses prophesy for 1,260 days. Later he uses Daniel's own phrase. All three point back to Daniel.
entries.same: The span of three and a half years. Daniel 7:25 in Greek gives the holy ones into the horn's hand for a set span (heos kairou kai kairon kai hemisy kairou). Daniel 12:7 has the same span. John's forty-two months and 1,260 days equal that, and 12:14 uses Daniel's wording.
entries.differs: John never uses Daniel's phrase in chapter 11. He counts the span in months and in days instead. Daniel's span is a time of oppression under a king; John uses it both for trampling (11:2) and for the witnesses' prophesying (11:3). Beale says the reason for the count in days is not clear.
entries.turn: Beale reads the number as a figure for the whole church age, from Christ's ascension to his return. For him it is a time of persecution under God's care. Forty-two may also recall Elijah's drought and Israel's forty-two camps in the desert, he says. Heiser says the numbers send readers back to Daniel and must be read with chapter 12.
entries.not: **Not a new number.** The span is Daniel's three and a half times, counted here in months and in days.
entries.deeper: Beale calls the forty-two months figurative for the time of tribulation Daniel prophesied (7:25; 9:27; 12:7, 11-12), and links forty-two to Elijah's drought (Luke 4:25; James 5:17) and to the forty-two stations of Numbers 33:5-49. Aune, as Heiser reads him, calls the period a symbolic number for a limited time of trial, derived from Daniel 7:25 and 12:7, and notes John's three ways of naming it. Keener says Daniel used all three figures and that a 360-day year makes them equal. The ESV Study Bible calls the span half a sabbatical cycle, and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible and the CSB Study Bible cite Daniel 7:25 and 12:7. Walton notes that the word times in Daniel 7:25 need not mean two. The vault's Greek Daniel 7:25 reads heos kairou kai kairon kai hemisy kairou. The grade is drawn here: the span is uniquely Daniel's, though the wording is John's.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Aune: the forty-two months, the 1,260 days and the time, times and half a time are three ways to name one period, from Daniel 7:25 and 12:7, so Revelation 11 must be read with Revelation 12. He then goes deep into Second Temple calendars, following Boccaccini, to show how Daniel's numbers fit a 360-day reckoning. His lesson is humility: prophecy is ambiguous at points by design, and every such alignment, he says, is speculation. His blunt advice: prophecy books that claim to know how it all plays out, without working through Daniel's calendar, should be thrown away.
entries.dissent: The CSB Study Bible says the 1,260 days of 11:3 must come before the beast's forty-two months, so the two periods differ; Beale holds they are the same period. Futurists, as the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible reports, read the literal last part of a future tribulation; Beale reads the whole church age. MacArthur reads the forty-two months as the second half of a future tribulation, the span of the Antichrist's open career, while God shelters the Jews in the wilderness (12:6, 14). He counts the 1,260 days of 11:3 as the same three and a half years.

entries.title: Revelation 11:3, my two witnesses
entries.summary: Two witnesses follow the law of Deuteronomy 19:15, which demands at least two witnesses to settle a case.
entries.plain: **A court will not convict on one person's word; it wants two.** The law of Moses said a charge stands only on the word of two or three witnesses. God gives authority to two witnesses, who prophesy in sackcloth. The number fits a court case. Their witness against a rebel world counts in God's court, and its rejection will be judged.
entries.same: Two witnesses (dyo martyres) as the minimum for valid testimony. Deuteronomy 19:15 in Greek says a matter stands on the mouth of two witnesses (dyo martyron); John has tois dysin martysin mou.
entries.differs: Deuteronomy sets a rule for Israel's courts. John names two prophets who speak for God against a hostile world. The law says two or three; John chooses two. He adds sackcloth, the dress of mourning, which the law does not mention.
entries.turn: Beale says the number stresses a just, legal witness, and he links it to Jesus sending disciples out two by two. In this court the world rejects the testimony, and that rejection becomes the ground of its judgment. The punishment then fits the crime, as the law of witnesses also required (Deuteronomy 19:19).
entries.not: **Not a court case from Deuteronomy.** John borrows the law's number for valid testimony, not its setting. His witnesses are prophets facing a hostile world, not accusers before Israel's judges.
entries.deeper: Beale says two comes from the law requiring at least two witnesses (Numbers 35:30; Deuteronomy 17:6; 19:15), carried into the New Testament (Matthew 18:16; John 8:17; 2 Corinthians 13:1). In 11:5 the penalty that matches the crime continues the allusion to Deuteronomy 19:15-19, and Numbers 35:30 may be echoed. Keener says two witnesses was the minimum under the law (Deuteronomy 17:6; 19:15). The ESV Study Bible cites Deuteronomy 19:15 and Matthew 18:16, and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible gives the number needed to establish a charge as one reason for two lampstands. Beale adds that sackcloth marks mourning over judgment, as worn by Elijah and John the Baptist. The vault's Septuagint of Deuteronomy 19:15 reads epi stomatos dyo martyron. The grade is drawn here: two witnesses as a legal phrase is uniquely the law's, but John supplies the setting.
entries.dissent: Who are the witnesses? Beale, Heiser and the ESV Study Bible read the people of God. The CSB Study Bible reads two individuals in Jerusalem before the beast's reign. Church fathers such as Hippolytus and Tertullian, the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible notes, named Enoch and Elijah; others name Moses and Elijah. MacArthur reads two individuals given power by God to preach judgment and salvation in the second half of the tribulation, the last word of God's witness to Israel.

entries.title: Revelation 11:4, the two olive trees and the two lampstands
entries.summary: The witnesses are the two olive trees and two lampstands standing before the Lord of the earth, wording that comes from Zechariah 4.
entries.plain: **A flag borrowed from an old uprising tells people whose cause you share.** Zechariah saw a gold lampstand with an olive tree on each side. The trees were two anointed men, a priest and a governor, who stood beside God, ruler of all lands. They would see the temple rebuilt by God's Spirit. John says his witnesses are two lampstands and two olive trees. They take up that work.
entries.same: Two olive trees (dyo elaiai), as in Zechariah 4:3 and 4:11, and a standing before the Lord of the earth. Zechariah 4:14 in Greek has paresteka si to kyrio pases tes ges; John has enopion tou kyriou tes ges hestotes. A lampstand (lychnia) stands in both.
entries.differs: Zechariah has one lampstand; John has two, to match the two trees. Zechariah's two are men, Joshua the priest and Zerubbabel; John's are his witnesses. John drops all from of all the earth. In Hebrew the two are sons of oil (bene hayyitshar), which the Greek renders sons of fatness; John says neither, only trees.
entries.turn: In Zechariah the priest and the governor rebuild the temple against opposition, not by might but by God's Spirit (4:6). John gives that picture to his witnesses. Beale applies it to the church, a kingdom and priests (1:6; 5:10), and notes that the lampstands mean churches in 1:20. MacArthur reads two prophets who will stir a revival, as the priest and the governor did after the exile.
entries.not: **Not the same two figures as in Zechariah.** Zechariah's olive trees are a priest and a governor of his own day. John gives the picture to his two witnesses.
entries.deeper: Beale says the olive trees and lampstands, with the closing clause, come from Zechariah 4:14 (also 4:2-3, 11-14). He reads the lampstand as the second temple and the trees as Joshua and Zerubbabel, supplying the Spirit's oil for its completion despite opposition (4:6-10). The masculine hestotes, he notes, may keep the order of Zechariah, where the feminine trees become the masculine two sons who stand (4:14), and Jewish writings read the lampstand as righteous Israel. The Hebrew of Zechariah 4:14 reads shene vene hayyitshar haomedim al adon kol haarets; the vault's Septuagint has hoi dyo huioi tes piotetos. Walton notes that the oil word means raw, unprocessed oil, not anointing oil. Keener calls the source clear and ties it to king and priest (Zechariah 6:13), as do the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the ESV Study Bible, the CSB Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible. The grade is drawn here: the wording is nearly identical and could come only from Zechariah 4.
entries.heiser: Heiser makes Zechariah 4 his main reason for reading the witnesses as symbols. The two witnesses are the two sons of oil, he says, in a heavenly vision where the seven lamps are the Lord's eyes, members of the divine council. Not by might but by my Spirit, he says, comes from Hosea 1:7, where God restores a people he had called not my people. So, in his words, "the two sons of oil represent heavenly people of God". He offers it as a direction to think in, not a proof.
entries.dissent: Individuals or the church? The CSB Study Bible reads two individuals; Keener holds both options open; the ESV Study Bible, Beale and Heiser read the church as priests and kings. Some, the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible notes, expect two future leaders like Joshua and Zerubbabel. Qumran looked for two anointed figures, a king and a priest, Keener says. MacArthur reads Zechariah's vision as fulfilled twice: first in the temple Joshua and Zerubbabel rebuilt, and last in the two witnesses, whose work points to Israel's restoration in the thousand years.

entries.title: Revelation 11:5, fire comes out of their mouth
entries.summary: Fire that comes out of the witnesses' mouths and consumes their enemies joins Elijah's fire from heaven to Jeremiah's words made fire in his mouth.
entries.plain: **A new song can join the chorus of one hit to the verse of another.** Elijah called down fire from heaven on soldiers sent to seize him. God told Jeremiah that his words would be fire in his mouth, and the people wood for it to burn. John joins the two. Fire comes from the witnesses' mouths and devours anyone who tries to harm them. Elijah's fire now comes from a prophet's mouth, as Jeremiah's did.
entries.same: Fire that devours enemies: 2 Kings 1:10 in Greek has fire come down and devour (katephagen) Elijah's foes. Fire in the mouth: Jeremiah 5:14 has my words in your mouth as fire (pyr), and it will devour (kataphagetai) them. John has fire coming out of their mouth that devours (katesthiei).
entries.differs: Elijah's fire falls from heaven; John's comes from the mouth, which is Jeremiah's picture. Jeremiah's fire is God's word aimed at Judah; John's guards the witnesses from anyone who harms them. John adds that anyone who tries to harm them must die in the same way, the law's rule that the penalty fit the deed.
entries.turn: Beale reads the fire as the witnesses' word of judgment: to reject it starts the enemies' doom. Two study Bibles say the mouth is Jeremiah's picture and the fire is Elijah's. Heiser uses the line to test readings that take the witnesses as two men. MacArthur reads real fire that keeps the two safe while they prophesy.
entries.not: **Not Elijah's fire from heaven.** Elijah called fire down from the sky. John's fire comes out of the witnesses' mouths, which is Jeremiah's picture of God's word.
entries.deeper: Beale says the clause is not literal but a legal pronouncement that begins the enemies' judgment, like the sword from Christ's mouth (1:16; 19:15) and Isaiah 11:4. He cites Jeremiah 5:14, where God gives his words into the prophet's mouth as fire to consume the people, noting the shared verb give in 11:3, and Elijah calling down fire in 2 Kings 1:10-17. The vault's Septuagint of Jeremiah 5:14 reads dedoka tous logous mou eis to stoma sou pyr, and then kataphagetai autous; 2 Kings 1:10 reads kateben pyr ek tou ouranou kai katephagen. Revelation 11:5 has pyr ekporeuetai ek tou stomatos auton kai katesthiei tous echthrous auton. Keener says the Elijah allusion is slightly changed, perhaps for powerful declarations of judgment (Jeremiah 5:10, 14). The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible and the CSB Study Bible cite both texts. The grade is drawn here: the fire and the mouth each have a clear source, joined by John.
entries.heiser: Heiser presses consistency. Readers who take the witnesses as two literal men, Moses and Elijah or Enoch and Elijah, read nearly every line literally but call the fire from their mouths figurative. If that line is figurative, he asks, why not the rest? He says this is not his main reason for a symbolic reading, which is Zechariah 4 and the day of the Lord material that follows, but it argues for being consistent.
entries.dissent: Is the fire literal? Beale reads a legal word of judgment, like the sword from Christ's mouth, and notes that no Old Testament prophet breathed fire. Heiser says readers who take the witnesses as two men still read this line as a figure, and asks why the rest is not. MacArthur, who reads two individuals, takes the fire as probably literal: no one can harm the witnesses while they prophesy, and the false prophet later copies the sign.

entries.title: Revelation 11:6, power to shut the sky and turn the waters into blood
entries.summary: The witnesses carry Elijah's power to stop the rain and Moses' power to turn water into blood and strike the land with every plague.
entries.plain: **A new band that plays the hits of two famous groups wants you to think of both.** Elijah told King Ahab there would be no rain except at his word. Moses struck the Nile, and the water turned to blood, the first plague on Egypt. John's witnesses can do both. The two great prophets who stood up to idol-serving kings live on in them.
entries.same: No rain during the prophets' days, as at Elijah's word in 1 Kings 17:1. Waters turned into blood (eis haima), as in Exodus 7:17-20. Striking with every plague: 1 Samuel 4:8 in Greek has the gods who struck Egypt with every plague (pataxantes ... en pase plege); John has pataxai ten gen en pase plege.
entries.differs: Elijah and Moses each had one power; John gives both powers to both witnesses, Beale notes. John's verb for turning, strepho, is not the verb of Exodus 7; Psalm 105:29 in Greek has a closer one, a likeness drawn here. Shutting the sky is not in 1 Kings 17 but echoes 1 Kings 8:35 and Deuteronomy 11:17. The plagues strike the whole earth, not Egypt alone.
entries.turn: Moses and Elijah both faced kings who persecuted God's people and served idols. Beale says those plagues punished hardened kings, and the church now carries that prophetic authority against a persecuting world. Wright reads the church's witness in their tradition, ending in martyrdom.
entries.not: **Not a retelling of Exodus or 1 Kings.** John takes one power from each prophet and gives both powers to both witnesses.
entries.deeper: Beale says the specific allusions are to Elijah's stopping the rain (1 Kings 17; Deuteronomy 11:16-17) and Moses turning water to blood (Exodus 7:17-25), and that the last clause follows the summary of the Egyptian plagues in 1 Samuel 4:8. He ties the three and a half years to Elijah's drought in Luke 4:25 and James 5:17. The vault's Septuagint of 1 Samuel 4:8 reads hoi pataxantes ten Aigypton en pase plege. Exodus 7:17 has metabalei eis haima, while Psalm 105:29 has metestrephe ta hydata auton eis haima, nearer John's strephein auta eis haima. 1 Kings 8:35 has the heavens shut and no rain. Keener, the ESV Study Bible, the CSB Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible name 1 Kings 17:1 and Exodus 7, and the CSB Study Bible's margin adds 1 Kings 8:35 and Deuteronomy 11:17. Walton notes that by withholding rain Yahweh showed his power over Baal, the storm god. Keener notes the hope for a prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15-18) and for Elijah's return (Malachi 4:5). The grade is drawn here: two famous miracles and a near quotation of 1 Samuel 4:8 point nowhere else.
entries.heiser: Heiser treats this verse as the basis of the popular view: shutting the sky, people say, Elijah did that; water to blood and plagues, Moses did that. He grants the echoes. His objection is to switching between literal and figurative halfway through the passage. He takes the witnesses as symbols of God's people, as Zechariah 4 and Revelation 12 suggest to him.
entries.dissent: Who are the witnesses? Literal readers name Moses and Elijah, or Enoch and Elijah, as the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible and Keener report, and the CSB Study Bible links Moses and Elijah through the transfiguration. Beale, Wright and Heiser read the church in the prophets' mantle. Beale also allows that Peter and Paul may be part of the model. MacArthur, without being dogmatic, gives six reasons they may be Moses and Elijah, among them the plagues, the drought of three and a half years, the transfiguration and Elijah taken up alive.

entries.title: Revelation 11:7, the beast from the Abyss will make war on them
entries.summary: The beast rising from the Abyss to make war on the witnesses and overpower them takes its words from Daniel 7, where beasts rise from the sea and the horn makes war on the holy ones.
entries.plain: **A villain who walks on wearing an old enemy's armor tells the crowd who he is.** In Daniel 7 four beasts rise from the sea. The last beast's horn makes war on God's holy ones and wins. John's beast comes up from the Abyss, makes war on the witnesses, overpowers them and kills them. It is Daniel's beast, named in Revelation here for the first time.
entries.same: Making war (poiein polemon) and winning against God's people. Daniel 7:21 in the vault's Greek reads the horn made war with the holy ones and prevailed against them (epoiei polemon meta ton hagion kai ischysen pros autous); John has poiesei met auton polemon kai nikesei autous. Daniel 7:3 has beasts going up (anebainon) from the sea; John's beast goes up (anabainon) from the Abyss.
entries.differs: Daniel's beasts rise from the sea; John's from the Abyss, the prison of 9:1. Daniel's prevailed becomes conquer (nikao), John's word for overcoming. Daniel's horn attacks the holy ones; John's beast, the two witnesses. John adds that the beast kills them, and only when their witness is finished.
entries.turn: Beale says the article, the beast, marks it as the one Daniel foresaw. Since Daniel's horn attacks a nation, he reads the witnesses as a community. 13:7 repeats the words with saints in place of witnesses. In Daniel the saints then receive the kingdom (7:22, 27), and the same turn follows in 11:11-15.
entries.not: **Not a new villain.** He is introduced with the article as one already known, and Revelation 13 and 17 describe him further from Daniel 7.
entries.deeper: Beale sets Daniel 7:3, 21 beside 11:7: the beast arising from the sea, the horn making war on the saints and overcoming them (7:21 in Theodotion, with a similar line in 7:8 in the Septuagint), and the beast ascending from the Abyss making war, overcoming and killing. Codex A, he notes, adds fourth to the beast, tightening the link. He reads the phrase as both the beast's work through the church age and its final attack (17:8; 20:7-10). The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible ties 11:7 to 13:1 and 13:7 and to Daniel 7:3, 21. The CSB Study Bible cites Daniel 7:20-21, 25 and lists 7:11. The ESV Study Bible uses the parallel with 13:7 to read the witnesses as the saints. The vault's Greek Daniel 7:21 reads epoiei polemon meta ton hagion kai ischyse pros autous. The grade is drawn here by Beale's definitions: the words are nearly identical and Revelation 13 confirms the source.
entries.dissent: When does the attack come? Beale says at the end of history, though the beast's spirit works throughout; the CSB Study Bible places it before the beast's forty-two months, in Jerusalem. Keener notes Jewish texts that expected a final war on God's people. MacArthur reads the beast as the Antichrist, one ruler whose power is satanic, who can kill the witnesses only when God lifts his protection at the end of their work.

entries.title: Revelation 11:8, the great city called Sodom and Egypt
entries.summary: Calling the great city Sodom and Egypt follows the prophets who named a rebellious Jerusalem Sodom and remembered Egypt as the oppressor of God's people.
entries.plain: **Calling a town Gotham tells readers it is crooked before anything happens.** Isaiah addressed Jerusalem's leaders as rulers of Sodom. Jeremiah said its prophets were like Sodom to God. Egypt was the land that enslaved Israel. John's witnesses lie dead in the main street of the great city. Spiritually it is Sodom and Egypt, the place where their Lord was crucified.
entries.same: Sodom (Sodoma) as a name for a city of God's people turned wicked. Isaiah 1:10 in Greek calls Jerusalem's leaders rulers of Sodom (archontes Sodomon); Jeremiah 23:14 says its people are like Sodom; Ezekiel 16:46 calls Sodom Jerusalem's sister.
entries.differs: The prophets call Jerusalem Sodom to shame it. John calls the great city Sodom and Egypt together, spiritually (pneumatikos), and adds the place where their Lord was crucified. Elsewhere in Revelation the great city is Babylon, so John may be merging cities, the sources say. Egypt has no single text; it stands for oppression of God's people.
entries.turn: Sodom means corruption ripe for judgment; Egypt means enslaving and persecuting God's people. Beale says the great city is the whole ungodly world, like Jerusalem in killing Christ. Keener and the CSB Study Bible read Jerusalem itself, and the ESV Study Bible thinks John merges Rome and Jerusalem.
entries.not: **Not a new name for a city.** John calls the city Sodom and Egypt spiritually, as the prophets called Jerusalem Sodom. The names describe its character.
entries.deeper: Beale says the city is like Sodom in wickedness and coming judgment (Deuteronomy 29:22-26; 32:28-33; Isaiah 1:9-15; 3:9; Jeremiah 23:14-15) and like Egypt in persecution. Joel 3:19 recalls violence done to Judah by Egypt, and Ezekiel 16:26, 44-57 joins Sodom and Egypt. He reads pneumatikos as seeing with spiritual eyes and the great city as Babylon, the world. Keener says the prophets often compared Jerusalem with Sodom (Isaiah 1:9-10; Jeremiah 23:14). The CSB Study Bible lists Isaiah 1:9-10; 3:9; Jeremiah 23:14; Ezekiel 16:46, 49, and Ezekiel 23 for Egypt. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible ties Sodom to fire (Genesis 19:24) and Egypt to the plagues. The vault's Septuagint of Isaiah 1:10 reads akousate logon kyriou, archontes Sodomon. The grade is drawn here: Sodom as a name for God's own city is uniquely the prophets', but John uses no one text.
entries.dissent: Which city? Keener, the CSB Study Bible and many commentators, Beale reports, read literal Jerusalem. Beale reads the ungodly world, with Rome first in John's day. The ESV Study Bible merges Rome and Jerusalem. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible says the city may stand for the world system. MacArthur reads Jerusalem, named for its wickedness, its Jewish people the focus of the witnesses' preaching.

entries.title: Revelation 11:9, no one may bury their bodies
entries.summary: Leaving the witnesses' bodies unburied echoes Psalm 79, where the nations defile the temple, kill God's servants around Jerusalem and leave no one to bury them.
entries.plain: **A team that leaves its fallen players on the field to be mocked has lost more than a game.** Psalm 79 mourns a disaster. The nations have defiled God's temple and ruined Jerusalem. They have left the bodies of God's servants to birds and beasts, and no one buries them. John's witnesses lie in the street three and a half days, and onlookers from every nation refuse them a tomb.
entries.same: God's faithful killed and left unburied while the nations look on. Psalm 79:3 in Greek says there was no one burying them (ouk en ho thapton); John says they do not let the bodies be put in a tomb (mnema).
entries.differs: The psalm's dead are many Israelites around Jerusalem; John's are the two witnesses in the great city's street. The psalm has birds and wild beasts (theria) eating the bodies; John has a beast (therion) that killed them. The psalm prays for revenge; John answers with resurrection in 11:11. The wording is close only in idea.
entries.turn: Beale finds the psalm's whole pattern in chapter 11: nations defile the temple, trample Jerusalem, kill God's servants, leave them unburied and mock them, and God is asked to repay. Revelation 6:10 already borrowed the psalm's cry, how long. For Beale that makes the witnesses a community. Their shame is about to be reversed.
entries.not: **Not a detail about burial customs alone.** Keener notes that refusing burial was the worst cruelty, but Beale and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible tie the scene to Psalm 79.
entries.deeper: Beale says the picture may come from Psalm 79:3b (78:3 in Greek), and that the parallels with the psalm cannot be accidental: the nations defiled the temple and laid Jerusalem in ruins (79:1), gave the bodies of God's servants to the birds and the beasts (79:2), poured out their blood around Jerusalem with none to bury them (79:3), and mocked the survivors (79:4). The psalm's cry for vengeance (79:5, 10) lies behind 6:10. 1 Maccabees 7:16-17 quotes Psalm 79:2-3 for the slaughter of godly Israelites, and 4Q176 applies it to the end time. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible compares Psalm 79:1-4. The vault's Septuagint of Psalm 79:2-3 has tois theriois tes ges and kai ouk en ho thapton. The grade is drawn here, following Beale's argument from the pattern; the wording is not close.
entries.dissent: Who lies unburied? Beale reads the whole pattern of Psalm 79 as a sign that the witnesses are a community of God's servants. MacArthur reads two dead prophets whose bodies the whole world watches for three and a half days, while the earth-dwellers celebrate their death.

entries.title: Revelation 11:11, the breath of life from God entered them
entries.summary: The witnesses' rising takes its words from Ezekiel 37:5 and 37:10, where the breath of life enters the dry bones and they stand on their feet.
entries.plain: **A comeback story can borrow the words of the most famous comeback ever told.** In Ezekiel 37 the prophet sees a valley of dry bones. God promises breath of life. Breath enters them, they live, and they stand up, a vast army. John says God's breath of life came into the dead witnesses, and up they stood. Israel's rising becomes theirs.
entries.same: Breath of life (pneuma zoes) comes from Ezekiel 37:5 in Greek. From 37:10 come the breath that entered (eiselthen) and the standing up (estesan epi ... podas auton). John has pneuma zoes ek tou theou eiselthen en autois, kai estesan epi tous podas auton.
entries.differs: John adds from God. Ezekiel's breath enters into them (eis autous); John's in them (en autois), and some scribes later changed John's text to match Ezekiel's Greek, Beale notes. Ezekiel's bones are a whole nation in exile; John's are two witnesses, three and a half days dead. Ezekiel ends with a great army; John's witnesses go up to heaven.
entries.turn: Ezekiel 37 promised Israel's return from exile as a resurrection. Beale says John sees it fulfilled in the faithful church, vindicated before its enemies at the end. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible and the ESV Study Bible read the church's resurrection here, if the witnesses are the church. Their enemies are seized with great fear.
entries.not: **Not a mere boost of morale.** Beale reads a figure for the church's vindication, and other texts, he says, show the saints raised in the body. MacArthur reads God raising the two prophets.
entries.deeper: Beale says the resurrection is taken directly from Ezekiel 37:5, 10 in the Septuagint, and that some copyists changed eiselthen en autois to eiselthen eis autous to match Ezekiel 37:10 exactly. Ezekiel 37:1-14 pictures exiled Israel as slain corpses brought back to life (37:9), and Judaism sometimes read it as the final resurrection. The vault's Septuagint has Ezekiel 37:5 pneuma zoes and 37:10 eiselthen eis autous to pneuma, and then estesan epi ton podon auton. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible says the verse alludes to Ezekiel 37:5, 10; the CSB Study Bible and the ESV Study Bible cite Ezekiel 37; Wright says Ezekiel's vision of breath coming into corpses will come true. Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible hear Genesis 2:7, God breathing life into Adam, and Keener adds perhaps Ezekiel 37. The grade is drawn here by Beale's definitions: the words are nearly identical to Ezekiel's Greek.
entries.dissent: Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible put Genesis 2:7 first, with Ezekiel 37 secondary; Beale, the CSB Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible put Ezekiel first. The CSB Study Bible reads two literal people and links their rising to Israel's conversion in 11:13; Beale reads the whole church. MacArthur reads God raising the two witnesses to vindicate them before the celebrating world.

entries.title: Revelation 11:12, they went up to heaven in the cloud
entries.summary: The witnesses taken up to heaven while their enemies watch recall Elijah taken up to heaven in a whirlwind as his prophetic career ended.
entries.plain: **A send-off in front of the whole company tells everyone the work was approved.** Elijah's ministry ended when a chariot of fire parted him from Elisha and a whirlwind took him up to heaven. John's witnesses hear a loud voice call them up. They rise to heaven in the cloud, and their enemies see it happen. The prophet's ending becomes theirs.
entries.same: A prophet taken up into heaven (eis ton ouranon) at the end of his ministry. 2 Kings 2:11 in Greek has Elijah taken up in a shaking (synseismo) into heaven; John has the witnesses going up into heaven in the cloud, followed by an earthquake (seismos) in 11:13.
entries.differs: Elijah goes up in a whirlwind beside a chariot of fire, seen only by Elisha. John's witnesses go up in a cloud after rising from death, while their enemies watch. Elijah had not died. John adds the voice from heaven, come up here, the words John himself heard in 4:1. The cloud recalls 10:1 and the ascension of Jesus.
entries.turn: Beale reads the ascent as God's public seal on the witnesses as true prophets, as Elijah's going up confirmed his authority. It also follows Jesus' own ascension in a cloud (Acts 1:9). Their enemies now see that the warnings were true.
entries.not: **Not Elijah's ascent repeated.** Elijah went up alive in a whirlwind, seen only by Elisha. The witnesses have died and risen, and their enemies watch them go.
entries.deeper: Beale says Elijah's prophetic authority was confirmed in the same way at the end of his ministry, when a storm wind took him up to heaven (2 Kings 2:11), and the storm wind belongs with theophany clouds, as in Ezekiel 1:4. Moses' end was also told as an ascent in Jewish tradition. He links come up here to John's own call in 4:1 and the cloud to 10:1. Keener says Elijah ascended in a chariot of fire (2 Kings 2:11). The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible calls Elijah's ascension (2 Kings 2:9-11) the best known. The CSB Study Bible lists 2 Kings 2:1 with Acts 1:9-10. Wright hears Daniel 7, God's people coming on a cloud. The vault's Septuagint of 2 Kings 2:11 reads anelemphthe Elias en synseismo hos eis ton ouranon. The grade is drawn here: an ascent at a prophet's end is uniquely Elijah's, though the words differ.
entries.dissent: Wright and the ESV Study Bible hear Daniel 7:13 and Acts 1:9 in the cloud; Keener, the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible and Beale hear Elijah. The two readings can stand together. MacArthur reads two prophets taken up while their enemies watch, and notes that God does not send them back to preach, since a rising from death convinces no one unwilling (Luke 16:31). Some, the CSB Study Bible notes, read the ascent as the church taken up halfway through the tribulation; the CSB Study Bible and MacArthur read two prophets taken up, and Beale reads the prophets' vindication.

entries.title: Revelation 11:13, a great earthquake
entries.summary: The great earthquake that follows the witnesses' rising takes its wording from Ezekiel 38:19, where a great earthquake marks God's judgment on Gog after Israel's revival.
entries.plain: **When a storyteller follows a revival with a final battle, readers who know the old tale expect the ending.** Ezekiel 37 brings dry bones to life. Ezekiel 38 follows with Gog's attack on restored Israel, and God answers with a great quake on Israel's soil. John keeps the same order. The witnesses rise, and in that hour a great earthquake strikes the city.
entries.same: A great earthquake (seismos megas) as God's judgment. Ezekiel 38:19 in Greek says there will be a great earthquake on the land of Israel; John has egeneto seismos megas.
entries.differs: Ezekiel's quake shakes the land as Gog attacks; John's brings down a tenth of the city and kills seven thousand. John has no Gog here; he saves Gog and Magog for 20:8. The phrase also occurs in Ezekiel 3:12 and Jeremiah 10:22, Beale notes, so it is the order of Ezekiel 37-38 that tips the link.
entries.turn: Beale reads the quake as the start of the final judgment. It is completed at the seventh trumpet, where an earthquake comes again (11:19). By following Ezekiel 37 with 38, Beale says, John sets the witnesses' rising at the end of history. He uses Ezekiel 38-39 that way again in 19:17 and 20:8-9.
entries.not: **Not Gog's war retold.** John takes Ezekiel's great earthquake and its place after the rising, but he saves Gog for 20:8.
entries.deeper: Beale says the wording actually comes from Ezekiel 38:19, where seismos megas is used of the final judgment of Gog when he tries to wipe out restored Israel. The link is natural, he says, since Ezekiel 37 pictures Israel's restoration as resurrection, and John follows the same order in 11:11-13. The phrase occurs otherwise only in Ezekiel 3:12 and Jeremiah 10:22. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible says the earthquake alludes to Ezekiel 38:19, and the CSB Study Bible lists Isaiah 29:6 and Ezekiel 38:19. Walton calls Ezekiel's quake a cosmic earthquake like those of Exodus 19 and Judges 5:4-5. The vault's Septuagint of Ezekiel 38:19 reads estai seismos megas epi ges Israel. The grade is drawn here: the phrase is common, but the sequence after Ezekiel 37 is unique to that book.
entries.dissent: When and where is the quake? Beale reads the start of the final judgment, tied to the quakes of 6:12 and 16:18 and completed at 11:19. MacArthur reads a real quake in Jerusalem that marks the prophets' going up, its dead perhaps mostly leaders of the Antichrist's forces.

entries.title: Revelation 11:13, seven thousand people were killed
entries.summary: Seven thousand killed may turn around the seven thousand in Israel whom God kept faithful in Elijah's day, though the sources differ on how.
entries.plain: **A reversal hits hardest when the number is one everyone remembers.** When Elijah thought he was the last faithful man, God told him that seven thousand in Israel had refused to bow to Baal. Those seven thousand were spared. In John's quake seven thousand people die, and the rest are terrified and give glory to God. Several sources hear Elijah's number, turned upside down.
entries.same: The number seven thousand (chiliades hepta) in a story of judgment and a faithful remnant. 1 Kings 19:18 in Greek has hepta chiliadas andron left in Israel.
entries.differs: In 1 Kings the seven thousand are the faithful who survive. In John seven thousand are killed and most of the city survives. Elijah's number marks a remnant kept by God; John's marks a tenth that falls. No wording beyond the number is shared.
entries.turn: The sources take the reversal two ways. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, on the line Bauckham argues, says a tenth dies and most turn to God. Beale, with Caird, reads a penalty to fit the crime. As the faithful witnesses were killed, so seven thousand persecutors die. The rest are terrified but not converted.
entries.not: **Not Elijah's seven thousand.** In 1 Kings they are the faithful who survive; here seven thousand die. Only the number is shared.
entries.deeper: Beale reports Caird's suggestion that the two witnesses are implicitly linked with the seven thousand faithful of Elijah's time, so that seven thousand killed is a matching penalty. Keener says some commentators see Israel's remnant here (1 Kings 19:18), and that seven thousand as a tenth fits Jerusalem better than Rome. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible says the number could stand for a remnant (1 Kings 19:18) and that prophets limited the surviving remnant to a tenth (Isaiah 6:13; Amos 5:3), while here the tenth dies. Wright recalls Elijah's seven thousand and the ten righteous Abraham asked for in Sodom. Beale also hears Daniel 4:34, 37, where Nebuchadnezzar gives glory to the King of heaven, and Jonah 1:9-16, where sailors fear the God of heaven, in his reading without true conversion. The vault's Septuagint of 1 Kings 19:18 has hepta chiliadas andron. The grade is possible: four sources raise the number, but only the number is shared.
entries.dissent: Do the survivors convert? Bauckham and others Beale lists, the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible and the CSB Study Bible (perhaps Israel's salvation, Romans 11:26) say yes. Beale says no: giving glory to the God of heaven can be forced acknowledgment, as with Nebuchadnezzar and Jonah's sailors. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible leaves both open. MacArthur reads the rest as the Jews still living, who now truly give glory to God, fulfilling Zechariah 12:10 and Romans 11:25-27.

entries.title: Revelation 11:15, the kingdom of the world has become the Lord's
entries.summary: The cry that the world's kingdom now belongs to the Lord, who will reign forever, announces the outcome Daniel 7 and Daniel 2 foresaw: earthly kingdoms handed over to God's everlasting rule.
entries.plain: **A sign on a shop that says under new management means the old owners are gone.** Daniel saw world empires as beasts. Then the kingdom was given to a figure like a son of man and to God's holy ones, and it would never end. Daniel 2 has God set up a kingdom no one can destroy. At the seventh trumpet loud voices say it has happened: the world's kingdom is now the Lord's.
entries.same: The kingdom (basileia) passing to God and lasting forever. Daniel 7:14 gives the son of man a kingdom that will not pass away, and 7:27 gives the kingdom to the holy ones forever. Daniel 2:44 in Greek has God raise a kingdom that stands into the ages (eis tous aionas); John has basileusei eis tous aionas ton aionon.
entries.differs: Daniel foresees the handover; John's voices say it has happened, in the past tense. Daniel speaks of kingdoms; John of the kingdom of the world (kosmos) as one. Daniel's kingdom goes to the son of man and the saints; John names our Lord and his Christ, the words of Psalm 2.
entries.turn: Beale says the change of rule from Daniel 7 is in view. 11:7 already used Daniel 7 for the beast that attacks the saints, and now its rule is replaced. Keener adds that the world system, Rome in John's day, is handed over to God's people. Heiser says this did not happen in AD 70.
entries.not: **Not a quotation of Daniel.** The voices take Daniel's handover of the kingdom but phrase it with the Lord and his Christ of Psalm 2.
entries.deeper: Beale says that if there is an Old Testament precedent it must be Daniel 7: the evil kingdoms are defeated and handed to the son of man, who reigns forever (7:13-14, 18, 22, 27). Daniel 2:44 in Theodotion, God raising a kingdom that lasts forever, may also be evoked, and so may Exodus 15:18. He reads the past tenses as prophetic perfects for the consummated kingdom. Keener cites Daniel 7:13-14, 17-18 and Isaiah 9:7, and notes that trumpets sounded at a king's accession (1 Kings 1:34). The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible cites Daniel 2:44 and 7:13-14, 17-18, and the CSB Study Bible lists Daniel 7:14, 18 with 2 Samuel 7:16 and Isaiah 37:16. Wright says Revelation, like Daniel, is all about the kingdom of God. The vault's Greek Daniel 2:44 reads basileian hetis eis tous aionas ou diaphtharesetai. The grade is drawn here: Beale hedges with if, but four sources name Daniel and the pattern is unique.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads the seventh trumpet as plain day of the Lord language. The world's kingdom becoming the Lord's, he says, certainly did not happen in AD 70 or 80; it sounds like the end of the world. That is his control on the whole chapter: since 11:15-19 is final judgment, the witnesses and the trampling before it should be read as end-time and symbolic, not as a datable event before 70.
entries.dissent: When does the reign begin? Beale reads the consummated kingdom at history's end. Some, he reports, see it fulfilled at Christ's death and resurrection, others at Jerusalem's fall in AD 70. The CSB Study Bible lists four readings, including Christ's earthly reign of 20:4-6. MacArthur reads the end of the world's long rebellion under Satan, when Christ returns to defeat his enemies and set up his kingdom; the seventh trumpet holds the bowls and all that leads to the thousand years.

entries.title: Revelation 11:15, our Lord and his Christ
entries.summary: Our Lord and his Christ, the raging nations and God's wrath come from Psalm 2, where the kings of the earth rise against the Lord and his anointed and he speaks to them in his anger.
entries.plain: **A film's last scene can answer the question its first scene asked.** Psalm 2 asks why the nations rage and the kings plot against the Lord and his anointed one. God laughs, speaks in his anger, and sets his king on Zion. John's heavenly voices sing the answer: the kingdom belongs to our Lord and his Christ. The nations raged, and God's wrath has come.
entries.same: The Lord and his anointed: Psalm 2:2 in Greek has tou kyriou kai ... tou christou autou, and John has tou kyriou hemon kai tou christou autou. Also the nations (ethne) of Psalm 2:1 and God's anger (orge) of Psalm 2:5; John has the nations were angry and your wrath (orge) came.
entries.differs: In Psalm 2 the kings are still plotting against the Lord's anointed; in John the kingdom is already his. The psalm's Greek verb for the nations is ephryaxan, they raged or snorted; John's orgisthesan, were angry, matches Exodus 15:14 in Greek instead. John adds our to Lord and spreads the psalm across two verses.
entries.turn: Psalm 2 was for early Christians a central prophecy of Jesus, Wright says. The New Testament reads it as begun at his first coming. Here, Beale argues, it is the final judgment. The nations' rage is met by God's wrath, the punishment fitting the crime. The ESV Study Bible says the song reverses the present, when rulers still rage against the Anointed.
entries.not: **Not a quotation of Psalm 2.** John takes its Lord and anointed, its raging nations and its wrath, and spreads them across two verses of a song.
entries.deeper: Beale notes the allusion to Psalm 2:2 in 11:15 and says the Lord and his anointed judge the nations for their rage, following Psalm 2:1-2, 5, 10-12; since Psalm 2 is used for final judgment in 19:15, the same is likely here. In the vault's Septuagint, Psalm 2:1 reads hinati ephryaxan ethne, 2:2 kata tou kyriou kai kata tou christou autou, and 2:5 en orge autou. Revelation 11:15 has tou kyriou hemon kai tou christou autou; 11:18 has ta ethne orgisthesan, kai elthen he orge sou. Keener says the raging nations, God's wrath and Christ's rule echo Psalm 2. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible says 11:15 may recall Psalm 2:2 and calls 11:18 a quotation from the Greek of Psalm 2:1, though that verse in the vault's Septuagint uses a different verb, a point drawn here. The ESV Study Bible cites Psalm 2:1-2, the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible Exodus 15:14 and Psalm 2:1, and the CSB Study Bible Psalm 2:1. The grade is drawn here by Beale's definitions: the Lord and his Christ is nearly word for word from Psalm 2:2.
entries.heiser: Reading 11:18, Heiser says the raging nations recall Psalm 2, why do the nations rage, and the early messianic psalms. The time for the dead to be judged is, he says, final judgment, day of the Lord language. Psalm 2 here belongs to the end, not to AD 70.
entries.dissent: Consummation or first coming? Beale says the setting of judgment points to the end, though Psalm 2 is fulfilled at Christ's first coming elsewhere in the New Testament (Acts 4:25-27; Hebrews 1:5). Some, he reports, read the reign as begun at the resurrection. MacArthur reads God's wrath as still future, spoken of as present because it is certain, and the nations' rage as leading to their last war on Christ (16:14; 19:17-21).

entries.title: Revelation 11:15, he will reign forever, and the nations were angry
entries.summary: The seventh trumpet's song borrows from the Song of Moses at the sea, where the nations heard and were angry, in the Greek, and the Lord will reign forever and ever.
entries.plain: **A victory parade can play the same march the city played after its first great win.** After the crossing of the sea, Moses sang that the nations heard and shook, and that the Lord will reign forever. The trumpets have followed the plagues on Egypt. The seventh ends where the Exodus story ended, with the song at the sea. The nations were angry, and the Lord reigns for good.
entries.same: The nations were angry: Exodus 15:14 in Greek reads ekousan ethne kai orgisthesan, and John has ta ethne orgisthesan. An everlasting reign: Exodus 15:18 has the Lord reigning forever and ever (basileuon ton aiona kai ep aiona), and John has basileusei eis tous aionas ton aionon.
entries.differs: The Hebrew of Exodus 15:14 says the peoples heard and trembled (yirgazun). The Greek translation made it they were angry, and John's word matches that Greek, a point drawn here. In Exodus the nations fear Israel's God; in John they rage against him. John's reign phrase is his own wording of the Exodus idea.
entries.turn: Beale says the seventh trumpet may be built around Exodus 15:13-18: God brings his people to his sanctuary despite the raging nations, and the Lord reigns forever. Since the first six trumpets copied the plagues on Egypt, the seventh fitly ends with the song at the sea. Revelation 15:3 later names the Song of Moses outright.
entries.not: **Not Psalm 2 alone.** The angry nations fit Exodus 15:14 in Greek more closely than Psalm 2:1.
entries.deeper: Beale says the acknowledgment of God's rule at the Red Sea rings in the background of 11:15 (Exodus 15:18, with Psalms 10:16; 145:13; 146:10 and Micah 4:7 as the other uses of the phrase). He says the seventh trumpet may be built around Exodus 15:13-18: the nations heard and were angry (15:14 in the Septuagint, as in Revelation 11:18), God brought his people into his sanctuary (15:17), and the Lord reigns forever (15:18), a verbatim parallel to 11:15. He notes that legontes also introduces the Song of Moses in Exodus 15:1, and adds Psalm 99:1, where the Lord reigns and the peoples rage. The vault's Septuagint of Exodus 15:14 reads ekousan ethne kai orgisthesan, and 15:18 kyrios basileuon ton aiona kai ep aiona kai eti. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible says the nations were angry recalls Exodus 15:14 and Psalm 2:1, and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible cites Exodus 15:18 for God's reign. The grade is drawn here: the Greek wording is close and Beale gives a motive, but he hedges with may.

entries.title: Revelation 11:17, you have begun to reign
entries.summary: The elders' thanks that God has taken his great power and begun to reign echoes the psalms' refrain, the Lord reigns, which Psalm 99 pairs with raging peoples.
entries.plain: **A crowd that chants the old team cheer on the day the title is won is finishing an old song.** Several psalms open with the Lord reigns. Psalm 99 adds, let the peoples tremble. The elders now thank God that he has taken up his power and begun to rule. What the psalms sang by faith, they sing as done. God's name drops who is to come, because he has come.
entries.same: God reigns (basileuo). The Greek of Psalms 97:1 and 99:1 opens ho kyrios ebasileusen, the Lord reigned; John has ebasileusas, you reigned. Psalm 99:1 goes on, let the peoples be angry (orgizesthosan laoi), close to the angry nations of 11:18.
entries.differs: The psalms say the Lord reigns as a lasting fact; John's elders thank God for taking up his power and beginning to reign at the end. John speaks to God, the psalms about him. He also cuts God's three-part name from 1:4: who is and who was, with no who is to come.
entries.turn: Beale says the change in the name and the past tense show this is the final kingdom, not God's rule through history. What the psalms of the Lord's reign sang, the end makes visible. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible says the last phrase drops out because God's coming reign is now real.
entries.not: **Not a claim that God did not reign before.** Beale and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible stress that the Bible already celebrates God's reign; this is its climax.
entries.deeper: Beale discerns behind and you reigned the repeated refrain the Lord reigns over the nations in the Septuagint psalms (46:9 [47:8]; 92:1 [93:1]; 95:10 [96:10]; 96:1 [97:1]; 98:1 [99:1]), following Jorns, and adds that Psalm 99:1-5 itself echoes Exodus 15 and joins the Lord reigns with let the people rage. He reads ebasileusas as an ingressive aorist, you began to reign. The vault's Septuagint of Psalm 99:1 reads ho kyrios ebasileusen; orgizesthosan laoi, and Psalm 97:1 ho kyrios ebasileusen; agalliastho he ge. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible cites Exodus 15:18 and Psalm 97:1 for God's reign. The grade is possible: two sources name the psalms, and the likeness is one common phrase.

entries.title: Revelation 11:18, those who fear your name, small and great
entries.summary: Rewarding those who fear God's name, small and great, echoes Psalm 115:13, where the Lord blesses those who fear him, the small with the great.
entries.plain: **A team photo that puts the rookies beside the stars says everyone counts.** Psalm 115 mocks the nations' idols, then promises that the Lord will bless those who fear him, the small with the great. John's elders sing of the reward for God's servants the prophets, his saints and all who fear his name, small and great. The psalm's contrast with idol worship fits the trumpets.
entries.same: Those who fear (phoboumenous) and the small and the great (tous mikrous ... megalous). Psalm 115:13 in the vault's Greek reads he blessed those fearing the Lord, the small with the great; John has tois phoboumenois to onoma sou, tous mikrous kai tous megalous.
entries.differs: The psalm says fear the Lord; John says fear your name. The psalm blesses; John rewards. The Greek translation in the vault joins small with great, while John has small and great, the form Beale gives. John also lists prophets and saints before them.
entries.turn: In Psalm 115 the line sets true Israel against idol worshipers, whose idols cannot see, hear or walk, the very list of 9:20. Beale says that is why it fits: the persecutors are idolaters. All of God's people, of every rank, are rewarded as the destroyers are destroyed.
entries.not: **Not the psalm's blessing repeated.** The psalm blesses those who fear the Lord. John rewards those who fear God's name, and he adds prophets and saints.
entries.deeper: Beale says Psalm 113:21 in the Septuagint's numbering (115:13 in English), the God-fearers, both small and great, probably stands behind the nearly identical phrase, and that in the psalm it contrasts true Israel with idolatrous nations. Some manuscripts change John's datives to accusatives to agree with the psalm, he notes. The CSB Study Bible lists Psalm 115:13 with 2 Kings 23:2 and Revelation 19:5. The vault's Septuagint of Psalm 115:13 reads tous phoboumenous ton kyrion, tous mikrous meta ton megalon. Revelation 19:5 repeats the pair. Beale reads your servants the prophets as another use of the formula of 10:7 (Amos 3:7), which the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible counts nearly twenty times in the Old Testament. The grade is drawn here: the phrase is close, and Beale shows a motive in the psalm's attack on idols.
entries.dissent: Who receives the reward? Mounce and Lenski, Beale reports, set the prophets apart from other believers; Beale reads one people described several ways. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible lists three readings of the prophets: Old Testament prophets, Christian prophets, or all believers. MacArthur reads the reward as given to the Old Testament saints, the church taken up at the rapture, and those saved in the tribulation.

entries.title: Revelation 11:18, to destroy those who destroy the earth
entries.summary: Destroying the destroyers of the earth echoes Jeremiah 51:25 in Greek, where God turns against Babylon, the destroying mountain that destroys the whole earth.
entries.plain: **A wrecking crew that ends up wrecked has met a fitting end.** In Jeremiah 51 God speaks to Babylon as a destroying mountain that ruins the whole earth. He will reach out against it and make it a burnt mountain. John's elders sing that the time has come to ruin the ruiners of the earth. The judgment fits the crime, and Babylon is its pattern.
entries.same: Destroying the earth, with the verb diaphtheiro. Jeremiah 51:25 in Greek (28:25 in its order) calls Babylon to oros to diephtharmenon, to diaphtheiron pasan ten gen, the destroying mountain that destroys all the earth; John has diaphtheirai tous diaphtheirontas ten gen.
entries.differs: Jeremiah speaks to one city, Babylon, as a mountain. John speaks of all who destroy the earth. He uses the verb twice, once for God's act and once for theirs, so the punishment mirrors the sin. Jeremiah's all the earth becomes the earth.
entries.turn: Beale reads the destroyers as those who destroy God's people. The matching verbs follow the rule of an eye for an eye. Babylon is a type of the world judged at the end, which ties this verse to the great city of 11:8 and 11:13. Keener adds that ruining the earth reverses the charge God gave humans in Genesis 1:26.
entries.not: **Not mainly a word about pollution.** Keener notes the misuse of creation, but Beale and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible read a Babylon-like empire that ruins the earth.
entries.deeper: Beale says this judgment, like those of 8:8 and 19:2, plainly follows Jeremiah's word against historical Babylon, setting Jeremiah 28:25 in the Septuagint beside 11:18. The same verb, he notes, describes the harlot who corrupted the earth in 19:2. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible says the phrase echoes the common Greek translation of Jeremiah 51:25, suggesting the evil empire, like Babylon, devastates the earth. The vault's Septuagint reads to oros to diephtharmenon, to diaphtheiron pasan ten gen. The ESV Study Bible links the destroyers to the final judgment of 20:14-15, and the CSB Study Bible identifies them with the earth-dwellers. Keener points to Genesis 1:26 and 2 Baruch 13:11. The grade is drawn here: the doubled verb with the earth matches the Greek of Jeremiah closely, and two sources name it.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads the destroyers of the earth as both human and supernatural rebels: "the Fallen Gods getting what they deserve". For him this is day of the Lord language, final judgment, which did not happen in AD 70. The study guide adds Deuteronomy 32 and Psalm 82 here, but in the lecture he cites no texts for the point.
entries.dissent: Who are the destroyers? Beale says the persecutors of God's people, Babylon's world. The CSB Study Bible says the earth-dwellers. Keener points to those who ruin creation. Heiser sees human and divine rebels together.
