entries.title: Revelation 11:19, lightning, rumblings, thunder, an earthquake and great hail
entries.summary: The opened temple with the ark in view, and the lightning, voices, thunder, earthquake and hail, bring back God's appearing at Sinai, where the covenant was made.
entries.plain: **Opening night in a new hall can replay the sound of the old hall's first concert.** At Sinai God came down amid thunder, lightning, a dark cloud and a trumpet, and the people shook. There he made his covenant, whose tablets went into the ark. Now God's temple in heaven opens. The ark of his covenant is seen, and lightning, rumblings, thunder, a quake and hail break out.
entries.same: Voices (phonai) and lightnings (astrapai) at God's appearing. Exodus 19:16 in Greek has phonai kai astrapai with a dark cloud and a trumpet; John has astrapai kai phonai kai brontai. Exodus 19:18 adds the smoke over the mountain.
entries.differs: Sinai had a trumpet and a thick cloud on a mountain. John has an open temple in heaven with the ark in view, which no one but the high priest saw in Israel. He adds great hail, which recalls the plague of hail on Egypt and the first trumpet. The five signs are John's fixed formula for the end (4:5; 8:5; 16:18).
entries.turn: Heiser says the scene is Sinai all over again: God making a covenant people anew. Beale says the formula marks the last judgment, and the ark marks both judgment and God's presence with his people. Keener adds that such Exodus language puts John's revelation on the level of Moses'.
entries.not: **Not a report that the lost ark was found.** Beale says the Old Testament looked for God's presence, not the box (Jeremiah 3:16-17); the ark here is a sign.
entries.deeper: Beale says the closing formula has marked the last judgment throughout (4:5; 8:5; 16:18), that in the Old Testament such cosmic signs mark theophanies, and that the formula is coined from Exodus 19:16-19, which also lies behind the seven thunders of 10:3-4. He suggests Jericho too: the ark appears between earthquakes after seven trumpets, as the ark followed the trumpets when Jericho's wall fell. Keener says this exodus language (Exodus 19:16; Ezekiel 1:4) puts John's revelation on the level of Moses'. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible says the lightning and thunder may evoke Sinai, and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible ties the hail to Exodus 9:22-25 and the first trumpet. The vault's Septuagint of Exodus 19:16 reads egenonto phonai kai astrapai kai nephelai gnophodeis, with the sound of the trumpet. The grade is drawn here: the signs fit Sinai uniquely, but John has made them a formula.
entries.heiser: Heiser says the scene is Sinai once more: God forming a covenant people, which ties the end back to the time he made his people new by bringing them out of Egypt. With the kingdom's arrival in 11:15, he says, this is plainly day of the Lord material, not AD 70.
entries.dissent: Beale reads the opened temple as final judgment and God's full presence. The ESV Study Bible reads it as the opening of the next vision, which shows the deepest conflict. Keener connects the ark with the covenant's curses on the disobedient. MacArthur reads the opened Most Holy Place in heaven as a sign of God's saving covenant in the midst of judgment, and the storm as part of the seventh bowl (16:17-21).

entries.title: Revelation 12:1, a woman crowned with twelve stars
entries.summary: The woman dressed in the sun with the moon at her feet and twelve stars on her head borrows Joseph's dream, where sun, moon and stars stand for Jacob's family.
entries.plain: **A team crest can say a whole history with one badge, if you know the story behind it.** In Genesis 37 Joseph dreams that the sun, the moon and eleven stars bow to him. His father knows at once that the dream means the family of Israel. John sees a woman wearing the sun and the moon, with a crown of twelve stars. Her crown carries all twelve tribes of Israel.
entries.same: The sun, the moon and the stars, together, as a picture of one family. The Greek words match the Greek of Genesis 37:9: helios (sun), selene (moon) and asteres (stars).
entries.differs: Joseph's dream has eleven stars, because Joseph himself is the twelfth son. John has twelve. In Genesis the lights bow down to Joseph. Here they dress a woman, who wears them as clothing, footstool and crown. The sources give no single reason for the change to twelve, beyond the twelve tribes being complete.
entries.turn: John dresses the woman in Israel's family badge, with all twelve tribes in her crown. Beale reads the bright clothing as heavenly status and protection. The woman suffers on earth, but she belongs to heaven. In the next verses she gives birth to the Messiah, then flees into the wilderness.
entries.not: **Not Mary alone.** Beale grants that Jesus' mother may be in mind in a secondary way. But the woman is persecuted and has other children, which the sources read as the faithful community.
entries.deeper: Beale bases the identification on Genesis 37:9 and notes that Philo calls Joseph the twelfth star of the dream. He also reports Jewish readings that made the twelve tribes the twelve signs of the zodiac, and Philo and Josephus explaining the high priest's robe by the sun, moon and twelve stars. Keener says the Genesis reference itself is clear enough to show the woman is Israel. The ESV Study Bible, the CSB Study Bible and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible all point to Joseph's dream. Beale adds Song of Songs 6:10 and Isaiah 60:19-20, where a bride or restored Zion shines like the sun and moon. The grade is drawn here: the three lights are shared and the family meaning is unique to Genesis 37, but the number and the scene differ.
entries.heiser: Heiser skips the sky imagery in this lecture and points to an earlier episode, though he says plainly that he thinks it intentional and meaningful. He starts at verse 6. The woman, he says, is Israel, the people of God, and not Mary, since the New Testament never tells of Mary being hunted into the wilderness. Because she bears the Messiah, the picture narrows to believers.
entries.dissent: The CSB Study Bible reads the woman as ethnic Israel or a believing remnant of Jews. MacArthur reads her as Israel, whom the prophets picture as God's wife, and says the context shows she is not the church; her twelve stars are the twelve tribes. Beale and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible read her as the faithful community before and after Christ. Catholic writers have long seen Mary; Beale allows her a secondary place only, and notes the Marian reading arose late. Keener and Beale both note pagan parallels: the goddess Leto, pursued by the dragon Python.

aw.s: A radiant woman, crowned with twelve stars and standing on the moon, labors to give birth while a great red dragon waits to devour her child. The child, destined to rule the nations, is caught up to God's throne, and the woman escapes to the wilderness, where she is kept safe for 1,260 days.

entries.title: Revelation 12:2, crying out in labor pains
entries.summary: The woman in labor draws on the prophets' picture of Zion as a mother in pain, whose child means rescue from captivity.
entries.plain: **A worried parent saying the waiting is the worst part puts a whole family's hope into one picture.** The prophets pictured Zion as a woman in labor. Her pains were the suffering of exile; the birth was the coming rescue. John's woman cries out as she is about to give birth. The sources hear Isaiah 26, Isaiah 66 and Micah 4 behind her, and the old promise to Eve beneath them all.
entries.same: A woman in labor who cries out as the birth comes near. The Greek of Isaiah 26:17 has the same three words John uses: odinousa (in labor), tekein (to give birth) and a verb for crying out. Micah 4:10 calls daughter Zion to writhe like a woman giving birth.
entries.differs: John adds a word no birth scene uses: basanizomene, being tormented. Beale notes it is never used of labor pains anywhere else, and in Revelation it means torment or persecution. So the pain becomes persecution. In Isaiah 26 the people cannot give birth to rescue; here the child does come. The setting moves from exile in Babylon to a woman in heaven.
entries.turn: The labor pains are the trials of God's people while they waited for the Messiah. In Isaiah and Micah a birth meant the end of captivity. John uses that hope for the birth of Christ, and Beale reads the mother as the faithful community of both Testaments.
entries.not: **Not a scene about the cross.** Beale notes that the woman suffers here, not the child. Her pains are the long wait of God's people, not Christ's death.
entries.deeper: Beale calls this an allusion to prophetic pictures of Israel as a pregnant mother whose pains stand for captivity and whose delivery stands for rescue (Isaiah 26:17-18; 66:7-9; Micah 4:9-10; 5:3). He notes the Targum of Isaiah explains the pains as distress, and that 4 Ezra 9-10 builds a similar vision of Zion in labor. He traces all these texts, and Revelation 12:2, back to Genesis 3:15-16. In the Greek of Isaiah 26:17 a travailing woman draws near to give birth and cries out in her pangs. Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible cite Isaiah 26, Isaiah 54 and 66 and Micah 5:3, and mention a Qumran hymn of a woman in labor. The CSB Study Bible also hears Isaiah 7:14, and Beale sets out the shared words sign, woman, with child and son. The grade is drawn here: several texts share the picture, and none alone supplies it.
entries.heiser: Reading Beale and McDonough, Heiser says the birth pangs are the suffering of foreign captivity, and the birth is the coming deliverance: the exile ends when the Messiah comes. He lists Isaiah 26, Isaiah 66 and Micah 4 and 5. He also follows them in tracing these texts to Genesis 3:15-16, and notes a Qumran hymn with the same picture.
entries.dissent: The CSB Study Bible links the birth pains to Genesis 3:15-16 and to Isaiah 7:14, the virgin birth. Beale sees Isaiah 7:14 as part of the pattern but holds that the woman is corporate, and Keener points to the remnant as mother. Beale also notes Feuillet's view, that the pains are Christ's at Calvary, and rejects it. MacArthur reads the mother as Israel, in pain through the centuries as she waited for the Messiah to defeat Satan, sin and death.

aw.s: A radiant woman, crowned with twelve stars and standing on the moon, labors to give birth while a great red dragon waits to devour her child. The child, destined to rule the nations, is caught up to God's throne, and the woman escapes to the wilderness, where she is kept safe for 1,260 days.

entries.title: Revelation 12:3, a great red dragon
entries.summary: The dragon takes the Old Testament's sea monster, the many-headed beast God crushed and the great dragon Pharaoh, and names it as the devil.
entries.plain: **A cartoonist who draws a country as a bear lets readers see a nation as one animal.** The Old Testament did this with a sea monster. Egypt's Pharaoh is called the great dragon in Ezekiel. Psalm 74 praises God for smashing the sea monsters' heads, and Isaiah 27 promises to kill the dragon on the last day. John's red dragon has seven heads. In verse 9 John says outright that it is the devil.
entries.same: The word dragon, drakon, is the Greek Old Testament's word for this monster. Great dragon in 12:3 and 12:9 matches the Greek of Ezekiel 29:3, ton drakonta ton megan, said of Pharaoh. Psalm 74 gives the monster more than one head.
entries.differs: In the Old Testament the dragon is a nation, mostly Egypt, or a chaos beast God beats. John says who stands behind them: the devil himself. He gives the beast exactly seven heads, seven crowns and ten horns, and colors it red. None of the Old Testament texts give these numbers. Beale ties the red to bloodshed, as with the red horse in 6:4.
entries.turn: The persecutors of God's people have one master behind them. John tells churches facing Rome that their trouble is the latest round of an old fight. God beat the dragon at the exodus, and Beale reads chapter 12 as an exodus replayed, with Rome now in Pharaoh's place.
entries.not: **Not a dinosaur or a literal reptile.** The sources agree the dragon is a symbol, and John names what it stands for in verse 9.
entries.deeper: Beale calls the description a mosaic of Old Testament images of evil kingdoms. He lists God defeating Pharaoh as a sea dragon (Psalm 74:13-14; 89:10; Isaiah 30:7; 51:9; Ezekiel 29:3; 32:2-3), and Babylon as the monster in Jeremiah 51:34. He stresses that great dragon is a title found only in Ezekiel 29:3 among the sea monster texts. Isaiah 27:1 promises the end-time defeat of the dragon, and the Targum compares that dragon to Pharaoh. In the vault's Greek Psalter, Psalm 74:13 breaks the heads of the dragons on the water. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cite the same Leviathan texts. The grade is drawn here: the word and the title are shared, but John combines several texts and adds his own numbers.
entries.heiser: Heiser, quoting Beale and McDonough, reads the dragon as the Old Testament sea monster, the Leviathan picture of chaos. It stands for evil kingdoms, Egypt above all, which God beat at the exodus. He stresses the Egypt link because the woman then escapes on eagles' wings, as Israel did. He keeps the devil in view, since verse 9 says who the dragon is.
entries.dissent: Some read the dragon as borrowed mainly from Near Eastern myth. Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible note the seven-headed Leviathan, or Lotan, of Canaanite myth, and the red dragon Typhon of Egypt. Walton's commentary cites the Ugaritic serpent with seven heads behind Isaiah 27:1. Beale grants that John may echo such myths for former pagans but rejects them as his main source, since the Daniel 7 sea beasts and other Old Testament texts are plainly there. MacArthur reads the dragon as Satan, and the heads and horns as figures for his rule over seven kingdoms of the past and ten still to come.

entries.title: Revelation 12:3, ten horns
entries.summary: The dragon's ten horns come from the fourth beast of Daniel 7, the terrifying empire that rose from the sea.
entries.plain: **A political cartoon can borrow one detail from an older cartoon, and readers know which villain is meant.** In Daniel 7 the fourth beast, the worst of the empires, has ten horns, which Daniel is told are ten kings. John gives the dragon the same ten horns. That marks the dragon as the power behind the empire Daniel feared most. In chapter 13 the beast from the sea will carry the same horns.
entries.same: Ten horns, kerata deka, the words used of the fourth beast in the Greek of Daniel 7:7. In both books the beast comes from the sea, and the horns stand for kings.
entries.differs: In Daniel the ten horns belong to the fourth beast, an earthly empire. John puts them on the dragon, the devil, and adds seven heads with seven crowns. Beale explains that John wants the reader to see the devil as the force behind the empires. The beast of 13:1 will then share the dragon's look.
entries.turn: John moves Daniel's horns from the empire to the dragon behind it. Jewish writers already read Daniel's fourth beast as Rome. Beale reads the horns as a sign that the dragon is, at least in part, first-century Rome. The crowns are claims to rule, set against the many crowns of Christ in 19:12.
entries.not: **Not the same beast as in Daniel.** Daniel's ten horns grow on an earthly empire. John sets them on the dragon itself, the power behind the empire.
entries.deeper: Beale says the dragon's home in the sea is confirmed by its ten horns, taken from the fourth beast of Daniel 7:7 and 7:24, which also came from the sea. He cites rabbinic texts that read that beast as Rome. He suggests the seven heads could also be a total of Daniel's beasts: one head each for three, and four for the leopard. The ESV Study Bible compares Daniel 7:6-7, and the CSB Study Bible cross-references Daniel 7:7, 20 and 24. The grade is drawn here: ten horns on a beast from the sea is Daniel's picture, and the same horns return in 13:1 and 17:3.
entries.dissent: Beale holds the seven heads may also come from Daniel 7, counting the leopard's four heads. Keener, the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible and Walton point instead to the seven-headed serpent of Canaanite myth. Beale allows that image a secondary place. On what the numbers stand for, Beale takes seven and ten as numbers of complete power, not a list of emperors. MacArthur reads the seven heads as seven kingdoms of the past and the ten horns as ten kingdoms still to come; at 17:12 he reads them as ten rulers under the Antichrist.

entries.title: Revelation 12:4, a third of the stars swept down
entries.summary: The dragon's tail throwing stars to earth borrows Daniel's vision of the horn that cast stars down; in verse 9 the dragon is thrown down himself.
entries.plain: **A bully who shoves others to the ground and then gets shoved there himself has met a fitting end.** In Daniel 8 a horn grows up to the sky and throws some of the stars to the earth. Beale links those stars to God's holy people, the victims of Daniel 8:24. John's dragon sweeps a third of the stars to earth with his tail. A few verses later the dragon is the one thrown to earth. Beale calls this a fitting reversal.
entries.same: An enemy of God reaches into heaven and throws stars down to the earth. In the Hebrew of Daniel 8:10 the horn throws part of the heavenly army and part of the stars to the ground. John has ebalen eis ten gen, he threw them to the earth.
entries.differs: Daniel's horn grows up to the sky and tramples the stars. John's dragon uses its tail and takes a third, a fraction he has used before in the trumpets. Beale reads Daniel's horn as Antiochus, and says John applies the picture to the devil behind him. Then John turns the image around: in 12:9 the dragon is thrown down to earth.
entries.turn: John gives Daniel's attack on the stars to the dragon. In his introduction Beale lists Daniel 8:10 in Revelation 12:4, 9 and 10 among John's ironic uses. The attacker suffers what he did, and his punishment mocks his pride.
entries.not: **Not Daniel's scene unchanged.** John keeps the stars thrown down to the earth, but the one who throws them is now the dragon, and he takes a third.
entries.deeper: Beale says the picture is taken from Daniel 8:10. Daniel 8:24 calls the victims the holy people, and Daniel 12:3 compares the righteous to stars. The Greek of Daniel 8:11 reads the fallen stars as Israel's captivity, to be ended. He cites 1 Enoch 46:7 and 2 Maccabees 9:10, which use Daniel's language for persecutors. On 12:9 he adds that the devil is punished through his own sin, since he threw the stars down. The vault's Greek of Daniel 8:10 (the version called Theodotion) reads it fell upon the earth, from the stars, and trampled them. The CSB Study Bible cross-references Daniel 8:10; Keener and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible point to it. The grade is drawn here: the scene is Daniel's, but John changes the agent and the share.
entries.dissent: The ESV Study Bible, the CSB Study Bible and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible read the stars as angels who fell with Satan, and some link this to a fall in the distant past. MacArthur reads them as the third of the angels who joined Satan's first rebellion and became demons. Beale reads them as persecuted saints, after Daniel 8. He says the Daniel background rules out a fall at the beginning here, and that the stars are not the dragon's angels of verses 7-9. Heiser, in Reversing Hermon, says the Bible records no angelic revolt before the Fall, and that Revelation 12:7-9 ties the war in heaven to the Messiah's coming.

entries.title: Revelation 12:5, ruling the nations with an iron rod
entries.summary: The child who will rule the nations with an iron rod is the king of Psalm 2, and John follows the Greek wording, shepherd, where the Hebrew has break.
entries.plain: **A coronation song can be sung again for a new king, and everyone knows whose crowning it was.** Psalm 2 is a song for the crowning of God's king, who will rule the nations with an iron rod. John's newborn son is that king. The vision skips from his birth straight to his rise to God's throne. John follows the old Greek wording of the psalm, which says the king will shepherd the nations, where the Hebrew says he will break them.
entries.same: The rod of iron and the nations. John's en rhabdo sidera matches the Greek of Psalm 2:9 word for word. Both use poimaino, to shepherd, for what the king does with the rod.
entries.differs: The Hebrew of Psalm 2:9 reads tero'em, you will break them, with the iron rod. The Greek translation reads you will shepherd them, and John follows the Greek. The psalm speaks to the king as you; John speaks of the child in the third person and says he will rule all the nations. He also leaves out the smashed pottery, which he used in 2:27.
entries.turn: John gives the psalm's king to the newborn son, who is caught up to God's throne. Beale says the birth and the ascension are pressed together because ruling is what the child was born for. He reads the psalm's promise as begun at the ascension and complete at 19:15.
entries.not: **Not a picture of a gentle shepherd only.** Beale notes the shepherd's rod can protect the flock and strike the enemy, and in 19:15 it strikes.
entries.deeper: Beale calls the destiny of the child an allusion to Psalm 2:7-9 and reads the scene as Christ's resurrection and ascent. On 2:27 he discusses the wording. The unpointed Hebrew tr'm can be read from the verb to break or the verb to shepherd; the Septuagint, the Syriac and the Vulgate took it as shepherd. John may follow the Greek, or the Greek may preserve an older reading. Beale suggests the word was chosen because it can carry both care and destruction. The Hebrew in Sefaria is tero'em beshevet barzel. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible says John cites Psalm 2:9; the CSB Study Bible and Wright call the words allusions to Psalm 2. The grade is drawn here: the phrase is nearly identical and could hardly come from elsewhere.
entries.dissent: The ESV Study Bible says the rod is a shepherd's club, not a royal scepter, used to shatter the nations. Beale allows that John may mean both care and judgment. On the child, some past interpreters read the church caught up for protection; Beale reads Christ, while noting the same psalm is given to believers in 2:26-27. MacArthur reads the child as Christ and the catching up as his ascension, and ties the iron rod to his crowning as king over the nations (11:15; 19:15).

entries.title: Revelation 12:5, she gave birth to a son, a male
entries.summary: John's odd phrase a son, a male copies Isaiah 66:7, where Zion gives birth to a male child before her labor begins.
entries.plain: **When a speaker keeps an old saying even though it breaks a grammar rule, the slip itself tells you he is quoting.** Isaiah 66 pictures Zion giving birth to a male child, a sign of a nation reborn. John writes that she bore a son, a male one. In Greek the word male is in the wrong gender for son. Beale reads the clash as a deliberate pointer back to Isaiah.
entries.same: In labor, to give birth, and she gave birth to a male. The Greek of Isaiah 66:7 has odinousan tekein and eteken arsen; John has odinousa, tekein and eteken huion arsen.
entries.differs: Isaiah's mother gives birth before her pains come. John's mother cries out in pain first. John adds son, huion, a masculine noun, and then keeps Isaiah's neuter arsen beside it, which breaks Greek agreement. Beale says the addition comes from Isaiah 66:8, where Zion bears sons. In 12:13 John writes the masculine form correctly, so the clash in 12:5 is not a slip.
entries.turn: In Isaiah the male child is Zion reborn, the nation restored after exile. John gives the promise to one person, Christ, who stands for Israel as its king. Beale ties this to verse 17, where the woman also has other children, as Zion bears sons in Isaiah 66:8.
entries.not: **Not careless Greek.** Beale points out that John uses the right form in 12:13, and others have concluded the odd neuter comes from Isaiah.
entries.deeper: Beale calls the allusion to Isaiah 66:7 evident from the verbal match and from the combination of son and male, based on the parallel of male in 66:7 and sons in 66:8 in the Hebrew. The Hebrew in Sefaria reads vehimlitah zakhar, she delivered a male, and then Zion bore et baneha, her sons. The Targum reads the male as Zion's king. Beale lists this among John's deliberate solecisms, like 1:4, meant to jolt the reader back to the source; he notes Fekkes reads arsen as a noun in apposition instead. Beale also links Zion's flight in Isaiah 66:7 Greek, exephyge, to the woman's flight in 12:6. Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible cite Isaiah 66:7-10. The grade is drawn here: the Greek is nearly verbatim and the grammar points to it.
entries.dissent: Fekkes, as Beale reports, sees no grammatical slip and takes arsen as a noun in apposition to son. Beale answers that John uses the masculine with the article in 12:13, so the neuter in 12:5 is best explained by Isaiah.

aw.n: Revelation 12:1-6, the woman, the child and the dragon
aw.s: A radiant woman, crowned with twelve stars and standing on the moon, labors to give birth while a great red dragon waits to devour her child. The child, destined to rule the nations, is caught up to God's throne, and the woman escapes to the wilderness, where she is kept safe for 1,260 days.

entries.title: Revelation 12:6, fleeing into the wilderness
entries.summary: The woman's flight into the wilderness, where God has a place ready and feeds her, replays Israel's exodus and the prophets' hope of a new one.
entries.plain: **A family that tells its own escape story every year hears it again in each new rescue.** Israel fled Egypt into the wilderness, and God fed the people there with manna. The prophets promised a second exodus through the desert. John's woman flees to the desert, to a place God has made ready, and she is fed there. Like Israel, she is kept safe and fed through a time of danger.
entries.same: God's people flee into the wilderness and are fed there by God. The word eremos, wilderness, is the word for Israel's desert years in the Greek Old Testament, and the feeding recalls the manna.
entries.differs: No Old Testament text has a woman flee to a place prepared by God. John joins the first exodus to the second one the prophets promised. Beale adds that the place, topos, is a common Greek word for the sanctuary, so the wilderness hides a temple. In John the flight comes after the child is caught up to God, not after a plague on Egypt.
entries.turn: John retells the exodus for the woman. She flees into the desert, to a place God has made ready, and she is fed there. In Israel's story the desert meant danger and care at once. Beale reads the woman as the church after the ascension. He says the protection is spiritual: believers may suffer in body, but God keeps their bond with him.
entries.not: **Not a copy of one exodus verse.** No Old Testament text has a woman flee to a place God prepared. John builds the scene from the whole wilderness story.
entries.deeper: Beale calls the flight a collective allusion to Israel's exodus and to the end-time exodus expected at Israel's restoration. He lists texts of God feeding Israel in the desert (Exodus 16:32; Deuteronomy 2:7; 8:3, 15-16; 29:5) and the end-time hope (Isaiah 32:15; 35:1; 40:3; 43:19-20; Hosea 2:14). He also notes Elijah and Moses fleeing to the desert, and Josephus' first-century movements that went out to the desert. Deuteronomy 8:15-16, with its serpents and manna, he thinks lies behind John's double view of the wilderness. The ESV Study Bible names Israel in Exodus 16 and Elijah. The CSB Study Bible, the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible point to the exodus. The grade is drawn here: the pattern is clear, the wording general.
entries.heiser: Following Beale and McDonough, Heiser reads the flight as both Israel's exodus and the end-time exodus, with God protecting and feeding his people. He notes the same pattern in Elijah and Moses. Since the flight comes after the ascension, he says, the woman now stands for all who call on the Lord, not ethnic Israel alone.
entries.dissent: The CSB Study Bible reads the woman as Jewish converts protected in the second half of a seven-year tribulation. The ESV Study Bible gives that view and the view that the period runs from the ascension to the end. Beale and Keener hold the second, and Beale rejects tying the flight to Christians fleeing to Pella or to a future remnant in hiding. MacArthur reads the woman as Israel, hidden by God in a wilderness east of the land, perhaps Moab, Ammon and Edom, for the last 1,260 days. That time begins, he says, when the Antichrist breaks his covenant with Israel at the middle of the tribulation.

entries.title: Revelation 12:7, Michael and his angels
entries.summary: Michael, who fights for John's side in heaven, is the angel prince of Daniel 10 and 12 who stands guard over God's people.
entries.plain: **A spokesperson for a team speaks for every member, and when the spokesperson wins, the whole team wins.** In Daniel, Michael is the great prince who stands up for Israel. He fights the angel princes of Persia and Greece, and in the last trouble he rises to defend God's people. John sees Michael and his angels fight the dragon in heaven and win. Beale says Michael now stands for the new Israel.
entries.same: The name Michael, which in the Old Testament appears only in Daniel. In both books he leads a battle in the unseen world on behalf of God's people.
entries.differs: In Daniel, Michael fights the princes of Persia and Greece and stands up in the final time of trouble. In John, his enemy is the dragon himself. In John's vision the war comes after the child is caught up to God's throne. Beale reads the dragon's angels as the evil princes of Daniel.
entries.turn: Beale reads the battle in heaven as the reflection of what Christ did on earth. Christ's death and resurrection win the victory, and Michael carries it out above. The hymn in verses 10-11 says the brothers win by the Lamb's blood.
entries.not: **Not the same enemy as in Daniel.** Daniel's Michael fights the angel princes of Persia and Greece. John's Michael fights the dragon himself.
entries.deeper: Beale says verse 7 develops Daniel's picture of Michael and the son of man fighting the angels of Persia and Greece (Daniel 10:13, 21; 12:1). In Daniel both are heavenly representatives of Israel, with Michael under the son of man. He cites Jewish texts that make Michael Israel's defender and Satan's opponent (1QM 17; Testament of Levi 5; Assumption of Moses 10), and a midrash that pictures Michael and Satan as lawyers before the heavenly court. In the vault's Greek of Daniel 12:1, Michael is ho archon ho megas, the great ruler, who stands over your people. Keener, the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible and the ESV Study Bible all point to Daniel 10 and 12; Wright calls him the archangel of Daniel 10. The grade is drawn here: the name is found only in Daniel.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Daniel 12:1-13 aloud, beginning with Michael the great prince, and says it sounds like Revelation 11 and 12 because that is where John gets it. He stresses that the unmatched time of trouble in Daniel 12:1 comes with the end and the resurrection, not the start of a seven-year period.
entries.dissent: The ESV Study Bible says many futurists see Michael's battle as the start of the great tribulation, and the CSB Study Bible places it near the middle of that tribulation. MacArthur sees a war that has gone on since Satan's fall and grows fiercer in the tribulation, perhaps as the saints taken up at the rapture pass through the devil's realm in the air. Beale and Keener tie the battle to Jesus' death and exaltation, not to a fall of angels at the beginning. Heiser, in Unseen Realm, says the passage clearly follows the Messiah's birth.

aw.n: Revelation 12:7-17, war in heaven and the accuser thrown down
aw.s: Michael and his angels fight the dragon and throw him out of heaven, and a voice celebrates the fall of the accuser of the brothers, defeated by the Lamb's blood and the witnesses' testimony. On earth the dragon chases the woman, who is given eagle's wings, and when the earth swallows the river he spews after her, he turns to make war on her other children.

entries.title: Revelation 12:7-8, the dragon was not strong enough
entries.summary: John describes the dragon's defeat with Daniel's words for the horn that made war on the saints and won, turned around, and adds Daniel 2's line that no place was found for them.
entries.plain: **A comedian can retell a rival's boast word for word and make it the punch line.** Daniel 7 says the horn made war with the holy ones and was stronger than they were. John takes the same words for the dragon's war in heaven, and says he was not strong enough. Then he adds a line from Daniel 2, where the broken kingdoms vanish and no place is found for them. The words of the enemy's victory now tell of his defeat.
entries.same: Make war with, polemos and meta, and ischyo, to be strong. These come from the Greek of Daniel 7:21. No place was found for them, topos ouch heurethe autois, is the Greek of Daniel 2:35, which John repeats almost exactly.
entries.differs: In Daniel the horn makes war on the saints and overpowers them. In John, Michael makes war on the dragon, and the dragon does not prevail. John adds a not, and swaps who fights whom. In Daniel 2 no place is found for the shattered statue's dust; John uses it for the dragon and his angels in heaven.
entries.turn: Beale calls this polemical irony. God defeats the enemy with the very language that told how the enemy began to defeat God's people. The devil is mocked by a parody of his own triumph. The same reversal of Daniel 7:21 returns in 17:14.
entries.not: **Not a loose memory of Daniel.** Beale argues John keeps Daniel's wording on purpose, even where it makes his Greek awkward, so the reader will notice.
entries.deeper: In his introduction Beale gives this as a model inverted use: Daniel 7:21 applied in reverse to Satan's overthrow, as a fitting punishment that matches the crime. He shows the parallel with the Greek of Daniel 7:21 (Theodotion) and Daniel 10:20, make war with the ruler of Persia. He says the odd infinitive in 12:7 and the not strong enough in 12:8 both keep Daniel's wording. Verse 8b, he adds, rests on the nearly identical words of Daniel 2:35, where the stone strikes the kingdoms; 20:11 repeats it at the last judgment. The vault's Greek of Daniel 7:21 reads the horn made war with the holy ones and prevailed against them. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible makes the same contrast with Daniel 7:21. The grade is drawn here: Beale calls the reverse use intentional, shown by the verbal likeness.
entries.dissent: The sources that discuss this verse agree it reverses Daniel 7:21. They differ on its timing: Beale ties it to Christ's resurrection, while futurists place it in a future tribulation, as the ESV Study Bible reports. MacArthur says Satan, thrown out at his first rebellion, has kept access to heaven; in the tribulation that access ends and he is barred for good.

entries.title: Revelation 12:9, that ancient serpent
entries.summary: Calling the dragon the ancient serpent who deceives the world names him as the serpent of Eden.
entries.plain: **Calling someone the original troublemaker sends everyone back to the first time trouble started.** The serpent in Genesis 3 deceived the first woman and called God a liar. John names the dragon the ancient serpent, the devil and Satan, who deceives the whole world. The new name ties the enemy of the church to the enemy in the garden. In this one verse the dragon, the serpent, the devil and Satan are joined.
entries.same: The serpent, ho ophis, the word of the Greek of Genesis 3:1. The serpent's work is deceit. In Genesis 3:13 the woman says the serpent deceived her. John calls him the one who deceives.
entries.differs: Genesis never calls the serpent Satan or the devil. John adds those names, and the word ancient to point back to the beginning. Beale notes the Greek Old Testament of Job 1-2 already rendered satan as diabolos, devil. The deceit grows from one woman to the whole world.
entries.turn: The enemy of the church is the same one who deceived in Eden. Beale says his two roles, slanderer and deceiver, both appear in Genesis 3. What he began in the garden he now does across the earth, and the rest of the chapter shows him trying to deceive the woman again.
entries.not: **Not a talking animal and nothing more.** John reads the serpent of Eden as a spiritual enemy, and Heiser in Unseen Realm reads Genesis 3 the same way.
entries.deeper: Beale says the ancient serpent identifies the dragon with the figure of Genesis 3:1 and 3:14, and compares the serpent deceived in Genesis 3:13 with John's the one deceiving. He cites the Talmud's primeval serpent and the Life of Adam and Eve, where the devil deceived Eve. He adds that the Greek of Job 1-2 renders satan as diabolos and that Zechariah 3:1 in Greek moves between the two names. Keener, the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible point to Genesis 3; the CSB Study Bible cross-references Genesis 3:1. Heiser, in Unseen Realm, notes this is the only verse that joins the terms Satan, devil and dragon. The grade is drawn here: the serpent who deceives could hardly come from anywhere but Genesis 3.
entries.dissent: Beale adds that John may have chosen a serpent also because snakes were linked with Asclepius, Dionysus and Zeus in Asia Minor, so the image also attacks pagan gods. The other sources do not discuss this.

entries.title: Revelation 12:10, the accuser of our brothers
entries.summary: The accuser thrown down is the satan of Job and Zechariah, the prosecutor in God's court, now struck from the case.
entries.plain: **A prosecutor who has lost every case can be struck off, and the accused walk free.** In Job and Zechariah the satan appears before God to accuse. He says Job serves God only for gain, and he stands to charge the high priest Joshua. John hears a voice in heaven say that the accuser of the brothers, who accused them day and night, has been thrown down. Christ's death, the sources say, has emptied his charges.
entries.same: An accuser who stands before God and brings charges against God's people. In the Greek of Job 1:6 and Zechariah 3:1 he is ho diabolos, the devil, the name John uses in 12:9.
entries.differs: In Job and Zechariah the accuser still has his place in the court. John announces that he has lost it. John coins his own noun for him, kategor, accuser, a word the Old Testament texts do not use. The charge also changes: Beale says he now argues that the saints deserve punishment, and Christ's death answers that.
entries.turn: The kingdom has come, the voice says, because the accuser is gone. Beale reads Michael's battle as a courtroom contest: a lawyer disbarred for using unfair means. Christ's death paid the penalty the accuser demanded. So the saints win by the Lamb's blood.
entries.not: **Not a promise that believers will never be accused on earth.** Beale says the saints are still charged in earthly courts; the verse speaks of the heavenly verdict.
entries.deeper: Beale draws the picture from Job 1:6-11; 2:1-6 and Zechariah 3:1-5, where Joshua's filthy clothes are replaced as God refutes the charge. He cites Jubilees and the Testament of Dan for Satan as accuser and Michael as Israel's advocate. Keener says Satan is a prosecuting attorney from Job on, and that later rabbis said he accused Israel day and night except on the Day of Atonement. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible cites Zechariah 3:1 and Job 1:6; the CSB Study Bible cross-references Job and Zechariah. Heiser, in Unseen Realm, links the satan of Job to this verse. The grade is drawn here: the courtroom role is unique to these texts, but John's words differ.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads the accuser thrown down with Luke 10:18, as a legal judgment on Satan when the kingdom began. A member of Christ's kingdom, he says, cannot be claimed by Satan, who may speak but has no ownership: "Satan has no claim on you". In Unseen Realm he links the phrase to the satan of Job 1-2.
entries.dissent: The ESV Study Bible gives three readings of the fall: the power of the cross, a defeat of demons that follows from it, or Satan's original expulsion. Beale and Keener tie it to Christ's finished work. The CSB Study Bible places the war near the middle of a future tribulation. MacArthur says the accusing stops because Satan loses his access to heaven, and that no charge stands against those forgiven through Christ's death.

entries.title: Revelation 12:12, rejoice, you heavens
entries.summary: The call for the heavens to rejoice repeats a phrase the Greek Old Testament uses when God saves his people and judges their enemies.
entries.plain: **Fans who sing the same victory chant every time their team wins are quoting every past win.** Several psalms and prophets call on the heavens to rejoice when God rescues his people. John uses the same call when the devil is thrown out of heaven. But the joy has a shadow. Land and sea are warned, because the angry devil has gone down to them.
entries.same: The plural heavens and the command to rejoice. John's euphrainesthe ouranoi is the exact Greek of Isaiah 49:13, be glad, O heavens. Isaiah 44:23 has a close form of the same call.
entries.differs: In Isaiah the heavens rejoice because God has shown mercy to his people. In John they rejoice because the accuser has fallen, and a woe on earth and sea follows. John adds those who dwell in the heavens. The sources give no reason for the change beyond the setting of the vision.
entries.turn: Beale says the plural heavens appears only here in Revelation, out of more than fifty uses of the word, and that it echoes this series of prophetic calls. The kingdom has come, and heaven celebrates. On earth the devil's short time begins.
entries.not: **Not a quotation of one verse.** The call to rejoice appears in several texts, so John may be echoing the whole group rather than one.
entries.deeper: Beale says the lone plural echoes a series of Old Testament prophecies that call the heavens to rejoice at God's kingdom and judgment: Deuteronomy 32:43, 1 Chronicles 16:31, Psalm 96:11 and Isaiah 44:23, 45:8 and 49:13 in Greek. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cites Psalm 96:10-11 and Isaiah 44:23, and the CSB Study Bible cross-references Psalm 96:11 and Isaiah 49:13. In the vault's Septuagint Isaiah 49:13 reads euphrainesthe ouranoi exactly as John does. The grade is drawn here as possible: the words match one text exactly but belong to a common formula.
entries.dissent: The sources agree on the echo but differ on its weight. Beale treats it as a group of texts; the study Bibles list single verses.

entries.title: Revelation 12:14, the two wings of the great eagle
entries.summary: The eagle's wings that carry the woman into the wilderness come from God's words at Sinai, where he says he carried Israel on eagles' wings.
entries.plain: **A grandparent who says I carried you before you could walk is telling a story of care.** At Sinai God reminds Israel that he bore them out of Egypt on eagles' wings, to himself. Deuteronomy 32 pictures God as an eagle spreading its wings over its young. John's woman is given the two wings of the great eagle to fly into the wilderness. She is carried to safety the way Israel was.
entries.same: Wings and an eagle that carry God's people into the wilderness. The Greek of Exodus 19:4 has epi pterygon aeton, on eagles' wings; John has hai dyo pteryges tou aetou, the two wings of the eagle.
entries.differs: In Exodus God is the one who carries; in John the wings are given to the woman, and she flies. John has two wings of the great eagle. Beale thinks the articles in the Greek point to a well-known image. Isaiah 40:31 adds the promise that the people will rise on wings like eagles in the second exodus.
entries.turn: What God did for Israel after Egypt he does for the woman. Beale lists this in his introduction among the analogies John draws from Israel's story. Heiser stresses the Egypt link: the dragon is the old Egypt monster, and the woman escapes as Israel did.
entries.not: **Not a hint that the woman literally flies.** The sources read the wings as God's protection, as in the Psalms, where God shelters people under his wings.
entries.deeper: Beale says the image of God as an eagle guarding Israel in the desert combines Exodus 19:4, Deuteronomy 1:31-33 and 32:10-12. He adds Isaiah 40:31, the return from Babylon on wings like eagles, and the Psalms where David asks to hide under God's wings. He notes the Targums on Exodus 19:4 read the eagle as God bringing Israel near to worship him. Keener, the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the ESV Study Bible, the CSB Study Bible, the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible and Wright all cite Exodus 19:4. Walton's commentary notes the bird may be a vulture rather than an eagle. The grade is drawn here: few words are shared, but wings, eagle and wilderness together point to Exodus 19:4.
entries.heiser: Following Beale and McDonough, Heiser reads the eagle's wings as Exodus 19:4 joined with Deuteronomy 1 and 32. It is God guarding his people in the desert. He also uses it against reading chapter 12 as fulfilled in the year 70. No rescue like the exodus came to Jews or Christians then, he says, so the rescue must still lie ahead.
entries.dissent: The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible adds that the wings could recall the dove's wings of Psalm 55:6-7, flight to the wilderness, and Beale also cites that psalm. The other sources hold to Exodus 19:4. They differ on who is carried. Beale reads the church, carried as Israel was. MacArthur reads Israel under God's care, and takes the eagles to be the large vulture-like birds of the land.

entries.title: Revelation 12:14, a time, times and half a time
entries.summary: The woman is fed for Daniel's three and a half years of trouble for God's people, a period 12:6 counts as 1,260 days.
entries.plain: **A countdown everyone knows by heart can be used for a new season.** Daniel twice speaks of a time, two times and half of a time. It is a limited period when the enemy oppresses the holy ones, three and a half years. John uses Daniel's phrase in 12:14 and the same length counted in days, 1,260, in 12:6. In Daniel it is the persecutor's time. Here it is also the time God protects and feeds his people.
entries.same: The same three and a half times. John's Greek kairon kai kairous kai hemisy kairou is the exact wording of Daniel 12:7 in the vault's Greek Daniel. The Aramaic of Daniel 7:25 is iddan veiddanin uflag iddan.
entries.differs: In Daniel the period is Israel's trouble under an arrogant king. John also makes it a time of protection: the woman is fed in the wilderness during it, while the dragon rages. Beale reads John as extending the span to the church worldwide, from Christ's resurrection to his return. MacArthur reads it as the last half of the tribulation.
entries.turn: The sources read the number as a limit God sets. The persecution is real but measured, and the devil's time is short (12:12). Beale ties it to 11:2-3 and 13:5, where the same span appears as 42 months and 1,260 days.
entries.not: **Not a span John made up.** He takes Daniel's three and a half times word for word, and in 12:6 he counts the same span as 1,260 days.
entries.deeper: Beale counts the three and a half years among his universalizing uses: Daniel 7:25 and 12:7 extended from Israel to the church worldwide. He says 12:6 is the clearest text for the period's limits, from the resurrection in verse 5 to the end. He adds that the forty-two months may echo Israel's forty-two stages in the desert (Numbers 33) and cites midrashim that link Hosea's wilderness to Daniel's period. Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible point to Daniel 7:25 and 12:7, as do the ESV Study Bible, the CSB Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible. The grade is drawn here: the phrase is word for word from Daniel.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Daniel 12 aloud and says it is where the numbers come from. He reads Revelation 11 and 12 together because they share the 1,260 days. Following Boccaccini, he sets Daniel's 1,260, 1,290 and 1,335 days on a 360-day calendar and floats links to Passover, Weeks and Booths, but he calls this speculation he cannot be sure of.
entries.dissent: The ESV Study Bible and the CSB Study Bible report the futurist view that the 1,260 days are the second half of a future tribulation. MacArthur reads the span as three and a half years, the last half of the tribulation, while God keeps Israel in the wilderness. Beale and Keener take the period as the whole time between Christ's comings. Keener notes that more than 1,260 days had passed since Jesus rose when John wrote, and that writers of such visions used numbers for the kind of time, not its length. Heiser holds that the persecution and rescue are already begun and not yet complete.

entries.title: Revelation 12:15, a river from the serpent's mouth
entries.summary: The flood the serpent spews after the woman uses the Psalms' picture of enemies as floodwater, and God's promise that the rivers will not sweep his people away.
entries.plain: **People say they are drowning in work, and everyone knows no water is involved.** In the Psalms enemies come like floods, and David calls Saul's pursuit torrents of destruction. Isaiah promises that when Israel passes through rivers they will not sweep her away. John's serpent pours water like a river from his mouth to carry the woman off. The sources read the flood as a figure for an attack, and God does not let it drown her.
entries.same: Floodwater as a picture of enemies who try to overwhelm God's people. Isaiah 43:2 has rivers that will not sweep God's people away, which is the outcome in John.
entries.differs: In the Psalms the flood comes from enemies; in John it comes out of a serpent's mouth. Beale reads the mouth as a clue that the flood is words: lies and false teaching, as the serpent deceived Eve. No Old Testament text has a river poured from a mouth. The sources give the picture, not a single verse.
entries.turn: The serpent tries to sweep the woman away. Beale reads the flood as persecution and deceit, and points to the false teachers of chapters 2 and 3, Jezebel and the Nicolaitans. The ESV Study Bible also reads the river as lies, like the serpent's words to Eve.
entries.not: **Not a real flood in the desert.** Beale rejects tying it to the Jordan flood Josephus describes in 68 and reads it as a figure.
entries.deeper: Beale lists three senses of the overflowing flood in the Old Testament: an army sweeping a land (Daniel 11; Isaiah 8:7-8), divine judgment (Psalm 32:6), and enemies of God's people from whom God saves them (2 Samuel 22:5; Psalms 18:4, 16; 69:1-2; 124:4-5; 144:7; Isaiah 43:2). He says the third is clearly meant. He also cites Qumran hymns that call the wicked's attacks waves of Belial, and adds the Red Sea and Daniel 9:26. Keener cites Psalms 32:6 and 69:15 and Isaiah 43:2. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible cites Psalms 18 and 69 and Isaiah 43:2; the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cites Psalm 144:7-8. The grade is drawn here as possible: the picture is common to many texts.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Beale and McDonough's three senses of the flood and agrees the third is in view: persecution of God's people. He points to Psalm 18:4, where David calls Saul's pursuit torrents of Belial, and notes Belial later becomes a name for Satan.
entries.dissent: Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible add a Greek parallel: in one form of the Leto story the dragon stirs the waters and the earth raises an island to help her. Beale reads the flood mainly as deceit; Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible as suffering and unjust opposition. MacArthur reads the flood as a great army sent against Israel, as Jeremiah pictures armies rising like a flood.

entries.title: Revelation 12:16, the earth swallowed the river
entries.summary: The earth opening its mouth to swallow the serpent's flood recalls the Song of the Sea, where the earth swallowed Pharaoh's army, and Korah's rebels swallowed in the desert.
entries.plain: **A story about a sinkhole saving a town would remind anyone of an older story with the same twist.** In the song after the Red Sea, Moses sings that God stretched out his hand and the earth swallowed the Egyptians. In the desert the ground opened and swallowed Korah's rebels. In John the ground opens its mouth and drinks down the serpent's river. The enemies of God's people go down again, as at the exodus.
entries.same: The earth swallows what threatens God's people. The verb is the same in Greek: katepien, swallowed, in Exodus 15:12 and Numbers 16:32, and in John. Numbers 16:32 also has the earth opening.
entries.differs: In Exodus the earth swallows the army; here it swallows the river the serpent spat out. In Numbers the earth swallows rebels inside Israel. John joins the two: the earth opens its mouth, as the serpent opened his. The sources do not say why John chose the river rather than the serpent himself.
entries.turn: God protects his people again as at the exodus. Beale reads it as God guarding the church from persecution and from teaching that would lead it astray, as he guarded Israel from Korah's lies.
entries.not: **Not nature taking sides on its own.** The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible notes that the earth here obeys God, unlike the Greek myth where the serpent is Earth's son.
entries.deeper: Beale calls the earth swallowing the flood a further allusion to the exodus and the wilderness: the earth swallowed the Egyptians (Exodus 15:12), and later Korah, Dathan and Abiram (Numbers 16:12-14, 32). He notes the Palestinian Targum expands Exodus 15:12 to the earth opened her mouth. He also cites Isaiah 51:9-10 and Psalm 74:13-14, where God cuts the dragon at the sea, and Jeremiah 51:34. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cites Exodus 15:12 and Numbers 16:30-33; the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible cites Exodus 15:10 and 12; Keener cites Numbers 16:31-32. The grade is drawn here: the verb is shared and the setting fits the exodus.
entries.heiser: Heiser calls this a believe-it-or-not moment. Exodus 15:12 says the earth swallowed the Egyptians, though we picture them drowning. He takes that as underworld language: the enemies are taken down to the realm of the dead. Revelation 12:16 uses the same picture, so the dragon's flood goes down as Egypt did.
entries.dissent: Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible add the Greek story where Earth raised the island of Delos for Leto, and Jewish tales of the earth hiding the temple vessels. Beale reads the scene from Exodus and Numbers alone. MacArthur reads the swallowing as the end of an army sent against Israel, perhaps through one of the many earthquakes of that time.

entries.title: Revelation 12:17, the rest of her offspring
entries.summary: The dragon's war on the woman's offspring plays out the first promise of Genesis 3:15: hostility between the serpent and the woman's seed.
entries.plain: **A family feud that started generations ago can still shape who fights whom today.** In Genesis 3:15 God puts hostility between the serpent and the woman, and between his seed and hers. Her seed will strike the serpent's head; the serpent will strike his heel. John's serpent, failing to destroy the woman, goes to war with the rest of her seed. The first promise in the Bible is playing out.
entries.same: A serpent, a woman, and her seed in conflict. John's word for offspring, sperma, is the word of the Greek of Genesis 3:15.
entries.differs: Genesis speaks of one line of descendants and one blow to the head. John has a first child, Christ, and then the rest of her seed, believers. He describes them as keeping God's commands and holding the testimony of Jesus. The war is the serpent's, and it has not ended, though its result is sure.
entries.turn: The woman's other children suffer because they belong to the child who defeated the serpent. Beale reads Genesis 3:15 as partly fulfilled here: the serpent bruises the seed, yet each time believers resist, he loses again. He cites the Targum, which reads the seed as those who keep the law.
entries.not: **Not the single line of Genesis kept as it was.** Genesis speaks of the woman's seed. John divides it into her first child and the rest of her offspring.
entries.deeper: Beale says verse 17 alludes to Genesis 3:15-16, where Eve's seed has both individual and corporate meaning, as Jewish readers also saw. The Targum Neofiti says the woman's sons will strike the serpent's head when they keep the law, in the days of King Messiah. He sees the same background behind 12:2 and the head wound of 13:3. Keener says the woman's seed alludes to Genesis 3:15; the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible says the verse echoes the promise; the CSB Study Bible cross-references it. The ESV Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible hear Genesis 3:15 already in 12:4. Wright sees Eve behind the woman. The grade is drawn here: three key words are shared and the idea is unique to Genesis 3:15.
entries.heiser: Reading Beale and McDonough, Heiser says the prophetic birth texts and Revelation 12 were inspired by Genesis 3:15-16, Eve bearing a seed who will strike the serpent's head. In Revelation 12, he says, that seed is Christ, the fulfillment.
entries.dissent: The CSB Study Bible reads the rest of her offspring as Gentile believers, apart from a believing Jewish remnant. MacArthur reads them as every follower of the Lamb, Jew or Gentile, whom Satan turns on in his rage. Beale rejects any national split and reads the woman and her offspring as the same church, seen in heaven and on earth. Kiddle, as Beale reports, limits the offspring to a group facing martyrdom; Beale disagrees.

entries.title: Revelation 13:1-2, a beast rising from the sea
entries.summary: The beast from the sea is Daniel 7 reworked: it has the ten horns of the fourth beast and the leopard, bear and lion of the other three, merged into one.
entries.plain: **A cartoonist can draw one monster with parts of every villain the readers fear.** In Daniel 7 four beasts rise from the sea: a lion, a bear, a leopard and a fourth beast with ten horns. They stand for four empires. John sees one beast from the sea, like a leopard, with a bear's feet and a lion's mouth, and ten horns. All Daniel's empires are folded into one.
entries.same: A beast rising from the sea, ten horns, and a leopard, a bear and a lion. The Greek matches the vault's Greek Daniel. It has anebainon ek tes thalasses (rising from the sea), pardalis (leopard), arkos (bear) and kerata deka (ten horns).
entries.differs: Daniel has four beasts, one after another. John has one, with parts of all four, and lists them in reverse order: leopard, bear, lion. He adds seven heads, crowns on the horns and blasphemous names. The dragon gives the beast its power and throne, a step Daniel does not have. Beale says the merging shows how fierce the beast is.
entries.turn: John folds Daniel's four empires into one beast, so it carries the strength of all of them at once. The dragon gives it power and a throne, which makes it the dragon's agent on earth. Jewish writers of John's day already read Daniel's fourth beast as Rome.
entries.not: **Not Daniel's four beasts kept apart.** John does not retell Daniel's vision. He merges its four beasts into one creature with parts of each.
entries.deeper: Beale calls verses 1-2 a creative reworking of Daniel 7:1-7. The beast from the sea and its ten horns are based on Daniel 7:2-3 and 7:7, 20, 24. The ten crowns point to the ten kings of 7:24, and the blasphemous names to the boastful horn of 7:8. In his introduction he names 13:1-8 as a combined allusion, and Daniel 7 as the pattern of chapter 13. He reads the seven heads as the total of the heads of Daniel's four beasts, with a sea-monster myth possibly in mind as well. Keener, the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the ESV Study Bible, the CSB Study Bible, the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible and Wright all trace the beast to Daniel 7. The grade is drawn here: Beale says the depiction is drawn mainly from Daniel 7, and the wording is close.
entries.heiser: Heiser calls the Daniel 7 background very likely, with secure roots, and reads Beale and McDonough's list. He adds a point of his own: set beside Daniel 2, the stone that ends the kingdoms comes in the time of the Messiah, when Rome ruled, so Rome is a secure anchor. He keeps a second background, Job's two beasts, on the table too.
entries.dissent: Many scholars, Beale reports, read the seven heads as the seven-headed sea monster of Ugaritic myth; Beale prefers a sum of Daniel's heads and allows the myth a secondary place. Keener and Wright read the beast as Rome. Beale and the ESV Study Bible read Rome in John's day and every empire that demands worship. The ESV Study Bible says most dispensationalists read a future political leader. MacArthur reads both a person, the Antichrist, and his final world empire, led by a revived Roman Empire. He takes the heads as empires from Egypt to Rome and then the Antichrist's, and the sea as the abyss.

entries.title: Revelation 13:1, two beasts, from the sea and from the land
entries.summary: Two beasts, one from the sea and one from the land, may echo Job's pair, Leviathan of the sea and Behemoth of the land.
entries.plain: **A story with two villains, one at sea and one on shore, reminds readers of other famous pairs.** Job 40 and 41 describe two great beasts: Behemoth on land and Leviathan in the sea. It is the only place in the Old Testament where two such beasts oppose God together. John sees a beast from the sea and then a beast from the earth. Beale and Heiser think Job's pair stands partly behind them.
entries.same: A pair of beasts, one of land and one of sea, opposed to God. The Greek of Job calls the land creature theria, beasts, and the sea creature drakon, dragon. John uses those words for the beast and the dragon.
entries.differs: Job's beasts are God's creatures, shown to humble Job. John's beasts serve the dragon and rule the earth. Daniel 7, not Job, supplies most of John's details. The Greek of Job says each beast was made to be mocked by the angels, a line John does not use.
entries.turn: If Job is in view, the beasts are chaos itself, beaten at the start and doomed at the end. Jewish tradition said God made Leviathan and Behemoth on the fifth day and would destroy them at the last judgment. Beale says that tradition may come into play here.
entries.not: **Not the main source of the beasts.** Beale says Daniel 7 predominates and Job is only part of the picture; Heiser calls the Job reading the minority view.
entries.deeper: Beale says the two beasts are based in part on Job 40-41, the only Old Testament picture of two satanic beasts opposing God. He lists echoes in the Greek: the land beast to be slain with a sword (40:19 in the Hebrew), the sea dragon's war waged by his mouth, fire from his mouth, nothing on earth like him, and both made to be mocked by the angels. He cites 1 Enoch 60:7-10, 4 Ezra 6:49-52 and 2 Baruch 29:4 for the fifth-day creation and final destruction. In the vault's interlinear, which numbers Job as English Bibles do, Job 40:19 and 41:33 both have the line about angels mocking. Keener mentions Leviathan served at the messianic banquet. Walton notes early Jewish readers took Behemoth as a mythic creature. The grade is drawn here as possible: the pair is suggestive, the wording general.
entries.heiser: Heiser starts with this less obvious background. Job 40-41 has the land and sea chaos monsters together, and he reads the Greek aloud. He then reads Pitre and 2 Baruch 29 on the end-time banquet where Leviathan and Behemoth are served as food: chaos itself devoured. He calls it the minority view, but keeps it on the table beside Daniel 7.
entries.dissent: Kline, as Beale reports, reads Behemoth and Leviathan as two names for one beast, God's champion against Job, not a satanic pair. Collins gives the Leviathan and Behemoth tradition much weight; Beale tempers it, following Caird, because Daniel 7 dominates the chapter.

entries.title: Revelation 13:3, a fatal wound healed
entries.summary: The beast's head struck with a deathblow, and later called the wound of the sword, may recall the serpent's crushed head of Genesis 3:15 and God's sword on the dragon in Isaiah 27:1.
entries.plain: **A defeated boxer who gets back up still lost the fight, even if the crowd cheers.** Genesis 3:15 promises that the woman's seed will strike the serpent's head. Isaiah 27 promises that God will bring his great sword on the dragon. John sees one of the beast's heads slain to death, and in 13:14 the wound is from a sword. Beale reads the blow as Christ's victory, and the healing as a fake comeback.
entries.same: A deadly blow to the head of the enemy. Isaiah 27:1 in Greek has machaira, sword, on the dragon, the same word as the sword of 13:14.
entries.differs: Neither Genesis nor Isaiah says the wound heals. John adds the healing, and the world's wonder at it. He also writes as slain, hos esphagmenen, the phrase used of the Lamb in 5:6, so the beast mimics Christ's death and rising. The Old Testament texts promise the enemy's end; John shows the enemy faking a recovery.
entries.turn: Beale says the deathblow was struck at the cross, and the devil's work goes on only in a beaten state. In his reading every return of an oppressive power looks like a recovery, but it is not one. Heiser stresses the counterfeit: the beasts copy Christ.
entries.not: **Not a healing the Old Testament promises.** Genesis and Isaiah speak of a blow to the enemy's head. The recovery, and the world's wonder at it, are John's own.
entries.deeper: Beale says a wound on the head of the great enemy reflects Genesis 3:15, especially with 12:17, and that the sword of 13:14 recalls Isaiah 27:1. He adds Psalm 74:13, where God breaks the heads of the sea monsters, and Habakkuk 3:13. The vault's Greek of Isaiah 27:1 has God bring the holy and great and strong sword on the dragon. Heiser, reading Beale and McDonough, calls the sword a clear allusion to Isaiah 27:1. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible call the healing a parody of Jesus' resurrection, and the ESV Study Bible compares 5:6. The grade is drawn here as possible: two sources propose the texts, and the shared words are few.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Beale and McDonough's link of the sword to Isaiah 27:1 and says it points back to the chaos monster reading. He then stresses that the beasts imitate Christ: a deadly wound healed, a granted authority, the counterfeit of Christ's own story.
entries.dissent: Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible link the healed head to rumors that Nero would return; the ESV Study Bible to Rome's recovery after Nero's death. Beale warns against tying the wound to one emperor, and says the Nero story does not fit, since the wound is struck by God and hurts the beast, not one ruler. Heiser reads it as counterfeit, not as Nero. MacArthur allows a fallen empire revived, such as Rome, but thinks it more likely a staged death and rising by the Antichrist, which draws the world to follow him.

entries.title: Revelation 13:4, who is like the beast?
entries.summary: The crowd's cry who is like the beast? copies Israel's song after the Red Sea, who is like you, O Lord?, and turns praise of God into praise of his enemy.
entries.plain: **Singing a hymn tune with new words for a dictator is worse than silence.** After the Red Sea, Israel sang: who is like you, O Lord, among the gods? The question praised God as beyond comparison. In John the world worships the beast with the same question: who is like the beast, and who can fight it? The praise that belongs to God is given to the enemy.
entries.same: The question who is like, tis homoios. These are the opening words of the Greek of Exodus 15:11, followed by the one praised.
entries.differs: Exodus asks which of the gods is like the Lord. John's crowd asks who is like the beast, and who can make war with it. The answer the song expects is no one but God; the crowd says no one but the beast. John adds the war, which Beale ties to the horn's war on the saints in Daniel 7.
entries.turn: Beale calls this an ironic use of the Old Testament's words for God's incomparability: the devil imitating God. In those texts God is set against false gods, so the beast's worshipers commit the worst blasphemy. And the question has an answer already in 12:7-8: Michael fought the dragon and won.
entries.not: **Not a harmless compliment.** The sources read the words as worship, given to a creature in place of God.
entries.deeper: Beale calls the expression an ironic use of phrasing applied to Yahweh (Exodus 8:10; 15:11; Deuteronomy 3:24; Isaiah 40:18, 25; 46:5; Psalms 35:10; 89:8; 113:5; Micah 7:18). In his introduction he lists Exodus 8:10 and 15:11 among John's retributive ironies. He cites the Talmud using such texts against Titus after the temple's fall. Keener, the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible and the ESV Study Bible all point to Exodus 15:11; the CSB Study Bible cross-references Exodus 15:11 and Isaiah 46:5; the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible adds Psalm 113:5. The ESV Study Bible notes that such cries greeted Caesar entering a city. The grade is drawn here: the question is the song's, and the sources agree on it.
entries.dissent: The sources agree on Exodus 15:11. They differ on how wide the echo is: Beale gives a long list of incomparability texts, while the study Bibles name one or two.

entries.title: Revelation 13:5-6, a mouth speaking great things for forty-two months
entries.summary: The beast's boastful mouth and its forty-two months come from Daniel's little horn, who speaks great things against the Most High for three and a half times.
entries.plain: **A tyrant's loud boasts and a fixed term in office tell you both his pride and his limit.** In Daniel 7 a little horn has a mouth speaking great things. It speaks against the Most High and oppresses the holy ones for three and a half times. John says the beast was given a boasting, blaspheming mouth, and power for forty-two months. Daniel's boaster and Daniel's limit both return.
entries.same: A mouth speaking great things, stoma laloun megala, word for word from the Greek of Daniel 7:8. Speaking against God, and a limited time that equals three and a half years.
entries.differs: Daniel counts three and a half times; John says forty-two months. John adds blasphemies against God's name, his dwelling and those who dwell in heaven. Daniel's horn speaks against the Most High and wears out the saints. Beale says John also blends in the horn of Daniel 8, so two of Daniel's tyrants become one.
entries.turn: Beale reads the boasting as self-worship and deceit, the beast claiming divine honors. The limit shows who is really in charge: the beast is given a mouth and a time. Only God sets times, Beale says, and the devil would never choose three and a half years.
entries.not: **Not a new span of time.** Forty-two months is Daniel's three and a half times counted in months. John keeps Daniel's limit and changes only the unit.
entries.deeper: Beale calls verse 5 a collective allusion to Daniel 7:6, 8, 11, 20 and 25. Much of it is word for word, and three elements, a blaspheming mouth, a given authority and a set time, occur together only in Daniel. He notes the Greek of 7:6 uses given (edothe) for the beast, as John does, and cites 1 Maccabees 1:24 for Antiochus speaking proudly. Verse 6 refers again to Daniel 7:25, and the dwelling recalls the sanctuary of Daniel 8:10-13. Keener, the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the ESV Study Bible, the CSB Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible all cite Daniel 7:8, 20 or 25. The grade is drawn here: the phrase is identical to the Greek of Daniel 7:8.
entries.heiser: Following Beale and McDonough, Heiser finds clear parallels to Daniel 7:6, 8, 11, 20 and 25 in the beast's speech. He notes that the odd word given comes straight from Daniel 7's language for the beasts.
entries.dissent: The ESV Study Bible says many futurists read the forty-two months as the second half of a future great tribulation. The CSB Study Bible reads them as the last three and a half years, after the two witnesses. MacArthur reads them as the last half of Daniel's seventieth week, the Great Tribulation. It begins, he says, with the abomination of desolation, and God allows the Antichrist to rage for that set time. Beale reads the period as the whole time from Christ's resurrection to his return. With Keener he takes it as a symbol of the whole church age.

entries.title: Revelation 13:7, war on the saints
entries.summary: The beast is allowed to make war on the saints and conquer them, as Daniel's horn made war with the holy ones and prevailed.
entries.plain: **A hard winter that was forecast is no less cold, but it does not catch you by surprise.** In Daniel 7 the little horn fights the holy ones and wins. Then God, the old judge on the throne, comes and gives the kingdom to the saints. John says the beast was permitted to fight the saints and defeat them. Daniel's war on the holy ones returns in John's vision.
entries.same: Make war with the saints, poiesai polemon meta ton hagion, the phrase of the Greek of Daniel 7:21. In both the persecutor wins for a time.
entries.differs: Daniel says the horn prevailed; John says the beast conquered, nikesai, the verb Revelation uses for the faithful who overcome. John adds that it was given to the beast, a reminder that God allows it. Beale notes the same words in 11:7, and the reverse in 12:7-8, where the dragon cannot win.
entries.turn: John takes Daniel's war on the holy ones and gives it to the beast. Beale says the war began with Christ's death and resurrection. Daniel promises that the persecutors will be judged and the saints will receive the kingdom, and John's readers are meant to remember the rest of the story.
entries.not: **Not defeat in the end.** The ESV Study Bible notes the irony: the saints are conquered in body, yet in 12:11 and 15:2 they are the ones who conquer.
entries.deeper: Beale says verse 7 returns to Daniel 7:8 in the Greek and 7:21, with the same wording as 11:7. After the mouth speaking great things, the Greek of 7:8 adds that the horn made war on the saints, and John follows the same order. The vault's Greek of Daniel 7:21 reads the horn made war with the holy ones and prevailed against them. Keener calls the figure of Daniel 7:21-22 antichristlike and applied first to Antiochus. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible point to Daniel 7:21. The grade is drawn here: the phrase is nearly word for word.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Daniel 7 beside the verse and says it is very clearly the source: the horn made war against the holy ones. He follows Beale and McDonough in tracing John's whole description back to Daniel 7.
entries.dissent: The CSB Study Bible reads the saints as Gentile believers in a future tribulation; Beale reads them as the church throughout the age. Keener reads the horn as Antiochus first, then his successors. MacArthur reads the war as the Antichrist's slaughter of God's people in the tribulation.

entries.title: Revelation 13:7-8, authority over every tribe, and worship
entries.summary: The beast is given authority over every tribe, people and language and is worshiped, a parody of the son of man in Daniel 7:14, to whom authority is given and all peoples serve.
entries.plain: **A copycat brand that steals a famous logo shows whom it wants to be mistaken for.** In Daniel 7:14 the son of man is given authority, and all peoples, nations and languages serve him. John gives the beast the same rule over all peoples, and says everyone on earth will worship it. The beast takes the son of man's crown for itself. Beale calls it a parody.
entries.same: Authority given to him, edothe auto exousia, and peoples, tribes and languages. The given authority matches the Greek of Daniel 7:14 and 7:6; the list of peoples matches the Greek of Daniel 7:14.
entries.differs: In Daniel the authority and the worship go to the son of man, and his kingdom never ends. John gives them to the beast, for a limited time. The same Greek word for given authority is used of Daniel's leopard in 7:6, and Beale thinks John noticed the irony already in Daniel.
entries.turn: The beast's rule is a mock version of the son of man's. Beale says readers should see it as a taunting prelude to Christ's victory. The beast's authority comes from the same God who will give the son of man the kingdom. The contrast is with 5:9, where the Lamb buys people from every tribe.
entries.not: **Not a true rival to Christ.** The sources stress the beast's power is given and temporary.
entries.deeper: Beale sets out the Greek of Daniel 7:14 beside Revelation 13:7b-8a and says the authorization clause is closer to the old Greek and the list of peoples closer to Theodotion. In his introduction he lists Daniel 7:14 in 13:7-8 among John's ironic uses. He also weighs Daniel 3:7, where all peoples worship the golden image, but holds that Daniel 7:14 is the strongest influence. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible links the verse to Daniel 3:7 and contrasts Daniel 7:14. The CSB Study Bible cross-references Daniel 7:6 and 14; the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible cites Daniel 7:13-14. The grade is drawn here: the authorization clause and the people list together point to Daniel 7:14.
entries.heiser: Heiser notes that the beasts imitate Christ, and that some of their language comes from Daniel 7's picture of the son of man being given the kingdom and an everlasting rule. To him it is illegitimate authority, a counterfeit.
entries.dissent: Beale treats Daniel 7:14 as the main source. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible point more to Daniel 3, the worship of Nebuchadnezzar's image. J. M. Ford, as Beale reports, sees Daniel 3:5-6 here.
