entries.title: Revelation 13:8, the book of life
entries.summary: The Lamb's book of life draws on Daniel's book of those to be delivered and the psalm's book of the living, from which the wicked are blotted out.
entries.plain: **A guest list decides who gets in, whatever the bouncer at the door says.** Daniel 12:1 promises rescue for everyone found written in the book. Psalm 69 asks that the wicked be erased from the record of the living. John says the beast's worshipers are those missing from the Lamb's book of life. That book belongs to the Lamb who was slain.
entries.same: A book in which God writes the names of his people. Psalm 69:28 links the book with life and keeps the wicked out of it; Daniel 12:1 ties it to rescue in the time of trouble.
entries.differs: John says the book belongs to the Lamb, a link to Christ none of the Old Testament texts make. He adds that the names were written, or left out, before the world was made. In Exodus 32 Moses asks to be blotted out for Israel's sake; John speaks of a book that keeps believers safe.
entries.turn: Those who are the Lamb's are kept from worshiping the beast. Beale says the book stands for the security of God's people, decided before history. The beast's worshipers show by their worship that their names are not there.
entries.not: **Not a list of good deeds.** Beale sets the book of life against the books of deeds in 20:12. It records who belongs to the Lamb.
entries.deeper: Beale says the context of Daniel 7 brings in the book of 7:10, which leads to the books of Daniel 12:1-2 in Theodotion and of Psalm 69:28 in the Greek, and that John's wording is closer to those two. Psalm 69 may predominate, since only it speaks of a book linked with life from which the wicked are excluded. He also cites Ezekiel 13:9 for false prophets left out of Israel's register. The ESV Study Bible lists Exodus 32:32-33 and Daniel 12:1; the CSB Study Bible cross-references Exodus 32:32-33 and Psalm 69:28; Keener cites Daniel 12:1. The grade is drawn here: the picture is shared, but John merges several texts.
entries.dissent: Readers divide over what from the foundation of the world goes with. The ESV Study Bible and Beale lean to the names written before creation, from the parallel in 17:8; the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible to the Lamb slain from creation, God's original plan.

aw.n: Revelation 13:1-10, the beast from the sea
aw.s: A beast with ten horns and seven heads rises from the sea, built from Daniel's leopard, bear and lion, and the dragon gives it his power. One head seems to have had a fatal wound that healed, the whole earth follows it in awe, and it is allowed to blaspheme and to make war on God's people for forty-two months.

entries.title: Revelation 13:10, captivity and the sword
entries.summary: The saying about going to captivity and dying by the sword joins two oracles of Jeremiah, once spoken against unfaithful Judah, now spoken to the faithful church.
entries.plain: **A proverb can change meaning depending on who says it to whom.** Jeremiah tells Judah that God has assigned each person a fate: death, sword, famine or captivity. It was a judgment for sin. John uses the same pattern: if anyone is for captivity, to captivity he goes; if for the sword, by the sword. Beale says it now speaks of the faithful, who must endure.
entries.same: The repeated pattern of captivity to captivity and sword to sword. The Greek of Jeremiah 15:2 has eis aichmalosian, eis aichmalosian, the same words John uses.
entries.differs: Jeremiah lists four fates and gives them as punishment on an unfaithful people. John keeps two, captivity and the sword, and speaks of the saints. He adds a call: here is the endurance and faith of the saints. The manuscripts differ in this verse, and some copies make it a warning that whoever kills will be killed.
entries.turn: Believers will suffer, and that suffering is part of God's plan, not a sign he has left them. Beale notes that even the faithful remnant shared Judah's exile. John calls them to endure without compromise and not to fight back.
entries.not: **Not a call to take up the sword.** In Beale's reading the saints suffer the sword; they do not use it.
entries.deeper: Beale calls the verse a paraphrase combining Jeremiah 15:2 and 43:11. He notes that most commentators wonder how texts of punishment can speak of believers, and answers from Ezekiel 14:12-23, where the faithful also go into exile. He suggests the beasts of the earth in the Greek of Jeremiah 15:3 drew John to the passage. He discusses the variants and prefers the reading of codex Alexandrinus. Keener, the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the CSB Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible all cite Jeremiah 15:2 and 43:11. The grade is drawn here: the pattern is Jeremiah's, nearly word for word.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Beale and McDonough: the saying combines Jeremiah 15:2 and 43:11, where Israel goes into exile for sin, and John applies it to believers persecuted for their witness. He sees the point: the people of God now suffer not for sin but under the beasts.
entries.dissent: Keener reads the judgment here as falling on the nations who rebel against God, to encourage the martyrs. Beale and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible read it as the suffering of faithful believers. Vos, as Beale reports, thinks a scribe made the second line match Jeremiah. MacArthur reads it as telling believers under the Antichrist to bear persecution patiently and not resist it.

aw.s: A beast with ten horns and seven heads rises from the sea, built from Daniel's leopard, bear and lion, and the dragon gives it his power. entries.title: Revelation 13:11, two horns like a lamb
entries.summary: The second beast's two horns recall the two-horned ram of Daniel 8, while its lamb-like look mocks the Lamb.
entries.plain: **A wolf in a sheep's costume still sounds like a wolf when it speaks.** In Daniel 8 a ram with two horns stands for an empire. John's second beast rises from the earth with a lamb's two horns, but it talks like a dragon. Beale hears Daniel's ram in the two horns. The lamb look is a disguise, a cheap copy of the Lamb with seven horns in chapter 5.
entries.same: A horned animal that stands for a ruling power, with exactly two horns. The Hebrew of Daniel 8:3 says the ram had qeranayim, two horns.
entries.differs: Daniel's ram is a ram; John's beast has horns like a lamb. The vault's Greek of Daniel 8:3 says only that the ram had horns, without the number; the Hebrew form gives two, and Beale cites the Hebrew. The comparison of Greek and Hebrew is drawn here. John adds that the beast speaks like a dragon.
entries.turn: The second beast looks harmless and talks like the devil. Beale reads it as the false prophet, who makes the first beast's claims sound persuasive, often from inside the church. Jesus warned of false prophets in sheep's clothing.
entries.not: **Not a gentle figure.** The lamb-like horns are a disguise; the dragon's voice shows what it is.
entries.deeper: Beale says the description is from the Hebrew of Daniel 8:3, a ram that had two horns, and adds Daniel 7:7 in the Greek, he had horns. Daniel's ram stands for Medo-Persia, the second kingdom, so the first beast is modeled on Daniel's fourth kingdom and the second on the ram, a pattern for later tyrants. He also says the two horns may mimic the two witnesses of chapter 11. Keener says the two horns might reflect Persia in Daniel 8; the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible says they may evoke the ram; the CSB Study Bible cross-references Daniel 8:3 and notes the word could be ram. The grade is drawn here: the two horns and the ruling animal match, but the lamb is John's own.
entries.dissent: Beale reads the second beast as including false teachers inside the church. Keener points mainly to the provincial council that ran the emperor's cult in Asia. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible reports both a preterist view, the cult's priests, and a futurist one, a religious leader beside a political one. MacArthur reads the second beast as the final false prophet, a religious leader beside the Antichrist, who is mainly a political one. Its two small horns show it is weaker than the ten-horned beast, and its lamb look marks a false Christ.

aw.n: Revelation 13:11-18, the beast from the earth, the mark and 666
aw.s: A second beast, harmless-looking like a lamb but speaking like the dragon, rises from the earth and drives everyone to worship the first beast, working wonders and making its statue speak. Trade is barred to anyone without its mark on hand or forehead, a mark tied to the beast's name and number, 666.

entries.title: Revelation 13:13, fire from heaven
entries.summary: The second beast calling down fire from heaven mimics Elijah on Mount Carmel, and its great signs mimic Moses, as Pharaoh's magicians once did.
entries.plain: **A forger copies the signature of the person you trust most.** Elijah called down fire from heaven on Mount Carmel to prove who the true God was. Moses did great signs in Egypt, and Pharaoh's magicians copied some of them. John's second beast does great signs and even makes fire come down from heaven. The beast fakes the proofs of a true prophet.
entries.same: Fire that comes down out of heaven in front of people, as proof. The Greek of 1 Kings 18:38 has pyr ek tou ouranou, fire out of heaven, as John does.
entries.differs: Elijah's fire proved the Lord was God; the beast's fire is meant to deceive. John adds that the beast does it to make people worship the first beast. In Exodus the magicians copied Moses' signs with secret arts; John makes the copy a weapon of the false prophet.
entries.turn: Beale calls it an ironic echo: the beast imitates the signs that proved Moses and Elijah true. Fire from heaven in 11:5 marks the true witnesses and in 20:9 God's judgment. The beast steals the sign. Believers must test signs, not trust them.
entries.not: **Not proof that the power is from God.** The sources read the signs as deceptive works, allowed by God for a time, as Deuteronomy 13 warned.
entries.deeper: Beale says the beast's activities are an ironic echo of the acts of Moses, whose authority was confirmed by great signs (Exodus 4:17, 30; 10:2; 11:10), copied by Pharaoh's magicians (Exodus 7:11). He adds that the Greek of Daniel 4:37 praises God for doing great signs. Fire from heaven recalls Elijah (1 Kings 18:38-39; 2 Kings 1:10-14). Keener points to the magicians in Exodus 7:11; the ESV Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible to 1 Kings 18:38 and 2 Kings 1:10; the CSB Study Bible cross-references them. The grade is drawn here: fire from heaven before people is Elijah's sign.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Beale and McDonough on Moses and Elijah, then goes further. Jesus is the greater Moses and greater than Elijah in the Gospels, so the beast poses as a new Moses and a new Elijah, a direct counterfeit of Jesus. He says the choice of what to imitate shows where true authority lies.
entries.dissent: Keener notes that wonders were not usually tied to the emperor cult in John's day, and reads the scene as a future blending of state religion and occult power. Beale reads the second beast as present already, including false teachers in the church. MacArthur reads the fire as counterfeit signs worked by the final false prophet, copying the two witnesses of 11:5.

entries.title: Revelation 13:14-15, worship the image or die
entries.summary: The order to make an image of the beast and kill all who will not worship it replays Nebuchadnezzar's golden statue in Daniel 3.
entries.plain: **A loyalty test where one side gets a job and the other a prison cell is old news.** In Daniel 3 King Nebuchadnezzar sets up a gold image and commands every people to bow to it or be thrown into the furnace. Daniel's three friends refuse. John's second beast orders an image of the first beast, gives it breath and has those who will not worship it killed. The old test returns in John's vision.
entries.same: An image set up by a ruler, a command to all peoples to worship it, and death for those who refuse. John's proskynesosin te eikoni, worship the image, matches the Greek of Daniel 3:5.
entries.differs: Nebuchadnezzar's image is gold and silent; John's image is given breath and speaks. Daniel's friends are rescued from the fire, but the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible notes that John warns many faithful will die. The ruler is not a Babylonian king but the beast, served by a false prophet.
entries.turn: John replays Daniel 3: an image, a command to worship it, and death for those who refuse. Beale says believers should persevere as Daniel's friends did, trusting that God will deliver them through death. Their reward is rescue from eternal fire.
entries.not: **Not Daniel 3 told again unchanged.** Nebuchadnezzar's statue is silent gold. John's image breathes and speaks, and a false prophet orders it, not a king.
entries.deeper: Beale says the beast killing those who will not worship the image comes from the king's order in Daniel 3, and that 13:16 echoes the groups summoned in Daniel 3:2-7. He notes 1 and 2 Maccabees also drew on Daniel 3, and that the image was later called a great dragon in a midrash. He cites Price on the colossal statue at Ephesus and Friesen's correction that it honored Titus. He also allows that the image's sixty cubits by six may lie behind 666. Keener, the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the ESV Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible all point to Daniel 3; the CSB Study Bible cross-references Daniel 3:5-6. Beale calls it a clear allusion.
entries.dissent: Beale reads the image as anything put in God's place, in any age, and sees the pressure to honor the emperor's image in John's day. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible dates a huge imperial statue at Ephesus to Domitian; Beale reports Friesen's view that the colossus honored Titus. MacArthur reads a future image of the Antichrist, tied to the throne he sets up in the Jerusalem temple at the abomination of desolation, halfway through the tribulation. Keener adds the Maccabean martyrs as a parallel. The sources agree on Daniel 3.

entries.title: Revelation 13:16, a mark on the hand or forehead
entries.summary: The beast's mark on the right hand or forehead parodies God's command to bind his law on the hand and between the eyes.
entries.plain: **A rival club that copies your team's jersey wants its fans to look loyal too.** God told Israel to keep his law as a sign on the hand and a reminder on the forehead. Later Jews wore small boxes of Scripture there. John's second beast makes everyone take a mark on the right hand or the forehead. Beale and others read it as a dark copy of the sign of loyalty to God.
entries.same: A sign of loyalty placed on the hand and the head. The Greek of Deuteronomy 6:8 and Exodus 13:9 has a sign on your hand, epi tes cheiros, the phrase John uses.
entries.differs: In the Torah the sign is God's law, kept in mind and practice. John's mark is the beast's name or number. The Greek of the Torah texts says before your eyes; John says forehead. In Ezekiel 9 a mark on the forehead saves the faithful; here the mark brings judgment.
entries.turn: Beale reads the mark as a travesty of the signs of belonging to God's people. The forehead stands for commitment, the hand for action. Those who bear the beast's mark give it full loyalty, as the 144,000 bear God's name in 14:1.
entries.not: **Not the Torah's sign copied.** The hand and the forehead are borrowed, but the beast's mark carries its own name, not God's law.
entries.deeper: Beale says God told Israel the Torah was to be a sign on the hand and a reminder on the forehead (Exodus 13:9, 16; Deuteronomy 6:8; 11:18), and calls the beast's mark a travesty of these signs. He contrasts the mark with the seal of 7:3 and the divine mark of Ezekiel 9, and cites Psalms of Solomon 15 for paired marks. He also weighs slave brands and the emperor's stamp on coins. The ESV Study Bible cites Deuteronomy 6:8 with Exodus 28:36-38 and Ezekiel 9:4; the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible says the mark may parody phylacteries. The grade is drawn here as possible: hand and forehead are the only shared words.
entries.heiser: Heiser says the key is bearing the name. Following Carmen Imes, he reads Numbers 6:27, where the priests put God's name on Israel, as the real background: the mark parodies bearing God's name. He grants Beale and McDonough's phylactery parallel as interesting, but thinks the blessing fits better. He reads the ban on buying and selling as persecution of those who will not deny Christ.
entries.dissent: Beale, the ESV Study Bible and Heiser read the mark as a sign of allegiance, whether or not it is ever seen. MacArthur reads a mark that must be visible on the hand or forehead, like the brands Roman slaves and soldiers wore, and that people will need to buy food and goods. Keener and Beale cite 3 Maccabees 2:28-29, where a king branded Jews with the ivy leaf of Dionysus. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible mentions slave and soldier brands, and Aune, as Heiser reports, Roman coins. Heiser finds these Greek and Roman parallels weak, since they have no Old Testament context.

entries.title: Revelation 13:18, the number 666
entries.summary: The only places 666 appears in the Old Testament are Solomon's yearly gold and a family list; Beale thinks Solomon's gold may be in view, and Heiser finds that unpersuasive.
entries.plain: **A number on a jersey can mean nothing, or it can honor a famous player, and fans argue about it for years.** First Kings 10 says Solomon received 666 talents of gold a year, just before it tells how his wealth and wives led him astray. Beale thinks that number may be in John's mind. Heiser rejects it. Nobody, he says, knows what the number means.
entries.same: The number six hundred sixty-six, and in the setting of a king's power and wealth.
entries.differs: Solomon's number counts gold; John's counts a name, the number of a man. First Kings does not call the gold evil. John gives no sign that he is pointing to Solomon. The link rests on what follows in 1 Kings: Solomon breaking the law for kings.
entries.turn: If Solomon's gold is in view, Beale says, the number marks kingship twisted by idolatry and greed. He also reads triple six as falling short of seven, the beast's failure to be what it claims. Wisdom means seeing through the beast.
entries.not: **Not a solved code.** Heiser stresses there is no secure Old Testament source for the number, and the sources list many readings without agreement.
entries.deeper: Beale says the mention of 666 talents in 1 Kings 10:14 may be in John's field of reference, since it comes at Solomon's peak and right before his breaking of Deuteronomy 17's rules for kings. He also cites Daniel 3:1, the image sixty cubits high and six wide, as a possible echo, after Irenaeus. He prefers a symbolic reading: six falling short of seven, three times over. Heiser reports Strawn and Bodner's 2020 article tying 666 to Solomon's gold. The other sources give gematria: Keener and the ESV Study Bible note Nero Caesar in Hebrew letters adds to 666. The grade is drawn here as possible: two sources propose the text, and one of them rejects it.
entries.heiser: Heiser says there is no secure Old Testament contribution to the number. He calls the Solomon proposal very weak, since Second Temple writers saw Solomon as a wise exorcist, the opposite of an antichrist. He doubts Nero too, because Irenaeus knew Nero yet ignored that solution, and to him spelling tricks feel "like cheating". He leans toward a link with Babel, via Irenaeus' Teitan, but admits nobody knows.
entries.dissent: Beale thinks Solomon's gold and Daniel's image may both stand behind the number. Heiser rejects Solomon. Keener and the ESV Study Bible give the Nero Caesar reading; Heiser notes it can also explain the variant 616, but he and Beale doubt it. The CSB Study Bible gives both gematria and the symbolic six. MacArthur reads 666 as the number of a man, six falling short of seven. He expects the Antichrist, once revealed, to be linked to it, perhaps by the value of his name, and warns against guessing beyond the text.

aw.n: Revelation 13:11-18, the beast from the earth, the mark and 666
aw.s: A second beast, harmless-looking like a lamb but speaking like the dragon, rises from the earth and drives everyone to worship the first beast, working wonders and making its statue speak. Trade is barred to anyone without its mark on hand or forehead, a mark tied to the beast's name and number, 666.

entries.title: Revelation 14:1, the Lamb standing on Mount Zion
entries.summary: The Lamb on Mount Zion is the king of Psalm 2, set on God's holy hill while the nations rage.
entries.plain: **A flag raised on a hill after a long battle tells everyone who holds the ground.** In Psalm 2 the nations plot against God and his anointed. God answers that he has set his king on Zion, his holy hill. After the raging beasts of chapter 13, John sees the Lamb on that mountain, with the 144,000 beside him. Wright and the ESV Study Bible say John is working with Psalm 2 again.
entries.same: God's king on Mount Zion, his holy mountain, while hostile powers rage. The Greek of Psalm 2:6 has Sion oros, Mount Zion, as John does.
entries.differs: The psalm's king is set on Zion by God; John's Lamb stands there with a whole people who bear his name and his Father's. The king of the psalm is God's son; John calls Christ the Lamb. Beale adds Joel 2:32, where survivors on Mount Zion call on the Lord's name.
entries.turn: The true king holds the true city, against the false lamb of 13:11. Beale says the Lamb's place on Zion shows he alone has a right to the throne, and the mention of his Father points to Psalm 2. Zion is the city where God keeps his people safe.
entries.not: **Not Psalm 2's scene unchanged.** The psalm sets one king on Zion. John adds a whole people beside the Lamb, bearing his name and his Father's.
entries.deeper: Beale says that in the last days God will install his Messiah on Zion, his holy mountain (Psalm 2:6-12), and that 4 Ezra 13 and 2 Baruch 40 build on this. He notes Mount Zion, as distinct from Zion, occurs nineteen times, often for a rescued remnant (Joel 2:32; Obadiah 17; Micah 4:7; Isaiah 24:23). Psalm 2's prophecy, he says, is applied to Christ's reign in Acts 13 and Revelation 2 and 12. The ESV Study Bible says the scene fulfills Psalm 2:6; Wright explains it from Psalm 2. The CSB Study Bible cross-references Isaiah 24:23 and Micah 4:7. The grade is drawn here: the king on Zion and the context of raging enemies point to Psalm 2.
entries.dissent: Beale reads the 144,000 as all God's people. Heiser, in his Revelation 7 lecture, reads them as Jews loyal to the Lamb, and the ESV Study Bible reports the dispensational view of Jewish believers in the tribulation. MacArthur reads them as redeemed Jews sent out as missionaries in the tribulation, and Mount Zion as Jerusalem, where the Messiah will return. Keener reads Zion as the heavenly temple pointing to the new Jerusalem. Beale weighs heaven, the old city and the new one, and favors a city that is here now and still to come.

entries.title: Revelation 14:2, like the sound of many waters
entries.summary: The sound from heaven like many waters and loud thunder uses Ezekiel's sound of God's glory, here for the song of the redeemed.
entries.plain: **A crowd in a stadium can sound like a waterfall.** Ezekiel heard the noise of many waters near God's throne, and in 43:2 God's own voice sounds like it. John hears a sound from heaven like many waters and loud thunder. This time it is the song of a great crowd with harps. The sound once used for God now comes from his people praising him.
entries.same: A sound like many waters, phone hydaton pollon. John used the same picture for Christ's voice in 1:15.
entries.differs: In Ezekiel 43:2 the sound is God's voice; in Ezekiel 1:24 it is the creatures' wings. Here it is the voice of the redeemed. John adds thunder and harps. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible says it could be God's voice, but in context it is probably the heavenly multitude.
entries.turn: The praise of the redeemed is loud with the weight of a great crowd. Beale ties it to 19:6, where the same sound praises God after Babylon's fall. Those who sing are the ones bought from the earth.
entries.not: **Not the voice of God himself here.** The sources read it as the song of the multitude.
entries.deeper: Beale compares 14:2 with 19:6, which uses nearly identical words for praise after the harlot's judgment, and says the voices are loud because they are the great multitude of 7:9. Keener notes Ezekiel heard the sound of many waters in heaven (Ezekiel 1:24; 43:2) and thunder at Sinai (Exodus 19:16). The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible cites Ezekiel 43:2, Ezekiel 1:24 and Daniel 10:6; the CSB Study Bible cross-references Ezekiel 1:24 and 43:2. The grade is drawn here: the phrase is Ezekiel's, but John uses it as a simile.
entries.dissent: Beale thinks the voice may come from angels first, and the redeemed learn the song, or from the redeemed themselves. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible reads it as the heavenly multitude's joyful praise.

entries.title: Revelation 14:3, a new song
entries.summary: The new song of the redeemed echoes the psalms' new song for God's victories.
entries.plain: **A new anthem gets written after a great victory, and only those who lived through it know why it matters.** The Psalms and Isaiah call for a new song to the Lord when he wins a victory or makes things new. John hears the redeemed sing a new song in front of God's throne. No one can learn it except the 144,000. It is a song only the rescued can sing.
entries.same: A new song sung to God for his victory. John's oden kainen and the psalms' asma kainon both mean a new song.
entries.differs: The psalms call all the earth to sing the new song. In John only the 144,000 can learn it. John's word for song, ode, differs from the psalms' asma and Isaiah's hymnos in the Greek. The sources give no reason for the restriction beyond that only the redeemed know what they sing about.
entries.turn: Beale says the new song in the Old Testament always praised God's victory over the enemy. Here it praises his final victory over sin and the beast. The ESV Study Bible says only those redeemed by the Lamb can sing it.
entries.not: **Not a quotation of one psalm.** The new song appears in several psalms and in Isaiah, so John echoes a familiar phrase.
entries.deeper: Beale lists the new song in Psalms 33:3, 40:3, 96:1, 98:1, 144:9 and 149:1 and Isaiah 42:10, and notes Jewish texts applied it to the Messiah's coming and the world to come. He ties 14:2-3 to 5:9 and 15:3. The ESV Study Bible cites Psalms 96:1, 98:1 and 144:9. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible refer back to their notes on 5:9. In the vault's Septuagint Psalm 96:1 has asma kainon and Isaiah 42:10 hymnon kainon. The grade is drawn here as possible: the phrase is common.
entries.dissent: The CSB Study Bible says this song differs from the song of 5:9-10, since only the 144,000 can learn it. Beale links the two. MacArthur hears all the redeemed singing it together in one great choir.

entries.title: Revelation 14:4, firstfruits to God
entries.summary: Calling the redeemed firstfruits to God recalls Jeremiah 2:3, where Israel was holy to the Lord, the first of his harvest.
entries.plain: **The first loaf from a new oven is often set aside as special.** In the Law the first part of the harvest belonged to God. Jeremiah 2:3 says Israel was set apart for the Lord, the first share of his crop, and that whoever devoured her was punished. John calls the redeemed a first share offered to God and to the Lamb. They are set apart as God's own, just before the harvest of the earth in verses 14-20.
entries.same: God's people called the first of his harvest, holy to him. The Greek of Jeremiah 2:3 uses arche, beginning, where John uses aparche, firstfruits.
entries.differs: Jeremiah speaks of Israel from the exodus; John speaks of those bought from among people for God and the Lamb. Jeremiah's word is not John's exact word. John joins the image to the Lamb, and sets it beside the harvest of judgment.
entries.turn: Beale reads the firstfruits as the whole people of God, set apart from a world about to be judged. Others read them as a first share, with more to come. Either way, they belong wholly to God.
entries.not: **Not Jeremiah's exact word.** Jeremiah calls Israel the first of the harvest. John borrows the idea but uses the word for a firstfruits offering.
entries.deeper: Beale says the holistic meaning of firstfruits fits Jeremiah 2:2-3, which calls the whole nation redeemed from Egypt holy to the Lord, the first of his harvest, and cites Philo and midrashim on the verse. He adds Ezekiel 20:40, where God accepts Israel's firstfruits on his holy mountain at the end. Keener says the term declares their holiness, citing Jeremiah 2:3. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible cites the firstfruits laws and Jeremiah 2:3; the CSB Study Bible cross-references Jeremiah 2:3. The grade is drawn here as possible: the idea is shared, the Greek word differs.
entries.dissent: Beale reads firstfruits as the totality of believers. Bauckham, as Beale reports, and the CSB Study Bible read them as a first group whose witness leads to a larger harvest. The ESV Study Bible says they foreshadow a greater harvest. MacArthur reads the 144,000 as Jewish evangelists set apart for special service, and reports that some see them as the first of a redeemed Israel, with more to follow.

entries.title: Revelation 14:5, no lie in their mouth
entries.summary: No lie found in their mouth joins Zephaniah's promise of a truthful remnant on Zion to Isaiah's servant, in whose mouth was no deceit.
entries.plain: **Children who copy a parent's honesty show whose family they belong to.** Zephaniah promises that the remnant on Zion will speak no lies, and no deceitful tongue will be found in their mouth. Isaiah says of the suffering servant that there was no deceit in his mouth. John says that among the 144,000 no lie was found in what they say. They share the truthfulness of the Lamb and of the faithful remnant.
entries.same: Nothing false found in their mouth. John's en to stomati auton ouch heurethe matches the Greek of Zephaniah 3:13, in their mouth shall not be found. Isaiah 53:9 has the same verb and mouth.
entries.differs: Zephaniah has a deceitful tongue and Isaiah deceit; John has pseudos, lie. Zephaniah speaks of the remnant, Isaiah of one servant; John joins them. He adds that they are blameless, amomoi, a word for an unblemished sacrifice.
entries.turn: The redeemed are like the Lamb, faithful witnesses who do not lie. Beale says the point is innocence before the world's false charges, as with the servant. Wright says the dragon's system runs on lies, and the Lamb's people stand apart from it.
entries.not: **Not a claim to sinless perfection.** Beale reads it as faithful witness and innocence of the world's charges, not moral flawlessness.
entries.deeper: Beale calls the line an allusion to the servant of Isaiah 53:9, right after the lamb led to slaughter in 53:7, and also to Zephaniah 3, which he thinks may itself echo Isaiah 53. He sets out the Greek of both. Zephaniah 3:11-14 speaks of a remnant on God's holy mountain in Zion in the last days, as here. First Peter 2:22 uses Isaiah 53:9 the same way. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible and the CSB Study Bible point to Zephaniah 3:13; the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible to both; the ESV Study Bible and Wright to Isaiah 53:9. The grade is drawn here: the wording of Zephaniah is close and the remnant on Zion fits.
entries.dissent: The study Bibles divide between Zephaniah and Isaiah as the main source. Beale holds both, with Zephaniah the closer wording. Keener reads the lie as including false doctrine.

entries.title: Revelation 14:6, an eternal gospel
entries.summary: The angel's eternal good news echoes the prophets' herald of good news, whose message was rescue for God's people and judgment on their enemies.
entries.plain: **News that the war is over is good for the prisoners, and bad for the jailers.** Isaiah and Nahum picture a runner on the mountains bringing good news: God reigns, and the oppressor is finished. John sees an angel flying overhead with an eternal gospel for every nation. Its message is to fear God, since the time for his judgment has arrived. The sources say it is good news because the judge is about to set things right.
entries.same: A herald announcing good news. John's euangelisai, to announce good news, is the verb of the Greek of Isaiah 52:7 and Nahum 1:15.
entries.differs: Isaiah's herald brings news to Zion; John's angel speaks to all peoples on earth. John calls the news eternal and makes judgment its content. The sources give no reason for the change beyond John's context of the end.
entries.turn: The good news includes judgment. Beale reads the angel as a messenger mainly of judgment, as in Isaiah's good news, which included the fall of God's enemies. Wright reads it as the Isaiah message that God reigns, now come true.
entries.not: **Not a different gospel from Jesus' gospel.** Beale says it is the same good news, which carries dire consequences if refused.
entries.deeper: Beale notes that even in the Greek of Isaiah the announcement of good news included judgment of the wicked (Isaiah 40:9; 52:7; 61:1; 60:6-14). He reads the eternal gospel as stressing judgment, and possibly as a contrast with the good news announced for Augustus' birthday. He also ties 14:6-7 to Daniel 4. Keener reads the good news as God's people vindicated, citing Nahum 1:15; the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible cites Isaiah 40:9, 41:27, 52:7, 61:1 and Nahum 1:15. Wright builds his reading on Isaiah 52:7-10. The grade is drawn here as possible: the verb is shared, the setting differs.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads gospel here as good news or good message. It is good news to the righteous, he says, because they are about to be vindicated and Babylon is about to fall. He reads the call to all nations to worship the Creator as the Psalm 82 judgment and the reversal of Deuteronomy 32: the gods judged and the nations brought back.
entries.dissent: Beale reads the gospel here mainly as a warning of judgment. The CSB Study Bible and Keener allow that it may also be a final call to faith before the end. Wright stresses good news for the oppressed.

aw.n: Revelation 14:6-20, Babylon fallen, the harvest and the winepress
aw.s: Three angels announce an eternal gospel, the fall of Babylon and the undiluted cup of God's wrath for those who worship the beast, and a voice blesses those who die in the Lord. Then one like a son of man reaps the earth's grain with a sickle, and an angel gathers its grapes into the great winepress, from which blood flows as high as the horses' bridles.

entries.title: Revelation 14:7, worship the one who made heaven and earth
entries.summary: The call to give God glory and worship the maker of heaven, earth and sea echoes the angel's word to Nebuchadnezzar in Daniel 4 and the psalm's praise of the Creator.
entries.plain: **A proud boss who must finally say who really owns the company is not exactly converted.** In the Greek of Daniel 4 an angel tells Nebuchadnezzar to give glory to the Most High. The humbled king then praises the maker of heaven, earth and seas. Psalm 146 praises the Lord as maker of heaven, earth and sea. John's angel calls everyone to fear God, honor him and worship the maker of all four.
entries.same: A call to give God glory and worship him as Creator of heaven, earth and sea. John's to poiesanti ton ouranon kai ten gen kai thalassan is close to the Greek of Psalm 146:6.
entries.differs: Beale's link is to the old Greek of Daniel 4. There an angel calls the king, and the king praises the maker of heaven, earth, seas and rivers. John has springs of water, and speaks to every nation, not one king. The vault's Greek of Daniel is the other version, Theodotion, so the old Greek wording rests on Beale's report.
entries.turn: Beale reads the call as a decree at the hour of judgment: those who refused God will be made to own him as judge and Creator, as Nebuchadnezzar was. If it is a last call to repent, the next verses show it ignored. Heiser hears the nations called back to the true God.
entries.not: **Not proof that everyone will turn.** Beale thinks Nebuchadnezzar's praise was forced, not a conversion, and so is this.
entries.deeper: Beale says 14:6-8 rests on a series of phrases about Nebuchadnezzar in Daniel 4: an angel telling the king to give glory to the Most High (4:34 in the old Greek), the king praising the maker of heaven, earth, seas and rivers (4:37 in the old Greek), the fourfold list of peoples, the hour of judgment, and Babylon the great (4:30). He sets the Greek side by side and reads the nominative saying as a deliberate clash that flags the allusion. The CSB Study Bible cross-references Psalm 146:6 and related psalms for the Creator line. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible contrasts true worship with worship of the beast. The grade is drawn here as possible: each text is proposed by one source.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads the angel's call as good news for the righteous. Fear God, give him glory, worship the maker of heaven and earth: to him this is the Psalm 82 judgment, and the reversal of the Deuteronomy 32 problem, with the nations brought back to worship the true God.
entries.dissent: Beale reads the command as a forced acknowledgment at the judgment, not a call to conversion, though he allows the second. The CSB Study Bible reads it as climactic preaching that calls people to fear God. Wright stresses the good news for the oppressed.

entries.title: Revelation 14:8, fallen, fallen is Babylon the great
entries.summary: The second angel's cry joins Isaiah's watchman, fallen, fallen is Babylon, to Nebuchadnezzar's boast in Daniel, Babylon the great.
entries.plain: **A headline can borrow a famous old headline and a dictator's own slogan at once.** In Isaiah 21 a watchman hears the news: fallen, fallen is Babylon, and her idols lie smashed on the ground. In Daniel 4 Nebuchadnezzar boasts of the great Babylon he built, and judgment falls on him that hour. John's angel joins the two: Babylon the great has fallen, twice over. Readers differ on whether the name points at Rome or at a kingdom still to come.
entries.same: The doubled cry fallen, fallen and the name Babylon. The Greek of Isaiah 21:9 has peptoke, peptoke, Babylon; John has epesen, epesen. Babylon the great, Babylon he megale, is the phrase of the Greek of Daniel 4:30 and appears nowhere else in the Old Testament.
entries.differs: Isaiah's Babylon fell long before John wrote; John uses the name for the Babylon of his vision. John uses a past tense for a fall still to come, as prophets did. He adds the nations drinking her wine, from Jeremiah 51. Daniel's line was a king's boast; John turns it into the city's epitaph.
entries.turn: The world system that leads the nations astray is doomed. Its fall is so sure that John speaks of it as done. Beale says Rome was called Babylon because, like Babylon, it burned the temple and sent Israel away. He reads John's Babylon as bigger than Rome: every proud system that wants worship.
entries.not: **Not Isaiah's Babylon.** Isaiah's city fell long before John wrote. John takes its fall, and Daniel's title for it, and gives them to a Babylon of his own vision.
entries.deeper: Beale says fallen, fallen is Babylon derives from Isaiah 21:9a, where it equals the destruction of Babylon's idols in 21:9b. The title Babylon the great is from Daniel 4:30 in both Greek versions, part of the king's self-glory. He lists Jewish texts that call Rome Babylon (2 Baruch 11:1; Sibylline Oracles 5; 1 Peter 5:13; 4 Ezra 3), and Jeremiah's word that historical Babylon would never rise. Keener notes the taunting dirge and Jeremiah 51:8. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the ESV Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible point to Isaiah 21:9, and the CSB Study Bible cross-references Daniel 4:30 and Isaiah 21:9. Wright reads Babylon through Isaiah and Jeremiah. The grade is drawn here: the cry is Isaiah's and the title is Daniel's.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Isaiah 21:9 and Beale and McDonough's merging of it with Daniel 4:30. In John's day, he says, Babylon is almost certainly a cipher for Rome, Daniel's fourth kingdom. He reports Aune's argument that Jewish texts call Rome Babylon only after 70, which would date Revelation late, and Aune's own counter from a Qumran text. He calls it not a slam dunk either way.
entries.dissent: Aune, as Heiser reports, notes that every Jewish text that calls Rome Babylon comes after the year 70. That would favor a late date for Revelation. But a Qumran commentary already uses Babylon as a code name for Assyria, so the habit is older. Beale and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible read Babylon as Rome and every system like it. The ESV Study Bible says its fall waits for the end. Beale cites Jeremiah's word that the old city would never rise again. MacArthur reads Babylon as the whole worldwide political, economic and religious kingdom of the Antichrist, whose capital city God will judge.

entries.title: Revelation 14:8, the wine that made the nations drunk
entries.summary: Babylon making the nations drink the wine of her passion comes from Jeremiah 51, where Babylon is a gold cup that made the whole earth drunk.
entries.plain: **A host who keeps everyone's glass full can make a whole room forget to ask questions.** In Jeremiah 51 Babylon is a golden cup held by the Lord. Everyone on earth got drunk from it, and the nations went mad. Then Babylon suddenly fell. John says Babylon got every nation drinking the wine of her lust for unfaithfulness. Beale reads the wine as the lure of wealth and security that numbs the nations.
entries.same: Babylon makes the nations drink her wine, and then she falls. The Greek of Jeremiah 51:7 has from her wine the nations drank; John has from the wine she made all the nations drink.
entries.differs: Jeremiah's Babylon is a cup in God's hand, God's tool of judgment. John's Babylon serves her own wine, of her passion for immorality, which the prophets used of unfaithful Israel. John drops the gold cup here and keeps it for 17:4.
entries.turn: Beale reads the wine as Babylon's offer of economic security for those who join her idolatry. Once drunk, people cannot resist her and do not fear judgment. In verse 10 God answers with his own cup.
entries.not: **Not mainly about drink or sex.** Beale and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible read the sin as idol worship and selling out for money, as chapter 18 shows.
entries.deeper: Beale says the metaphor of drunkenness comes from Jeremiah 51:7-8, joined with Jeremiah 25:15-16, which is also used in 14:10. He notes Jeremiah's madness comes from terror at Babylon's oppression, and he cites Hosea 4:11-12, where harlotry and wine take away understanding, and Isaiah 23 on Tyre as a harlot paid by the nations. Keener says the allusion here is to Jeremiah 51:7. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible notes Jeremiah warns God's people to flee Babylon. The CSB Study Bible cross-references Jeremiah 51:7-8, and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cites Jeremiah 51:7. The grade is drawn here: the picture is Jeremiah's, the wording John's own.
entries.dissent: Some read the phrase as the wine of God's wrath on her immorality, Beale reports, but he rejects that as anticipating verse 10 too early. The ESV Study Bible reads the passion as society's lure of prosperity and pleasure.

entries.title: Revelation 14:10, the cup of God's wrath
entries.summary: Whoever worships the beast will drink God's wine, mixed undiluted in the cup of his anger, the cup of the Psalms and Jeremiah.
entries.plain: **People who pour drinks for others may one day be handed a stronger one.** Psalm 75 says the Lord holds a cup of strong wine. The wicked of the earth must drink it to the dregs. In Jeremiah 25 God tells the prophet to pass his cup of anger to the nations. John's third angel says the beast's worshipers will drink God's own wine, full strength, from that cup.
entries.same: God's cup of wine given to the wicked as judgment. The Greek of Psalm 75:8 and Jeremiah 25:15 both call it unmixed wine, akratos, the word John uses. Isaiah 51:17 has the cup of his wrath, tou thymou autou.
entries.differs: John writes mixed unmixed, kekerasmenou akratou, a phrase that sounds like a contradiction; Beale says it means prepared at full strength. In Isaiah the cup is taken from Jerusalem's hand and given to her tormentors; here it goes to the beast's worshipers. John adds fire, sulfur and the presence of the Lamb.
entries.turn: The punishment fits the crime. Those who drank Babylon's wine (verse 8) now drink God's. Beale says Babylon's wine numbed them for a while; God's wine makes them submit to his judgment for good.
entries.not: **Not a picture of God getting people drunk for fun.** In the Old Testament texts the cup is a standard image of judgment that crushes the proud.
entries.deeper: Beale says the image is inspired by the wording of Psalm 75:8, Jeremiah 25:15 and Jeremiah 51:7, which Jewish interpreters grouped and applied to the wicked in the age to come (Midrash Rabbah on Genesis 88.5). He lists Psalm 60:3, Isaiah 51:17, 21-23 and 63:6 too. He reads mixed unmixed as an allusion to the unmixed cup of Jeremiah 25:15 and Psalm 75:8 in the Greek. In the vault's Septuagint, Psalm 75:8 reads a cup of undiluted wine, full of mixture. Keener, the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the CSB Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cite Psalm 75:8 and Jeremiah 25:15. The grade is drawn here: akratos and the cup together point to these texts.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Beale and McDonough on the cup: Psalm 75:8 and Jeremiah 25:15 and 51:7 in particular, grouped by Jewish tradition. He then says the verse does not settle the debate between eternal torment and annihilation. It is apocalyptic language from the same texts, and both views, he says, remain on the table.
entries.dissent: Beale holds that verses 10-11 teach eternal conscious punishment. Heiser says the apocalyptic language can support either view. The ESV Study Bible says the wicked are not annihilated. Keener notes that the text does not stop people repenting before death.

entries.title: Revelation 14:10, fire and sulfur
entries.summary: Torment with fire and sulfur recalls the fire and sulfur God rained on Sodom.
entries.plain: **Naming a famous disaster is shorthand for total ruin.** In Genesis 19 the Lord rains sulfur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah, and their smoke goes up like a furnace. Prophets later used Sodom as the model of complete judgment. John says the beast's worshipers will be tormented with fire and sulfur before the angels and the Lamb. Revelation already called the great city spiritually Sodom.
entries.same: Fire and sulfur as God's judgment. The Greek of Genesis 19:24 has theion kai pyr, sulfur and fire; John has pyri kai theio, fire and sulfur.
entries.differs: In Genesis the fire falls once and destroys the cities. John speaks of torment, before witnesses, and verse 11 adds that it goes on. He reverses the order of the two words. The sources do not explain the change.
entries.turn: The worshipers of the beast face a Sodom-like judgment. Keener says fire and sulfur suit a spiritual Sodom (11:8), though the image may be broader. The same pair returns in the lake of fire.
entries.not: **Not a weather report.** The sources read fire and sulfur as a figure of judgment drawn from Sodom's story.
entries.deeper: Beale says that in the Old Testament fire and brimstone, sometimes with smoke, mark a fatal judgment (Genesis 19:24, 28; Deuteronomy 29:23; Psalm 11:6; Isaiah 34:9-10; Ezekiel 38:22). Keener links fire and brimstone to a spiritual Sodom, citing Genesis 19:24 and Ezekiel 38:22. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible both point to Genesis 19:24; the CSB Study Bible cross-references Luke 17:29, which mentions Sodom. The grade is drawn here as possible: the pair of words is common to several judgment texts.
entries.dissent: The sources agree on Sodom as background. They differ on what the fire means: Beale reads ongoing torment, while Fudge, as Beale reports, reads a judgment that ends in destruction and is remembered forever.

entries.title: Revelation 14:11, the smoke goes up forever
entries.summary: The smoke of torment rising forever, with no rest day or night, comes from Isaiah 34's picture of Edom burning night and day, its smoke rising for all time.
entries.plain: **A burned-out ruin left standing can be a reminder for generations.** Isaiah 34 pictures Edom judged. Its land turns to burning pitch and sulfur, the fire is never put out, and its smoke rises forever. John says the smoke of the torment of the beast's worshipers rises without end, and they get no rest. The sources agree on Isaiah, and disagree on what the image means for punishment.
entries.same: Smoke rising forever, and no end night and day. The Greek of Isaiah 34:10 has night and day, its smoke shall go up, and for a long time; John has the smoke goes up forever and no rest day and night.
entries.differs: Isaiah speaks of a land, Edom, laid waste. John speaks of people, the beast's worshipers. Isaiah's smoke marks a desolation; John adds torment and no rest. He moves from one nation to all who worship the beast.
entries.turn: Beale says Isaiah's picture of one nation is widened to the final judgment of all unbelievers. The restless nights are the dark mirror of the endless praise of 4:8. They also stand against the rest promised to the faithful in 14:13.
entries.not: **Not agreed by all readers to mean the same thing.** Keener notes the meaning shifts from Isaiah's desolation to burning and torment, and others read a lasting memorial.
entries.deeper: Beale says verse 11a is drawn from Isaiah 34:9-10, God's judgment of Edom, and that the Targum and midrashim applied the passage to Rome. He discusses whether the smoke is a memorial of a finished destruction, as in Isaiah, or of ongoing torment, and argues for ongoing torment from 20:10 and the word torment. He notes the phrase no rest day and night repeats 4:8. Keener says the eternal smoking of Edom is described in similar terms in Isaiah 34:10. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible and the CSB Study Bible all point to Isaiah 34:10. The grade is drawn here: the smoke rising forever is Isaiah's.
entries.dissent: Beale and the ESV Study Bible read eternal conscious punishment. Fudge, as Beale reports, reads a judgment remembered forever, as with Edom. Keener says the meaning shifts from Isaiah's desolation to eternal burning. Heiser says the apocalyptic language can support either view.

entries.title: Revelation 14:14, one like a son of man on a cloud
entries.summary: The crowned figure seated on a white cloud, one like a son of man, is Daniel 7:13's figure, come now to reap the earth.
entries.plain: **A judge's robe tells you who will hand down the verdict.** In Daniel 7 a human figure comes with the clouds before God, the Ancient of Days, and is given the kingdom. John sees a figure like a son of man seated on a white cloud, with a gold crown and a sharp sickle. The same figure who walked among the lampstands in chapter 1 now comes to harvest the earth.
entries.same: One like a son of man and the clouds. John's homoion huion anthropou is the phrase of 1:13, from Daniel 7:13, with the same odd case in Greek.
entries.differs: In Daniel the figure comes with the clouds to receive the kingdom. In John he sits on a single white cloud, wears a gold crown and holds a sickle. Daniel's figure is presented to God; John's carries out the judgment. Beale says the context leaves only the role of judge in view here.
entries.turn: The son of man of Daniel 7, whom Revelation 1 showed as the divine Christ, now comes to judge. Beale ties it to Jesus' sayings about his own return with the clouds. The crown marks him as king, and the sickle as the one who reaps.
entries.not: **Not one more angel among many.** Beale, the CSB Study Bible and Heiser read the figure as Christ, though the next angel speaks to him.
entries.deeper: Beale calls the figure an allusion to Daniel 7:13, in the tradition of Matthew 24:30. He notes seven heavenly beings in 14:6-20 and grants that some read the son of man as an angel, but answers that 1:13 uses the same words for the divine Christ and that the son of man on the clouds is always Christ in the Gospels. He reads the out-of-place nominative having as a stylistic flag pointing back to Daniel and to 1:13-16. The vault's Greek of Daniel 7:13 reads with the clouds of heaven, as a son of man. The CSB Study Bible calls it a clear allusion to Daniel 7:13; the ESV Study Bible and Wright also cite Daniel 7. The grade is drawn here: the phrase is Daniel's word for word.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Aune: seated on a cloud may join Psalm 110:1, sitting at God's right hand, to Daniel 7:13, as Jesus did at his trial in Mark 14:62. With Beale, he takes the figure as Christ. Even if it were angelic language, he says, that would not lower Christ, since in the Old Testament Yahweh appears as the angel of the Lord.
entries.dissent: Keener says one like a son of man could mean only a human-looking figure, and that Christ would not take orders from an angel. Kiddle and Muller, as Beale reports, read an angel. Beale, the CSB Study Bible and Heiser read Christ, with the angel only passing on God's timing.

entries.title: Revelation 14:15-16, put in your sickle, for the harvest is ripe
entries.summary: The command to send the sickle because the harvest is ripe, and then to gather the grapes, follows Joel 3:13, the only Old Testament text with both the sickle and the winepress as judgment.
entries.plain: **Farmers know when a field is ready, and a good farmer does not wait.** Joel 3 pictures the nations gathered for judgment: put in the sickle, the harvest is ripe; come and tread, the winepress is full, for their evil is great. John sees two reapings. The son of man is told to put in his sickle because the harvest is ripe, then an angel gathers the earth's grapes for the winepress. Joel's double picture becomes two scenes.
entries.same: Send the sickle, for the harvest is ripe, and then the full winepress. John's drepanon, sickle, is the word of the Greek of Joel 3:13. The order, harvest and then grapes, is Joel's.
entries.differs: The Hebrew of Joel says ki vashal katsir, the harvest is ripe, a grain harvest. The Greek translation turns it into the vintage, ho trygetos. John has ho therismos, the harvest, which agrees with the Hebrew; the comparison is drawn here. John splits Joel's one command into two scenes with two reapers. He adds a crown and a cloud.
entries.turn: Beale says both reapings are judgment, as in Joel: God's judgment of the nations when their evil is full. The repeating stresses how complete it is. Others read the first reaping as the gathering of God's people.
entries.not: **Not agreed by all readers to be two pictures of judgment.** Beale, Heiser and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible read both as judgment; Bauckham, Wright and the ESV Study Bible read the grain harvest as salvation.
entries.deeper: Beale says both 14:14-16 and 14:17-20 depend on Joel 4:13 (3:13 in English Bibles), the only Old Testament passage where harvesting with a sickle is used as a figure, and the only one where harvest and winepress appear together. He sets out the Greek, notes Joel's plural sickles, and cites Mark 4:29, which quotes Joel with harvest. He adds Jeremiah 51:33 and Isaiah 18:5. The Hebrew in Sefaria reads shilchu maggal ki vashal katsir. The CSB Study Bible cross-references Joel 3:13; Keener, the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the ESV Study Bible and Wright all point to Joel 3. Beale calls the Joel text the model for the twofold picture. The grade is drawn here: the sickle and the ripe harvest occur together only in Joel.
entries.heiser: Heiser calls Joel 3:13 an important passage and reads it as plainly Day of the Lord language: the nations surrounding Jerusalem, the valley of decision. It answers the question whether the sickle brings salvation or judgment, he says: it is pretty clearly judgment of the wicked. He adds Jeremiah 51:33 and Micah 4:12-13.
entries.dissent: Bauckham, as Beale reports, reads the grain harvest of verses 14-16 as the gathering of God's people, and only the grapes as judgment. The ESV Study Bible, the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible and Wright lean the same way. Beale, Heiser and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible read both as judgment, since both of Joel's images are judgment.

Then one like a son of man reaps the earth's grain with a sickle, and an angel gathers its grapes into the great winepress, from which blood flows as high as the horses' bridles.

entries.title: Revelation 14:19-20, the great winepress of God's wrath
entries.summary: The winepress trodden outside the city, with blood up to the horses' bridles, draws on Isaiah 63, where the Lord treads the nations like grapes, alone, and their blood stains his clothes.
entries.plain: **Grape juice on a farmer's boots looks like blood, and the prophets noticed.** In Isaiah 63 someone comes from Edom in red-stained clothes. He has trodden the winepress alone, trampled the nations in his anger, and their blood has spattered his robes. John sees the earth's grapes thrown into the great winepress, which stands for God's anger. It is trodden outside the city, and blood flows as high as a horse's bridle.
entries.same: A winepress trodden in God's anger, with blood instead of wine. The Greek of Isaiah 63:2-3 has a trampled winepress, lenos, I trampled them, and their blood on the earth; John has the winepress was trampled, epatethe he lenos, and blood came out.
entries.differs: In Isaiah the one who treads is the Lord, alone. John says it is trodden outside the city, and adds the bridles and 1,600 stadia. The winepress is great, megan, in a masculine form that does not agree with its noun; Beale thinks Isaiah 63's Hebrew and Greek explain the clash. In 19:15 Christ is the one who treads.
entries.turn: John tells readers who the divine warrior of Isaiah 63 is: Christ. Heiser stresses the point. The judgment of the nations happens outside the city, where the faithful are safe, as in Joel's valley near Jerusalem. Beale, Heiser and Keener read the blood to the bridles as a stock way to say the slaughter is beyond counting.
entries.not: **Not Isaiah's scene unchanged.** In Isaiah the Lord treads the winepress alone. John sets it outside the city and adds the bridles and the 1,600 stadia.
entries.deeper: Beale says the first part of verse 20 is based on Joel 3:13b together with Isaiah 63:2-3, and cites Lamentations 1:15, where the Lord trod the winepress of Judah. He sets out the Greek of Isaiah 63:2-3 and argues the masculine great may point to Isaiah, where the Hebrew winepress, purah, is followed by a masculine them. He compares 1 Enoch 100:3, where horses walk up to their chests in sinners' blood. Keener says the image is particularly from Isaiah 63:1-6, and the CSB Study Bible cross-references it; the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the ESV Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible point to it. Heiser, after Aune, calls it an allusion to Isaiah 63:1-6. The grade is drawn here: the winepress of wrath trodden is Isaiah's picture.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Aune: the winepress alludes to Isaiah 63:1-6, the divine warrior with blood-stained clothes, and 19:15 shows the rider treads it. By putting Jesus in that role, John says who the divine warrior is: in the Old Testament there is only one, God, or the angel of the Lord. He cites Tremper Longman and says Jesus "does not come back blowing kisses".
entries.dissent: Wright reads the vintage as the martyrs' own blood, shed outside the city as Jesus' was, and so as salvation through suffering. Caird, as Beale reports, also reads martyrdom. Beale, Keener and Heiser read judgment on the nations, from Isaiah 63 and Joel 3. MacArthur places the slaughter at Armageddon, on the Plain of Esdraelon, outside Jerusalem. He takes the blood as splashing about four feet high, or running in channels that deep, and the 1,600 stadia as about the distance from Armageddon to Edom.

entries.title: Revelation 15:2, a sea of glass mixed with fire
entries.summary: The glassy sea where the victors stand recalls the Red Sea of the exodus and the crystal expanse under God's throne in Ezekiel 1.
entries.plain: **A town that builds its new park on the spot where a flood once broke through is telling a story without words.** John sees a sea like glass, mixed with fire, and the victors standing by it with harps. The picture borrows the Red Sea, where Israel stood safe on the far shore and sang. It also borrows the clear floor under God's throne in Ezekiel 1. John sets the victors beside it, singing as Israel sang.
entries.same: A sea, a people who have come through, and a song that follows. In Exodus 14-15 Israel crosses the sea and Moses leads the singing. In Revelation 15:2-3 the victors stand by a glassy sea and sing the song of Moses. Ezekiel 1:22 adds the clear, crystal-like expanse spread over the living creatures.
entries.differs: Exodus never calls the Red Sea glass. Beale points to later Jewish teaching that the sea set hard like glass when the waters piled up (Exodus 15:8). The fire is John's own addition. Beale says fire in Revelation stands for judgment, so this is the sea where the Lamb judged the beast. Ezekiel's expanse sits over the creatures' heads; John's sea lies before the throne, as in 4:6. And the singers are no longer Israel alone but everyone who refused the beast.
entries.turn: At the Red Sea Israel watched God beat Pharaoh. Here the church has won its own fight against the beast, though only through the Lamb's victory. John retells the old rescue so that believers under pressure know how their story ends. Beale adds that the sea in Revelation often stands for evil, so a calm sea shows evil brought under God's control.
entries.not: **Not a quotation of Exodus.** No Old Testament text calls the Red Sea glass. The link runs through the scene: a sea, a people brought through it, and the song of Moses that follows.
entries.deeper: Beale says the heavenly counterpart of the Red Sea is uppermost in mind, and that the song of Moses in the next verse confirms it. He allows a side glance at the bronze basin called the sea in Solomon's temple. He cites the Mekilta and other rabbinic texts, which said the sea at the exodus hardened and looked like glass, reading Exodus 15:8, where the deeps congealed. The image could also rest on Ezekiel 1:22, where the Greek translation compares the expanse to the look of crystal (krystallou); Revelation 4:6 has a sea like crystal. Beale adds Daniel 7:10, where a river of fire runs before the throne as the beast is judged, and Keener links the fire to Jewish pictures of fiery rivers before God's throne drawn from Daniel 7:9-10. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible hears a new exodus from the sea monster (Psalm 74:13-14; Isaiah 51:9-10). The ESV Study Bible reads the sea as the clear pavement around the throne (Exodus 24:10; Ezekiel 1:22). The grade is drawn here: the sea, the victors and the song together trace back to the exodus, though the wording is not close.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Beale and McDonough on the scene: the sea of glass points first to the Red Sea, and the first exodus from under Pharaoh is replayed as a final exodus from under the beast. He adds Ezekiel 1:22, the crystal platform for God's throne, as a cue that the judgment is still the council meeting of chapters 4 and 5. With Beale he says the sea does double duty: it is the beast's home and a picture of chaos, yet God masters it, as he did at the Red Sea.
entries.dissent: The sources agree on the exodus but weigh the second picture differently. Beale and Heiser add Ezekiel 1:22 and read the sea as a sign of evil subdued. Keener stresses the rivers of fire before God's throne in Daniel 7 and Jewish tradition. The CSB Study Bible reads the fire as a preview of the fire that later burns Babylon. Beale rejects readings that make the fire the saints' trials or their baptism. MacArthur reads the sea of glass as the clear crystal floor that stretches out before God's throne, as at 4:6, and the victors as saints from every nation, Israel included, who overcome the Antichrist through faith in Christ.

aw.n: Revelation 15:1-16:11, the song of Moses and the first bowls
aw.s: Those who have overcome the beast stand beside a sea of glass mixed with fire and sing the song of Moses and of the Lamb. Seven angels dressed like priests come out of the heavenly temple with seven golden bowls of God's wrath, and the first five bring sores, seas and rivers turned to blood, scorching sun and darkness on the beast's throne.

entries.title: Revelation 15:3, the song of Moses the servant of God
entries.summary: The victors sing the song of Moses, the song Israel sang after crossing the sea, now joined to the song of the Lamb.
entries.plain: **A national anthem sung after a new victory carries the memory of the first one.** After the Red Sea, Moses and Israel sang to God for throwing Pharaoh's horses and riders into the water. John hears the victors sing the song of Moses, God's servant, joined to a song for the Lamb. The old rescue from Egypt and the new rescue by the Lamb are praised together.
entries.same: A song sung by a sea after God beats an enemy, and the name of Moses. Exodus 14:31 calls Moses the Lord's servant just before the song begins. Revelation names the song of Moses, God's servant. Both groups of singers praise God, not themselves.
entries.differs: John names the song but does not quote it. Beale shows that the words that follow come from other Old Testament texts. Exodus 14:31 in Greek calls Moses God's attendant (therapon); John calls him God's slave or servant (doulos). He adds the song of the Lamb, which no one had sung before. And the singers stand by a sea in heaven, not on the shore of Egypt. Deuteronomy 32, the other song of Moses, may be in view as well.
entries.turn: John says the exodus has happened again on a larger scale. Israel escaped Pharaoh; the church escapes the beast. Beale reads the Lamb's victory as the thing the Red Sea rescue pointed toward. For believers under Rome the point is plain: the God who drowned Pharaoh's army will not fail them.
entries.not: **Not a quotation of the song.** John names the song of Moses, yet the words the singers sing come from other Old Testament texts, not from Exodus 15.
entries.deeper: Beale calls the song in 15:3-4 an imitation of the song Moses sang after the Red Sea victory (Exodus 15:1-18). The title servant of God, he says, comes from Exodus 14:31, which stands right before that song. He reads the and between the two songs as explanatory, so there is one song: the saints praise the Lamb's victory as what the Red Sea pointed to. Deuteronomy 32 is also called a song of Moses (Deuteronomy 31:19, 22, 30; 32:44), and Beale includes it, since it ends with God avenging the blood of his servants (32:43). Jewish writings linked the song of Exodus 15:1 to a new song in the age to come (Midrash on Psalms) and even to the singers' resurrection (b. Sanhedrin 91b). The Greek of Revelation reads ten oden Mouseos tou doulou tou theou; Exodus 15:1 in the Greek translation has ten oden tauten, this song. Keener thinks Exodus 15:1-18 is almost surely meant. The ESV Study Bible says the song of Moses is fulfilled in the song of the Lamb, and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible adds the Passover lamb of Exodus 12. The grade is drawn here: John names the song outright.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Beale and McDonough: this song answers, in the last days, the song Moses sang in Exodus 15, and naming it settles that the scene is set at the Red Sea of a new exodus. He uses it to tie the bowls to the plagues on Egypt that follow in chapter 16.
entries.dissent: Beale includes Deuteronomy 32 in the allusion, since it is also called a song of Moses and it describes judgment. Keener grants that Deuteronomy 32 was used in Jewish worship but thinks the context points to Exodus 15. Wright says the song owes something to Deuteronomy 32 while the focus stays on the exodus. Beale reports De Moor's proposal of an Aramaic song of the Lamb about David and Goliath and finds it intriguing but unproven. Beale takes the and between the songs as meaning even, so the two are one song. MacArthur reads two songs for two rescues: Israel freed from Egypt through Moses, and sinners freed from sin through Christ.

entries.title: Revelation 15:3, great and marvelous are your works
entries.summary: The song's first line gathers phrases from Moses' warning of great and marvelous plagues and from psalms that praise God's great works.
entries.plain: **A sports announcer can call a comeback amazing in words that old fans recognize from a famous broadcast.** The singers open by calling God's works great and marvelous. Moses had warned Israel that disobedience would bring plagues on them like Egypt's, great and marvelous. Psalms praise God's great works and the wonders he does. John's line gathers those phrases into praise, just as the bowls of plagues are about to fall.
entries.same: Two adjectives side by side, great (megala) and marvelous (thaumasta). The Greek of Deuteronomy 28:59 calls Israel's coming plagues great and marvelous (megalas kai thaumastas). Psalm 111:2 says the Lord's works are great, and Psalm 86:10 says God is great and does marvelous things.
entries.differs: In Deuteronomy the two words describe plagues; John applies them to God's works. In Deuteronomy the plagues fall on unfaithful Israel; in Revelation they fall on those who follow the beast. The psalms spread the two words across a verse, while John sets them in one short line. No single text has John's exact phrase, which is why the sources point to more than one.
entries.turn: The bowls about to fall are Egypt's plagues come again. By praising God's works as great and marvelous, the singers call those judgments right before they happen. Beale says the line shows God's acts as moral expressions of his character, not displays of raw power.
entries.not: **Not a quotation of one verse.** The phrase is built from several, and the sources do not agree which one counts most.
entries.deeper: Beale calls the first line an allusion to Deuteronomy 28:59-60 in the Greek translation, which predicts that Israel's future judgment will follow the pattern of the plagues on Egypt. He also hears Psalm 111:2-4, which praises the Lord's great works and wonders at the Red Sea, and notes that this psalm may itself recall Exodus 34:10 and Exodus 15:11, where God is marvelous in glories. Psalm 86:10 could also be included, he says, because verse 4 cites that psalm in full. He points out that Tobit 12:22 has wording even closer than any of these but does not refer to the exodus. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible says the words come especially from Psalm 86:9-10, which itself evokes Exodus 15:11. Keener ties the great and wonderful works to the plagues of 15:1 and compares Exodus 15:11. The grade is drawn here: the pair of words is traceable to texts about the exodus, but no one source supplies it whole.
entries.dissent: The sources name different sources for the line. Beale leads with Deuteronomy 28:59-60 and Psalm 111. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible leads with Psalm 86:10. Keener points to Exodus 15:11. Beale himself allows that the psalm cited in verse 4 may be what brought the phrase to mind.

entries.title: Revelation 15:3, just and true are your ways
entries.summary: Moses' second song calls God's works true and his ways just; the singers say it of God's ways, and the altar says it of his judgments.
entries.plain: **A family motto stitched on a sampler can turn up again in a wedding toast years later.** Moses' second song, in Deuteronomy 32, praises God: his works are true, his ways are justice, and he is just and holy. The singers in Revelation say nearly the same about God's ways. Later, as the bowls fall, an angel calls God just and holy, and the altar calls his judgments true and just. Each time the point is that God judges fairly.
entries.same: The pair true and just, with holy beside it. In the Greek of Deuteronomy 32:4 his works are true (alethina) and his ways are judgment. The Lord is just (dikaios) and holy (hosios). Revelation 15:3 has just and true your ways; 16:5 calls God just and the holy one; 16:7 has true and just your judgments.
entries.differs: Deuteronomy speaks about God; Revelation speaks to him. In 15:3 John reverses the order of true and just, and in 16:7 he puts judgments where Moses had ways. In 16:5 holy one takes the place of who is to come, the third part of the name used for God in 1:4. Beale says the change shows that God has begun to judge.
entries.turn: Deuteronomy 32 ends with God avenging the blood of his servants. John calls on that song as the bowls fall on those who shed the blood of the saints (16:6). The angel of the waters and the altar agree: what God does is right. The saints' cry from under the altar (6:10) is being answered.
entries.not: **Not a celebration of cruelty.** Both Deuteronomy and Revelation tie God's judgment to his fairness. Beale calls the acts moral expressions of God's just character.
entries.deeper: Beale says the noun clause in 15:3 echoes Deuteronomy 32:4 in the Greek translation, and that the same verse lies behind the identical words in 16:7. He notes that Deuteronomy 32 is introduced as a song in 31:30 and that the Talmud (b. Taanith 11a) applies it to judgment and reward in the world to come. The Greek of Deuteronomy 32:4 has true, judgment, just and holy in one verse; Beale reads holy (hosios) in 16:5 as a near synonym for just, as in that verse and Psalm 145:17. He adds that Daniel 3:27 in the Greek also seems to recall Deuteronomy 32:4, and that Psalm 119:75 and 119:137-138 join the same words. The ESV Study Bible cites the later song of Moses, especially Deuteronomy 32:4, and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible cites Deuteronomy 32:4 at 15:3-4 and 16:5. The grade is drawn here: the pair of words is common, but only this verse joins it to a song of Moses.
entries.dissent: The CSB Study Bible's cross-references at 16:7 point instead to Psalm 19:9, where the Lord's judgments are true and righteous. Beale also cites Psalm 119. Keener reads the angel's praise against the psalms in which the oppressed thank God for vindicating them. The sources agree on the meaning; they differ on which text John had in mind.

entries.title: Revelation 15:3-4, who will not fear you, King of the nations
entries.summary: The question who will not fear you, joined to the title King of the nations, comes from Jeremiah's mockery of idols.
entries.plain: **A tribute that borrows a line from an old hymn lets the hymn finish the thought.** Jeremiah mocks idols that cannot walk or speak, then turns to God and asks who would not fear him, the king of the nations. The singers in Revelation ask the same question. In both places the answer is plain: everyone should. John sets the true God against the beast and its image, which the world has worshiped.
entries.same: The title King of the nations and the question who will not fear you. Jeremiah 10:7 in the Greek translation reads tis ou phobethesetai se, basileu ethnon. Revelation 15:4 asks tis ou me phobethe, with the title at the end of 15:3.
entries.differs: The SBL Greek text prints King of the ages at 15:3, not of the nations; copies differ here. Beale argues that nations is original, because Jeremiah's wording runs on into verse 4. John adds a second verb, glorify your name, and a reason: you alone are holy. In Jeremiah the question sits inside a mockery of idols made by craftsmen. In Revelation it rings out in a victory song.
entries.turn: Jeremiah sets the living God against lifeless idols. Beale says John does the same with the beast and its image. The question is aimed at the earth's people, who will refuse to give God glory when the bowls fall (16:9).
entries.not: **Not a change in meaning.** Some copies read nations and some read ages. Both titles call God king. The choice touches the link to Jeremiah, not the sense of the line.
entries.deeper: Beale sets the two texts side by side and says the opening of verse 4, with the end of verse 3, recalls Jeremiah 10:7. Jeremiah 10:1-16 contrasts Israel's God with idols and says there is none like him (10:6-7). Beale adds that the formula who is like you goes back to the exodus (Exodus 15:11), so it fits a song of Moses. On the text he judges King of the nations original: copyists took it for King of the ages, perhaps under the influence of 1 Timothy 1:17, and one late copy reads saints. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible says the words come secondarily from Jeremiah 10:7, after Psalm 86. The ESV Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible also cite Jeremiah 10:7, the latter adding Exodus 15:14, 18. The grade is drawn here: the question and the title appear together only in this verse of Jeremiah.
entries.dissent: Beale, the ESV Study Bible and most English versions read King of the nations. The SBL Greek text prints King of the ages, with nations as a variant. Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible discuss the reading king of the ages or of the world as a common Jewish title for God, while still tying the line to the Old Testament. The choice affects the Jeremiah link but not the line's sense. MacArthur also reads King of the nations and points to Jeremiah 10:7.
