entries.title: Revelation 15:4, all the nations will come and worship
entries.summary: The hope that every nation will come and bow before God is taken from Psalm 86:9-10, almost word for word in the Greek.
entries.plain: **A school that paints its founder's prayer on the new gym wall is saying the prayer is coming true.** Psalm 86 hopes that every nation God made will come, bow before him and honor his name, because he alone is God. The singers in Revelation use nearly the same words. Every nation, they sing, will arrive and kneel in God's presence, because he alone is holy. A lonely man's prayer becomes a victory song.
entries.same: The Greek follows the psalm closely: all the nations (panta ta ethne) will come (hexousin) and worship (proskynesousin) before you (enopion sou), as in Psalm 86:9 in the Greek translation. Both join this to glorifying God's name. Both give a reason built on God standing alone. The psalm says alone God (86:10); John says alone holy (15:4).
entries.differs: John drops the psalm's words about the nations God made and its address, O Lord. He splits the psalm: glorifying God's name comes first, inside his question, and the coming of the nations second. The psalm's you alone are God becomes you alone are holy. The psalmist prays in trouble; John's singers stand after the victory.
entries.turn: In the psalm one troubled man hopes the nations will someday honor God. John puts that hope in the mouths of people who have already won. Beale reads all the nations as many from every nation, not every person: some come willingly, others are made to admit God's glory.
entries.not: **Not Psalm 86 word for word.** John drops the psalm's nations whom God made and its address to the Lord. He changes you alone are God to you alone are holy.
entries.deeper: Beale says most of the language of verse 4 rests on Psalm 86:9-10, and that the psalm's words great and marvelous may already lie behind verse 3. He adds the psalm's formula there is none like you among the gods (86:8) and suggests Isaiah 2:2 as a further echo. The theme of the nations streaming to Zion runs through the prophets (Isaiah 2:3; 49:22-23; 60:14; 66:23; Micah 4:2; Zechariah 8:20-22; 14:16). Later Jewish writings (Midrash on Psalms 66.1) link Psalm 86:9-10 to Exodus 15, which Beale thinks may reflect an older tradition, though John may have been first. In the Greek translation the psalm reads panta ta ethne hosa epoiesas hexousi kai proskynesousin enopion sou; John has panta ta ethne hexousin kai proskynesousin enopion sou. Keener, the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the ESV Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible all point to Psalm 86:9, and the CSB Study Bible's cross-references list it. The grade is drawn here: the wording is nearly the psalm's own.
entries.dissent: Bauckham, as Beale reports, argues that John shifts the new exodus toward the nations coming to know the true God. Caird, also reported by Beale, says the point is only the nations' conversion. Beale holds that judgment and salvation both remain: all will acknowledge God, some willingly and some by force. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible stresses that God, not the beast, receives the worldwide worship. MacArthur places the worship after God's judgment is complete, when Christ's thousand-year kingdom is set up on earth and the chosen from every nation come to worship him.

entries.title: Revelation 15:4, your righteous acts have been revealed
entries.summary: The song's last line may recall Psalm 98:2, where God shows his righteousness before the nations after a new song for his victory.
entries.plain: **A news alert that says the verdict is in uses different words from the court clerk, but reports the same event.** Psalm 98 sings that the Lord has made his saving help known and shown his justice before the nations. The song in Revelation ends the same way. The nations come because God's just acts are now in plain view. The psalm also opens with a new song and harps after a victory, like the scene John sees.
entries.same: God's justice made public before the nations. Psalm 98:2 has the nations, God's righteousness and the verb revealed. Revelation 15:4 has the nations, God's righteous acts (dikaiomata) and the verb made manifest. Both the psalm and Revelation begin with a new song and harps (Psalm 98:1, 5; Revelation 15:2-3).
entries.differs: The Greek words differ. The psalm has righteousness (dikaiosyne) and revealed (apekalypse); John has righteous acts or verdicts and made manifest (ephanerothesan). In the psalm God shows his saving help for Israel. In Revelation the acts are verdicts of judgment, Beale says. The likeness lies in the thought more than the words, so this is only a possible echo.
entries.turn: Psalm 98 ends with God coming to judge the world. Beale finds the same movement here: the song of the first exodus becomes the pattern for the last judgment. The singers praise God because his verdicts are now open for everyone to see.
entries.not: **Not a word-for-word borrowing.** The vocabulary is different. The link rests on the same order of ideas: a new song, a victory, and justice shown to the nations.
entries.deeper: Beale calls the end of verse 4 another reminiscence of the exodus, from Psalm 98:2, and sets the two side by side. He notes that the psalm's second verse follows an opening that recalls Exodus 15:1, 6, 12, that the psalm calls for harps (98:5), and that it ends with God judging the world in righteousness (98:9). He reads the righteous acts as God's vindication of his people by condemning their opponents, an answer to the prayer of 6:9-10, and notes that the word group in the Greek Old Testament can mean either vindication or just condemnation. The ESV Study Bible cites Psalm 98:2 for the righteous acts of judgment, and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible lists it among the psalms behind the song. Wright recalls Psalms 96 and 98, where creation sings because God is coming to judge the earth. The grade is drawn here: several sources name the psalm, but the wording differs.

entries.title: Revelation 15:5, the tent of testimony in heaven
entries.summary: John calls the heavenly sanctuary the tent of testimony, the name the Greek translation gives Israel's desert tent, which the Hebrew calls the tent of meeting.
entries.plain: **When two languages name the same building differently, the name a writer uses shows which language he learned it in.** The Hebrew Bible calls Israel's desert tent the tent of meeting, where God met Moses. The old Greek translation usually calls it the tent of testimony. John sees the sanctuary of that tent opened in heaven, and he uses the Greek name. The tent of the exodus becomes the place the last plagues come from.
entries.same: The phrase tent of testimony (skene tou martyriou). The Greek of Exodus 38:21 and 40:34-35 uses it for the tent in the wilderness. Beale counts about 140 uses in the Greek Old Testament, most of them in Exodus through Deuteronomy.
entries.differs: The Hebrew of Exodus 40:34 says ohel moed, tent of meeting. The Greek translators wrote tent of testimony, which points to the tablets of the law kept inside. John follows the Greek name. He also places the tent in heaven and calls its inner room the sanctuary (naos). In Exodus the tent was where God dwelt in mercy; here it sends out judgment, Beale says.
entries.turn: The setting stays in the exodus: the sea, the song, and now the tent. Beale says the testimony includes God's law and also the testimony of Jesus. God now shows his just will by judging those who reject it. The sanctuary that once stood for mercy is opened to release the bowls.
entries.not: **Not a second temple in heaven.** John's tent is the heavenly original of Israel's tent, the same sanctuary seen opened in 11:19.
entries.deeper: Beale reads the phrase as the sanctuary, which is the tabernacle, the heavenly counterpart of the tent that went with Israel in the wilderness, continuing the exodus scene of 15:2-4. He counts about 140 uses of tent of testimony in the Greek Old Testament, 130 of them in Exodus to Deuteronomy, and explains that the testimony was the ten commandments placed in the ark (Exodus 25:21; 31:18; 32:15). The tent also stood for mercy, since sacrifices were made there, but for John it now witnesses to judgment. The Hebrew of Exodus 40:34 has ohel moed, while the Greek translation of the same verse has ten skenen tou martyriou; that John follows the Greek name is a comparison drawn here, not by the sources. The CSB Study Bible's cross-references cite Exodus 38:21 and Numbers 17:7 and 18:2. Wright recalls Sinai, where God gave Moses instructions for the tent of meeting. The grade is drawn here: the phrase is the Greek Old Testament's own name for the tent.

entries.title: Revelation 15:6, angels in linen with golden sashes
entries.summary: The seven angels wear linen and gold sashes like the man in linen of Daniel 10 and the Son of Man in Revelation 1.
entries.plain: **When the waiters in a famous restaurant wear the chef's jacket, diners know whose kitchen they serve.** Daniel saw a man by the river dressed in linen, with gold around his waist. Ezekiel saw a man in linen among the angels sent to punish Jerusalem. John's seven angels come out of the temple in clean, shining linen with gold sashes across the chest, dressed like Jesus in 1:13. They are priests of the heavenly temple, sent out to judge.
entries.same: Linen and gold around the body. Daniel 10:5 has a man clothed in linen (baddin in the Greek) and girded with gold. Revelation 15:6 has angels clothed in linen (linon), girded around the chest with gold sashes (zonas chrysas), almost the words used of the Son of Man in 1:13.
entries.differs: Daniel has one man, girded at the waist; John has seven angels with sashes across the chest. Some early copies read stone (lithon) instead of linen (linon). Beale thinks stone may be original, which would recall the jeweled covering in Ezekiel 28:13. Ezekiel 9:2 supplies a man in linen among six destroyers, but in the Greek his belt is of sapphire, not gold.
entries.turn: Beale says the shared clothing makes the angels Christ's agents: they carry out the judgment of the figure in 1:13. Their priestly dress fits their work in the heavenly temple. Ezekiel 9 adds the setting of angels sent out from God's house to judge.
entries.not: **Not a sign that the angels are Christ.** They share his clothing because they act for him. Beale calls them his representatives.
entries.deeper: Beale says the description is almost identical to the Son of Man's in 1:13 and that both allude to the Greek of Daniel 10:5, 16, which he sets beside 1:13 and 15:6. He weighs a textual problem: stone (lithon) has strong support (A, C, 2053, 2062), while linen (linon or linoun) has p47 and Sinaiticus. He judges stone the harder reading and possibly original, recalling Ezekiel 28:13, where the guardian cherub is covered with stone, or the high priest's breastplate; Metzger, as Beale reports, thinks stone a copying slip. The word pure is used of the gold on the high priest's ephod in Exodus 28. Keener notes that Jewish texts dressed both angels and priests in white linen. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible compares the priestly sash of Exodus 39:8, and the ESV Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cite Daniel 10:5, the latter adding Leviticus 16:4. The grade is drawn here: the picture is traceable to Daniel 10 through Revelation 1.
entries.heiser: Heiser says the angels' clothing is drawn from Levitical priestly garments, and lists Ezekiel 9:2-3, 9:11, 10:2, Daniel 10:5 and 12:6-7. He recalls his earlier suggestion that the 144,000, described in priestly terms, may be a priestly class set against the Watchers, and says some of that could be in play here too. He offers that second point loosely.
entries.dissent: The sources split over the text. The SBL Greek text and most translations read linen, and Metzger, as Beale reports, calls stone a copying error that makes no sense. Beale argues stone is the harder and perhaps original reading, linked to Ezekiel 28:13. Either way the sources agree the angels are dressed as priests.

entries.title: Revelation 15:7, seven golden bowls full of God's wrath
entries.summary: The bowls of God's anger draw on Isaiah's cup of wrath, which God takes from Jerusalem and hands to her oppressors, and on the gold bowls of the temple.
entries.plain: **A waiter who brings the bill on the same tray as the dessert links the two in your mind.** In Isaiah, Jerusalem has drunk the bowl of God's anger to the bottom. Then God takes it from her hand and gives it to those who tormented her. John's seven angels receive gold bowls full of God's anger. The bowls also look like the gold vessels of the temple, so worship and judgment meet in one picture.
entries.same: A vessel filled with God's anger (thymos). The Greek of Isaiah 51:17 and 51:22 speaks of the cup of God's rage (to poterion tou thymou). Revelation 15:7 speaks of bowls full of the rage of God (phialas ... tou thymou tou theou), and 16:19 calls it a cup.
entries.differs: Isaiah's Greek has cup (poterion) and drinking cup (kondy). John has bowl (phiale), the word for the shallow bowls of temple service. Beale notes that Isaiah's Hebrew word for bowl is a borrowed Assyrian word found only there, and that the Aramaic paraphrase of Isaiah renders it with a loanword from the Greek phiale. In Isaiah the bowl passes from Jerusalem to her enemies; John hands it to angels to pour out.
entries.turn: The bowls echo the gold bowls of incense in 5:8, which held the saints' prayers. Beale reads the bowls of anger as God's answer to those prayers for justice (6:9-11). Isaiah's twist, where the cup moves from the victims to their oppressors, fits bowls aimed at Babylon.
entries.not: **Not kitchen bowls.** Aune, as Heiser reports, renders the word as bowls used in offerings, and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible agrees. They are temple vessels.
entries.deeper: Beale says the image of bowls comes partly from the Old Testament, where bowls appear about thirty times in the priestly service at the altar, probably to carry out the ashes and fat of sacrifices. Some are tied to the tent of witness (Numbers 4:14-15; 7:13-89) and some are called gold bowls (1 Chronicles 28:17; 2 Chronicles 4:8, 22). The image also derives in part, he says, from Isaiah 51:17, 22, where the bowl of the cup of God's wrath, once poured on sinful Israel, is now poured on her tormentors, Babylon. He adds that bowl and cup can be synonyms (Proverbs 23:31 in the Greek). Keener thinks of the incense bowls of the temple and of the cup of wrath at 14:9-10. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible calls them bowls used in offerings, and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible links them to the bowls of prayers in 5:8. The grade is drawn here: the picture of a vessel of wrath moving to the oppressor is traceable to Isaiah 51.
entries.heiser: Heiser follows Aune. The word is better rendered as bowls used in offerings. It appears twelve times in Revelation, mostly in scenes set in the heavenly tent. In the Old Testament such bowls likely carried ashes and fat out of the holy place. So, he says, the earth is about to be cleaned and made ready. The Messiah will live there, and it will be holy ground again.
entries.dissent: Keener derives the bowls mainly from the temple's incense bowls. Beale joins the temple bowls to Isaiah's cup of wrath. Heiser, after Aune, stresses offering bowls and reads them as cleansing the earth. The views overlap more than they clash.

entries.title: Revelation 15:8, the temple filled with smoke from God's glory
entries.summary: Smoke fills the heavenly temple and no one can enter, as when God's glory filled Moses' tent, Isaiah's temple and Ezekiel's temple before judgment.
entries.plain: **At a stadium, a cloud of fireworks smoke at kickoff tells everyone the main event has begun.** When Moses finished the desert tent, God's glory filled it and Moses could not go in. Isaiah saw the temple fill with smoke when he was called. Ezekiel saw a cloud fill the temple before judgment fell on Jerusalem. John sees the heavenly temple fill with smoke from God's glory, and no one can enter until the plagues are over.
entries.same: A sanctuary filled with God's presence, and no one able to enter. Exodus 40:35 in the Greek: Moses was not able to go in (ouk edynethe ... eiselthein), for the glory filled the tent. Revelation 15:8: no one was able to go in (oudeis edynato eiselthein). Isaiah 6:4 has the house filled with smoke (kapnou), the same word John uses.
entries.differs: Exodus speaks of cloud and glory, not smoke; Isaiah supplies the smoke. Beale notes that Isaiah 6:1, 4 are the only Old Testament verses where smoke fills the temple. Exodus and 1 Kings describe the dedication of a sanctuary, while Ezekiel 10 and Isaiah 6 lead into words of judgment, closer to John's scene. John adds a time limit: until the seven plagues are finished.
entries.turn: God himself stands behind the plagues; the angels only carry them out. Beale reads the closed temple as a sign that no one can hold back God's hand once he judges. The saints' plea for justice need not be made again, because it is being answered.
entries.not: **Not one Old Testament scene.** Exodus 40, Isaiah 6 and Ezekiel 10 each supply a part: the glory filling the house, the smoke, and the setting just before judgment.
entries.deeper: Beale lists the parallels: Exodus 40:34-35, 1 Kings 8:10-11, 2 Chronicles 5:13 and Isaiah 6:1, 4 in the Greek. He calls the description a collective echo of these scenes, though the focus may be Ezekiel 10:2-4, where a being clothed in linen stands near the cherubim and the temple fills with the cloud. That scene introduces judgment, which brings it closer to Revelation 15, and he thinks John joins it to Isaiah 6. The priests who cannot stand in the glory in Exodus, Kings and Chronicles fit the priestly angels here. He also says 15:8-16:21 is modeled in part on Ezekiel 9:1-10:6, where seven angelic figures punish all who lack God's mark. Keener recalls the dedications of the tent and temple and cites Ezekiel 10:3-4 for the glory's departure. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the ESV Study Bible, the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible and the CSB Study Bible cite Exodus 40:34-35 and the temple texts, and Wright names the tent, Isaiah 6 and Solomon's dedication. The grade is drawn here: several scenes stand behind it, none supplies all of it.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Beale and McDonough on the smoke and their list of parallels. He stresses their focus on Ezekiel 10, where an angel in linen stands by the cherubim before judgment is announced. He ties this to the priests' clothing and the offering bowls. The scene is a cleansing, he says, but of the earth, not the temple in heaven. The earth is being made ready to be holy ground again.
entries.dissent: The sources share the texts but differ on the tone. Keener reads Ezekiel 10:3-4 as the glory withdrawing from the temple. The ESV Study Bible compares the consecration of the tent and the temple. Beale holds that Ezekiel 10 joined to Isaiah 6 is the closest model, because both lead into judgment.

entries.title: Revelation 16:1, a loud voice from the temple
entries.summary: The voice from the temple that starts and ends the bowls recalls Isaiah 66:6, the voice of the Lord from the temple repaying his enemies.
entries.plain: **A whistle from the referee's booth tells everyone the call comes from the top.** Isaiah hears a voice from the temple, and it belongs to the Lord, who is repaying his enemies. John hears a great voice ring out of the temple, telling the seven angels to go and pour out their bowls. When the seventh bowl falls, a voice from the temple and the throne says, It is done. The bowls start and end with God's own word.
entries.same: A voice that comes out of the temple and announces judgment. The Greek of Isaiah 66:6 has a voice from the temple (phone ek naou), the voice of the Lord repaying his adversaries. Revelation 16:1 has a great voice from the temple (megales phones ek tou naou). In 16:17 the great voice comes from the temple and the throne.
entries.differs: Isaiah hears three sounds: from the city, from the temple, from the Lord. John hears one loud voice and does not name the speaker. Beale thinks it is God's, since it comes from the temple God has just filled (15:8). In Isaiah the voice repays enemies directly; in John it sends angels with bowls. Many copies change from the temple to from heaven, Beale notes.
entries.turn: The judgments are God's decision, not the angels' and not Satan's. Beale says the Isaiah background points to God as the speaker. The same voice that starts the bowls ends them at 16:17, so the whole series is framed by God's command.
entries.not: **Not Isaiah's three sounds.** Isaiah hears three: the city, the temple and the Lord himself. John hears one great voice and does not name who speaks.
entries.deeper: Beale says God as speaker is suggested by the allusion to Isaiah 66:6, where the Lord's voice sounds from the temple as he repays his enemies, which the Midrash on Psalms (18.11) applies to the judgment of Rome. The command to pour out God's wrath uses a stock Greek Old Testament phrase for judgment (Ezekiel 14:19; Jeremiah 10:25; Zephaniah 3:8), and Beale sets Jeremiah 10:25, pour out your rage on the nations, beside 16:1. He thinks Psalm 79:6, 12 may also have shaped the verse, since 16:6 alludes to the same psalm. Keener says the Old Testament commonly speaks of pouring out wrath, especially in Jeremiah and Ezekiel. Beale also hears the priest pouring out blood at the altar in Leviticus 4: as that cleansed the tent, the bowls cleanse the earth. On the text, he notes that scribes changed from the temple to from heaven because the temple seemed odd. The CSB Study Bible's cross-references cite Isaiah 66:6 at 16:17. The grade is drawn here: the wording is close and the setting the same, but the phrase is short.
entries.dissent: Keener treats pour out wrath as common prophetic language with no single source. Beale names Jeremiah 10:25 and Psalm 79:6 for that phrase and Isaiah 66:6 for the voice. Some interpreters, Beale reports, take the speaker as an angel or a cherub; he prefers God or Christ. MacArthur, at 16:17, takes the voice from the temple as God's own.

aw.n: Revelation 16:12-21, the Euphrates dried and Armageddon
aw.s: The sixth bowl dries up the Euphrates to make way for the kings from the east, and three frog-like spirits from the dragon, the beast and the false prophet gather the kings of the world to battle at the place called Armageddon. The seventh bowl brings a voice saying it is done, the greatest earthquake ever, the splitting of the great city and hundred-pound hailstones.

entries.title: Revelation 16:2, painful sores on those with the mark
entries.summary: The first bowl brings Egypt's plague of boils, described in the words Deuteronomy uses, on everyone who took the beast's mark.
entries.plain: **A judge who sentences graffiti vandals to scrub walls makes the punishment match the crime.** In Egypt, Moses threw soot in the air and painful boils broke out on both people and cattle. Moses later warned Israel that unfaithfulness would bring the same evil sores on them. John's first bowl brings evil, painful sores on those who took the beast's mark. Those who chose one mark now receive another.
entries.same: Sores that break out on people as a plague from God. The Greek of Exodus 9:9-10 has sores (helke) on people and animals. Deuteronomy 28:35 in Greek has the Lord striking with an evil sore (helkei ponero). Revelation 16:2 has a bad and evil sore (helkos kakon kai poneron).
entries.differs: Exodus strikes the Egyptians and their animals. John strikes only those who bear the beast's mark and worship its image. The word evil (poneron) comes from Deuteronomy's summary, not from Exodus. John drops the soot and the furnace. Beale reads the sore as a picture of suffering, like the torment of the fifth trumpet, more than a skin disease.
entries.turn: Heiser and Beale both see the irony: the mark of the beast is answered by a mark from God. Egypt's plague now falls on everyone who sides with the beast, wherever they live. The ESV Study Bible notes that this bowl hits people, not the land, unlike the first trumpet.
entries.not: **Not a new kind of plague.** The sore is the one that struck Egypt, now aimed only at those who bear the beast's mark.
entries.deeper: Beale says the bowl's effect rests on the literal plague of boils in Egypt (Exodus 9:9-11), which Deuteronomy 28:27, 35 sums up as an evil sore. The punishment fits the crime: an idolatrous mark is met by a penal one. Jewish retellings stress the torment of the boils: Josephus (Antiquities 2.304) and Philo (Life of Moses 1.127-28) say the Egyptians suffered in soul as much as in body, and Pesikta Rabbati says the plague would come again on Rome. Beale rejects Job 2 as the background, since Job suffered for righteousness. Keener calls the sores the sixth plague of Exodus 9:10. The ESV Study Bible, the CSB Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cite Exodus 9:8-12 and Deuteronomy 28:27, 35. The grade is drawn here: the plague is plainly Egypt's, and John's adjective matches the Greek of Deuteronomy.
entries.heiser: Heiser calls the plague of boils on Egypt the immediate point of reference and stresses an ironic reversal. In Egypt the Egyptians got the boils; now those who take the beast's idolatrous mark are marked with boils by God. He thinks John wants readers to catch it: you took the mark, so God marks you.
entries.dissent: The sources agree on Egypt. Wall, as Beale reports, reads the sore against Job 2:7, and Beale rejects that. The CSB Study Bible's cross-references add Job 2:7 and Isaiah 1:6 beside Exodus and Deuteronomy. MacArthur notes that the Greek Old Testament uses the same word for Egypt's boils and for Job's, and Luke uses it for the sores of Lazarus. He reads the bowl as real open sores on the beast's worshipers all over the world. Beale reads the sore as a picture of suffering more than a skin disease.

aw.s: Those who have overcome the beast stand beside a sea of glass mixed with fire and sing the song of Moses and of the Lamb. entries.title: Revelation 16:3-4, the sea and the rivers turned to blood
entries.summary: The second and third bowls repeat Egypt's first plague, the Nile turned to blood, on all the sea and all the rivers and springs.
entries.plain: **A disaster film that floods a whole city starts from one burst pipe.** In Egypt, Aaron struck the Nile with his staff, its water became blood, and the fish died. John's second bowl turns the whole sea to blood like a corpse's, and every living thing in it dies. The third turns the rivers and springs to blood. What struck one river now strikes all the world's waters.
entries.same: Water turned to blood, and the death of what lives in it. The Greek of Exodus 7:20-21 has the river's water changed into blood (eis haima) and the fish dying. Revelation 16:3 has the sea becoming blood and every living soul in it dying. In 16:4 the rivers and springs become blood.
entries.differs: Exodus strikes the Nile; John strikes the sea, then the rivers and springs. In Exodus the fish die; in 16:3 every living soul (psyche) dies, which Beale takes to include people who live by the sea. John adds blood like a dead man's. The second and third trumpets (8:8-11) used the same plague on a third; the bowls are total.
entries.turn: Beale reads the sea and waters as pictures of the ungodly world and its trade, as in 17:15, where the waters are peoples. So the bowls strike the people who live off Babylon's economy. An angel then explains the third bowl as a fitting punishment for shed blood (16:5-6).
entries.not: **Not a quotation of Exodus.** John takes the plague, not its words. The Nile becomes the whole sea and then the rivers, and the dying fish become every living thing.
entries.deeper: Beale says both the second trumpet and the second bowl are based on Exodus 7:17-21, where Moses turns the Nile to blood and its fish die. Philo (Life of Moses 1.100) widened that plague to the death of people, as Revelation does. The difference between trumpet and bowl is partial against total effect. Beale argues the sea stands for ungodly humanity: the many waters of 17:1 are peoples and nations (17:15), the beast rises from the sea of nations (13:1), and blood in Revelation always stands for the suffering either of the wicked or of Christ and his people. He ties the bowls to Babylon's sea trade in chapter 18. The third bowl, on rivers and springs, rests on the same plague (Exodus 7:17-21; Psalm 78:44). Keener, the ESV Study Bible, the CSB Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible all name the first plague on Egypt, and Wright notes that John again draws on the plagues of Egypt. The grade is drawn here: the plague is unmistakable, only its reach has grown.
entries.heiser: Heiser follows Beale closely. The second and third bowls take readers back to the Nile turned to blood, and he cites Philo's widening of the plague to people. He then argues with Beale that the waters stand for the mass of nations opposed to God, read through his Deuteronomy 32 picture of nations under hostile spiritual powers. The target is the people who took the mark; the water is the picture.
entries.dissent: The sources agree that the bowls repeat the Nile plague. They read the waters differently. Beale and Heiser take the sea as a picture of the ungodly world and its trade, so the blood falls on the people who bear the mark. MacArthur reads the second bowl as the world's oceans turned thick and dark like a dead man's blood, with the sea's creatures dying, and the third as fresh water spoiled the same way, so the beast's worshipers have nothing clean to drink.

entries.title: Revelation 16:6, blood to drink
entries.summary: The angel's verdict, that those who poured out the saints' blood are given blood to drink, joins Psalm 79's lament over Jerusalem with Isaiah's promise against Israel's oppressors.
entries.plain: **An old saying holds that those who live by the sword will die by it.** Psalm 79 grieves that the nations poured out the blood of God's people like water around Jerusalem, and asks God to avenge it. Isaiah promises that Israel's oppressors will drink their own blood like wine. The angel of the waters says the same of the third bowl. The persecutors spilled the blood of God's people and his prophets, so God now hands them blood to drink.
entries.same: Blood poured out, then blood given to drink. The Greek of Psalm 79:3 says they poured out (exechean) their blood like water. Revelation 16:6 says they poured out (exechean) the blood of saints and prophets. Isaiah 49:26 has the oppressors drinking their own blood (pionetai ... to haima).
entries.differs: The psalm asks God to avenge his servants' blood (79:10); John hears an angel declare that God has done it. Isaiah's oppressors drink their own blood like new wine and get drunk; John has God give them blood to drink. John names the victims saints and prophets, the whole church in Beale's reading, and adds a short verdict: they deserve it.
entries.turn: The psalm was prayed after Babylon wrecked Jerusalem. Now the same kind of judgment falls on the new Babylon and its followers. Beale and Heiser call it a reversal: the persecutors receive what they gave. The third bowl answers the martyrs' cry of 6:10.
entries.not: **Not a call for believers to take revenge.** In the psalm and in Revelation God does the avenging. Wright stresses that vengeance belongs to God, not to the Lamb's followers.
entries.deeper: Beale says Isaiah 49:26 probably stands behind the wording, and that the Midrash Rabbah on Leviticus applies it to the judgment of the nations in the time to come. Psalm 79:3, 10, 12 is also echoed: they poured out their blood like water; let the avenging of your servants' blood be known among the nations. Beale reads both kinds of blood as suffering of every kind, death included. He notes the Jewish tradition that God turned Egypt's water to blood because Pharaoh had killed Israel's infants (Wisdom 11:5-7), and that Wisdom uses deserving for the Egyptians' punishment. Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible cite the same tradition. The ESV Study Bible cites Isaiah 49:26. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible lists Deuteronomy 32:43, 2 Kings 9:7, Psalm 79:10, 12 and Isaiah 49:26, and the CSB Study Bible's cross-references give Isaiah 49:26 and 2 Kings 9:7. The grade is drawn here: two texts supply the two halves of the line.
entries.heiser: Heiser calls 16:6 a citation of Psalm 79:3, a psalm from after Babylon's conquest, and reads it as reversal: what Babylon did to God's people now happens to those who bear the beast's mark. He then adds Deuteronomy 32:43, which Beale does not mention: the heavenly ones rejoice, the gods bow, and God avenges his children's blood. He calls that verse a microcosm of the bowls and of the day when the gods are destroyed.
entries.dissent: The sources name different texts. Beale leads with Isaiah 49:26 and Psalm 79. Heiser leads with Psalm 79 and adds Deuteronomy 32:43, which the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible also lists. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible stresses the exodus pattern of blood for blood. Beale allows that the persecutors may also shed one another's blood, as in 17:16.

entries.title: Revelation 16:8-9, scorched by the sun
entries.summary: The fourth bowl turns around the promise of Isaiah 49:10, given to the saints in Revelation 7:16, that sun and heat would not strike God's people.
entries.plain: **A promise of shade on a hot day becomes a warning when the shade is taken away.** Isaiah promised that God's returning people would not be struck by burning heat or sun. A psalm says the sun will not harm those God keeps. Revelation 7:16 gives that promise to the saints. The fourth bowl turns it around: the sun is allowed to scorch those who follow the beast.
entries.same: Sun and burning heat. The Greek of Isaiah 49:10 says neither burning heat (kauson) nor sun will strike them. Revelation 7:16 promises the saints that neither the sun nor any heat (kauma) will fall on them. In 16:8-9 the sun scorches (kaumatisai) people with great heat (kauma mega).
entries.differs: Isaiah and the psalm promise protection; the fourth bowl removes it from the beast's followers. John does not quote either text; the link runs through his own promise in 7:16. Burning heat is not one of Egypt's plagues, as Keener notes. Beale reads the heat as hardship and loss of security, the reverse of the relief from want promised in 7:16.
entries.turn: Those protected in 7:16 are spared; those outside God's care are exposed. Yet the scorched do not repent. They curse God's name, Heiser notes, having taken the beast's name instead. Beale compares their hardening to Pharaoh's.
entries.not: **Not a quotation of Isaiah.** The words reach John through his own promise in 7:16, which he now turns around. Isaiah's verse is not repeated.
entries.deeper: Beale compares 7:16, where the sun and heat no longer strike the redeemed, with 16:8-9, where the same words are turned against the ungodly; 7:16 alludes to Isaiah 49:10, which speaks of an end to hunger and thirst. He adds Deuteronomy 32:24, where the covenant curses include being consumed by burning heat, tied to famine. Since the pouring of each bowl is figurative, he argues, its effect is too; the Greek Old Testament often follows pouring out wrath with fire as a figure of destruction. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible makes the contrast with 7:16 and cites Psalm 121:6 and Isaiah 49:10. Keener notes that heat struck field workers and desert travelers (Psalm 121:6) but was not a plague on Egypt. The grade is possible: two sources tie the bowl to the reversed promise, but John's words come through 7:16, not straight from Isaiah.
entries.heiser: Heiser follows Aune. In 16:1 the bowls are poured on the earth, yet the fourth hits the sun and the seventh the air, because the bowls strike the four elements of ancient thought: earth, water, fire and air. That is a way of saying every follower of the beast is judged. It cannot be literal, he argues: "Believers are under the same sun and they breathe the same air". He also notes the irony that those who took the beast's name curse God's.
entries.dissent: Keener reads the heat as an image of common suffering, not a reversed promise. Beale and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible see the reversal of 7:16 and Isaiah 49:10. Heiser, after Aune, focuses on the four elements rather than on any Old Testament text. MacArthur reads the bowl as real heat from the sun, deadly to people with no fresh water left, and suggests it could melt the polar ice and flood coastal cities. Heiser, after Aune, holds that the bowls cannot be literal, since believers live under the same sun.

entries.title: Revelation 16:10-11, darkness on the beast's kingdom
entries.summary: The fifth bowl brings Egypt's ninth plague, a darkness that could be felt, on the throne and kingdom of the beast.
entries.plain: **A blackout across a whole city puts even the mayor's office in the dark.** In Egypt, Moses stretched out his hand and a darkness came that could be felt, for three days. The fifth bowl is poured on the beast's throne, and his whole realm goes dark. People gnaw their tongues in pain and curse God. The plague that struck Pharaoh's land now strikes the beast's whole realm.
entries.same: Darkness sent on a kingdom as a plague. The Greek of Exodus 10:22 says darkness (skotos) came on all the land of Egypt. Revelation 16:10 says the beast's kingdom was darkened (eskotomene). In both, the ruler of the land is the real target.
entries.differs: Exodus darkens Egypt for three days; John darkens the beast's kingdom with no time given. John adds pain: people gnaw their tongues, then curse the God of heaven for their pains and sores. Exodus says the darkness could be felt (10:21), which Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible connect to the pain. The fourth trumpet (8:12) used the same plague on a third.
entries.turn: Beale reads the throne as the beast's power to rule anywhere, so the bowl strikes his whole system. He reads the darkness as the anguish of people who sense they are cut off from God, an early taste of the outer darkness Jesus warned of. Like Pharaoh, they still do not repent.
entries.not: **Not a quotation of Exodus.** John keeps the plague of darkness, drops the three days, and adds people gnawing their tongues in pain.
entries.deeper: Beale says this woe, like the fourth trumpet, is based on Exodus 10:22, a plague partly aimed at the sun god Ra, of whom Pharaoh was thought an incarnation. He identifies the beast's throne with Satan's throne in 2:13. Wisdom 17 reads Egypt's darkness as a picture of separation from God and of the darkness of hell, and Beale follows that line: the pain stands for the horror of knowing one is cut off from God, a precursor of the outer darkness of Matthew 8:12; 22:13; 25:30. Jewish writings applied the plague of darkness to Rome (Midrash Rabbah on Leviticus 6.6; Pesikta Rabbati 17.8). Beale also cites Isaiah 8:21-22 and Jeremiah 13:16, where darkness and anguish fall on idolaters. Keener calls it the ninth plague. The ESV Study Bible, the CSB Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cite Exodus 10:21-23, the last adding the darkness that marks the Lord's day in Joel 2:1-2 and Amos 5:20. The grade is drawn here: the plague is plainly Egypt's ninth.
entries.heiser: Heiser follows Beale: the throne stands for the beast's rule over his whole realm, so the bowl cripples his power everywhere. He links it to the ninth plague (Exodus 10:21-29), to the fourth trumpet, and to the darkening on the day of the Lord in Aune's list (Isaiah 13:10; Joel 2:10; Amos 8:9). He finds Beale's reading of the pain as spiritual anguish, a foretaste of outer darkness, reasonable.
entries.dissent: The sources differ on the pain. Beale reads it as the anguish of separation from God. The CSB Study Bible suggests cold, the earlier sores, the burns of the fourth bowl, or all three. Aune, as Heiser reports, notes the problem without solving it. MacArthur reads the throne as the Antichrist's own throne or capital, with real darkness spreading from it over his whole kingdom, and the gnawing of tongues as a vain attempt to ease the pain of sores, drought and heat.

aw.s: Those who have overcome the beast stand beside a sea of glass mixed with fire and sing the song of Moses and of the Lamb. Seven angels dressed like priests come out of the heavenly temple with seven golden bowls of God's wrath, and the first five bring sores, seas and rivers turned to blood, scorching sun and darkness on the beast's throne.

entries.title: Revelation 16:12, the Euphrates dried up for the kings from the east
entries.summary: The sixth bowl dries up the Euphrates for kings from the east, as Isaiah and Jeremiah foretold God would dry Babylon's river before Cyrus took the city.
entries.plain: **A bridge that lets an army cross can mean rescue or ruin, depending on who crosses.** God dried the Red Sea so Israel could escape Egypt. Isaiah and Jeremiah foretold that God would dry up Babylon's river, and Cyrus came from the east and took the city. The sixth bowl dries up the Euphrates to clear the road for kings from the east. The way is open for the last battle and for Babylon's fall.
entries.same: The Euphrates dried up, and kings from the east. Isaiah 44:27 in Greek: I will dry up (xerano) your rivers. Jeremiah 51:36: I will dry up her spring. Revelation 16:12: its water was dried up (exeranthe). Isaiah names Cyrus, raised up from the east (41:2, 25) against Babylon.
entries.differs: In the prophets the drying leaves historical Babylon open to Cyrus and frees Israel. John keeps Babylon as the target but widens it: the kings become those of the entire inhabited world (16:14). Unlike the Red Sea crossing, this dry riverbed leads the crossers to their own judgment. Beale reads the river, like Babylon, as a symbol, not the river in modern Iraq.
entries.turn: Beale says the drying pictures Babylon's many followers turning against her, a prelude to her fall (17:16). The kings think they gather to destroy God's people, but God gathers them for judgment. Heiser presses the geography: to John's readers, the east meant Babylon.
entries.not: **Not a quotation.** No prophet says the Euphrates dries up for kings from the east. John joins the dried rivers of Isaiah and Jeremiah to the conqueror Isaiah saw coming from the east.
entries.deeper: Beale says the sixth bowl follows the prophecies of Babylon's judgment and Israel's release, themselves patterned on the drying of the Red Sea (Exodus 14:21-22; Isaiah 11:15; 44:27; 50:2; 51:10). The prophets foretold the drying of the Euphrates (Isaiah 11:15; 44:27; Jeremiah 50:38; 51:36), fulfilled when Cyrus diverted the river and took Babylon (Herodotus 1.190-91). God raised up Cyrus and his princes from the east (Isaiah 41:2, 25; 46:11). Beale holds that John universalizes the pattern: Babylon is the world system, the Euphrates its peoples (17:1, 15), and the kings those of the whole earth. The Aramaic paraphrase of Jeremiah 51:36 already reads the drying as a figure for peoples. The ESV Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cite Isaiah 44:27-28, Jeremiah 50:38 and 51:36, and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible adds Isaiah 11:15-16. The CSB Study Bible suggests the Red Sea crossing. Wright calls it a very different kind of exodus. The grade is drawn here: the wording is general, but the pattern is plainly Babylon's fall.
entries.heiser: Heiser ties the sixth bowl to the sixth trumpet and to Babylon: the Euphrates and the kings of the east point to the land of the Babylonians and the Persians, as anyone in John's day would know. "I got news for you it's not China," he says. The whole series uses Babylon as the chief picture of chaos, the system set against God, not any modern nation.
entries.dissent: Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible read the kings of the east as the Parthians, Rome's feared enemy beyond the Euphrates. Beale and Heiser read them through Babylon and Cyrus, and Beale makes them all the world's kings. Some, Beale reports, see the Nero legend behind them; others take them as good angels, which he rejects. MacArthur reads the river as the real Euphrates, the eastern edge of the land promised to Israel, which God will dry up so that an army from the east can reach the land for Armageddon. He suggests they may come to rebel against the Antichrist or to attack Israel.

aw.n: Revelation 16:12-21, the Euphrates dried and Armageddon
aw.s: The sixth bowl dries up the Euphrates to make way for the kings from the east, and three frog-like spirits from the dragon, the beast and the false prophet gather the kings of the world to battle at the place called Armageddon. The seventh bowl brings a voice saying it is done, the greatest earthquake ever, the splitting of the great city and hundred-pound hailstones.

entries.title: Revelation 16:13-14, unclean spirits like frogs
entries.summary: Egypt's plague of frogs returns as three demonic spirits from the mouths of the unholy three, who deceive the world's kings.
entries.plain: **A cartoon that draws a politician's promises as croaking frogs needs no caption.** In Egypt, the second plague filled the land with frogs, and Pharaoh's magicians copied it with their secret arts. John sees three foul spirits that look like frogs. They come out of the mouths of the dragon, the sea beast and the lying prophet. They do signs and go out to gather the world's kings for war. Egypt's plague has become a plague of lies.
entries.same: Frogs as a plague, and signs that fool kings. The Greek word for frog (batrachos) appears in the Greek Old Testament only in accounts of Egypt's plague (Exodus 8:2-11; Psalms 78:45; 105:30), Beale notes. In Exodus 8:7 Pharaoh's magicians produce frogs; in Revelation 16:13-14 the frogs are spirits doing signs.
entries.differs: In Exodus the frogs come out of the Nile; in Revelation they come out of three mouths. They are no longer animals but unclean spirits, demons. In Exodus the frogs plague the king; here they deceive the kings and lead them to war. Beale calls this one of the clearest cases in Revelation of a literal plague reapplied and spiritualized.
entries.turn: The unholy three speak, and what comes out is lies. Beale says the frogs' loud, empty croaking fits deception. As Pharaoh's magicians copied God's signs, these spirits do counterfeit signs, and the world's rulers believe them.
entries.not: **Not three literal frogs.** The text calls them demonic spirits. The frog is the picture; deception is the point.
entries.deeper: Beale notes that the only uses of frog in the Greek Old Testament are in the Egyptian plague. The frogs seem harmless yet corrupt (Psalm 78:45), and Pharaoh's magicians could reproduce them (Exodus 8:7), a fitting picture of deceptive signs. Frogs were unclean (Leviticus 11:9-12, 41-47), and in Egypt the goddess Heqt was shown as a frog. Jewish writers read the croaking as confusion and empty speech (Philo, On Dreams 2.259-60). Beale also notes that Zechariah 13:2 in the Greek puts false prophets and the unclean spirit in the land when the nations gather, and that 1 Kings 22:22-23 has a lying spirit in the mouths of Ahab's prophets, luring the king to war. The CSB Study Bible's cross-references list 1 Kings 22:20-23. Keener thinks the frogs recall the second plague, which John had no room for earlier. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the ESV Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cite Exodus 8, the last adding the magicians' counterfeit signs, and Wright hears another echo of Egypt. The grade is drawn here: the frog and the plague belong to Exodus alone.
entries.dissent: Keener notes that frogs were negative symbols in Greek writers too. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible says that if the frogs recall Egypt, they are transformed. Beale ties them closely to Exodus 8 and to the magicians. None doubts the exodus link; they differ on how much weight it bears.

entries.title: Revelation 16:14, gathering the kings for the war of the great day
entries.summary: The kings are gathered for war on God's great day, as the prophets foretold God would gather the nations against Jerusalem to judge them.
entries.plain: **A trap works best when the prey thinks it is the hunter.** The prophets foretold a day when God would gather the nations to fight against Jerusalem, only to judge them there. Demonic spirits now go out to the rulers of the entire world and gather them for the war on God's great day. The kings think they are marching to win. God is gathering them to lose.
entries.same: Nations gathered for war on God's day. The Greek of Zechariah 14:2 reads I will gather all the nations against Jerusalem for war (eis polemon). Joel 3:2 has I will gather all the nations, and Zephaniah 3:8 speaks of gathering nations and drawing in kings. Revelation 16:14 has the spirits gathering the kings for the war (eis ton polemon).
entries.differs: In Zechariah God himself gathers the nations; in Revelation demonic spirits do it, though Beale says God stands behind them. John says kings, not nations, and the kings of the whole inhabited world. The article in the war marks it as the well-known war of the end, Beale says. John names no place here; he keeps that for 16:16.
entries.turn: The prophets said God would gather the nations to judge them. John says that gathering is under way. Beale links this war to 19:19 and 20:8: one final battle against Christ and his people, seen three times. The nations are fooled into thinking they will wipe out the saints.
entries.not: **Not a quotation of Zechariah.** The idea of God gathering the nations is the prophets'. John's wording is his own, and in his scene spirits do the gathering.
entries.deeper: Beale says the three references to the war (16:14; 19:19; 20:8) rest on Old Testament prophecy, especially Zechariah 12-14 and possibly Zephaniah 3, where God gathers the nations to Israel for history's final war. He sets out Zechariah 14:2 in Greek, adds 12:3-4 and 14:13-14, and notes Zephaniah 3:8, where God gathers nations and draws in kings to pour out his anger on them. Ezekiel 38-39, Joel 3:2, 9, 12, Micah 4:11-12 and Psalm 2:2 belong to the same picture, and 4 Ezra 13 alludes to Zechariah 14:2. The great day of God means decisive judgment, as in Joel 2:11, 31 and Zephaniah 1:14. Keener cites Joel 3:2, 11 and Zephaniah 3:8 as the prophets' language of judgment. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible adds Micah 4:11-13 and Zechariah 12:3-4; 14:2-3. The CSB Study Bible's cross-references list Ezekiel 38-39, Joel 2:11; 3:2 and Zechariah 14:2, and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible recalls Psalm 2. The grade is drawn here: the idea is the prophets' own and the wording is close to Zechariah.
entries.dissent: The sources pick different lead texts. Beale leads with Zechariah 14:2 and Zephaniah 3:8. Keener leads with Joel 3. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible points to Psalm 2, where the kings gather against the Lord's anointed. They agree on the picture. Beale reads 16:14, 19:19 and 20:8 as one battle seen three times. MacArthur reads a real gathering of the world's armies in the land of Israel for Armageddon, ended when Christ arrives (19:17-20), and keeps the rebellion of 20:7-10, after the thousand years, apart from it.

entries.title: Revelation 16:15, so that he does not walk naked
entries.summary: The warning to keep one's clothes, so that others do not see one's shame, uses the language of Ezekiel's sentence on faithless Jerusalem.
entries.plain: **A coach who tells the team to stay dressed and ready is warning them not to be caught out.** Ezekiel warned faithless Jerusalem that God would gather her lovers against her, strip her and leave her naked for all to see her shame. In the middle of the bowls Jesus breaks in: he comes like a thief. Happy are those who keep watch and keep their clothes on. Otherwise they will be caught naked, and others will see their shame.
entries.same: Nakedness, shame, and others seeing it. The Greek of Ezekiel 16:37 has God gathering her lovers so that they see all her shame. Ezekiel 16:39 leaves her naked (gymnen) and stripped of her garments (himatia). Revelation 16:15 speaks of keeping one's garments (himatia), walking naked (gymnos) and people seeing one's shame.
entries.differs: Ezekiel announces a sentence on Jerusalem for idolatry; John gives believers a warning so that it need not happen to them. The thief picture comes from Jesus' sayings, not from Ezekiel. Beale notes that Ezekiel 16:37 also has God gathering nations against the city, as in 16:14, 16. John's word for shame (aschemosyne) is close to Ezekiel's word for left indecent in 16:39.
entries.turn: Beale reads the garments as faithfulness under pressure: refusing the beast's demands, as in 3:4-5 and 3:18. Those who compromise will be shown up as idolaters, like the harlot stripped bare in 17:16. The warning sits in the middle of the gathering for war. The final attack will test the church.
entries.not: **Not advice about clothing.** The garments stand for faithful lives, and the shame for being exposed as an idolater. The ESV Study Bible links it to Christ's rebukes of Sardis and Laodicea.
entries.deeper: Beale says Ezekiel 16:36-39, cited by Wettstein as a general parallel, is probably alluded to, and lists the links in the Greek: idolatry has made Israel a harlot; her shame is uncovered; God gathers nations against her round about; they see all her shame; her garments are stripped; she is left naked and bare. He thinks the verse also develops 3:3-5 and 3:18 and the Gospel saying about the thief (Matthew 24:43; Luke 12:39-40; 1 Thessalonians 5:2). He weighs and sets aside the custom of burning the clothes of temple guards found asleep (Mishnah Middot 1.2). Keener traces the nakedness to the stripping of captives or of an unfaithful woman (Isaiah 47:3; Ezekiel 16:37; Habakkuk 2:16). The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible cites Ezekiel 16:37, Hosea 2:3 and Isaiah 47:3. The grade is drawn here: Beale says probably, and the key words are shared.
entries.dissent: Beale finds the main background in the letters to Sardis and Laodicea and in Ezekiel 16. Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible also name Isaiah 47:3, where Babylon is stripped, and Keener adds Habakkuk 2:16. Some, Beale reports, read the temple-guard custom behind the verse.

entries.title: Revelation 16:16, the place called in Hebrew Armageddon
entries.summary: Armageddon, mountain of Megiddo, draws on Megiddo's battles and Zechariah 12:11, though Heiser reads it as the mount of assembly, Zion.
entries.plain: **A place name can carry a whole history, so that saying it is enough to call up old battles.** John says the kings gather at a place called in Hebrew Armageddon, mountain of Megiddo. Megiddo was where kings fought Israel in Deborah's day and where good King Josiah fell. Zechariah used the mourning at Megiddo to describe the grief in Jerusalem on the last day. Heiser reads the name another way: the mount of assembly, Zion.
entries.same: The name Megiddo spelled with a final n. The Hebrew of Zechariah 12:11 has megiddon, the only Old Testament spelling with n, as Beale reports from J. Day. Revelation 16:16 has Harmagedon and says the name is Hebrew. Judges 5:19 has kings fighting by the waters of Megiddo.
entries.differs: No mountain of Megiddo appears in the Old Testament; Megiddo sat on a plain. The Greek translation of Zechariah 12:11 does not even have the name; it reads a plain being cut down. That may be why John says in Hebrew. Beale argues, after Day, that the mountain comes from Ezekiel 38-39, where the last enemy falls on the mountains of Israel. John joins the two.
entries.turn: John uses a name full of history. Kings fought near Megiddo in Deborah's day, and Josiah fell there. Zechariah used its mourning for the last day. The kings gathered in 16:14 meet their defeat at this place. Readers differ on what the name marks: a real battlefield, a symbol of the last battle, or Zion, God's mountain.
entries.not: **Not a name spelled out in the Old Testament.** No Old Testament text has the word Armageddon. John marks it as Hebrew and leaves readers to trace it.
entries.deeper: Beale weighs the options. Har-megiddon means mount of Megiddo, though no such mountain is known. Megiddo is where wicked kings fought Israel (Judges 5:19; 2 Kings 23:29; 2 Chronicles 35:20-22); Judges 5 is a likely model, since there God defeats an overwhelming foe. He reports J. Day's case that Zechariah 12:11 is the precise source: it alone puts Megiddo in an end-time setting of God destroying the nations, it alone spells the name with n, and John uses Zechariah elsewhere. Day adds that mountain comes from Ezekiel 38:8 and 39:2, 4, 17. Beale calls the argument probable and keeps the other Megiddo texts in the background. He rejects the reading har moed, mount of assembly (Isaiah 14:13), as too remote in form, though he grants that Kline's case from the context is plausible. Keener and the ESV Study Bible cite Judges 5:19, and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible adds 2 Kings 23:29 and Zechariah 12:11. The Hebrew of Zechariah 12:11 reads bevikat megiddon, in the plain of Megiddon, while the Greek translation lacks the name; that observation is drawn here from the two texts. The grade follows Beale's probable for Day's argument.
entries.heiser: Heiser rejects Megiddo outright. In The Unseen Realm he argues that the g in magedon can stand for the Hebrew letter ayin, so that har magedon is har moed, the mount of assembly of Isaiah 14:13, the mountain of God's council. That mountain is Zion. Zechariah 12:11, he says, places the final battle at Jerusalem and names Megiddo only as a comparison for mourning, on a plain. In the lecture he calls it the place of the divine council, where Babylon's forces march on Jerusalem.
entries.dissent: The sources disagree sharply. Beale, after Day, takes the name from Zechariah 12:11 and Megiddo's battles, read as symbols. Heiser, and Kline as Beale reports, read har moed, the mount of assembly, Zion; Beale calls that derivation too remote in form. Keener thinks a site near the valley of Megiddo the most common view. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible mentions a pun on the Greek word for chariot as less likely. MacArthur reads Armageddon as Mount Megiddo, about 60 miles north of Jerusalem, with the battle fought on the plains nearby, where Barak and Gideon won, and spreading the length of the land (14:20).

entries.title: Revelation 16:18, an earthquake such as never was
entries.summary: The seventh bowl's storm and quake join the thunder and lightning of Sinai with Daniel's time of trouble such as never was.
entries.plain: **A newspaper that calls a storm the worst since records began is using a formula people trust.** At Mount Sinai there were thunders, lightnings and a trembling mountain when God came down. Daniel foretold a time of trouble like none since nations began. The seventh bowl brings lightning, rumbling, thunder and an earthquake like none since people have lived on the earth. Sinai's storm and Daniel's last trouble meet.
entries.same: Lightning, voices, thunder and quaking, and the formula never before. Exodus 19:16 in Greek has voices (phonai) and lightnings (astrapai). Daniel 12:1 in Greek has a time of affliction such as has not happened (oia ou gegonen) since there was a nation on the earth (epi tes ges). Revelation 16:18 has such as did not happen (hoios ouk egeneto) since people were on the earth (epi tes ges).
entries.differs: Exodus has thunder and lightning, and the quake is in the mountain. Daniel's formula describes distress; John applies it to an earthquake. Beale notes that Daniel's formula itself comes from Exodus 9:18, 24, the plague of hail, which John uses three verses later. John swaps nation for humankind, widening it to all people.
entries.turn: Sinai was where God came down; the bowls end with God appearing to judge. Beale says the link to Daniel 12 makes clear this is the last judgment, when God's people are delivered and the wicked are raised to shame. Babylon falls, and with it the cities of every nation.
entries.not: **Not a quotation of Daniel.** John borrows Daniel's formula, such as never was, and applies it to an earthquake in place of a time of distress.
entries.deeper: Beale says lightnings, sounds, thunders and a great earthquake are based in large part on the Sinai scene of Exodus 19:16-18, which the Old Testament and Jewish writings reuse for the last judgment, as Revelation does at 4:5, 8:5 and 11:19. He calls it beyond chance that the wording such as had not been since humanity came to be on the earth comes from Daniel 12:1, the end-time distress after which God's people are delivered. Daniel's formula is itself a typological use of Exodus 9:18, 24 (compare Exodus 10:6, 14; 11:6), and it appears again in Matthew 24:21, Mark 13:19 and the War Scroll (1QM 1.11-12). Keener says the language suggests God's appearing at Sinai (Exodus 19:16). The CSB Study Bible's cross-references give Exodus 19:16-19. The Greek of Daniel 12:1 in the vault's interlinear (the version called Theodotion) reads oia ou gegonen aph' hou gegenetai ethnos epi tes ges, close to John's wording. The grade is drawn here: the Sinai picture is general, the Daniel formula close.
entries.dissent: Beale finds both Sinai and Daniel 12:1 here. Keener names only Sinai. Bauckham, as Beale reports, explains why hail closes the series: it was joined to the Sinai scene in the exodus story, and Joshua 10:11 and Ezekiel 38:19-22 may also have shaped it. Beale reads the storm and quake as the stock picture of God coming to judge, as at 4:5, 8:5 and 11:19. MacArthur reads a real earthquake, the strongest in the earth's history, that ends God's wrath just before Christ returns.

The seventh bowl brings a voice saying it is done, the greatest earthquake ever, the splitting of the great city and hundred-pound hailstones.

entries.title: Revelation 16:20, every island fled and the mountains were gone
entries.summary: The quake that topples cities and removes mountains may draw on Ezekiel's great earthquake when God judges Gog.
entries.plain: **When a map is redrawn after a war, old borders vanish as if they never were.** Ezekiel foretold a great quake in the land of Israel when Gog attacks: mountains thrown down, walls fallen. The seventh bowl's quake splits the great city and brings down the cities of the nations. Then the islands flee and the mountains are no longer found. Ezekiel's last battle ends in a shaking that undoes the land itself.
entries.same: A great earthquake (seismos megas), mountains overturned, and judgment on the last enemy. Ezekiel 38:19-20 in Greek has a great quake on the land of Israel, mountains torn and every wall falling. Revelation 16:18-20 has a great quake, the cities of the nations falling, and the mountains not found.
entries.differs: Ezekiel's quake shakes the land of Israel and all its creatures; John's is worldwide, splitting the great city and toppling the cities of the nations. Ezekiel says the mountains will be torn; John says they cannot be found. The fleeing islands come from John's own picture in 6:14, Beale notes, not from Ezekiel.
entries.turn: Ezekiel's chapters on Gog stand behind the battles of 19:17-21 and 20:8. Here they shape the end of the bowls: the world itself gives way before God. Beale reads the vanishing islands and mountains as the end of the present world.
entries.not: **Not a quotation of Ezekiel.** The quake and the thrown-down mountains are Ezekiel's picture. The fleeing islands and the wording are John's own.
entries.deeper: Beale says God's end-time defeat of Israel's enemy in Ezekiel 38:19-22 may also be in mind in 16:18-21: a great earthquake, mountains thrown down, every wall fallen, and hailstones rained on the enemy. Jewish writings cite Ezekiel 38:19-22 together with the hail of Egypt as a type of the last judgment (Midrash Rabbah on Exodus 12.2; Pesikta de Rab Kahana 7.11, applied to Rome), and the Sibylline Oracles apply it to the breakup of the world. He compares 6:14 and 20:11 for the fleeing islands and mountains, and notes the expectation of an earthquake at God's final coming (Haggai 2:6; Zechariah 14:4). The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible cites Ezekiel 38:19-20 and Zechariah 14:4-5 at 16:20. The CSB Study Bible's cross-references give Ezekiel 38:20 at 16:20 and Ezekiel 38:22 at 16:21. The grade is possible: the picture is shared, the wording only general.
entries.dissent: Beale reads the fleeing islands and lost mountains as the end of the present world, one picture of the last judgment with the quake and the hail. MacArthur reads a real earthquake that reshapes the surface of the whole earth, preparing it for Christ's thousand-year kingdom.

aw.s: The sixth bowl dries up the Euphrates to make way for the kings from the east, and three frog-like spirits from the dragon, the beast and the false prophet gather the kings of the world to battle at the place called Armageddon. entries.title: Revelation 16:21, huge hailstones from heaven
entries.summary: The seventh bowl ends with Egypt's plague of hail, described as very great, now falling on people across the world.
entries.plain: **A storm that breaks a hundred-year record is measured against the last great one.** In Egypt God sent hail so heavy that nothing like it had fallen since the nation began. The seventh bowl ends with huge hail, each stone about a talent in weight, falling on people. They curse God because the plague is so terrible. Egypt's seventh plague returns, far heavier.
entries.same: Hail from the sky as a plague, described twice as very great. The Greek of Exodus 9:18, 24 has very great hail (chalazan pollen sphodra). Revelation 16:21 has great hail and says its plague is very great (megale ... sphodra). Both call it a plague (plege).
entries.differs: Exodus's hail falls on Egypt's fields, people and animals; John's falls on people across the world. John gives the weight of each stone, about a talent, between about 45 and 130 pounds by ancient measures, Beale says. In Exodus Pharaoh briefly admits his sin (9:27); John's people only curse God.
entries.turn: Beale asks why hail, not the death of the firstborn, comes last. Following Bauckham, he says the hail is joined to the Sinai storm of 16:18, because God's appearing at Sinai followed the plagues. Joshua 10:11 and Ezekiel 38:22 add hail on God's enemies in battle. So the series ends with God appearing in judgment.
entries.not: **Not Egypt's last plague.** Egypt's plagues end with the death of the firstborn. John closes the bowls with the hail, joined to the Sinai storm of 16:18.
entries.deeper: Beale says the exodus plague of hail is replicated but now strikes all who oppose God (Exodus 9:19-35). Both texts stress the size twice: very great hail and the hail was very great (Exodus 9:18, 24), great hail and the plague is very great. Jewish tradition said Egypt's hail fell in bowls and cups, and the Midrash Rabbah on Numbers even calls them phials, John's word for bowl. Following Bauckham, he explains why hail comes last: it is combined with the Sinai storm of Exodus 19, which follows the plagues, and with the hail on the Amorites in Joshua 10:11 and on Gog in Ezekiel 38:19-22. Keener says this hail is far more severe than in Exodus 9:24, and that people's refusal to repent shows they deserved it (compare Exodus 7:22). The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible cites Exodus 9:19, and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cites Exodus 9:22-25 and Joshua 10:11. Heiser also traces the hail to the plagues on Egypt. The grade is drawn here: the doubled very great matches Exodus.
entries.heiser: Heiser keeps the sixth and seventh bowls distinct, because the hail is a separate element that takes readers back to the plagues on Egypt. He knows some commentators fold the seventh bowl into a summary of the whole series and does not follow them.
entries.dissent: The sources read the hail differently. Beale reads the plagues as figures, and with Bauckham explains the hail's place by the Sinai storm. Keener says hail of that weight would crush everything, a judgment far heavier than Egypt's that belongs to the end of the age. MacArthur reads real hailstones of about a hundred pounds, from storms like none before, causing ruin and death.

entries.title: Revelation 17:1, the great prostitute who sits on many waters
entries.summary: The prostitute seated on many waters takes Jeremiah's words about historical Babylon, the city that dwelt by many waters.
entries.plain: **A nickname that once described a real harbor town can stick to a city long after the docks are gone.** Jeremiah spoke to Babylon as the city that lives by many waters, rich in treasure, whose end has come. Babylon really did sit on the Euphrates and its canals. John's angel shows him the great prostitute seated on many waters. Later the angel explains: the waters are peoples and nations.
entries.same: Sitting or dwelling on many waters. The Greek of Jeremiah 51:13 (51:13 in English Bibles, 28:13 in the Greek order) addresses those who dwell on many waters (eph' hydasi pollois). Revelation 17:1 has the prostitute seated on many waters (epi hydaton pollon).
entries.differs: Jeremiah addresses a real city with rivers and canals that made it rich and safe. John speaks of a woman, a prostitute, and 17:15 turns the waters into peoples, crowds, nations and languages. Jeremiah's verb is dwell; John's is sit, which Beale reads as ruling, as in 18:7, where she says she sits as a queen.
entries.turn: John names the enemy with Babylon's own address. Beale notes that the waters were Babylon's wealth and defense, as the peoples are now the basis of her trade and security. Readers differ on who she is: Rome and the system behind it, or a city and a religious system still to come.
entries.not: **Not Jeremiah's city by its river.** Jeremiah spoke to the real Babylon on the Euphrates and its canals. John gives that address to a woman, and the angel turns the waters into peoples (17:15).
entries.deeper: Beale traces this picture of Babylon's coming judgment to Jeremiah 51:13, where Jeremiah foretells the complete judgment of historical Babylon, those dwelling on many waters (28:11-13 in the Greek). In 17:15 he notes that the waters were the Euphrates and the canals around the city, which brought wealth and protection, and that Jeremiah 51:13 and the Aramaic paraphrase tie the waters to Babylon's treasures. Babylon sits because she rules, as in 18:7. Keener notes that ancient art pictured cities as goddesses enthroned by a river, and that Rome's empire spread around the Mediterranean (compare Psalm 65:7; Isaiah 17:12-13). The ESV Study Bible reads the many waters as the peoples Babylon rules. The CSB Study Bible's cross-references cite Jeremiah 51:13. The grade is drawn here: the phrase is Jeremiah's and the city is the same.
entries.heiser: Heiser lists this as one of the features that rule out Jerusalem. Following Beale and McDonough, he says the many waters come from Jeremiah 51, 28 in the Greek order, where the prophet foretells the utter judgment of historical Babylon dwelling on many waters. The description belongs to Babylon, and through Babylon to Rome, not to Jerusalem.
entries.dissent: Beale and Keener read the woman on many waters as Rome, whose empire ringed the sea, and Beale reads her as the world system Rome stood for. Heiser reads Babylon through Rome and rules out Jerusalem. MacArthur reads the prostitute as the final world system of false religion, seated as a ruler over the nations, which the waters stand for. He calls this Babylon distinct from the historical city, and makes Babylon the capital of the Antichrist's coming empire (17:18).

aw.s: An angel carries John into a wilderness to see the great prostitute who sits on many waters, riding a scarlet beast full of blasphemous names. entries.title: Revelation 17:2, the kings of the earth committed immorality with her
entries.summary: The kings' immorality with Babylon borrows Isaiah's picture of Tyre, the trading city that sold herself to every kingdom on earth.
entries.plain: **Calling a business deal a love affair says something about who is seducing whom.** Isaiah said that Tyre, the great trading port, would return to her trade and play the harlot with every kingdom on earth. Nahum called Nineveh a harlot who sold nations. John says the world's kings slept with Babylon. Beale reads the sin as trade and idol worship bound together, for the sake of wealth.
entries.same: A city that sells itself to all the kingdoms of the earth. The Hebrew of Isaiah 23:17 says Tyre will play the harlot (zanetah) with all the kingdoms of the earth. Revelation 17:2 and 18:3 say the kings of the earth committed fornication (eporneusan) with Babylon. Nahum 3:4 in Greek calls Nineveh a harlot (porne) who sells nations.
entries.differs: Isaiah speaks of Tyre, a port, not Babylon. John moves the picture to Babylon, and makes the kings the ones who commit the act. The Greek translation of Isaiah 23:17 drops the harlot and says Tyre will be a market for all the kingdoms. Beale notes that John's next words, the merchants grew rich (18:3), fit that Greek reading. John keeps both senses.
entries.turn: Beale says the sin is about trade and religion at once. To deal with Babylon meant to honor her gods. Heiser stresses that the prostitute is the one who seduces. He reads her as an empire that draws nations into idol worship, as Nineveh and Tyre did, and that was Rome in John's day.
entries.not: **Not about sex.** Beale and Heiser read the word as the Old Testament's picture of idol worship and crooked trade.
entries.deeper: Beale says the economic sense of fornication is confirmed by an allusion to Isaiah 23:17b, where Tyre plays the harlot with all the kingdoms of the earth. Among the harlot pictures of the Old Testament, most of which describe Israel, this one is closest in wording to Revelation. The Greek translation renders it as Tyre being a market (emporion), which fits the merchants of 18:3. He adds Isaiah 23:15-18 and Nahum 3:4: Tyre and Nineveh are harlots because they dominate nations by trade and lead them into idolatry, and Tyre's wages will one day be set apart to the Lord (23:18). Revelation 18 draws repeatedly on Ezekiel 26-28 about Tyre and alludes to Isaiah 23:8 in 18:23. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible names Nineveh (Nahum 3:4) and Tyre (Isaiah 23:17) as the two prostitutes of the Old Testament who are not Israel. The CSB Study Bible's cross-references list Isaiah 23:16-17 and Nahum 3:4. The Hebrew of Isaiah 23:17 reads vezanetah et kol mamlekhot haarets, she will play the harlot with all the kingdoms of the earth. The grade is drawn here: Beale says allusion, and the wording is close to the Hebrew.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Keener's application commentary on Revelation: in two Old Testament cases the prostitute is a world empire, not Israel. Nineveh seduces nations with harlotry and witchcraft (Nahum 3:4), and Tyre plays the harlot with all the kingdoms (Isaiah 23:17). He adds Ezekiel 28, where Tyre's gems and wealth draw nations under its sway. Beale and McDonough, he notes, say the harlot idea is an illicit relationship, religious, economic or political.
entries.dissent: Keener lists the Old Testament uses of harlot for God's people and then for mercantile or military centers like Tyre and Nineveh, citing a passage on Tyre in Isaiah. Beale gives Isaiah 23 the closest wording. Some commentators, Beale reports, limit the harlot to the apostate church or to apostate Israel; Beale includes the pagan world and those who cooperate with it. MacArthur reads the immorality as idolatry and the harlot as a false religious system that wins over the world's rulers and its peoples, and keeps the commercial side for chapter 18.

entries.title: Revelation 17:3, carried away in the Spirit
entries.summary: The angel carries John away in the Spirit, in the words that describe Ezekiel being lifted and carried by the Spirit to see visions.
entries.plain: **A new reporter who uses the paper's old byline is claiming the same beat.** Ezekiel says the Spirit lifted him and carried him off to see visions of God, often visions of judgment. John says the angel took him, in the Spirit, to a desert place. He tells his call in Ezekiel's words, and what he sees next is judgment on Babylon.
entries.same: A prophet carried off by the Spirit to see a vision. The Greek of Ezekiel 11:24 says the Spirit took him up and led him, in a vision, by God's Spirit (en pneumati theou). Revelation 17:3 says he carried me away in the Spirit (en pneumati). Ezekiel 3:12 has the Spirit taking him up.
entries.differs: In Ezekiel the Spirit itself lifts the prophet; in Revelation the angel carries John, and the Spirit is the sphere. Ezekiel is taken to the exiles or to Jerusalem's temple; John is taken to a wilderness. The same formula returns in 21:10, where John is carried to a high mountain to see the bride, the opposite of this scene.
entries.turn: Beale reads the words as a claim to speak for God, like the times Ezekiel was sent to warn of judgment. As with Ezekiel, John's message here is judgment. The ESV Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible note that it opens a new vision.
entries.not: **Not a physical trip.** John is taken in a vision, as Ezekiel was.
entries.deeper: Beale says the angel carried John in and by the Spirit to another dimension to view the vision, a formula of prophetic commission based on Ezekiel's repeated commissions (Ezekiel 2:2; 3:12, 14, 24; 11:1; 43:5). In each, except 43:5, Ezekiel is sent with authority to announce judgment on Israel, and John's message here is likewise judgment. He links 1:10, 4:2 and especially 21:10, which uses Ezekiel in the same way. Keener cites Ezekiel 8:3 and 11:1, 24 for being carried away in visions by the Spirit. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible cites Ezekiel 8:3; 11:1, 24, the ESV Study Bible Ezekiel 3:12 and 11:24, and the CSB Study Bible's cross-references list Ezekiel 8:3 and 11:24. The grade is drawn here: the formula is Ezekiel's, the wording close.
