entries.title: Revelation 17:3, into a wilderness
entries.summary: John sees Babylon in a wilderness though she sits on many waters, because Isaiah 21 joins wilderness and sea in an oracle on Babylon's fall.
entries.plain: **A riddle that seems to contradict itself often hides a clue.** The woman sits on many waters, yet John is taken to a wilderness to see her. Isaiah 21 opens with an oracle about the wilderness of the sea and goes on to cry that Babylon has fallen. By putting desert and water together, John points to that oracle. The scene is about Babylon.
entries.same: A wilderness (eremos) tied to a vision of Babylon's fall. The Greek of Isaiah 21:1 heads the oracle the vision of the wilderness (eremou). Revelation 17:3 has into a wilderness (eis eremon). Isaiah 21:9 has fallen, fallen is Babylon, which Revelation repeats in 14:8 and 18:2.
entries.differs: In Isaiah the vision comes out of the desert. John, by contrast, is brought into the desert to see his. The Hebrew of Isaiah 21:1 reads midbar yam, wilderness of the sea, joining desert and water; the Greek in the vault has only wilderness. John's waters come from Jeremiah 51:13 (17:1). He sets the two images side by side without explaining them.
entries.turn: Beale says Isaiah 21:1 alone joins desert and sea and ties them to Babylon, and Revelation 17 does the same. The desert is a place of evil spirits and judgment. Babylon herself will become a desolate haunt (18:2). Heiser reads both pictures as anti-Eden: the desert where you die and the sea where no one can live.
entries.not: **Not a geography mistake.** Beale calls it symbolic geography, and Heiser and Keener also read the clash of water and desert as deliberate.
entries.deeper: Beale says being taken into the desert alludes to Isaiah 21:1-2, a vision coming from the desert. It is not coincidental, he argues: Isaiah 21:1-10 is a vision of judgment on Babylon, and fallen, fallen is Babylon (21:9) appears in 14:8 and 18:2. Isaiah 21:1 alone joins desert and sea in its heading, in the Hebrew and some Greek copies. Later Jewish writings read the sea and wilderness of Isaiah 21:1 as the place the beastly kingdoms of Daniel 7:3 would rise from (Midrash Rabbah on the Song of Songs 3.4). Beale grants Beckwith's point that a desert is a common place for visions but finds more here. The Hebrew of Isaiah 21:1 reads massa midbar yam; the Greek in the vault reads to horama tes eremou, the vision of the wilderness. Walton notes the Hebrew may mean wilderness by the sea, the marshland of southern Mesopotamia near Babylon. Keener suggests the woman who thought she sat on many waters would end desolate like the desert. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cites Isaiah 21:9. The grade is drawn here: Beale says allusion, and the pairing of desert and sea is Isaiah's.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Beale and McDonough: John takes two items from Isaiah 21, verses 1 and 9, and uses both, because only there are the desert and the fall of Babylon found together. That tells readers the subject is Babylon, not Jerusalem. He adds Isaiah 17:12-13, which Beale does not mention, where many nations roar like many waters. The desert and the sea, he says, are both anti-Eden: places of death, a recipe for chaos.
entries.dissent: Beckwith, as Beale reports, treats the desert as a common setting for visions with no special meaning. Beale reads it as a place of judgment and evil, though also of the saints' protection, as in 12:6. The ESV Study Bible reads it as a place of protection where John can see through Babylon's beauty. Keener links it to the woman's coming desolation. MacArthur says the Spirit carried John to a lonely, desolate wasteland, perhaps so that he could understand the vision better.

entries.title: Revelation 17:4-5, dressed in scarlet, a name on her forehead
entries.summary: The woman's scarlet dress, gold and forehead name draw on Jeremiah's portrait of faithless Judah as a harlot.
entries.plain: **A costume borrowed from a famous play tells the audience which character to watch.** Jeremiah pictured faithless Judah as a harlot with a harlot's forehead, dressed in scarlet and decked with gold to win lovers who would turn on her. John's woman wears purple and scarlet, gold, jewels and pearls, and a name on her forehead. He borrows the costume, though Heiser and Beale stress that this woman seduces others.
entries.same: Scarlet, gold, and a harlot's forehead. The Greek of Jeremiah 4:30 says if you put on scarlet (kokkinon) and adorn yourself with gold. Revelation 17:4 has the woman clothed in scarlet (kokkinon) and gilded with gold. Jeremiah 3:3 speaks of the look of a harlot, a harlot's forehead in the Hebrew; Revelation 17:5 has a name written on her forehead.
entries.differs: Jeremiah speaks of Judah, God's own people gone astray; John speaks of Babylon. John adds purple, precious stones and pearls, the goods of trade listed in 18:12, and a golden cup. Jeremiah's harlot dresses up in vain because her lovers seek her life; John's is powerful and rides the beast. Her forehead bears a written name: Babylon the Great, mother of harlots.
entries.turn: Beale says the costume shows a seducer whose wealth and charm hide her bloodstained character. Behind the royal red lies the red of persecution (17:6). Heiser draws a line: Israel in the prophets is the one seduced; this woman is the one who seduces.
entries.not: **Not Jeremiah's harlot unchanged.** Jeremiah's woman is Judah, dressed up in vain for lovers who want her dead. John borrows the costume for a woman who rules and seduces.
entries.deeper: Beale says the expensive clothing reflects the way harlots try to seduce (Jeremiah 4:30: dressed in scarlet, decked with gold), and that perhaps not by accident Jeremiah's harlot also has a scarlet dress and blood on her skirts (2:34). In his comments on 17:16 he says the whole portrait draws on Jeremiah 2:20-4:30: a harlot (2:20) with a harlot's forehead (3:3), causing others to sin, dressed in scarlet and gold, whose lovers despise her (4:30). He also notes that the Greek Old Testament describes the high priest's clothing with the same five words, gold, purple, scarlet, linen and stones, in deliberate contrast with the bride of chapter 21. Keener cites Jeremiah 4:30 for the scarlet and Jeremiah 3:3 for the harlot's forehead. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible cites Jeremiah 4:30 and 3:3. The CSB Study Bible's cross-references add Ezekiel 28:13. The grade is drawn here: the colors and the forehead together point to Jeremiah 2-4.
entries.heiser: Heiser rejects the view that Babylon is Jerusalem, calling it "an unfortunate anti-semitic trajectory". He reads Beale and McDonough on Jeremiah 2-4, where Judah is a harlot with a harlot's forehead, scarlet dress and gold. But Israel, he argues, is the one seduced, as in Deuteronomy 32:16-17, not the one who seduces nations. A faithless wife is not the same as a prostitute, and this woman is the engine of chaos.
entries.dissent: Ford, as Beale reports, sees the whole portrait drawn from Jeremiah's harlot Judah, and some limit the harlot to apostate Israel or the apostate church. Beale includes those groups only as parts of the world system. Heiser and Keener exclude Jerusalem, since Revelation contrasts the bride, the new Jerusalem, with the prostitute, Babylon. MacArthur reads the woman as Babylon, the world's final system of false religion, grown rich and dressed in fine clothes and jewels to lure the nations.

entries.title: Revelation 17:4, a golden cup in her hand
entries.summary: The woman's golden cup and the wine that makes the nations drunk come from Jeremiah's picture of Babylon as a golden cup in the Lord's hand.
entries.plain: **A trophy cup can be a prize or a poison, depending on what is poured into it.** Jeremiah called Babylon a gold cup held by the Lord, and the whole world got drunk from it. The nations drank, and they lost their minds. John sees the woman holding a golden cup full of the filth of her immorality. The nations have drunk the wine of her passion. The cup that Jeremiah put in God's hand now sits in hers.
entries.same: A golden cup held in a hand, and nations drunk on its wine. The Greek of Jeremiah 51:7 reads a golden cup (poterion chrysoun), Babylon, in the hand of the Lord. It makes all the earth drunk, and the nations drink her wine. Revelation 17:4 has a golden cup (poterion chrysoun) in her hand. In 18:3 the nations drink the wine of her immorality.
entries.differs: In Jeremiah, Babylon is the cup and the Lord holds it. In Revelation the woman holds the cup. Jeremiah's cup carries God's judgment to the nations; John's is full of abominations and impurity, the idolatry she spreads. Beale says the wine still comes ultimately from God's hand, as does her destruction (17:17).
entries.turn: The cup stands for Babylon's promise of prosperity, which numbs people to her evil, Beale says. Jeremiah's next words, Babylon has suddenly fallen (51:8), are echoed in 18:2. The drinkers will soon drink God's cup of wrath instead (16:19; 18:6).
entries.not: **Not a literal drinking party.** Beale reads the wine as the lure of wealth and idolatry. MacArthur reads it as the world swept up into a false religion.
entries.deeper: Beale calls this a partial allusion to Jeremiah 51:7-8, where historical Babylon is a gold cup held in the Lord's hand that makes the whole earth drunk, the nations drink her wine and go mad, and then Babylon suddenly falls. The wine comes from Babylon's hand but ultimately from God's, as does her destruction. He links the cup's contents, abominations, to idolatry, since abomination is a common Greek Old Testament word for idols, and unclean things to the unclean spirits of 16:13. At 18:3 he again cites Jeremiah 51:7 and 25:15 for drinking. Keener cites Jeremiah 51:7 for the nations made drunk on Babylon's wine. The ESV Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cite Jeremiah 51:7 at 17:4, and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible cites it at 18:3. Some copies read the fornication of the earth in 17:4, which Beale thinks is a scribe's attempt to bring the verse closer to Jeremiah. The grade is drawn here: golden cup in the hand is word for word in the Greek.

entries.title: Revelation 17:5, Babylon the Great, a mystery
entries.summary: The name Babylon the Great comes from Nebuchadnezzar's boast in Daniel 4:30, the pride that was judged in one hour.
entries.plain: **A boast that once went before a famous fall can become a nickname for pride itself.** In Daniel 4 King Nebuchadnezzar looks over his city and boasts that he built this great Babylon by his own power. That same hour he is struck down to live like an animal. John reads the woman's name: mystery, Babylon the Great. The title carries the king's pride and his fall.
entries.same: The words Babylon the Great (Babylon he megale). The Greek of Daniel 4:30 has the king's question: is not this Babylon the great (Babylon he megale), which I built? Revelation 17:5 writes the same two words as the woman's name, and 16:19, 18:2 and 18:10 repeat them.
entries.differs: In Daniel the words are the king's boast about his city; in Revelation they are a name written on a woman's forehead. John adds mystery, a word that in the Greek Old Testament carries end-time meaning only in Daniel 2, Beale says. Daniel's Babylon was one city. Beale and the CSB Study Bible read John's Babylon as Rome and, beyond it, the proud world system.
entries.turn: Beale says that as the king was judged for pride, so end-time Babylon is about to be judged. Daniel 4 runs through the chapter: John's amazement (17:6-7), the one hour (17:12; 18:10) and the title Lord of lords (17:14). For Beale the mystery is how the kingdom of evil will fall: by turning on itself (17:16-17).
entries.not: **Not Daniel's Babylon itself.** In Daniel the words name the city the king built. John writes them as a title on a woman's forehead and calls it a mystery.
entries.deeper: Beale says the first part of the name, Babylon the Great, was already seen in 14:8 as an allusion to Daniel 4:30 (4:27 in the Aramaic numbering), where it shows the reach of the king's power and glory and is part of the self-praise for which he is judged. The prefix mystery confirms the Daniel background: it introduces the account of the king's pride in Daniel 4:9 in the Greek version called Theodotion, and it carries end-time meaning only in Daniel 2:18-19, 27-30, 47. John's great amazement in 17:6 also matches Daniel's reaction in Daniel 4:19 in the Greek, which the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible notes too. The CSB Study Bible says the phrase is taken from Nebuchadnezzar's boast in Daniel 4:30, and its cross-references at 18:2 cite Daniel 4:30. The Greek of Daniel 4:30 in the vault reads ouch aute esti Babylon he megale. The grade is drawn here: the two words match, and the setting is Babylon's pride and fall.
entries.heiser: Heiser's first point against reading the woman as Jerusalem is the name itself: she is identified as Babylon the Great, which takes the ambiguity out. For John, he says, the city of Babylon no longer mattered. Babylon is a symbol for Rome and, behind Rome, for the whole system opposed to God.
entries.dissent: The CSB Study Bible allows three readings: a rebuilt end-time city (which Jeremiah 51:26 makes unlikely), a code name for Rome, or any proud society. Beale reads it as the world's economic and religious system across the ages, focused in Rome. Some, as Beale reports, distinguish the Babylon of chapter 17 from that of chapter 18; he rejects this. MacArthur holds that this Babylon is distinct from the historical city, that its true identity is still to be revealed, and that all false religion flows from Babel. He makes Babylon the capital of the Antichrist's empire (16:19; 17:18), and separates religious Babylon in chapter 17 from commercial Babylon in chapter 18.

entries.title: Revelation 17:6, drunk with the blood of the saints
entries.summary: The prophets pictured God's sword and land drunk with his enemies' blood; John turns the image around, so Babylon is drunk on the blood of God's people.
entries.plain: **A slogan from one side of a war can be turned around and thrown back by the other.** Isaiah and Jeremiah pictured God's judgment as a sword or a land drunk with the blood of his enemies. Isaiah also said Israel's oppressors would drink their own blood. John sees the woman drunk on the blood of God's people, the witnesses to Jesus. The image of God's judgment now describes Babylon's crime, which will be judged by the same picture.
entries.same: Drunkenness with blood. The Greek of Isaiah 34:7 says the land will be drunk with blood (methysthesetai ... apo tou haimatos). Jeremiah 46:10 says the sword will be drunk with their blood. Isaiah 49:26 has the oppressors drunk on their own blood. Revelation 17:6 has the woman drunk (methyousan) with the blood of the saints.
entries.differs: In the prophets the one drunk with blood is God's sword, a land under judgment, or oppressors punished. In Revelation it is the oppressor herself, drunk with the blood of the faithful. Beale says the imagery is applied in reverse, so that Babylon will be punished by her own sin. John names the victims as saints and witnesses of Jesus.
entries.turn: The woman's cup of filth (17:4) includes the blood of believers, and she enjoys it. Beale reads the blood as every kind of persecution, including death. Because she drank blood, she will be given blood to drink, as 16:6 already announced.
entries.not: **Not cannibalism.** The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible notes that drinking blood was a picture of violence, and Beale calls it an ancient idiom for oppression.
entries.deeper: Beale says the metaphor of drunkenness with blood is developed from the Greek of Isaiah 34:5-7, 49:26 and Jeremiah 46:10 (26:10 in the Greek order), where it describes God's judgment of the wicked. John applies it in reverse to show that Babylon will be punished by her own sin, as 16:6 reveals. He adds that 1 Enoch 62:12 uses the Isaiah 34 and Jeremiah 46 passages for the judgment of oppressors, and that drinking blood was an idiom for oppression in Josephus and Philo. Ancient writers called Rome drunk with the blood of citizens. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible cites Deuteronomy 32:42, Isaiah 49:26 and Ezekiel 39:19 for the terrifying prophetic picture. The CSB Study Bible's cross-references list Deuteronomy 32:42, Isaiah 49:26, 63:6 and Ezekiel 39:19. The grade is drawn here: the picture is the prophets', the target reversed.
entries.dissent: The sources point to different prophetic texts. Beale names Isaiah 34, Isaiah 49:26 and Jeremiah 46:10. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible and the CSB Study Bible add Deuteronomy 32:42 and Ezekiel 39:19, where God's arrows and the birds of prey are drunk with blood. Keener reads the verse against Rome's bloody arena games. MacArthur reads the victims as the witnesses of the tribulation and the woman as a murderer: false religion has killed believers through the centuries, and its final form will be deadlier still.

entries.title: Revelation 17:8, the beast comes up and goes to destruction
entries.summary: The beast that rises from the abyss and goes to destruction follows Daniel 7, where beasts rise from the sea and the last is destroyed.
entries.plain: **A villain who keeps coming back in a film series still has a final scene written for him.** In Daniel 7 four great beasts come up out of the sea, and the last is killed and its body burned. John is told that the beast he saw was, is not, and is about to come up from the abyss and go to destruction. The words mock God's own name in 1:4, the one who is, who was and who is coming. The beast's comeback ends where Daniel's beast ended.
entries.same: A beast that comes up and is destroyed. The Greek of Daniel 7:3 says four beasts came up (anebainon) from the sea; 7:11 says the beast was destroyed (apoleto). Revelation 17:8 says the beast is about to come up (anabainein) from the abyss and goes to destruction (apoleian).
entries.differs: Daniel's beasts come up from the sea; John's from the abyss, the realm of demons (9:1-2). Daniel sees four beasts in turn; John sees one beast that gathers their features. John adds the pattern was, is not, will come, a mocking copy of God's name in 1:4 and of Christ's death and rising (1:18). Daniel's beast is burned; John's simply goes to destruction, with burning kept for the woman (17:16).
entries.turn: Beale says the threefold pattern mocks the beast: he imitates Christ's death and resurrection, but his comeback ends in ruin, not eternal life. The world marvels at him, but those whose names God has recorded for life are not fooled. His power is real but short.
entries.not: **Not a beast who cannot be stopped.** Every source reads the beast's rise as already doomed. The text says he goes to destruction.
entries.deeper: Beale traces the longer third part, rising and then going to ruin, to Daniel 7, which shows the last beast three times coming up onto the stage of history and then being destroyed (7:3, 11, 17-18, 23, 26). He calls 17:8a a collective allusion to these portrayals and sets the Greek of Daniel 7:11, the beast was destroyed, beside John's goes to destruction. The same Daniel texts lie behind 11:7, where the beast rises from the abyss to make war on the witnesses. Jewish writings applied Daniel 7:11 to Rome's judgment. The threefold formula parodies the divine name of 1:4, 8 and 4:8, as Keener, the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible also note. The ESV Study Bible says the beast's future appearance in unprecedented violence will be short-lived. The vault's Greek of Daniel 7:3 (the version called Theodotion) has anebainon ek tes thalasses; 7:11 has apoleto. The grade is drawn here: Beale names the source, and the shared verbs are close.
entries.dissent: The sources read the beast's was and is not differently. Beale says is not means the lasting effect of his defeat at the cross and resurrection, and the formula shows a beast at work from the start of history to its end. The ESV Study Bible says the beast once received a mortal wound and came back to life, and its future rise will be brief. MacArthur reads the words as the Antichrist's faked death and return to life, after which a demon from the abyss possesses him; the beast is both a king and his kingdom.

aw.n: Revelation 17:7-18, seven hills and seven kings
aw.s: The angel explains the woman and the beast: the beast once was, now is not and will come up from the Abyss; its seven heads are seven hills and also seven kings, five fallen, one living and one still to come, and the beast is an eighth who belongs to the seven. Its ten horns are ten kings who will make war on the Lamb, and in the end the beast and the horns turn on the woman, the great city that rules the kings of the earth, and burn her.

entries.title: Revelation 17:9-10, seven heads are seven mountains and seven kings
entries.summary: The beast's seven heads come from the beasts of Daniel 7, whose heads add up to seven, and are explained as mountains and kings, as Daniel explains beasts as kings.
entries.plain: **A riddle with two answers can point to a city and to a whole history at once.** In Daniel 7 the four beasts have seven heads among them, and the angel explains that the beasts are kings. John's angel explains the seven heads as seven mountains and also seven kings. Rome was famous as the city on seven hills. Mountains in the prophets also stand for kingdoms, as when Jeremiah calls Babylon a destroying mountain.
entries.same: Heads that stand for kings, and a mountain that stands for a kingdom. Daniel 7:6 gives the third beast four heads, making seven among the four beasts, as Beale counts. Daniel 7:17 explains the beasts as kings (in the vault's Greek, kingdoms). Revelation 17:10 says the heads are seven kings. Jeremiah 51:25 calls Babylon a destroying mountain.
entries.differs: Daniel spreads the heads across four beasts; John puts all seven on one beast. Daniel explains beasts as kings; John explains heads as both mountains and kings, a double meaning Daniel does not have. Many readers hear Rome's seven hills, a city Daniel never names. John adds a count: five have fallen, one is, one is still to come.
entries.turn: Beale reads the seven as a number of completeness: the oppressive power of world empires across history, with Rome its form in John's day. Keener and Heiser stress the plain reference to Rome's seven hills. Either way the beast's kingdoms are numbered and their end is near.
entries.not: **Not a list to be matched to emperors with certainty.** Beale, Keener and the ESV Study Bible show that attempts to count the kings give conflicting results.
entries.deeper: Beale says the seven heads are identified first as seven mountains, which can mean Rome's hills, but in Revelation mountain always means mountain and figures strength. Mountains symbolize kingdoms in the Old Testament (Isaiah 2:2; Jeremiah 51:25; Ezekiel 35:3; Daniel 2:35, 45; Zechariah 4:7). The kingdoms are confirmed by Daniel 7:4-7, where the four beasts have seven heads among them, the source of the heads in 13:1, and by Daniel 7:17, 23, where beasts are kings and kingdoms. He allows Rome's seven hills as a secondary reference (Virgil, Cicero, the Sibylline Oracles). Keener says every reader would know the seven hills meant Rome. The ESV Study Bible cites Jeremiah 51:24-25 and Daniel 2:35, 44-45 for mountains as seats of power. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible note the seven hills. The grade is drawn here: the pattern is traceable to Daniel 7, the mountains to the prophets' picture of kingdoms.
entries.heiser: Heiser treats the seven hills as the clincher against reading Babylon as Jerusalem: Jerusalem does not have seven hills, nor did Babylon, but Rome does, as coins and other sources of the period show. He reads the beast itself from Daniel 7: the fourth beast persecutes the faithful, matches the fourth kingdom of Daniel 2, and is Rome, in whose time God's kingdom arrives.
entries.dissent: Keener, Heiser and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible stress the seven hills of Rome. Beale treats the hills as secondary and the seven kings as a figure for oppressive rule throughout history. The CSB Study Bible lists Roman emperors or seven world empires. Keener thinks Nero's expected return is in view; Beale doubts any count of emperors works. MacArthur takes the seven mountains as the seven kingdoms of 17:10 and lists them: Egypt, Assyria, Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, Rome and the Antichrist's empire still to come. He allows that the final false religion includes Rome without being limited to it.

entries.title: Revelation 17:12, the ten horns are ten kings
entries.summary: The angel explains the beast's ten horns as ten kings, just as the angel in Daniel 7:24 explains the fourth beast's ten horns.
entries.plain: **A sequel that answers a question the first film left open ties the two stories together.** Daniel saw a fourth beast with ten horns, and an angel told him that ten kings would rise from that kingdom. John's angel explains the beast's ten horns the same way: they stand for ten kings, still waiting to be given their thrones. Their rule with the beast will be brief. Daniel's riddle gets its next chapter.
entries.same: Ten horns explained as ten kings. Daniel 7:7 gives the fourth beast ten horns, and 7:24 explains them as ten kings to come. Revelation 17:12 explains its ten horns as ten kings (deka basileis), not yet crowned.
entries.differs: Daniel's kings arise from the fourth kingdom; John's have not yet received royal power and rule only for one hour, with the beast. Daniel's little horn rises among them; John's kings hand their power to the beast and make war on the Lamb (17:13-14). Daniel names no city; John ties the kings to Babylon, whom they will finally destroy (17:16).
entries.turn: Beale says John begins to show how Daniel's prophecy will be fulfilled. He reads ten as a figure for great power. These kings serve the beast, yet God puts it into their hearts to do his purpose (17:17).
entries.not: **Not Daniel's vision retold whole.** John takes Daniel's explanation of the horns as kings, then gives his own details: kings not yet crowned, ruling one hour with the beast.
entries.deeper: Beale finds the ten horns in Daniel 7:7-8, 20, 24, just as he found the seven heads in Daniel 7:4-7. Revelation 17:12, like Daniel, reads the horns as kings, and so starts to unfold how Daniel's prophecy will come true. He reads ten as figurative for great power, as the Lamb's seven horns (5:6) also allude to Daniel 7, and the kings as the same as the kings of the earth in 16:14 and 19:19. Walton notes that Daniel 7:24 makes plain that the horns are kings, whether Alexander's successors or Rome's. Keener notes that in Roman times most Jewish readers took Daniel's fourth kingdom to be Rome. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the CSB Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cite Daniel 7:7, 20, 24. The grade is drawn here: John repeats Daniel's explanation word for word.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Beale and McDonough, who find the seven heads in Daniel 7:4-7 and the ten horns in Daniel 7:7-8, 20 and 24. Revelation, like Daniel, explains the horns as kings. He adds that the fourth kingdom is Rome, not Jerusalem: Jerusalem lies within the fourth kingdom, which the kingdom of God destroys.
entries.dissent: Keener suggests Rome's client kings, while noting a proposal of the Parthian satraps. Beale reads the ten kings as all the earth's kings allied with the beast across the ages. The ESV Study Bible notes the dispensational reading that ties the horns to the ten toes of Daniel 2 and to a future alliance. MacArthur reads ten kings who will rule under the Antichrist, his empire divided into ten districts. Since they have not yet received power, he says, no figure in history can be named as one of them.

entries.title: Revelation 17:12, for one hour
entries.summary: The kings rule for one hour, and Babylon falls in one hour, an echo of the one hour in the Greek of Daniel 4, the story of Nebuchadnezzar's fall.
entries.plain: **A phrase from an old story can come back with its whole meaning attached.** In the Greek version of Daniel 4 the phrase one hour appears in the story of Nebuchadnezzar, the proud king of Babylon who was made like a beast. John uses one hour for the reign of the ten kings with the beast. Then the mourners cry three times that Babylon's judgment came in one hour. Babylon's old king and the new Babylon share the same brief clock.
entries.same: The phrase one hour (mia hora). Beale cites the old Greek of Daniel 4:17a, one hour, for the time God made Nebuchadnezzar like a beast. In the other Greek version of Daniel 4:19, Daniel is struck dumb for about one hour (horan mian). Revelation 17:12 has one hour (mian horan); 18:10, 17 and 19 have in one hour (mia hora).
entries.differs: The phrase stands only in the Greek of Daniel 4, not in the Aramaic or in English Bibles. Daniel 4:17a is a line found only in the old Greek. In Daniel the hour belongs to the king's beastlike period or to Daniel's dismay; in John it is the kings' brief reign and Babylon's sudden fall. John repeats it as a refrain.
entries.turn: Beale says God is sovereign even over the ungodly kings who ally with the beast, as he was over Nebuchadnezzar. The one hour also marks Babylon's judgment: her prosperity is stripped away in a moment, like the king's. The repeated cry of the mourners rings with Daniel's story.
entries.not: **Not a sixty-minute timetable.** Beale says the hour was the shortest unit of time ancient people knew and here means a brief time.
entries.deeper: Beale says the kings' reign for one hour echoes Daniel 4:17a in the old Greek (hora mia), the period in which God made Nebuchadnezzar like a beast. One hour is repeated in chapter 18 for the time Babylon the Great was judged (18:10, 17, 19), a combined allusion to the one hour of Daniel 4:17a and to Babylon the Great in Daniel 4:30. He adds that Daniel 4:19 in both Greek versions has one hour for Daniel's amazement at the vision of the king's judgment. In Daniel the king's beastliness is linked with the beasts of Daniel 7, which may be why John joins the two chapters. The vault's interlinear prints only the Greek version called Theodotion, which lacks 4:17a, so that line is cited here from Beale. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible links the kings' one hour to Babylon's ruin in one hour. The CSB Study Bible compares the hour of testing (3:10). The grade is drawn here: the phrase is short, but Beale and Heiser both trace it to Daniel 4.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Beale and McDonough on 17:12. The kings rule for one hour, the time in the Greek of Daniel 4:17 when God made King Nebuchadnezzar like a beast. God rules even the kings who side with the beast against the Messiah. The same one hour returns for Babylon's judgment in 18:10, 17 and 19, which also draws on Daniel 4.
entries.dissent: The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible and the CSB Study Bible read one hour simply as a very short time, with no Daniel background named. The CSB Study Bible ties it to the beast's forty-two months. Beale and Heiser trace it to Daniel 4. MacArthur reads the one hour of 17:12 as a figure for the brief three and a half years of the beast's rule, and the single hour of chapter 18 as a short time of swift judgment.

aw.n: Revelation 18:9-24, kings, merchants and the cargo list
aw.s: The kings, the merchants and the sea captains stand far off and mourn as Babylon burns, because no one buys their cargoes any more, a long list of luxuries that ends with human beings. An angel hurls a great millstone into the sea, and the sounds of music, craftsmen, the mill, the lamp and the wedding fall silent in the city where the blood of prophets and saints was found.

entries.title: Revelation 17:14, they will make war on the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them
entries.summary: Daniel saw the horn make war on the saints and prevail; John turns the words around, so the Lamb conquers those who make war on him.
entries.plain: **A chant from the other team's stands can be turned around after the final whistle.** Daniel watched a horn make war against God's holy ones and prevail over them. John uses the same words, then flips the ending. The kings make war on the Lamb, and the Lamb conquers them. The enemy's victory in Daniel becomes the enemy's defeat.
entries.same: Making war, and one side overcoming. In the Greek of Daniel 7:21 that horn made war with the saints (epoiei polemon meta ton hagion) and beat them. Revelation 17:14 says they will make war with the Lamb (meta tou arniou polemesousin) and the Lamb will conquer them.
entries.differs: In Daniel the horn wins against the saints. In John the kings fight the Lamb and lose. John keeps Daniel's unusual war with (meta) and reverses the outcome. He uses conquer (nikao) where Daniel's Greek has prevailed. The called, chosen and faithful, the saints Daniel saw defeated, now share the Lamb's victory.
entries.turn: Beale says the reversal is deliberate irony: the beast is defeated by the same warlike means he used against the saints. Revelation 13:7 and 11:7 used Daniel 7:21 for the beast's victory; here the line is turned. It answers the question of 13:4: who can fight against the beast?
entries.not: **Not careless Scripture-twisting.** Beale calls the reversal intentional, a way to show the beast punished by his own sin.
entries.deeper: Beale says the battle wording comes from Daniel 7:21, sets the Greek of Daniel beside 17:14a, and notes that here, as in Daniel, kings appear as horns. The change does not cancel the allusion: Beale says Daniel's ending is turned around and given to the saints' champion, as in 12:7-8 and 1 Enoch 90:12-13, where a lamblike figure also defeats beasts. The prediction of the beast's victory becomes an ironic type of his defeat. Daniel 7:22, where judgment is given to the saints, lies behind the faithful who share the victory. Beale also argues that war with (meta) reflects the precise allusion to Daniel, not a general Semitic idiom. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible says the verse reverses 13:7 and cites Daniel 7:21-22. The grade is drawn here: the wording is Daniel's, the outcome turned.

entries.title: Revelation 17:14, Lord of lords and King of kings
entries.summary: The Lamb's title, Lord of lords and King of kings, matches the title the old Greek of Daniel 4:37 gives God after he humbles Babylon's king.
entries.plain: **A title once claimed by an emperor can be handed to the one who outranks him.** Babylon's kings called themselves king of kings. In the Greek version of Daniel 4, after God humbles Nebuchadnezzar, the king praises God as the God above all gods, the Lord over all lords and the King over all kings. John gives the Lamb the same two titles, Lord of lords and also King of kings. The God who humbled old Babylon's king now appears as the Lamb who conquers the new one.
entries.same: The pair Lord of lords and King of kings. Beale cites the old Greek of Daniel 4:37: because he is God of gods, Lord of lords and King of kings. Revelation 17:14 says because he is Lord of lords (kyrios kyrion) and King of kings (basileus basileon). Deuteronomy 10:17 calls the Lord God of gods and Lord of lords.
entries.differs: The title in this form stands in the old Greek of Daniel 4:37, not in the Aramaic, which says King of heaven; the vault's Greek version also lacks it. John drops God of gods and gives the title to the Lamb. In 19:16 he reverses the order, putting King of kings first.
entries.turn: In Daniel the title belongs to the God who exposed Nebuchadnezzar as an empty copy of real power. Beale says the title now passes to the Lamb, who judges the beast that carries Babylon. It also answers the emperors who claimed divine titles, Domitian among them.
entries.not: **Not a title borrowed from Rome.** Beale and the sources trace it to the Old Testament, though it also answers the claims of kings and emperors.
entries.deeper: Beale says the same title occurs only twice in biblical writings before the New Testament, in 1 Enoch 9:4 and the old Greek of Daniel 4:37, and judges Daniel the more likely influence. The wording is closer (because he is). In Daniel and Revelation the title grounds God's power to remove evil kings. Almost the same title is used for the Babylonian king in Daniel 2:37 and 3:2 and for God in 2:47, and the Daniel formula of universality follows the title as it follows 17:14 in 17:15. 1 Enoch 9:4 may itself allude to Daniel 4:37. The vault's interlinear has only the Greek version called Theodotion, whose 4:37 reads King of heaven, so the old Greek wording is cited here from Beale. Keener notes that king of kings was the title of Eastern rulers (Ezekiel 26:7; Daniel 2:37) and that Jews applied such titles to God from Deuteronomy 10:17. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible cites Deuteronomy 10:17 and Psalm 136:3, and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible adds Daniel 2:47 and 4:37. The grade is drawn here, after Beale's judgment that Daniel is the likelier source.
entries.dissent: The sources point to different origins. Beale prefers the old Greek of Daniel 4:37, with 1 Enoch 9:4 as a second candidate. Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible lead with Deuteronomy 10:17 and Psalm 136:3. The CSB Study Bible's cross-references list Deuteronomy 10:17, Psalm 136:2-3 and Daniel 2:47. Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible add that king of kings was the Parthian ruler's title.

entries.title: Revelation 17:15, the waters are peoples and nations
entries.summary: The angel explains the many waters as peoples and nations, a picture Isaiah uses when the nations roar like many waters.
entries.plain: **When a crowd surges at a stadium gate, people say it moved like a wave.** Isaiah pictured the noise of many nations roaring like the roar of mighty waters. John's angel explains the waters where the prostitute sits: they are peoples, crowds, nations and languages. The many waters of Babylon become the many peoples she rules.
entries.same: Many waters as many nations. The Greek of Isaiah 17:13 reads many nations like much water (hos hydor poly ethne polla). Revelation 17:15 says the waters are peoples, crowds, nations and languages (laoi kai ochloi ... kai ethne kai glossai).
entries.differs: Isaiah compares the nations to roaring waters; John explains the waters as nations outright. Isaiah's nations rush against Zion and are driven off; John's peoples are ruled by Babylon. John's fourfold list follows the pattern of Daniel, where it names the subjects of Babylon's king (Daniel 5:19), not Isaiah's wording.
entries.turn: Beale says the waters were Babylon's source of wealth and defense, and now the peoples are the basis of her trade and power. He links this to 16:12: when the kings turn the peoples against her, the waters dry up. Heiser hears the language of Babel: peoples, nations and languages.
entries.not: **Not a map of rivers.** The angel gives the meaning himself: the waters are peoples.
entries.deeper: Beale says the formula of universality comes from Daniel, where it names the subjects of the Babylonian king (Daniel 5:19, and in the Greek 3:2 and 4:37), and identifies here those under the harlot's influence. Isaiah 17:12-13 also uses many waters for many nations (compare Isaiah 8:7; 23:10; Jeremiah 46:7-9; 47:2). The many waters already allude to Jeremiah 51:13, the Euphrates and canals of Babylon, which the Aramaic paraphrase calls the house of her treasures. Jewish texts read many waters as hostile nations (the Aramaic paraphrases of Song of Songs 8:7 and Isaiah 21:1). Keener cites Isaiah 17:12-13 at 17:1. The CSB Study Bible's cross-references list Isaiah 17:12 and Jeremiah 51:13, and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cites Jeremiah 51:13. The grade is drawn here: the equation of waters and nations is Isaiah's, the list is Daniel's.
entries.heiser: Heiser adds Isaiah 17:12-13, which Beale does not mention: the many nations sound like many waters. He reads the list of peoples, nations and languages as the language of the Tower of Babel and Deuteronomy 32, where the nations were divided and placed under other gods. So Babylon's waters are the nations of the Babel rebellion, part of what he calls a recipe for chaos.
entries.dissent: The sources agree that the waters here are peoples, as the angel says. They read the river of 16:12 differently. Beale ties the two together: the dried Euphrates pictures the peoples turning on Babylon. MacArthur reads the waters of 17:15 as the world's nations under the harlot's rule, and the drying of 16:12 as God drying the real river for the armies from the east.

entries.title: Revelation 17:16, they will hate the prostitute and leave her naked
entries.summary: The beast and the kings strip, devour and burn the prostitute, as Ezekiel foretold that Jerusalem's lovers would turn on her.
entries.plain: **Partners in crime often end up turning on each other.** Ezekiel warned faithless Jerusalem that her lovers would turn on her in hatred, strip her naked, take all she had and burn her houses. John says the ten horns and the beast will hate the prostitute, leave her ruined and naked, devour her body and set her on fire. Ezekiel's sentence on Jerusalem is carried out on Babylon by her own allies.
entries.same: Former lovers who hate the harlot, strip her and burn. The Greek of Ezekiel 23:29 says they will deal with you in hatred (en misei) and you will be naked (gymne). Ezekiel 23:25 has fire devouring the rest. Revelation 17:16 says they will hate (misesousin) the prostitute, make her naked (gymnen) and burn her with fire (en pyri).
entries.differs: Ezekiel's harlot is Jerusalem, judged by God through Babylon. John's harlot is Babylon, destroyed by the beast and kings. Ezekiel has noses and ears cut off; John has her flesh eaten, which recalls Jezebel's end (2 Kings 9:36), Beale says. John adds that God put it into their hearts (17:17).
entries.turn: Beale calls this the mystery: evil destroys itself, the political side of the world system turning on its economic and religious side. Wright and Keener note that empires' allies often turn on them. God uses even the beast to carry out his word.
entries.not: **Not a quotation of Ezekiel.** John follows the order of Ezekiel's scene, hatred, stripping and burning, without repeating its words, and he adds that God put it into their hearts.
entries.deeper: Beale says the harlot's ruin is sketched on the outline of Ezekiel 23:25-29, 47, apostate Jerusalem's judgment: survivors devoured by fire, clothes stripped, dealt with in hatred, left naked and bare, houses burned. Ezekiel 16:37-41 adds lovers gathered against her, her house of harlotry broken down and her houses burned, and Ezekiel 23:31-34 even gives her a cup. Hosea 2:3, Jeremiah 41:22 in the Greek, and Nahum 3:4-5 about Nineveh add to the picture. Eating her flesh recalls Jezebel (2 Kings 9:36), whom Beale compares to the harlot in eleven ways. He reads three metaphors combined: a whore exposed, a victim devoured, a city burned. The ESV Study Bible cites Ezekiel 16:39-41, and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cites Ezekiel 16:35-42 and 23:28-30. The CSB Study Bible's cross-references list Ezekiel 23:22-35, and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible Ezekiel 16:39 and 23:26-29. Keener cites Ezekiel 23:9. Walton notes the Assyrian laws that let a husband disfigure an unfaithful wife. The grade is drawn here: the sequence of hatred, stripping and burning follows Ezekiel 23.
entries.dissent: The sources weigh the Jerusalem background differently. Beale grants that the imagery once described Israel and that unbelieving Israel and the apostate church belong to Babylon in part. Some commentators, he reports, limit the harlot to apostate Israel, and Chilton reads Rome's destruction of Jerusalem here; Beale rejects both. Heiser and Keener see no Jerusalem reference in the harlot at all. MacArthur reads the Antichrist and his ten under-rulers turning on the false religious system they used to unite the world, plundering it and taking all worship for themselves, as God intends.

aw.n: Revelation 17:7-18, seven hills and seven kings
aw.s: The angel explains the woman and the beast: the beast once was, now is not and will come up from the Abyss; its seven heads are seven hills and also seven kings, five fallen, one living and one still to come, and the beast is an eighth who belongs to the seven. Its ten horns are ten kings who will make war on the Lamb, and in the end the beast and the horns turn on the woman, the great city that rules the kings of the earth, and burn her.

entries.title: Revelation 17:16, they will burn her with fire
entries.summary: The burning of the prostitute may recall the law that a priest's daughter who turns to harlotry is to be burned with fire.
entries.plain: **A punishment written into an old rulebook can be invoked against a new offender.** The law of Moses said that a priest's daughter who disgraced herself by harlotry was to be burned with fire. John says the beast and the kings will burn the prostitute with fire. Several sources hear that law, though most also note that burning was simply how conquered cities were destroyed.
entries.same: Burning with fire as the penalty for harlotry. In the Greek of Leviticus 21:9 a priest's daughter who sells herself shall be burned with fire (epi pyros katakauthesetai). Revelation 17:16 says they will burn her with fire (katakausousin en pyri). In 18:8 she will be burned (katakauthesetai), the same verb form as in Leviticus.
entries.differs: Leviticus speaks of one woman in a priest's family under Israel's law; John speaks of a city-woman and of enemies, not judges, doing the burning. John does not mention priests. Since burning was the normal fate of captured cities, the picture works without Leviticus, so this is only a possible echo.
entries.turn: If the law is in view, Beale says, it fits the part of Babylon made up of compromisers within the church, a kingdom of priests (1:6). Wright reads the scene as drawn partly from the law's punishment of a whore and partly from Isaiah's fall of Babylon. Either way her end is just.
entries.not: **Not the only reading.** Keener thinks Daniel 7:11, where the beast's body is burned, a likelier source, and the CSB Study Bible's cross-references also cite Leviticus 20:14.
entries.deeper: Beale suggests Leviticus 21:9 contributed to the picture of the harlot's burning, since there the daughter of a priest who profanes herself by harlotry is to be burned. He thinks it especially apt for the compromisers in the church, a kingdom of priests, and notes that the harlot's attire matches the high priest's clothing in the Greek of Exodus 28. Keener mentions the suggestion as worthy of note but less likely than Daniel 7:11, the burning of the beast, or the normal burning of captured cities (Amos 1:4), and the rumor that Nero burned Rome. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible lists Genesis 38:24, Leviticus 20:14 and 21:9 for burning as the penalty for disgraceful promiscuity, as well as conquered cities (Joshua 6:24) and the beast (Daniel 7:11). The CSB Study Bible's cross-references give Leviticus 20:14 and 21:9. Wright says the scene is drawn partly from the biblical punishment of a whore (Leviticus 21:9). Katakauthesetai in 18:8 is the same form as in the Greek of Leviticus 21:9, a point drawn here. The grade is possible: four sources name it, but the picture fits other backgrounds too.
entries.dissent: Beale and Wright accept a link to Leviticus 21:9. Keener calls it less likely than Daniel 7:11. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible lists it beside the burning of cities and of the beast without choosing. The sources agree that the burning is God's judgment carried out through her allies.

entries.title: Revelation 18:1, the earth lit up by his glory
entries.summary: The angel whose glory lights up the earth recalls Ezekiel 43:2, where the earth shines with the glory of God returning to his temple.
entries.plain: **When the stadium lights come on, everyone knows the main event is about to start.** Ezekiel saw God's glory come back to the temple from the east, and the earth shone with his glory. John sees an angel come down from heaven with great authority, and the earth is lit up by his glory. Before Babylon's fall is announced, the light of God's presence fills the scene.
entries.same: The earth made bright by glory. The Hebrew of Ezekiel 43:2 says the earth shone from his glory (vehaarets heirah mikkevodo). Revelation 18:1 says the earth was lit from his glory (he ge ephotisthe ek tes doxes autou).
entries.differs: In Ezekiel the glory is God's own, returning to the temple; in Revelation it belongs to an angel. The Greek translation of Ezekiel 43:2 says the earth shone like brightness in the glory round about; John's from his glory is closer to the Hebrew, a comparison drawn here. Ezekiel's scene is the return of God to his people. John's is the prelude to Babylon's fall.
entries.turn: Beale says the borrowing fits a chapter that calls God's people to leave Babylon and come back to him (18:4). It also points ahead to 21:23, where God's glory lights the new city. The angel's true glory outshines Babylon's false glory (18:7).
entries.not: **Not proof that the angel is God.** Beale thinks the angel may be Christ, since glory in Revelation belongs to God or Christ, but allows that he may be an angel reflecting God's glory.
entries.deeper: Beale says the earth shining with the glory around God, when Ezekiel saw the end-time return of God to his land and temple (Ezekiel 43:2, also with a loud voice), provides a fitting allusion to open a chapter whose theme is separation from the world and restoration to the Lord. He suggests the figure may be Christ, like the angel of the Lord, because every ascription of glory to a heavenly figure in Revelation is to God or Christ, though a mere angel reflecting God's glory is possible. Following Sweet, he notes that the allusion anticipates 21:10-23, which is based on Ezekiel 40-48. Keener notes that powerful angels were described as shining like lightning or the sun (Daniel 10:6). The CSB Study Bible's cross-references cite Daniel 4:13, 23, where a holy watcher comes down from heaven. The Hebrew of Ezekiel 43:2 reads vehaarets heirah mikkevodo; the Greek in the vault reads he ge exelampen hos phengos; that John's from his glory matches the Hebrew is drawn here. The grade is drawn here: the wording is close, and the scene is Ezekiel's.
entries.dissent: Beale reads the angel as perhaps Christ and the scene as Ezekiel's glory. Keener compares the shining angel of Daniel 10:6. The CSB Study Bible's cross-references point instead to the holy watcher who comes down from heaven in Daniel 4:13, 23, another Babylon chapter. None of them makes the angel God himself. MacArthur reads another angel, not the one of 17:1, whose brightness stands out against the darkness the fifth bowl left on the world.

aw.n: Revelation 18:1-8, come out of her, my people
aw.s: A shining angel announces that Babylon the great has fallen and become a haunt of demons and unclean birds, because the nations drank her wine and the merchants grew rich on her luxury. A voice calls God's people to come out of her, and to pay her back double, since she boasts that she sits as a queen and will never be a widow.

entries.title: Revelation 18:2, fallen, fallen is Babylon the Great
entries.summary: The angel's cry, fallen, fallen is Babylon, repeats the watchman's report in Isaiah 21:9 and Jeremiah's word that Babylon has suddenly fallen.
entries.plain: **A newspaper headline written before the result is in shows how sure the editors are.** Isaiah's watchman sees a rider coming and cries that Babylon has fallen, fallen, with all her idols smashed. Jeremiah says Babylon has suddenly fallen and been broken. John's angel cries the same double word over Babylon the Great. The fall is announced as if it were already done.
entries.same: The doubled verb fallen, fallen and the name Babylon. The Greek of Isaiah 21:9 has peptoke, peptoke Babylon. Revelation 18:2 has epesen, epesen Babylon he megale. Jeremiah 51:8 has suddenly Babylon fell (epese).
entries.differs: John uses a different tense from Isaiah's Greek but keeps the doubling. He adds the Great, from Daniel 4:30. Isaiah's Babylon falls with its carved idols; John's falls and becomes a home for demons. Isaiah spoke of the ancient city. Beale reads John's as the city that stands for Rome and the world system.
entries.turn: Beale says the past tense works like a prophet's certainty: the fall is so sure that only its results are told. Old Babylon fell as foretold, so the new Babylon will too. The idols of Isaiah 21:9 fit John's charge of idolatry against her.
entries.not: **Not a report of a past event.** The verb is past, but the sources read it as a promise of what God will surely do.
entries.deeper: Beale says the repeated announcement of Babylon's fall, from 14:8 on, stresses its certainty; fallen, fallen is Babylon the Great alludes to Isaiah 21:9. Isaiah 21:9 may still be in mind in 18:2b, since it goes on: all her images and idols are crushed. The prophecy and fulfillment of Babylon's past fall are a pattern for the fall of a much larger Babylon, and the past tense works like the Hebrew prophetic perfect. He notes that a few Greek copies of Isaiah 21:9 even read Babylon the Great. Keener says John takes this taunt directly from Isaiah 21:9 (compare Jeremiah 51:8). The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the ESV Study Bible and the CSB Study Bible's cross-references cite Isaiah 21:9, and Wright hears Isaiah 21:9 and Jeremiah 51:8. The Greek of Isaiah 21:9 in the vault reads peptoke, peptoke Babylon; Revelation has the aorist epesen. The grade is drawn here: the doubled cry is unmistakable.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Beale and McDonough. The cry from Isaiah 21, Babylon has fallen, comes in 18:2 and in 14:8. Joined to the desert of Isaiah 21:1, it shows that the city is Babylon. It is not Jerusalem.
entries.dissent: Beale reads the fall of historical Babylon as a pattern for the fall of a far larger Babylon, the world system. Heiser reads the city as Babylon, a figure for Rome, and rules out Jerusalem. MacArthur reads Babylon as the worldwide kingdom of the Antichrist, and 18:2 as the seventh bowl's destruction of it, told as if already done though still to come, after which only demons live there.

entries.title: Revelation 18:2, a home for demons and every unclean bird
entries.summary: Fallen Babylon becomes a lair of demons, unclean birds and beasts, as Isaiah foretold for ruined Babylon and Edom, in words the Greek translation renders as demons.
entries.plain: **An abandoned mall taken over by pigeons and stray dogs tells you the money has gone.** Isaiah foretold that ruined Babylon would be home to wild beasts and owls, with wild goats dancing there. He said the same of Edom. The Greek translation calls some of those creatures demons. John says fallen Babylon has become a den of demons, where every foul spirit, bird and beast lives.
entries.same: A ruined city full of demons, birds and beasts. The Greek of Isaiah 13:21 has wild beasts (theria) resting there and demons (daimonia) dancing. Isaiah 34:14 has demons (daimonia) meeting satyrs, and 34:11 birds dwelling. Revelation 18:2 has a dwelling of demons (daimonion) and a haunt of every unclean bird and beast (theriou).
entries.differs: The Hebrew of Isaiah 13:21 names desert creatures, owls and goat-like beings (seirim); the Greek translation renders some of them as demons and sirens. John follows that Greek sense. He adds unclean spirits and calls every creature unclean, which Beale ties to Babylon's idolatry. Isaiah describes a deserted ruin. Beale reads John's scene as the truth behind Babylon's beauty.
entries.turn: Beale says the final stripping of Babylon's luxury shows her skeleton, inhabited by demonic creatures. What guided her all along is revealed. The desert of 17:3 becomes her own condition.
entries.not: **Not a nature report.** The sources read the creatures as signs of complete ruin and of the demonic power behind Babylon.
entries.deeper: Beale says the desolation most resembles Isaiah's pictures of the judgment of Babylon and Edom (Isaiah 13:21; 34:11, 14), viewed as types of universal Babylon's judgment. He sets out the Greek: wild beasts rest there, demons dance (Isaiah 13:21-22); birds and ravens dwell there (34:11, 13-14). Jewish interpreters read these creatures as demons (the Aramaic paraphrase of Isaiah 13:21; Midrash Rabbah on Leviticus). He adds Baruch 4:35, Babylon inhabited by demons, and Jeremiah 50:39 and 51:37, and notes that Fekkes sees these texts as the combined inspiration. Isaiah 34 was used earlier in 14:11. The word for haunt (phylake) means a place of watching, as in Daniel 4:25 in the old Greek. Keener cites Isaiah 34:9-15 and Jeremiah 50:13; 51:29, 37. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible notes that the Greek translation calls some creatures demons in Isaiah 34:14 and 13:21. The ESV Study Bible cites Isaiah 13:21-22, and the CSB Study Bible's cross-references Isaiah 13:20-22. The Hebrew of Isaiah 13:21 has tsiyim and seirim, desert creatures and goat-like beings. The grade is drawn here: the creatures and the demons follow Isaiah's Greek.
entries.dissent: The sources lean on different prophets. Beale gives Isaiah 13 and 34 the closest wording. Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible add Jeremiah's oracles against Babylon (50:13; 51:29, 37). The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cites Isaiah 13:19-22 and Jeremiah 51:37. They agree on the meaning.

entries.title: Revelation 18:3, the merchants of the earth grew rich
entries.summary: The merchants who grew rich from Babylon's luxury come from Ezekiel's lament over Tyre, whose trade enriched the kings of the earth.
entries.plain: **A shopping mall that closes takes a whole town's jobs with it.** Ezekiel described Tyre as a great trading city. Her wealth made the world's kings rich, and her merchants came from every land. John says the world's traders made their fortunes from Babylon's vast wealth. From here on, chapter 18 keeps returning to Ezekiel's songs about Tyre.
entries.same: Merchants and kings made rich by a trading city. The Greek of Ezekiel 27:33 says Tyre enriched (eploutisas) all the kings of the earth. Ezekiel 27:12 speaks of merchants (emporoi) trading with Tyre because of her great strength. Revelation 18:3 says the merchants of the earth (emporoi) grew rich (eploutesan) from the power of her luxury.
entries.differs: Ezekiel praises Tyre's trade in a funeral song; John speaks of Babylon. In Ezekiel the kings are enriched; in John the merchants grow rich and the kings commit immorality with her. John adds luxury (strenos), a word for wealth that breeds arrogance, Beale says. Isaiah's Greek of 23:17, where Tyre becomes a market, may also stand behind the merchants.
entries.turn: Beale says the verse gives the cause of Babylon's judgment: she drew nations and rulers into idolatry through the promise of economic security. Heiser reads the merchants as those who use wealth to enslave others. The trade that made them rich will be the reason they mourn.
entries.not: **Not a condemnation of all trade.** Beale says the sin is idolatrous trust in wealth and the security it brings, not owning wealth as such.
entries.deeper: Beale says John's merchants, grown rich from her wealth and power, recall Ezekiel 27:12, where merchants traded with Tyre because of her great power, and Ezekiel 27:33, where Tyre made the world's kings rich. He counts it the first of many uses of Ezekiel 26-28 in the chapter. He adds that the Greek of Isaiah 23:17, which makes Tyre a market for all the kingdoms, is even closer to the merchants of 18:3. He reads luxury (strenos) as wealth, given the link with power and with becoming rich, and possibly arrogance. Rome's peace, he says, mainly secured prosperity for the elite who benefited from the system. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible says the merchants growing rich recalls the lament over Tyre (Ezekiel 27:12, 27). The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible ties the verse to Jeremiah 51:7-8 and notes that Rome's propaganda claimed to bring good to many peoples. The CSB Study Bible's cross-references cite Ezekiel 16:29. The grade is drawn here: the pairing of merchants and enrichment is Ezekiel's.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads 18:3 as the point where the merchants enter: those who use wealth to victimize and enslave others. He ties the chapter's economic picture to Psalm 82, where God judges the gods for abusing the weak. When a system of power owns you through what you can buy or eat, he says, you are trapped, and behind the human power brokers stands a darker intelligence.
entries.dissent: Beale reads the merchants against Rome's peace, which mainly made the elite rich, and treats the Babylon of chapters 17 and 18 as one. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible recalls Rome's claim to bring good to many peoples. MacArthur separates the two: religious Babylon in chapter 17 draws the nations into false worship, and commercial Babylon in chapter 18 lulls the world into a love of goods, with rulers and business leaders swept into its trade.

entries.title: Revelation 18:4, come out of her, my people
entries.summary: The call to God's people to leave Babylon before her plagues fall repeats Jeremiah's and Isaiah's call to the exiles to flee Babylon.
entries.plain: **A fire alarm is a kindness, because it tells people to leave before the building burns.** Jeremiah told the exiles in Babylon to run from the city and save their lives from God's anger. Isaiah told them to leave and touch nothing unclean. A voice from heaven gives John's readers the same call: leave Babylon, so you do not share her sins or her plagues.
entries.same: A command to God's people to come out of Babylon. The Greek of Jeremiah 51:45 reads come forth from her midst, my people (exelthete ek mesou autes, laos emos). Revelation 18:4 reads come out of her, my people (exelthate, ho laos mou, ex autes). Isaiah 52:11 adds go forth and touch nothing unclean.
entries.differs: Jeremiah's exiles were to leave a real city when its fall came. Beale says John's readers are to separate from Babylon's sins, not move house: their escape is moral, not physical. Jeremiah gives one reason, to escape God's anger. John gives two: not to share her sins and not to receive her plagues.
entries.turn: Beale says the call is aimed at wavering believers inside the church, tempted to join Babylon's idolatrous trade. They are to stay in the world as witnesses but not belong to it. The unclean of Isaiah 52:11 fits the unclean spirits of 18:2.
entries.not: **Not a call to leave society.** Beale says Christians are not told to withdraw from economic life, though they may be shut out of it for refusing to compromise.
entries.deeper: Beale says the call is patterned after the repeated calls of Isaiah and Jeremiah, especially Jeremiah 51:45, with Isaiah 48:20, 52:11 and Jeremiah 50:8 and 51:6. In Jeremiah 51 the coming judgment is the reason for leaving, and the city becomes a haunt of jackals (51:37), as in 18:2. Isaiah 52:11 adds touch nothing unclean, meaning Babylon's idols, which fits the threefold unclean of 18:2. Paul uses Isaiah 52:11 in 2 Corinthians 6:17. Beale also hears the angel's word to Lot to get out of Sodom (Genesis 19:15), and possibly Abraham leaving Ur. Keener cites Jeremiah 51:6, 45 and notes Zechariah 2:7 and Genesis 19:17. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible ties the call to Jeremiah 51:6 and 51:45, the ESV Study Bible to Isaiah 52:11 and Jeremiah 51:6-9, 45, and the CSB Study Bible's cross-references list Isaiah 52:11 and Jeremiah 50:8; 51:6, 9, 45. Wright hears Isaiah 48:20 and 52:11-12 and above all Jeremiah 51:45. The grade is drawn here: the words are Jeremiah's almost exactly.
entries.dissent: The sources agree on Jeremiah. They differ on who is addressed. Beale says it is believers within the confessing church. The CSB Study Bible mentions a few who see the rapture here. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible notes that Jeremiah meant a prophecy of future flight, since he had told the exiles to settle in Babylon (Jeremiah 29:7). MacArthur reads a call to God's people to break free of the system before it is destroyed, and perhaps also a call to the chosen to come to faith.

entries.title: Revelation 18:5, her sins are piled up to heaven
entries.summary: Babylon's sins have reached heaven, as Jeremiah said Babylon's judgment reached to heaven and as Sodom's outcry rose to God.
entries.plain: **A pile of unpaid bills eventually reaches a height no one can ignore.** Jeremiah said Babylon could not be healed, because her judgment had reached to heaven and risen to the clouds. John says Babylon's sins are stacked as high as the sky. God has not forgotten what she did. Jeremiah's word judgment becomes John's word sins, the cause behind the sentence.
entries.same: Something of Babylon's reaching up to heaven. The Greek of Jeremiah 51:9 says her judgment has drawn near to heaven (eis ouranon). Revelation 18:5 says her sins have reached up to heaven (achri tou ouranou). Genesis 18:20 speaks of Sodom's great outcry and very great sins.
entries.differs: Jeremiah says judgment; John says sins. Beale says Jeremiah put judgment, the effect of sin, for the sin itself; John goes back to the cause. John's verb (ekollethesan) means clung together or piled up, a different picture from Jeremiah's drew near. John adds that God remembered her wrongs.
entries.turn: Beale says the sins in heaven remind God to punish them. Because Babylon multiplied her sins, God multiplies his judgments to keep his justice. The call to leave her (18:4) makes sense: the reckoning has come.
entries.not: **Not a picture of God forgetting until reminded.** Remembering sins is an Old Testament way of speaking of judgment (Psalm 109:14; Hosea 9:9), Beale notes.
entries.deeper: Beale says appeal is again made to Jeremiah 51: Babylon's judgment has reached to heaven and is lifted up to the skies (51:9), with Genesis 18:20 and 19:13 also in view. Being lifted up was an idiom for an extreme level of corporate sin (Jonah 1:2; Ezra 9:6). He confirms the Jeremiah allusion from the neighboring allusions to Jeremiah 51:7 in 18:3 and 51:45 in 18:4, and reads the aorist verbs as prophetic perfects. Keener notes the Jewish belief that God stores up judgment until sin reaches its full measure (Genesis 15:16). The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cite Jeremiah 51:9, and the CSB Study Bible's cross-references give Jeremiah 51:9. Wright compares Lot near Sodom (Genesis 18). The Greek of Jeremiah 51:9 in the vault reads engiken eis ouranon to krima autes. The grade is drawn here: the setting is the same chapter of Jeremiah, the wording reworked.

entries.title: Revelation 18:6, pay her back as she paid
entries.summary: The call to repay Babylon as she repaid others comes from Jeremiah's oracle on Babylon and Psalm 137, and the double portion from Jeremiah and Isaiah.
entries.plain: **A refund policy that matches what you paid is fair by design.** Jeremiah called for Babylon to be repaid for her deeds, done to as she had done. Psalm 137 blesses whoever repays Babylon for what she did to God's people. John hears a voice say to repay Babylon as she repaid, and to pour her a double share in her own cup. The old prayers for justice against Babylon are now answered.
entries.same: Repayment in kind. The Greek of Jeremiah 50:29 says repay her (antapodote aute) according to her works. Psalm 137:8 blesses the one who repays you the repayment you repaid us. Revelation 18:6 says repay her (apodote aute) as she also repaid, according to her works. Jeremiah 16:18 says God will repay double (diplas).
entries.differs: Jeremiah addresses archers attacking Babylon; the psalmist blesses an unnamed avenger; John's command has no named hearer, and Beale thinks God's agents and ultimately God are meant. Jeremiah 16:18 speaks of Judah repaid double; John turns it on Babylon. John adds the cup she mixed, filled for her in turn.
entries.turn: Beale says the punishment fits the crime. He follows Kline, who argues the word usually rendered double means a matching equivalent. Babylon's sins are balanced by equal punishment in God's scales. Keener reads double as more than complete repayment.
entries.not: **Not permission for believers to take revenge.** Beale and Wright say God himself carries out the repayment.
entries.deeper: Beale says the wording first evokes Psalm 137:8 in the Greek, which he sets beside 18:6a, and then Jeremiah 50:29 (repay her according to her works) and 51:24 (I will repay Babylon), so that historical Babylon's punishment becomes a type of the final one. On double he follows Kline: in the Hebrew kapal and the Greek diploo, the sense is a duplicate or matching equivalent, shown in texts John may allude to (Isaiah 40:2; Jeremiah 16:18). That removes the clash with the measure-for-measure principle in 18:6-7. He adds the cups of Ezekiel 23:31-35, Psalm 75:8 and Habakkuk 2:15-16. Keener cites Jeremiah 50:15, 29 and Isaiah 40:2 and says double meant more than complete. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the ESV Study Bible, the CSB Study Bible's cross-references and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible all cite Isaiah 40:2 and Jeremiah 16:18, and the last adds Psalm 137:8 and Jeremiah 50:29; 51:24. The grade is drawn here: the repayment wording follows Jeremiah and the psalm closely.
entries.dissent: The sources disagree on double. Beale, after Kline, reads it as an exact equivalent, keeping the punishment equal to the crime. Keener reads it as more than complete. The ESV Study Bible calls it a just repayment that duplicates the violence Babylon did, and the CSB Study Bible says full measure and more. Beale also weighs whether God's people, angels or God are addressed. MacArthur reads double as full or overflowing, so that the punishment fits the crime.

aw.s: A shining angel announces that Babylon the great has fallen and become a haunt of demons and unclean birds, because the nations drank her wine and the merchants grew rich on her luxury. entries.title: Revelation 18:7, I sit as a queen; I am no widow
entries.summary: Babylon's boast that she sits as a queen, is no widow and will never mourn repeats the boast of Babylon in Isaiah 47:7-8.
entries.plain: **A company that brags it is too big to fail often fails in a single day.** In Isaiah, Babylon tells herself she will rule as a lady forever. She will never sit as a widow or lose her children. John's Babylon tells herself she sits as a queen. She is no widow, and she will never see grief. The old boast is put in a new mouth, and it will meet the same end.
entries.same: A boast spoken in the heart about sitting secure and never being a widow. The Greek of Isaiah 47:8 has her saying in her heart (en te kardia autes) that she will not sit as a widow (chera). Revelation 18:7 has the same phrase in her heart. Then comes I sit as a queen, and widow I am not (chera ouk eimi).
entries.differs: Isaiah's Hebrew calls Babylon a lady or mistress (gevaret) forever; the Greek has I will rule forever. John has queen (basilissa). Isaiah's Babylon will not know loss of children; John's will not see mourning. John also joins the boast to self-glory and luxury, which the voice says must be repaid with torment and grief.
entries.turn: Beale says the pride and fall of historical Babylon become a pattern for the world system's arrogance and downfall. Her confidence in her own security is self-worship. Beale and the ESV Study Bible both see a warning to the church: Laodicea said much the same of itself (3:17).
entries.not: **Not a boast about marriage.** Widowhood and bereavement are pictures of a city's ruin. The point is pride in permanent security.
entries.deeper: Beale says the basis for the judgment is patterned after the prediction of historical Babylon's fall in Isaiah 47, and sets the Greek of Isaiah 47:7-8 beside 18:7b. Like old Babylon, the latter-day city sees herself as mother of her people and expects never to lose them; her security will be removed suddenly (Isaiah 47:9-11; Jeremiah 50:31-32). The Sibylline Oracles (5.168-77) apply the same picture to Rome, the city that believed she could never fall. He also notes Zephaniah 2:15, where Nineveh boasts in her heart that she alone exists. Keener says John cites Isaiah 47:8-9 here. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the ESV Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cite Isaiah 47:7-8, and the CSB Study Bible's cross-references add Ezekiel 28:2-8 and Zephaniah 2:15. Walton notes the Babylonian boast I am in Isaiah 47:8 echoes the divine name of Exodus 3:14, and that an Assyrian king listed eleven I am titles for himself. Wright also hears Isaiah 47:8-9. The grade is drawn here: the boast follows Isaiah almost line for line.

entries.title: Revelation 18:8, her plagues will come in one day
entries.summary: Babylon's plagues come in one day and she is burned with fire, as Isaiah 47 foretold for Babylon, and her judge is mighty, as Jeremiah 50:34 says.
entries.plain: **A bank that collapses overnight shows how thin its confidence was.** Isaiah told proud Babylon that losing her children and her husband would both come on her in one day. Fire would burn her helpers like stubble. Jeremiah called Israel's redeemer strong, the Lord who would plead their cause against Babylon. John says Babylon's plagues will come in a single day and she will burn, because the Lord God who judges her is mighty.
entries.same: Calamities that come in one day on proud Babylon. The Greek of Isaiah 47:9 says these two things will come (hexei) on you suddenly in one day (en hemera mia). Revelation 18:8 says in one day (en mia hemera) her plagues will come (hexousin). Jeremiah 50:34 in Greek calls the redeemer strong (ischyros), the Lord who will judge; John says strong is the Lord God who judged her.
entries.differs: Isaiah names two losses, children and widowhood; John names three plagues, death, mourning and famine. Isaiah's fire burns Babylon's astrologers like stubble (47:14); John's burns the city herself, as 17:16 foretold. Jeremiah's strong one is Israel's redeemer; John's mighty Lord is Babylon's judge.
entries.turn: Beale says the speed of the fall exposes how empty her proud confidence was. It also echoes Babylon's fall in one night to Cyrus (Daniel 5:30), Keener and Beale note. God's might is the final reason: he is able to do what he says.
entries.not: **Not a fixed twenty-four-hour schedule.** One day stresses suddenness, as the one hour of 18:10 does. Some copies even read one hour here, Beale notes.
entries.deeper: Beale says the sudden ruin in one day keeps following Isaiah 47, where both losses arrive in a single day (47:9) and all of them burn in the fire (47:14). Even the words about God come from a prophecy against Babylon, Jeremiah 50:34 (27:34 in the Greek order), where Israel's strong redeemer is the Lord who will judge. Jeremiah 50:27, 31, the day has come, may also stand behind in one day. Babylon was conquered in a single night (Daniel 5:30). Keener recalls the same night and says this new Babylon would be judged by fire. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible cites Isaiah 47:9 and Jeremiah 50:34. The ESV Study Bible cites Isaiah 47:7-9, and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible says the verse alludes to Isaiah 47:9. The CSB Study Bible's cross-references add Isaiah 47:14. The grade is drawn here: one day and the verb come follow Isaiah's Greek closely.

entries.title: Revelation 18:9-10, the kings stand far off and lament
entries.summary: The kings who mourn Babylon from a distance follow Ezekiel's lament over Tyre, where princes tremble and the kings of the coasts are appalled.
entries.plain: **At a business collapse, the partners who profited from it watch from across the street and worry about themselves.** Ezekiel pictured the princes of the sea coming down from their thrones, trembling and mourning when Tyre fell. The kings of the coasts were shocked. John's kings shared Babylon's sin and luxury. Now they weep as the smoke of the burning city rises. They stand far off in fear and cry woe for the great city.
entries.same: Rulers who mourn a fallen trading city, afraid for themselves. The Greek of Ezekiel 26:16-17 has the princes of the sea fearing their own ruin. They groan and lament: how you were destroyed, the praised city that was strong. Revelation 18:9-10 has the kings weeping and standing far off in fear. They cry, the great city, the strong city.
entries.differs: Ezekiel mourns Tyre; John mourns Babylon. Ezekiel's princes leave their thrones and sit on the ground; John's kings stand far off. John adds the smoke of her burning, which Beale links to Sodom (Genesis 19:28) and Edom (Isaiah 34:10). The cry woe, woe and in one hour are John's.
entries.turn: Beale says the whole lament in 18:9-19 is modeled on Ezekiel 26-27, and the three groups who mourn, kings, merchants and sailors, mourn Tyre there too. The mourners grieve for themselves: Babylon's fall means their own ruin. No sympathy for Babylon is stirred; the saints are told to rejoice (18:20).
entries.not: **Not a lament John shares.** Beale says the mourning is selfish and marks the mourners for judgment, in contrast to the saints' praise.
entries.deeper: Beale says Ezekiel 26-27, the oracle on Tyre's fall, is the model for 18:9-19 and runs on to 18:22; in Ezekiel 27:29-30, 35-36 the same three groups mourn Tyre. Verses 9-10 follow the pattern of Ezekiel 26:16-18 in the Greek, where princes fear, groan and lament over Tyre, and the Greek adds that they will fear their own destruction. The kings living in luxury is a partial allusion to Ezekiel 27:33, and the weeping echoes Jeremiah 51:8, wail for her. Keener notes that the client kings had reason to mourn Rome, whose favor kept them in power, and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible cites Ezekiel 26:18 for their terror. The CSB Study Bible's cross-references give Ezekiel 26:16-18. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible says 18:9-20 closely resembles the prophecy against Tyre in Ezekiel 26-27. The grade is drawn here: the sequence of the scene follows Ezekiel, the wording only in part.
entries.dissent: The sources read the kings against different settings. Keener notes that client kings had reason to mourn Rome, whose favor kept them in power. Beale stresses that they mourn for themselves, as Ezekiel's princes did over Tyre. MacArthur reads the world's political leaders weeping because the fall of the Antichrist's capital means that his empire, and their own power, is finished.
