aw.n: Revelation 18:9-24, kings, merchants and the cargo list
aw.s: The kings, the merchants and the sea captains stand far off and mourn as Babylon burns, because no one buys their cargoes any more, a long list of luxuries that ends with human beings. An angel hurls a great millstone into the sea, and the sounds of music, craftsmen, the mill, the lamp and the wedding fall silent in the city where the blood of prophets and saints was found.

entries.title: Revelation 18:11-13, no one buys their cargo any more
entries.summary: The merchants' lament and the long list of cargo, ending with human beings, follow Ezekiel 27's inventory of Tyre's trade.
entries.plain: **A warehouse inventory can read like an accusation when the last line is people.** Ezekiel 27 lists the goods that flowed into Tyre from every land: silver, iron, linen, ivory, spices, horses, and the lives of human beings. John's merchants weep because no one buys their cargo any more, and he gives their list: gold, silver, jewels, linen, purple, spices, wine, grain, horses, chariots, bodies. It ends with human souls.
entries.same: Merchants and a list of trade goods, including people. Ezekiel 27:12-24 names many of the same goods and the merchants (emporoi) who trade them. The Greek of Ezekiel 27:13 says they traded with you in souls of men (en psychais anthropon). Revelation 18:13 ends its list with souls of men (psychas anthropon).
entries.differs: Beale counts fifteen of John's twenty-nine items in Ezekiel's list and says the rest fit Rome's real trade. Ezekiel places slaves early among bronze goods; John puts them last, after livestock. John adds bodies, the Greek word for slaves, before souls of men. Ezekiel's list praises Tyre's reach; John's indicts Babylon's values.
entries.turn: Beale says the goods are good in themselves. The slaves at the end show how the system uses them. Sweet, as Beale reports, sees the list in falling order of value, with human souls among the livestock. Heiser reads it as the picture of a system that enslaves people through what they can buy and own.
entries.not: **Not a shopping list for its own sake.** Beale and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible read the list as a charge against an empire living in luxury at others' cost.
entries.deeper: Beale says the list rests partly on Ezekiel 27:7-25, which has fifteen of John's twenty-nine goods and the merchants too, and that repeated allusions to Ezekiel 26-27 before and after confirm it. The items missing from Ezekiel reflect the real trade of John's time. The phrase bodies and souls of men refers to slaves, as Ezekiel 27:13 shows, where souls of men are traded for bronze; Gundry, as Beale reports, sees the Greek idiom bodies and the Hebrew idiom souls of men joined. Keener traces the image of merchants mourning a trade center to Isaiah 23:1-8 and especially Ezekiel 27, and lists the sources of the goods in Roman trade. The ESV Study Bible says the list resembles the goods of Tyre's merchants in Ezekiel 27. The CSB Study Bible notes the inventory is like Ezekiel 27, and its cross-references cite Ezekiel 27:12-22. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cites Ezekiel 27:13-22, and Wright says John draws on Isaiah 23 and Ezekiel 27. Walton places Javan, Tubal and Meshech of Ezekiel 27:13 in the Greek world and Anatolia. The grade is drawn here: the shape of the list is Ezekiel's.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads the cargo list as the economic side of Babylon: those who hold power enslave people through what they can eat, own or buy. He ties it to Psalm 82:2-5, where the gods are judged for injustice to the weak, and says God is not in favor of coercive, abusive power. Behind the human power brokers, he argues, stands "a more sinister intelligence".
entries.dissent: Beale and Keener read the goods beyond Ezekiel's list against Rome's real trade in John's time. MacArthur also finds over half the goods in Ezekiel 27:12-22, and reads the list as the trade of a world system still to come, in which the slave trade, long banned, returns.

entries.title: Revelation 18:16, clothed in linen, purple and scarlet; woe, woe
entries.summary: The merchants' double woe over the city dressed in linen, purple, scarlet, gold and jewels draws on Ezekiel's pictures of adorned Tyre and adorned, unfaithful Jerusalem.
entries.plain: **A designer label means little once the store is boarded up.** Ezekiel described Jerusalem dressed by God in fine linen, gold and silver, before she trusted her beauty and turned to harlotry, and then cried woe, woe over her. He pictured Tyre's king covered in every precious stone. John's merchants cry woe, woe over the great city, once dressed in fine linen, purple, scarlet, gold, jewels and pearls.
entries.same: A city dressed in linen and gold, and a double woe. In the Greek of Ezekiel 16:13 Jerusalem is decked in gold and silver and dressed in fine linen (byssina). Ezekiel 16:23 has woe, woe to you (ouai, ouai soi). Ezekiel 28:13 has every precious stone as Tyre's covering. Revelation 18:16 has woe, woe (ouai ouai), the great city clothed in fine linen (byssinon) and gilded with gold and precious stone.
entries.differs: Ezekiel 16 speaks of Jerusalem, Ezekiel 28 of Tyre's king; John speaks of Babylon. John's six goods include purple, scarlet and pearls, which Ezekiel 16:13 lacks. Ezekiel's woe comes from God; John's comes from the merchants who profited. John repeats the costume of 17:4, adding linen.
entries.turn: Beale says the city's clothing pictures her wealth. The same five words describe the high priest's garments in the Greek of Exodus, so the religious side of the system shows too. The harlot city is set against the pure bride city adorned with jewels in 21:18-21. The merchants mourn lost wealth, not lost goodness.
entries.not: **Not a judgment on fine clothes.** The clothing pictures a city that trusted in her wealth, as Jerusalem trusted in her beauty in Ezekiel 16:15.
entries.deeper: Beale says the list of six goods follows the pattern of Ezekiel 27:12-24, where some goods are pictured as Tyre's clothing (27:7), and is partly inspired by Ezekiel 28:13, where every precious stone covered Tyre's king. He adds Ezekiel 16:13, where God adorned Israel with gold, silver, fine linen and silk before she played the harlot (16:15), and calls Ezekiel 16:23, woe, woe to you, the probable inspiration for the double woe, which he says is put beyond doubt. The same five words, gold, purple, scarlet, linen and stones, describe the high priest's garments in the Greek of Exodus 25-28, which brings out the religious side of the system and the contrast with the bride. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cites Ezekiel 27:7 and 28:13. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible cites Ezekiel 16:23 for the double woe. The CSB Study Bible's cross-references link 18:16 to 17:4. The grade is drawn here: the woe and the costume trace back to Ezekiel.

entries.title: Revelation 18:17-19, the sailors throw dust on their heads
entries.summary: The sea captains and sailors who stand far off, throw dust on their heads and cry, what city was like the great city, follow Ezekiel's lament of the sailors over Tyre.
entries.plain: **When a great ship sinks, the crews of other ships stop to watch from a distance.** Ezekiel pictured Tyre's oarsmen and pilots coming ashore and crying bitterly. They put earth on their heads and lamented: who was ever like Tyre? John's captains and sailors stand far off and watch the smoke rise. They pour dust over their heads and cry: what city was like the great city? In one hour the wealth that made them rich is gone.
entries.same: Sailors who stand off, cry out, throw dust on their heads and ask who was like the city. The Greek of Ezekiel 27:29-30 has the rowers and captains standing on land. They cry bitterly and put earth on their heads. Ezekiel 27:32 asks who is like Tyre (tis hosper Tyros). Revelation 18:18-19 asks who is like the great city (tis homoia) and has them cast dust on their heads.
entries.differs: Ezekiel's sailors mourn Tyre, the port they worked from; John's mourn Babylon, the market that made them rich. Ezekiel's sailors spread ashes as a bed; John's simply weep. John adds the smoke of her burning and the refrain in one hour she was laid waste, where Ezekiel 26:19 has the city made desolate.
entries.turn: Beale says the sailors, like the merchants, weep for themselves: their trade is finished. Their question, who is like the great city, echoes the world's worship of the beast (13:4), the ESV Study Bible notes. Now it is a cry of loss. Beale adds that Tyre pictures economic idolatry in general, not sea trade alone.
entries.not: **Not Ezekiel's lament copied whole.** John keeps the steps: standing off, crying out, dust on the head, and who is like the city. He drops the ashes and adds the smoke and the one hour.
entries.deeper: Beale says the pattern of Ezekiel 27 continues: those who do Tyre's sea trade lament and throw dust on their heads because Tyre's end means the end of their living. He sets Ezekiel 27:28-33 beside 18:17b-19 and lists the shared steps: the pilots and sailors, standing on land, crying bitterly, casting dust on their heads, weeping and mourning, and asking who is like Tyre, whose wealth enriched the kings of the earth. Laid waste (eremothe) follows Ezekiel 26:19, I will make you a desolate city. Ezekiel 27:26-27 focuses more on the ruin of the sailors themselves. The ESV Study Bible says the cry, what city was like the great city, now mourns incomparable destruction (Ezekiel 27:32). The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cite Ezekiel 27:30 for the dust, and the latter cites Ezekiel 26:19 for brought to ruin. The CSB Study Bible's cross-references give Ezekiel 27:30 and 27:32. The grade is drawn here: the scene follows Ezekiel step by step.
entries.dissent: Beale reads Babylon as more than Rome, with Tyre standing for economic idolatry and Rome's sea trade in view. MacArthur reads ship captains mourning the loss of Babylon, the capital of the coming empire, and of the shipping trade that made them rich, and the one hour as a brief time of swift judgment.

entries.title: Revelation 18:20, rejoice over her, heaven
entries.summary: The call for heaven and the saints to rejoice over Babylon's fall comes from Jeremiah 51:48, where heaven and earth shout for joy over Babylon.
entries.plain: **When a long court case ends in justice, the families of the victims hug on the courthouse steps.** Jeremiah said that heaven and earth and all in them would shout for joy over Babylon when her destroyers came. John hears the call for heaven to celebrate, with the saints, apostles and prophets. God has given the verdict against her on their behalf. The mourners on earth weep; heaven celebrates.
entries.same: Heaven told to rejoice over Babylon's fall. The Greek of Jeremiah 51:48 says the heavens and the earth will be glad (euphranthesontai) over Babylon (epi Babylona). Revelation 18:20 says be glad (euphrainou) over her (ep' aute), heaven. Deuteronomy 32:43 in Greek calls the heavens to be glad because God avenges his sons' blood.
entries.differs: Jeremiah has heaven and earth rejoice; John keeps heaven and replaces earth with the saints, apostles and prophets, the new people of God, Beale says. Jeremiah's reason is that destroyers come from the north; John's is that God has judged Babylon for her treatment of them. The verb changes from future to command.
entries.turn: Beale says the joy is not revenge but delight in God's justice, which shows the saints' faith was right. It answers the martyrs' cry of 6:10, and the rejoicing reverses the world's glee over the two witnesses (11:10). The section closes with Jeremiah 51:49 in 18:24, about blood shed.
entries.not: **Not gloating over suffering.** Beale says the focus is the outcome of God's justice. Keener calls the judgment of the wicked the vindication of the righteous.
entries.deeper: Beale says the segment opens with an allusion to Jeremiah 51:48, heaven and earth shouting for joy over Babylon's destruction, and ends with Jeremiah 51:49, persecution as a reason for judgment. He says believers in general are meant, as heaven and earth in Jeremiah meant all Israel. He hears secondary echoes of Isaiah 44:23 and 49:13, where heaven rejoices at the release from Babylon, and of Deuteronomy 32:43 in the Greek, with its double call to rejoice because God avenges the blood of his sons. The difficult clause, God judged your judgment from her, may allude to a reading of Jeremiah 50:34 (27:34 in the Greek). He reports six possible translations. Keener reads it as God applying to Rome the verdict its courts passed on Christians. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cites Jeremiah 51:48. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible lists Deuteronomy 32:43, 2 Kings 9:7, Psalm 79:10 and Joel 3:21 for vengeance on those who shed his people's blood. Wright reads it as the law of malicious witness in Deuteronomy 19:16-20. The grade is drawn here: the verb and the object follow Jeremiah's Greek.
entries.dissent: The sources read the clause about judgment differently. Beale lists six translations and leans to God judging her for the saints' sake. Keener and Wright read it as the verdict Rome passed on the saints now passed on Rome, after the law of false witness. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible sets Deuteronomy 32:43 beside Jeremiah. MacArthur reads the call as addressed to the martyrs of the tribulation (6:9-11), who rejoice because God's justice has prevailed, not over the deaths of the lost.

entries.title: Revelation 18:21, a great millstone thrown into the sea
entries.summary: The angel throws a great millstone into the sea, as Jeremiah's messenger threw a stone into the Euphrates, saying Babylon would sink and never rise.
entries.plain: **A judge who snaps a pencil to show a deal is dead makes the point without a speech.** Jeremiah told his messenger to tie a stone to the scroll against Babylon. He was to throw it into the river and say that Babylon would sink the same way. John sees a mighty angel lift a huge stone, the size of a millstone. He hurls it into the sea and says Babylon will go down like that, never to be found.
entries.same: A stone thrown into water as a sign, with the word so, explained of Babylon. The Greek of Jeremiah 51:63-64 has toss it into the Euphrates. Then say: so (houtos) Babylon will sink and not rise. Revelation 18:21 has he threw it into the sea, saying: so (houtos) Babylon will be thrown down and never found again. Ezekiel 26:21 in Greek has you will not be found (ouch heurethese) for ever.
entries.differs: Jeremiah's stone is small and tied to a scroll; John's is like a great millstone. The Euphrates becomes the sea. A man does it in Jeremiah; a mighty angel in John. John takes never found again from Ezekiel's word on Tyre. Beale thinks the great millstone came from Jesus' saying about a millstone and the sea (Matthew 18:6).
entries.turn: Beale says the historical judgments of Tyre and Babylon picture the fall of the last world kingdom. Jesus' saying links the image to those who cause others to stumble, a warning to deceivers in the church (2:14, 20). The repeated never found again begins the closing silence of 18:21-23.
entries.not: **Not a stone small enough to recover.** The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible notes the word means the huge millstone turned by a mule. Nothing will bring Babylon back up.
entries.deeper: Beale says the picture is based on Jeremiah 51:63, where Seraiah binds a stone to the book of Babylon's judgment and casts it into the Euphrates. The angel's so matches the so of Jeremiah 51:64 in the Greek. The Ezekiel 26 background joins Jeremiah: Ezekiel 26:12 has stones cast into the sea and 26:21 never found again. Both may themselves echo Egypt's army hurled like a stone into the depths (Nehemiah 9:11; Exodus 15:4-5). He thinks John also evokes Matthew 18:6-7, with its millstone, sea and woe, and that the third strong angel completes the scrolls of 5:2 and 10:1. Keener cites Jeremiah 51:63-64 and Mark 9:42. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible cites Jeremiah 51:63-64 and Jesus' warning. The ESV Study Bible cites Jeremiah 51:63-64 and Ezekiel 26:21, and the CSB Study Bible's cross-references Jeremiah 51:59-64. Wright compares Jeremiah's act and Jesus' millstone saying. The grade is drawn here: the sign and its so follow Jeremiah.

entries.title: Revelation 18:22, the sound of harpists will never be heard again
entries.summary: The silencing of Babylon's music joins Isaiah 24:8, where the harp falls silent, with Ezekiel 26:13, where Tyre's songs are heard no more.
entries.plain: **A concert hall with a padlock on the door says more than any review.** Isaiah foretold a ruined earth where the joy of tambourines and the sound of the harp would stop. Ezekiel told Tyre that the music of its songs would end and its harps never be heard again. John hears the angel say that harps, singers, flutes and trumpets will fall silent in Babylon for good.
entries.same: Music that stops for good. The Greek of Isaiah 24:8 says the sound of the harp (phone kitharas) has ceased. Ezekiel 26:13 in Greek says the sound of your harps will by no means be heard any longer (ou me akousthe eti). Revelation 18:22 says the sound of harpists (phone kitharodon) will by no means be heard (ou me akousthe) in you any longer (eti).
entries.differs: Isaiah speaks of the whole earth's joy ending; Ezekiel of Tyre's music; John of Babylon's. John lists four kinds of musicians and adds craftsmen and the sound of the mill. Isaiah's verb is has ceased; John uses Ezekiel's emphatic will by no means be heard, and repeats it as a refrain.
entries.turn: Beale says the silence is fitting punishment. Babylon pushed faithful believers out of the trades and took the pleasures of life from them; now her own workers and music are taken away. The punishment fits the crime.
entries.not: **Not a verdict on music.** The silence pictures a city emptied of life and joy, Keener says, as in Isaiah 13:20-22.
entries.deeper: Beale says the use of Isaiah 24:8 and its context stresses both lost wealth and the lost joy that goes with it (Isaiah 24:6 speaks of the earth's people made poor). Isaiah 24:8 is joined to Ezekiel 26:13, where Tyre's musicians are ended and its harps silenced, and whose Greek matches John's ou me akousthe en soi eti. He reads the removal of craftsmen as payback for the trade guilds' exclusion of Christians who would not honor the guild gods. Keener reads the silence as complete devastation, as in Isaiah 13:20-22. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible says the verses recall Isaiah 24:8 and Ezekiel 26:13, and the CSB Study Bible's cross-references give Isaiah 24:8. The grade is drawn here: the wording joins the two texts closely.

entries.title: Revelation 18:22-23, the millstone, the lamp, the bridegroom and the bride
entries.summary: The silence of mill, lamp, bridegroom and bride repeats Jeremiah 25:10, where God takes those sounds from Judah through Babylon; now Babylon loses them.
entries.plain: **A town after a flood has no wedding music, no kitchen noise and no light in the windows.** Jeremiah warned that God would take from Judah the sounds of joy and of weddings, the grinding of the mill and the glow of the lamp. Babylon would be his tool. John hears the same list spoken over Babylon. What Babylon did to Jerusalem is now done to her.
entries.same: The voices of groom and bride, the mill and the lamp, all taken away. The Greek of Jeremiah 25:10 has the voice of the groom (phonen nymphiou), the voice of the bride (phonen nymphes) and the light of a lamp (phos lychnou). Revelation 18:23 has the voice of groom and bride (phone nymphiou kai nymphes). It has the light of a lamp (phos lychnou). In 18:22 there is the sound of a mill.
entries.differs: In Jeremiah the loss falls on Judah, and Babylon is God's instrument. In Revelation it falls on Babylon herself. The Hebrew of Jeremiah 25:10 has the sound of millstones (kol rechayim), which the vault's Greek gives as the scent of perfume; John has the sound of a mill. John reverses Jeremiah's order and shortens the double voice.
entries.turn: The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible says Babylon reaps what it sowed: Jerusalem lost these sounds when Babylon conquered it. Beale reads the loss as the end of the joys of prosperity. The silence contrasts with the wedding of the Lamb that follows (19:7).
entries.not: **Not a ban on weddings.** The bridegroom and the bride stand for ordinary joy, which the prophets used to picture a city's ruin, Keener says.
entries.deeper: Beale says loss of joy through lost prosperity is echoed from Jeremiah 25:10 in 18:22b-23a, with Jeremiah 7:34 and 16:9 likely included, where loss is also pictured in wedding terms (compare Jeremiah 33:11). He notes that some copies repeat the word voice before the bride, bringing it closer to Jeremiah, and judges the shorter reading original. The passages from Jeremiah, Ezekiel and Isaiah together point to the fall of the world system. Keener cites Jeremiah 16:9 and 25:10 and Joel 1:8 for the image of stifled joy. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible cites Jeremiah 25:10 and 16:9 and says Babylon now reaps what it sowed. The ESV Study Bible cites Jeremiah 7:34 and 25:10, the CSB Study Bible's cross-references give Jeremiah 25:10, and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible says the verse alludes to Jeremiah 25:10. That the vault's Greek of 25:10 reads perfume where the sense of the Hebrew and John is millstones is noted here from the interlinear. The grade is drawn here: four items of the list match Jeremiah.
entries.dissent: The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible stresses the reversal: Babylon, which silenced Jerusalem, is silenced. Beale stresses the loss of prosperity and joy for the world system. Keener treats the image as a general prophetic picture of destruction. The three readings fit together.

aw.n: Revelation 18:9-24, kings, merchants and the cargo list
aw.s: The kings, the merchants and the sea captains stand far off and mourn as Babylon burns, because no one buys their cargoes any more, a long list of luxuries that ends with human beings. An angel hurls a great millstone into the sea, and the sounds of music, craftsmen, the mill, the lamp and the wedding fall silent in the city where the blood of prophets and saints was found.

entries.title: Revelation 18:23, your merchants were the great ones of the earth
entries.summary: The charge that Babylon's merchants were the great ones of the earth repeats Isaiah 23:8, where Tyre's merchants were princes, honored on earth.
entries.plain: **A city whose bankers are treated like royalty has its priorities on display.** Isaiah asked who planned the fall of Tyre, the city whose merchants were princes and whose traders were honored on earth. His answer: the Lord, to humble all pride. John gives the first reason for Babylon's fall in the same words. Her merchants were the great ones of the earth.
entries.same: Merchants who were the earth's great men. The Greek of Isaiah 23:8 says her merchants (hoi emporoi autes) were the glorious rulers of the earth (tes ges). Revelation 18:23 says your merchants (hoi emporoi sou) were the great ones of the earth (hoi megistanes tes ges).
entries.differs: Isaiah speaks of Tyre; John of Babylon. Isaiah's Greek calls them glorious rulers; John calls them great ones, a word Isaiah's Greek pairs with rulers in 34:12. Isaiah asks a question and answers it in the next verse; John states the charge as a reason for judgment, beginning with because.
entries.turn: Beale says the merchants are judged because they gave glory to themselves, not to God. Isaiah 23:9 says the Lord plans to bring down all pride. In Ezekiel 28:5, 9 Tyre's wealth makes its heart claim to be a god. Calling oneself great, in Revelation, claims a title that belongs to God alone.
entries.not: **Not a charge against merchants as such.** Beale locates the sin in self-glorying pride and in oppression, not in trading.
entries.deeper: Beale says the reason lies in the allusion to Isaiah 23:8, her merchants were the glorious rulers of the earth, and notes that Isaiah 34:12 sets rulers and great ones side by side. The context of the allusion supports self-glory as the charge: the Lord of hosts purposed to bring down the pride of the glorious ones (Isaiah 23:9), and Tyre's heart was lifted up by its riches (Ezekiel 28:5, 9). He adds that Jewish tradition held that Tyre's merchants oppressed the saints (b. Baba Bathra 75a; the Aramaic paraphrase of Isaiah 23:12), and that some rabbis equated Tyre with Rome. Keener traces the merchants' mourning to Isaiah 23:1-8 and Ezekiel 27. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible ties the chapter to Tyre as economic prostitute (Isaiah 23:15-17). Wright says John drew together material from Isaiah 23 and Ezekiel 27. The grade is drawn here: the sentence follows Isaiah's wording, with one word changed.

entries.title: Revelation 18:23, all nations were deceived by your sorcery
entries.summary: Babylon's sorcery that deceived the nations recalls Isaiah 47:9, Babylon's spells, and Nahum 3:4, Nineveh the harlot who sold nations by her sorceries.
entries.plain: **A con artist's charm works only until the trick is exposed.** Isaiah told Babylon that her many spells and great enchantments would not save her. Nahum called Nineveh a harlot and mistress of sorceries who sold nations by her harlotry and peoples by her spells. John gives a second reason for Babylon's fall. By her sorcery every nation was led astray.
entries.same: Sorcery (pharmakeia) that leads nations astray. The Greek of Nahum 3:4 has a harlot leading in potions (pharmakon), who sells nations by her harlotry and tribes by her potions. Isaiah 47:9 in Greek has in your sorcery (en te pharmakeia sou). Revelation 18:23 has by your sorcery (en te pharmakeia sou) all the nations were deceived.
entries.differs: Isaiah speaks of Babylon's magic that cannot save her; Nahum speaks of Nineveh selling nations. John joins them: Babylon's sorcery deceived nations. Nahum's sells becomes John's deceived. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible says Isaiah supplies the concept and Nahum the language.
entries.turn: Beale says the stress is on fooling people into idol worship, not on magic as such. Sorcery sits next to idols in 9:20-21 and next to harlotry in Nahum. Babylon is punished because she charmed the world into false worship and false security.
entries.not: **Not mainly about spells and potions.** The sources read sorcery as the deceptive power that drew nations into idolatry. Keener allows love potions or pagan rites as part of the picture.
entries.deeper: Beale says the wording of 18:23 comes from Isaiah 47:9, where ruin comes on Babylon in her sorcery, and Nahum 3:4, Nineveh skilled in sorcery, selling nations by her fornication and peoples by her sorceries. Nahum equates sorcery with fornication, and the Aramaic paraphrase renders she sells nations by her fornication as betraying nations with her idols. Qumran applied Nahum's Nineveh to Jerusalem's false teachers. Isaiah 47:9-10 ties sorcery to Babylon's trust in herself (I am, and there is no other), already used in 18:7-8, and Jezebel's harlotries and sorceries (2 Kings 9:22) link the harlot to 2:20-21. Keener cites Isaiah 47:8-9 and Nahum 3:4. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible says Isaiah supplies the concept and Nahum the language, and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cites Nahum 3:4. The vault's Greek of Isaiah 47:9 reads en te pharmakeia sou, the same three words as John. The grade is drawn here: the phrase matches Isaiah's Greek, the picture Nahum's.

entries.title: Revelation 18:24, in her was found the blood of prophets and saints
entries.summary: Babylon falls because the blood of the saints and of all the slain is found in her, as Jeremiah said Babylon must fall for Israel's slain and the slain of all the earth.
entries.plain: **A crime scene is closed only when the evidence is found.** Jeremiah said that as Babylon made Israel's dead fall, so the dead of the whole world would fall in Babylon. John gives the last reason for Babylon's ruin. The blood of prophets, of God's people and of everyone killed on earth was found in her. The city that hid nothing will be found no more, because blood was found in her.
entries.same: Babylon held to account for the slain of Israel and of all the earth. The Greek of Jeremiah 51:49 has the slain of Israel and the slain of all the earth (pases tes ges). Revelation 18:24 has the blood of prophets and saints. It adds everyone slain on the earth (epi tes ges).
entries.differs: Jeremiah speaks of Babylon's fall matching the fall of the slain; John speaks of blood found in her. Jeremiah's victims are Israel's; John's are prophets and saints. John adds the verb was found, playing on the refrain will never be found of 18:21-23, Beale says. Nahum 3:1 calls Nineveh a city of blood; John fixes that charge on Babylon.
entries.turn: Beale says Nineveh and Babylon, both judged for bloodshed, foreshadow the end of the last corrupt world system. Nothing will be found in her again, because her guilt was found in her. The verse answers the souls under the altar (6:10).
entries.not: **Not Jeremiah's verse repeated.** Jeremiah counts Israel's slain. John counts prophets, saints and all the slain on earth, and says their blood was found in her.
entries.deeper: Beale says the city fell for the same reason as Nineveh, which was skilled in sorcery and a city of blood (Nahum 3:1, 4). Historical Babylon came to an end because of Israel's slain (Jeremiah 51:49a), and 51:49b, which speaks of the slain of the whole earth falling, probably helped shape 18:24b, with secondary echoes of Ezekiel 24:7 and Matthew 23:35, 37. The section opened with Jeremiah 51:48 in 18:20 and closes with 51:49. He reads blood and death as figures for all persecution. Keener cites Jeremiah 2:34 and Matthew 23:35. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible says Babylon would fall for killing God's people, as she had killed many throughout the earth (Jeremiah 51:49), and the CSB Study Bible notes she bears the guilt of all the martyrs. The grade is drawn here: the slain of all the earth is Jeremiah's phrase.
entries.dissent: Keener notes that Rome took on the guilt for the slaughter as the present form of the oppressing empire. Beale reads the blood as every kind of persecution by the world system, foreshadowed by Nineveh and old Babylon. MacArthur reads the blood as the atrocities that the religious and commercial systems of the coming Babylon will commit against God's people, which God will avenge (19:2).

entries.title: Revelation 19:1, hallelujah over the fall of the wicked
entries.summary: The first hallelujah may echo the last line of Psalm 104, where the psalm ends with hallelujah once sinners are gone from the earth.
entries.plain: **A crowd that bursts into an old hymn at a victory parade is borrowing the hymn's mood as well as its words.** Hallelujah is a Hebrew shout that means praise the Lord. It appears only here in the New Testament, four times in a row. Beale thinks John may be recalling Psalm 104, which ends with that same shout after the wicked are swept away. Here the shout greets the end of Babylon.
entries.same: The word hallelujah (halleloyia in John's Greek), and the reason for it. In Psalm 104:35 the shout follows the prayer that sinners vanish from the earth. In Revelation 19:1-3 it follows the judgment of Babylon.
entries.differs: Psalm 104 closes a song about creation with one hallelujah. John has a heavenly crowd shout it again and again, in a scene of judgment. Hallelujah is common in the Psalms, so the word alone cannot point to one psalm. Beale also notes a proposal that John has the Hallel psalms, 113 to 118, in view. No source settles which psalm John means.
entries.turn: The praise is for a verdict. God has judged the city that corrupted the earth and killed his servants. The crowd sings the old temple shout because the old hope has come true: the wicked are gone, as the psalm prayed.
entries.not: **Not a word John invented.** Hallelujah was already a fixed shout of worship, at home in the Psalms and in Jewish praise. The echo, if there is one, lies in the setting.
entries.deeper: Beale names two views. Johnson, as Beale reports, hears the Hallel psalms (113 to 118, especially 113:1 and 115:13), which recall the exodus and which Jewish writings tied to the final defeat of the wicked. Beale thinks Psalm 104:35 more likely, because there the hallelujah answers the end of sinners, and rabbinic texts read that verse of the last judgment. He adds that Tobit 13 has the streets of the end-time Jerusalem cry hallelujah, a link to the bride-city of 21:2. The CSB Study Bible's cross-references give Psalm 104:35 and 106:1, 48. The ESV Study Bible notes the word is Hebrew for praise Yahweh, frequent in Psalms 113 to 118. The grade is possible, as Beale's own phrase is the possibility of allusion.
entries.dissent: Johnson, as Beale reports him, points to the Hallel psalms; Beale prefers Psalm 104:35. The ESV Study Bible names Psalms 113 to 118 only as where the word is common, without calling it an echo. Keener treats hallelujah as a general call to worship found across the Psalms.

aw.n: Revelation 19:1-10, the marriage supper of the Lamb
aw.s: A vast heavenly crowd shouts hallelujah because God has judged the great prostitute, and again because the Lamb's wedding day has arrived and his bride stands ready in fine linen. The angel declares those invited to the wedding feast blessed, and when John bows to him, tells him to worship God alone.

entries.title: Revelation 19:2, the city that ruined the earth
entries.summary: Babylon is the one who corrupted the earth, in words that Beale traces to Jeremiah's oracle against Babylon, the mountain that destroys the whole earth.
entries.plain: **A judge who reads out the same charge that sank an old gang is telling the new gang how its trial will end.** Jeremiah called Babylon a destroying mountain that ruins the whole earth. John says the great prostitute corrupted the earth. Beale hears Jeremiah in this charge. Old Babylon fell for wrecking the world, and the new Babylon will fall for the same crime.
entries.same: The verb to corrupt or destroy (phtheiro, diaphtheiro) with the whole earth as its object. In the Greek of Jeremiah 51:25 (28:25 in the Greek numbering) Babylon is the mountain that corrupts all the earth. John has the prostitute who corrupted the earth.
entries.differs: Jeremiah speaks to a mountain; John to a woman, the prostitute. Jeremiah's Greek doubles the verb, the corrupted mountain that corrupts. John uses the plain verb and adds by her immorality. Beale says the verb carries both senses, ruin by vice and ruin by violence, since the next clause speaks of blood. Revelation 11:18 uses the same Jeremiah wording for those who destroy the earth.
entries.turn: Old Babylon's fall becomes the pattern for the new one. Beale reads the new Babylon as the empire of John's day, which will meet the old city's end. The charge is twofold: it corrupted the nations with its ways and it destroyed the earth.
entries.not: **Not a quotation of Jeremiah's oracle.** John borrows one charge, ruining the whole earth, and lays it on the great prostitute. He leaves out Jeremiah's picture of a mountain set on fire.
entries.deeper: The vault's Greek of Jeremiah 51:25 reads to oros to diephtharmenon to diaphtheiron pasan ten gen, the corrupted mountain that corrupts all the earth. Revelation 19:2 has hetis ephtheiren ten gen en te porneia autes. Beale says both 11:18 and 19:2 depend on this verse, which he calls an almost identical phrase used of historical Babylon's judgment. Keener points instead to Jeremiah 51:48-49, heaven rejoicing over Babylon's fall, for the same vindication theme. The CSB Study Bible's table of Jeremiah in Revelation links Jeremiah 51 to Revelation 14, 18 and 21 in several places, though not to this verse. The grade is drawn here by Beale's definitions: a phrase traceable to one oracle, with a shared verb but not identical wording. Beale's category is analogical use: old Babylon as the pattern for the new.
entries.dissent: Beale and Keener read Babylon in chapters 17 to 19 as the whole world system set against God, and Beale sees it first in the Roman empire of John's day. MacArthur reads Babylon as the Antichrist's kingdom across the world, at once political, economic and religious, still to come, with a capital city at its center. He says it is not the old city on the Euphrates, and that no city in history so far fits John's details.

entries.title: Revelation 19:2, avenged the blood of his servants
entries.summary: God avenges the blood of his servants on the prostitute, in words close to God's charge against Jezebel in 2 Kings 9:7, with the prayer of Psalm 79:10 behind it.
entries.plain: **A family that finally hears a guilty verdict may repeat the words their grandparents prayed.** In 2 Kings 9, God sends Jehu to pay back Jezebel for killing the prophets and the Lord's servants. John uses almost the same words for Babylon, who has already been painted as a Jezebel. Psalm 79 adds the old prayer that God avenge his servants' blood. Here that prayer is answered.
entries.same: Avenge, the blood, his servants, and from her hand. The Greek of 2 Kings 9:7 has ekdikeseis ta haimata ton doulon ... ek cheiros Iezabel; John has exedikesen to haima ton doulon autou ek cheiros autes. Psalm 79:10 asks for vengeance for the poured out blood of your servants.
entries.differs: In 2 Kings, Jehu is sent to do the avenging. In John, God does it himself. Jezebel's name drops out, and the prostitute takes her place. John has blood in the singular where the Greek of Kings has bloods. The phrase from her hand is unclear; Beale takes it as blood shed by her hand.
entries.turn: The martyrs under the altar asked how long until God avenged their blood (6:10). This verse is the answer. Babylon, like Jezebel, killed God's prophets and led people into false worship. Like Jezebel, she is now judged.
entries.not: **Not a call for Christians to take revenge.** In every text here the vengeance belongs to God. The saints only pray and praise.
entries.deeper: Beale calls the allusion to 2 Kings 9:7 clear, given the near identical wording and since Jezebel the prostitute has already been alluded to around this verse (2:20; 17:16). He reads from her hand by the Hebrew idiom, where hand means power, so the blood was shed by her. He adds Psalm 79:10 (78:10 in the Greek) as a possible further allusion, which supports the same sense, and notes that 6:10 alluded to the same psalm and 16:6 develops it. Keener cites Deuteronomy 32:43 and Psalm 79:10 for vindication of the righteous. The CSB Study Bible's cross-references list Deuteronomy 32:43 and 2 Kings 9:7. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible says God answers the martyrs' prayers of 6:10. The grade is Beale's: clear for 2 Kings 9:7.
entries.dissent: The sources agree on the vengeance theme. They differ on the main text. Beale puts 2 Kings 9:7 first and Psalm 79:10 second. Keener names Deuteronomy 32:43 and Psalm 79:10 and does not mention Jezebel. The English versions Beale lists read the phrase as vengeance on her, while he prefers blood shed by her hand.

entries.title: Revelation 19:3, her smoke goes up forever
entries.summary: The smoke rising from Babylon forever comes from Isaiah 34:10, where Edom burns and its smoke never stops.
entries.plain: **A ruined castle kept as a monument tells every visitor that the war is over for good.** Isaiah 34 pictures Edom burning night and day, its smoke rising for all time. John takes that picture for Babylon. Her smoke goes up forever. The city will never be rebuilt. Edom's ruin becomes the pattern for Babylon's end.
entries.same: Her smoke goes up, without end. The Greek of Isaiah 34:10 has anabesetai ho kapnos autes, her smoke shall go up. John has ho kapnos autes anabainei eis tous aionas ton aionon, her smoke goes up to the ages of the ages.
entries.differs: Isaiah's smoke rises from Edom; John's from Babylon. Isaiah's verb is future, shall go up. John's is present, goes up. Isaiah's Greek speaks of a long time and many generations. John uses the book's strongest phrase for endless time, the ages of the ages. Revelation 14:11 already used this verse for the beast's worshipers.
entries.turn: Beale reads Edom's fall as a pattern: the world system, once judged, stays down for good. The smoke is a lasting memorial of God's verdict. John may also be answering Rome's claim to be the eternal city, which the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible and Beale both note.
entries.not: **Not a picture of a city still burning in the new creation.** The ESV Study Bible reads the smoke as a sign of judgment that cannot be undone.
entries.deeper: Beale says the wording comes from Isaiah 34:9-10, where the ascending smoke is a permanent memorial of Edom's punishment, and that 14:11 alludes to the same text. Keener calls it a quotation of Isaiah 34:10, naturally applied to every city that sinned the same way. Beale notes the Targum of Isaiah 34:9 and later rabbinic writings already read the verse as a type of Rome's fall. Walton notes that pitch and burning sulfur, both found near the Dead Sea, fit a picture of God's wrath. The CSB Study Bible's cross-references give Isaiah 34:8-10 and Revelation 14:11. The grade is drawn here by Beale's definitions: he says the wording comes from Isaiah, and the shared phrase is close in Greek.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads the smoke of 19:3 with 14:11 in his debate over final judgment. Such lines are often taken to settle that the lost are punished forever. He says they do not settle it. The smoke could mean ongoing vengeance, or it could mean a judgment that is permanent and cannot be reversed. He keeps both views on the table and leans slightly toward the second.
entries.dissent: The sources agree on Isaiah 34. They differ on what forever means. Beale reads the smoke, with 14:11 and 20:10, as unending punishment. Heiser says the same words may mean only that the verdict is final.

entries.title: Revelation 19:4, amen, hallelujah
entries.summary: The elders' amen and hallelujah echo the close of Psalm 106, where all the people answer God's rescue with the same two words.
entries.plain: **A congregation that answers a prayer with the closing words of a well-known hymn is joining an older choir.** Psalm 106 ends with all the people saying amen and praise the Lord, after God gathered them back from their enemies. In Revelation 19 the elders and the living creatures around the throne say the same pair, amen and hallelujah. They seal the crowd's praise for the judgment of Babylon.
entries.same: The pair amen and hallelujah as a closing response of worship. In Hebrew Psalm 106:48 ends with amen and hallelu-yah. John has amen halleluia.
entries.differs: In the psalm the whole people speak. In Revelation the heavenly elders answer, with the creatures around the throne. The old Greek translation of the psalm does not keep hallelujah at this point; it has may it be, twice. So John's pair matches the Hebrew line, a point drawn here.
entries.turn: Beale says the pairing fits its setting. In the psalm the people thank God for gathering them after rescue from their oppressors. In Revelation the heavenly council does the same after God judges the city that oppressed the saints.
entries.not: **Not a quotation of a whole verse.** Only the closing pair of words is shared, with the setting of thanks after rescue.
entries.deeper: Beale says the declaration echoes Psalm 106:48 and that the wording is not haphazard, since the psalm's thanks follows God's gathering of his people from oppressors (106:42-48). The ESV Study Bible says amen expresses confident certainty or strong agreement. The CSB Study Bible's cross-references list Psalm 106:48 at this verse. In the vault's Septuagint, Psalm 106:48 closes with genoito genoito, may it be, may it be, the usual Greek rendering of amen there; hallelujah does not appear at that point. The Hebrew of the verse ends ve'amar kol ha'am amen hallelu-yah, and all the people shall say amen, hallelujah. The grade is drawn here by Beale's definitions: a short pair that is common in worship, made likely by the shared setting.
entries.dissent: Beale and the CSB Study Bible tie the words to Psalm 106:48. The ESV Study Bible treats them as standard words of worship and names no psalm.

entries.title: Revelation 19:5, all his servants, small and great
entries.summary: The call to praise from the throne gathers psalm phrases: all you his servants from Psalms 134 and 135, and those who fear him, small and great, from Psalm 115:13.
entries.plain: **A host who calls everyone to the dance floor, young and old, is using an invitation older than the party.** A voice from the throne calls God's people to praise. The words sound like the Psalms. All his servants is how Psalms 134 and 135 address worshipers. Those who fear him, small and great, comes from Psalm 115. John gathers these psalm calls into one invitation.
entries.same: Praise our God, all his servants, those who fear him, the small and the great. The Greek of Psalm 115:13 has tous phoboumenous ton kyrion, tous mikrous meta ton megalon, those fearing the Lord, the small with the great. John has hoi phoboumenoi auton, hoi mikroi kai hoi megaloi.
entries.differs: The psalms speak of fearing the Lord; John has fearing him. Psalm 115 says small with great; John says small and great. The psalm blesses those who fear; John calls them to praise. Revelation 11:18 uses the same string of names for the believing community.
entries.turn: The servants whose blood was shed in verse 2 are the ones called to praise in verse 5. Beale reads the titles as names for all believers, not a special class. The small and the great means everyone, high or low.
entries.not: **Not proof that the voice is God speaking of himself.** The voice says our God. Beale leaves open whether it is Christ, an angel or another heavenly figure.
entries.deeper: Beale calls all his servants a collective allusion to Psalms 22:23, 134:1 and 135:1, 20 in the Greek, and links those who fear him, small and great, to Psalm 115, as at 11:18. He notes Charles's point that praise God (aineo with theos) sometimes renders the Hebrew hallelu-YHWH in the Septuagint, so the call may be another hallelujah. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible says the praise may echo Psalm 134:1 and 115:13. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible calls praise our God the equivalent of hallelujah. The CSB Study Bible's cross-references list Psalm 115:13. The grade is drawn here by Beale's definitions: the phrases are traceable to these psalms, though each is short.

entries.title: Revelation 19:6, the Lord our God reigns
entries.summary: The shout that the Lord God Almighty has begun to reign gathers a refrain from the enthronement psalms, the Song of the Sea and Isaiah 52:7.
entries.plain: **A chant that a whole stadium knows by heart needs only its first words to be recognized.** The Psalms often cry out that the Lord reigns. Moses sang it after the Red Sea. Isaiah's messenger runs to Zion to say that God reigns. The heavenly crowd now shouts it again. God has begun to reign, because Babylon has fallen.
entries.same: The verb for reigning with the Lord as subject. The Greek of Psalm 93:1 (92:1 in the Greek) opens ho kyrios ebasileusen, the Lord reigned; John has ebasileusen kyrios ho theos. The Greek of Isaiah 52:7 has basileusei sou ho theos, your God shall reign.
entries.differs: John's verb is past tense in form. Beale takes it as began to reign. John puts the verb before the name, as Isaiah 52:7 and Psalm 47 do. He adds the Almighty, the title of 11:17. In the Psalms the reign follows the defeat of Israel's enemies. In John it follows the fall of Babylon.
entries.turn: Wright compares the shout to Isaiah 52:7: God has become king at last, by overthrowing Babylon. Beale reads it as the reign announced in 11:15-17 now in force. The reign of God is shown in a real act of judgment, and the wedding of the Lamb follows.
entries.not: **Not a single quoted verse.** The shout is a refrain found in many places, and the sources list several. None claims John means only one.
entries.deeper: Beale calls the phrase a sweeping allusion to psalms and other texts where God establishes his kingship after judging Israel's enemies: Psalms 93:1, 96:10 and 97:1, 1 Chronicles 16:31, perhaps Psalms 47 and 99. He adds Isaiah 52:7 and Zechariah 14:9 for the end time, and Exodus 15:17-18, where the Red Sea victory leads to God's reign. He thinks Isaiah 52:7 may stand out most. He also reads the grammar as a flag: the participle legonton disagrees with its noun, as John does elsewhere to mark an Old Testament allusion. Keener lists Psalm 97:1, Exodus 15:18, Isaiah 24:23 and 52:7, and Micah 4:7. The grade is possible: the refrain is common, so it cannot be traced to one passage.
entries.dissent: Beale and Wright give Isaiah 52:7 the lead. Keener lists Isaiah 52:7 among several and gives no lead text. The ESV Study Bible names no Old Testament text and says God reigns throughout history but is praised here for a reign without rival. The CSB Study Bible's cross-references list seven texts.

aw.s: A vast heavenly crowd shouts hallelujah because God has judged the great prostitute, and again because the Lamb's wedding day has arrived and his bride stands ready in fine linen. entries.title: Revelation 19:7-8, the bride clothed in fine linen
entries.summary: The bride dressed in bright, clean linen draws on Isaiah 61:10, where God clothes his people in salvation and righteousness like a bride in her jewels.
entries.plain: **A wedding dress handed down through a family carries the story of every bride who wore it.** In Isaiah 61, God's people rejoice because he has clothed them with salvation and wrapped them in righteousness, like a groom and a bride dressed for the wedding. John sees the Lamb's bride ready, given fine linen to wear. The linen is the righteous deeds of the saints.
entries.same: Joy, a bride, and clothing that stands for righteousness. Isaiah 61:10 rejoices because God has clothed the speaker, as a bride is adorned. John's bride rejoices, is made ready, and is given linen that stands for righteousness (dikaiomata).
entries.differs: Isaiah's speaker is restored Israel. John's bride is the Lamb's people. Isaiah speaks of garments of salvation and a robe of righteousness. John names fine linen, bright and pure, and calls it the righteous deeds of the saints. John adds that it was given to her, which stresses God's gift. John also says the marriage of the Lamb has come, which Isaiah does not have.
entries.turn: The bride stands against the prostitute. Both wear linen, but the prostitute's comes from trade and sin. The bride's is a gift, and Beale reads it as both faithful deeds and God's vindication of the saints. She becomes the new Jerusalem of 21:2.
entries.not: **Not righteousness earned by good works.** The linen was given to her. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible and the ESV Study Bible both say her deeds answer God's grace and do not buy it.
entries.deeper: Beale says Isaiah 61:10 forms the basis for 19:8 and sets the two texts side by side. In the vault's Septuagint the verse reads that God clothed me with a garment of salvation and adorned me as a bride with ornament, which stresses God's action, as John does with was given. Beale adds that Isaiah 62:1-5 carries the same marriage picture, and that Jewish readers took the garments of Isaiah 61:10 both as Israel's righteousness and as God's. He notes Fekkes supports the allusion. He also hears Ezekiel 16:8-10, where God covers Israel with fine linen, and Psalm 45. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible says John draws on Isaiah 61:10 to 62:5. Walton notes that in ancient Israel both bride and groom wore ceremonial clothing. The grade is drawn here: the wording differs, but the bride clothed in righteousness is traceable to Isaiah 61.
entries.dissent: The sources agree on Isaiah 61:10 but grade it differently: Beale calls it the basis of the verse, the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible says it may recall it. They differ on the linen. Beale reads it as both the saints' deeds and God's acts for them. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible stresses moral purity. Keener links it to the linen of the high priest. MacArthur reads the linen as the saints' deeds, the fruit of the righteousness given to them, not that gift itself. He takes the bride here as the church, presented to Christ at the rapture, with the wedding meal at the start of the thousand-year kingdom; later in the book the bride widens to all the redeemed.

entries.title: Revelation 19:9, the marriage supper of the Lamb
entries.summary: The blessing on those invited to the Lamb's wedding supper takes up Isaiah 25:6-8, the feast God makes for all peoples on his mountain, where death is swallowed up.
entries.plain: **An invitation that names the old family table, not the restaurant, tells guests what kind of dinner it will be.** Isaiah 25 promises a great feast that God will host on his mountain for all peoples. At that meal he swallows up death and wipes away tears. Revelation 19 pronounces a blessing on the guests called to the Lamb's wedding meal. The study Bibles hear Isaiah's banquet here.
entries.same: A feast hosted by God at the end of the age, for guests from every people. Isaiah 25:6 speaks of a banquet for all the nations; John speaks of the guests at the Lamb's supper (deipnon).
entries.differs: Isaiah's feast is rich food and aged wine. John names no food at all. Isaiah has no wedding; John makes it the Lamb's marriage. Isaiah has God as host. John has the Lamb as groom. The wedding picture comes from other texts the sources name, such as Isaiah 54 and 62 and Hosea 2, and from Jesus' parables.
entries.turn: The long promise of a meal with God at the end now has a date and a host. Wright joins two old hopes here: Israel as God's bride and God's feast for all. The guests are believers from every nation, the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible says. The supper of verse 17 is its grim opposite.
entries.not: **Not the same meal as the great supper of God in verse 17.** That one is a feast of birds on the defeated. Heiser and Beale both set the two side by side as opposites.
entries.deeper: Beale says the end-time banquet of Isaiah 25:6-7 and 65:13-17 is perhaps echoed, together with the wedding parable of Matthew 22:1-14. Keener is firmer: the banquet here is from Isaiah 25:6. He adds that in Isaiah 25:9 God's people say let us rejoice and be glad, close to 19:7. The ESV Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cite Isaiah 25:6-9, and Wright cites Isaiah 25:6-10. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible says the wedding banquet was a common Jewish picture of the messianic age, and that later teachers even served Leviathan at it. In the vault's Septuagint, Isaiah 25:6 says the Lord shall make a feast for all the nations on this mountain. The grade is drawn here by Beale's definitions: no shared words, but a God-hosted feast for all peoples at the end traces to Isaiah 25.
entries.heiser: Heiser places the marriage supper at the end of the Bible's long story of meals with God, from Eden's tree of life to Abraham's meal in Genesis 18 and the elders on Sinai in Exodus 24. After Brant Pitre, he calls Isaiah 24 to 27 the fullest Old Testament end-time banquet. It is on Zion, for all peoples, and death is swallowed up (25:8). The elders of 24:23 he reads as the divine council. He sets this meal against the supper of 19:17, where birds eat the defeated. He places the actual wedding supper in the new Eden.
entries.dissent: Beale grades the Isaiah link with perhaps; Keener says the banquet is from Isaiah 25:6. On the wedding theme, Heiser after Smith names Isaiah 54:5 to 55:5, Wright names Isaiah 54 and 55, and Beale names Isaiah 62 and Hosea 2. MacArthur separates the guests from the bride. The bride is the church; the guests are believers from before Pentecost, with saints of the tribulation, and he calls it a difference of picture, not of standing.

entries.title: Revelation 19:11, in righteousness he judges
entries.summary: The rider who judges in righteousness takes a favorite psalm line about God judging the world rightly, also given to the king from Jesse's stem in Isaiah 11:4.
entries.plain: **A new judge who takes the oath of office repeats words that every good judge before her swore.** The Psalms say again and again that God will rule the world with justice. Isaiah 11 gives that task to the coming king from David's family. John says the rider on the white horse judges in righteousness and makes war. The judge of the Psalms is now on horseback.
entries.same: To judge in righteousness. The Greek of Psalm 96:13 (95:13 in the Greek) and Psalm 9:8 uses krinei with en dikaiosyne; John has en dikaiosyne krinei. Isaiah 11:4 also has the king judging the lowly.
entries.differs: In the Psalms God judges. In John the rider does, and he also makes war. John reverses the word order and puts righteousness first. The Psalms judge the world; John's rider judges the nations who follow the beast. Isaiah 11:4 in Greek speaks of judging the case of the lowly, not of righteousness.
entries.turn: Beale reads the war as a legal battle: the rider's judgment vindicates his people and condemns their oppressors. A task that belonged to God, and in Psalm 72 to the king's son, is carried out by Christ. The same Isaiah 11 text returns in verse 15.
entries.not: **Not a borrowing of a whole psalm.** John takes one phrase, judging in righteousness, which the psalms use of God and Isaiah 11:4 uses of the king. The war around it is John's own scene.
entries.deeper: Beale calls the phrase a collective allusion to a favorite psalm expression for God vindicating his afflicted people: Psalms 9:8, 72:2, 96:13 and 98:9 in the Greek, with Isaiah 11:4. He notes Acts 17:31 uses the same psalm texts for the day Christ will judge. He adds that Zechariah 9:9-10, the king who rides to victory, could be partly formative. The CSB Study Bible's cross-references list Psalms 9:8 and 96:13. Keener reads the rider as God going out as a warrior for his people (Isaiah 59:16-18; Zechariah 14:3). The grade is possible: the phrase is shared, but it is a formula found in several psalms.
entries.dissent: Beale finds the psalms and Isaiah 11:4 behind the phrase. Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible put the weight on the divine warrior texts, Isaiah 42:13 and 59:16-18 and Habakkuk 3. Beale also proposes 3 Maccabees 2:11 for the title faithful and true. Beale reads the war as a legal battle, not combat on a battlefield. MacArthur reads the scene as Christ's return to earth with his saints, all judgment, and sets it apart from the rapture, when he meets his own in the air.

aw.n: Revelation 19:11-21, the rider on the white horse
aw.s: Heaven opens and a rider on a white horse, named Faithful and True and the Word of God, leads heaven's armies, his robe stained with blood and a sword coming from his mouth, his title King of kings. Birds are summoned to feast on the fallen, the beast and the false prophet are seized and cast into the fiery lake, and their armies fall to the rider's sword.

entries.title: Revelation 19:12, eyes like a flame of fire
entries.summary: The rider's fiery eyes repeat the son of man's eyes from 1:14, which come from the shining man of Daniel 10:6.
entries.plain: **A film that brings back a hero in his famous coat needs no introduction.** In Daniel 10 a shining man has eyes like torches of fire. John used that picture for the risen Jesus in chapter 1 and again in chapter 2. Now the rider has the same fiery eyes. The reader knows at once who he is: the judge who sees everything.
entries.same: Eyes like fire. The Greek of Daniel 10:6 has hoi ophthalmoi autou hosei lampades pyros, his eyes as lamps of fire. John has hoi ophthalmoi autou phlox pyros, his eyes a flame of fire.
entries.differs: Daniel has lamps or torches; John has flame, as in 1:14 and 2:18. Here John even drops the word like. In Daniel the shining man brings a message about the last days. In John the eyes belong to the rider who judges.
entries.turn: Beale reads the eyes as the judge who knows the true state of everyone, as in the letter to Thyatira (2:18-23). The same eyes judged false believers there. So those judged here may include people inside the churches.
entries.not: **Not a new figure.** The fiery eyes tie the rider to the son of man of chapter 1, the CSB Study Bible and the ESV Study Bible both note.
entries.deeper: Beale says the judging role is enforced by Daniel 10:6, which John already used in 1:14 and 2:18. In Daniel 10 the heavenly figure reveals that Israel's persecutors will be judged in the latter days, which fits the judgment here. Keener refers back to 1:14 and Daniel 10:6. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible says fiery eyes suggested divinity and fury to ancient readers. The grade is drawn here: the picture is Daniel's and repeats 1:14, but the word is changed.
entries.heiser: Heiser passes over the eyes quickly. He says they draw on language from Daniel used earlier in the book for the risen Christ, and that by this point such Old Testament references are easy to pick out.

entries.title: Revelation 19:12, many crowns and a name no one knows
entries.summary: The crowns and the hidden name may recall Isaiah 62:2-3, where Zion is promised a new name and a royal diadem.
entries.plain: **A ring engraved with a private name means more to the couple than to anyone who reads it.** In Isaiah 62 God promises Jerusalem a new name that he will give, and calls her a royal crown in his hand. The rider wears many crowns and a written name that only he knows. Beale and one study Bible hear Isaiah's promise here.
entries.same: A crown (diadema) and a name. The Greek of Isaiah 62:3 has diadema basileias, a diadem of kingship, and 62:2 promises a new name (onoma kainon). Isaiah 65:15 promises God's servants a new name. John has diademata polla and onoma gegrammenon, many diadems and a written name.
entries.differs: Isaiah gives the new name and the crown to Jerusalem, God's people. John gives them to the rider. Isaiah's name is new; John's is unknown to all but the rider. Isaiah has one diadem, held in God's hand; the rider wears many on his head.
entries.turn: Beale reads Christ as standing for his people: Israel's promised name and crown are fulfilled in him first, and believers share his name (2:17; 3:12). The many crowns outrank the dragon's seven and the beast's ten. He alone is king of all.
entries.not: **Not a secret password the saved must learn.** Beale says the hidden name is about Christ's character being fully shown in judgment, not a word kept from everyone.
entries.deeper: Beale says that if there is an Old Testament background for the diadems and the secret name, it is Isaiah 62:2-3, supported by the allusion to Isaiah 63:1-3 in the next verse, with Isaiah 65:15 perhaps in mind. He links 19:12 with 2:17, where the wording is nearly the same. He then suggests the name may be the divine name, written as Yahweh's name was written on the high priest's forehead plate (Wisdom of Solomon 18:24). He notes a Targum on Exodus 6:3 says the name of the Word of the Lord was not known, which is close to 19:12-13. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible says the name recalls the new name promised to Israel (Isaiah 62:2; 65:15) and that the many crowns echo Isaiah 62:3. The grade is possible: Beale himself writes if there is a background.
entries.heiser: Heiser says the rider is marked with the name of Yahweh, as the beast's followers are marked with the beast's name. On the name by which he is called, he says most scholars opt for I am that I am, the divine name.
entries.dissent: Beale and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible hear Isaiah 62. Keener reads the unknown name against ancient magic, where knowing a name gave power over its bearer. The ESV Study Bible reads it as the part of the Son's being that can never be fully known. The CSB Study Bible says it shows God has not revealed everything (Deuteronomy 29:29).

entries.title: Revelation 19:13, a robe dipped in blood and the winepress
entries.summary: The rider's blood-soaked robe and his treading of the winepress come from Isaiah 63:1-3, where God returns from Edom with garments stained from trampling the nations.
entries.plain: **A soldier coming home in a mud-caked uniform tells the town what battle he has fought.** In Isaiah 63 a figure comes from Edom in red garments. He has trampled the grapes alone, and the nations' blood has spattered his clothes. That figure is God himself. John's rider wears a bloodied robe and tramples the grapes of God's anger. Isaiah's divine warrior is Jesus.
entries.same: A garment stained with blood, and a lone figure treading the winepress (lenos) as judgment on the nations. Isaiah 63:2-3 asks why the garments are red. The answer is that the nations' blood stained them. John's rider wears a bloodied robe and treads the winepress of God's fury.
entries.differs: Isaiah's warrior is God; John's is Christ. Isaiah says the blood was spattered on the garments. John says the robe was dipped. Beale calls dipped John's own equivalent of the Hebrew sprinkled; some copies of Revelation change it back to sprinkled. Isaiah tells the story after the battle. John shows the stained robe before the battle is told.
entries.turn: Beale reads the stains as God's justice, about to be carried out on the oppressors of his people. In Isaiah the warrior acts for vengeance and redemption; both are here. John does not soften the picture, but he puts it in the hands of the Lamb.
entries.not: **Not proof that the blood must be the enemy's alone.** Some readers take it as Christ's own blood or the martyrs'. Beale and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible think the enemy's blood most likely.
entries.deeper: Beale calls this a clear allusion to Isaiah 63:1-3 and says the allusion continues in verse 15 with the winepress of God's wrath (Isaiah 63:2-6). The Hebrew of Isaiah 63:3 reads veyez nitzcham al begaday, their juice spattered on my garments. The vault's Septuagint has my garments are defiled, without spattered. Beale notes a Palestinian Targum on Genesis 49:11 also changes the verb to dipped when it uses Isaiah 63 of the Messiah. He says Jewish readers took Isaiah 63 of the final judgment, sometimes of Rome or of Gog and Magog. Keener, the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the ESV Study Bible, the CSB Study Bible and Wright all name Isaiah 63. Walton notes Assyrian kings boasted of lands dyed red with enemy blood. The grade is Beale's: clear allusion.
entries.dissent: Whose blood? Beale and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible say the enemy's, as in Isaiah 63. The CSB Study Bible says the robe looks back to Jesus' death and forward to the winepress. Wright reads the real weapons as Jesus' own blood and self-giving love. Caird and Sweet, as Beale reports, take it as the blood of Christ or the martyrs. MacArthur says the blood is the enemies' but not from Armageddon, which begins only in verse 15; it stands for the battles Christ has already won over sin, Satan and death.

entries.title: Revelation 19:14, the armies of heaven follow him
entries.summary: The armies of heaven riding behind the rider may recall Zechariah 14:5, where the Lord comes with all his holy ones.
entries.plain: **A parade where the hometown team marches behind the champion lets everyone share the win.** Zechariah 14 says the Lord will come, and all his holy ones with him. John sees the armies of heaven on white horses, dressed in clean white linen, following the rider. Two sources hear Zechariah here. They also note that the linen is the bride's linen from verse 8.
entries.same: The Lord comes with a heavenly company behind him to judge. Zechariah 14:5 speaks of all the holy ones with him; John speaks of the armies in heaven following him.
entries.differs: Zechariah names holy ones, a word that can mean angels. John names armies and dresses them in the linen of the bride, which marks them as saints. Zechariah's Lord comes to the Mount of Olives; John's rider comes from an opened heaven. The armies do not fight. Only the rider strikes the enemy.
entries.turn: The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible says the army may include angels, as in Zechariah, but must include believers. Those who conquered the beast by dying now share Christ's victory. The armies win nothing by force; the rider's word does it.
entries.not: **Not an army of believers taking up swords.** The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible notes that the heavenly armies carry out no violence; Jesus alone strikes the wicked.
entries.deeper: The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible cites Zechariah 14:5 for the angels in the army, and Heiser points back to Zechariah 14 for the Lord coming with his holy ones. Beale weighs angels against saints. He notes that angel armies come with Christ elsewhere in the New Testament (Matthew 25:31; 2 Thessalonians 1:7). But he thinks 17:14 shows the followers are saints, since there the called and faithful come with the King of kings. He suggests both may be in view. Keener lists Old Testament heavenly armies (2 Kings 6:17; Isaiah 66:15; Habakkuk 3:8) and leans toward the angelic host. The grade is possible: no shared words, and two sources propose Zechariah.
entries.heiser: Heiser says the rider's company recalls the earlier use of Zechariah 14, the Lord coming with all his holy ones. He adds that the holy ones in white linen include believers. Rule with a rod of iron in verse 15 was promised to the one who overcomes (2:26-27), and Jesus shares his throne with him (3:21). So the returning holy ones are the divine council, human and heavenly, with Christ.
entries.dissent: Who rides? Keener thinks the image is mainly the angelic host. Beale, the ESV Study Bible, the CSB Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible put the saints first, because of the bride's linen. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible and Heiser include both. MacArthur lists the church, saints of the tribulation, believers of Old Testament times and angels, coming unarmed to reign with him, not to fight.

entries.title: Revelation 19:15, a sharp sword from his mouth
entries.summary: The sharp sword from the rider's mouth joins the servant's sword-like mouth in Isaiah 49:2 with the king who strikes the earth by his word in Isaiah 11:4.
entries.plain: **A headline that settles a case can do more damage than any weapon.** Isaiah 49 says God made his servant's mouth like a sharp sword. Isaiah 11 says the coming king will strike the land with a rod that comes from his lips. John joins the two. A sharp sword comes from the rider's mouth to strike the nations. At the end of the chapter that sword kills the beast's army.
entries.same: A sharp sword linked with the mouth, from Isaiah 49:2 (machairan oxeian in the Greek). Striking by what comes from the mouth, from Isaiah 11:4, where the Greek has pataxei ... to logo tou stomatos autou, he will strike with the word of his mouth. John has hromphaia oxeia ... pataxe ta ethne.
entries.differs: Isaiah 49 makes the servant's mouth like a sword. John puts a real sword in the mouth. Isaiah 11 strikes the earth; John strikes the nations. The Hebrew of Isaiah 11:4 says the rod of his mouth. The Greek says the word of his mouth. Beale thinks that Greek reading fits the rider's name, the Word of God. John's word for sword is not Isaiah's.
entries.turn: The rider wins by speaking. Beale reads the sword as God's word of accusation, a verdict that condemns. Jesus is the servant of Isaiah 49 and the king of Isaiah 11 at once. The sword that warned the churches in chapters 1 and 2 now judges the world.
entries.not: **Not a call to holy war.** Every source reads the sword as speech. Keener cites Hosea 6:5, God slaying by the words of his mouth.
entries.deeper: Beale says four Old Testament allusions shape this verse. The sword from the mouth is based on Isaiah 49:2, where the servant restores Israel and saves the nations by his word. The depiction is completed by an echo of Isaiah 11:4. The Hebrew there has shevet piv, the rod of his mouth; the Greek reads the word of his mouth, and the Targum follows the Greek. Beale adds 1 Enoch 62:2, which applies Isaiah 11:4 to the son of man, and Psalms of Solomon 17. He calls verse 21 a repeated allusion to both texts. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible says a well-known earlier Jewish work already linked Psalm 2:9 with Isaiah 11:4. The CSB Study Bible's cross-references list both Isaiah texts. The grade is drawn here: two texts woven together, neither repeated word for word.
entries.dissent: The sources agree on the two Isaiah texts. Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible add the Wisdom of Solomon 18:15-16, God's word leaping from heaven like a warrior with a sharp sword. The CSB Study Bible hears strike the nations as Psalm 2:9.

entries.title: Revelation 19:15, rule them with a rod of iron
entries.summary: The rider shepherds the nations with a rod of iron, the promise of Psalm 2:9 in the wording of the Greek translation.
entries.plain: **A translation that picks one meaning of a tricky word can steer every later reader.** In Psalm 2 God tells his anointed king that he will break the rebel nations with a rod of iron. The old Greek translation read the Hebrew verb as shepherd instead of break. John follows the Greek. The rider will shepherd the nations with an iron rod. Here that means to crush.
entries.same: A rod of iron used on the nations. The Greek of Psalm 2:9 reads poimaneis autous en rhabdo sidera, you will shepherd them with a rod of iron. John has poimanei autous en rhabdo sidera, almost word for word.
entries.differs: The psalm speaks to the king, you will. John speaks of the rider, he will. The Hebrew reads tero'em, you will break them. The Greek, and John with it, has shepherd. Beale says the Hebrew letters can be read either way. Here John means destroy, not care for.
entries.turn: Psalm 2 promises God's son victory over the rulers who plot against God and his anointed. John says Jesus fulfills it. Yet in 2:26-27 the same promise is made to believers who overcome, and in 12:5 to the child born of the woman. The rule of the Messiah is shared with his people.
entries.not: **Not gentle shepherding.** In other texts the verb means tending a flock. Here, with an iron rod and a sword, Beale says the main sense is destruction.
entries.deeper: Beale calls this an allusion and later an undoubted reference to Psalm 2:9. The vault's Septuagint has poimaneis, you shall shepherd; the Hebrew of Psalm 2:9 is tero'em beshevet barzel, you shall break them with a rod of iron. Beale thinks the translator, or John, saw in the unpointed Hebrew both shepherd and break, and chose shepherd to hold both ideas. He notes the Greek uses the same verb for devastate in Micah 5:6 and Jeremiah 6:3 and 22:22. He points to Psalms of Solomon 17:24, which joins Psalm 2:9 to the word of the king's mouth, as John does. The ESV Study Bible, the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible and Wright all name Psalm 2. The grade is drawn here by Beale's definitions: the wording is almost identical to the Greek psalm.
entries.heiser: Heiser notes that rule with a rod of iron is applied here to the returning Christ, but in 2:26-27 to believers who overcome. With 3:21, where Jesus shares his throne, he calls it a shared messianic rule. The white-clad holy ones who return with him, he says, include us.
entries.dissent: The sources agree on Psalm 2:9 and on the Greek wording. They differ on whether any saving sense remains in shepherd. Beale sees no hint of salvation here, only judgment. Wright stresses that Jesus wins with his own blood and self-giving love.

entries.title: Revelation 19:16, King of kings and Lord of lords
entries.summary: The name on the rider's robe and thigh is a title the Old Testament gives to God, in Deuteronomy 10:17 and in Daniel, where Beale finds it in the Greek of Daniel 4:37.
entries.plain: **A title once given to the real owner, and later stolen by a pretender, means more when it is handed back.** Eastern kings called themselves king of kings. Deuteronomy 10 calls Israel's God Lord of lords. In Daniel the pagan king learns that God is the true king of heaven. Now the rider wears the full double title, king over all kings and lord over all lords. It belongs to him alone.
entries.same: Lord of lords, a title for the one God over every ruler, in Deuteronomy 10:17 (kyrios ton kyrion in the Greek). Daniel 2:47 calls God Lord of kings. John has basileus basileon kai kyrios kyrion.
entries.differs: Deuteronomy pairs God over all gods with Lord over all lords. John pairs king over all kings with lord over all lords. Beale says John's full pair is found in the old Greek of Daniel 4:37. The Greek Daniel kept in the vault is a later version. It has only king of heaven at 4:37, so the full pair could not be checked there. John gives the title to Christ, as he did in 17:14.
entries.turn: Nebuchadnezzar, king of the first Babylon, was hailed as king of kings until God humbled him. Beale reads the title as handed to Christ, who judges the latter-day Babylon. Rome's emperors, and the Parthian kings who used the same title, are shown up as pretenders.
entries.not: **Not a title borrowed from Parthia.** Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible note the Parthian kings used it, but Jewish tradition had given it to God long before.
entries.deeper: Beale says the name is taken from the Greek of Daniel 4:37, where it is a title for God, and is applied to Christ typologically, so God's handling of Nebuchadnezzar foreshadows Jesus' handling of the latter Babylon. The vault's Daniel, the version called Theodotion, reads at 4:37 ton basilea tou ouranou, the king of heaven. Beale's reading of the old Greek is reported, not checked, here. Keener cites Deuteronomy 10:17, Daniel 2:47 and Zechariah 14:9. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible adds Psalm 136:3 and notes the title was used of eastern monarchs (Ezra 7:12; Ezekiel 26:7; Daniel 2:37). The CSB Study Bible's cross-references give Deuteronomy 10:17, Daniel 2:47 and 1 Timothy 6:15. Applied to someone new is the label drawn here, since the old Greek wording could not be checked. The grade is drawn here: the pair is a stock title, but its use for God against a Babylonian king points to Daniel.
entries.dissent: Beale traces the title to the Greek of Daniel 4:37. Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible name Deuteronomy 10:17 and Daniel 2:47 and stress the Parthian royal title as the setting. The ESV Study Bible names no Old Testament source.
