entries.title: Revelation 19:17-18, the great supper of God
entries.summary: The angel's call to the birds to eat the flesh of kings, horses and warriors is Ezekiel 39's summons to the birds after the defeat of Gog.
entries.plain: **A second invitation printed in the same type as the first, but for a very different event, is meant to make readers shudder.** In Ezekiel 39, after Gog's army falls, God tells the birds and beasts to gather and feast on fallen warriors and the blood of princes. John's angel calls the birds to the great supper of God. They will eat kings, captains, horses and riders. John gives Gog's end to the beast's army.
entries.same: The summons to every bird to gather (synachthete in both Greek texts) and eat the flesh of the fallen. The list of the dead: kings or princes, mighty men, horses and their riders. Ezekiel 39:20 says they will be filled at God's table; John says the birds were filled (echortasthesan) with their flesh.
entries.differs: Ezekiel calls birds and beasts; John calls only birds, flying in midheaven like the eagle of 8:13. Ezekiel calls it God's sacrifice; John calls it the great supper of God. John adds free and slave, small and great. Ezekiel's enemy is Gog; John's is the beast, the false prophet and their armies.
entries.turn: Beale says the angel updates Ezekiel. The prophecy still waited, and now Christ is the one who wins and the beast is Gog. In Ezekiel the defeat makes God's holy name known to Israel and the nations. The same theme of the name runs through 19:11-16.
entries.not: **Not the marriage supper of verse 9.** The two meals are opposites. Beale calls this one a macabre parody of the wedding feast.
entries.deeper: Beale sets Ezekiel 39:4 and 17-20 beside 19:17-18 and says the angel announces the beast's defeat with the same imagery as Gog's. The vault's Septuagint of Ezekiel 39:17 has eipon panti orneo ... synachthete kai erchesthe, speak to every bird ... gather and come; 39:20 has you shall be filled at my table with horse and rider. Beale adds that Jewish readers applied the passage to Rome, and one midrash paired it with the wedding of the righteous. Keener, the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the ESV Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible all name Ezekiel 39:17-20; the ESV Study Bible adds the covenant curse of Deuteronomy 28:26. Walton notes that lying unburied for birds was the worst curse imaginable in the ancient world. The grade is drawn here: the summons, the guest list and the meal could hardly come from anywhere else.
entries.heiser: Heiser, following Meredith Kline, says there is only one Old Testament passage where birds and beasts are summoned to feed on the dead at the cosmic mountain: Ezekiel 39, Gog and Magog. Kline also lists the earthquake, sword, hail and burning sulfur of Ezekiel 38:19-22. So chapters 16, 19 and 20 all retell the one Gog battle. Heiser calls this repetition, not a line of separate events. He also links the birds to Psalm 74:14, where animals eat Leviathan, chaos consumed.
entries.dissent: The sources agree on Ezekiel 39. They differ on what it means for the order of events. Beale, after Kline, and Heiser hold that 19:17-21 and 20:7-10 tell the same battle. Others Beale names see two battles, or treat Gog as a broad label for God's enemies. MacArthur sees two: this is the battle of Armageddon at the close of the tribulation, and the Gog and Magog revolt of 20:8 comes a thousand years later.

entries.title: Revelation 19:19, the kings of the earth gathered for war
entries.summary: The beast and the earth's kings gathered to make war on the rider recall Psalm 2:2, with the gathering of nations in Ezekiel 38 and Zechariah 14.
entries.plain: **A crowd that boos the referee at the start of a final it cannot win is following an old script.** Psalm 2 opens with the kings of the earth gathering against the Lord and his anointed. Ezekiel and Zechariah foresee nations gathered for a last war. John sees the beast and the earth's kings massed with their armies against the rider. The outcome was settled long ago.
entries.same: The kings of the earth gathered (synago) against God's anointed. The Greek of Psalm 2:2 has hoi basileis tes ges ... synechthesan; John has tous basileis tes ges ... synegmena. Ezekiel 38:7-8 uses the same perfect passive participle for Gog's gathered army.
entries.differs: The psalm's kings gather against the Lord and his anointed. John's gather against the rider and his army, and the beast leads them. The psalm has no battle scene. John uses the war, with the article, as if readers already know which war. Zechariah's nations gather against Jerusalem; John names no city here.
entries.turn: Beale says the kings do not gather on their own. Demonic spirits and Satan stir them, as 16:14 and 20:8 show. Behind it all, God is the one who draws them. The psalm settled the result: the Messiah wins.
entries.not: **Not a quotation of Psalm 2.** John borrows the psalm's picture of earth's kings massing against God's anointed king, and joins it to the gathered armies of Ezekiel and Zechariah.
entries.deeper: Beale says Psalm 2:2 rings in the background, and the undoubted use of Psalm 2:9 in verse 15 supports the further allusion. He reads 16:14, 19:19 and 20:8 as one battle, the final war the prophets foretold. Behind it he places God gathering the nations, from Zechariah 12 to 14 and perhaps Zephaniah 3, and from Ezekiel 38:2-9 and 39:2. Of all the parallels, only Ezekiel 38:7-8 has the perfect passive participle that John uses. Later Jewish readers, he notes, took the rebels of Psalm 2:2 as Gog and Magog. The ESV Study Bible links the battle back to 16:14. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cites Psalm 2:12 at verse 21. The grade is drawn here: the kings of the earth gathered against God's Messiah trace to Psalm 2, though the wording is only partly shared.
entries.dissent: Beale finds Psalm 2:2 beside Ezekiel and Zechariah, and reads 16:14, 19:19 and 20:8 as one final battle told in the same words. MacArthur takes 16:14 and 19:19 as the battle of Armageddon and 20:8 as a separate revolt at the end of the thousand years. Keener names no Old Testament text but notes that Jewish views of the final war tried to fit different Old Testament pictures together. The CSB Study Bible's cross-references list other gathering texts (Numbers 27:3; Judges 6:33; Isaiah 13:4).

entries.title: Revelation 19:20, thrown alive into the lake of fire
entries.summary: The beast thrown into the burning lake of fire recalls Daniel 7:11, where the beast is slain and given to the burning fire, beside the river of fire before God's throne.
entries.plain: **A sequel that ends with the villain falling into the same fire as the first story makes the link plain.** In Daniel 7 the fourth beast is killed and its body handed over to be burned. A river of fire flows from God's throne. John's beast and false prophet are seized and hurled, still living, into a burning lake of sulfur. Daniel's beast meets its end again.
entries.same: The beast (therion) given over to fire. The Greek of Daniel 7:11 has the beast destroyed and given eis kausin pyros, to the burning of fire. John has the beast thrown eis ten limnen tou pyros tes kaiomenes, into the lake of fire that burns. Daniel 7:10 has a river of fire before the throne.
entries.differs: Daniel's beast is killed first, then burned. John's beast is thrown in alive, with the false prophet. Daniel has a river of fire; John has a lake. John adds sulfur. Beale says John reads Daniel's brief burning in the light of the endless punishment of 14:10-11 and 20:10.
entries.turn: The beast of Daniel stood for kingdoms that crushed God's people. Its end is now carried out on the beast of Revelation. The devil follows in 20:10, and death and Hades in 20:14. Beale notes that the throne and the opened books of 20:11-12, also from Daniel 7, sit right beside that lake.
entries.not: **Not Daniel's scene retold word for word.** In Daniel the beast is slain and its body burned. John has the beast and its false prophet thrown, still living, into the burning lake.
entries.deeper: Beale says John highlights an allusion to Ezekiel 38 and especially Daniel 7:11, perhaps with Daniel 7:9-10. He suggests the lake that burns joins the beast's burning in Daniel 7:11 with the river of fire before the throne. A Greek variant of Daniel 7:9-10, a burning fire, a river of fire, may have helped. So may the burning furnace phrases of Daniel 3. The vault's Daniel (Theodotion) has 7:11 edothe eis kausin pyros. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible says in Daniel 7:11 the beast was slain and thrown into fire, and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible and Keener cite Daniel 7:11. Keener adds Isaiah 30:33. On 20:14 the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible notes that a lake usually holds water, and points again to the river of fire from God's throne; the Aramaic of Daniel 7:10 is nehar di nur, a river of fire. The grade is drawn here: the beast handed to fire is traceable to Daniel 7, though the lake is new.
entries.heiser: Heiser does not discuss Daniel 7 at this verse. In the Revelation 20 lecture he reports Justin Bass's suggestion that the lake of fire may be the river of fire of Daniel 7:9-10, where the beast is judged. Heiser treats this as a suggestion.
entries.dissent: Beale reads the pair as all who play the part of beast and false prophet at the end. MacArthur reads the beast as the Antichrist and the false prophet as his religious partner, thrown in alive with changed bodies; since they are still there in 20:10, he says, annihilation is ruled out. Beale and the study Bibles read the lake as endless conscious punishment, citing 20:10. Heiser keeps open whether the second death means final destruction or endless torment. Wright hears the fate of Sodom and Gomorrah in the burning sulfur.

entries.title: Revelation 19:20, fire and sulfur
entries.summary: The burning sulfur of the lake may echo Ezekiel 38:22, where God rains fire and sulfur on Gog and his armies.
entries.plain: **Two words that always come as a pair can carry a whole story with them.** In Ezekiel 38 God judges Gog with plague, hail, fire and sulfur rained down on him and his troops. John's lake burns with sulfur. Beale, and Heiser after Kline, hear Ezekiel's judgment of Gog here, since the birds of verses 17 and 18 come from the next chapter.
entries.same: Fire and sulfur together as God's weapon against the end-time enemy. The Greek of Ezekiel 38:22 has pyr kai theion; John has tou pyros ... en theio.
entries.differs: In Ezekiel the fire and sulfur rain down from above. In John they fill a lake. Ezekiel lists plague, blood, rain and hailstones too; John keeps only the pair. Gog's whole army is struck in Ezekiel. In John only the two leaders go into the lake; their army dies by the sword.
entries.turn: The pair ties the beast's end to the Gog story that shapes this whole battle. Kline, as Heiser reports him, lists Ezekiel's weapons that John reuses. They include the sword, the hail and the burning sulfur.
entries.not: **Not a link that rests on Ezekiel alone.** Fire and sulfur also fell on Sodom, and the pair is common in judgment scenes. The echo is possible because the next chapter of Ezekiel is plainly in view.
entries.deeper: Beale says fire and brimstone echo Ezekiel 38:22, where the same two words describe the judgment of Gog and Magog, which is clearly alluded to in 19:17-18 and 21. He notes the participle burning agrees with lake in gender but with fire in case, perhaps on purpose. He cites Ezekiel 38:22 and 39:6 again when he argues that 19:17-21 and 20:7-10 are the same battle, by sword and by fire. Heiser reads Kline's list: sword (Ezekiel 38:21), hail and fiery sulfur (38:22; 39:6), set against 16:21 and 19:20. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible notes that Jewish tradition pictured Gehenna as burning. The grade is possible: a common pair of words, proposed by two sources.
entries.heiser: Reading Kline, Heiser lists the instruments of judgment shared by Ezekiel and John: earthquakes (Ezekiel 38:19-20), the sword (38:21), and hail with fiery sulfur (38:22; 39:6). He sets the last against Revelation 16:21 and 19:20. For him this is part of the proof that Revelation 16, 19 and 20 recycle one Gog event.
entries.dissent: Beale and Heiser tie the sulfur to Ezekiel 38:22. Wright hears the fate of Sodom and Gomorrah. Keener treats judgment by fire as a standard feature of Jewish accounts of the end.

entries.title: Revelation 20:2-3, the powers locked in the pit
entries.summary: The dragon seized, bound and shut in the abyss until a set time echoes Isaiah's day when the powers above and the kings below are herded into a pit and punished after many days.
entries.plain: **A judge who orders a dangerous man held in custody until trial has not finished the case, only paused it.** Isaiah 24 tells of a day when God punishes the rebel powers in the heavens and the kings on earth. They are rounded up like prisoners and shut in a pit. Only after many days are they punished. John sees an angel seize the dragon and lock him in the abyss. He stays there a thousand years before his end.
entries.same: In both scenes a cosmic enemy is captured and held in a pit. He is kept there a long time before the last sentence. Beale reads Isaiah 27:1 as the sequel. Its Greek names the foe the dragon and the serpent. John gives him the same two names.
entries.differs: Isaiah speaks of a whole crowd: rebel powers above and rulers below. John names one prisoner, the dragon, Satan himself. Isaiah gives many days; John gives a thousand years. Isaiah has no angel with a key and a chain, and no sealing of the door. John also adds a short release before the end, which Isaiah does not mention. The sources give no reason for these changes.
entries.turn: Isaiah saw the powers above and the kings below rounded up, locked in a pit and sentenced after a long time. John follows the same order. Satan is seized and shut away, and his final sentence comes later, in 20:10. The sources differ on when the binding happens.
entries.not: **Not a quotation of Isaiah.** John borrows the order of Isaiah 24:21-22, capture, prison and a late sentence, with the dragon and serpent of Isaiah 27:1. Isaiah's prisoners are many; John's is one.
entries.deeper: Beale says Isaiah 24:21-22 is the basis for Revelation 20:2-3 and finds its fulfillment there. The Hebrew of 24:22 reads ve'ussefu asefah asir al bor, gathered as prisoners in a pit, vesuggeru al masger, shut up in a prison, and umerov yamim yippakedu, after many days they will be punished. The Greek translation turns the pit into a fortress and a jail and the many days into many generations, but keeps a verb of locking (apokleiso) related to John's ekleisen, he shut. Beale ties in Isaiah 27:1, since the Hebrew for in that day the Lord will punish occurs only there and in 24:21; the Greek of 27:1 reads ton drakonta ophin, the dragon, the serpent, close to John's ton drakonta, ho ophis ho archaios. He also notes that Isaiah and Revelation 20 both have two stages of punishment for the evil powers. Later Jewish writings read Isaiah's host on high as evil angels. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible says the binding alludes to Isaiah 24:21-22 and 27:1, and Keener finds the interval of 20:5 suggested by the same passage. 1 Enoch 10 has angels binding the Watchers in a pit until judgment. The grade is drawn here: the pattern of capture, prison and delayed sentence is traceable to Isaiah.
entries.dissent: Beale holds the binding began at the cross and limits only Satan's power to rally the nations for the final war; Satan is not removed from the world. MacArthur reads it as future, after Christ returns: Satan and his demons are locked away for a literal thousand years while Christ reigns on earth. He argues that a number joined to years in Scripture always means real years. The ESV Study Bible sets out three readings: premillennial interpreters see a complete removal of Satan in a future age, while amillennial interpreters tie the binding to Jesus' first coming. The CSB Study Bible thinks the present-binding view has been weakened. Keener follows the order of the story as it stands and leaves the question open.

aw.n: Revelation 20:1-6, Satan bound and the thousand years
aw.s: An angel with the key to the Abyss and a great chain seizes the dragon, binds him for a thousand years and seals him in the Abyss so that he cannot deceive the nations. Those beheaded for their witness, who refused the beast and its mark, come to life and reign with Christ for the thousand years, the first resurrection, over which the second death has no power.

entries.title: Revelation 20:2, that ancient serpent
entries.summary: Calling the dragon the ancient serpent and stopping him from deceiving points back to the serpent of Eden, whose lie brought the first fall.
entries.plain: **A detective who files a new arrest under an old case number is saying this is the same offender.** John calls the dragon the ancient serpent, the same title he used in 12:9. That points back to the garden, where the serpent lied to Eve and Adam. Now the angel locks him up so he can no longer deceive the nations. The first deceiver is finally restrained.
entries.same: The serpent (ophis) and the act of deceiving. In Genesis the serpent deceives the woman; in 20:3 and 20:8 the serpent is stopped from deceiving, then released to deceive again. The Greek of Genesis 3:1 uses the same word for serpent.
entries.differs: Genesis never calls the serpent the devil or Satan, and never calls it ancient. John adds those names and joins the serpent to the dragon. In Eden the serpent deceives two people. In John it deceives whole nations. The sources give no reason beyond the identification already made in 12:9.
entries.turn: Beale reads the restraint as a reversal of Eden. The serpent ruined the first human pair and their task of ruling the earth for God. Jesus, the last Adam, now holds back the deceiver so that the people of God can carry out that task among the nations.
entries.not: **Not a new enemy.** The dragon of this chapter is the same figure as in chapter 12. John does not introduce a second devil for the end.
entries.deeper: Beale says the name the ancient serpent in 20:2, with deception in 20:3, is an allusion to Genesis 3:1 and 3:14, as he argued on 12:9. In Genesis 3:4-5 the serpent says God's command is untrue and God's motive is selfish; the deception led to the fall. Beale argues that the binding restrains the serpent from repeating, among the nations, what he did in Eden. The CSB Study Bible lists Genesis 3:13 among its cross-references for deceive in 20:8. The ESV Study Bible links the titles to 12:9-17. In the Greek of Genesis 3:1 the serpent is ho ophis; John has ho ophis ho archaios. The grade is drawn here: the title and the act of deceiving point to one passage.
entries.dissent: Beale reads the restraint as partial and present: the serpent is kept from blinding the nations to the gospel. Other readers of the binding, as the ESV Study Bible sets out, take it as a complete removal still to come. MacArthur reads it as a full removal in a future thousand-year kingdom, with the demons locked away too, so that their influence is gone from the world.

entries.title: Revelation 20:4, thrones and judgment given
entries.summary: The thrones and the judgment given to those seated on them come from Daniel 7, where thrones are set and the verdict is given for the holy ones, who then take the kingdom.
entries.plain: **A courtroom drawing shows the bench, the judges and the people the verdict is for.** In Daniel 7 thrones are set up, the court sits, and a verdict is given in favour of God's holy people. Then they receive the kingdom. John sees thrones too, and judgment given. But now God's people sit on the thrones themselves, and they reign with Christ.
entries.same: Thrones, plural, set for a court, as in Daniel 7:9. Judgment given (krima edothe), as in the Greek of Daniel 7:22, where judgment is given to the holy ones. In both the verdict leads to the saints reigning.
entries.differs: In Daniel the court sits and gives the verdict for the holy ones; the people and the judges are distinct. In John the faithful dead sit on the thrones, so they share the judging. Daniel's holy ones are Israel's faithful; John's are those who refused the beast, the martyrs among them. John adds a thousand years, which Daniel does not have.
entries.turn: Daniel saw thrones set in place and judgment given for the saints, who then received the kingdom. John sees that courtroom again. The faithful who refused the beast are vindicated and reign with Christ. The sources differ on where and when that reign takes place.
entries.not: **Not a courtroom John made up.** The thrones and the verdict come from Daniel's courtroom, as Beale, Wright and three study Bibles note.
entries.deeper: Beale calls the wording a partial allusion to Daniel 7:22, widened by I saw thrones to include Daniel 7:9. The Greek of Daniel 7:22 reads to krima edoken hagiois, he gave judgment to the holy ones; John has krima edothe autois, judgment was given to them. Daniel 7:9 has thronoi etethesan, thrones were set; the Aramaic has korsavan remiv. Beale lists five views of who sits on the thrones and prefers exalted believers with angels, since the only other plural thrones in Revelation are the elders' in 4:4 and 11:16; a Talmud passage views Daniel's court as God, angels and the Messiah. He notes the vindication in Daniel 7 leads to the kingdom (7:18, 27). The ESV Study Bible names the echoes of Daniel 7:9 and 22; the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible says amillennialists read vv 4-6 as fulfilling them; the CSB Study Bible lists Daniel 7:18, 22 and 27. The grade is drawn here: plural thrones with judgment given are traceable to Daniel 7.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads the plural thrones as the divine council, widened to include believers. He walks through Beale's five options and agrees with the fifth: angels and exalted believers together. After Aune he adds that the verb they sat has no stated subject, pointing back to Daniel 7:9-10, where the son of man, the holy ones and their people all inherit the rule. His pastoral conclusion: a believer who dies now joins the council's rule at once.
entries.dissent: Who sits on the thrones? Beale lists martyrs, all believers, the angelic court of Daniel 7, angels standing for saints, and his own choice, believers with angels. Beale and Wright read the reign as heavenly, during the present age. MacArthur reads the souls as martyrs of the tribulation who reign on earth for the thousand years, with the redeemed of both Testaments. The ESV Study Bible notes that premillennial interpreters place the thrones on earth in a future reign, while amillennial interpreters read the Daniel echoes as putting them in heaven. Keener follows the narrative as most naturally future and leaves the figure open.

entries.title: Revelation 20:4, they came to life
entries.summary: The last chapters of Revelation follow the order of Ezekiel's last chapters, and the word for came to life is the word Ezekiel uses when the dry bones live.
entries.plain: **A film that follows the chapters of a famous novel in order is retelling that book, even when the dialogue is new.** Ezekiel ends with four scenes. Dry bones come to life. God's king rules his people. Gog attacks and is destroyed. Then a new temple and city appear. Revelation 20 to 22 runs in the same order. In 20:4 the faithful come to life, the same verb Ezekiel uses for the bones.
entries.same: The verb ezesan, they lived, is in the Greek of Ezekiel 37:10 and in Revelation 20:4. Both times God's people come to life. The order matches too. First life from the dead, then a kingdom, then Gog and Magog, then the new city.
entries.differs: Ezekiel's bones are the whole house of Israel, raised as a nation and brought home. John's are those who stayed faithful to Jesus. Ezekiel's kingdom has David as king with no length given; John's lasts a thousand years. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible notes the match is not exact: Ezekiel has no thousand years, and John's city has no temple.
entries.turn: By following Ezekiel's order John tells readers that the end he describes is the end Ezekiel saw. Beale reads the coming to life, like Ezekiel's, as a picture of restoration that John applies to the church. Wright says this is why the Gog episode must come after the first resurrection.
entries.not: **Not a quotation of the dry bones vision.** The link rests on one verb and on the order of scenes, which Keener, Beale and Wright all note.
entries.deeper: Beale sets out a fourfold ending: resurrection of God's people (Revelation 20:4a; Ezekiel 37:1-14), messianic kingdom (20:4b-6; Ezekiel 37:15-28), the battle with Gog and Magog (20:7-10; Ezekiel 38-39), and the new temple and city on a high mountain (21:1-22:5; Ezekiel 40-48). In that light he reads ezesan in 20:4 as an echo of the same form in the Greek of Ezekiel 37:10, with future forms in 37:6 and 14. Since Ezekiel's resurrection pictures Israel's return from exile, he takes 20:4-6 as a spiritual resurrection, universalized and applied to the church; Ezekiel 37:10 is also used figuratively in 11:11. Keener says Revelation 20 onward especially expounds Ezekiel 37-48, and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible says John follows that sequence to some degree. Wright notes Ezekiel 38 comes straight after the return from exile pictured as resurrection. The grade is drawn here: the order of ideas is traceable to Ezekiel alone.
entries.dissent: Beale reads the coming to life as spiritual: the faithful dead live with Christ in heaven. He reports that Fiorenza grants the Ezekiel echo but takes it as a bodily rising, as the same verb is in 2:8. The ESV Study Bible sets the premillennial bodily reading against the amillennial heavenly one. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible says the parallel with Ezekiel is partial. MacArthur reads it as a bodily rising: the martyrs enter the thousand-year kingdom in raised bodies.

entries.title: Revelation 20:5, the first resurrection
entries.summary: The rest of the dead and the first resurrection may draw on Daniel 12:2, where many who sleep in the dust wake, some to life and some to shame.
entries.plain: **Two invitations can come from one wedding, one to the feast and one to the door.** Daniel 12 says many who sleep in the dust will wake. Some wake to a life that lasts forever. Others wake to disgrace. John speaks of a first resurrection for the faithful and of the rest of the dead, who come to life later and face the second death. The sources hear Daniel's two groups behind John's words.
entries.same: The dead rising, with two outcomes: life for one group and judgment for the other. Daniel 12:2 and Revelation 20 both speak of the dead coming back in two kinds.
entries.differs: Daniel gives one waking with two outcomes. John separates the faithful who come to life in 20:4 from the rest of the dead, who wait until the thousand years end. He calls the first a resurrection and the end of the others the second death. Daniel uses neither phrase. Keener notes Daniel does not separate the two in time.
entries.turn: John promises the faithful that death has no claim on them. The resurrection Daniel waited for is theirs first. The others will rise too, but to judgment before the great white throne in 20:11-15.
entries.not: **Not a quotation of Daniel 12:2.** John takes up Daniel's hope of the dead rising to two outcomes, in his own terms: a first resurrection and a second death. The phrase second resurrection never occurs, as Heiser stresses.
entries.deeper: The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible says Daniel had predicted a resurrection of the damned, citing Daniel 12:2, with 2 Baruch 51 and John 5:29. Beale reads 20:12 as assuming the last great resurrection of righteous and unrighteous, in light of 20:5 and Daniel 12:2. Keener says the punishment of the rest after an interval may come from Isaiah 24:21-22, though Daniel 12:2 has no gap between the two. In the vault's Greek Daniel, 12:2 reads houtoi eis zoen aionion, kai houtoi eis oneidismon, these to everlasting life and these to reproach. John's word for came to life is ezesan; Daniel's verb for waking is exegerthesontai. Beale himself takes the first resurrection in 20:4-6 as spiritual and the rising of 20:12-13 as bodily. The grade is possible: the wording is only generally similar, and two sources name Daniel.
entries.heiser: Heiser says the first resurrection is the general resurrection the Old Testament expected, as in Daniel 12. The second death is the final judgment, either endless dying or annihilation; he keeps both open. He points out that the phrase second resurrection never occurs. In his reading 20:11-15 describes the same general resurrection again from the side of judgment, and Aune's survey shows the two-sided resurrection already in Second Temple writings, before the rabbis.
entries.dissent: Beale takes the first resurrection as spiritual life with Christ after death, and the rising of 20:12-13 as the bodily resurrection of all. Heiser reads the first resurrection as the general bodily one of Daniel 12, after Christ's return. The ESV Study Bible sets out the premillennial view of two bodily resurrections a thousand years apart. The CSB Study Bible notes that first implies a second resurrection to come. MacArthur sees two kinds of resurrection. The first, for the redeemed of the Old Testament, the church and the tribulation, comes before the thousand years; the second, for unbelievers, comes at the great white throne.

entries.title: Revelation 20:6, priests of God and of Christ
entries.summary: Those in the first resurrection will be priests and will reign, the promise of Exodus 19:6 given to those raised first, with Isaiah 61:6's end-time priests and Daniel's reigning saints.
entries.plain: **A family motto carved over the door of a new house tells you who lives there now.** At Sinai God told Israel they would be his kingdom of priests. Isaiah 61 promised that one day the whole nation would bear the name of the Lord's priests. John says those raised first will serve as priests to God and to Christ. They will also reign with him. He used the promise twice before, in 1:6 and 5:10.
entries.same: Priests and reigning together, as in Exodus 19:6, where Israel is a royal priesthood. Hiereis, priests, the word of the Greek of Isaiah 61:6. The kingdom given to the holy ones in Daniel 7:27.
entries.differs: Exodus has one phrase, a kingdom of priests or royal priesthood; John has two verbs, they will be priests and they will reign. Isaiah names them priests of the Lord. John names both God and Christ as the ones they serve, setting Christ beside God. Exodus speaks to Israel at Sinai. John speaks to all who share the first resurrection.
entries.turn: The promise to Israel at Sinai now belongs to the whole church, Jew and Gentile, as in 1:6 and 5:10. Beale reads the reign as already begun for the faithful dead in heaven. It will be completed at the end.
entries.not: **Not a reward for martyrs only.** Beale argues that the use of Exodus 19:6 and Isaiah 61:6, both about the whole people, points to all the faithful.
entries.deeper: Beale says the promise is based on Exodus 19:6, already applied to the whole community in 1:6 and 5:9-10, and makes a partial allusion to Isaiah 61:6, where the whole nation in the end time will be called priests of the Lord. The Greek of Isaiah 61:6 reads hymeis de hiereis kyriou klethesesthe; John has esontai hiereis tou theou kai tou christou. The Greek of Exodus 19:6 has basileion hierateuma, royal priesthood. The Targum of Isaiah 61:3-6 adds that the nation will be princes wearing diadems. Beale also names Daniel 7:27, the kingdom given to the holy ones, and Zechariah 6:13, a priest on his throne. Against Elliott, who denies that 20:6 alludes to Exodus 19:6 because it speaks only of martyrs, Beale argues the promise covers the whole church. Keener and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible point back to their notes on 1:6. The grade is drawn here: priests and reign together are traceable to Exodus 19:6, as in 1:6.
entries.heiser: In his Revelation 19 lecture Heiser lists Exodus 19:6 as the clearest case of John giving Israel's language to the church: the kingdom of priests in 1:6, 5:10 and 20:6 includes Gentiles. He uses it to argue that Revelation's people of God are not a Jewish group only.
entries.dissent: Elliott, as Beale reports, holds that 20:6 does not allude to Exodus 19:6, since he limits the promise to martyrs and to a future reign. Beale rejects both points. The ESV Study Bible reads the priests as the victors who resist the beast and reign with Christ through the era of the binding. MacArthur reads the reign as the thousand-year kingdom on earth, shared by the redeemed of every era, and the blessing as entry into it.

entries.title: Revelation 20:8, Gog and Magog
entries.summary: Satan gathers the nations for battle under the names Gog and Magog, Ezekiel's last enemy, now drawn from the four corners of the earth.
entries.plain: **When people call a tyrant a new Pharaoh, everyone knows which story they mean.** Ezekiel 38 and 39 tell of Gog, ruler of the land of Magog, who leads a vast army from the far north against God's restored people. God destroys him. John names Gog and Magog outright. But now they are the nations of the whole earth, gathered by Satan for one last war against God's people.
entries.same: The names Gog and Magog. A gathering of nations for war against God's people, as in Ezekiel 38-39, where God gathers Gog and leads him against the mountains of Israel. Beale traces John's gathering for the war to Ezekiel 38:2-8 and 39:2.
entries.differs: In Ezekiel, Gog is a ruler and Magog his land, and they come from the far north with named allies. John treats Gog and Magog as two names for all the nations, from every direction on earth. Ezekiel's victim is Israel in its land; John's is the camp of the saints. In Ezekiel God draws Gog out; in John Satan deceives the nations and leads them.
entries.turn: Beale and Heiser, after Kline, read this as the same last battle already told in 16:14 and 19:17-21, now told a third time. The names show that Ezekiel's unfulfilled prophecy is meant. The end is sure: the attack fails at once, and the deceiver is judged.
entries.not: **Not a retelling of Ezekiel 38 in every detail.** John takes the names Gog and Magog and the picture of a vast army against God's people. He leaves out Ezekiel's list of nations.
entries.deeper: Beale calls the gathering a fulfillment of the prophecy of Gog and Magog and derives the wording from Ezekiel 38:2-8 and 39:2. He adds Zechariah 12-14 and Zephaniah 3, texts he also finds behind 16:14 and 19:19. The Greek of Ezekiel 38:2 names Gog and the land of Magog; John has ton Gog kai Magog, the two names side by side. Beale sees universalization: Ezekiel's northern foe becomes all nations, and oppressed Israel becomes the church. The Qumran War Scroll and a scroll of Isaiah also place Gog and Magog with the nations. He argues against two separate battles: Ezekiel itself describes Gog's defeat both by sword and by fire, which John splits between 19:17-21 and 20:9. Walton traces Gog to Gyges, a king of Lydia called Gugu in Assyrian texts, and Magog to land of Gugu. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible and the CSB Study Bible both refer the verse to Ezekiel 38-39. The grade is drawn here: the names occur nowhere else.
entries.heiser: Heiser, following Meredith Kline, holds that Ezekiel 38-39 shapes Revelation 16, 19 and 20, so these are one battle told three times, not three events. He calls a second Gog and Magog event ridiculous. Kline notes that, as in Ezekiel 38:8, the assault comes after a long age of safety for God's people. Heiser also defines the deception of 20:3 by this release: what Satan was kept from doing is leading the nations against Zion.
entries.dissent: Beale argues 20:8-10 retells the battle of 19:17-21, and the ESV Study Bible gives this as the amillennial view; premillennial readers see a later, separate battle. MacArthur is one: he sets this revolt at the end of the thousand years, like Ezekiel's battle but not the same, and places ancient Magog north of the Black and Caspian Seas. Beale argues the names cannot be fixed on a modern nation, and that Rosh in Ezekiel 38:3 means chief, not Russia. Webb, as Beale reports, takes Gog and Magog as a general name for God's enemies. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible says the correspondence with Ezekiel is not exact.

aw.n: Revelation 20:7-15, Gog and Magog and the great white throne
aw.s: Released at the end of the thousand years, Satan gathers Gog and Magog, the nations from the four corners of the earth, around the camp of God's people, but fire from heaven consumes them and the devil is thrown into the lake of fire. Before a great white throne the dead, given up by the sea, death and Hades, are judged from the books, and anyone not found in the book of life is thrown into the lake of fire, the second death.

entries.title: Revelation 20:8, as the sand of the sea
entries.summary: The countless army, like sand on the shore, uses the picture the Old Testament gives the hordes that came against Israel in Joshua, Judges and Samuel.
entries.plain: **Calling a crowd a sea of faces borrows a picture everyone has heard before.** When the kings of Canaan, the Midianites and the Philistines came against Israel, the writers said their numbers were like sand on the seashore. John uses the same picture for the nations Satan gathers. The odds look hopeless for God's people, as they did in those old battles.
entries.same: The comparison of an enemy army to sand by the sea. The Greek of Judges 7:12 has hosper he ammos he epi to cheilos tes thalasses; John has hos he ammos tes thalasses.
entries.differs: In the old stories the army is one nation or a league of kings in Canaan. In John it is the nations of the whole earth. John keeps only the comparison and drops the shore and the camels. The sources give no reason for the wording beyond the common picture.
entries.turn: The old battles ended with Israel rescued against huge odds. John's version ends the same way, only faster: fire from heaven ends it before a blow is struck.
entries.not: **Not the promise to Abraham.** Genesis 22:17 uses the same picture for his children. But Beale and a study Bible point to the armies that came against Israel.
entries.deeper: Beale notes that Joshua 11:4, Judges 7:12 and 1 Samuel 13:5 use the same metaphor for the nations arrayed against Israel, and that the Greek of Joshua 11:4-5 and 1 Samuel 13:5 also has gathering to war and encamping. He suggests these early attacks may have shaped Ezekiel 38-39 and could well belong to the background of Revelation 20:8-9, working by analogy. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible calls it a common hyperbole for a countless multitude, citing Genesis 22:17, Judges 7:12 and 1 Samuel 13:5. The ESV Study Bible compares 12:17, where the dragon stands on the sand of the sea. The grade is possible: the picture is common, and two sources name these texts.
entries.dissent: Beale reads the comparison as a deliberate link to Israel's old enemies. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible treats it as a stock phrase. The CSB Study Bible's cross-references list instead the promise texts about Abraham's descendants and Israel's numbers (Genesis 32:12; Hosea 1:10), which would make it an ironic reversal; no source draws that out.

entries.title: Revelation 20:9, up over the breadth of the earth
entries.summary: The armies going up over the breadth of the earth to surround God's people borrow Gog's going up against the land in Ezekiel 38 and the Babylonian march across the breadth of the earth in Habakkuk 1:6.
entries.plain: **A news report can borrow the wording of an old war bulletin to tell you who the new invader is like.** Ezekiel says Gog will come up against God's people like a cloud. Habakkuk says the Babylonians march over the wide spaces of the world to seize homes not theirs. John joins the two. The nations march up over the whole width of the land and ring God's people.
entries.same: The verb went up against (anabaino with epi) is in the Greek of Ezekiel 38:11 and 38:16. Then the breadth of the earth (to platos tes ges). Habakkuk 1:6 in Greek has the same phrase in the plural.
entries.differs: Habakkuk has the plural, breadths; John has the singular. Ezekiel's army comes up against one land; John's spreads across the whole earth. Habakkuk speaks of Babylon conquering Judah; John speaks of the last enemy attacking God's people. Beale's reason: the earlier invasion foreshadows the last one.
entries.turn: Babylon and Gog were the great invaders of Israel's history and prophecy. John sets the final attack on the church in their line. Beale reads the breadth of the earth as worldwide, so the camp under siege is the church scattered everywhere.
entries.not: **Not a borrowing of one siege story.** John's wording recalls two invasions. Gog marches on the land in Ezekiel, and Babylon across the earth in Habakkuk.
entries.deeper: Beale finds a unique parallel in Ezekiel 38-39, a countless end-time enemy that goes up upon the land (38:11, 16; 39:2) and is judged by fire from heaven. Some Greek copies of Ezekiel 38:11 even call the land a city. For the phrase itself he says the wording of Habakkuk 1:6 in Greek, Babylon going on the plain of the earth, is drawn on here. The vault's Greek has epi ta plate tes ges; the Hebrew has lemerchavei erets, to the broad places of the earth, so here the Greek and the Hebrew agree. Beale adds that the old Greek of Daniel 12:2 uses the same phrase for the whole earth, but the vault's Greek Daniel is the version called Theodotion, which reads differently there. The CSB Study Bible cross-references Ezekiel 38:16, Joel 3:2 and Zechariah 14:2. The grade is drawn here: the shared phrase and verb point to these texts.
entries.dissent: Beale reads the beloved city as the church worldwide. Wright reads the place as the people of God in all the world. He says it has no more to do with a map than the thousand years with a calendar. MacArthur and the CSB Study Bible take it as Jerusalem, the seat of Christ's thousand-year reign, with the saints living around it. Then the going up would be toward one place.

entries.title: Revelation 20:9, the camp of the saints and the beloved city
entries.summary: The besieged people are called a camp, like Israel's wilderness camp with God in its midst, and the beloved city, the Zion the Lord loves in Psalm 87.
entries.plain: **Calling a team the home side tells you whose ground it is, wherever the game is played.** The armies surround the camp of the saints and the beloved city. Israel in the wilderness lived in a camp with God among them. Psalm 87 says God loves Zion's gates more than any other dwelling. John gives both names to God's people under attack.
entries.same: A city the Lord loves. The Greek of Psalm 87:2 (86 in the Greek numbering) has agapa kyrios, the Lord loves. John has ten polin ten egapemenen, the city that is loved. A camp (parembole) is the word for Israel's wilderness encampment.
entries.differs: The psalm speaks of the gates of Zion and the dwellings of Jacob. John says only the beloved city and never names Jerusalem or Zion. Deuteronomy's camp is Israel's tribes around the tabernacle; John's is the saints, a name he uses for believers from every nation.
entries.turn: Beale reads both names as the church throughout the world. It is a people in the wilderness with God among them. It is also the true Zion. If the psalm is in view, the point is stronger. Psalm 87 counts people of other nations as born in Zion.
entries.not: **Not a certain echo.** Beale says the phrase may echo Psalm 87, and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible gives it only as a comparison.
entries.deeper: Beale says the beloved city may echo Psalm 87:2-3, the Lord loving the gates of Zion, the city of God (compare Psalm 122:6; Isaiah 66:10; Zephaniah 3:14-17), and notes beloved city in Sirach 24:11. The Hebrew of 87:2 is ohev YHWH sha'arei tsiyyon. For the camp he points to Israel's wilderness encampment and above all Deuteronomy 23:14, where God walks in the midst of the camp to rescue and to defeat enemies, so the camp must be holy; the Qumran War Scroll projects that camp into the last battle. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible gives Psalms 78:68 and 87:2 for the city and Exodus 16:13 and 33:7 for the camp. Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible both compare Israel in the wilderness. The grade is possible: the wording is generally similar, and two sources name the psalm.
entries.dissent: The CSB Study Bible reads the beloved city as Jerusalem renewed for the thousand-year reign. MacArthur, who also cites Psalm 87:2, reads it as Jerusalem, the seat of that reign. Beale, the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible and Wright read it as the people of God, the pilgrim church. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible notes camp is military language and could recall either the exodus or a unit of war.

entries.title: Revelation 20:9, fire came down from heaven
entries.summary: Fire comes down from heaven and consumes the attackers, in the words of Elijah's fire on the king's soldiers and on the pattern of Gog's end by fire in Ezekiel.
entries.plain: **A fire alarm needs no explaining, because everyone knows what it means.** When King Ahaziah sent soldiers to seize Elijah, flames fell from the sky and burned them up. Ezekiel says God will rain fire and burning sulfur on Gog and send fire on Magog. John borrows Elijah's exact words for Ezekiel's ending. The nations ring God's people, and flames fall from the sky and destroy them.
entries.same: The Greek words katebe pyr ek tou ouranou kai katephagen, fire came down from heaven and ate. They are the same in 2 Kings 1:10 and 1:12 and in John. From Ezekiel 38:22 and 39:6 comes fire as God's weapon against Gog and Magog.
entries.differs: In 2 Kings the fire falls on fifty soldiers at a prophet's word. In John it falls on the armies of the whole earth, and no prophet calls it down. Ezekiel's fire comes with plague, hail and sulfur; John has fire alone. Some copies of Revelation add from God, which brings the line closer to 2 Kings 1:12.
entries.turn: The final war never happens. As fire saved Elijah from the king's men, it saves the church from the nations. Beale notes the same Elijah story stands behind the witnesses' fire in 11:5; here it is the last judgment.
entries.not: **Not a copy of the Elijah story.** In 2 Kings 1 fire falls on soldiers sent to seize one prophet. John keeps the fire from heaven and turns it on the nations around God's people.
entries.deeper: Beale says the defeat follows Ezekiel's pattern, where Israel's enemy is destroyed by fire, and that the actual wording is drawn from 2 Kings 1:10-14. The Greek of 2 Kings 1:10 reads kai katebe pyr ek tou ouranou kai katephagen auton; John has kai katebe pyr ek tou ouranou kai katephagen autous. The Hebrew is vatered esh min hashamayim vatochal, and fire came down from heaven and ate. Some manuscripts add apo tou theou, as in 2 Kings 1:12. Ezekiel 38:22 has fire and sulfur rained on Gog, and 39:6 fire sent on Magog. The ESV Study Bible, the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible all cite Ezekiel 38:22 and 39:6; Keener also cites 2 Kings 1:10 and Genesis 19:24; the CSB Study Bible lists both. Wright calls it an Elijah-like move. The Palestinian Targum on Numbers 11:26 also has Magog destroyed by fire. The grade is drawn here: the wording is identical to 2 Kings.
entries.dissent: Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible also hear Sodom's fire (Genesis 19:24), and MacArthur names both Sodom and Elijah. Beale and Wright put the weight on Elijah. Beale reads the fire as a figure for God's judgment rescuing his people, whatever form it takes. The CSB Study Bible pictures a rebellion around a renewed Jerusalem put down by fire, and MacArthur reads it as God's judgment on a final revolt against Jerusalem at the end of the thousand years.

entries.title: Revelation 20:11, a great white throne
entries.summary: The great white throne and the one seated on it recall the throne of the Ancient of Days in Daniel 7:9, whose robe is white as snow and before whom the books are opened.
entries.plain: **When the clerk calls the room to rise, everyone knows the judge is coming in.** In Daniel 7 the Ancient of Days takes his seat on a blazing throne, dressed in white. Then the court sits and the books are opened. John sees a great white throne and one seated on it. As in Daniel, the books are opened next, and the dead are judged.
entries.same: A throne in heaven, one seated on it, white as a mark of the judge's purity, and books opened next. Daniel 7:9 has the Ancient of Days sitting, his clothing white (leukon); John has a white throne (thronon megan leukon).
entries.differs: In Daniel the clothing and the hair are white and the throne is fire. John moves the white to the throne and calls it great. Daniel sets up many thrones; John sees one. John does not name the one seated, though Beale thinks it is God, as the Ancient of Days.
entries.turn: The throne of chapters 4 and 5 returns for the last judgment. Beale reads it as the climax of every earlier judgment in the book. Its whiteness signals that the verdict will punish evil and vindicate God's persecuted people.
entries.not: **Not a new throne.** The great white throne takes up the throne of Daniel 7:9 and the throne room of chapters 4 and 5, now set for the last judgment.
entries.deeper: Beale ties the vision to 4:2 and 5:7, where God's throne alludes chiefly to Daniel 7:9 and Ezekiel 1:26-28, and that Daniel 7 is again in view here, because the books of Daniel 7:10 are opened next. He reads the white as holiness and vindication, compares God's alabaster throne in 1 Enoch 18 and the white clothing of Daniel 7:9, 1 Enoch 14 and 3 Enoch 28, and notes Jesus could also be the one seated (22:1-3; Matthew 25:31). The ESV Study Bible links the throne to the Ancient of Days and his purity; the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible says Jewish traditions describing the day of judgment before a throne sometimes follow Daniel 7:9. The grade is drawn here: the throne with books following is traceable to Daniel 7.
entries.dissent: The CSB Study Bible says the dead here rise in a second resurrection implied in 20:5. Beale and the ESV Study Bible see all the dead before the throne, great and small, with the book of life sparing the faithful. MacArthur reads it as the judgment of unbelievers of every age only, held between the end of the present universe and the new creation. Heiser reads 20:11-15 as the same general resurrection seen from the side of judgment.

entries.title: Revelation 20:11, no place was found for them
entries.summary: Earth and heaven flee and no place is found for them, the words Daniel 2:35 uses when the wind blows away the broken statue of the empires.
entries.plain: **A demolition crew can leave a lot so clean that you cannot tell a building stood there.** In Daniel 2 a stone smashes the great statue of the empires. The pieces blow away like chaff, and no place is found for them. John uses the same words for the whole old world. Earth and sky flee from the face of the one on the throne, and no place is found for them.
entries.same: The words topos ouch heurethe autois, no place was found for them. They are the same in the Greek of Daniel 2:35 and in Revelation 20:11.
entries.differs: In Daniel the words describe the broken pieces of a statue that stands for four empires. John applies them to earth and heaven. Daniel's pieces are blown away by wind; John's world flees from God's face. John used the same words in 12:8 for the dragon and his angels thrown out of heaven.
entries.turn: Daniel's stone ends the empires and becomes a mountain filling the earth. John widens the scene to the end of the whole evil world order, making room for the new heaven and new earth of 21:1. Beale says this probably, though not necessarily, includes the material world.
entries.not: **Not a picture invented for this scene.** The words are Daniel's, as Beale shows, and John has already used them once in 12:8.
entries.deeper: Beale says the phrase is from Daniel 2:35 in the version called Theodotion, used there of the end-time destruction of the wicked kingdoms; 12:8 uses it of the devil's defeat at the cross, and here it covers the complete destruction of the evil world system. The vault's Greek Daniel (the same version) reads kai topos ouch heurethe autois, and John has kai topos ouch heurethe autois, word for word. The Aramaic is vechol atar la hishtechach lehon, and no trace at all was found of them. Beale notes almost identical language for the last judgment in 6:14 and 16:20 and ties the flight of heaven and earth to Psalm 102:25-27, Isaiah 51:6 and 2 Peter 3. The ESV Study Bible and the CSB Study Bible link the passing away to 21:1 and Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22. The grade is drawn here: the wording is identical.
entries.dissent: Is the old creation destroyed or renewed? Beale says the flight probably, not necessarily, includes the material cosmos, and leaves the literal question to 6:12-15. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible reads the flight as sinners fleeing the face no mortal can see. The ESV Study Bible ties it to the shaking foretold in Haggai 2:6. MacArthur reads the flight as the old universe going out of existence before God makes a new one.

entries.title: Revelation 20:12, the books and the book of life
entries.summary: Books are opened and another book, the book of life, joining Daniel 7:10, where the court sits and books are opened, with Daniel 12:1, where everyone found written in the book is rescued.
entries.plain: **A teacher can hold two lists at once, a record of the year's work and the class roll.** Daniel 7 shows a heavenly court where books are opened before the judgment. Daniel 12 promises that everyone found written in God's book will be rescued. John puts the two together. The books record what the dead have done. The book of life holds the names of those who belong to the Lamb.
entries.same: Books opened (biblia enoichthesan), as in the Greek of Daniel 7:10 (bibloi eneochthesan). Found written in the book, as in Daniel 12:1 (ho heuretheis gegrammenos en te biblo). John's 20:15 turns it to the negative.
entries.differs: Daniel 7 opens the books on the beast's crimes; John opens them on all the dead. Daniel 12 speaks of the book; John calls it the book of life, a name it carries through Revelation. Daniel's book rescues Israel's faithful; John's holds the names of the Lamb's people. John also turns Daniel 12:1 around: whoever is not found written is thrown into the fire.
entries.turn: Judgment and rescue sit side by side. The books show that God forgets nothing. The book of life shows that he forgets no one who belongs to the Lamb, who was slain for them. Beale reads the scene as the end of a judgment already set in motion by the cross.
entries.not: **Not salvation by a record of good works.** Beale, the CSB Study Bible and the ESV Study Bible all say the names in the book of life are there because of the Lamb, not their record.
entries.deeper: Beale says the line combines an allusion to Daniel 7:10 and Daniel 12:1-2. The books of Daniel 7 record the evil deeds of the persecutor; Walton notes royal courts kept records of the king's acts, now brought as evidence. The book of Daniel 12 is redemptive; Walton ties it to the book Moses offers to be erased from in Exodus 32:32-33. The Aramaic of 7:10 reads dina yetiv vesifrin petichu, the court sat and books were opened; the Hebrew of 12:1 reads kol hannimtsa katuv basefer, everyone found written in the book. Beale cites 1 Enoch 47:3, where the books of the living open before the Head of Days, as confirming the Daniel source, and Daniel 12:1 for the positive form of 20:15. Keener adds Exodus 32:32-33 and Malachi 3:16; Beale and the CSB Study Bible add Isaiah 4:3. The ESV Study Bible, the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible all cite Daniel 7:10. The grade is drawn here: books opened is Daniel's wording.
entries.dissent: Who is judged here? Beale and the ESV Study Bible include believers, spared through the book of life. The CSB Study Bible says the dead here rise in a second resurrection implied in 20:5. Heiser sees one general resurrection, told again from the side of judgment. MacArthur reads the dead here as unbelievers only, judged as guilty by the record of their deeds, with the book of life listing the redeemed.

entries.title: Revelation 20:12, judged by what they had done
entries.summary: The dead are judged according to their works, the Old Testament's standard phrase for God repaying each person, as in Psalm 62:12 and Jeremiah 17:10.
entries.plain: **A saying your grandmother used becomes yours without anyone noticing the source.** The psalms and prophets often say that God repays each person by what they have done. Psalm 62 and Jeremiah 17 are two of the best known. John uses the same measure twice at the last judgment. The dead are judged by what is written in the books, by what they did.
entries.same: Judgment by deeds, with the phrase according to their works (kata ta erga). The Greek of Psalm 62:12 (61:13 in the Greek numbering) has kata ta erga autou, according to his works.
entries.differs: The psalm speaks of God repaying each person; John speaks of the dead being judged. John ties the deeds to books in heaven, which the psalm does not mention. Jeremiah adds that God searches the heart, a point John does not make here.
entries.turn: The final judgment will be fair. Nothing done is forgotten. Wright says this matches the rest of Scripture, and the ESV Study Bible adds that the deeds of believers show their trust in Christ.
entries.not: **Not a quotation of one verse.** The phrase is a common way of speaking in the Old Testament, so the sources give several texts, not one source.
entries.deeper: Keener says all would be judged according to their works, citing Psalm 62:12, Proverbs 24:12, Jeremiah 17:10 and 32:19, and Ezekiel 18:30, and adds that former sins cancelled by repentance would not count (Ezekiel 18:21-22). The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cites Psalm 62:12 with Matthew 16:27 and Romans 2:6-11, and the CSB Study Bible lists Psalm 62:12 and Jeremiah 17:10. Beale refers to his comment on 2:23 for the Old Testament idiom and cites Sirach 16:12-14 for judging each by deeds alongside cosmic dissolution. The Greek of Psalm 62:12 reads hoti sy apodoseis hekasto kata ta erga autou; John has ekrithesan hekastos kata ta erga auton in 20:13. The grade is possible: the idiom is common, and several sources name these texts.
entries.dissent: How do works and grace fit? The CSB Study Bible says no one is saved by works, which would leave room for boasting. Wright says worried Protestant teachers miss the point: judgment by the whole of a life is the language of all Scripture. The ESV Study Bible says believers' deeds attest their trust in Christ and set their rewards.

aw.n: Revelation 20:7-15, Gog and Magog and the great white throne
aw.s: Released at the end of the thousand years, Satan gathers Gog and Magog, the nations from the four corners of the earth, around the camp of God's people, but fire from heaven consumes them and the devil is thrown into the lake of fire. Before a great white throne the dead, given up by the sea, death and Hades, are judged from the books, and anyone not found in the book of life is thrown into the lake of fire, the second death.

entries.title: Revelation 20:14, the second death
entries.summary: The second death, the lake of fire, may come from the end of Isaiah, with its undying worm and unquenched fire for the rebels, as the old Aramaic paraphrase of Isaiah read it.
entries.plain: **A phrase from an old sermon can stay in a family long after the sermon is forgotten.** Isaiah ends with the new heavens and new earth. Then come the bodies of the rebels, whose worm never dies and whose fire is never put out. The Aramaic paraphrase read in synagogues spoke there of a second death. John uses that name for the lake of fire, two verses before his own new heaven and earth.
entries.same: A fiery punishment of the wicked that does not end, set right next to the promise of a new heaven and earth. Isaiah 66:24 has a fire that will not be quenched (to pyr auton ou sbesthesetai); John has the lake of fire.
entries.differs: The Hebrew and Greek of Isaiah never say second death. That phrase comes from the Aramaic paraphrase of Isaiah 65, as Beale reports McNamara. Isaiah shows corpses outside the city; John speaks of death and Hades themselves thrown into the lake.
entries.turn: The new creation of chapter 21 has an outside. As in Isaiah, the last word about the rebels comes beside the promise of a world made new. Death and Hades, which held the dead, are themselves ended.
entries.not: **Not a phrase from the Hebrew Bible.** Second death appears in the Aramaic paraphrase, not in Isaiah's Hebrew or Greek; the link is through that reading.
entries.deeper: Beale agrees with McNamara that the phrase is derived from Isaiah 65:14-18 and 66:22-24 and their targumic tradition, not from a general Jewish idea. He notes that two verses later John alludes to the new creation of Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22 (21:1), that the Targum of Isaiah 65:6 and 15 names the second death just before the new creation prophecy, and that the Targum of 66:24 says the spirits of the ungodly live on in a fire that stays lit. The Greek of 66:24 reads ho gar skolex auton ou teleutesei, kai to pyr auton ou sbesthesetai. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cites Isaiah 66:24 and Mark 9:47-48. Keener notes that some Jewish texts used the phrase second death for the fate of the wicked. The grade is possible: the phrase is not in the Hebrew or Greek text, and the echo runs through the Targum.
entries.heiser: Heiser, reading Justin Bass, says fiery punishment in the afterlife may begin in Deuteronomy 32:22 and shows most clearly in Isaiah 33:14 and 66:24. He reads Isaiah 66:22-24 aloud, the new heavens and earth and then the worm that does not die, and notes Jesus uses that language for Gehenna. These are data points, he says, for an idea developed later. He leaves the second death open between endless dying and annihilation.
entries.dissent: Does the second death mean endless torment or final destruction? Beale holds the Isaiah background supports endless suffering, though he grants the Targum of 66:24 may set a limit. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible reads it as eternal conscious torment. Heiser keeps both views open, asking how death can go on if death is no more (21:4).

entries.title: Revelation 21:1, a new heaven and a new earth
entries.summary: John's first sight of the world to come is Isaiah's promise of new heavens and a new earth, now seen as done.
entries.plain: **A family that finally moves into the house they have been sketching for years still calls it by the name on the old plans.** Isaiah 65 and 66 promised that God would create a fresh heaven and earth, where the old troubles would be forgotten. John opens his last vision with those words. What Isaiah announced, John now sees in front of him. The first world has gone, and the new one has come.
entries.same: A new heaven and a new earth, in the same Greek words in both books: ouranos kainos and ge kaine. Both texts set the new world against a former one that is gone or forgotten.
entries.differs: Isaiah speaks in the future: God will create, and the old things will not be remembered. John reports what he saw, and says the first heaven and earth had passed away. He keeps the singular heaven, as the Greek of Isaiah has it. He also adds a line Isaiah does not have, that the sea was gone. Beale says Isaiah's newness is about quality: the new world lasts, the old did not.
entries.turn: In Isaiah the promise answered the exile. The new creation was God's comfort for a people dragged off to Babylon. John uses it for the end of all exile. Beale notes that Revelation 3:14 already ties this promise to Jesus rising from the dead. Here it reaches its full size, for the whole people of God and the whole world.
entries.not: **Not a promise new with John.** The new heaven and new earth are Isaiah's (65:17; 66:22). What John adds is their place at the end of the whole story, after the last judgment.
entries.deeper: Isaiah 65:17 in Hebrew reads hineni bore shamayim chadashim va'arets chadashah: God announces that he is creating heavens and an earth that are new. The Greek translation turns it into a plain forecast, estai gar ho ouranos kainos kai he ge kaine, meaning a new heaven and earth will exist. Revelation 21:1 has ouranon kainon kai gen kainen, matching the Greek's singular heaven. Isaiah 66:22 adds that the new heaven and earth will remain before God. Beale lists 21:1 among the clear allusions to Isaiah 40-66 in this vision, and in his introduction he names Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22 in Revelation 21:1 as one of the clearest cases of a prophecy John expects to be fulfilled only at the end. He notes that kainos usually means new in kind, and that Jewish writers reading Isaiah 65 (Jubilees, 1 Enoch, 2 Baruch) also pictured a renewed creation. The Jewish Study Bible says Isaiah 65:17-25 goes beyond the earlier chapters: the world itself is transformed in the new age. Keener adds that Isaiah 65:18 puts the new Jerusalem at the center of that new world, as John does in 21:2.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Isaiah 65 and 66 as the source John repurposes, after Pilchan Lee. In Isaiah 65:17-18 God gives a new creation and a new Jerusalem together, as the answer to the Babylonian exile, not a rebuilt temple. He follows Beale and McDonough: Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22 stand behind the wording of 21:1, and 66:22 adds that the new world remains. His point is that the prophets never separate a restored Jerusalem from a restored creation.
entries.dissent: How new is the new creation? Beale reads a real renewal of the old cosmos, changed at its core. Keener thinks Revelation leans toward replacement rather than renewal, and notes that Jewish texts held both views. The ESV Study Bible sets out both options and leaves them open. The CSB Study Bible says the new world will be like the present one in some ways but very different in others. MacArthur reads replacement: the present universe is destroyed and God creates a new one that lasts forever.

aw.s: John sees a new heaven and a new earth, with no more sea, and the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down from God like a bride dressed for her husband. A voice announces that God's dwelling is now with people, that he will wipe away every tear, and that he makes all things new; the thirsty will drink freely, while the cowardly, the faithless, murderers, sorcerers, idolaters and liars have their place in the lake of fire.

entries.title: Revelation 21:1, and the sea was no more
entries.summary: The missing sea may recall Isaiah 51, where God dried up the sea for the exodus and then promised that sorrow would flee.
entries.plain: **An old enemy's name can carry the whole story of what a people once feared.** In the Old Testament the sea is the wild, hostile water that God tames, home of monsters like Rahab. Isaiah 51 recalls God drying up the sea so his people could cross. Then it promises that sorrow will run away. John says the new world has no sea at all.
entries.same: The sea as the thing that stands in the way of God's people, and its removal. Isaiah 51:10 speaks of God drying up the sea and the deep water; Isaiah 51:9 and 27:1 name the sea monsters God defeats.
entries.differs: No Old Testament verse says there will be no sea. John's words are his own: the sea is not any longer. Isaiah 65:17, which John has just used, does not mention the sea at all. Beale links the line to Isaiah 51:10-11, where drying the sea and ending sorrow sit side by side. Keener and others offer other reasons, so the echo is uncertain.
entries.turn: Beale reads the sea as a picture of every threat God's people faced: evil, hostile nations, death, and the trade that fed Babylon. In the new world none of these remain. Verse 4 then spells out the same point without the picture: no death, no grief, no pain.
entries.not: **Not a line taken from one verse.** No Old Testament text says the sea will be gone. John draws the idea from Isaiah's pictures of the sea and its monsters as a threat that God overcomes.
entries.deeper: The Greek of 21:1 is he thalassa ouk estin eti, the sea is no longer. Beale notes the same pattern, ouk estai eti, in 21:4 for death and grief, and in 22:3 and 22:5 for the curse and the night. He sees 21:4 as unpacking 21:1, both framed by a line about the first things passing away. The echo, he says, is of Isaiah 51:10-11, where the sea dried at the exodus stands for the removal of sorrow at the last day. In the Greek of Isaiah 51:10 God is the one making the sea desolate and setting a road through its depths. Beale also cites the Assumption of Moses 10:6, where at the new creation the sea retreats into the abyss, and Jeremiah 51:36, where God dries up Babylon's sea. The grade is drawn here: the idea is shared but the wording is not, and the sources name different texts.
entries.heiser: Heiser calls this one of his favorite verses. The sea, he says, was the Old Testament's picture of chaos: untamable, unpredictable and hostile to life. Reading from the Dictionary of Biblical Imagery, he lists the sea monsters behind it: the dragon of Job 7:12 and Psalm 74:13, Leviathan in Psalm 74:14, Rahab in Psalm 89:10 and Isaiah 51, and the serpent of Isaiah 27:1. No more sea means no more chaos, enemy, sin or death. He calls the literal reading, no salt water, ridiculous.
entries.dissent: Why no sea? Beale reads it as every past threat to God's people, with Isaiah 51 behind it, and adds that a literal sea would not contradict that. Heiser reads it as the end of chaos. MacArthur reads it literally: the new world will not be water-based and will have a different climate. Keener offers two reasons: Isaiah 65:17, read literally, names only heaven and earth; or the sea stood for evil powers, as in 13:1. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible thinks the river of life in 22:1 replaces it. Mealy, as Beale reports, sees the heavenly sea of 4:6 removed as a veil. The CSB Study Bible cross-references Isaiah 57:20, the restless sea of the wicked.

entries.title: Revelation 21:2, the holy city, prepared as a bride
entries.summary: The new Jerusalem comes down dressed as a bride, from Isaiah's holy city Jerusalem and the bride God adorns in Isaiah 61:10.
entries.plain: **A wedding speech can borrow a line from the couple's favorite book, and everyone in the room hears it.** Isaiah called Jerusalem the holy city and told her to put on her beautiful clothes. Later he pictures God's people dressed like a bride for her wedding. John sees the holy city come down from God, and she is dressed as a bride. Isaiah's promises to a broken city now describe the city of God's people at the end.
entries.same: The holy city Jerusalem: Isaiah 52:1 in Greek has Ierousalem, polis he hagia, and John has ten polin ten hagian Ierousalem. The bride and her adornment: Isaiah 61:10 in Greek has hos nymphen katekosmese me, as a bride he adorned me, and John has hos nymphen kekosmemenen, as a bride adorned.
entries.differs: John adds new to Jerusalem. Beale traces that to Isaiah 62:2, where Jerusalem gets a new name, explained in 62:4-5 as a new marriage with God. In Isaiah, Zion is told to rise and dress. In John the city comes down out of heaven, already made ready by God. John also names the husband: in 21:9 the bride is the Lamb's wife.
entries.turn: Isaiah was speaking to a city wrecked by Babylon, promising that God would take her back like a bride. John gives that promise its final form. Beale and Keener read the city as its people: the bride is the whole company of the redeemed, Jewish and Gentile, wearing the salvation God gives. Revelation 19:7-8 used the same Isaiah passage when the Lamb's marriage came.
entries.not: **Not a quotation of one verse.** John joins two of Isaiah's pictures, the holy city Jerusalem and the bride God adorns, in a sentence of his own.
entries.deeper: Beale finds three allusions to one stretch of Isaiah in this verse. The holy city Jerusalem is Isaiah 52:1, which in the Greek reads endysai ten doxan sou, Ierousalem, polis he hagia, put on your glory, O Jerusalem, holy city. The added new comes from Isaiah 62:1-2, where Jerusalem is called by a new name. The bride adorned for her husband is Isaiah 61:10, where Zion says in the Greek hos nymphen katekosmese me kosmo, as a bride he adorned me with ornament. Revelation has hetoimasmenen hos nymphen kekosmemenen to andri autes, made ready like a bride dressed for the man she marries. Beale lists 21:1-2 among the clear allusions to Isaiah 40-66. He notes that 4 Ezra 10 also pictures the coming Jerusalem as a woman, and that Revelation 3:12 already calls the church of Philadelphia, Jews and Gentiles, the new Jerusalem. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible and the CSB Study Bible both point to Isaiah 52:1 and 61:10; the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cites Isaiah 52:1.
entries.heiser: Heiser notes that Isaiah 52 already calls Jerusalem the holy city, at a time when the real city faced judgment. He reads the title as a hint of Jerusalem's restored future, with the promise that the unclean will no longer enter her. The language, he says, comes straight out of the Old Testament, and he points to Isaiah 61:10 and Isaiah 62 for the bride.
entries.dissent: Keener notes the title holy city was common for Jerusalem in Jewish writings and on Jewish coins, so it need not point to Isaiah alone; he also cites Isaiah 48:2 and 62:12. The sources also differ on the city: Beale and the ESV Study Bible read it as the church, while the CSB Study Bible treats the bride and city as a picture of the people in a place God prepares. Keener notes that Jerusalem meant both the place and its people, and Beale reads the picture as a figure for God's people in a real new world. MacArthur reads the new Jerusalem as a real city, the capital of heaven, already in existence and now coming down; the whole city, with all its saints, is called the bride.

entries.title: Revelation 21:3, God will dwell with them
entries.summary: The voice from the throne repeats the covenant promise of Ezekiel 37:27 and Leviticus 26:11-12, that God will live among his people, and widens his people to peoples.
entries.plain: **A family promise made to one child can be kept, years later, for every grandchild at the table.** God told Israel in Leviticus and again in Ezekiel that he would set his dwelling among them. He would be their God, and they his people. John hears the same promise from the throne. But he changes one word. Where the prophets said people, he says peoples, so the promise covers every nation.
entries.same: God's dwelling among them, and the two-part covenant promise that he belongs to them and they belong to him. The Greek of Ezekiel 37:27 has kataskenosis, a dwelling, and the Greek of Leviticus 26:11 has skene, a tent. John has skene and the verb skenoo, to pitch a tent or dwell.
entries.differs: The prophets always say people, singular, meaning Israel. John writes laoi, peoples. Beale calls the change deliberate: promises once aimed at Israel are kept for every tribe and nation. Some copyists changed it back to the singular to match the Old Testament. Ezekiel's dwelling sat inside a temple only a few priests could approach. In John there is no temple wall; God lives among all of them.
entries.turn: This is the center of the whole vision. Beale reads verse 3 as the meaning of the city and the bride in verse 2: God and his people living together for good. Zechariah 2:11 had already said many nations would become God's people. John sees that hope done. It also prepares for 21:22, where the city has no temple at all.
entries.not: **Not one verse quoted.** The promise that God will live among his people runs through the Law and the Prophets. John may be using that shared formula rather than one text.
entries.deeper: Ezekiel 37:27 in Hebrew reads vehayah mishkani aleihem, my dwelling will be over them, then vehayiti lahem lelohim vehemmah yihyu li le'am, the two-sided covenant promise. The Greek has estai he kataskenosis mou en autois, my dwelling will be among them. Revelation reads idou he skene tou theou meta ton anthropon kai skenosei met' auton, kai autoi laoi autou esontai. Beale says Ezekiel 43:7, the temple where God will dwell among Israel forever, is echoed, but that the more specific allusion is to Ezekiel 37:27 and Leviticus 26:11-12. Jubilees 1:17 quotes the same Ezekiel promise and ties it to the new creation. In his introduction Beale gives this verse as an example of universalization: the end-time temple promised to Israel extends its benefits to the nations. He also notes that skene may play on the Hebrew shakan, to dwell, behind the later word shekinah. The grade is drawn here: the two-part formula and the dwelling word are nearly identical.
entries.heiser: Heiser treats Ezekiel 43:7, God's throne and dwelling in Ezekiel's temple, as a key verse for chapter 21, fulfilled by a city and a new earth, not a temple. With Beale and McDonough he adds Leviticus 26:11-12 and Ezekiel 37:26-28. Those words were spoken to Israelites about living in the land. In Revelation they are spoken to every believer, Jew or Gentile. He notes the verb to tabernacle is the one John 1:14 uses for the Word becoming flesh.
entries.dissent: Which text leads? Beale finds Ezekiel 43:7 echoed but Ezekiel 37:27 and Leviticus 26:11-12 the main source. Heiser foregrounds Ezekiel 43:7. The study Bibles give long lists of the covenant formula (Exodus 29:45, Jeremiah 7:23, Zechariah 8:8), so the wording may be a shared formula rather than one verse. On the text, manuscripts are split between peoples and people; Beale favors peoples. Beale holds that the nations share Israel's promises through Jesus, the true seed of Abraham; Heiser stresses one people of God made of Jews and Gentiles. MacArthur reads the dwelling as God's own house, and holds that the saints of the Old Testament, the tribulation and the thousand years are by now all gathered into the bride.
