entries.title: Revelation 21:4, he will wipe every tear
entries.summary: God wiping every tear and ending death comes from Isaiah 25:8, the feast where death is swallowed up.
entries.plain: **A parent kneeling to dry a child's face does more than any speech about comfort.** Isaiah 25 pictures a feast on God's mountain. There God swallows up death and wipes the tears from every face. John says the same of the new world. God himself wipes away every tear, and death is gone. The promise Isaiah gave to Israel now belongs to all of God's people.
entries.same: Every tear (pan dakryon), wiped or taken away by God, and death ended. The Greek of Isaiah 25:8 has the Lord God removing every tear from every face, right after death is swallowed up.
entries.differs: Isaiah says from every face; John says from their eyes. Isaiah's verb in Greek is to take away; John's is to wipe out. Isaiah puts death being swallowed first, then the tears. John puts the tears first and then says death will be no more. Some copyists added God before every tear to match Isaiah more closely, Beale notes.
entries.turn: In Isaiah the tears were Israel's, under exile and death. John gives the promise its final reach: no more death for anyone in the new world. Revelation 7:17 already used this verse for the great crowd before the throne. Here it is the settled state of the world to come.
entries.not: **Not a promise that grief never mattered.** The tears are wiped, which means they were real. Beale reads them as the sufferings of God's people in the old world, now ended.
entries.deeper: The Hebrew of Isaiah 25:8 reads billa hammavet lanetsach, he has swallowed up death forever, umachah adonai YHWH dimah me'al kol panim, and the Lord God will wipe the tear from every face. The verb machah means to wipe, which John's exaleipsei matches more closely than the Greek translation's apheile, removed; that link to the Hebrew is drawn here. The Greek has pan dakryon apo pantos prosopou, every tear from every face. Beale calls Revelation 21:4 a fulfillment of Isaiah 25:8, lists 21:4 among the clear allusions to Isaiah in this vision, and in his introduction names Isaiah 25:8 in 21:4 among the clearest cases of a prophecy expected to be fulfilled at the end. He notes that later Jewish readers took Isaiah 25:8 of the resurrection. Exodus Rabbah 15.21, like John, joins it with 35:10 and 65:19. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible both say the verse alludes to Isaiah 25:8.
entries.heiser: Heiser calls this line a specific fulfillment of Isaiah 25:8. He notes it was already echoed in Revelation 7, with the crowd before the throne. A promise given to Israelites, he says, is here given to every believer.

entries.title: Revelation 21:4, no more mourning, crying or pain
entries.summary: The list of what will be gone draws on Isaiah 35:10, 51:11 and 65:19, where grief and the sound of weeping flee from the redeemed.
entries.plain: **When a hospital ward finally closes because no one is sick, the empty beds say more than the doctors can.** Isaiah promised that those God rescues will come home singing, and that grief and groaning will run away. In Isaiah 65 no sound of weeping or crying is heard in the new Jerusalem. John gathers these into one line. No mourning, no crying, no pain, because the first things have gone.
entries.same: A list of sorrows that will no longer exist when God restores his people. Isaiah 65:19 in Greek has no longer a voice of krauge, crying, and John has krauge too. The phrase the first things echoes the former things of Isaiah 65:17.
entries.differs: The Hebrew of Isaiah 35:10 and 51:11 names two things that flee, sorrow and sighing. The Greek translation and John both have three. John's three words differ from the Greek's, though Beale calls them synonyms. Isaiah says the sorrows flee away; John says they will not be any longer, a formula Beale traces to Isaiah 65:19-20. John adds death to the list.
entries.turn: In Isaiah these lines describe exiles coming home to Zion. John uses them for the whole redeemed people in the new creation. The line ends with the reason: the first things have passed away. That closes the frame opened in verse 1, where the first heaven and earth passed away.
entries.not: **Not one verse quoted.** John blends at least three Isaiah texts into a single sentence of his own, as Beale and Keener both show.
entries.deeper: Beale sets out the pieces. Isaiah 35:10 and 51:11 promise everlasting joy when grief and groaning flee; in the Greek, odyne kai lype kai stenagmos, pain and grief and groaning, ran away. Revelation has penthos, krauge and ponos, mourning, crying and pain. Isaiah 65:19 in Greek reads ouketi me akousthe en aute phone klauthmou oude phone krauges, no longer will be heard in her the voice of weeping nor the voice of crying. Isaiah 65:20 continues with no longer will there be, the shape of John's ouk estai eti. Beale also hears Isaiah 60:20, the days of mourning ended. The closing ta prota apelthan, the first things passed away, recalls Isaiah 65:17 and 43:18. Beale lists 21:4 among the clear allusions to Isaiah in this vision. Keener names Isaiah 25:8, 35:10, 51:11 and 65:16-19 together, and the ESV Study Bible cites Isaiah 65:19-20.
entries.heiser: Heiser notes that Isaiah 35:10 and 51:11 predict that pain, grief and groaning will flee in the coming new creation. These were promises to Israelites, he says, but in Revelation they belong to all believers.
entries.dissent: The sources agree on Isaiah but not on the weight of each text. Keener and the CSB Study Bible list Isaiah 25:8, 35:10, 51:11 and 65:19 together. Beale adds Isaiah 60:20 and 65:20. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible reads the first things as the former things of Isaiah 65:16-17, the past troubles that will be forgotten.

entries.title: Revelation 21:5, I am making all things new
entries.summary: God's announcement from the throne takes up Isaiah 43:19, behold I make new things, and adds all.
entries.plain: **A builder who once promised a new kitchen can stand in the finished house and say every room is new.** In Isaiah 43 God told the exiles to look, because he was doing a new thing, a road in the desert. In John the one on the throne speaks again. Look, he says, I am making all things new. One small word, all, turns Isaiah's new thing into a whole new world.
entries.same: The opening look, the speaker God, the word new, and the verb make in the present tense. The Greek of Isaiah 43:19 has idou ego poio kaina, behold I make new things. John has idou kaina poio panta.
entries.differs: John adds panta, all. Beale says the addition marks full fulfillment, the end of what was begun, and not that everyone is saved. Isaiah's new thing was a way home from Babylon through the wilderness. John's is the whole new creation. Beale also hears Isaiah 66:22, the new heaven and earth that I make.
entries.turn: Beale notes that God speaks in his own voice only twice in Revelation, here and in 1:8. The present tense, I am making, is a prophetic present: it makes the future certain. Paul uses the same Isaiah promise in 2 Corinthians 5:17 for the new creation that has already begun in Christ.
entries.not: **Not Isaiah's line repeated exactly.** Isaiah 43:19 has new things; John has all things made new, spoken by God from the throne.
entries.deeper: Isaiah 43:19 in Greek reads idou ego poio kaina ha nyn anatelei, behold I make new things which will now spring up. Revelation 21:5 reads idou kaina poio panta. Beale notes that the Isaiah texts behind 21:1, 4-5 all use present poio as a prophetic present (43:19; 65:17-18; 66:22 in Greek). He lists 21:4-5 among the clear allusions to Isaiah. The next line, these words are faithful and true, Beale roots in Isaiah 65:16, where God is the God of amen; Aquila and Symmachus render that word as faithfulness and amen. He adds that Pirke de Rabbi Eliezer 51 applied Isaiah 43:19 to the renewal of the future temple. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible says the verse alludes to Isaiah 43:19; the CSB Study Bible links it to 2 Corinthians 5:17.
entries.dissent: Beale reads I am making as a future made certain. Mulholland, as Beale reports, reads it as renewal happening within history now. The CSB Study Bible holds both: believers are already a new creation, and everything will be made new later. Keener points to Wisdom of Solomon 7:27, where Wisdom renews all things in the present.

entries.title: Revelation 21:6, water from the spring of life without cost
entries.summary: God's gift of water to the thirsty, free of charge, joins Isaiah 49:10, springs of water for the returning exiles, with Isaiah 55:1, come to the waters without money.
entries.plain: **A town well with a sign that says free to all tells you who owns the water.** In Isaiah 49 God leads his people home past springs so they never thirst. In Isaiah 55 he calls the thirsty to come and drink without money. John joins the two. God gives the thirsty water from the spring of life, and it costs them nothing.
entries.same: The thirsty, given water by God, at no cost. Isaiah 55:1 in Greek calls hoi dipsontes, the thirsty, and John has to dipsonti, the one who thirsts. Isaiah 49:10 has pegon hydaton, springs of waters; John has tes peges tou hydatos, the spring of the water.
entries.differs: Isaiah's springs become one spring whose water is life. Isaiah 55:1 says without money and without price; John uses one word, dorean, as a gift. Isaiah calls people to come and buy; John has God giving. Beale suggests the free gift may also come from the line before the springs in Isaiah 49:10, he who has mercy on them.
entries.turn: Jewish teachers often read the water of Isaiah 55:1 as the Torah, Beale notes. John reads it as eternal life in God's presence, given by grace. In Isaiah the promise was for returning exiles. In John it is for anyone who thirsts and overcomes, and 22:17 repeats the invitation.
entries.not: **Not a reward for martyrs only.** Beale answers that view: 22:17 opens the same water to the whole redeemed community.
entries.deeper: Isaiah 49:10 in Greek reads they will not hunger or thirst, for he who has mercy on them will comfort them and lead them through springs of waters. Isaiah 55:1 reads hoi dipsontes, poreuesthe eph' hydor, you who thirst, go to the water, and buy without money. Revelation has ego to dipsonti doso ek tes peges tou hydatos tes zoes dorean. Beale calls Isaiah 49:10 the basis of the water image and says Isaiah 55:1 is combined with it. He reads tes zoes as water that is life, from God and the Lamb (22:1, 17; Jeremiah 2:13; Psalm 36:9). Rabbinic texts he cites (Mekilta, Midrash on Psalms) take the water of Isaiah 55:1 as the Torah. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible says the line probably echoes Isaiah 55:1; the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cites Isaiah 49:10 and 55:1; Keener and the ESV Study Bible cite Isaiah 55:1. The grade is drawn here: the free water to the thirsty is distinctive to Isaiah 55:1, but the wording is reshaped.
entries.dissent: The sources agree on Isaiah 55:1. Beale makes Isaiah 49:10 the base text; the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible names only Isaiah 55:1. Keener sets it beside the abundant water of the age to come in Isaiah 35:1-2 and Ezekiel 47:1-12. Some, as Beale reports, limit the water to martyrs; he rejects that.

entries.title: Revelation 21:7, I will be his God and he will be my son
entries.summary: The promise to the one who overcomes takes the promise to David's son in 2 Samuel 7:14 and gives it to each believer.
entries.plain: **A family name handed down to an heir can be shared, by adoption, with every child the family takes in.** In 2 Samuel 7 God promised David that he would be a father to David's son, and the son would be his son. That promise belonged to the king. John hears God say it of everyone who overcomes. Each one will be God's son and inherit with him.
entries.same: God speaks of himself in the first person and of the heir in the third: I will be to him, and he will be to me a son. The Greek of 2 Samuel 7:14 reads autos estai moi eis huion; John has autos estai moi huios.
entries.differs: Samuel says I will be his father; John says I will be his God. That swap blends the Davidic promise with the covenant formula of verse 3, I will be their God. John also adds inheritance: the overcomer will inherit these things. In Samuel the son is one royal heir; in John the son is any believer.
entries.turn: Beale explains the shift by corporate representation. Christ is the Son who inherits the earth, as Psalm 2 says. Those he represents share what he receives. Verse 3 spoke of all God's people together; verse 7 speaks to each one. The promises made to overcomers in chapters 2 and 3 are summed up here.
entries.not: **Not a claim that believers become divine like the Son.** Beale says Christ stays God's unique Son; those in him receive the privileges of his sonship.
entries.deeper: The Greek of 2 Samuel 7:14 reads ego esomai auto eis patera, kai autos estai moi eis huion, I will be to him for a father and he will be to me for a son. Revelation 21:7 reads esomai auto theos kai autos estai moi huios. Beale says 2 Samuel 7:14 is now more clearly in mind, combined with the covenant formula, and he notes Psalm 89:26-29 and Psalm 2:7. He finds a hint of Isaiah 55:1-3 too, since the thirsty of 55:1 are promised the sure mercies of David in 55:3. The ESV Study Bible and the CSB Study Bible both point to 2 Samuel 7:14; the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible notes that Israel was God's son as a nation but that here each believer is called God's child. The grade is drawn here: the wording follows the Greek of Samuel closely, but John has changed its key word.
entries.dissent: The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible read the line mainly as the covenant formula, I will be their God, adapted to sonship. Beale and the ESV Study Bible hear the Davidic promise of 2 Samuel 7:14 behind it. Some scribes, Beale notes, turned the singular into plurals because they saw it applied to all God's people.

entries.title: Revelation 21:10, carried in the Spirit to a great, high mountain
entries.summary: John is taken to a high mountain to see the city, as Ezekiel was taken to a very high mountain to see the temple of the future.
entries.plain: **A guide who starts the tour from the same hilltop as the first explorer tells you whose map you are following.** Ezekiel 40 begins his long vision of the future temple. God's hand sets him on a towering peak, and he sees something like a city. John too is carried by the Spirit up a vast, lofty mountain. From there he sees the holy city. Everything he sees next, Beale says, is Ezekiel's vision, read again.
entries.same: A prophet carried by God's Spirit to a very high mountain, where he sees a city. The Greek of Ezekiel 40:2 has oros hypselon sphodra, a very high mountain, and a city-like building opposite. John has oros mega kai hypselon. Ezekiel 43:5 has the Spirit taking the prophet up.
entries.differs: Ezekiel saw a temple, with a city beside it. John sees only a city, and later says it has no temple. He moves from Ezekiel's hand of the Lord to his own phrase in the Spirit. In Ezekiel the mountain is in the land of Israel; in John the city comes down from heaven.
entries.turn: By borrowing the opening of Ezekiel 40, John tells the reader how to read the rest of chapter 21. The city is the fulfillment of Ezekiel's temple, with its gates, walls and measurements. The same angel scene opened the vision of Babylon in 17:1-3. The prostitute was seen from a wilderness; the bride is seen from a mountain.
entries.not: **Not a new setting for a vision.** The great high mountain is where Ezekiel stood to see his temple (40:2). John is taken to the same kind of place to see the city.
entries.deeper: Beale says 21:10 combines Ezekiel 43:5, the Spirit took me up, with 40:1-2, where the Lord's hand sets the prophet on a towering peak, and that the combination shows beyond doubt that the vision that follows is Ezekiel 40-48's future temple. The Greek of Ezekiel 40:2 reads etheke me ep' orous hypselou sphodra, kai ep' autou hos oikodome poleos: a towering peak, with something like a city built on it. Revelation reads apenenken me en pneumati epi oros mega kai hypselon. Beale also links John's repeated in the Spirit to Ezekiel's commissions (2:2; 3:12, 14; 11:1; 43:5). He gathers other Old Testament texts that set the end-time city on a high mountain: Isaiah 2:2-3, Micah 4:1-2, Psalm 48:2, and Ezekiel 28:14, where Eden itself is a mountain. Keener says the image is rooted in Ezekiel 40:2. The grade is drawn here: the setting and wording match Ezekiel's opening, and Beale calls the link certain.
entries.heiser: Heiser asks why a high mountain, when Zion is not tall. His answer is the cosmic mountain, the place where God dwells, and the first cosmic mountain was Eden, called a mountain in Ezekiel 28. With Beale and McDonough he cites the combination of Ezekiel 43:5 and 40:1-2. John wants readers to think of Ezekiel's temple vision, he says, though he describes a city and a new creation. That works only if you think of the cosmic mountain, not a building project.
entries.dissent: The sources agree on Ezekiel 40:2. The ESV Study Bible notes that in Ezekiel this mountain vision comes right after the defeat of Gog and Magog, as in Revelation. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible adds Isaiah 2:2-3 and contrasts this mountain with the seven hills Babylon sits on.

aw.n: Revelation 21:9-27, the city of gold and twelve stones
aw.s: An angel carries John to a high mountain to show him the bride, the holy city Jerusalem, shining with God's glory, with twelve gates named for Israel's tribes and twelve foundations named for the Lamb's apostles. The city is a cube of pure gold, its foundations set with twelve precious stones and its gates each a single pearl; it has no temple, since God and the Lamb are its temple, and its gates never shut as the nations bring their glory into it.

entries.title: Revelation 21:11, having the glory of God
entries.summary: The city shines with God's glory, from Isaiah 60's promise that the Lord's glory would rise on Jerusalem and Ezekiel 43's glory returning to the temple.
entries.plain: **A lamp in a window can make a plain house look like the brightest one on the street.** Isaiah 60 tells Jerusalem to shine, since the Lord's glory has dawned over her. In Ezekiel 43 God's glory comes back to the temple and the earth shines with it. John sees the holy city shining with the glory of God, like a rare jewel. The light is not the city's own. It is God's presence.
entries.same: The glory of God (he doxa tou theou) resting on the end-time city and making it shine. The Greek of Isaiah 60:1 has he doxa kyriou risen on Jerusalem; Ezekiel 43:2 has the earth shining with God's glory.
entries.differs: Isaiah has the glory of the Lord; John has the glory of God. Isaiah speaks of light rising on the city; John compares the city's brilliance to jasper as bright as crystal, a picture neither prophet uses here. Ezekiel's glory fills a temple; John's fills a city with no temple.
entries.turn: Beale reads the glory as God's own presence, once kept inside the temple, now resting on his people, who are both the city and the temple. The glory is the bride's adornment from verse 2. The jasper also ties the city back to the throne room of 4:3, where God shines like jasper.
entries.not: **Not glory the city earns.** Beale stresses that the bride's brightness is God's glory reflected in his people.
entries.deeper: Beale says that, given the clear allusions to Isaiah 40-66 in this vision, the glory of God must come from Isaiah 58:8 and 60:1-2, 19, where the Lord's glory dwells in the latter-day Jerusalem. The Greek of Isaiah 60:1 reads photizou, photizou, Ierousalem, hekei gar sou to phos, kai he doxa kyriou epi se anatetalken. Beale adds that the shining also continues the allusion to Ezekiel 43:2, 4-5, where the glory enters the new temple and the earth shines. Revelation reads echousan ten doxan tou theou, ho phoster autes homoios litho timiotato. Beale compares phoster, luminary, with Daniel 12:3 in Greek, where the wise shine as lights. Keener cites Isaiah 60:1-3; the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cites Isaiah 60:1 and Ezekiel 43:5. The grade is drawn here: the idea is distinctive to these texts, but the wording is short and general.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads with Beale here: the city having the glory of God and shining like jasper continues the allusion to Ezekiel 43, where the glory enters the new temple and the earth shines. Isaiah, Ezekiel and Revelation, he says, all use the same bright gem language for the place where God is.
entries.dissent: Beale gives Isaiah 60 the lead and Ezekiel 43 a supporting part. Heiser, after Beale and McDonough, foregrounds Ezekiel 43. The ESV Study Bible links the jasper only to Revelation 4:3 and names no Old Testament text.

entries.title: Revelation 21:12-13, twelve gates with the names of the tribes
entries.summary: The city's twelve gates, three on each side and each named for a tribe of Israel, come from Ezekiel's city in Ezekiel 48:30-35.
entries.plain: **A school that names each of its doors after its founders tells every pupil whose story they walk into.** Ezekiel's vision ends with a city that has twelve gates, three on each side. Each gate carries the name of one of Israel's tribes. John's city has the same twelve gates and the same names. He adds an angel at every gate. And in verse 14 he writes the names of Jesus' twelve apostles on the foundations.
entries.same: Twelve gates, three facing each direction, each one carrying a tribe's name. The Greek of Ezekiel 48:31 has the gates of the city by the names of the tribes of Israel; John has names written on them of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel.
entries.differs: Ezekiel lists the gates starting from the north; John goes east, north, south, west, an order Beale traces to the measuring in Ezekiel 42:15-19. Ezekiel has no angels at the gates; John has twelve. Ezekiel's city sits beside a temple; John's city has none. John also adds the apostles on the foundations, which Ezekiel could not have.
entries.turn: Beale reads the tribes and apostles together as one people of God, the true Israel, made of Jews and Gentiles in Christ. The apostles are the foundation and the tribes are the gates. Beale calls that a reversal: Israel's promises reach their goal in Christ. Heiser makes the same point: one people of God, as in Eden.
entries.not: **Not Ezekiel's gates alone.** John keeps Ezekiel's twelve gates named for Israel's tribes and adds twelve foundations bearing the apostles' names.
entries.deeper: Ezekiel 48:31-34 in Greek reads hai pylai tes poleos ep' onomasi phylon tou Israel, gates named for Israel's tribes, three to the north, three to the east, three to the south and three to the west. Revelation 21:12 reads onomata epigegrammena, ha estin ton dodeka phylon huion Israel. Beale says Ezekiel's many temple gates (chapter 40) and the twelve city gates of 48:31-34 are merged into one set around one city-temple. He links the angels to the watchmen on Jerusalem's walls in Isaiah 62:6, as Mounce and Sweet suggest, and to the cherubim at Eden's gate in Genesis 3:24, though Fekkes doubts the Isaiah link. Keener notes that the Temple Scroll from Qumran also puts the tribes on twelve gates of the new temple, and that 1 Enoch ties twelve heavenly gates to the zodiac, while John ties his to the tribes. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible both cite Ezekiel 48. The grade is drawn here: twelve gates named for the tribes, three to a side, is Ezekiel's picture alone.
entries.heiser: Heiser, reading Keener, notes that the gates bear the twelve tribes as in Ezekiel 48:31-34, an element of Ezekiel's temple prophecy now used of a city. The foundations carry the apostles. He sees how easily something given to the tribes is applied to the apostles: Israel and the church, one circumcision-neutral people of God.
entries.dissent: Beale reads the twelve tribes on the gates as the whole redeemed church. The CSB Study Bible thinks the gates and foundations imply that Israel and the church keep distinct covenant promises forever. The ESV Study Bible reads the pairing as the unity of Old Testament and New Testament believers.

entries.title: Revelation 21:15-17, a golden measuring rod
entries.summary: An angel measures the city with a rod, as the man with a measuring reed measured Ezekiel's temple and as an angel measured Jerusalem in Zechariah 2.
entries.plain: **A surveyor who walks the boundary of your land is telling you it is yours and protected.** In Ezekiel 40 a shining man with a measuring reed walks the future temple and measures every wall and gate. In Zechariah 2 a man goes out to measure Jerusalem. John's angel has a measuring rod of gold. He measures the whole city with its gateways and wall, and the wall is given in a human measure that is also the angel's.
entries.same: A heavenly figure with a measuring reed (kalamos) who measures the city, its gates and wall. Ezekiel 40:3 in Greek has kalamos metron, a measuring reed; John has metron kalamon chrysoun, a golden reed for measuring.
entries.differs: Ezekiel's reed is plain; John's is gold. Ezekiel never says his measuring man is an angel; John does, and Beale reads of an angel in verse 17 as making that explicit. Ezekiel measures a temple complex in fine detail; John measures a city, with numbers built on twelve and far larger than Ezekiel's.
entries.turn: In Ezekiel the measuring promised that the temple would really be built and kept safe. Beale reads John's measuring the same way: God guarantees his presence with his people and their safety from anything unclean. In 11:1 John measured the temple during the church's trials. Now the whole city is measured and secure.
entries.not: **Not a copy of Ezekiel's measuring scene.** Ezekiel's guide measures a temple with a reed; John's angel measures a whole city with a reed of gold.
entries.deeper: Ezekiel 40:3 in Greek reads en te cheiri autou en spartion oikodomon kai kalamos metron, in his hand a builder's line and a measuring reed. Revelation 21:15 has eichen metron kalamon chrysoun hina metrese ten polin. Beale calls this a continued allusion to Ezekiel 40:3-5, where measuring promises the temple's establishment and protection; the Greek of Ezekiel uses the verb and noun for measure about thirty times each. For 21:16-17 he adds Zechariah 2:2, where an angelic figure goes to measure Jerusalem's breadth and length, and Ezekiel 40:5, where the wall's breadth and height equal one reed. He reads human measurement as a hint that redeemed humanity, Gentiles included, belongs to the city. Keener says the rod comes from Ezekiel 40:3 and that the measurements were meant to produce awe and repentance (Ezekiel 40:4; 43:10-11). The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible names Zechariah 2:1-2 and Ezekiel 40-41. The grade is drawn here: the scene is Ezekiel's, but measuring with a reed is not unique to it.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads Keener here: the rod recalls the measuring of Jerusalem in Zechariah 2:1-2 and of the temple in Ezekiel 40-41. Ezekiel's city was eighteen thousand cubits around; John's is nearly two thousand times larger. The numbers twelve thousand and one hundred forty-four recall the hundred forty-four thousand, so they speak of God's people, not a building. He also likes Bauckham's contrast, through Keener: the human measure that is also an angel's answers the beast's human number in 13:18.
entries.dissent: Beale, Keener and Heiser read the numbers as symbols, since a wall of 144 cubits makes no sense around a city that size. The ESV Study Bible leaves open that they may be literal dimensions. MacArthur takes them as real: the rod is a standard measure of about ten feet, the measuring marks the city as God's own, and 144 cubits is likely the wall's width. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible and Heiser, after Bauckham, read 21:17 against 13:18: the beast lowers humanity, the city lifts it to an angelic level.

entries.title: Revelation 21:16, its length, width and height are equal
entries.summary: The city is a perfect cube, like the inner sanctuary of Solomon's temple in 1 Kings 6:20, and square like Ezekiel's holy area.
entries.plain: **When a family makes the whole house the room where the guests of honor sit, everyone gets the best seat.** Solomon's temple had one inner room that was a perfect cube, the most holy place, where God's presence was. Only the high priest could enter, once a year. Ezekiel's temple area was square. John's city is square too, but it is also a cube. The whole city has the shape of the most holy place.
entries.same: A square (tetragonos) measured by length and breadth, from Ezekiel 45:2 and 48:20 in Greek. Length, breadth and height all equal, as in the inner sanctuary of 1 Kings 6:20.
entries.differs: Ezekiel's sanctuary is square on the ground, and he never measures a height. John adds height and makes the city a cube. Solomon's inner room was twenty cubits each way; John's city is twelve thousand stadia, about fifteen hundred miles. No Old Testament text makes a whole city the shape of the inner sanctuary; that step is John's.
entries.turn: The cube says the city is the most holy place. Keener reads it as God's presence with his people at full strength, always. Beale adds that the high priest alone once stood there; now all God's people do. That is why, in 21:22, John sees no temple: the whole city already is one.
entries.not: **Not Ezekiel's square alone.** Ezekiel's holy area is square. John's city is a cube, equal in length, width and height, like the inner room of Solomon's temple.
entries.deeper: Beale traces the square to Ezekiel 45:2-3, where the holy area is tetragonos and measured by length and width, and to Ezekiel 41:21, 43:16 and 48:20 in Greek, where the same word is used of the temple, the altar and the holy allotment. Ezekiel 40:5 measures breadth and height equal, a source for 21:17. Revelation reads he polis tetragonos keitai ... to mekos kai to platos kai to hypsos autes isa estin. Beale says the equal length, breadth and height echo the inner sanctuary of 1 Kings 6:20, and that the high priest's breastpiece was also tetragonos, measured by length and breadth (Exodus 28:16). Some Jewish traditions, Keener and Beale note, expected the new Jerusalem to grow huge, reading Isaiah 54:2 and Ezekiel 41:7; Baba Bathra 75b makes it twelve miles high. Keener, the ESV Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible all cite 1 Kings 6:20. The grade is drawn here: the equal three dimensions point to one room, but no wording is shared.
entries.heiser: Heiser, reading Keener, says the city is not merely square but a cube, recalling the most holy place. The whole city is like a temple and like its holiest room. A city fifteen hundred miles high defies literalism, he says. With Beale and McDonough he reads God's glory, once kept in the back room of the temple, as now filling the whole new creation.
entries.dissent: Beale also weighs a minority view that the city is a pyramid, like a Babylonian ziggurat, which would set it against Babylon; he does not adopt it. Keener, the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible and Heiser read the dimensions as symbolic, and Keener notes that no one could breathe at that height. The ESV Study Bible allows that they may be literal. MacArthur takes them as real: about two million square miles of ground, room for all the saints, in the shape of the most holy place.

entries.title: Revelation 21:18-21, foundations of precious stones and gates of pearl
entries.summary: A city built of jewels, with jasper walls, jeweled foundations and gates of single pearls, comes from God's promise to rebuild Jerusalem in Isaiah 54:11-12.
entries.plain: **A ring made from a grandmother's stones keeps her promise in a new setting.** In Isaiah 54 God speaks to Jerusalem as a wife who was left alone and grieving. He promises to rebuild her with precious stones: foundations of sapphire, battlements of jasper, gates of shining stones. John sees that city. Its wall is jasper, its foundations are jewels, and each gate is one huge pearl.
entries.same: A city whose foundations, walls and gates are made of precious stones. The Greek of Isaiah 54:11-12 has sappheiros for the foundations and iaspis, jasper, for the battlements. John's wall is jasper, his first foundation jasper and his second sapphire.
entries.differs: In the Greek translation Isaiah's gates are crystal stones; John's are pearls. Isaiah names a few stones; John lists twelve, drawn from the high priest's breastpiece. Isaiah promised a rebuilt earthly Jerusalem; John's city comes from heaven. John adds gold like clear glass, from Solomon's gold-covered temple, Beale says.
entries.turn: Isaiah 54 is about a wife restored. God is the husband, the city is the bride, and the stones stand for lasting peace and safety. Beale reads John the same way: the jewels show that the bride is secure forever in God's presence. Since 21:9 she is the wife of the Lamb.
entries.not: **Not Isaiah's list repeated.** Isaiah 54 names a few stones for the foundations, walls and gates. John builds a whole city of gold and jewels.
entries.deeper: Isaiah 54:11-12 in Greek reads I prepare for you carbuncle for your stone and sapphire for your foundations, and I will make your battlements jasper, your gates crystal stones, and your wall choice stones. Revelation 21:18-19 reads he endomesis tou teichous autes iaspis ... hoi themelioi tou teichous tes poleos panti litho timio kekosmemenoi, the wall built of jasper and the foundations adorned with every precious stone. Beale lists 21:19-21 among the clear allusions to Isaiah 40-66. He notes that Isaiah 54 begins with God as Israel's husband and calls her a wife, gyne, as Revelation 21:9 does. The Qumran commentary on Isaiah 54 reads the stones as the community's twelve priests and tribal heads, and later rabbis (Baba Bathra 75a) expected literal gates of gems and pearls. Keener calls Isaiah 54:11-12 the main source for the stones; the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible also cite it. Tobit 13:16-17 pictures the new Jerusalem built with sapphire, emerald and gold.
entries.dissent: The sources agree on Isaiah 54. They differ on what the stones mean. Beale reads them as the safety and glory of God's people, and calls pearls large enough for gates on so high a wall a sign that the picture is figurative. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible stresses the contrast with Babylon's pearls in 17:4 and 18:16. Rabbinic readers, as Keener and Beale report, took the gems literally. MacArthur takes the materials at face value: a wall of clear diamond, gold you can see through, and gates each made of one pearl almost 1,400 miles high, recalling Christ's suffering.

entries.title: Revelation 21:19-20, the twelve stones of the foundations
entries.summary: The twelve foundation stones follow the twelve stones on the high priest's breastpiece in Exodus 28:17-20, with a likely glance at the stones of Eden in Ezekiel 28:13.
entries.plain: **A team that wears the founders' colors on a new kit is saying it carries the same story.** The high priest wore a breastpiece with twelve stones in four rows. Each stone bore the name of a tribe of Israel. John lists twelve stones for the city's foundations, and most of them match that breastpiece. The foundations carry the apostles' names. So the stones that once stood for Israel's tribes now hold up the whole people of God.
entries.same: Twelve precious stones, set out in an ordered list, standing for God's people. Eight of the Exodus 28:17-20 stones reappear in John's list, Beale says, and the others are equivalents. Jasper, sapphire and emerald appear in both.
entries.differs: John lists the stones in a different order from Exodus. He puts them on the city's foundations, not on a priest's chest. In Exodus the stones bear the tribes' names; in John the foundations bear the apostles' names. The gem list of Ezekiel 28:13, describing Eden's splendor, also overlaps with John's.
entries.turn: The high priest carried Israel's names into God's presence. Now the whole people stands there, built into the city. Beale reads it as the priesthood of all believers made final, as 22:3-4 will say. If Ezekiel 28 is in view too, the city is also Eden restored, the first garden on God's mountain.
entries.not: **Not the high priest's list copied out.** Eight of John's twelve stones appear on the breastpiece of Exodus 28, Beale and MacArthur note. The rest differ in name.
entries.deeper: Beale says the jewel list is based on Exodus 28:17-20 and 39:8-14, the breastpiece of judgment. Josephus gives the breastpiece stones in two other orders, so a new order does not rule out the allusion. Each stone bore a tribe's name (Exodus 28:21). In Revelation 21:19 the first foundation is iaspis, the second sappheiros, the third chalkedon, the fourth smaragdos. Beale also finds Ezekiel 28:13 partly in mind: its Greek lists eleven of the Exodus stones in nearly the same order, and it pictures a perfect figure in Eden, the garden on God's mountain. He links 1 Kings 7:9-10, where Solomon laid the temple's foundation with costly stones. The ESV Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible name both Exodus 28 and Ezekiel 28:13. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible counts nine stones shared by both lists. The grade is drawn here: twelve named stones standing for God's people point to the breastpiece.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads the stones against Ezekiel 28, not the breastpiece. In Unseen Realm, he says, he compared the lists: the stones of Ezekiel 28:13 match John's, while the high priest's list does not fit as well. So the gems describe a place, God's cosmic home in Eden, not a person. John describes the new Jerusalem in Eden terms on purpose. He cites Beale that Ezekiel 28:14 and 16 set Eden on a mountain of precious stones.
entries.dissent: Which list? Beale, Keener and the CSB Study Bible make Exodus 28 the main source, and MacArthur finds eight of the twelve on the breastpiece; Keener thinks Ezekiel 28:13 informs 17:4 rather than this list. Heiser argues the opposite: the match is with Ezekiel 28 and its Eden, not the high priest. The ESV Study Bible, the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible hold both together. Some ancient writers tied the breastpiece stones to the twelve signs of the zodiac; Keener says John avoids those links, and Beale doubts the pagan lists ever existed.

entries.title: Revelation 21:22, I saw no temple in the city
entries.summary: The city has no temple because God and the Lamb are its temple, a turn the sources trace to Jeremiah 3:16-17, where the ark is not remade and Jerusalem itself becomes the Lord's throne.
entries.plain: **A church that has outgrown its building may meet in a park and find God there just the same.** Everyone expected the new Jerusalem to have a great temple, as Ezekiel had pictured. John looks and sees none. God himself, with the Lamb, takes its place. Jeremiah 3 had already hinted at this. It says nobody will build the ark again, and the whole city will be named the Lord's throne.
entries.same: The holy object at the center of worship is no longer needed, because God's presence fills the city. In Jeremiah the ark will not be missed or remade; in John the temple is not there. In both, the nations come to the city (Jeremiah 3:17; Revelation 21:24).
entries.differs: There are no shared words. Jeremiah speaks of the ark, not the temple, and calls Jerusalem the Lord's throne. John speaks of the temple and names God and the Lamb as the temple itself. The link is one of ideas, which is why the grade is only possible.
entries.turn: Ezekiel spent four chapters on a temple. John sums them up in one line: the temple is God himself, with the Lamb. Beale reads this as the goal the old temple always pointed to. Jesus had called his body the temple (John 2:19-22). Now God's presence is no longer behind a curtain but everywhere in the city.
entries.not: **Not a quotation of Jeremiah.** No Old Testament verse says the city will have no temple. John draws the point from Jeremiah 3:16-17, where the ark is not remade, and says it in his own words.
entries.deeper: Jeremiah 3:16 in Greek says they will no longer say ark of the covenant of the holy one of Israel; it will not come to heart, nor be named, nor be made again. Verse 17 names Jerusalem thronos kyriou, the Lord's throne, the place where every nation gathers. Revelation 21:22 reads kai naon ouk eidon en aute, ho gar kyrios ho theos ho pantokrator naos autes estin kai to arnion. Beale names Jeremiah 3:16-17, with Haggai 2:9 and the Targum on Zechariah 4:7, as the Old Testament and Jewish texts closest to John's thought. He notes that Jeremiah's not remember and not come to mind are repeated almost word for word in Isaiah 65:17. The Jewish Study Bible notes the ark stood for God's presence and had vanished before the temple fell. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cites Jeremiah 3:16-17. The grade is possible: two sources and Heiser name the text, but the link rests on ideas.
entries.heiser: Heiser calls Jeremiah 3:16-17 the clearest preview and a rarely cited one. The ark, God's throne or footstool, will not be made again, and Jerusalem will be called the Lord's throne. Temple talk morphs into the whole city, which sounds like Revelation 21. On 21:22 itself he reads Beale and McDonough: John saw no material temple, because God and the Lamb fill the whole new creation. He adds that a third temple could still be built in Jerusalem, for political or religious reasons, but in his view it would not fulfill prophecy.
entries.dissent: Keener links 21:22 to Ezekiel 40-48 and Zechariah 14:21, and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible to Ezekiel 41-48, rather than to Jeremiah. Beale says a temple-free hope was mostly a break with Judaism, which kept looking for a greater material temple (1 Enoch 90:28-29; Tobit 13-14). The Jewish Study Bible reads Isaiah 66:1 as saying God never needed a building. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible and Heiser read the verse as a greater picture than Ezekiel's, not a rejection of it. MacArthur notes that earlier verses place a temple in heaven (7:15; 11:19) and reads this as the eternal state, where God himself is the temple.

entries.title: Revelation 21:23, no need of sun or moon
entries.summary: The city needs no sun or moon because God's glory lights it, taken from Isaiah 60:19-20, with the Lamb as its lamp.
entries.plain: **A stage lit from within the set needs no spotlights over the audience.** Isaiah 60 told Jerusalem that one day the sun and moon would no longer be her light. The Lord would be her light forever, and her God her glory. John sees exactly this. The city does not need sun or moon. God's glory lights it. Then John adds his own line: the Lamb is its lamp.
entries.same: No need of the sun or the moon, because God is the city's light. Isaiah 60:19 names the sun and the moon (helios, selene) and the Lord as everlasting light; John names helios and selene and the glory of God.
entries.differs: Isaiah's last line makes God the city's beauty. John replaces it with the Lamb is its lamp. Beale says the swap puts the Lamb beside God as the source of light, a mark of his deity. Isaiah says the sun will not be for light by day; John says the city has no need of it.
entries.turn: Beale and the ESV Study Bible read the light as God's presence, with Christ as the one through whom it shines. The same promise returns in 22:5, where there is no night. It also explains 21:25: the gates never close, because night never comes.
entries.not: **Not a claim that the sun is destroyed.** The city has no need of it; Beale reads the point as God's glory being enough to make his people glorious.
entries.deeper: Isaiah 60:19 in Hebrew reads lo yihyeh lach od hashemesh le'or yomam ... vehayah lach YHWH le'or olam velohayich letif'artech: the sun stops being the daytime light, and the Lord becomes a light that lasts forever. The Greek follows closely. Revelation reads he polis ou chreian echei tou heliou oude tes selenes ... he gar doxa tou theou ephotisen auten, kai ho lychnos autes to arnion. Beale says the wording of the whole verse is based directly on Isaiah 60:19, with Isaiah 24:23 perhaps in mind too, and that 4 Ezra 7:39-42 also alludes to Isaiah 60:19. Later Jewish writers, he notes, said the light of Isaiah 60:19 first shone in Eden. Keener says the line is taken directly from Isaiah 60:19-20. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the ESV Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible agree. Beale lists 21:23-26 among the clear allusions to Isaiah.
entries.dissent: The sources agree on Isaiah 60:19-20. The CSB Study Bible adds Isaiah 24:23, 30:26 and Zechariah 14:6-7. The CSB Study Bible also reads the light against Genesis 1:3, where light came before the sun and moon were made.

entries.title: Revelation 21:24, the nations walk by its light
entries.summary: Nations walking by the city's light and kings bringing their glory into it come from Isaiah 60:3, 5, the pilgrimage of the nations to Zion.
entries.plain: **A lighthouse that once guided one harbor's boats can end up guiding ships from every country.** Isaiah 60 pictures nations coming to Jerusalem's light and kings to her shining dawn. They bring their wealth with them. John sees the nations walking by the city's light. The kings of the earth bring their glory into it. In Revelation, kings of the earth were Babylon's allies. Here kings come to worship.
entries.same: Nations (ethne) and kings coming to the city because of its light. The Greek of Isaiah 60:3 has nations going by your light (to photi sou) and kings by your brightness; John has the nations walking through its light (dia tou photos autes) and the kings of the earth.
entries.differs: Isaiah's nations bring their wealth, the Hebrew chayil. John says they bring their glory. Beale notes that the Greek translation never renders chayil as glory, so the change is John's: the nations bring themselves as worshipers more than goods. John also adds of the earth to Isaiah's kings, the phrase used earlier for Babylon's allies.
entries.turn: In Isaiah the nations come to serve Israel and see God in Zion. John sees redeemed people from the nations inside the new Jerusalem with God's people from Israel. Beale reads the kings as converted, set against the kings who brought their glory to Babylon in chapter 18. Wright hears Psalm 72 too.
entries.not: **Not a quotation of Isaiah 60.** John takes up Isaiah's nations and kings drawn to the city's light, in words of his own.
entries.deeper: Isaiah 60:3 in Greek reads kai poreusontai ethne to photi sou, kai basileis te lamproteti sou, nations will go by your light and kings by your brightness. Isaiah 60:5 has the wealth of the sea and of nations coming to Zion. Revelation 21:24 reads kai peripatesousin ta ethne dia tou photos autes, kai hoi basileis tes ges pherousin ten doxan auton eis auten. Beale sets the texts side by side and says the parallels, with Isaiah 60:19 in 21:23, show the vision keeps alluding to Isaiah 60. He adds Isaiah 2:2-5, where nations stream to Zion and walk in the Lord's light. Rissi, as Beale reports, takes kings of the earth from Psalm 89:27; Beale finds Isaiah 60 better. Keener cites Isaiah 60:3-22 and 66:12. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible says the verse recalls Isaiah 60:3, 5, 11. Wright names Isaiah 60 above all, with Psalm 72, Isaiah 49:6-7 and Zechariah 14:16-17.
entries.dissent: Rissi and Vogelgesang, as Beale reports, read the open city as a sign that even the judged will one day come in; Beale rejects that as too literal. Fekkes suggests John left glory ambiguous: the nations' riches against Revelation 18, and their worship. The ESV Study Bible reads the kings as those whose names are in the Lamb's book of life. Beale reads the picture as a figure: the nations are saved along with Israel, not later. MacArthur reads the nations as redeemed people of every ethnic group, living in the city's light with no divisions between them.

entries.title: Revelation 21:25-26, its gates will never be shut
entries.summary: The gates that are never shut, through which the glory and honor of the nations is brought, come from Isaiah 60:11.
entries.plain: **A front door left open all night tells you the neighbors have nothing left to fear.** Ancient cities closed their gates at night against attack. Isaiah 60 promised Jerusalem that her gates would stay open day and night, so the wealth of the nations could come in. John sees gates that are never shut in the day. Then he adds that there is no night there at all.
entries.same: Gates that are never shut, and the nations' riches brought in. The Greek of Isaiah 60:11 has the gates not shut (ou kleisthesontai) day and night; John has ou me kleisthosin, they will never be shut. Both speak of what belongs to the nations being brought into the city.
entries.differs: Isaiah says the gates stay open day and night. John says they are not shut by day, and then explains there is no night. Isaiah has the force or wealth of the nations brought in; John has their glory and honor. John leaves out Isaiah's picture of kings led in procession.
entries.turn: Open gates mean perfect safety: no enemy remains, and nothing evil can get in, as verse 27 says. Beale also reads them as lasting welcome. The nations will never again be shut out of God's presence. Genesis 3:24 barred the road back to Eden's tree. Here the gates stand open.
entries.not: **Not a picture of a long line still waiting outside.** Beale says the open gates show eternal access, not people entering bit by bit over endless time.
entries.deeper: Isaiah 60:11 in Greek reads kai anoichthesontai hai pylai sou diapantos, hemeras kai nyktos ou kleisthesontai, eisagagein pros se dynamin ethnon, your gates will be open continually; day and night they will not be shut, to bring to you the power of the nations. Revelation 21:25-26 reads hoi pylones autes ou me kleisthosin hemeras, nyx gar ouk estai ekei, kai oisousin ten doxan kai ten timen ton ethnon eis auten. Beale prints the two side by side and says the wording of 21:26 is based on Isaiah 60:11. He notes the phrase glory and honor appears elsewhere in Revelation only in the praise of God and the Lamb (4:9, 11; 5:12-13), which supports reading the nations' gift as worship. He cites 1QM 12.12-15, which also alludes to Isaiah 60:11-12 for end-time Zion. Keener, the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible and the CSB Study Bible all name Isaiah 60:11.
entries.dissent: Who brings the glory, the kings or the nations? Beale says Isaiah 60:11 does not settle it and the point does not depend on it. The CSB Study Bible reads the verses as showing that nations and rulers keep their distinctions in the eternal state; Beale reads them as figurative. MacArthur, on 21:24, says all peoples merge into the one people of God, with no more divisions.

entries.title: Revelation 21:27, nothing unclean will enter
entries.summary: The ban on anything unclean entering the city recalls Isaiah 52:1 and 35:8, where the unclean will no longer pass through Zion or walk the holy way.
entries.plain: **A clean room in a lab has a door that only the properly dressed can pass.** Isaiah 52 tells Jerusalem that the unclean will never again walk through her. Isaiah 35 describes a holy road home where nothing unclean will travel. John says nothing unclean will enter the new city. Only those whose names the Lamb has written in his book go in.
entries.same: The unclean kept out of the holy city for good. Isaiah 52:1 in Greek promises that no longer will the uncircumcised and unclean (akathartos) pass through Jerusalem.
entries.differs: John's word for unclean is koinon, common or defiled, not Isaiah's akathartos. Isaiah names the uncircumcised and the unclean; John names whoever practices what is detestable or false. Isaiah has no book; John adds the Lamb's book of life, which Beale links partly to Isaiah 4:3, those written for life in Jerusalem.
entries.turn: Isaiah's line was about foreign armies and ritual impurity. John makes it moral and spiritual: the liars and idolaters of 21:8 stay outside. Beale says the warning is mainly for those who claim faith but live against it. Just as the unclean could not enter the old temple, the unclean will not enter the eternal one.
entries.not: **Not a ban on the nations.** Verses 24-26 have just brought the nations in. The ban is on uncleanness, as Keener notes, not on any people group.
entries.deeper: Isaiah 52:1 in Greek ends ouketi prostethesetai dielthein dia sou aperitmetos kai akathartos, no longer will the uncircumcised and unclean go through you. Revelation 21:27 reads kai ou me eiselthe eis auten pan koinon kai poion bdelygma kai pseudos. Beale says the verse alludes partly to Isaiah 35:8 and 52:1, both of which keep the unclean off the way into end-time Jerusalem, and adds Ezekiel 44:9, which bars the uncircumcised from the sanctuary. The allusion is supported, he notes, by the use of Isaiah 52:1 in 21:2 and 21:10. He also links the stones of 21:18-20 to righteousness, citing Isaiah 52:1, 60:20-21, Ezekiel 44:9 and Zechariah 14:21. The CSB Study Bible cross-references Isaiah 35:8 and 52:1. The grade is drawn here: the idea is distinctive, but John's words differ from the Greek.
entries.dissent: Keener hears Zechariah 14:21, no more traders or abominations in God's house, and Joel 3:17, no strangers in Jerusalem, rather than Isaiah. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible sets the verse beside Zechariah 5:3-4, where the wicked are banished.

entries.title: Revelation 22:1, the river of the water of life
entries.summary: The river that runs from God's throne is Ezekiel's river from the temple, joined to Zechariah's living water and the river that watered Eden.
entries.plain: **A town that rebuilds its old fountain on a grander square keeps the old shape in a new setting.** Ezekiel saw a river run out from under the temple, getting deeper as it went and bringing life wherever it reached. Zechariah saw living water flow out of Jerusalem. Genesis has a river going out of Eden. John sees one clear, shining river. Its source is the throne that God and the Lamb share.
entries.same: A river that starts at God's house and gives life. In the Greek both Ezekiel 47:9 and Genesis 2:10 use potamos, river, and Genesis says it goes out (ekporeuetai), the same verb John uses (ekporeuomenon). Zechariah 14:8 calls it living water.
entries.differs: In Ezekiel the water comes from under the temple door. In John it comes from the throne, because God and the Lamb are now the temple (21:22). Ezekiel's river freshens the Dead Sea and fills it with fish; John leaves out the sea and the fish. Genesis has one river that splits into four; John has one river running down the city's main street. The sources give no reason for each change beyond the temple now being God himself.
entries.turn: John ends the Bible's story where it began, with a river from God's presence. Beale reads the water as eternal life, the close company of God and the Lamb that nothing can break. Keener and Beale add that John may also mean the Spirit. Jesus spoke of living water in John 7.
entries.not: **Not a plain water supply.** Ancient cities needed water, the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible notes, but this river stands for life with God, not plumbing.
entries.deeper: Beale says the verse combines the pictures of living water flowing out of the end-time city and its temple in Ezekiel 47:1-9 and Zechariah 14:8, with Joel 3:18 as a third, and that Ezekiel is clearly in mind because chapters 21-22 keep returning to Ezekiel 40-48. He adds that it reaches back further, to Genesis 2:10, so that the end is made like the beginning, on a larger scale. Keener calls Ezekiel 47 the immediate allusion and names Genesis 2:10 and Psalm 46:4 as background; the ESV Study Bible, the CSB Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible point to the same texts. Walton notes that some ancient temples were said to be founded on springs, so a temple with water flowing from it was a known picture. In Greek the shared words are potamos (river) and the verb ekporeuomai (go out). Beale does not use a grade word here; the grade is drawn here by his definitions, since river, source and life-giving power all match Ezekiel 47.
entries.heiser: Heiser's last episode stops before chapter 22, so he never walks through this verse. In it he says that everything from 21:9 to 22:5 grows out of the hope for a restored temple, worked out as a new city and a new creation, and draws much of its imagery from Ezekiel 40-48. In his Revelation 5 lecture he points to 22:1 as the one place where the Lamb shares the throne the river flows from.
entries.dissent: Is the water the Holy Spirit? The ESV Study Bible says the Spirit carries this life, citing John 7:38-39, and the CSB Study Bible links it to the same promise. Beale grants the Spirit may be in mind but reads the water mainly as eternal fellowship with God. Keener leaves it as a possibility.

aw.n: Revelation 22:1-5, river and tree of life
aw.s: The angel shows John a clear, life-giving river running from God's throne through the middle of the city, with the tree of life on both banks, fruiting every month and healing the nations with its leaves. Nothing cursed remains; God's servants will see him face to face, carry his name and reign for ever in his light.

entries.title: Revelation 22:2, leaves for the healing of the nations
entries.summary: Ezekiel's fruit trees by the temple river become the tree of life from Eden, and leaves meant for healing are now for the healing of the nations.
entries.plain: **A family recipe handed to the whole street is the same dish served to more people.** Ezekiel saw fruit trees lining the river, bearing every month, with leaves that heal. John sees Eden's tree of life lining it. Then he adds what Ezekiel does not have. The leaves now heal the nations.
entries.same: Trees on each bank, fruit every month, leaves for healing. All of that is Ezekiel 47:12. The tree of life (xylon zoes) is Genesis 2:9's name for the tree in the garden's center.
entries.differs: Ezekiel speaks of every kind of fruit tree; John names the tree of life from Genesis. Ezekiel's leaves simply heal; John's heal the nations. The Greek of Ezekiel uses a word for health (hygieia); John uses therapeia, healing. Beale reads the single tree as standing for many trees, since one tree cannot grow on both banks. Twelve crops, one each month, fits the book's twelves.
entries.turn: The tree Adam lost is open again, and now it serves the whole world. In Ezekiel the river renews Israel's land. In John the healing reaches people from every nation who belong to the Lamb. Beale reads the healing as the finished work of Christ's death, given once and for all, since there is no more sickness or death in the new creation (21:4).
entries.not: **Not a medicine for ongoing illness.** Beale says the healing does not go on forever, since there will be no more pain (21:4). It pictures a cure already complete.
entries.deeper: Beale says the leaves for healing are based on Ezekiel 47:12, which is itself modeled on Eden's garden and river in Genesis 2:9-10, and that the tree of life shows John read Ezekiel's fruitful land as Eden restored (Genesis 3:22, 24). In his introduction he gives this verse as an example of universalization: leaves promised to Israel become leaves for the nations. The Hebrew of Ezekiel 47:12 ends vealehu litrufah, its leaf for healing. Some manuscripts of Revelation drop of the nations, which Beale thinks brings it closer to Ezekiel. Keener says John changes Ezekiel's trees to bring in the tree of life from Genesis, and that some Jewish writers counted twelve trees, a tree per month. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible notes the added of the nations; Wright calls this one of John's most moving reworkings. Beale gives no grade word here; the grade is drawn here: trees, river banks, monthly fruit and healing leaves could only come from Ezekiel 47:12.
entries.heiser: Heiser does not reach 22:2 in a full reading. In other episodes he calls the healing of the nations the end point of the Deuteronomy 32 story: the nations are judged, then healed, in a new Eden. In the Revelation 19 lecture he begins the Bible's meal with God at the tree of life, in Eden, which he calls God's house. In the Revelation 12 lecture he floats a link with Israel's feast calendar, then says he cannot be sure of it.
entries.dissent: One tree or many? Beale and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible read the single tree as a kind of tree filling the city, after Ezekiel's many trees. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible thinks John means one tree on purpose, because eternal life has one source, Jesus. Beale also notes a reading of verse 2 with one tree standing between two branches of the river.

entries.title: Revelation 22:3, no more curse
entries.summary: John takes Zechariah's promise that Jerusalem will never again lie under a ban of destruction and sets it in Eden, where the curse of Genesis 3 is lifted.
entries.plain: **A town that tears down the sign announcing its demolition has had more than a reprieve.** Zechariah promised that rebuilt Jerusalem would never again be put under God's ban and destroyed. John uses Zechariah's words. But he places them in the restored garden, so they also answer the curse that fell on the ground after Adam sinned.
entries.same: The words match Zechariah 14:11 almost exactly in Greek. Both say ouk estai eti, there will be no more. Only the word for curse differs.
entries.differs: For curse the Greek of Zechariah has anathema; John has katathema. Beale says both words render the Hebrew cherem, the ban that marks something for destruction. Zechariah speaks of one city, safe at last after a final attack. John widens it to the whole new creation, and the setting of a river and the tree of life calls up the curse on the ground in Genesis 3:17.
entries.turn: John says nothing will ever again fall under God's sentence. Beale reads it as the end of the curse of death that Adam brought, now removed by the Lamb. The reason given is the throne of God and the Lamb in the city: where God fully reigns, no curse remains.
entries.not: **Not a promise to one city only.** In Zechariah the promise belongs to Jerusalem. John applies it to the whole new creation and to everyone who lives there.
entries.deeper: Beale says the phrase is from Zechariah 14:11, where the Greek reads anathema ouk estai eti and John reads katathema ouk estai eti. The Hebrew is vecherem lo yihyeh od, and no ban will be again. Cherem was the ban of total destruction placed on what was devoted to judgment. Beale thinks John may also have Isaiah 34:1-2 in mind, where the nations are put under the ban. Keener says the removal of the curse comes from Zechariah 14:11 and here means the reversal of Eden's curse (Genesis 3:16-19). The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible says it evokes the Greek translation of Zechariah 14:11 and also the fall; the ESV Study Bible and the CSB Study Bible point to Genesis 3; the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible names both. The grade is drawn here: Beale says the phrase is from Zechariah, and the wording differs by one word.
entries.dissent: The sources agree on Zechariah and differ on the weight given to Genesis. Keener and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible put the Eden curse at the center. Beale centers on Zechariah's ban and adds a possible echo of Isaiah 34:2, which no other source names.

entries.title: Revelation 22:3, his servants will serve him
entries.summary: Isaiah's promise that Israel will be called priests of the Lord is fulfilled when all God's servants serve him in the temple-city.
entries.plain: **A title once held by a few can be handed to everyone in the room.** Isaiah promised that Israel's people would bear the title of the Lord's priests. In Revelation 22 all of God's servants serve him before his throne. John's verb is the word for priestly service in a temple, so the whole people now do what priests once did.
entries.same: God's people serving him as priests. The shared idea is a whole people in priestly service.
entries.differs: Isaiah uses the nouns priests and ministers. John uses a verb, latreuo, to serve in worship, as in 7:15. Isaiah promises Israel the wealth of the nations; John says nothing of wealth. The sources give no reason for the change of wording.
entries.turn: In the old temple only priests came near. Now every servant of God serves him face to face, because the city itself is the temple. Beale and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible read the service as priestly, the fulfillment of a promise first made to Israel.
entries.not: **Not a word for slavery.** The servants here are God's people, and their service is worship in his presence, as in 7:15.
entries.deeper: Beale says the priestly service echoes Isaiah 61:6, and that Isaiah is in mind because John weaves Isaiah through 21:1-22:5, with Isaiah 61:10 in 21:2 and Isaiah 60 in 21:23-26 and 22:5. He compares 7:15, where the saints already do priestly service in the heavenly temple. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible also cites Isaiah 61:6 for priestly service in God's temple-city, and the ESV Study Bible calls the servants priests in a city that has become a temple. The Greek of Isaiah 61:6 has hiereis kyriou, priests of the Lord, and leitourgoi, ministers; John's verb is latreusousin. The grade is drawn here: Beale's wording, evident, fits his probable grade, since the idea is traceable to Isaiah though the words differ.
entries.dissent: The sources agree the service is priestly. They do not discuss a rival source.

entries.title: Revelation 22:4, they will see his face
entries.summary: God told Moses no one could see his face and live; John says God's servants will see it.
entries.plain: **A door marked no entry that later swings open on its own changes the meaning of the old sign.** At Sinai Moses asked to see God's glory. God said no one could see his face and live. John says all God's servants will see it. What was closed even to Moses is now open to everyone in the city.
entries.same: Seeing God's face. The Greek of Exodus 33:20 has idein to prosopon mou, to see my face; John has opsontai to prosopon autou, they will see his face.
entries.differs: Exodus says no one can. John says they will. He gives no condition and no limit. Psalm 17:15 and other psalms only hope for it. The sources give the reason in what has changed: the people are now made clean and the whole city is the holy place.
entries.turn: Seeing God's face is the highest blessing of the age to come, the ESV Study Bible says. Beale calls it the answer to the old prayer that God would shine his face on his people. What would have killed a sinner now brings life.
entries.not: **Not a contradiction of Exodus.** Exodus speaks of sinful people in the old world. John speaks of a cleansed people in a new one, the ESV Study Bible and Beale both say.
entries.deeper: Keener says God's once-hidden face (Exodus 33:20) will now be fully shown; the ESV Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible make the same contrast with Moses. Beale says the hope of seeing God's face runs through the psalms (Psalms 11:4-7; 17:15; 27:4) and Jewish writings, and that a revelation that would once bring death (Exodus 33:20) now brings eternal life. He hears the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:25-27 behind 22:4-5, where God's face shines and his name is placed on Israel. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible notes Jewish hopes of seeing God's face at the end. The grade is drawn here as possible: the words are general, and the sources name Exodus as a contrast more than as a source.
entries.dissent: Beale makes the priestly blessing of Numbers 6 the text most in mind; Keener, the ESV Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible point to Moses at Sinai. The sources do not say whether the face is God's or the Lamb's; Beale says it is unclear and that both are present.

entries.title: Revelation 22:4, his name on their foreheads
entries.summary: The gold plate on the high priest's forehead, marked holy to the Lord, becomes God's name on the forehead of every servant.
entries.plain: **A badge once pinned only on the head of a department can end up on every staff member's jacket.** In Exodus the high priest wore a gold plate on his forehead, engraved holy to the Lord, so Israel could be accepted before God. John sees God's name on the foreheads of all his servants. Each one now has the access the high priest had.
entries.same: A divine name worn on the forehead. The Greek of Exodus 28:38 places the plate on the metopon, the forehead, the same word John uses.
entries.differs: Exodus engraves holy to the Lord on one man's plate. John has only God's name, on everyone. Beale answers that Philo and Josephus both say the high priest's plate carried the name Yahweh alone. The plate in Exodus let the priest bear Israel's guilt; John says nothing of guilt, since the people are already clean.
entries.turn: What only Aaron wore, all God's people wear. Beale reads it as access to God's presence. Once it was kept for the high priest. Now the whole people have it. The name also marks them as his and keeps them safe, as the seal of 7:3 and the name of 14:1 did.
entries.not: **Not a tattoo or a visible mark.** Beale reads the name as a picture of belonging to God and of his presence with his people, not ink on skin.
entries.deeper: Beale says it is beyond coincidence that God's name was on the high priest's forehead in Exodus 28:36-38, and that 22:4 grants every saint what was reserved for the high priest, as 21:18-20 did with the breastpiece stones. The Greek of Exodus 28:38 has epi tou metopou Aaron, on Aaron's forehead, and dekton, accepted. Beale also links the new names given to end-time Zion in Isaiah 62 and 65, and the name written on the overcomer in 3:12. Keener points back to 7:3 and says the point is that God's people belong to him alone. The CSB Study Bible's word study notes that forehead marks in the ancient world showed ownership or loyalty to a god. Only Beale names Exodus 28; the grade is drawn here as probable from his wording, beyond coincidence, and the shared rare detail of the forehead.
entries.dissent: The sources differ on what the name chiefly means. Beale stresses priestly access. Keener and the CSB Study Bible stress ownership, God claiming his servants, against the mark of the beast (13:16).

entries.title: Revelation 22:5, no night, for the Lord God gives them light
entries.summary: Isaiah's promise that the Lord, not the sun, will be his people's light, and Zechariah's day without night, close John's vision of the city.
entries.plain: **People who live near the far north know summer weeks when the sun never sets.** Isaiah promised Jerusalem that the sun and moon would no longer be its light, because the Lord would be its everlasting light. Zechariah saw a day with no night. John repeats both. The servants need no lamp and no sun, because God himself shines on them.
entries.same: No need of sun, because the Lord gives light, from Isaiah 60:19-20. No night, from Zechariah 14:7. In Greek both John and Zechariah use nyx, night.
entries.differs: Isaiah speaks of the sun and moon; John speaks of a lamp and the sun. Isaiah promises the Lord as everlasting light; John says God will shine on them. Zechariah's single day, neither day nor night, becomes simply no night. John has used Isaiah 60 already in 21:23-25 and repeats it here.
entries.turn: Nothing from the old world can dim God's presence any more. Beale reads it as the full answer to the prayer that God's face would shine on his people. The light leads straight into the reign that follows in the same verse.
entries.not: **Not a claim about astronomy.** Beale says the point is not whether the sun exists in the new world but that nothing will hide God's glory.
entries.deeper: Beale calls this a repeated allusion to Isaiah 60:19-20, already used in 21:23, and says the language is figurative. The Greek of Isaiah 60:19 reads ouk estai soi eti ho helios eis phos hemeras, the sun will no longer be your light by day, and estai soi kyrios phos aionion, the Lord will be your everlasting light. John has ou chreia photos lychnou kai photos heliou, no need of lamplight or sunlight, hoti kyrios ho theos photisei, for the Lord God will shine. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cites both Isaiah 60:19-20 and Zechariah 14:7 here. Beale adds the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:25-27, God making his face shine, as uppermost in mind. Keener notes Jewish visions of the righteous shining in the future. The grade is drawn here as probable: the idea is Isaiah's, the wording John's own.
entries.dissent: Beale holds open whether there will be no sun at all or a sun outshone by God's light, and says the text does not settle it. Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible point instead to Jewish hopes of the righteous shining (Daniel 12:3), a different focus.

entries.title: Revelation 22:5, they will reign forever and ever
entries.summary: Daniel's holy ones receive the kingdom forever; John ends his vision with God's servants reigning forever and ever.
entries.plain: **A promise kept long after it was made makes the old words sound new.** Daniel saw the holy ones of the Most High receive the kingdom and hold it forever. John's last word about the city is that God's servants will reign forever and ever. Daniel's promise has come true.
entries.same: God's people ruling for all ages. Daniel 7:18 in Greek has heos aionos ton aionon, to the age of the ages; John has eis tous aionas ton aionon, forever and ever.
entries.differs: Daniel says the holy ones will receive and possess the kingdom. John uses the verb reign (basileuo), and he names no kingdom and no subjects. Daniel's kingdom comes after four beasts are judged. John's reign comes after the whole old order has passed.
entries.turn: The servants in 22:3 are also kings. Beale says the reign is eternal and so cannot be the thousand years of 20:4-6; it is the climax of Daniel's promise and of Jesus' word in 3:21. The ESV Study Bible says believers reign over the new earth with Jesus.
entries.not: **Not the thousand-year reign.** Beale separates this reign from 20:4-6, which has an end and a final revolt. This one never ends.
entries.deeper: Beale calls the reign a climactic fulfillment of Daniel 7:18 and 27, already begun for the saints in the church age (1:6; 5:10) and in heaven (20:4-6). He suggests the reign is best read with a corporate sense of Zechariah 14:9, the Lord king over all the earth, and compares Adam's charge to rule the earth (Genesis 1:28). The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cites Daniel 7:27 and Revelation 20:4. The Greek of Daniel 7:27 (the version called Theodotion) has basileia aionios, an everlasting kingdom, given to the holy ones of the Most High. The grade is drawn here as probable: the idea of the holy ones ruling forever is traceable to Daniel 7, while the wording is general.
entries.heiser: Heiser reads the rule in the Revelation 20 lecture. He says Christ will rule on earth forever, not for a thousand years, and believers will rule with him forever in a new Eden spread over the whole globe. He ties the thrones to Daniel 7, where the holy ones sit and rule together as God's council. Believers who die join that council now; what they wait for is shared rule on a new earth.
entries.dissent: Beale reads the thousand years of 20:4-6 as the church age and this reign as the eternal state after it. Heiser reads the binding of 20:1-6 as the present age but says the reign of 20:6 cannot be, since it follows the first resurrection, and he holds the rule after the last battle to be forever. The ESV Study Bible links this verse to 5:10. MacArthur reads the thousand years as a future reign on earth after Christ returns, and this reign as the eternal state that follows it.

aw.n: Revelation 22:1-5, river and tree of life
aw.s: The angel shows John a clear, life-giving river running from God's throne through the middle of the city, with the tree of life on both banks, fruiting every month and healing the nations with its leaves. Nothing cursed remains; God's servants will see him face to face, carry his name and reign for ever in his light.

entries.title: Revelation 22:6, what must soon take place
entries.summary: The closing words repeat the opening of the book, Daniel's what must take place, with Daniel's true and faithful added.
entries.plain: **A speech that ends with the line it began with tells the audience the whole thing hangs together.** Revelation opened with Daniel's words about God showing what must happen. It closes with them too. The angel adds that these words are faithful and true, much as Daniel told the king his dream was true and its meaning sure.
entries.same: The Greek phrase ha dei genesthai, what must take place, as in Daniel 2:28-29 and 45. Daniel 2:45 also pairs alethinos, true, with pistos, faithful.
entries.differs: Daniel says after these things, or in the last days. John says en tachei, soon, exactly as in 1:1. Daniel speaks of a dream and its meaning; John speaks of the words of this book. Daniel's God makes it known to a king; John's God sends an angel to his servants.
entries.turn: The book is framed by Daniel 2 at both ends. Like Daniel's dream, Beale says, Revelation is about God's kingdom filling the earth and the judgment of the world's kingdoms. Beale reads the change to soon as a hint that the fulfillment has already started.
entries.not: **Not a new prophecy tacked on.** The verse repeats 1:1 almost word for word. It closes the book; it does not add to it.
entries.deeper: Beale says 22:6b is clearly drawn from Daniel 2:28-29, 45, and reproduces the exact wording of 1:1, so it should be read as the formal conclusion of the whole book. He hears Daniel 2:45 Theodotion in 22:6a: the dream is true (alethinon) and its interpretation faithful (piste). He also ties faithful and true to Isaiah 65:16 through 21:5. He finds the same Daniel formula at 1:1, 1:19 and 4:1, and in his introduction he lists these as possible indirect fulfillment: Daniel's prophecy referred to as beginning to come true. Keener reads faithful and true as a formula for sworn testimony. The ESV Study Bible and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible note the echo of 1:1 as a closing bracket. The grade is drawn here: the phrase matches Daniel word for word, as in 1:1, which is graded clear.
entries.dissent: The sources agree on Daniel 2. Beale hears Daniel 2:45 in faithful and true; Keener reads the pair as an oath formula (Jeremiah 42:5). MacArthur reads soon as the imminence of Christ's return, and the things to take place as the whole of the book.
