entries.title: Revelation 22:6, the God of the spirits of the prophets
entries.summary: The title God of the spirits of the prophets may adapt a title Moses uses, which names God over the spirits of all people.
entries.plain: **A familiar title with one word swapped can point to a new group.** Twice in Numbers, Moses names God as the one over the spirits of every living person. John calls God the Lord of the spirits of the prophets. The old title covered all people. John narrows it to the ones God speaks through.
entries.same: God of the spirits. The Greek of Numbers 27:16 has ho theos ton pneumaton, the same words John uses before of the prophets.
entries.differs: Numbers goes on to name all flesh; John names the prophets. In Numbers 27 Moses asks God to appoint a leader after him; in Numbers 16 he pleads for the people. John uses the title to say God stands behind the prophets who bring his word.
entries.turn: The God who chose Joshua after Moses has sent this message. If the echo stands, Beale says, the spirits are God's Spirit speaking through the prophets. That puts John in the line of Israel's prophets.
entries.not: **Not a sure link.** Beale writes of it with an if, and Keener names the title without saying John borrowed it.
entries.deeper: Beale suggests an echo of Numbers 27:16, where the Lord God of the spirits and of all flesh is asked to name Joshua as Israel's next prophetic leader, and notes the same title in Numbers 16:22. If the echo is real, he says, the phrase means God's Spirit speaking through the prophets. He also notes that Lord of Spirits is a title for God about a hundred times in the Similitudes of 1 Enoch. Keener calls God of the spirits of all flesh an Old Testament title (Numbers 16:22), found later in Jewish and Samaritan texts, and says John ties it to the prophets. The grade is possible: two sources propose the link, and the wording is only partly the same.
entries.dissent: Beale weighs whether the prophets are a special office or all believers, and leans to an office because Daniel 2 brackets the phrase. Some manuscripts change it to holy prophets. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cross-references 1 Corinthians 14:32 rather than Numbers.

entries.title: Revelation 22:10, do not seal up the words
entries.summary: Daniel was told to seal his book until the time of the end; John is told not to seal his, because the time is near.
entries.plain: **A sealed letter waits for its day, but an open one is meant to be read at once.** Daniel was told to close his words and seal his book until the end came. John hears the opposite command. He must not seal his book, because the time is near. What Daniel had to keep closed is now open.
entries.same: The sealing of a prophet's words. The Greek of Daniel 12:4 has sphragison, seal; John has me sphragises, do not seal. Both speak of the words (logoi) of a book.
entries.differs: Daniel is commanded to seal; John is commanded not to. Daniel's sealing lasts until the end comes; John's reason is that the time is near (ho kairos engys), the words of 1:3. Daniel did not understand what he saw; John's readers are meant to understand now.
entries.turn: Daniel was told to seal his words until the end; John is told to leave his book open. Beale reads that as a sign that Daniel's prophecies have started to come true through Christ's death and resurrection, so they can now be understood. The churches must hear the book read and obey it.
entries.not: **Not a quotation of Daniel.** John reverses Daniel's command in words of his own. The link is the sealing, not a shared sentence.
entries.deeper: Beale links the command to Daniel 12:4 (in Theodotion, the words are shut and the book sealed until the end), with 12:9 and 8:26. The Hebrew of 12:4 is setom hadevarim vachatom hasefer ad et qets. In his introduction Beale files the verse under possible indirect fulfillment: the use intensifies 1:1-3 and is tied to the verbatim repeat of 1:1 in 22:6. Keener says some of Daniel's visions applied only to the future, while John's book is for his own generation. Walton notes that in Daniel sealing concerns authentication once the set time has passed. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the ESV Study Bible, the CSB Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible all name Daniel 12:4 or 12:9. The command reverses Daniel's, but Beale's point is fulfillment, so the reason given here is read as coming true. The grade is drawn here: the sealing of a prophetic book until the end is unique to Daniel 12.
entries.dissent: Beale reads the time as near because fulfillment has begun and continues through history. MacArthur reads near as imminence, meaning the end is the next event; the book stays open so that it can be preached and obeyed. The ESV Study Bible says the end is near for every generation because the dragon was defeated at the cross. The CSB Study Bible stresses imminence; the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible says Jesus fulfills what was sealed.

entries.title: Revelation 22:11, let the wrongdoer still do wrong
entries.summary: Daniel foretold that the wicked would go on in wickedness while the wise understand; John turns the forecast into commands.
entries.plain: **A weather forecast and an order to take an umbrella say the same thing in two moods.** Daniel was told that in the last days the wicked would keep acting wickedly, while the wise would understand. John repeats the pattern as commands. The wrongdoer is told to keep at it, and the holy one to stay holy.
entries.same: Two groups who stay as they are: the wicked go on in wrong, the righteous in right. Both texts follow the sealing of Daniel's book.
entries.differs: Daniel predicts; John commands. Daniel speaks of the lawless who will not understand and the wise who will. John uses four pairs: wrongdoing, filth, righteousness, holiness. Ezekiel 3:27 gives the command form, let the one who hears hear and the one who refuses refuse. Beale says the change from forecast to command shows that Daniel's prophecy is already coming true.
entries.turn: The wicked are left to their choice. The faithful are urged on. Beale reads the commands as the double effect of God's word: it hardens those who reject it and wakes up those who belong to him. Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible call the tone ironic, a challenge to the unrepentant.
entries.not: **Not God inviting people to sin.** The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible says the language is ironic, as in the prophets, a challenge to people who refuse to repent.
entries.deeper: Beale says 22:11 makes explicit allusion to Daniel 12:10, right after the use of Daniel 12:4, 9 in 22:10, and that it may also echo Ezekiel 3:27, part of the Isaiah 6 hardening theme. The Greek of Daniel 12:10 (Theodotion) has anomesosin anomoi, the lawless will act lawlessly, and hoi noemones synesousin, the wise will understand. John has ho adikon adikesato eti, let the wrongdoer still do wrong. Beale notes the Greek of Daniel 12:4 ends with the earth filled with injustice (adikia). Keener, the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the ESV Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible all cite Daniel 12:10, most with Ezekiel 3:27. The grade is drawn here as probable: the pattern of two fixed groups is traceable to Daniel 12:10, but the words differ.
entries.dissent: Beale reads the commands as real, a judgment of hardening on apostates and a call to the faithful. Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible read them as ironic. The ESV Study Bible says patterns of behavior will at last become fixed. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible gives both readings.

entries.title: Revelation 22:12, my reward is with me
entries.summary: Isaiah's picture of the Lord coming with his reward is spoken by Jesus of himself, with the Old Testament rule that each is repaid by his works.
entries.plain: **When a deputy says the boss's line in the first person, the listeners know who he claims to be.** Isaiah announced that the Lord was coming, with his reward with him. Jesus says it of himself, in the first person, with the reward as his own. He adds that he will repay each person for what they have done, a rule the psalms say belongs to God.
entries.same: Look, coming, and his reward with him. The Greek of Isaiah 40:10 reads idou ... ho misthos autou met' autou; John has idou ... ho misthos mou met' emou. Isaiah 62:11 repeats it. Psalm 62:12 has repaying each according to works.
entries.differs: Isaiah speaks of the Lord in the third person; Jesus speaks in the first. Isaiah adds that his work is before him; John turns work into each person's deeds. The Greek of Isaiah 62:11 already says the saviour comes, which Beale thinks helped John apply the line to Jesus. The judging by works comes from Psalm 62:12, Proverbs 24:12 and Jeremiah 17:10.
entries.turn: What was said of the Lord is now said by Jesus. Beale calls it another claim to deity. In Isaiah the reward is salvation for God's people; in John it covers reward and judgment, since Jesus repays each person by their works.
entries.not: **Not salvation earned by deeds.** Beale says works show who has been washed in the Lamb's blood (22:14); the reward in Isaiah was salvation God gives.
entries.deeper: Beale sets Isaiah 40:10 in the Greek beside 22:12 and says what Isaiah foretold of the Lord is fulfilled in Jesus. He adds Isaiah 62:11, where the Greek reads behold, the saviour has come, having his reward with him, and says the Targum and some Greek copies already read the work as each person's work. The Hebrew of Isaiah 40:10 is hinneh secharo itto, his wage is with him. For repayment by works he points to 2:23 and texts such as Proverbs 24:12. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible names Isaiah 40:10, 62:11, Psalm 62:12, Proverbs 24:12 and Jeremiah 17:10 and says the divine role is applied to Jesus. Keener cites Psalm 62:12; the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cites Isaiah 40:10 and 62:11. The grade is drawn here: the phrase matches Isaiah almost word for word.
entries.dissent: The ESV Study Bible reads Jesus here as the Divine Warrior of Isaiah 62:10-63:6, bringing reward and punishment, with degrees of each. Beale stresses that Isaiah's reward is salvation and that judgment is only implied there. Beale also hears Matthew 16:27.

entries.title: Revelation 22:13, the first and the last
entries.summary: Jesus gathers into one sentence the titles Isaiah gives the Lord alone, the first and the last, with the Alpha and the Omega and the beginning and the end.
entries.plain: **A signature that combines three family seals leaves no doubt whose letter it is.** In Isaiah the Lord calls himself first and last, and says there is no other God. Revelation has used these titles one at a time, for God and for Jesus. Here Jesus claims all three together.
entries.same: First and last, from Isaiah 44:6 and 48:12. John's Greek is ho protos kai ho eschatos.
entries.differs: Isaiah has first and last only. John adds Alpha and Omega, the opening and closing letters of the Greek alphabet. He also adds beginning and end. In Isaiah the Lord speaks; here Jesus speaks.
entries.turn: Titles Isaiah kept for the one God now belong to Jesus. Beale says the pairs mean he rules the start and the end of history and everything between. That is why he can promise to come and to judge in the verse before.
entries.not: **Not a title for a lesser being.** In Isaiah the first and the last means the only God; the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible and Beale read it as a divine title applied to Jesus.
entries.deeper: Beale notes that the book has already given God the titles Alpha and Omega (1:8; 21:6) and beginning and end (21:6), and given Christ the title first and last (1:17; 2:8). Here all three, used of God in the Old Testament, are joined and given to Christ. He refers back to his comments on 1:4, 8 and 17 for the Old Testament background, where Isaiah 41:4, 44:6 and 48:12 are the source. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible names those three Isaiah texts and says the divine titles belong to Jesus. The ESV Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible call them divine titles. The grade follows chapter 1, where Beale calls the use of Isaiah in 1:17 a clear reference.
entries.dissent: The sources agree. Keener reads the titles as an inclusio, framing the book with its opening in 1:8.

entries.title: Revelation 22:14, the right to the tree of life
entries.summary: Adam was driven out so he could not reach the tree of life; those who wash their robes are given the right to it.
entries.plain: **A gate that once had a guard posted to keep people out can end up with a welcome mat.** After Adam sinned, God sent him out of the garden. Cherubim with a flaming sword kept him from the tree. John blesses those who wash their robes. They get the right to the tree and walk in through the city's gates.
entries.same: The tree of life (xylon tes zoes) and the way into it. The Greek of Genesis 3:24 uses the same words for the tree.
entries.differs: Genesis bars the way; John grants the right (exousia) to it. Genesis has cherubim and a flaming sword; John has open gates. Beale adds that the words about going through the gates come from the Greek of Isaiah 62:10, go through my gates. Genesis 3 has no city.
entries.turn: The expulsion from Eden is undone for those made clean by the Lamb. Washing robes points back to 7:14, where they are made white in his blood. Those outside in 22:15 stay outside, so the banishment of Genesis 3 lasts for the wicked, Beale says.
entries.not: **Not entry earned by good behavior.** The robes are washed in the Lamb's blood (7:14), the sources say; the right is a gift.
entries.deeper: Beale says the tree of life and the open gates pick up the Isaiah 60 and Genesis 3 imagery of 21:24-22:3, and that the gates are taken specifically from Isaiah 62:10 in Greek (poreuesthe dia ton pylon mou), perhaps with Isaiah 26:2 and Psalm 118:20. On 22:15 he says the casting out of the garden in Genesis 3:23-24 continues for the wicked. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible says access to the tree reverses the banishment of Genesis 3:24, and the CSB Study Bible says it is what Adam and Eve were cut off from. The ESV Study Bible calls the tree once banned to humanity. Beale notes Testament of Levi 18:10-11, where a messianic figure opens paradise and feeds the saints from the tree of life. The grade is drawn here as probable: the tree and the access are uniquely Genesis 3, though no sentence is repeated.
entries.dissent: Beale leans on Isaiah 62:10 for the gates and on 7:14 for the robes. The other sources name Genesis 3 alone. Some manuscripts read those who keep his commandments instead of those who wash their robes; Beale thinks the change began by accident.

entries.title: Revelation 22:15, outside are the dogs
entries.summary: The dogs shut out of the city may recall Deuteronomy's ban on bringing a dog's wages into God's house.
entries.plain: **An old insult can carry the weight of the rule it first came from.** Deuteronomy forbade Israel to bring a prostitute's fee or a dog's wages into the Lord's house. John lists dogs first among those left outside the city. The word ties the outsiders to the uncleanness once barred from God's house.
entries.same: Dogs (kyon, kynes) kept out of God's dwelling. The Greek of Deuteronomy 23:18 forbids the price of a dog in the house of the Lord.
entries.differs: Deuteronomy bans a dog's wage from the temple; John bars dogs from the city. Deuteronomy pairs the dog with a prostitute's fee; John puts the dogs at the head of a list of sorcerers, the sexually immoral, murderers, idolaters and liars. The sources do not agree on who the dogs are.
entries.turn: The city is the holy place, so what was unclean for the temple stays out. Beale reads the dogs as people who claim faith but serve idols. Paul uses the word that way in Philippians 3:2.
entries.not: **Not about animals.** All the sources take dogs as a name for people, a common insult in the ancient world.
entries.deeper: Beale says John's dogs, with those doing abomination in 21:27, suggest that Deuteronomy 23:18 is echoed, where the wages of a dog are linked with a harlot's fee and called an abomination not to be brought into the temple. He also cites Psalm 59:6, 14 and Isaiah 56:10-11, and hears the sin list of Malachi 3:5. Keener reads dogs as probably the sexually immoral, specifically unrepentant prostitutes, citing Deuteronomy 23:17-18. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible makes the same link and notes that dog was a common Greek insult. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible cross-references Deuteronomy 23:18. The grade is possible: the shared word is one image, though several sources name the text.
entries.dissent: Keener and the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible read the dogs as male prostitutes. Beale reads them as apostates driven by greed. The NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible and the CSB Study Bible say false teachers, after Philippians 3:2. The ESV Study Bible names no Old Testament text.

entries.title: Revelation 22:16, the root of David and the bright morning star
entries.summary: Jesus names himself with two royal prophecies at once: the root from Jesse's line in Isaiah 11 and the star out of Jacob in Numbers 24.
entries.plain: **A new king who signs with two old seals of his family claims both inheritances.** Isaiah promised a shoot from the root of Jesse, David's father, who would rule the nations. Balaam saw a star come from Jacob and a ruler's rod from Israel. Jesus calls himself David's root and descendant, and the shining star of the morning. He claims both promises.
entries.same: Root (rhiza) from Isaiah 11:1 and 11:10, the root of Jesse. Star (aster in John, astron in the Greek of Numbers 24:17) rising from Jacob.
entries.differs: Isaiah names Jesse; John names David. John adds offspring (genos), which Beale says makes root mean a descendant. Numbers has a star out of Jacob that crushes Moab; John's star is bright and of the morning, with no battle. John already used these titles one at a time, in 5:5 and 2:28; here he joins them.
entries.turn: Jesus says, in the present tense, that he is the king these prophecies promised. Beale reads it as a sign that the messianic victory has begun and will be completed. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible notes that Gentiles worshiped the morning star as a god; Jesus takes the title for the Messiah.
entries.not: **Not Venus or a pagan star god.** Keener says the morning star is Venus, herald of the dawn, but the title here points to the star from Jacob in Numbers 24:17.
entries.deeper: Beale says the titles combine two Old Testament prophecies, Numbers 24:17 and Isaiah 11:1, 10, about the messianic king's triumph. The Greek of Isaiah 11:10 has he rhiza tou Iessai, the root of Jesse, and the one rising to rule the nations. Numbers 24:17 has anatelei astron ex Iakob, a star will rise out of Jacob. Keener names Isaiah 11:1 and probably Numbers 24:17, and notes the Dead Sea Scrolls applied Numbers 24:17 to a conquering messiah. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible says interpreters linked the two texts through the shared word for sceptre. The ESV Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible name the same texts. Beale gives no grade word; the grade is drawn here as probable, since each title is traceable to one text but the wording is adapted.
entries.heiser: In the Revelation 4 lecture Heiser reads from his own book. He says the morning star in 2:28 is messianic and points to a divine king from Judah, read through Numbers 24:17, where a star goes out from Jacob. That verse was taken as messianic in Judaism apart from the New Testament, so readers would hear a coming king, not brightness. He then cites 22:16 as Jesus claiming that standing himself.
entries.dissent: Does root mean David's source or David's descendant? The ESV Study Bible says Jesus is David's descendant and also his Lord, from whom his kingship comes, and Keener notes that some read root that way. Beale argues that root here means descendant, since offspring explains it. Heiser hears divine standing in the star language as well.

entries.title: Revelation 22:17, let the thirsty come
entries.summary: Isaiah's call to everyone who is thirsty to come to the waters and take without money echoes in the book's last invitation.
entries.plain: **A last line that repeats the first invitation sends the guests home with it ringing in their ears.** Isaiah called out to the thirsty to come to the waters, and to buy without money. John ends his book with the same invitation. Whoever is thirsty may come, and whoever wants may take the water of life as a free gift.
entries.same: The thirsty, the call to come, water, and no cost. Isaiah has hoi dipsontes, those who thirst, in Greek; John has ho dipson, the one who thirsts.
entries.differs: Isaiah says buy without money; John says take as a gift (dorean). Isaiah offers wine and milk; John offers the water of life from 22:1. Isaiah says go; John says come, three times. Beale thinks Isaiah's repeated calls are the model for John's.
entries.turn: The whole book closes with an open door. The Spirit and the bride call people to the life the vision has shown. Beale reads all the calls to come as invitations to people; Wright hears the church inviting its neighbours while there is still time.
entries.not: **Not a quotation of Isaiah 55.** John borrows Isaiah's open call to the thirsty, to come and take water at no cost, in words of his own.
entries.deeper: Beale says John leans on Isaiah 55:1 more plainly here than in 21:6, and that Isaiah's repeated commands to come likely shaped John's three. The Greek of Isaiah 55:1 opens hoi dipsontes, poreuesthe eph' hydor, you who thirst, go to the water, and ends aneu argyriou, without money. John has ho dipson erchestho, ho thelon labeto hydor zoes dorean. Keener cites Isaiah 55:1 and the water of 22:1. The ESV Study Bible says the water is freely given by grace, citing Isaiah 55:1, and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible says the verse alludes to it. The grade is drawn here as probable: thirst, water and no price together point to Isaiah 55:1.
entries.dissent: Who is told to come? Beale takes all the calls as addressed to people, and weighs the reading where the first two calls go to Jesus and the last two to people. The ESV Study Bible separates this come, an invitation to the thirsty, from the prayer of verse 20. MacArthur reads the first come as the Spirit and the church answering Christ's promise to return, and the rest as a free offer to anyone who thirsts.

entries.title: Revelation 22:18, do not add or take away
entries.summary: Moses' warning not to add to or take from God's commands, with the curses written in his book, becomes the warning that guards John's book.
entries.plain: **A contract that ends with the same clause as an old charter claims the same force.** Moses told Israel not to add to God's commands or take anything away. Anyone who turned to other gods would bring on himself every curse written in the book. John closes his book the same way. Add to it, and the plagues in it come on you; take from it, and you lose your place at the tree of life.
entries.same: Adding and taking away. The Greek of Deuteronomy 4:2 has ou prosthesete and ouk aphelete, do not add, do not remove; John uses epitithemi, add, and aphaireo, take away. Deuteronomy 29:20 has the curses written in this book.
entries.differs: Moses guards his commandments; John guards the words of this prophecy. Deuteronomy threatens the curses of the covenant; John threatens the plagues described in his book. Deuteronomy says the Lord will blot out the man's name; John says God will remove that person's part in the tree and the city. John also makes the penalty match the crime: add, and plagues are added.
entries.turn: John presents his book with the authority of Moses' law. Beale reads it as law for a renewed Israel, modeled on the old. The warning aims at false teaching that makes room for idols, as in Deuteronomy. Disobeying it brings every plague the book describes.
entries.not: **Not a new kind of warning.** Moses guarded his law the same way (Deuteronomy 4:2; 12:32), and John applies that warning to his own book.
entries.deeper: Beale says John alludes to a series of warnings across Deuteronomy, beyond chapter 4: Deuteronomy 4:1-2, 12:32 and 29:19-20, and possibly 28:58-61. He sets them beside 22:18-19 and notes three links: both warn against idolatry, both promise life in a new land, and both speak of plagues (Deuteronomy 29:21). Deuteronomy 12:32 introduces chapter 13 on false prophets in the Hebrew numbering. He also cites Proverbs 30:6 and Josephus, Against Apion 1.42-43. Keener names Deuteronomy 4:2, 12:32 and 29:20 and notes such warnings in other books (1 Enoch; the Letter of Aristeas). The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, the ESV Study Bible and the NIV Biblical Theology Study Bible name Deuteronomy 4:2 and 12:32. The grade is drawn here: the pairing of add and take away with a written book of curses could hardly come from anywhere else.
entries.dissent: What counts as adding or taking away? Beale says it means following false teaching about the written word, as in Deuteronomy 13, and that it covers John's book, not all later prophecy. The CSB Study Bible doubts it refers to the canon. MacArthur reads the warnings as marking the close of the New Testament canon, aimed at anyone who changes or twists the truth. The ESV Study Bible links it to speaking without God's authority (Deuteronomy 18:20-22). The CSB Study Bible hears Genesis 3, where Eve added to God's word and the serpent took away from it.

entries.title: Revelation 22:20, surely I am coming soon
entries.summary: Malachi's promise that the Lord will send his messenger and come suddenly may lie behind Jesus' sending his angel and his promise to come soon.
entries.plain: **A host who says he is on his way after a long wait sounds like the guest an old letter promised.** Malachi said God would send his messenger, and then the Lord would come suddenly to his temple. In John's last chapter Jesus has sent his angel, and he says three times that he is coming soon. The order of events matches Malachi.
entries.same: A messenger sent, then the Lord coming quickly. The Greek of Malachi 3:1 has idou ... erchetai, look, he comes; John has idou erchomai tachy in 22:7. Jesus sent his angel (aggelos) in 22:16; Malachi's God sends his messenger (aggelos).
entries.differs: In Malachi God sends the messenger and the Lord comes to his temple. In John Jesus sends the angel and Jesus comes. Malachi's coming is to judge; John's is to judge and reward. Malachi says suddenly; John says soon. The sources give no reason beyond applying the Lord's coming to Jesus.
entries.turn: The coming of the Lord that Malachi promised is the coming of Jesus. Beale reads the use of Malachi as another sign of Christ's divinity. Wright hears the long hope of God's return to his temple, fulfilled in Jesus and still awaited.
entries.not: **Not a firm link.** Beale writes that verse 20 echoes Malachi and that verse 16 may be modeled on it; the link rests on a shared sequence, not shared sentences.
entries.deeper: Beale says verse 20 echoes Malachi 3:1, where the Lord's coming quickly as a witness against falsehood is foretold, and that the link is strengthened by 22:16 (I will send my angel) and 22:7 (look, he is coming), and by the sin list of Malachi 3:5 recalled in 22:15. The Greek of Malachi 3:1 has idou exapostello ton angelon mou, look, I send my messenger, and exaiphnes hexei, he will come suddenly. Wright reads Malachi's promise that the Lord would come suddenly to his temple as the hope Jesus fulfilled and the book still awaits. The grade is possible: two sources name the link, and the wording is only generally similar.
entries.dissent: Beale and Wright hear Malachi. The other sources read 22:20 against 1 Corinthians 16:22, the Aramaic prayer marana tha, and name no Old Testament text.
